The citations by Edwards occur without apparent caveat regarding the role that Locke ascribed to reason in the interpretation of Scripture. Edwards found Locke's notes, which he frequently cited verbatim, highly instructive.[^002-note147]

In his study of Scripture, Edwards continually sought aids to assist with the task of translating and interpreting the Hebrew and Greek texts of the Old and New Testament. The "Blank Bible" documents his pursuit and use of lexicons, concordances, and dictionaries. Among the concordances

<!-- p. 68 -->

he utilized at different times were well-established volumes by such distinguished scholars as Johann Buxtorf (1564–1629) and Abraham Trommius (1633–1719).[^002-note148] Buxtorf, an Orientalist and student of rabbinics who taught at the University of Basel, was well-known for his defense of the Hebrew text as superior to the Vulgate and the Septuagint. Edwards took note of the Dutch scholar Trommius's Greek concordance because it was mentioned positively by Alexander Cruden (1701–70), a Scot who migrated to London and worked as a proofreader before publishing a biblical concordance himself. Edwards' annotation in the "Catalogue" noted that Cruden's volume, which he also cited in the "Blank Bible," was "said to be more useful than any book of this kind hitherto published."[^002-note149] Additional concordances noted in the "Catalogue" include volumes by Erasmus Schmid (1570–1637) and Christian Nold (1626–83).[^002-note150] Edwards also made use of the "dictionary" published by Thomas Wilson (1563–1622), an Anglican divine who ministered at Canterbury.[^002-note151] His publication was one of the earliest attempts at a concordance of the English Bible.

Edwards watched for the appearance of new resources. One such item was *The Hebrew Concordance, Adapted to the English Bible; Disposed after the Manner of Buxtorf*, by John Taylor, the same John Taylor whose other works Edwards knew well.[^002-note152] Edwards profited from consulting general dictionaries, including the *Cyclopaedia* by Ephraim Chambers (c. 1680–1740).[^002-note153] He used Chambers, for example, to identify the proper color of the sapphire stone mentioned in Exodus 24:10; from the description of that color he then derived a typological link to the heavenly sphere (p. 240).

<!-- p. 69 -->

We know that Edwards acquired Chambers' volumes no earlier than late summer 1737, for in August of that year he wrote a Boston merchant requesting that he secure the publication for him from England.[^002-note154]

Edwards also sought works that addressed issues of geography and chronology in his effort to understand and interpret the biblical text. In the "Blank Bible," for example, he has references to two volumes by Edward Wells (1667–1727), an Anglican divine and geographer whose publications relating to the two Testaments were valuable aids to him.[^002-note155] Edwards also consulted the work of Herman Moll (d. 1732), a Dutch mapmaker and geographer who came to London near the end of the seventeenth century.[^002-note156] In one instance he drew upon Moll's description of the height of a palm tree in his interpretation of the spouse in Canticles (p. 625). Biblical exegesis often intersected with the study of the chronology of the ancient world. Chronology was a preoccupation of many writers during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Edwards was especially beholden to the work of Arthur Bedford (1668–1745), an Anglican divine who served as chaplain to the Prince of Wales. In his *Scripture Chronology*, Bedford defended the reliability and authority of the biblical record against a growing number of critics. Edwards learned of Bedford's volume while reading an issue of the *Republick of Letters*.[^002-note157]

In the world of eighteenth-century biblical scholarship, chronology and history were close companions. Authors who published on one or the other topic often viewed the two as related. Edwards spent a lifetime reading books on history as part of his study of Scripture. The historical works he cited in the "Blank Bible" range across human history from ancient times to his own century. He sought historical information on the ancient world, biblical Israel, early Christianity, the Christian church in the Middle Ages, the Protestant Reformation, the Roman Catholic Church in the modern period, and contemporary religious developments in America and the rest of the world. And he was successful in securing publications that addressed most of these topics.

Among the historians Edwards cited in the "Blank Bible" was Henry Winder (1693–1752), a Dissenting divine who served congregations in

<!-- p. 70 -->

Liverpool and wrote on the history of the Bible.[^002-note158] One example of Edwards' use of Winder involved citations from a variety of ancient sources, including the works of the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus (37–95) and the Roman writer Varro (116–27 B.C.E.), in an attempt to understand the judgment in Genesis 5 that ancients lived nearly a thousand years (p. 144). Samuel Shuckford (c. 1694–1754), an Anglican, was another contemporary of Edwards whose work focused on both sacred and secular history between the time of creation and the end of the Jewish kingdoms.[^002-note159] On one occasion Edwards cited Shuckford's comment regarding the role of hunting in training the potential leaders in ancient Persia (p. 153). Edwards read closely the historical work of Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724), an Anglican who achieved prominence in the realm of both scholarship and the established church's hierarchy, rising to the position of Dean of Norwich in 1702. In his publications Prideaux defended Anglican orders, attacked the deists, and attempted to resolve chronological difficulties in biblical history, focusing his attention especially on the transitional period between the two Testaments. Edwards cited Prideaux's *Connection* seventy-one times in the "Blank Bible."[^002-note160] He may have learned of this work through Cotton Mather's *Manuductio*, which recommended it as occasional reading.[^002-note161]

Edwards turned to the work of William Reading (1674–1744), an Anglican and the librarian at Sion College, for details related to the early life of Christ.[^002-note162] In one instance Edwards took note of the tradition conveyed by Eusebius (c. 260–c. 340) and others that when the infant Jesus was carried into a temple in Egypt, all the idols fell down (p. 649). Another historian Edwards cited was Nathaniel Lardner (1684–1768), a

<!-- p. 71 -->

Nonconforming divine trained on the continent who gained a reputation as a conservative Christian apologist. His principal work set out to confirm the reliability of the internal evidence for the historical character of the New Testament.[^002-note163] In his work Lardner addressed a range of issues related to dating and authorship. Lardner also used history to support his belief in trinitarianism and the miraculous. On one occasion Edwards quoted from Lardner the description of a heretic derived from the third-century church father Cyprian (d. 258) (p. 1135). Edwards turned to the volumes of the historian Robert Millar (d. 1752) for information bearing on the expansion of Christianity in the period after the New Testament.[^002-note164] One reference by Edwards to Millar points to a discussion of pagan practices involving processions, images, and feasts in different cultures, including ancient Israel (p. 794).

There are other kinds of historical resources in the "Blank Bible." Edwards cited several historians whose works are narrowly defined. He referred, for example, to historical studies of the Jews, infant baptism, and the papacy.[^002-note165] He has references to ancient writers, both pagan and Christian.[^002-note166] Several historical sources that Edwards turned to frequently in the "Blank Bible" defy easy categorization. For example, *The Court of the Gentiles*, by Theophilus Gale (1628–78), an English Nonconformist divine and scholar, provided Edwards with information on a wide variety of topics related to the ancient world and especially to religious traditions in those times. One such reference contains a pagan account of creation involving the emergence of the universe out of chaos (pp. 124–25). Another

<!-- p. 72 -->

such work that does not classify easily is *The Divine Legation of Moses*, by William Warburton (1698–1779), an Anglican divine who became the Bishop of Gloucester in 1759.[^002-note167] Warburton's career brought both prominence and controversy. He supported both the Anglican establishment and toleration of Dissenters and defended Mosaic law against criticisms from the deists. Late in his career he attacked the enthusiasm of Methodism. One example of Edwards' use of Warburton involves the latter's suggestion that God taught Adam to speak by directing him to name the animals (p. 134).

There are several works cited in the "Blank Bible" that reflect specific interpretive interests of Edwards. Typology, an interpretive method that linked the Old and New Testaments by the identification of "types" in the former and "antitypes" or fulfillments in the latter, was a lifelong concern for him and an approach he used repeatedly to understand and interpret biblical texts and to apply them to the world he knew firsthand. His commentary "Notes on Scripture" also illustrates the centrality of this interpretive approach for him.[^002-note168] His notebook on "Types" is even more striking evidence of the same.[^002-note169] In the "Blank Bible" Edwards cited *The Figures and Types of the Old. Testament*, by Samuel Mather (1626–71), an English Nonconforming divine.[^002-note170]

Issues related to the canonicity of the books in the New Testament were also a concern of Edwards. He turned to the work of the Welsh minister and biblical scholar Jeremiah Jones (1693–1724) for historical details on the reception of the biblical writings in the early Christian church.[^002-note171] Prophecy and its relationship to eschatology were additional issues of primary interest to Edwards over many years. Among the sources addressing those concerns directly was *The Use and Intent of Prophecy*, by Thomas Sherlock (1678–1761), an Anglican educator and subsequently

<!-- p. 73 -->

a bishop in various dioceses, including London, beginning in 1748.[^002-note172] Another publication Edwards consulted dealing with some of the same eschatological concerns was written by Samuel Collett.[^002-note173]

The point here is not to provide a full listing of the sources Edwards used in the "Blank Bible" but rather to suggest the variety of works he found relevant to scriptural study. That variety goes far beyond commentaries, exegetical aids, historical works, and specialized studies. It reflects the full range of his theological and ministerial interests. In the "Blank Bible" Edwards' reading in specialized theological topics is evident, for example, in works that deal with creation, the person and work of Christ, the work of the Holy Spirit, divine attributes, and human nature.[^002-note174] These topics were central issues to systematic theologians, whether writing in Latin or English, whether the publication was called an "Institutes" or "A Complete Body of Divinity." Edwards cited examples of both kinds of systematic theological works in the "Blank Bible."[^002-note175] Apologetics

<!-- p. 74 -->

was also a category much in use in Edwards' day as theologians defended their views against opponents.[^002-note176]

Edwards' commentary was never far removed from life circumstances or the application of biblical ideas and principles to life situations. It is not surprising, therefore, that among his sources in the "Blank Bible" are individual sermons and collections of sermons by contemporaries or distinguished preachers.[^002-note177] The close association between exegesis and preaching was a given in Protestant theology. There are also works cited in the interleaved Bible that might be described as devotional or meditational, inviting personal contemplation and application of the biblical text to the Christian life.[^002-note178]

Finally, among the sources cited by Edwards are a number of examples of collected works by distinguished authors. Such collections, usually leather-bound, multiple volumes in folio, are among the most impressive publications from the eighteenth century and earlier. Such collections offered diverse resources. In the "Blank Bible" Edwards cited the collected works of Isaac Barrow (1630–77), Joseph Mede (1586–1638),

<!-- p. 75 -->

John Glas (1695–1773), Stephen Charnock (1628–80), John Lightfoot (1602–75), John Tillotson (1630–94), Thomas Goodwin (1600–1680), Isaac Watts (1674–1748), John Locke, and John Owen. It is not difficult to imagine that Edwards may have contemplated that someday his own writings would appear in such an edition.

Three closing observations regarding the sources discussed above and others cited in the "Blank Bible" are appropriate. First, it is striking that the authors Edwards was reading did not belong exclusively to one religious party or faction but rather spanned a wide range of theological views, including Anglicans and Puritans, Calvinists and Arminians, evangelicals and free-thinkers—even Roman Catholics. He does not seem to have paid primary attention to religious affiliations. Second, it is remarkable that Edwards was able to gain physical access to such a diverse set of published materials, especially after he relocated from Northampton to Stockbridge, on the frontier of western Massachusetts. His success in securing these publications is relevant for the study of the diffusion of print culture in early America. Finally, despite the wealth of scholarship devoted to Edwards, the study of certain aspects of his religious thought is only beginning. This is certainly the case with respect to the exegetical dimension of his theology. The juxtaposition of newly edited texts in this edition with the sources he read makes possible a new round of research into the influence of particular authors on his interpretation and application of the Bible.

### Edwards' Reputation Through the Ages

The call for additional research on Jonathan Edwards as an exegete needs to be set against the evolution of his reputation over the past 250 years. Edwards' eminence as a preacher has been secure ever since the 1730s, when he emerged publicly on the colonial scene in New England. His first Boston sermon in 1731 was published almost immediately.[^002-note179] Subsequent sermons confirmed that he was both a powerful and a skilled homiletician. Edwards' prestige as an evangelical supporter of religious awakenings has been widespread ever since the mid-1730s and the early 1740s, when he described and celebrated the religious stirrings in Northampton and then defended and analyzed the revivals in New England. His publications brought him prominence throughout the American

<!-- p. 76 -->

colonies as well as in the larger transatlantic world.[^002-note180] Edwards' stature as a Reformed theologian rose incrementally during the last twelve years of his life with the appearance sequentially of publications in which he identified the marks of true religion or genuine piety, defined a proper ecclesiology and understanding of the sacraments, defended the classic Calvinist position on the bondage of the human will against Arminian notions, and maintained the universality of depravity and its transmission to new generations.[^002-note181]

In the years after his death in 1758, a steady stream of posthumous publications expanded his reputation further, both in America and abroad. The two dissertations published by Samuel Hopkins in 1765 demonstrated that Edwards was not simply following in the footsteps of earlier thinkers but breaking new ground.[^002-note182] Similarly, in 1774 the appearance in Scotland of an edition of his sermons on the history of redemption confirmed that he had been engaged in a creative search for new ways to do theology and that his international reputation was continuing to expand.[^002-note183] The publication by Jonathan Edwards, Jr., of selections from his father's sermons and private notebooks in the closing decades of the eighteenth century evidenced further the growing interest in the writings of Edwards, Sr.[^002-note184]

In the nineteenth century the appearance of multiple multivolume editions of Edwards' *Works*, beginning in 1806 with the first volume of the Leeds edition and extending through 1881 with the last reprint of the Worcester revised edition, confirmed the stature Edwards enjoyed during that century as a Protestant theologian and ranking figure in the evangelical world.[^002-note185] These editions also demonstrated the presence of a

<!-- p. 77 -->

ready market for his writings. In addition, several previously unpublished texts appeared, including volumes edited by Tryon Edwards (1809–94)[^002-note186] and Alexander B. Grosart (1827–99).[^002-note187] Edwards' life of David Brainerd (1718–47), the most popular of all his works during the nineteenth century, established him as an advocate of Christian missions, a growing concern.[^002-note188] By 1900 his stature among many was unquestioned. Even William James, who did not share his judgments on religious experience, acknowledged Edwards' prominence in the history of American religious life and thought.[^002-note189]

It was perhaps inevitable that dissenting judgments would appear side by side with the positive accounts of Edwards' life and writings. From the beginning, individuals who did not share his theological or philosophical perspectives criticized rather than celebrated him. In the eighteenth century religious opponents attacked his support of ecstatic activity in the revivals.[^002-note190] In the nineteenth, philosophically-minded critics challenged his metaphysical and moral assumptions.[^002-note191] In the twentieth century, scholars repulsed by Calvinism dismissed him as preoccupied with issues from the past.[^002-note192] Prominent public figures with little ear for the concerns that drove Edwards sometimes denounced him in vigorous prose.[^002-note193]

<!-- p. 78 -->

Adjectives like "antiquated" and "tragic" were often applied to Edwards and his career. The scholar Vernon L. Parrington, for example, declared Edwards "an anachronism," his "great powers baffled and wasted," in effect dismissing his significance for the development of the subsequent American republic.[^002-note194] Others, even those more sympathetic to Edwards' thought, branded his ideas "impractical" and "absurd."[^002-note195] These opposing views of Edwards have existed side by side continuously.

In the years near the mid-twentieth century, a strong new current of interest and admiration pulsed among those who attempted a fuller recovery of Edwards' context, biography, writings, and significance. Three scholars deserve special mention because of their prominence and their diverse motivations. In 1937 H. Richard Niebuhr featured Edwards' understanding of the sovereignty of God as an anticipation of Neo-Orthodox theology in his classic study of American Christianity.[^002-note196] In 1940 Ola Elizabeth Winslow wrote a prize-winning biography of Edwards, depicting him as a man of immense interest and complexity.[^002-note197] And in 1949, in perhaps the most significant study of Edwards ever written, Perry Miller declared him a gifted and perceptive intellectual, a modern thinker whose ideas shaped the American experience.[^002-note198] These three thinkers contributed to the rising wave of interest in Edwards during the second half of the twentieth century, a scholarly surge that cut across theological, intellectual, disciplinary, and interpretive lines. This new scholarship found expression in journals, dissertations, monographs, biographies, and thematic studies as well as in the volumes of the Yale Edition of *The Works of Jonathan Edwards*, launched in 1957.[^002-note199] Nearly half a century later, in 2003—the tercentenary of Edwards' birth—this surge of interest showed little sign of abating.[^002-note200]

<!-- p. 79 -->

Despite the astonishing volume and diversity of publications, to date only a modest amount of attention has been paid to Edwards' biblical interests.[^002-note201] Much research remains to be done. Resources are newly available to assist with that task. But even now, many of his writings that feature biblical issues are not available in published or critical format, including more than twelve hundred manuscript sermons, a score or more of thematic notebooks, and the "Miscellanies" entries dealing with "Prophecies of the Messiah" and "Fulfillment of Prophecies of the Messiah." Widespread access to these materials awaits the completion of an electronic edition of Edwards' *Works*. When that planned enterprise becomes a reality, more definitive judgments will be possible regarding Edwards the exegete.

In the meantime, steps need to be taken to rectify the oversight of Edwards' exegetical writings. Several clusters of his writings require fresh examination with an eye toward the role that biblical interpretation plays in them. In an order of descending public prominence, these materials include major treatises published during his lifetime and posthumously; sermons, both those published before and after his death and those still in manuscript; private notebooks, published and unpublished; and other incidental or personal writings, some of which have been published in whole or in part and some of which remain in manuscript.

It would be impossible to identify two more important treatises published during Edwards' lifetime than *Freedom of the Will* and *Religious Affections*. Both have appeared in critical editions in the Yale Edition, volumes 1 and 2, edited by the distinguished scholars Paul Ramsey and John E. Smith. Despite his acknowledgement that biblical evidence for God's foreknowledge formed a major part of Edwards' argument against the Arminian notion of freedom of the will, Ramsey barely touched on the

<!-- p. 80 -->

scriptural aspect of the subject. The more than three hundred biblical citations in the treatise therefore invite examination with respect to the manner in which Edwards used them as proof texts in support of the concept of necessity. For example, in the treatise he cited Luke 19:41 in support of the judgment that God "foretold the future moral conduct of nations and people" when Christ spoke prophetically of his deliverance into the hands of his enemies.[^002-note202] The "Blank Bible" entry on Luke 19:41, however, is drawn from Doddridge, no advocate of Calvinist orthodoxy or of necessity (p. 916). In *Freedom of the Will*, Edwards also argued for foreknowledge on the basis of predictions regarding the martyrdom of some of Christ's disciples, including Peter.[^002-note203] The entry in the "Blank Bible" on John 21:19 offers a way of understanding that martyrdom as consistent with Christ's will (p. 966). By contrast with Ramsey's introduction to *Freedom of the Will*, Smith's introduction to *Religious Affections* devoted more attention to the biblical basis for the thesis of the treatise, namely, "True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections."[^002-note204] And the more than eleven hundred biblical citations figure in Smith's analysis of the argument. Edwards' support, for example, of the Twelth Sign—"Gracious and holy affections have their exercise and fruit in Christian practice"—makes use of extensive biblical argumentation.[^002-note205] One contrast to Christian practice is "slothfulness," which Edwards condemned, using the account in Matthew 25 of the wicked servant who hid his talent in the ground.[^002-note206] The "Blank Bible" entry on Matthew 25:24–27 asserts that the unfaithful servant "ought to have made what gain he could of the talent that he had" (p. 871). Hundreds of biblical passages related to the argument in *Religious Affections* invite similar examination. The outcome of such research is likely to reorient the standard depiction of the argument of this important treatise.

Edwards' extant sermons, numbering nearly 1,250, represent a huge cache of writings that contain large sections devoted to the exposition and citation of biblical materials. His standard sermon outline included an initial exposition of the scriptural text on which the sermon was based, followed by a statement of doctrine and its elaboration, and then a section which improved or applied the doctrine to life circumstances. Although the central place of the Bible has been recognized in Edwards'

<!-- p. 81 -->

sermons, there has been only limited examination of the use of Scripture. Relatively little of that research has been correlated with his exegetical notebooks.[^002-note207] One example will suffice to suggest what can be undertaken with potentially profitable results. In May 1739 Edwards preached a sermon on Malachi 4:1–2 entitled *Christ the Spiritual Sun*. The exposition of the text identified Malachi as the last of the prophets in the Old Testament canon who, in a period of spiritual darkness, wrote about a coming time of "gospel light." That light was to come from the rising of the Sun of righteousness who will bring both "light and heat," comfort to the righteous and fire to the wicked.[^002-note208] Edwards' exposition of the text in Malachi and his development of the sermon's doctrine—"That same spiritual Sun, whose beams are most comfortable and beneficial to believers, will burn and destroy unbelievers"—drew on exegetical entries that he had written in both "Notes on Scripture" and the "Blank Bible."[^002-note209] His sermon and the related exegetical entries demonstrate in striking fashion the impact of his private study of Scripture on the public side of his ministry. They also document the creative homilectical use he made of scriptural metaphor and typology. Close textual study of the relationships among his exegetical notebooks and the texts of his sermons will dramatically enhance our understanding of the role of the Bible in his ministry. Hundreds of Edwards' sermons await such examination.

Edwards' private notebooks hold great promise for the further study of his exegesis. Four volumes of "Miscellanies," three scriptural notebooks, two sets of notes on "Types," and a variety of topical notebooks have been published in the Yale Edition. Other unpublished manuscripts include "Harmony of the Old and New Testaments," "Prophecies of the Messiah" and "Fulfillment of the Prophecies of the Messiah," notebooks on the "History of Redemption," the "Catalogue" of reading, and the "Account Book." All of these in different ways shed light on the centrality of the Bible in Edwards' life and thought. Individually, these documents cast light on his study and interpretation of particular biblical texts. Many of these manuscripts also intersect thematically. The full extent

<!-- p. 82 -->

of such intersections has yet to be discovered. As a result, only a limited sense of the relative importance of the Bible and its interpretation for Edwards' thought and ministry is possible at this moment. Much research remains to be done.

It is possible to suggest that as an exegete Edwards was probably without peer in America in the middle of the eighteenth century. He did not, however, achieve widespread prestige in this field during his lifetime. His prominence came as an advocate and defender of evangelical awakenings, as a successful preacher, and as a theologian in the Reformed tradition. It is at best speculative to suggest that had Edwards lived another decade he might have gained a reputation as a learned exegete. Nonetheless, some summary observations concerning Edwards as an exegete are appropriate now, based on the materials available in this edition of the "Blank Bible" and contextualized within the wider framework of his published commentaries and notebooks as well as his other publications in the Yale Edition.

Edwards' exegetical interests are highly traditional, reflected in the topics and issues he addressed in the "Blank Bible." He stood firmly within the tradition of Protestant exegesis stretching back to the Reformation. For example, he considered the patriarchs of ancient Israel models for the devout life and believed that the circumstances of the children of Israel anticipated those of the Christian church, that the Hebrew prophets' proclamations were saturated with gospel imagery, and that the apostles gave explicit voice to Reformed theological concerns such as justification by faith and predestination. Edwards was not the first to articulate these scriptural motifs. In that respect it is inappropriate to declare his observations uniquely insightful into the meaning, interpretation, or application of the Bible. The fact that he drew so heavily on the commentaries of Matthew Poole, Matthew Henry, and Philip Doddridge, among others, is further evidence that he stood firmly in a long tradition.

Despite the traditional character of his exegetical observations, Edwards did not restrict himself to any one interpretive approach to the biblical text. In that respect it is possible to describe him as a creative and imaginative exegete whose interpretations of particular passages ranged across a variety of ways of understanding them. He drew on the force of the original Hebrew and Greek texts, employing lexicons and concordances in his quest for clear translation and precise meaning. He probed the historical circumstances and cultural contexts of the ancient Near East and the Mediterranean world, turning to works that featured the

<!-- p. 83 -->

chronology of events and the geography of places related to the biblical accounts. He found anticipations of his own era by reading evangelical religion—conversions and revivals—back into the biblical text. He discovered the rationale for contemporary social arrangements, including ministerial authority, patriarchal responsibility, and racial slavery, in particular biblical passages. He thought that his own life circumstances were addressed in various ways in the text. For example, he repeatedly detected scriptural injunctions that called for parishioners to provide adequate salaries for ministers of the gospel. Likewise, his capacity for uncovering symbolical or figurative associations within the biblical text seems infinite. And finally, some of his commentary is simply the product of random thoughts. Edwards gave none of these approaches priority in the "Blank Bible." They all appear at different times and in diverse combinations.

The task of the exegete varies from moment to moment, and for that reason it is often impossible to determine the compelling reason for Edwards' observations on a particular biblical text. The contexts surrounding his exegetical activities varied immensely. He was responsible for preparing sermons on a weekly basis, a task which called for him to explain and proclaim scriptural truths to his auditors. In that role theological abstractions were of less value than clear practical applications. But he also spent a large amount of time and energy during his lifetime writing theological treatises for publication. In that context the clear exposition of Scripture became a primary line of support for his various theological arguments. He also read the Bible as an act of personal devotion and for spiritual edification. What he saw in the biblical text at those moments therefore depended in part on his mood and interior stale. On the basis of the written commentary alone, it is often—in fact, usually—impossible to determine his precise circumstances when he wrote a particular entry.

Edwards was a convinced Protestant theologian, and therefore he viewed the Bible as the authoritative source of Christian theology and the inspired Word of God. He brought this high view of the scriptural text to his activity as a commentator. That does not mean that he ascribed only one meaning to any given text. In fact, what is most striking about the "Blank Bible" is the variety of meanings he discovered in the biblical passages. He was also aware of the contested quality of the interpretation of Scripture in his day, an issue of rising religious significance during his lifetime. The impact of the new scholarship deriving from the Enlightenment was mixed on him, as he often drew insights from commentators

<!-- p. 84 -->

who contested vigorously his theological positions, but whose insights he found useful. At the same time, he consistently rejected the radical implications of the new emerging historical criticism. Therefore it is inaccurate and inappropriate to construe Edwards as either a modern critical exegete or a fundamentalist hermeneut. His approach to the biblical text was eclectic and often dictated by circumstance. Yet there was no ambiguity in his mind regarding the authority of the Bible for his religious judgments. It is that role of the Bible which has not been sufficiently acknowledged in many of the accounts of Edwards' religious thought.

Finally, the entries in Edwards' "Blank Bible" confirm the richness of the Christian exegetical tradition, the various appropriations Edwards made of that tradition, and his creative adaptations and applications of scriptural insights. But it is also apparent from the "Blank Bible" how often Edwards used the scriptural accounts to assert and support his hostility toward—even hatred of—other religious traditions and theological positions. Edwards was deeply prejudiced against Roman Catholics and especially the papacy, and he continually verbalized that enmity, cloaking his antagonism in the language of Scripture and sanctioning it with various theological rationalizations. Edwards denied ultimate legitimacy to Judaism as a religion by casting it in a framework that found its sole ultimate meaning in its anticipation of Christianity. Edwards paid less attention to Islam in the "Blank Bible," but his references to it are consistently negative and virulent. These unattractive dimensions of Edwards' exegesis cannot be overlooked or rationalized. They are, in fact, repulsive and reflect negatively on his understanding of the Christian tradition of which he was a part. Unfortunately, they represent a significant element in his cultural and theological legacy.

### Note on the Text

#### Description of the Manuscript

The "Blank Bible" is physically unique among Edwards' manuscripts. It is a tan, leather-bound, hard-covered, interleaved volume, booklike in external appearance. By contrast with his typical notebooks, which were constructed from gatherings of folded sheets or a collection of infolded quires or signatures of foolscap stitched together by him, this manuscript was put together by someone knowledgeable about traditional bookbinding. Constituted of more than twenty-five signatures, the volume measures on the cover 24×18 cm. and is approximately 7 cm. thick. The

<!-- p. 85 -->

outer leather binding is now worn, heavily frayed on the edges, and literally threadbare on the spine. There is no lettering on either the front or the spine of the volume (see the frontispiece).[^002-note210]

Inside the hard covers, interleaved and bound together in signatures, are 398 sheets comprising 796 unnumbered pages of a small King James Version of the Bible and 455 sheets of trimmed foolscap numbered 1 to 904.[^002-note211] In the course of the latter, there are six errors in the numbering of the pages, bringing the total page count of the foolscap to 910.[^002-note212] Page numbers have been written on the upper outer margins of the foolscap sheets. Some of the foolscap sheets bear fragments of a watermark, showing on the upper portion a crown and on the lower portion an attached intersecting "WR."[^002-note213] The title pages of the Old Testament and the New Testament in the interleaved King James Bible bear the London imprint, "Printed by the Companie of Stationers"; they are dated 1652 and 1653, respectively.[^002-note214] The regular pages of the small printed Bible, which include two parallel columns of text, measure 14.75×8.25 cm. The larger sheets of trimmed foolscap have been ruled vertically down the center with a red ink line, creating two parallel columns.

Despite the worn binding, the "Blank Bible" is in remarkably good repair. The wear appears to be the product of use rather than abuse. All four outside corners are worn through the leather binding. The central sections of the front and back covers are soiled from handling. But there are only a few holes and tears in the foolscap sheets. A few more of the much thinner sheets of paper on which the small Bible was printed show damage. Some of the foolscap sheets have yellowed with age; others remain strikingly white more than 275 years after being assembled in this interleaved configuration.

There is reason to believe that the "Blank Bible" was rebound at some point during Edwards' years of possession. The most compelling evidence for this judgment is the fact that a few of the entries trail into the interior margins on the interleaved foolscap sheets and are now bound into those margins.[^002-note215] Perhaps Edwards used the Bible from 1730 until sometime in 1748, at which point he decided, because of wear, to have

<!-- p. 86 -->

it rebound. At that point he may have signed the title page "Jonathan Edwards. His Book 1748," which is a possible explanation for the presence of that date there. If this assumption is correct, Edwards' heavy use of the Bible over the next ten years would account, in part, for its present worn appearance. No known independent evidence for this dating of the rebinding process exists apart from the tight margins and the date of his signature on the title page.[^002-note216]

Edwards' entries in the interleaved Bible, which span the last twenty-eight years of his lifetime, document the diversity of his handwriting during those three decades. He wrote some entries in a small, carefully formed, sharply defined round script that generally in this manuscript signals an early entry. Other, later entries are in a less carefully formed, more angular, less sharply defined script that is also very small. By contrast, Edwards wrote still other entries in a large but clear vertically oriented handwriting. And there are entries that are large, poorly formed, sloppily written, in an angular or slanted script that speaks of haste and lack of care. This final pattern, generally, marks entries from the last years of his use of the manuscript. One other factor affecting his script was the amount of space available for a particular entry. There are many notes squeezed into open spaces between two existing entries. In all cases, the sharpness of Edwards' quill affects the visual appearance of the writing, as does the consistency and color of the ink.[^002-note217]

A great deal has been written about Edwards' crabbed and difficult to read handwriting—a legitimate complaint, but one that is surmountable by the investment of time and patience. In the "Blank Bible," only a few words cannot be confirmed absolutely; these conjectures are all identified in the notes. One other observation related to Edwards' handwriting and to the difficulty of deciphering it involves the bleeding of the inks through the paper. The problem of bleeding ink is much greater on the thin sheets of the printed Bible than on the heavier sheets of foolscap.

The construction of the "Blank Bible" customarily positions a page of printed biblical text opposite an interleaved page of foolscap. This arrangement called for Edwards, following Benjamin Pierpont's example, to write an entry, a note, or a reference bearing on a particular passage on the page of the printed Bible opposite it on the larger facing page of

<!-- p. 87 -->

foolscap. For example, the text of James 4:6 in the KJV reads, "But he giveth more grace, wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble." This passage is located three-fourths of the way down the righthand column on the printed page. Edwards wrote his brief comment on the facing foolscap interleaved sheet, page 874, in the analogous location three-fourths of the way down the righthand column. It reads, "James 4:6. 'But he giveth more grace.'] I.e. they to whom God has given sonic true grace, the grand note of which is humility, he rewardeth it with more grace, which is agreeable to what Christ says so often, To him that hath, shall be given" (p. 1175).[^002-note218] This is the primary pattern Edwards followed throughout the manuscript.

On that same foolscap page 874 is Edwards' entry on James 3:13, which includes seven lines of text at the top of the lefthand column and nine additional lines of text in the middle of the righthand column. He flagged the continuation of his entry at the end of the former location and at the beginning of the latter by the use of directional notations: "∗See next col.," and "∗See last col." Edwards employed a variety of such directional notations—some consisting of symbols only, others accompanied by words or phrases—to guide himself through the labyrinth of increasingly full columns and pages to displaced entries, continuations of entries, or later additions to earlier entries. The longer he used the "Blank Bible," the fuller many of the columns and foolscap pages became, especially in those sections of the Bible that most attracted his attention. As a result, with the passage of years, more and more entries were displaced from their appropriate position to locations in other columns or on other pages that had not been filled by commentary. In the manuscript Edwards' directional notations provide an essential guide to the displaced and scattered entries. In this published edition of the "Blank Bible," all the entries have been rearranged in canonical order, thereby eliminating the visual confusion that often confronts the reader of the manuscript. Canonical reference was, in fact, Edwards' primary—perhaps even exclusive—organizing principle for the commentary.

One other structural arrangement in the "Blank Bible" addresses the problem created by some columns and pages on the foolscap sheets filling up more quickly than others because their corresponding sections of the Bible attracted Edwards' special attention. The original designer of the manuscript chose to include supplementary blank pages that did

<!-- p. 88 -->

not face pages of printed biblical text. These extra foolscap pages, also ruled into two vertical columns, provided additional space for larger entries or for entries that did not fit in the designated positions. These open or extra pages occur in clusters of two beginning with pages 16–17 of the manuscript. Two such extra pages are found every twenty-five pages until page 688, at which location a cluster often extra pages is inserted. Between that ten-page cluster and the close of the manuscript, three additional clusters of ten extra pages, two additional clusters of two extra pages, and one instance of three extra pages occur. In toto, of the 910 foolscap pages in the manuscript, 109 have no facing page of biblical text. All of the entries on these extra pages employ canonical or locational referencing devices to integrate them properly into the biblical canon.[^002-note219]

But it is not only on the foolscap sheets that canonical cross-references or directional notations occur. In the margins of the small printed King James Version of the Bible Edwards also referenced displaced entries, biblical citations, and other notations. He made these entries in several different ways. Sometimes he wrote an abbreviated note at the side of a verse, such as "See next vacant p., #." Other times he wrote out a reference, for example, "See note on Matthew 5:32." Many times he placed a mark, similar to "+" or "∗," over a word in the printed text or at the start of a phrase, and then wrote a marginal reference beginning with the same mark on the margin, sometimes with a canonical reference, often with only the abbreviation "SSS," the latter signaling Matthew Poole's *Synopsis Criticorum* as the location to be consulted. Hundreds of marginal entries occur on the pages of the small printed Bible. The problem of ink bleeding through the thin paper compounds the difficulty of reading some of these very small entries.

Perhaps the most interesting pages in the "Blank Bible" from the standpoint of Edwards' biography are three closing numbered pages 902–4, which follow the section of commentary on the book of Revelation.[^002-note220] On these pages, over the years that he possessed the manuscript, Edwards recorded financial accounts for each of his children (see Appendix C). These accounts tabulate what he borrowed from his offspring and when he repaid them. The earliest account noted is that of his oldest daughter Sarah (1728–1805), an account that began on September

<!-- p. 89 -->

24, 1732. That account eventually includes the following citation: "Note that what was borrowed of Sarah was all paid in an emerald ring in the year 1748." Perhaps Edwards was not as oblivious to economic matters as is sometimes depicted. In daughter Lucy's account, he wrote, "All due to her, allowing for the fall of money, and interest, and all. May 24, 1749." Unfortunately, these accounts have received little attention from biographers.[^002-note221]

Only modest textual evidence in the manuscript documents the ownership of the "Blank Bible" after Edwards' death. There are a few editorial changes in the text attributed to Jonathan Edwards, Jr. (1745–1801). These occurrences are identified in the footnotes.[^002-note222] Two other kinds of markings in the text signal the presence of later readers who wished to identify particular entries for one reason or another. Some entries have been marked with large X's in red pencil or ink as well as with gray pencil or light ink. Many of these markings appear to be the work of Alexander B. Grosart, who marked entries while reading the text, some of which he subsequently printed in his limited edition of selected writings.[^002-note223]

Two other distinctive markings on the manuscript signal the possession of the interleaved Bible after Edwards. The first is on the inside of the front cover of the volume. It is a book label documenting the transfer to the Yale College Library that reads, "Deposited by the heirs of Jonathan Edwards 1900." The second, on the inner margin on the last sheet of the children's accounts, page 904, written in a vertical line parallel to the spine of the volume, reads, "God's word here is." This is not written in Edwards' handwriting. Perhaps it is the judgment of some family member, devoted disciple, or admiring scholar.

#### History of the Manuscript

The interleaved Bible was originally the possession of Benjamin Pierpont, Edwards' brother-in-law, the brother of Sarah Pierpont, who became Edwards' wife in 1727. Benjamin Pierpont's bold signature with the words "His Book" and the date of 1728 on the title page declare ownership

<!-- p. 90 -->

with a flourish.[^002-note224] In addition, sixty-eight scattered exegetical entries in the same hand as well as two initial clusters of isagogical materials at the beginnings of the Old and New Testament confirm both Pierpont's possession and his limited use of the manuscript (see Appendix A). Lacking evidence to the contrary, it is assumed that Pierpont either conceived or adopted the plan for the manuscript, interleaving the larger blank sheets of trimmed foolscap ruled vertically down the middle with a red ink line between the pages of the small King James Version of the Bible. No other direct independent evidence is available concerning the provenance or the construction of this unusual manuscript.[^002-note225]

Pierpont's use of the interleaved Bible grew naturally out of his vocational choice. The son of James Pierpont (1660–1714), minister of the Congregational church on the green in New Haven, Connecticut, Benjamin was born to the cloth, or so it seemed. After graduation from Yale College, he read theology in preparation for the ministry, perhaps with his brother-in-law, perhaps with instructors at Yale.[^002-note226] By August 1729 Pierpont was supplying the vacant pulpit of Deerfield, Massachusetts. In January 1730 the congregation decided "That the Worthy Mr. Benjamin Pierpont Shall have a Call to Settle Among us to be our Pastor and teacher."[^002-note227] But within two months opposition to his candidacy developed among a minority in the community. Charges were leveled against Pierpont, declaring him "not of Prudent, Grave & Sober Conversation" as well as "vain, apish & jovial, particularly among females."[^002-note228] These and other particulars resulted in the congregation's withdrawal of the offer to settle in October 1730 and the effective end to his candidacy for the ministry. The leading men of the town issued a public statement in support of Pierpont's character, stating that despite "the Injuries his Reputation has suffered… he was accounted a person of good character," and that the reports circulated were not "looked upon by Sober & Judicious men as worthy to be regarded."[^002-note229] Nevertheless, the controversy and dismissal ended Pierpont's stay in Deerfield and his plans for the ministry.

<!-- p. 91 -->

Within a few years, he was reported to have died in the West Indies, although the date of his death is uncertain.[^002-note230]

How and precisely when the manuscript passed from Pierpont to Edwards remains uncertain. Pierpont may have given it to his brother-in-law at a point when the young supply's situation in Deerfield was eroding. Edwards, who undoubtedly knew of Pierpont's troubled candidacy may have solicited it. Perhaps Sarah Edwards played a role in the transfer. What is clear is that the interleaved Bible was in Edwards' possession by the middle to late months of 1730, according to dating by Thomas A. Schafer.[^002-note231]

The ownership of the manuscript thus passed from a failed ministerial candidate into the hands of a promising young minister who, little more than a year earlier, had taken over sole responsibility for the prestigious pastorate in Northampton, Massachusetts, held previously by his grandfather Solomon Stoddard. One might assume, given this contrast, that Edwards would change dramatically the uses made of the interleaved Bible. This was not the case. Pierpont had written exegetical entries that addressed time-honored scriptural issues, some hinging on the original Hebrew and Greek texts. His comment, for example, on the title, "The Gospel of Matthew," included the following: "In ye original it is Ευανγελὶον; i.e.: good, or joy full news. The Syriack is בָשׂר i.e.: good speech."[^002-note232] Several times Pierpont recorded the observations of earlier commentators from his reading of their works. His entry on Acts 19:5, which discussed the phrase "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," cited two sources, including the *Institutiones theologicae* of Gulielmus Bucanus (fl. 1591–1605), a professor at the University of Lausanne.[^002-note233] Pierpont also offered his own observations on the meaning of biblical passages. And occasionally he gave voice to personal thoughts and feelings.[^002-note234] With reference to this last use of the manuscript, it is impossible to read

<!-- p. 92 -->

his comment on the phrase "light my candle" in Psalms 18:28, "I.e.: renew my comforts, alter my sad estate at present and chase trouble," without thinking of his difficulties in Deerfield.[^002-note235] Similarly, one wonders whether his entry on Luke 17:27, dealing with the sinful world before the flood, was constructed biographically. Pierpont wrote," A deluge of sensuality and excess digs a channel for a deluge of wrath to come down."[^002-note236] Rather than changing the function of the manuscript, Edwards, in fact, followed his brother-in-law closely in his use of the interleaved Bible. For that reason, failed or not as a ministerial candidate, Benjamin Pierpont played a formative role in the story of Edwards' most unusual manuscript.

From 1730 until his death, Edwards wrote some 5,506 notes and entries in what he came to call his "Blank Bible."[^002-note237] The diverse nature of those entries has been described. One issue that arises in this context relates to the relationship between the interleaved Bible and Edwards' earlier biblical notebook. The "Blank Bible" is patently complementary to the "Notes on Scripture," a fact that raises several questions relating to Edwards' usage of the two. What differences, for example, separated the biblical manuscripts in his mind? Is a distinction evident in their respective contents? How did the contrasting physical nature of the two bear on the history and use of the "Blank Bible"? Some answers are possible. Beginning in 1730, with a few notable exceptions, the exegetical entries in the "Notes on Scripture" after nos. 192–94 tended to be longer, more discursive notes. Some in that series—for example, no. 416, "Whether the PENTATEUCH was written by Moses," and no. 419, Genesis 10-11, "The Dispersion and First Settlement of the Nations"—are virtually free-standing essays.[^002-note238] The general contrast between the length of entries in the "Notes on Scripture" and the "Blank Bible" is striking. Many notes in the latter are a single word, an abbreviation, or a few words. Many other entries are a few lines only. But there are also some long entries in the "Blank Bible" that are the product of multiple additions written over an extended period of time. Among the longest entries in the interleaved Bible are Edwards' notes on Genesis 41:40–57, 2 Samuel 15-18, and Galatians 5:17. After 1730, however, the general rule is that Edwards tended to write longer entries in the "Notes on Scripture" and shorter entries in the "Blank Bible."

We might speculate on whether practical considerations influenced

<!-- p. 93 -->

the way Edwards used the two manuscripts. The leather-bound volume was more convenient for travel than the gatherings and quires of double leaves of foolscap that made up the manuscript booklets of the "Notes on Scripture." And Edwards was frequently on the road. The "Blank Bible" potentially provided him with both a copy of the text of Scripture and a location for writing brief notes or reflections while away from his scrutore, or writing desk, which normally housed his manuscripts."[^002-note239] There is, however, no known record of Edwards' taking the "Blank Bible" on a journey with him, so we are forced to focus on the contents of me manuscript rather than on any speculations regarding its use.

One unexpected role that the "Blank Bible" played for Edwards had no equivalent in Pierpont's use. Beginning perhaps in September 1732 and continuing throughout his lifetime, Edwards used the closing blank pages, numbered 902–4, as a place to keep track of financial accounts with his children. It appears that he routinely borrowed money from them, noting carefully the successive amounts he owed each. He began these accounts on page 904; with the passage of time and the growing number of children in his family, he proceeded backward in the manuscript, opening new accounts successively on pages 903 and 902. The individual accounts for the eleven children do not follow a pattern. These records shed light on the lifestyle of the Edwards children. Son Timothy's (1738–1813) account, for example, notes, "Silver buckles taken from above this mark."[^002-note240] It was not simply currency that figured in these exchanges. In the case of Eunice (1743–1822), Edwards wrote, "She was paid all, and overpaid in a pair of gold buttons. March 1756."[^002-note241] In the case of Jerusha (1730–47), the account notes, "for progress in reading." The children's accounts tend to shed a soft light on Edwards' relationships with his children.[^002-note242]

Edwards' ultimate plans for the materials in the "Blank Bible" are not explicit from comments in the manuscript itself or from other writings. But he provided important clues concerning his future projects in the letter to the Trustees of the College of New Jersey before he assumed presidential responsibilities in Princeton. His description of the particulars of the two contemplated great works, *A History of the Work of Redemption* and *The Harmony of the Old and New Testament*, confirms the central

<!-- p. 94 -->

role that Edwards' biblical commentaries, including the "Blank Bible," were to play in his future plans.[^002-note243]

Edwards' premature and unexpected death on March 22, 1758, prevented him from completing these projects as well as from recording a clear final wish about the destination and use of his diverse manuscripts. Edwards' will, signed on March 14, 1753, established Sarah as the "Sole Executrix" of his estate; to her he gave all his manuscripts and some of his printed books. His library, by contrast, was to be hers only if one of his sons did not take a college degree.[^002-note244] The inventory of his estate listed his manuscripts as 15 folios, 15 quartos, and 1,074 sermons, but it offered no identifiable reference to the interleaved Bible. Although Jonathan's will placed responsibility for guardianship of his written legacy primarily in the hands of Sarah, subsequent to the date his will was probated, May 13, 1758, and sometime before her own untimely death on October 2, 1758, Sarah entrusted the manuscripts and library to his close friend and former student Samuel Hopkins. Hopkins undertook the task of writing a biography, which he published seven years later. In the section of the *Life* dealing with the manuscripts, Hopkins took note of Edwards' writing plans. He observed that his mentor had written "a great deal on the Bible… by opening his thoughts on particular passages of it, as they occur'd to him in reading or meditation."[^002-note245] Hopkins, however, made no specific mention of the "Blank Bible."

Sarah's will specified that on her death Edwards' "Papers and Writings" were to be put into the hands of a family member, thereby formally continuing the trust she had been given by her husband.[^002-note246] Nearly nine years later Sarah's desire was carried out when Jonathan Edwards, Jr., took custody of his father's papers. Jonathan Jr. graduated from the College of New Jersey in 1765 and subsequently studied theology with both Hopkins and Joseph Bellamy (1719–1790), another student and ministerial colleague of his father. The younger Edwards served as a tutor at Princeton from 1766 to 1768. In March 1767 he was chosen by the Edwards family to take possession of his father's manuscripts and papers. During the ensuing years Jonathan Jr. was instrumental in publication efforts in America and Great Britain that resulted in the appearance of several works by his father, including *A History of the Work of Redemption*,

<!-- p. 95 -->

two volumes of selected sermons, and some entries from the "Miscellanies."[^002-note247]

Several years after the death of Jonathan Edwards, Jr., in 1801, the collection of papers and manuscripts was placed in the hands of Timothy Dwight (1752–1817), a grandson of Edwards and president of Yale College from 1795 until his death. He aspired to write a biography of his grandfather. During the years of Dwight's custody of the papers, the first two collected editions of Edwards' works appeared, both entitled *The Works of President Edwards*, both in eight volumes, one published in Leeds, England (1806–11), and the other in Worcester, Massachusetts (1808–1809).[^002-note248] In volume 6 of the Worcester edition, under the title "Observations upon Particular Passages of Scripture," the editor Samuel Austin (1760–1830) printed twenty-one excerpted entries from the "Blank Bible," filling twelve printed pages.[^002-note249] This was the first time any portion of the interleaved Bible appeared in print. Dwight's aspirations notwithstanding, he was reduced to being a patron of and subscriber to the Worcester edition.[^002-note250] The biography he had hoped to write and the new American edition of his grandfather's works he had hoped to publish were tasks that fell to his son Sereno E. Dwight (1786–1850), who became the minister at Park Street Church in Boston in 1817. Sereno Dwight's *Life of President Edwards* appeared in 1829, followed the next year by his ten-volume edition of *The Works of President Edwards with a Memoir of his Life*.[^002-note251] Volume 9 included the text of "Types of the Messiah," which is, "Miscellanies," no. 1069, and a shortened and rearranged version of "Notes on Scripture," retitled "Notes on the Bible."[^002-note252] Dwight did not publish any entries from the "Blank Bible." In fact, he retained only one of five explicit references to the title "Blank Bible" in his edition of "Notes on the Bible."[^002-note253] The Worcester revised edition, by contrast, which appeared for a first time in 1843 in four volumes in New York and in several

<!-- p. 96 -->

subsequent nineteenth-century editions, reprinted the entries from the interleaved Bible that first appeared in 1809.[^002-note254]

After 1830 the collection of manuscripts and papers continued for a time in Sereno Dwight's possession, although other members of the extended Edwards family expressed concern regarding their security and use. As a result of concerted family action, in 1847 Tryon Edwards, a great-grandson of Edwards and a minister in New London, Connecticut, assumed "*legal & moral*" responsibility for the manuscripts. Five years later, in 1852, he edited and published *Charity and Its Fruits; Or, Christian Love as Manifested in Heart and Life*, a series of Edwards' sermons on the Christian moral life which appeared in both New York and London.[^002-note255]

The attention Edwards' manuscripts were gaining abroad because of publications in both England and Scotland became the occasion for an unplanned transatlantic odyssey of the "Blank Bible." A publishing house in Edinburgh contracted with Tryon Edwards for permission to publish "a *new & enlarged* edition" of Edwards' works. As a result, the firm sent a young man, Alexander B. Grosart, to America in mid-1853 to work on the project. Grosart collaborated closely with Tryon Edwards and Edwards Amasa Park (1808–1900), a prominent Edwardsean theologian at Andover Seminary, as well as with other members of the extended Edwards family. Grosart copied manuscripts and collected papers bearing on Edwards' biography. But controversy broke out among these parties concerning Grosart's intentions. By the fall of 1854 Grosart was back in Scotland, having carried with him several manuscripts that had been in the custody of Tryon Edwards, including the "Blank Bible." When the firm backing the project collapsed, the plan for a new edition of Edwards' works was abandoned.

Grosart's account of his activities in America and in Scotland appears in the "Introduction" to a work he published more than a decade later, a volume entitled *Selections from the Unpublished Writings of Jonathan Edwards of America*.[^002-note256] In it he wrote, "The treasure of the whole proved to be a Treatise on Grace, carefully finished and prepared for the press: and second to it, if second, an interleaved Bible, containing numerous annotations." In further comments on these annotations, Grosart stated, incorrectly it turns out, "*that not one of these has been hitherto printed*." Though he cited the publication of the "Observations" in the Worcester

<!-- p. 97 -->

edition, he failed to recognize their provenance in the interleaved Bible. In the same vein, he stated that "the present *is a wholly independent series*,—the old Bible having been in the possession of one of the grandchildren until the general committing of all in 1849–50 to Dr Tryon Edwards.… In the 'Notes on the Bible'… there are various references to 'the Blank Bible,' which were not understood, but now are, in the light of our recovery of the present Annotations."[^002-note257]

Grosart then offered his evaluation of Edwards' exegetical entries, a judgment that warrants quotation because it is one of the earliest public statements regarding the "Blank Bible." He wrote, "Students of Edwards have always prized 'above rubies' the 'Notes' and 'Observations' already extant; and I run no great hazard in anticipating that those now for the first time printed, will be equally valued. They seem to us to be of a more richly *experimental character* than the others, while there is the same acumen, quickness in discernment of Scriptural harmonies and parallelisms, soundness of interpretation of difficulties, happy accommodation, sweetness and tenderness of enforcement, overshadowed at times with solemn appeal, and rare ingenuity of 'improvement,'—as the Puritans were wont to call it."[^002-note258]

Grosart held a high view of Edwards' biblical reflections. He selected and printed 324 entries from the "Blank Bible," arranged in canonical order, filling 122 pages in his volume. He chose his selections principally from books of the Bible that had attracted a great deal of attention from Edwards. For instance, he included thirty-five entries from Genesis, twenty-seven from Matthew, twenty-five from Exodus, and twenty-three from Isaiah. Surprisingly, there are no entries among his selections from the book of Revelation. Grosart, who went on to a career as a prominent editor of Puritan and Victorian authors, included a defense of his editorial practices in the introduction to his volume. He spoke of his "*scrupulous accuracy*" in the editing, including the retention of traditional contractions such as "'tis." Although he regarded some of Edwards' constructions as "ungrammatical" and "clumsy," nevertheless he asserted that he retained them, lest he allow nineteenth-century conventions to intrude on the eighteenth century. Grosart thought Edwards' concern with truth overrode the issue of "the form of expression."[^002-note259]

<!-- p. 98 -->

The Grosart story did not end in 1865. Decades later Tryon Edwards accused Grosart of having misled him regarding his intentions when he took Edwards' manuscripts to Scotland. Those charges have been compounded by the speculation of later scholars that Grosart may have been responsible for the loss of valuable manuscripts and letters. During the four decades the "Blank Bible" was in Scotland, family members, interested scholars, and educational institutions competed for access, possession, and control of Edwards' scattered papers. Following controversy among the descendants of Edwards and scholars interested in using the papers, Edward Amasa Park, who was assembling materials for a biography, approached Grosart on behalf of the family and asked him to return the manuscripts in his possession. Sometime in the 1890s a small cluster of manuscripts, including the "Blank Bible," was returned to Park, thereby completing the Scottish saga of the interleaved Bible. Whether there were other manuscripts and letters that were not returned remains unclear.[^002-note260]

Concern for the preservation and security of Edwards' papers proved a catalyst for action by members of the family, who gathered signatures from eighteen of Edwards' great-grandchildren agreeing to deposit his manuscripts at Yale University Library. But even that plan, formulated in 1890, was thwarted for years by the unwillingness of Park to surrender the papers in his possession. Finally, following his death on June 4, 1900, his daughter sent those items, including the "Blank Bible," to the Yale Library, where the interleaved Bible and the majority of Edwards' papers are now located. There is also a significant, though much smaller collection of Edwards' manuscripts at the library of Andover-Newton Theological School.[^002-note261]

In the twentieth century only modest notice was given to the interleaved Bible before the closing decades, when the impact of the new Yale Edition of the *Works* began to be felt. Even then, because the initial focus of the Edition was upon Edwards' published writings, only limited attention was given to his manuscripts. Perry Miller's influence on Edwards scholarship in the second half of the twentieth century was another reason for limited interest in the manuscripts. As author of the

<!-- p. 99 -->

most influential study of Edwards in the twentieth century and as first General Editor of the Yale University Press edition of *The Works of Jonathan Edwards*, Miller played a formative role in shaping the scholarly agenda. He focused attention on Edwards as a philosopher and a controversialist. But his attitude also biased readers against certain traditional theological concerns, including biblical interpretation. He had little interest in the role of the Bible in Edwards' thought. His biography included a brief, three-sentence paragraph referencing the interleaved Bible and "Notes on the Scriptures," a paragraph that contains a mistaken account of the origin of the "Blank Bible" and its relationship to the "Notes on Scripture": "He [Edwards] also took a King James version of the Bible that had belonged to Sarah's father—probably this project was begun after his marriage—and interleaved it with blank folio pages. He started to annotate crucial passages. Eventually he filled up his pages, and then three more manuscript volumes. These 'Notes on the Scriptures' were also meticulously indexed."[^002-note262] In fact, the three manuscripts are part of the "Notes on Scripture," a series Edwards began seven years before he wrote the first entry in the "Blank Bible." He never "filled up" the pages of the interleaved Bible completely.[^002-note263]

In view of this situation, it is not surprising that even some of the most important scholarship dealing with Edwards in the following decades failed to reckon with the "Blank Bible." For example, in the mid-1960s Conrad Cherry's instructive historical account of Edwards' Calvinism, which focused on his concept of faith, took seriously the biblical element in Edwards' theology; but Cherry did not cite or acknowledge the existence of the "Blank Bible."[^002-note264] Later that same decade Roland André Delattre listed the "Interleaved Bible" in the bibliography of his important study of the concept of beauty in Edwards' philosophical, theological, and ethical thought, but there is no evidence that the manuscript figured in his analysis.[^002-note265] In the mid-1970s Karl Dieterich Pfisterer's examination of Edwards' view of history, which drew heavily on his biblical reflections, used only published sources and showed no recognition of the "Blank Bible."[^002-note266] Late in the 1970s Sacvan Bercovitch described the role

<!-- p. 100 -->

of the jeremiad in early American culture, including the role that Edwards' millennial and scriptural preoccupations played in the process, but there is no mention of the existence of the "Blank Bible" among his sources.[^002-note267] In 1980 Mason I. Lowance, Jr., examined the prophetic and metaphorical language used in New England between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, a study in which Edwards'; interests in typology and exegesis figured centrally, but he has no reference to the "Blank Bible."[^002-note268] In the late 1980s M. X. Lesser's volume on Edwards in Twayne's United States Authors Series included the suggestion that while at Yale, Edwards began "foraging in the Bible, keeping 'Notes on Scripture.'" Later in the same decade, Lesser continued, "he began to interleave the family Bible with 'miscellaneous observations' and textual explications that in time grew to over nine hundred manuscript pages"—an unfortunately inaccurate description of the "Blank Bible."[^002-note269] Michael J. McClymond's study of Edwards' theology and its interaction with eighteenth-century intellectual developments fails to deal with the evidence in either the "Notes on Scripture" or the "Blank Bible."[^002-note270]

Perhaps it is unfair to criticize these scholars for failing to deal with something that was still in manuscript. Biographers, too, in general, have offered little more than passing reference to the "Blank Bible." Ola Elizabeth Winslow, for example, included in the bibliography of her prize-winning biography a brief description of the "Interleaved Bible," an entry that features the children's accounts at the end of the manuscript. Elsewhere she characterized the accounts "kept in his hand" as "charmingly" suggestive evidence of Edwards' relationship with his children.[^002-note271] Winslow, however, took no account of the manuscript as a biblical commentary. Iain H. Murray, whose high regard for the contemporary relevance of "Edwards' life and writings" was evident throughout his biography, mentioned the "Notes on Scripture" and the "Blank Bible" in tandem, citing Alexander Grosart's opinion of the importance of the latter,

<!-- p. 101 -->

which he described as a 900–page "interleaved study Bible."[^002-note272] Neither Harold Simonson nor Robert W. Jenson engaged manuscript materials in their biographical studies of Edwards.[^002-note273]

Gradually, however, the publication of the volumes of the Yale Edition in the 1960s and 1970s began to change this situation. Schafer's pioneering studies of Edwards' manuscripts brought new attention to the "Miscellanies" as well as to a number of other virtually unknown texts, among which was the interleaved Bible. Schafer assisted other editors in the Yale Edition with manuscript questions.[^002-note274] The first formal references in the Edition to the interleaved Bible occur in Clyde A. Holbrook's introduction to *Original Sin*, published in 1970.[^002-note275] Later that decade the first physical description of the "Blank Bible" in the Edition appeared in *Apocalyptic Writings*.[^002-note276] In that same volume extensive cross-references occurred to the interleaved Bible, showing the direct and complicated links among Edwards' scriptural commentaries. Subsequent volumes in the Edition have almost uniformly had index entries documenting the substantive connections between the documents featured in those volumes and the "Blank Bible."[^002-note277] The fullest use of entries from or references to the "Blank Bible" has been in the edited volumes of "Miscellanies," "Notes on Scripture," "Notes on the Apocalypse," and "Images of Divine Things." The practical effect of the Edition's citation of biblical references has been a growing recognition by scholars—both those connected and those unconnected with the Edition—of these exegetical resources. For example, John Smith's short but valuable book-length introduction to Edwards as a philosopher and philosophical theologian alerts the reader to the range of manuscript resources dealing with Edwards' scriptural interpretation.[^002-note278]

One exception to the pattern of neglect and oversight of Edwards' views on the Bible outside the circle of the Yale Edition and its editors was John H. Gerstner. He, however, was not really an exception to that rule because for many years Gerstner was under contract to edit three volumes of sermons as part of the Yale Edition. In 1974 he departed from

<!-- p. 102 -->

the editorial project, but not before he had immersed himself in the manuscripts. Over the course of the 1970s and 1980s he published a series of essays dealing with Edwards and the Bible.[^002-note279] Gerstner's research on Edwards ultimately gave rise to a three-volume study published in the early 1990s that he described as "the first full-scale theology of Edwards ever published." He consciously chose to present his work in "the traditional orthodox theological form." Gerstner's volumes, the product of four decades of "fascination" with Edwards' "wisdom," left no ambiguity about his admiration for the man and his theology.[^002-note280] He declared that on the basis of his accomplishments Edwards may have been "the greatest Christian since the apostolic age," an attitude that colors the entire exposition.[^002-note281] Gerstner devoted attention to a variety of issues related to Edwards' views on the Bible, including the relationship between reason and revelation as well as the inspiration, canon, and interpretation of Scripture—all issues of theological concern also to Gerstner. Perhaps the most unusual element in the three volumes was a 234–page section in volume 1 entitled "A 'Commentary' on Hebrews" in which Gerstner collated and commented upon every citation he could find written by Edwards relating to the book of Hebrews. He arranged the excerpts canonically.[^002-note282] There is both a creative and a distortive quality to this "reconstruction." Edwards never wrote a systematic commentary on Hebrews or any other book of the Bible. His exegetical work was infinitely more occasional and happenstance. In his reconstruction, Gerstner cited extensively from the "Blank Bible" on Hebrews. A close check of his transcriptions from the interleaved Bible, however, reveals that they are filled with numerous errors, making highly suspect the reliability of his citation of manuscripts throughout his volumes.[^002-note283]

<!-- p. 103 -->

A more significant engagement with the "Blank Bible" comes in the recent monograph of Robert E. Brown.[^002-note284] Brown's approach differs dramatically from that of Gerstner. The latter's conviction concerning the contemporary religious relevance of the commentary is countered by Brown's preoccupation with the ways Edwards was engaged with and influenced by "the early and transformative impact of critical historical interpretation on American religious thought."[^002-note285] Brown argues that Edwards was aware of problems attendant on the rise of biblical criticism. Even though he rejected the radical implications derived from that criticism, Brown contends that his "conservative participation in the transformation to modern interpretative strategies" is significant. He describes Edwards' approach to the new interpretation as "a kind of hybrid traditionalism" and characterizes him as "modestly critical," which he equates with being "judicious."[^002-note286] Unfortunately, all parties involved in the controversies over modern biblical criticism, even in its earliest stages, thought their positions wise and based on sound judgment. What Brown does make clear is that "Edwards had markedly absorbed the historical sensibilities of the age," even if he then went on to reject the leading implications of those sensibilities as they bore on scriptural interpretation.[^002-note287] Brown's study makes excellent use of the biblical manuscripts—both "Notes on Scripture" and the "Blank Bible." His work challenges the next generation of scholars to construct new and appropriate categories for Edwards' engagement with critical approaches to the Bible.

The contrast between Gerstner and Brown could not be greater. Gerstner places Edwards in a line of Reformed thinkers and exegetes that includes Charles Hodge (1797–1878) and Benjamin Warfield (1851–1921), nineteenth-century predecessors of American fundamentalists; Brown situates Edwards in a world of thinkers increasingly influenced by the rise of historical and critical thought, embracing exegetes as diverse from his own theological views as John Locke and Anthony Collins. These two contrasting perspectives are instructive in another way: they illustrate the diversity of the motivations operating among the persons who have turned attention to Edwards' biblical materials.
