Some seek to celebrate his theology while others hope to understand his intellectual or religious ideas.

<!-- p. 104 -->

#### Dating of the Manuscript

Ever since Thomas A. Schafer's groundbreaking research on the dating of the "Miscellanies" and the other early manuscripts, readers of volumes in the Yale Edition have almost come to expect a month by month, year by year, chronology of Edwards' writings. Schafer used handwriting, ink, orthography, watermarks, citations, and content analysis to unlock the chronology of the earliest manuscripts of the young Edwards.[^002-note288] All editors of volumes in the Edition, including those published before Schafer's volume 13, have been beholden to Schafer for his decades of work. Editors of subsequent volumes in the Edition have acknowledged the standard set by Schafer's remarkable scholarship and have also identified the increasing complexity involved in dating later materials as precisely, in part because Edwards constructed notebooks from paper stock in advance of rather than at the time of composition, thereby eliminating a major element in Schafer's system.[^002-note289] In the case of the "Blank Bible," of course, Edwards inherited a fully constructed interleaved manuscript, so paper stock is not helpful for dating his entries.

Dating hundreds of entries in manuscripts such as the "Miscellanies," "Images and Shadows of Divine Things," and "Notes on Scripture, written more or less in series over four decades, has posed a major challenge for editors of the Edition.[^002-note290] Dating more than five thousand entries written randomly in the interleaved Bible in scattered fashion over a period of nearly three decades represents a scholarly challenge of a wholly different magnitude. The "Blank Bible" is a chronological puzzle and an editor's nightmare. For that reason the decision to set limits on the amount of chronological data supplied has been both necessary and expedient. The goal of this volume is to provide the reader with select aids that will assist in dating some of the entries. No attempt has been made to date all the entries—a goal not justifiable in terms of the required investment, the anticipated results, or the additional insights. Furthermore, full chronological data on every entry are not necessary for reading, understanding, appreciating, or using this book.

Edwards obtained the "Blank Bible" in 1730, and for the next twenty-seven-plus years he wrote entries on its pages. The manuscript contains a variety of diverse information and clues bearing on the dating of many

<!-- p. 105 -->

of the entries. A limited amount of this chronological information is virtually explicit with respect to the possible dates of composition for some entries. A large amount of the data bearing on the time when Edwards wrote specific entries is indirect or proximate, allowing the reader, at best, to make reasonable judgments about the possible date of composition. The majority of the entries lack immediately apparent explicit or indirect evidence regarding the date when Edwards entered the notes or comments. This last fact does not mean that it would be impossible by one means or another to date these entries. But that task has not been undertaken uniformly in this volume; nor is it assumed to be a reasonable expectation for any edition of this manuscript. Research that demands an exact time for the composition of any one particular entry in the interleaved Bible may require direct examination of the holograph itself. That option remains available at the Beinecke Library for the interested scholar. For most readers, however, the information that follows will be sufficient for identifying significant chronological patterns among the entries in the interleaved Bible.

Some few entries in the "Blank Bible" can be linked to explicit chronological data found elsewhere. The best examples of this pattern involve references to Edwards' own sermons. The interleaved Bible contains twenty-five entries citing sermons identified by canonical references. In nearly every case the sermons in question, part of Edwards' manuscript corpus, have notations identifying when they were preached. For example, the "Blank Bible" entry on Numbers 14:22–23 reads, "See sermon on the words" (p. 267). Edwards preached that sermon in the winter or summer of 1730.[^002-note291] This very early entry in the manuscript was written in a small carefully formed script. The same comment, "See sermon on the words," occurs at 2 Corinthians 5:17, referencing a sermon Edwards preached in September 1751 (p. 1073).[^002-note292] The handwriting of the latter entry contrasts sharply with that of the note in Numbers. The approximate dates for these entries in the interleaved Bible therefore derive from notations on the sermons. This kind of specific chronological information for individual entries in the manuscript is the striking exception to the general pattern.

Perhaps the most significant data bearing indirectly on the dating of hundreds of entries in the "Blank Bible" are Edwards' own cross-references to his other manuscript series, manuscripts that have been dated

<!-- p. 106 -->

by editors in the Edition, namely, the "Miscellanies," "Notes on Scripture," "Notes on the Apocalypse," and "Images and Shadows of Divine Things." In toto, 896 references to these four series are present in the "Blank Bible." Where such cross-references are integral to an entry in the interleaved Bible, Edwards wrote the entry in question after the referenced note. Where such cross-references are later additions to an entry in the interleaved Bible, the likelihood is high that Edwards wrote the entry in question before the referenced note. Two examples will illustrate these patterns. Edwards wrote an entry on Matthew 22:32 in which he argued that Abraham and the other patriarchs see God's promises to them fulfilled in "their seed on earth," and thus they "share in the glory of the church on earth," a theme that he developed more fully in "Miscellanies," no. 811, which he cross-referenced in the "Blank Bible," a cross-reference integral to the entry. He also added a later cross-reference to "Scripture," no. 379, which continues the discussion by focusing on the ways in which God's covenant with the patriarchs was fulfilled in blessings given to their posterity (p. 864).[^002-note293] "Miscellanies," no. 811, has been dated by Ava Chamberlain as written no earlier than August 1739; "Scripture," no. 381, has been dated by me as written after August 1739. These dates strongly suggest that the Matthew 22:32 entry in the "Blank Bible" was written around August 1739.[^002-note294]

A second example involves Edwards' integral cross-reference to "Images," no. 141, in his brief note on Job 7:7, an entry that equates Job's reference to "wind" with "the breath" (p. 431).[^002-note295] In the same sentence Edwards also referenced other entries in the "Blank Bible" on Psalms 78:39 (p. 513) and James 4:14 (p. 1175). The three cross-references, which are integral to the entry, appear contemporary with one another; and therefore all probably were written by Edwards sometime between April and September 1742, as determined by Wallace E. Anderson's dating of "Images," no. 141.[^002-note296] In sum, cross-references to dated manuscript series provide the possibility of triangulating probable dates for composition by careful consideration of the chronological order of the entries.

For that reason the following chronological tables derived from the four edited manuscript series are useful. The dates of composition for the select entries have been determined by editors of the earlier volumes in the Yale Edition.

One additional chronological observation concerning the relations among Edwards' three biblical commentaries—"Notes on Scripture," "Notes on the Apocalypse," and the "Blank Bible"—is in order. Edwards' entries in the "Notes on Scripture" tail off dramatically in the late 1740s.[^002-note301] Moreover, even earlier, by August 1746, he had altered the basic function of "Notes on the Apocalypse" as a commentary, using it primarily after that date as a location in which he recorded extensive "Extracts" from Moses Lowman's commentary on the book of Revelation, "Events Probably Fulfilling the Sixth Vial on the River Euphrates" which he read in newspapers beginning in October 1747, and other "Events of an Hopeful Aspect on the State of Religion" which he learned of by correspondence or reading public accounts.[^002-note302] These changes in the two manuscripts did not signal an end to Edwards' interest in the study of the Bible or to his pursuit of exegetical insight wherever it might be found. But they do show that increasingly he turned to the "Blank Bible" when recording general comments and observations. In other words, the interleaved Bible became the primary location for his biblical observations during his last years in Northampton and his years in Stockbridge. It is also appropriate, however, to take note of the continuing presence of exegetical

<!-- p. 110 -->

entries in his "Miscellanies" written during these later years.[^002-note303] Finally, one factor no doubt contributing to these changes in his study habits was the huge investment Edwards was making during the last decade of his life in writing the defenses of his communion practice in Northampton, in addressing administrative issues concerning the Native American mission in Stockbridge, and in composing several major treatises.[^002-note304]

Edwards' citations of published sources provide additional chronological data relating to the composition of particular entries in the manuscript. Of the 109 publications cited by Edwards in the "Blank Bible," many were first published between 1730, the year he acquired the interleaved Bible, and 1758, the year of his death. The publication dates of those particular sources thus provide the termini a quo. However, some publications that Edwards cited appeared in multiple editions; unless we know which edition he used, we cannot use them for establishing chronology.

Fortunately, by this point in the history of the Yale Edition, considerable information exists in earlier volumes regarding Edwards' various sources and the time periods in which he was engaged with them. That information aids immeasurably in the task of dating his use of those sources in the "Blank Bible." On the basis of data drawn from earlier volumes in the Edition and from entries in the interleaved Bible, the approximate dates by which Edwards made use of select sources cited in the "Blank Bible" can be established tentatively. Of course, Edwards could and often did return to these publications on later occasions. He may also have used these sources earlier in manuscripts that have not yet been edited or in citations that have not been identified. Table 7[^002-note305] contains three diverse pieces of information for several sources Edwards cited in the "Blank Bible": the date of publication, which for many of these publications falls between 1730 and 1758; a reference to publications in Edwards' writings that can be linked to a date; and the location in the volumes of the Yale Edition that provides information regarding that date.

One source Edwards used extensively, Philip Doddridge's *Family Expositor*, possesses a special advantage for the reader interested in the dating of "Blank Bible" entries. The six volumes of Doddridge's commentary on the New Testament were published sequentially in 1739, 1740, 1748, 1753, 1756, and 1756, respectively. Edwards cited these volumes more than 300 times in the interleaved Bible. In each case, therefore, the publication date of the volume provides a specific terminus a quo for Edwards' use of Doddridge in that entry. His extensive use of Doddridge's later volumes is additional evidence of the concentration of his exegetical activities in the "Blank Bible" during the last decade of his life.

Two other manuscripts by Edwards, kept by him over many years, provide important supplementary information with chronological implications for a number of entries in the "Blank Bible." The two manuscripts are his "Catalogue" of reading and his "Account Book."[^002-note306] These rich bibliographical documents have very different natures. The "Catalogue," begun by Edwards in 1724 while a tutor at Yale College, includes references to books and other publications that interested him, that he wanted to acquire, or that he learned about in one way or another. Some of these he eventually purchased and owned, or borrowed, and then read or cited. Others simply remained on his list.[^002-note307]

The "Account Book," begun by Edwards in 1733 and continued for the balance of his life, provides a rich dated record of financial transactions, including salary payments, cattle purchases, debts, and other domestic expenses. In it Edwards also kept a record of the marriages he performed. In addition, he noted the titles and dates on which he lent publications to friends and colleagues. These last items provide valuable information regarding his library and the years by which he had acquired particular titles.

Several examples illustrate the usefulness of the information found in these two manuscripts. The "Catalogue," for example, tells how Edwards learned about Lowman's commentary on the book of Revelation from his uncle William Williams (1665–1741), who had received correspondence from Benjamin Colman (1673–1747) in Boston describing a

<!-- p. 114 -->

forthcoming publication by an author named "Lawman."[^002-note308] This first reference in the "Catalogue" to Lowman is on the same manuscript page as two notes dated specifically in late 1737, suggesting a slightly earlier timeframe for the writing of the note.[^002-note309] The "Catalogue" entry confirms that Edwards learned of Lowman's work almost immediately after its publication in 1737. Other references in the "Catalogue" relate to one of the "Blank Bible" entries on Exodus 17:6 which quotes from the November 1752 issue of *The Monthly Review; or, Literary Journal* (p. 230). Edwards apparently had that publication in hand no later than 1753, as witnessed by numerous entries to various 1752–53 issues of the *Monthly Review* in the "Catalogue."[^002-note310] The presence of the references in the "Catalogue" confirms the timeframe implied in the "Blank Bible" citation. Entries in the "Account Book" are also valuable for confirming dates by which Edwards clearly had access to the books mentioned. One entry reads, "Lent to Mr. Vanhorn the 1st vol. of the *History of Popery*, June 28, 1750."[^002-note311] Another entry reads, "Lent Warburton's *Divine Legation of Moses* to Mr. Bellamy, Feb. 1750/51."[^002-note312]

The diversity of Edwards' handwriting in the manuscript and the different inks he used in the entries are not as helpful in dating these entries as they are for other manuscripts.. The usual assumptions concerning the size, shape, and apparent care, or lack of care, evident in his script are less valid when applied to the "Blank Bible" because he was often constrained by the size of the space available in a specific column and adjusted his script to accommodate the spatial limitations. Similarly, the advantage of identifying contiguous entries written with the same ink as contemporary is often lost where entries are neither contiguous nor even physically proximate. Hand and ink in isolation from other factors therefore offer a less firm basis for chronological decisions in the "Blank Bible" than perhaps in other manuscripts. In addition, each page of the interleaved Bible reflects a chronological puzzle of its own, depending on the order in which the random entries were written on the page. First entries usually were located in the appropriate positions in the columns analogous to the printed biblical texts, but subsequent entries often were either displaced to alternate open spaces or begun at one location and continued at one or more other openings. It is often possible to reconstruct

<!-- p. 115 -->

the order of entries on a given manuscript page, which reflects the sequence of entries but not the actual time periods when Edwards wrote the comments. On other occasions, reconstructing that order is virtually impossible. Finally, there is much to be gained by simple content analysis of the entries, thereby linking themes and ideas across the pages of the interleaved Bible. But such connections are at best suggestive of similar times of composition.

#### Editing of the Manuscript

The distinctive physical makeup of the interleaved Bible and the scattered random placement of Edwards' entries on its pages have required editorial decisions unique to the nature and content of this manuscript. Most notably, all the entries have been rearranged to follow the canonical order of the King James Version of the Bible. All entries in this edition, whether originally written at the correct site for the comment on the facing interleaved foolscap page, at a different location on such a page or on another page because of space constraints, or at the margin of the small printed Bible, now appear in canonical order, regardless of size, date of composition, or content. The editorial justification for this rearrangement of the text is self-evident: canonical biblical references were Edwards' exclusive organizing scheme for the manuscript. The jumbled sequence of the entries on the manuscript was the result of space constraints, not of inherent or substantive relationships between physically adjacent entries.

Another significant editorial decision has involved the question of whether to attempt in this volume a physical replication of the manuscript, which is distinctive by virtue of the presence of the printed text of the Bible facing double columns of manuscript entries. For two reasons the decision was made against such an attempt. First, it was impractical and unnecessary to reprint the entire text of the King James Version, which remains readily accessible despite the plethora of new English translations, paraphrases, and niche bibles available today. Second, a two-column edited text would pose both space and design problems without any appreciable benefit. Photographs of select pages from the "Blank Bible," which have been provided in this edition, are a more accurate way to depict the physical nature of the manuscript.

Nevertheless, at times it may be useful for readers to have access to a copy of the King James Version of the Bible even though it is not necessary for understanding all of Edwards' entries. For some entries, no specific textual referent is required. The comment may be self-contained or

<!-- p. 116 -->

may not hinge on the biblical text. In other instances, Edwards cited the word, phrase, or sentence in the biblical passage that is the focus of his commentary; again, consultation with the KJV is unnecessary. There are, however, countless entries where Edwards, who had the biblical text on the facing page in the manuscript, began his comment without any textual excerpt or citation. In those instances, it may be useful to read the biblical passage in question in the KJV alongside Edwards' commentary.

When Edwards wrote several separate entries on the same biblical passage or on the same excerpt of biblical text, those entries appear under a single canonical reference with paragraph divisions and footnotes signaling the separations. The canonical reference or excerpted text is not repeated. Edwards' directional annotations for referencing continuations, later additions, or related entries have been retained in this edition only when they provide some substantive link between entries. His placement of notes and entries in the manuscript did not signal relative importance or substantive subordination.

The disparate contents of the "Blank Bible" raise a variety of additional editorial questions. The standard conventions employed by the Yale Edition, a brief statement of which appears above in the "Note to the Reader," answer many of them. Others require special attention in the "Blank Bible." The large number of authors Edwards cited in the manuscript poses a particular challenge. Often these citations contain other sources cited at second and third hand. The convention established in the Edition is to identify the immediate source of Edwards' quotes or references. Second—and thirdhand sources are not regularly identified unless they pose a special problem. This pattern, which also has been followed in the four-volume edition of Edwards' "Miscellanies," seeks a balance between the edited text and the annotations. It is sensitive both to the needs of the readers and to the constraints of space. Wherever possible, the editions of the particular works Edwards used or had access to are identified in the footnotes. In many instances, when the edition he used cannot be positively identified, the first edition or possible subsequent editions he may have used will be cited. The collective efforts of the editors of the preceding volumes in the Edition deserve mention as a major source of assistance in this identification task.

Edwards frequently included Latin, Greek, and Hebrew words or citations in his commentary on the biblical text, some drawn from the sources he was reading, others from the ancient texts themselves. The convention followed in this edition is to provide an accurate text and a translation when needed. Edwards himself often provided the latter in

<!-- p. 117 -->

his comments. Throughout, the level of annotation employed is intended to assist the general reader of the text as well as the scholar seeking more specialized information. That dual purpose has informed the Edition throughout its history, and it remains primary for the "Blank Bible."

## The Old Testament

### Genesis

Ch.JE acquired the "Blank Bible" in 1730, but signed the title page in 1748. Across the top of the title page he wrote two procedural notes. The first reads, "Vol. 2 of 'Notes' begins with no. 291. Vol. 3 begins with no. 413." It references the first entries in the second and third MSS of the "Notes on Scripture" (*Works, 15*). The second reads, "Note that this mark, SSS, is a reference to Poole's *Synopsis* in a place at a place [sic] marked in the margin." It identifies JE's short reference for Matthew Poole's *Synopsis Criticorum*. JE's personal copy of the *Synopsis Criticorum* has not been located. 1.]JE wrote three additional procedural notes on the margins of p. 2 of the MS. The first reads, "This mark for back [<], and this for forward [>]." The second is a vertical list of thirty-five symbols for cross-referencing text additions or citations. Included in the list are such iconic symbols as #, ∗, †, ‡, etc. The third reads, "Note when there are quotations in the margin with these three letters written under them, viz. (har), 'tis to signify that the quotation is to show the harmony there is between the Old and New Testament." JE marked this note with a vertical line. See how many things in the manner of the old creation are typical of the work of redemption. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, §§1–2; MS: "No. 702. p. 37. 38. 39. 40. 41. 42." *Works, 18*, 283–89. the reasonableness of this account and history of the creation, "Miscellanies," no. 1048.This second reference is a later addition. *Works, 20*, 389–91.

Genesis 1:1. "In the beginning God created," etc.] The word is Elohim from the radix אָלָה, "adjurare," signifying the three persons of the Trinity confederated together as to the grand scheme and design of the creation, as they are in the eternal covenant of redemption. The word is in the plural number (see *Republic of Letters*, vol. 5, p. 380)."An Essay upon four Tracts lately publish'd, intitled, An account of Moses's Principia, Part I. & II.; The Natural History of the Bible; and Moses's Sine-Principio. By J. H.," *The Present Stale of the Republick of Letters* 5 (May 1730), 380. And also from אֵל, *deus*, from the radix איל, *fortitudo*, signifying the power of the Creator. Elohim is the plural number of El, with the insertion of the letter ה out of the name Jehovah, as was in the change of the names of Abraham and Sarah. See Mastricht.Peter van Mastricht (1630–1706), a professor of theology at Utrecht, discusses the use of the plural noun אֱלהִים with the singular form of the verb בָּדָא, explaining the link as evidence of the involvement of the three persons of the Trinity in the creation. Book 3, ch. 5, of *Theoretico-Practica Theologia: qua, per singula capita Theologica, pars exegetica, dogmatica, elenchtica & practica, successione conjugantur* (Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715) contains an extended explanation of Genesis 1:1 under the title "De Creatione in Genere" (pp. 311–19). For more on Mastricht, see *Works, 13*, 319, n. 2. On the issue of the Trinity, see Amy Plantinga Pauw, *The Supreme Harmony of All: The Trinitarian Theology of Jonathan Edwards* (Grand Rapids, Mich., Eerdmans, 2002).

<!-- p. 124 -->

See reasons why we should suppose that the world was CREATED in SEPTEMBER, SSS on Exodus 12:2.This sentence is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 359.

Genesis 1:2. "And the earth was without form," etc.] There were many traditions among the heathen of what is contained in this verse. Thus SanchoniathonA Phoenician writer in the 14th–13th centuries B.C.E. whose works on ancient mythology and beliefs were known through Philo in the 1st century C.E. says, "that in the beginning of things, there was a spirit of dark air, which he calls χάος ἐρεβῶδες, i.e. says Bochart (*Can., lib*. 2, *cap*. 2),On Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a learned French orientalist and biblical scholar, see *Works, 5*, 229, n. 8, and *15*, 170, n. 7. In the "Blank Bible" JE cites Bochart numerous times, drawing citations principally from his reading of Theophilus Gale. in the Phoenician tongue, ערב בהות, *chauth ereb*, 'evening darkness.' The notion 'chaos' is taken from Genesis 1:2, the word ἐρεβῶδες from ἔρεβος (as Plato and Hesiod read it), and ἐρεβος from Genesis 1:5, *ereb*, 'evening.' Thus Hesiod.An early Greek didactic poet who lived around 700 B.C.E. First of all things, chaos was produced; whence follows, from chaos sprung *erebos*, the evening and dark night. Whence second, 'tis added in Sanchoniathon, 'From the conversion of the spirit with the chaos, there emerged *mōt*, i.e. slime, a corrupt, watery mixture which some call *ilus*. This *mōt*, first matter or chaos, is expressed much in the same manner by Plato, who calls it ἀμορφόν τι, 'somewhat without form,' and ἄτακτον εἶδος, 'a confused mass.' Also he says it was ἔρεβος, 'darkness,' to which we may add that of Ovid,Ovid (43 B.C.E.–17 C.E.), a popular Roman poet. *Metamorphoses, lib*. 1, *fab*. 1.

*Quern dixere chaos rudis indigestaque moles*."Which state is called chaos, a rough, unordered mass of things."

"It follows in Sanchoniathon, 'Out of this *mōt* or chaos proceeded the whole seed of the creation, or generation of the universe.' The chaos is mentioned by Orpheus in *Argonaut* thus. 'In this beginning was the ancient chaos.' Then it follows in Orpheus, that the chaos changed its natures, and out of this chaos there was first of all segregated ὠρανός, the heaven or heavenly substance, i.e. light from אור, *ōr*, light." See Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 3, pp. 40–41.Second edition. "Orpheus says, of water

<!-- p. 125 -->

ἰλὺς, slime, was made; and Apollonius, out of slime the earth was made. Where the Scholiast tells us, that the chaos, or first matter, was water, which settling became slime; and the slime condensed became earth. Hence Thales held water to be the first matter of all things."The variety of diverse personal references—mythic figures, ancient writers, classical philosophers, historians of all periods—here and elsewhere documents JE's interest in the past. Ibid., p. 42.

Sanchoniathon calls the "motion of the spirit" on the chaos "'a dark and blustering wind.' Take the whole together, as we find it, in Eusebius,Eusebius (c. 260–c. 340), Bishop of Caesarea and author of the *Ecclesiastical History*, dealing with the history of early Christianity. *lib*. 1, 10, where the first moving principle of the universe is made to be a dark blustering spirit or wind, who finding the chaos confused, and involved in darkness, without bonds or order, being moved with love of his own principle,MS: "principe." he made a contexture called Love, whence the first production of all things proceeded (though the spirit itself had no generation). From this connection of the spirit was produced *mōt*, which some call *ilus*, slime, or watery mixture; and of this was made the seed of all creatures, and the generation of all things." Aristotle speaks of Parmenides as making "love, or cupidity, the first principle." Ibid., p. 43. The ancient "poets and philosophers held the night to be older than the day. So Plutarch, *Symp*., 4. They account that darkness was more ancient than light. Thus StanleyThomas Stanley (1625–78), the author of *The History of Philosophy* (London, 1655). tells us, that Thales [held] the night was elder than the day. This circumstance of the creation was held also by Orpheus and Hesiod, who had it from the Phoenicians." Ibid., pp. 49–50.

Megasthenes,Megasthenes (c. 350–290 B.C.E.), a Greek historian and diplomat who wrote about ancient India. in his fifteenth book of Strabo,Strabo (64/63 B.C.E.–23 C.E.), a Greek geographer and historian. expresses the opinion of the Indians thus. "That in many things they agree with the Greeks; as, that the world had a beginning, and will have an end; that it is of a spherical figure; that God, the Creator and Governor of it, penetrates all things; that all things had different beginnings; and that the world was made of water." Grotius, *De veritate*, Bk. 1, sec. 16, notes.*Truth of the Christian Religion*, 29. Hugo Grotius (1583–1645), was a prominent Dutch jurist, theologian, and historian.

"Without form and void." See no. 448.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 530.

Genesis 1:2–3.] See "Shadows of Divine Things," no. 72.*Works, 11*, 74–75.

<!-- p. 126 -->

Genesis 1:3. "And God said, Let there be," etc.] "That all things were made by the word of God is asserted by Epicharmus,Epicharmus (530–440 B.C.E.), a Greek poet. and the Platonists; and before them, by the most ancient writer (I don't mean of those hymns that go under his name), but of those verses which were of old called Orpheus's, not because Orpheus composed them, but because they contained his doctrines. The verses are these.

> I swear by that first word the Father spake,  When the foundation of the earth was laid."Grotius, *Truth of the Christian Religion*, 35–37.

Genesis 1:26.] See John 1:1–4, Isaiah 40:13–14, Isaiah 9:6, 1 Corinthians 2:10–11, John 5:17–19, Isaiah 6:8, Proverbs 8:27–31, John 17:21–22.This paragraph was written after the following paragraph.

"Let us make man." Here is a consultation of the persons of the Trinity about the creation of man, for every person had his particular and distinct concern in it, as well as in the redemption of man. The Father employed the Son and the Holy Ghost in this work. The Son endued man with understanding and reason. The Holy Ghost endued him with a holy will and inclination, with original righteousness.This paragraph, a separate entry, was written before the preceding paragraph.

Genesis 1:27.] "Plato in his *Critias* affirms that in the days of old, there flourished in the first men Θεοῦ μοῖρα, a particle of God, also Θεῖα φύσις, a divine nature, which rendered them blessed, and more particularly in his *Theætetus*, discoursing of this likeness of man to God, makes it to consist in this, that man be holy with wisdom and righteousness," agreeable to Ephesians 4:24 and Colossians 3:10. "Man's creation after the image of God is set forth by Ovid in his *Metamorphoses*.

"Sanctius his animal mentisque capacius altaæ deerat adhuc et quod dominari in cetera posset, quo natus homo est, sive hunc divino semine fecit.""A living being of finer stuff than these, more capable of lofty thought, one who could have dominion over all the rest, was lacking yet. Then man was born, made of his divine substance" (*Metamorphoses*, Bk. I, lines 76–78). Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 4, pp. 54–56.Second edition.

Of Adam the first man. Heathen fables of Saturn seem, many of them, to be taken from the story of Adam. "Saturn is supposed to be so called from סָתַר, *latuit*, whence he was styled *Deus Latius*, and his proper seat was *Latium*," which arises from Adam's hiding himself. "Sanchoniathon, discoursing of Saturn's names and genealogy, says, That the great God

<!-- p. 127 -->

Eliun, called the Most High, generated the heaven and the earth. Eliun, עֶלְיוֹן, is one of God's proper names, and signifies 'most high.' Bochart, *Can., lib*. 2, ch. 2, *fol*. 784, supposeth this passage to have been taken from those words, Genesis 14:19, Genesis 14:22, 'the most high God possessor,' or (as Bochart) 'generator of heaven and earth,' it being so rendered by the LXX, Zechariah 12:1. The wife of Eliun, Sanchoniathon makes to be Beruth, i.e. *berith*, whence we read of the Phoenician goddess Berith," which is a wordבְּרְית that signifies "covenant." "The blind Canaanites, hearing much of God's *berith*, God's covenant, grossly conceited that this *berith* was a goddess," and that by God's *berith* they intended one that was his wife. "Saturn's immediate parent was Ouranos. Whence it follows in Sanchoniathon, that the first-born son of heaven was Ilos, who also was called Saturn. This name Ilos, given to Saturn, Bochart makes to be the same with the Hebrew EL, a proper name of the true God. And that the Phoenicians called Saturn EL is manifest by the words of Damascus in Phot. Thus the Phoenicians and Syrians call Saturn EL, and *Bel*, and *Bolathes*." That Saturn is Adam is agreeable to what the heathens held of his reigning in the Golden Age. (See note on Genesis 2:8–9.) As Adam was driven from his government and paradise, so Saturn was driven from his kingdom. Adam turned an husbandman; so Saturn is said to be the first that taught men husbandry. "And Stephanus, speaking of Kronos Saturn, says that he was called Adanus, and that this Adanus was son of heaven and earth, which is a perfect description of Adam's production by God out of the earth. The name Adanus seems to be the same with Adam. For the Greeks, having no words terminating in 'm,' for 'Adam' they pronounced 'Adan.' Adam is called the 'son of God'; so Saturn is called the 'son of heaven.' Adam was formed out of the dust of the earth; so Saturn's mother was called Tellus,I., e. earth. as Hesiod and Orpheus tell us." Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 1, pp. 4–7.Second edition. This paragraph and the following four are a separate entry.

But many of the heathen fables of Saturn seem also evidently to be taken from the story of "Noah, according to that excellent parallel drawn by Bochart, *Phaleg, lib*. 1, *cap*. 1, *fol*. 1. That Noah (says he) passed among the heathens under the name of Saturn, there are so many things to prove it that there is scarce left room for doubting. 1. Saturn is "πανγενητὼρ, the 'father of all'; so was Noah." (This name agrees both to Adam and Noah, though to Adam more eminently.) "2. Saturn, as Noah, was

<!-- p. 128 -->

styled a preacher of righteousness. 3. Under Saturn's reign, as under Noah's, all things were common and undivided. 4. All men enjoyed the highest peace under Saturn, as under Noah. 5. In Saturn's time all men used one speech." (As it is said before the building of Babel, "The whole earth was of one language, and one speech" [Genesis 11:1]. Note these three last agree with Adam as well as Noah.) "6. Saturn's wife was called Rhea, or earth; because Noah was called a man of the earth (Genesis 9:20), according to the Hebrew idiom, 'an husbandman,' which the mythologists took in a proper sense for, ὅ άνὴρ της γῆς, 'the husband of the earth,' whence Saturn, the same with Noah, is made the husband of Rhea, i.e. the earth. 7. Saturn is also said to be an husbandman and planter of vines, as Noah was. 8. Saturn is styled the president of drunkenness, from Noah's being drunk. 9. Hence also came the Saturnalia, or revels, consecrated to the memory of Saturn. 10. Saturn also is said to be the author of the law, which forbad the gods to behold men naked, which was but a tradition of the curse on ChamI.e. Ham. for beholding his father's nakedness [Genesis 9:24–26]. 11. Saturn is said to arise, together with his wife and children, out of the sea, a tradition of Noah with his wife and children, their deliverance from the deluge. 12. Hence a ship became Saturn's symbol; and Saturn is said by Sanchoniathon to sail about the world, as Noah in the ark. 13. Saturn is said to foretell Deucalion's flood,In Greek legend, Deucalion, the son of Prometheus, constructed an ark and thereby survived a flood caused by Zeus. making use of a dove, etc., answerable to that of Noah, etc. 14. Saturn is said to have devoured all his children besides three, viz. Jupiter Hammon, the same with Ham; Neptune, the same with Japheth; and Pluto, the same with Shem." Gale's *Court of the Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 1, p. 9.Second edition. The heathens held that "Saturn and his three sons divided the government of the world amongst themselves." So Bochart, in Gale, Pt. 1, Bk. 1, ch. 2, p. 13.*Court of the Gentiles*, 2nd edition.

Some of the heathenish fables concerning Saturn seem also evidently to be taken from the story of Abraham. "So Sanchoniathon says that Saturn offered up his only begotten son, and also circumcised the privy parts, and forced his companions to do the same, which evidently refers to the story of Abraham. And so 'tis more fully explained by Porphyry in his book "περί ᾽Ιουδαίων quoted by Eusebius, *Præpar. Evang., lib*. 1, *cap*. 9, where he makes Saturn, who after his death became a planet, to be

<!-- p. 129 -->

called Israel. His words are these: "Saturn, whom the Phoenicians call Israel, after his death was consecrated into a star," etc. Then he adds, That the same Saturn had, by a nymph called Anobret, an only son whom for this they called Jeoud, as he is so called to this day by the Phoenicians. This only [son] (says he), being clothed with a royal habit, was sacrificed by his father, being under great calamity. This Phoenician fable is excellently well deciphered by Bochart, and applied to the story of Abraham's offering up Isaac. Thus Jeoud among the Hebrews is Jehid, which is the epithetאֶת־יְחִידְךָ אֶת־בִּנְךָ given to Isaac (Genesis 22:2), concerning whom it is evident that Porphyry treats. Then he adds, this only son was offered by his father. So Sanchoniathon. Thence this Saturn, the same with Abraham whom the Scripture styles a prince of God (Genesis 23:6), the Phoenicians made the principal god. And they called him Israel; and they consecrated unto him one day in seven as holy, i.e. the sabbath day, which was sacred amongst the Jews; and they sacrificed their sons unto him, after a wicked kind of manner, wherein they would imitate Abraham. The nymph Anobret, or according to the Phoenician name ענברת הן, Annoberet, signifies 'conceiving by grace,' which is an appellation properly belonging to Sarah, as Hebrews 11:11. Abraham is here called by the name of his posterity, Israel, Isaac, Jeoud. So Genesis 22:2, 'Take thy son, Jehid, which is the same with the Phoenician Jeoud. In Orphaicis, Abraham is μονογενὲς, where Abraham and Isaac are confounded, as here Abraham and Jacob." See Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 1, pp. 4–9.Second edition.

'Tis easy to be accounted for why the Phoenicians (those near neighbors to Israel, and that were the most friendly to 'em of any of their heathen neighbors), in conversing with them, and hearing from them of Adam, Noah, and Abraham, and not distinctly understanding, should confound 'em together, and apply things spoken of each of these to the same person, and all to their Saturn, whose original notion with them was that he was the son of heaven and earth, the first-born son of heaven, and the πανγεννέτωρ,Literally, "the father" or "parent of all." or the grand progenitor or father of mankind. So was Adam, and so was Noah. And no wonder that when the Phoenicians heard the Israelites speaking of Abraham their father, they should understand them of the same πανγεννέτωρ, or grand progenitor, for his name Abram signifies "high father" or "great father"; and his name Abraham signifies that he is "the father of a multitude," and the great promise

<!-- p. 130 -->

to him was that he should be the "father of many nations" [Genesis 17:5]. They were all of them, according to the Hebrew idiom, sons of the covenant, or sons of *Berith*, which might lead the Phoenicians to suppose Berith to be God's wife. God did particularly in a remarkable manner establish his covenant with each of these: Adam, Noah, and Abraham. And they possibly might look back upon Abraham as the son of heaven and earth, as they asserted of Saturn, or Adam. Genesis 14:19, "Blessed be Abraham of the most high God, the generator of heaven and earth," as Bochart renders it. And the Phoenicians, hearing the Israelites speaking of Abraham as their great father, and also Israel, might easily confound them.

Noah and Abraham also were as it were driven out of their own country to hide themselves from the idolatrous corruptions of Ham and his posterity in Babylon. Noah fled eastward towards China, according to Bedford.Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, 249. Concerning Bedford, see *Works, 5*, 64–65. The heathens suppose that Saturn was driven out of his kingdom by his own son Jupiter. So Noah wasJE deleted "driven out of his." dispossessedMS: "dispossed." of his paternal dominion over his posterity by the posterity of Ham (the heathen Jupiter), particularly by Nimrod, who rebelled against his father Noah [Genesis 10:8–9] (for the name comes from the Hebrew *Morad*,מָרַד which signifies "to rebel"), and "usurped an universal empire over his brethren." See Gale, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 3, p. 32.Second edition. Abraham also was bid to depart out of his own country by Jehovah,Conjecture for illegible word. whose name the heathens gave to Jupiter, i.e. Jeu-pater,MS: "Jau-pater." Gale has an extended discussion of these names. See *Court of the Gentiles* (2nd ed.), Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 1, p. 12. [Abraham, whom] God sent into the land of Canaan where he lay hid from his former acquaintance.

Genesis 1:31-2:2.] The heathens had traditions of this rest of God when he had finished his work. Plato's words are remarkably cited in Gale's *Court of the Gentiles*, Pt. 2, Bk. 2, ch. 8, p. 182. "God willed that all things should be good, and nothing bad. Neither is it lawful to suppose that God, who is best, should make the world but in the best and most beautiful manner." And then concludes, fol. 37, Thus, "after the father of the universe had beheld his workmanship, the framed visible image of the eternal invisible gods, he recreated and reposed himself therein."Theophilus Gale, *The Court of the Gentiles* (Oxford, 1670), Pt. 2, Bk. 2, ch. 8, p. 182.

<!-- p. 131 -->

Genesis 2:3.] It is rendered very probable by Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology* that this first sabbath, being the first day of Adam's life, and so the first day from whence he began to reckon time, was the first day of his week; and so, that the first day of the week was the day that God sanctified to be kept by all nations and ages, excepting the change that was made of the day of the sabbath for the Israelitish nation after the coming out of Egypt, till the resurrection of Christ. And also that the deep sleep that was fallen on Adam, in which God took from him one of his ribs and made Eve of it, was on the night before. If so, then as Christ rose from the dead on the first day of the week, so Adam on the same day rose from his first sleep. As Christ on that day rose from that death that he died, by which he purchased and obtained the church, being by that means created anew, so Adam rose from that deep sleep that he slept, which made way for her formation and by which he obtained her. As when Adam arose from his deep sleep, God brought the woman to him, whose being his deep sleep had made way for, and gave her to him; so when Christ rose from the dead, God brought the church to him. It was gathered and brought home to Christ in an extraordinary manner soon after his resurrection. As Adam rose and received his wife, "bone of his bone, and flesh of his flesh" [Genesis 2:23], and when out of himself from near his heart, so Christ received his church that is "of his flesh, and of his bone" (Ephesians 5:30), and as the product of his most dear dying love. As this day was a day wherein God was refreshed and rejoiced in beholding his works, and a day of rejoicing to Adam in that he then received his wife, and a day of rejoicing to Eve, being then first received into union with her companion, so the day of Christ's resurrection was a day of rejoicing to God the Father, to Christ, and also to the church, which was then begotten again to a living hope by his resurrection [1 Peter 1:3]*Scripture Chronology*, 120–21.

See also what traditions there were of this seventh-day sabbath among the heathen, "Miscellanies," no. 961.This sentence is a later addition. *Works, 20*, 241–42.

Genesis 2:5.] "Scripture," no. 451.*Works, 15*, 532.

Genesis 2:7.] The wiser heathens held this by tradition. Sanchoniathon speaks of the "first parent of mankind as one sprung out of the earth." And Plato speaks of it as what was affirmed by the Phoenicians, "that man sprung out of the earth. And Plato says expressly that the first man was produced out of the earth." Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 4, p. 52.Second edition.

"And breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul." "Aristotle, in *Libris de Generat. Animal*., says that the mind came from without. Sanchoniathon says, 'The first men were made ἐκ τοῦ κολπία ἀνέμου, of the colpia of the wind, or spirit. Bochart, *Can., lib*. 2, *cap*. 2, *fol*. 784, gives this account hereof. Colpiah is the same: *Col-pijah*,יה פּי קול the voice of God's mouth, by whose inspiration and word man was made. Orpheus also speaks thus: Mankind was framed by God himself, out of the earth, and received from him a rational soul." Ibid., p. 53.Gale, *Court of the Gentiles* (2nd ed.), Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 4, p. 53.

The soul of man is from God by a nobler manner of communication than the matter of his body. 'Tis as it were a communication from God, as rays from the sun. 'Tis breath of God's breath, spirit of his Spirit. The spirit of man is the candle of the Lord. It came from God, as one light is lighted up by another, as a light is lit up by the beams of the sun. The soul is in the image of God, as the image of the sun is reflected by his beams.This paragraph is a separate entry, written earlier than the preceding two paragraphs.

Genesis 2:8. "And there he put the man whom he had formed."] "Scripture," no. 343.*Works, 15*, 326.

Genesis 2:8–9.] Concerning "the state of man in paradise." Plato, speaking of the Golden Age, speaks of man as living on the fruits of the trees of which there was abundance, and speaks of there being "a soil very fruitful, that yielded these fruits of its own accord without the labor of agriculture, and speaks also of men's then living naked, and that they then conversed not only with men but beasts (which probably came from God's bringing the beasts to Adam to see what he would call them, and Eve's conference with the serpent), and speaks of men's enjoying vigor and a perfect state, the first man being of all men φιλοσοφότατος,"Extremely wisdom-loving." and speaking of these things as ancient traditions. Says he, "Our first ancestors, who sprang up immediately after the first revolution, delivered these things unto us, which fables many nowadays, not rightly, disbelieve. The Golden Age is also livelily painted forth by Ovid, *Metamorphoses*.

> Aurea prima sata est ætas, quae vindice nullo,  Sponte sua, sine lege fidem rectumque colebat.

<!-- p. 133 -->

Nondum præcipites cingebant oppida fossæ. Non galeæ, non ensis erat. Ispa quoque immunis, rostroque intacta, nec ullis Saucia vomeribus, per se dabat omnia tellus; Contentique cibis nullo cogente creatis, etc.""Golden was that first age, which, with no one to compel, without a law, of its own will, kept faith and did the right. Nor yet were cities begirt with steep trenches. There were no helmets or swords. The earth herself, without compulsion, untouched by hoe or plowshare, of herself gave all things needful. And men were content with food which came from no one's seeking."

This Golden Age was in the reign of Saturn, which is the same with Adam. See note on Genesis 1:27.

Some suppose "the Elysian fields, so much talked of by the poets, to be but a corrupt imitation of paradise. That which makes for this conjecture is an observation in Bochart, *Can., lib*. 1, *cap*. 34, *fol*. 664. "That this fable of the Elysian fields is Phoenician, may be gathered from the very name, which is of Phoenician extract, for amongst the Hebrews עָלַז and עָלַס signifies to 'exult' and 'rejoice.' Thence עַלּיז, *alis*, joyful, whence Elysius, for 'twas usual among the ancients to change 'A' into 'E,' as Enakim for Anakim, etc. This suits with the import of the Hebrew 'Eden,' which signifies a garden of delight and pleasure. Others have conceived that the story of paradise was preserved amongst the heathen under the fable of Adonis's garden, which comes near to that of Eden. So Stillingfleet."Edward Stillingfleet (1635–99), appointed Bishop of Worcester in 1689, was the author of numerous works, including the *Origines Sacrae* (1662) which addressed the authority of Scripture. See Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 4, pp. 56–59.Second edition.

JE's second sermon on Genesis 3:11, preached Feb. 1739, with the doctrine: "The act of our first father Adam in eating.… Twofold heinousness. 1. That which only concerned Adam personally. 2. That which equally belongs" (MS, p. 23). On pp. 8–11 JE discusses God's command to Adam, which "was not only express, but very preemptory," and "delivered with great solemnity" and authority. It was accompanied by the terrible threat that Adam would surely die if he violated the command. JE asserts that the Hebrew idiom translated in the margin, "dying thou shalt die," denotes both the certainty and the extremity of the threatened death. The Hebrew implies the superlative—"a most dreadful death." JE also suggests that it may imply "more deaths than one," namely, temporal death of the body and eternal death of the soul.

"In the day that thou eatest."] It don't seem to me necessary that we should understand this, that death should be executed upon him in that day when he eats, but that it may be understood in the same manner as Solomon's words to Shimei, 1 Kings 2:37. "For it shall be, on the day thou goest out, and passest over the brook Kidron, that thou shalt know for certain that thou shalt surely die." Death was executed upon Shimei many days after he had done that thing. The thing that God would signify to Adam by this expression seems to me to be, that if he but once presumed to taste that fruit, he should die. You shall not be waited upon to see whether you will do it again; but as soon as ever you have eaten, that very day shall death be made sure to you. You shall be bound to die, given over to death without any more waiting upon you, as that was what Solomon would signify to Shimei, that if he but once went over the brook Kidron, he should die. See notes on 1 Kings 2:37.This reference and the following sentence are a later addition. And so these words signify that perfect obedience was the condition of God's covenant that was made with Adam, as they signify that for one act of disobedience he should die.The remainder of this entry is another later addition. Genesis 2:19–20.] See Warburton, *Divine Legation*, vol. 2, pp. 81–82.William Warburton uses the account of Adam's naming the creatures in the Garden of Eden to argue against those who maintained that humans lived for some time in the manner of animals without language. It is his building, built up for him with a great deal of art and architecture. In Ephesians 2, *ultimo*, the Apostle useth the very same expression. 'Ye are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom all the building fitly framed' (or as the wordσυναρμολογουμένη. is, 'artificially framed harmoniously,' with all the art and curiosity that can be), 'groweth into an holy temple in the Lord, in whom ye also are built together for an habitation of God' Ephesians 2:20–22]."

Genesis 2:22–23.] "אשה in Hebrew, with the addition of ה, the sign of the feminine gender to איש, 'man,' there is the letter י, which is not in אשה, 'woman.' And in the word אשה, there is the letter ה, which is not in the word איש, man. From whence we may observe that one is in a state of imperfection without the other. That when these two letters are joined together,

<!-- p. 136 -->

they make יה, the name of the great God, to show that God is in reality with such, who are thus joined together, especially in his fear and love, and according to his injunction. But if it is not so, and God is not amongst them, there only remains אש, or 'fire,' in common to both." Bedford's *Scripture Chronology*, p. 120.

Genesis 3:1. "The serpent was more subtile."] No. 251.*Works, 15*, 202–3.

The beast and the devil were united in man's temptation, and procuring his fall; and by his fall he became like them both. He has the image of both the beast and the devil. The serpent that tempted man was a talking, reasoning beast, and an incarnate devil; and such is man now become.This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 3:6. "Saw that the tree was good for food."] There was "the lust of the flesh." "And that it was pleasant to the eyes." There was "the lust of the eyes." "And a tree to be desired to make one wise." There was "the pride of life," as in 1 John 2:16.

Concerning the woman's being the occasion of man's fall. Hereto may belong "that relation in Hesiod concerning man's being thrown into a miserable state, because of a rapine committed against God's will, and that by means of a woman sent down, who with her hands opened the lid of a great vessel, and thence dispersed sad disasters and sorrows among men." Barrow's *Works*, vol. 2, p. 92.Fourth edition. This paragraph is a separate entry.

Genesis 3:7. "They knew that they were naked."] It is probable that not only Adam and Eve immediately lost the beauty and that kind of luster that was on their bodies as soon as they had sinned, but that one effect of their eating this fruit, which immediately followed, was their voiding excrements, and that they never had done this before, in which they saw an image of their spiritual filthiness which came forth, as Christ says, from within, and proceeded out of their hearts, and fixed an idea of vileness as connected with those parts of their bodies, which it did the more deeply, as this effect, which they looked upon as the evidence of the debasing of their nature, they also looked upon as the fruit of their guilt,

<!-- p. 137 -->

which their minds were now under a strong impression of. So that this external filthiness was connected with a sense of spiritual filthiness, which greatly affected 'em

Here is one end why God suffered man to fall: that he might see his own nakedness; that is, that he might be sensible of his absolute dependence on God for righteousness and all good, and that he has nothing from himself or in a dependence on himself, but so considered is naked. "And they sewed fig leaves together," "which in Eastern countries are very broad, and as Strabo tells us, as big as a shield." Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 122.This paragraph is a separate entry written earlier than the preceding paragraph.

Genesis 3:7–8.] They first sew fig leaves to cover their nakedness; and then, when that don't satisfy, they can't rest, in that when they hear the terrible voice of God coming to them, they hide themselves among the trees of the garden, which well represents the manner of sinners' flying from one refuge to another when awakened with apprehensions of God's approaching wrath. The trees of the garden well represent the ordinances and duties of religion that God has appointed in his church to be means of grace and of our spiritual nourishment. That garden was a type of the church, and the trees of the garden were what yielded outward nourishment for men. Sinners under awakenings are wont to fly to those to hide their nakedness from God.

Genesis 3:14. "Upon thy belly shalt thou go."] Probably before that, serpents used to fly, and to be a shining, glorious, harmless creature. The serpent's fall therefore well represented the fall of the angels. Before their fall they were seraphim, which signifies fiery flying serpents; but when they sinned, they fell like lightning from heaven to the earth. The "fiery serpents" (Numbers 21:6) are in the Hebrew "seraphim."שְׂרָפַים See SSS on Numbers 21:6.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 692.

"Upon thy belly shall thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life." No. 452.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 532–33.

Genesis 3:14–15.] No. 456;*Works, 15*, 537. Poole's *Synopis, in loc*., places marked in margin.*Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 38–46.

Genesis 3:15.] By the "woman" is not only here meant the woman literally, but the church, that woman spoken of in the Revelation 12, against whom the dragon had such enmity; and her "seed" is that man-child there spoken of, that she brought forth [Revelation 12:5]. The seed of the woman is twofold. 'Tis either Christ, who became the son of the church, and then his heel is his human nature, or believers, and then their heel that Satan bruises is their bodies, for he cannot hurt their souls.

"I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; *he* shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel." "Here the pronoun 'he,' the verb 'bruise,' and the affix 'his' are all of the singular number," as Bedford observes in p. 166 of his *Scripture Chronology*, which shows that by "seed" is meant a particular person and not her posterity in general. Which observation is agreeable to that which the apostle Paul makes, Galatians 3:16, "He saith not, To seeds, as of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ"; referring to what is said, Genesis 22:17–18, where the singular pronoun or affix "his," and the singular verb "possess," is in like manner used when speaking of that seed of Abraham, who should "possess the gate of his enemies, and in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed."This paragraph and the two following are; a separate entry.

Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology* says the Jewish *Paraphrasts*I.e. Targums. express this text thus. "There shall be a remedy to mankind, but there shall be no remedy to thee, the serpent. But there shall be a remedy to them in the latter age of the world, even in the days of king Messiah, who shall remember what thou didst in the beginning of the world." And [Bedford] says that "Maimonides,Moses Maimonides (1135–1204), the foremost Jewish medieval philosopher. a learned Jew, justly admires that the seed of the woman should be only mentioned, and not of Adam, without whom she could have no seed, and which must therefore be his seed, and that it should be said of her seed, not of his, that it bruised the serpent's head. This (saith he) is one of the passages in Scripture which is most wonderful, and not to be understood according to the letter, but contains great wisdom in it."*Bedford, Scripture Chronology*, 166.

In the old creation the woman was taken out of the man; in the new creation the man is taken out of the woman. Believers that are new creatures are all taken out of the woman. God in the new creation honors the inferior, as man, the inferior nature, is honored above the angels.

Genesis 3:16. "In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children."] This is fulfilled in a literal and in a mystical sense, of which the former is a type.JE marked this entry with an "X."

Genesis 3:20. "And Adam called his wife's name Eve."] Nos. 322 and 399.*Works, 15*, 304–6, 396–99.

Genesis 3:21.] Our first parents, who were become naked, were clothed at the expense of life. Beasts were slain and resigned up their lives to afford them clothing to cover their nakedness. The skin signifies the life, as in Job, "skin for skin" [Job 2:4], i.e. life for life. Those beasts typified Jesus Christ; probably they were beasts slain in sacrifice. But if not, if they were slain by God on purpose to clothe Adam and Eve, the type is no less lively. See Exodus 26:14.

Genesis 3:22. "And the Lord God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us."] By this, together with the words of the serpent here referred to, viz. "Ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil" [Genesis 3:5], it is evident that by the word ELOHIM a plurality of persons in the Godhead is signified. To make this evident, I would repeat the words of Dr. Knight in his *Sermons*, p. 30,James Knight (1672–1735), the vicar of St. Sepulchres in London, was the author of *Eight Sermons Preached at the Cathedral Church of St. Paul, in Defence of the Divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit* (London, 1721). as quoted by Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology*, p. 165.

"It may be worthwhile to reflect on the words which the serpent spake to deceive our first parents. 'God doth know (saith he) that in the day you eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods (or rather as God, the one God), knowing good and evil.' For the word Elohim is so used from the beginning of Genesis to this very place for the one God, and the design of the tempter was to make them believe that by tasting of the fruit, which God had forbidden, they might come to the knowledge and wisdom of God, even of the same God who gave them the precept. When therefore God saith, 'The man is become as one of us,' the meaning is this: he is become as God, for he hints at the promise that the serpent had made, which was a likeness to God [Genesis 3:5] and not to angels. But 'one of us' is an indefinite term, and equally applicable to each of the persons meant and comprehended in the name God, and consequently one with the true God."

By this it is evident, so that the serpent said, "Ye shall become like Elohim" [Genesis 3:5], he had respect to a plurality. In that word [is] signified

<!-- p. 140 -->

that he should become like one of that plurality, because when God refers to his words, he speaks of a plurality, saying, "Behold, the man is become as one of us." And so that the word Elohim, as 'tis a word in the plural number, so does properly carry a plurality of persons in its signification, for the word "us" denotes a plurality of persons.

2. Hereby 'tis also evident that when God says, "The man is become as one of us," he has respect to persons in the same Godhead, for that the words signify a plurality of persons is self-evident. Nothing can be more evident than that the expression, "one of us," has respect to more than one. And 'tis evident by the words of the serpent referred to in them, that the plurality that the expression denotes is not God and angels. God don't in them speak to angels or any superior order of creatures, but the plurality denotes the plurality that is comprehended in that one name of God, Elohim, which the serpent used when he said, "Ye shall become as Elohim," which words God here refers to. God's own words self-evidently denote a plurality of persons; and the words of the serpent, they refer to confiningMS: "Confine." the plurality to the deity.

OrigenOrigen (185–254), an Alexandrian theologian and biblical critic who wrote an apologetic work against Celsus. (*Contra Celsum, lib*. 4) conceives that Plato, by his conversation with the Jews in Egypt, understood the history of man's fall, which he (according to the Egyptian mode), in his Symposiacs, expresseth under the fable of Porus (i.e. Adam), his being drunk with nectar, and then going into Jupiter's garden, and being circumvented by Penia (i.e. the serpent), was thence cast out, etc., which seems an evident vestigium of Adam's fall and being cast out of paradise. Genesis 4:23–24. "And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice, ye wives of Lamech.… I have slain a man to my wounding," etc.] The probable design of the Holy Ghost in relating this is to show the great increase of the depravity and corruption of the world, of Cain's posterity, and those that adhered to them at that day in the generations next to the flood. This is shown in the particular instance of Lamech, the chief man of Cain's posterity in his day. Lamech had been guilty of murder. He had slain some man that he had a quarrel with; and he justifies himself in it, and endeavors to satisfy his wives that he shall escape with impunity from the instance of Cain, whose life God protected, and even took special care that no man should kill him, and had declared if any man killed him, vengeance should be taken on him sevenfold [Genesis 4:15

<!-- p. 142 -->

Genesis 4:15], though the man he slew was his brother, and a righteous man, and had done him no injury. But this man he had slain "'in' or 'for' his wounding" (As the wordsלְפִצְעִי are interpreted by some learned men. See Poole's *Synopsis, in loc*., places marked.*Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 64–66, especially 65. The remaining portion of this parenthesis is a later interpolation. See instances, Joshua 24:32, קְשִׂיםָה בְּמֵאָה, "for an hundred pieces of silver."), that is, the man he had slain, had injured and wounded him; and therefore if Cain should be avenged sevenfold, doubtless he seventy and sevenfold. By this speech to his wives he shows his impenitence, presumption, and great insensibility. When Cain had slain his brother, his conscience greatly troubled him; but Lamech, with great obduracy, shakes off all remorse, and as it were bids defiance to all fear and trouble about the matter. That he should set the price of his life so high, that he should imagine that the vengeance due to the man that should take it away ought to be so vastly beyond that which was threatened for the killing of Cain, must be owing to a prodigious pride of heart, esteeming himself a man of such great value, and accounting it so very heinous a thing for any to hurt or wound him. And then it shows a vile abuse of God's goodness, longsuffering, and forbearance in the instance of Cain, which ought to have led men to repentance. But instead of this, that instance of God's forbearance probably was so abused as to be one great occasion of that violence that the earth was filled with in Lamech's days. The sins for which the old world was destroyed were chiefly sensuality, pride, violence, presumption, a stupid seared conscience, and busing God's patience, of each of which Lamech (the head of that wicked world) is here set forth an example, in his polygamy, and his murder (which probably was some way occasioned by his polygamy), and in this speech to his wives about what he had done. It need not be wondered at that Lamech should express his mind to his wives, any more than that Ahab and Haman should express the wicked workings of their hearts to their wives (1 Kings 21:5–6 and Esther 5:10–14). And it is the less to be wondered at in Lamech's case. For 'tis natural to suppose that his wives, knowing what he had done, were full of fear lest the friends of the person murdered would avenge themselves on him and his family, and that they themselves should lose their lives by the means, which would be more natural still if the quarrel he had with the young man that was slain was about his wives, as is probable. This may well account for the earnestness of Lamech's speech to his wives, as may

<!-- p. 143 -->

well suppose it would require some pains to remove their fears in such a case.

Genesis 4:25.] Eve don't say, "God hath appointed us another seed," but "hath appointed ME [another seed]." She speaks of Abel and Seth, the righteous children of Adam and Eve, as "her seed"; and so the church or generation of the righteous, which was to proceed from Seth, she calls "her seed," doubtless with respect to the promise (Genesis 3:15).

Genesis 4:26. "And to Seth, to him also was born a son; and he called his name Enos. Then men began to call upon the name of the Lord."] The right translation probably is, "Then began men to call by the name of the Lord, or 'in' the name of the Lord"; i.e. then they began to call themselves and their children "by" or "in" his name, signifying that then the people of God, of whom Seth was the principal man, and as it were their head, leader, and chief priest, being with his posterity appointed another seed (seed or generation of God) instead of Abel, I say, then the people of God, openly to distinguish themselves from the wicked apostate world of the posterity of Cain and those that joined with them,MS: "them &." began to appear as a visibly distinct society, being called the children of God when the others were called the children of men. The children and posterity were looked upon as being in the name of the fathex, and upholding his name. See Numbers 27:4, Deuteronomy 9:14 and Deuteronomy 25:7, 1 Samuel 24:21, 2 Samuel 14:7 and 2 Samuel 18:18, Ruth 4:5, Job 18:17, Isaiah 14:22, Genesis 48:16, compared with Numbers 6:27. On the birth of Enos, it probably first began to be a custom for parents openly to dedicate their children to God, and call them by his name, and as it were insert them into his name by bringing [them] to the place of public worship, the transaction being performed by the parents' solemn declaration and covenant attended with prayer and sacrifice. See Poole's *Synopsis, in loc*., place marked in the margin.*Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 67–68,

Genesis 7:7. "And Noah went in, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives."] When Adam was created, and the world was empty of people and needed to be peopled, yet God made him but one wife. And so from the beginning it was so, that one man had but one wife. And when the world was made empty again and needed to be repeopled, and there was but four men in the world, Noah and his three sons, they each of them, had but one wife, as is yet more evident by Genesis 7:13. So from the beginning of the new world it was likewise so that one man had but one woman, which are strong arguments against a plurality of wives. Henry.Ibid., 33.

Genesis 7:8–9, Genesis 7:14–16.] Concerning the resorting of all kinds of birds and beasts, etc., to the ark before the flood, see no. 354.*Works, 15*, 340–41.

Genesis 7:9.] The brute creatures readily went into the ark; they fled for refuge to save themselves. The ox knew his owner, and the ass his protector's crib. Nay, even the wildest creatures flocked to the ark. Thus God made the brute creatures to rebuke the stupidity and folly of men, as he made Balaam's ass rebuke the madness of the prophet [Numbers 22]. Men more brutish than the brutes themselves did not know, did not consider.

<!-- p. 148 -->

Genesis 7:16. "And the Lord shut him in," for these ends. 1. For the security of those within, the door must be close shut, that no water might come in. 2. To shut out others. It had stood open till now; and if they had believed and fled for refuge to the ark, they might have been admitted (as those that believed the word of Moses in Egypt, and fled home, saved themselves from those dreadful storms [Exodus 9:20]). But now their day was past; if they come afterwards, the door was shut. And it was in vain for 'em to come to the door, and cry for entrance; for God shuts, and none can open. Doubtless when the storms began to come on, many fled to the ark, hoping to have entrance, but in vain. 3. To prevent any that were within the ark from coming out, and so perishing. God put Adam into paradise, but he did not shut him in, and so he threw himself out. But when he put Noah into the ark, and so when he brings a soul to Christ, he ensures the salvation. 'Tis not in our own keeping, but in the Mediator's hand. Henry.*Exposition, I* (1725), 34.

Genesis 7:17. "The waters bare up the ark."] "*Obs*. 1. The waters which broke down everything else, bare up the ark. That which to unbelievers is a savor of death unto death, is to the faithful a savor of life unto life. 2. The more the waters increased, the higher the ark was lifted up towards heaven. Thus sanctified afflictions are spiritual promotions; and as troubles abound, consolations much more abound." Henry.Ibid.

Genesis 7:19.] As this deluge was in many things a type of that deluge of wrath that shall come on wicked men in another world, so it was in this in particular, that it was an ocean without any shore, signifying the same with the bottomlessness of the pit, which represents that their misery will have no end, and that it will [be] as it were infinite in degree because it will be objectively infinite. What they will have to apprehend and think of will be infinite, viz. the wrath and hatred of an infinite God and its endless duration causing absolute despair, which will as it were be an infinite present suffering, so far as a finite spirit will be capable of apprehending an object that is infinite.

Genesis 8:9.] The dove esteemed the ark as her place of confinement; before she went forth, she was weary of that confinement. So the saints are in danger of growing weary of the strictness of a close walk with God. Corrupt nature will strongly remonstrate against it. But the dove, after she took liberty, and departed from the ark, and wandered in the wide world a while, esteemed the ark as her refuge and resting place. So the saints, after they have yielded to temptation and given the reins a while to their lusts, are glad to return to Christ for refuge and rest from those storms and tempests they meet with in a way of sin.

Genesis 9:12–15.] Such a promise of God that he would no more destroy the earth by a flood of waters, and such a token of this covenant, was very

<!-- p. 150 -->

necessary for the comfort of Noah and his sons after they had been so terrified by such an awful dispensation of God. For probably before the flood, they had never seen any such thick clouds and such showers of rain as are common since, the air and fluids of the earth being then so much purer, as not to be disposed thus to such thick and dark condensing of vapors. God's way of watering the ground seems to be that mentioned in Genesis 2:6, of causing mist to go up and descend in great dews. The rainbow here seems to be a new thing, which it would not have been if there had been such clouds and showers before the flood as since. Noah and his sons therefore would have been likely to have been put into a terrible consternation from time to time, when they saw the heavens all covered with thick and dark clouds, and the water descending in great showers of rain, for fear the world was going to be drowned again with a flood. But God, having told Noah, as in these verses, their seeing the rainbow, as was common after showers, especially great showers, would be a great comfort to 'em. See no. 238Ibid., 189.

That beautiful, pleasant appearance, the rainbow was a token of the covenant. So God's covenant with his people is represented by the staff called "Beauty," in Zechariah 11:10.

Genesis 9:27. "God shall enlarge Japheth,… and Canaan shall be his servant."] "Pursuant to this prediction, the Greeks and Romans made themselves masters of the residue of Canaan. Tyre built by the Sydonians, and Thebes by Cadmus, were both destroyed by Alexander the Grecian. Alexander laid siege to the city of Thebes, took it by storm, and entirely destroyed it, slaying ninety thousand of the inhabitants, and selling the rest, to the number of thirty thousand more, into slavery. Carthage, founded by Dido, was, after a long succession of losses and a vast effusion of blood, demolished by Scipio the Roman, which losses made Hannibal, a child of Canaan, cry out with a mixture of astonishment and despondency, '*Agnosco fortunam Carthaginis*.'"This paragraph is a separate entry. For a version of this account, including a translation of the Latin as, "I acknowledge the fate of Carthage," see Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 290. Sometime Fellow of Christ's Colledge in Cambridge* (4th ed., London. 1677), Bk. I, pp. 283–84. These accounts confirm widespread interest in the link between the children of Noah and the subsequent distribution of nations.

Concerning Canaan. Canaan is the same with Mercury of the heathens. "1. Mercury, as to his genealogy, was said to be the son of Jupiter Hammon, i.e. Ham, as Canaan was. 2. Mercury is derived, by the learned, from מכר, *macar*, to merchandise or sell, which exactly answers to the Hebrew 'Canaan,'כְּנַעַן which signifies a merchant. 3. Hence also Mercury is made the god of trade and merchandise, as likewise famous for thievery, all which alludes to the great trading, merchandising piracies and craft of Canaan's posterity, the Phoenicians. 4. Mercury is painted with wings, which some refer to the ships of the Phoenicians. 5. Mercury is brought in as always employed in servile messages, which is supposed to be an allusion to the curse of Canaan." Genesis 9:25, "A servant of servants shall he be to his brethren." Thus Bochart. "Plato in his *Phaedrus* terms him Πατὴρ γραμμάτων, the 'father of letters,'" because the Phoenicians, Canaan's posterity, first brought letters into Greece.
