Genesis 14:5–6.] Thus God is pleased to honor his servant Abraham. First, he orders that in providence that shows the great strength of the enemy by giving the victory over so many people, and those that were so mighty. They subdue the race of the giants that were in these lands. And then he gives 'em an easy prey to Abraham and his family, his little flock, and shows that the weakness of God is stronger than the greatest strength of men, when hand join in hand and mighty princes are combined together. Abraham takes them in their greatest glory, and just after they had taken their richest prize, that which they took from that wealthy

<!-- p. 156 -->

country of the plain of Sodom. In their highest pride, and exaltation, and triumph, they are suddenly brought down, as Nebuchadnezzar [Daniel 4:33] and Belshazzar [Daniel 5:30] were. Thus God often deals with men.

There seems to be a special hand of God with them, to enable 'em to conquer these giants, from the favor he bore to his servants, Abraham and Lot, and to evacuate those countries of them, that he designed to give to their posterity for a possession. See Deuteronomy 2:18–19 ff. They gave not God the glory of this great victory, but took it to themselves, as Nebuchadnezzar did the building of Babylon. Therefore God destroyed them. That race of giants that was in and about Canaan was probably the only race of giants upon earth. God had long war with them, and they were all destroyed for the sake of his people. The race was entirely extirpated in the days of David. They seem to have been raised up for that end, that they might be types of the devils, and that their being destroyed before his people might be a type of the victory Christ obtains over the devils for the sake of his people. See note on Joshua 10, no. 402.*Works, 15*, 405–11.

So he dealt with the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah.

Genesis 15:1.] In what God says to Abraham, he has respect to what is related in the Genesis 14. There it is related how wonderfully God had protected him from his enemies, and given him the victory over them. And therefore God on this occasion bids Abraham not to fear, and tells him that he is his "shield." In the Genesis 14, it is also related how that Abraham had refused the reward that the king of Sodom had offered him Genesis 14:23]. And therefore God here tells him that he is his "exceeding great reward," which he was sufficient for, being "the possessor of heaven and earth," as Abraham on that occasion observed (Genesis 14:19 and Genesis 14:22).

The same that God promises here, or Jesus Christ, that is called here "the word of the Lord," was typified in the Genesis 14 by Melchizedek's bringing forth bread and wine to Abraham Genesis 14:18], for Melchizedek is a type of Christ. And the bread and wine typifies the blessings Christ bestows on his people,JE deleted "or the way in which he bestows them, viz. as having that are." both their defense and happiness, which are both by his body and blood. And 'tis also agreeable to the blessing that Melchizedek gave him in the name of the Lord, in the Genesis 14:19.This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 17:10. "Every man-child," etc.] This is an evidence of original sin, for let the Scripture be its own interpreter; and we are in many places taught that the foreskin represents sin or lust. Leviticus 26:41, "If then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled." "Theodorus teaches us in his poem upon the Jews, that the precept of circumcision was first given to Abraham, in these verses which Eusebius has preserved in his *Gosp. Prep*., Bk. 9, ch. 22.

The FORESKIN that was cut off in circumcision fitly represented corruption, not only as it aptly represented lust in general, being a special spot of the lust of the flesh, and we know how often corruption in general is called THE FLESH, but because that especially is men's NAKEDNESS, and is called their SHAME, which terms are often used in Scripture to signify SIN.This and the preceding paragraph are a later addition.

"And he that is eight days old shall be circumcised."] One reason why they were not to be circumcised till they were eight days old was because the child was legally impure till then, and it was seven days before it was clean. Genesis 17:14. "That soul shall be cut off from his people."] This and other parallel texts in the law of Moses ben't necessarily to be understood of death. 'Tis very agreeable to the use of such expressions elsewhere, that he that is excommunicated, deprived either by the judgment ofJE deleted "the authority of the." ecclesiastical judges, or by the immediate judgment of God, of all union and communion with the congregation or church of God's people, should be said to "be cut off from his people," and CUT OFF from the congregation of the Lord. Joshua says to the Gibeonites, Joshua 9:23, "Now therefore ye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen." In the original, it is, "There shall not be cut off from you a bondman" (The word "cut off," in the original,כָּרַת being the same as in the other case.), i.e. no one of you shall be separated from the rest of your company so as not to partake with him, or have communion with him, in servitude. So God says, Numbers 4:18, "Cut ye not off the tribe of the families of the Kohathites from among the Levites," i.e. let 'em not be separated from them, and from a participation in their privileges. Here again the word in the original is the same, as it also is, Zechariah 14:2. "Half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the city shall not be cut off from the city," where it is implied that not only those that are dead, but those who areJE deleted "expelled or." separated from the inhabitants and benefits of the city by captivity, are cut off from the city. So divorcement in Scripture is "cutting off," the word being from the same root in the original (Deuteronomy 24:1, Deuteronomy 24:3, and Isaiah 50:1). However, God's depriving his people of church privileges, or of the privileges of his visible people, [is] compared to this very thing.

Genesis 18:18–19.] By these verses it is manifest: 1. That absolute promises already made may yet in a sort depend on future condition, for the promise here mentioned had been made already absolutely over and over. But yet Abraham's future commanding "his children and his household after him" is mentioned as the condition of it; and then after that, remains another condition, viz. "that they keep the way of the Lord, to do justice and judgment."

2. That the promise is absolutely made, before the performance of all the conditions, because the performance of the future conditions is so certainly connected with what was already found in Abraham, that it was certainly consequent, and taken as already fulfilled. This may illustrate the dependence of a sinner's salvation on his future universal obedience and perseverance, though it be already absolutely promised.

3. Hereby 'tis manifest that ordinarily a thorough care and endeavor in the education of children will be successful.

4. That when God admits children into covenant with their parents, and so admits 'em to be the subjects of the visible seal of the covenant, it is as it were on a dependence on the future religion and piety of those children as so ordinarily consequent on it, that it may be looked upon as virtually included in it.

Genesis 18:25 "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?"] In the title of "fudge of all the earth" is implied God's being the fountain of all right, that the universal rule of right is from him. He is the author of all laws of righteousness, revealed laws, and laws of nature, he by whom kings rule, and princes decree justice, and all the judges of the earth [judge]. He is the author of that reason and conscience that is in men, that naturally suggests what is right and wrong, that approves of right, and condemns wrong, whereby men are a law to themselves. All knowledge of right, all approbation of it, all dislike of wrong in the universe, is from him, as well as all rewards of right and punishment of wrong. And take the meaning of the phrase in this extensive sense, and so the reasoning is very strong.

Genesis 19:1. "And there came two angels," etc.] Probably from hence and other like instance which we have an account of in Scripture, came that notion among the heathen nations which Homer expresses in his *Odyssey*. "The gods themselves, like unto wandering strangers (seeing they are everywhere), do come and visit cities, beholding what is done right or wrong among men." See Dr. Owen, on Hebrews 13:3, pp. 210e and 211a.John Owen, Hebrews 11–13.

<!-- p. 162 -->

"And Lot sat in the gate of Sodom." Where he probably sat exhorting and reproving the people. For the gate of the city seems of old to be the place of resort on all public occasions, not only the place the judges sat to judge the people, but where their teachers sat to instruct and reprove them. Isaiah 29:21, "That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate." Amos 5:10, "They hate him that rebuketh in the gate, and they abhor him that speaketh uprightly." The judges might properly do this, but others might also do it who did not take upon the office of judges. If Lot was now reproving the people, and striving to persuade 'em to repent and reform, he thusGrosart interlined "showed that he." had no fellowship with the unfruitful, with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reproved them. And God rewarded his withstanding and resisting the stream of the general wickedness of that people by sending angels on a most kind and merciful errand to him, while in the exercise of his fortitude and opposition. And 'tis also observable that just before the destruction of the people, God used extraordinary means to reclaim 'em by Lot's reproofs (who was "a preacher of righteousness," as well as Noah, 2 Peter 2:5–9); and their destruction came upon them just on the manifestation of the highest and most desperate degree of obstinacy in them, in their despising his reproofs, and most horrid wickedness towards Lot and the angels immediately after. Lot, having lately been reproving the people in the gate, the place of judgment, made them the more ready to say, as they do in Genesis 19:9, "This fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Genesis 19:15–17.] As these angels did, so should ministers, the angels of the churches, do. They should hasten persons' escape out of the spiritual Sodom by warning of them of the great danger of their being consumed with the city. They should charge 'em to escape for their lives, and not to look behind them, nor to stay at all by the way, but escape to the mountain, lest they be consumed. Yea, they should as it were compel them while they see them linger; they should as it were lay hold on them, and hale them forth.

Genesis 19:20–22.] Zoar is a type of the church; and Lot, in that which is here mentioned of him, is a type of Christ. Lot intercedes that Zoar, one of the cities of the plain, might be saved for his sake, that he might flee

<!-- p. 163 -->

thither, and that that city might not be burnt. As Lot by interceding for this little city saved it, so Christ saves the church by his intercession. And so Lot saved Zoar from being consumed by the fire and brimstone by coming to it, coming into the city, and being among the citizens. So Christ saves men by coming into the world to them, by taking on him men's nature. He saves the church by uniting himself to it, being one of the church, becoming the brother of the elect. Lot comes out of burning Sodom, out of that sink of sin and wickedness, and as it were out of the midst of the fire of God's wrath, with salvation to Zoar. So Christ was made sin for us, and comes as it were out of the fire of God's wrath, rises from the dead, and as it were from hell, and comes to his people with salvation. Zoar was a little city; so the church is a little city. Christ's people are a "little flock" [Luke 12:32]. Lot pleads this as an argument why Zoar should be saved for his sake, that it was a "little one" Genesis 19:20]. He can be more bold to ask that mercy, that a few should be saved for his sake than that many should.

and New Testament, in that 'tis according to the Old Testament as well as New, that 'tis not unreasonable that God himself should provide the sacrifice by which sins against himself should [be] atoned, and his own anger appeased.
