This has its greatest fulfillment in Christ's ascension ("Fulfillment of Prophecies of Messiah," p. 69a).In "Miscellanies," no. 1068, a treatise entitled "Fulfillment of the Prophecies of the Messiah" (Andover coll.), JE cites Old Testament passages, including this one, in support of the proposition: "By the ancient prophecies, the Messiah, after his rising from the dead, was to ascend into heaven; and in his exaltation… he was to have his throne in heaven" (pp. 65–69).

"Gone up." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 294.

Genesis 49:10.] Traditions among the heathen taken from this prophecy, see Gale's *Court of the Gentiles*, pp. 67 ff.Second edition, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 6, pp. 67–70.

"The scepter shall not depart from Judah." Concerning the meaning of the word translated "scepter,"שֵׁבֶט see Dickinson's *Reasonableness of Christianity*, p. 88.This and the following paragraph are a separate entry. Dickinson, quoting the Cambridge biblical scholar Joseph Mede (1586–1638), defines a scepter as "any power or Majesty of government," no matter what its name, the ensign or symbol of which was a rod or staff. On Mede, see *Works, 5*, 5–6.

"And unto him shall the gathering of the people be." I.e. of the Gentile nations. Till Christ came, the Gentiles were far off, but by Christ they were made nigh. The Gentiles were as stray sheep, wandering from the flock; but Christ is the shepherd that gathered them to his flock, so that there is one sheepfold of both Jews and Gentiles under Christ, one shepherd.

<!-- p. 199 -->

The Gentiles were as it [were] banished like Cain. They were aliens and strangers, but Christ called [them] back from their banishment, broke down the wall of partition, and "gathered together in one all things" (Ephesians 1:10). The Gentiles, before Christ came, were "not gathered," as the phrase is (Isaiah 49:5). The calling of the Gentiles is spoken of in the Prophets and also in the New Testament by gathering together his people from the four quarters of the world. Christ said if he was lift up from the earth, he would draw all men unto him [John 12:32].

See concerning this prophecy, Bp. Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, pp. 307 ff.;Thomas Sherlock asserts that ancient sources all agree that the scepter was "already in the Hand of *Judah*," which this prophecy confirms. It also assumes "Continuance of the Sceptre of *Judah*… to the *very last Days* of the *Jewish* State" (*Use and Intent of Prophecy* [5th ed., London, 1749], pp. 307–9). Dissertation III treats "The Blessing of Judah, Genesis 49" (pp. 307–60). and Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 3, pp. 129–46Kidder's essay on this verse focuses on the time when the Messiah was to come. In opposition to Jewish views cited from a variety of rabbinic sources, he sets out to prove that the Messiah has already come, that the promise of the Messiah was an absolute, and that Jesus' coming was in the last days, the proper time of the Messiah. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 129–46. and SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum*, *I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 294–304. These three references in this paragraph are later additions.

"Unto him shall the gathering of the people be." Hosea 1:11, "Then shall the children of Israel and the children of Judah be gathered together, and appoint over them one head," compared with Ezekiel 37:22, Ezekiel 37:24.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Genesis 49:11. "Binding his foal to the vine, and his ass's colt to the choice vine, he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes."] I.e. Shiloh, the great lawgiver, judge, and savior spoken of in the foregoing verse. He comes to his people to judge and save them, riding on an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass, representing the great burden that he bears, and the hard labor with which he comes. "The ass was the hieroglyphic of drudgery, hard labor, and bearing of burdens; in which respect it was figurative of the stupendous servile office of Christ for us, who was to bear the burden of our sin and sorrow, the iniquity of us all being laid upon him." (See Merrick's sermon on *The True Vine*, p. 14.)Merrick, *Parable of the Vineyard* This prince and savior finishes his toilsome journey at the winepress where he binds his foal to the vine. Christ is the True Vine; especially his divine nature is that by which the blessed fruit of the vine is produced. The vine that yields the fruit that produces the reviving wine signifies the

<!-- p. 200 -->

same as the altar that sanctifies the gift. There is a twofold coming to Christ to Zion as her lawgiver, judge, and Savior. One was in his suffering state, the other in exaltation and triumph; in both he comes as it were on an ass. In the former, he comes with labor and toil; in the other, he comes in the virtue of his labors and sufferings. His triumph and glory is wholly on that foundation, so that still he is fitly represented as riding on an ass. He comes in both these journeys to wash his garments "in the blood of grapes." He ends his first toilsome travail at the winepress where, in union with the divinity, he washes his garments in his own blood. In the other he treads the winepress of his Father's wrath, and dyes his garments with the blood of his enemies, and also washes his garments in wine, the happy and glorious fruit of his own suffering, as all the joy and glory in which he and his people shall appear at Christ's triumphant coming, at the fall of Antichrist and at the end of the world, is as it were the new wine expressed from the True Vine as the consequence of the shedding of Christ's own blood.JE deleted "See Revelation 7:14, " a later interlineation.

If we understand the words of this verse as referring not to Shiloh, spoken of in the foregoing verse, but as spoken of Judah, of whose blessing they are a part, then they may be understood of the church, or people of Christ, who are sometimes in the book of Psalms called by the name of Judah. Then this may represent the saints' washing their robes, and making them white in the blood of the Lamb, and as it were swimming in that joy that is through the blood of Christ, and is called the fruit of the vine and new wine, which they especially do partake of who go through great labor and suffering for Christ's sake, represented by their riding on an ass. They tie their ass to the choice vine as they suffer for Christ, and in a dependence on him who is the True Vine.

"His foal unto the vine." Zechariah 9:9.

"Washed his garments in wine." Isaiah 63:2–3.This and the preceding reference are separate entries.

Genesis 49:12. "His eyes shall be red with wine."] Isaiah 55:1.

Genesis 49:16.] Fulfilled in Sampson, who was of that tribe.

Genesis 49:17.] Fulfilled in Sampson, and also in the story we have of the Danites, in the Judges 18. When Sampson pulled the house down under the Philistines that were upon the roof of it, by breaking

<!-- p. 201 -->

the pillars on which it stood, he as it were made the house throw his rider, by wounding his legs.This sentence is a later addition.

"An adder." SSS.Poole *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 306. This reference is a separate entry.

Genesis 49:18. "I have waited for thy salvation, O Lord."] Jacob says this here because the event foretold in the immediately preceding words, viz. Sampson's slaying the Philistines, and destroying the temple of Dagon at his death, was a remarkable type of that great salvation by Christ so often promised in the blessing God gave to Abraham, Isaac, and to him, and that he had been so supported by through the many troubles of his wearisome pilgrimage. See Bp. Sherlock's explanation of this and the preceding verse, *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, pp. 296 ff.;Sherlock interprets the promise to multiply Abraham and his seed and to give them Canaan as a possession as implying "necessarily a Promise of temporal Power and Dominion. For a People cannot possess a Land without some Form, or rule of Government among them." The promise therefore points to victory over their enemies (*Use and Intent of Prophecy* [5th ed.], pp. 296–303). and Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. *4–5*This reference, written at the bottom of the page, may read "4. c." or 4. 5. "*Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 4–5. and SSS.This and the preceding reference are later additions. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 306–307.

Genesis 49:19.] Fulfilled in Jephthah'sJE crossed out this word with two "x's." time, who was of this tribe [Judges 11-12]; and it may be also in what we have account of in 1 Chronicles 5:18–22. See also 1 Chronicles 12:8, 1 Chronicles 12:15.

Genesis 49:21.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 308.

Genesis 49:22. "Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well, whose branches run over the wall."] The wordבְּנוֹת which is translated "branches" properly signifies daughters; and the wordשְוּר which is translated "wall" signifies both a wall and also an enemy, so that the words may be translated either "whose branches run over the wall," or "whose daughters go over to the enemy." But let it be translated either of the ways, the event referred to doubtless is the tribe of Benjamin's being supplied with wives

<!-- p. 202 -->

[Judges 21:14]. For their wives, that they were supplied with from Jabesh Gilead, were of this tribe, for Jabesh Gilead was in the half tribe of Manasseh. And the daughters of Shiloh, which they catched when they came out in dances, were of the tribe of Ephraim, for Shiloh was in that tribe. Thus their daughters went over to the enemy, or the tribe of Benjamin, who were enemies to the other tribes of Israel in that war in which their women and most of the men were destroyed. Thus also the branches or daughters of this fruitful bough or vine run over the wall. As the whole people of Israel are several times in Scripture compared to a vineyard, so here a particular tribe in Israel seems to be compared to a distinct enclosure of fruit trees or vineyard, that was walled in (as vineyards were wont to be), and so separated from other vineyards. Joseph is compared here to an exceeding flourishing bough or vine, whose daughters or branches run over the wall, and get out of the enclosure, and run into another vineyard.

In that it is said, his "branches run over the wall." And the same word that signifies "branches," also signifying (and more properly signifying) "daughters," it seems to show which way his branches shall run over the wall, viz. by his daughters' breaking over the enclosure, or limits of the tribe, and going to another tribe.This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 49:24. "But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob."] This was remarkably verified in Joshua and Gideon, who were of this tribe, as appears with respect to Joshua by Numbers 13:8, and with respect to Gideon by Judges 6:11, with Joshua 17:2 and Judges 6:35. They were wonderful instances of those whose "bow abode in strength," and the arms of whose hands were strengthened "by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob," who were strengthened and succeeded by immediate help from God, as appears by their whole story. Jephthah the Gileadite was also of Joseph, being of the tribe of Manasseh.

"From thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel." These words seem to have a remarkable fulfillment in Joshua, who was as it were the shepherd of Israel, who led them into Canaan to their pasture, and conquered their enemies for them, and was in a subordinate sense the rock of Israel's salvation, who bore the name of Christ, Joshua or Jesus or the Savior, and was a remarkable type of Christ, and who had Christ with him, and acted by his influence, and fought by his strength, and had his spirit

<!-- p. 203 -->

to guide him. It may also have respect to the ark and tabernacle being kept at Shiloh, as it was till the days of Samuel, for Shiloh was in the tribe of Ephraim (Psalms 78:60, Psalms 78:67). The ark was the type and symbol of Christ, the shepherd and rock of Israel; and the tabernacle and the mercy seat over the ark was the place of his presence.

"From thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel." I.e. from the mighty God of Jacob, mentioned in the immediately preceding words. It seems evidently to be explained by the words immediately following, from "the God of thy father," and he "will help thee," for so the wordsוְיַעְזְרֶךָּ     אָבִיךָ     מֵאֵל     יִשְׂרָאֵל     אֶבֶן     רֹעֶה     מִשָּׁם are literally translated, *misham rougneh ebhen Israel meel abhik vejangzerekah*. "The arms of his hands were made strong" (thus he "helped thee") "by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob" (who was Joseph's father). From thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel, even from the God of Jacob thy father; and he (the shepherd, the stone of Israel) will help thee, and by him shall the arms of thine hands be made strong. He, the Messiah, is the hand or the arm of the Lord (as he is sometimes called), which shall strengthen thine arms. See SSS on Genesis 49:25.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 310. This paragraph is a later addition.

Genesis 49:26. "The blessings of thy father have prevailed above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills. They shall be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him who was separated from his brethren."] The blessings of his progenitors, by which they had the everlasting hills of Canaan given to them, and the everlasting hills of the heavenly Canaan were given to but one of their children. Abraham's blessing reached Isaac only. Ishmael and his other children were separated from Isaac, and sent forth out of Canaan as having no part there. And so Isaac had but one blessing, which was given to Jacob as the only heir of Canaan. Esau was separated and sent away out of the land. But Jacob had a blessing for all his sons, and one even for Joseph, that seemed in the providence of God to be separated from his brethren, and sent out of Canaan, as if he had no part in it, like Esau, and Ishmael, and the sons of Keturah. But yet the blessing of his father reached him. He had a part given him in Canaan, yea, an everlasting inheritance in it, and in the most eminent blessings that appertained to it, to the very summit, and utmost bounds, and duration of its everlasting hills. See the following three paragraphs.

<!-- p. 204 -->

"Unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills." In the original,תַּאֳוַדְ "to the 'term' or 'ends' of the everlasting hills." I.e. 1. To the highest top and summit of these hills, figuratively representing the height and excellency of the blessing, agreeable to the style of Scripture, which speaks of God's mercy, righteousness, as being like the great mountains reaching to the clouds, etc.

2. To the end or final period of these everlastingMS: "lasting." hills, representing the durableness of the blessing. And I doubt not but the Spirit of God here has respect to the blessings of heaven, which is very often in the Old Testament represented by a mountain, an high mountain, and is called the mountain of the height of Israel, etc., and is in a most absolute sense an everlasting mountain.

3. The words may have respect to the extent of the possessions of Joseph. The distant mountains seemed to be the ends of the earth. The posterity of Joseph reigned over the bigger part of the land of Canaan, that hilly country; and that was terminated by hills: Mt. Carmel and other mountains by the sea, and Mt. Libanus on the north, and Mt. Shenir and Hermon, etc., on the east. But the Spirit of God has probably also a reference to the extent of the spiritual dominion God's people have in Christ Jesus, and as they sit together in heavenly places with him, and reign with him, in and through whom, and with whom, they possess all things, and reign over the nations. And the kingdom, and dominion, and the greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven shall be given into their hands; yea, all heaven, the hills of that celestial Canaan, even to their utmost bounds, shall be theirs.

Genesis 49:27. Exodus 2:10. "Because I drew him out of the water."] Moses' being preserved thus in the midst of great waters in an ark when a poor, little, helpless infant, and being saved out of the water, it typifies God's remarkable preservation of his church, or of Christ mystical, when in the midst of great affliction and surrounded with danger, and the church is small, and weak, and unable to defend or help themselves (as indeed man is at all times a helpless creature). And particularly it represents the preservation of the church of Israel in Egypt, and their redemption out of their affliction and danger there, where they were as it were in the midst of great waters continually ready to overwhelm them. But God bore them on eagles' wings [Exodus 19:4], and was as it were an ark to them to keep the waters from overwhelming them. God has promised his people that when they pass through the waters, they shall not overflow them [Isaiah 43:2]. This was a figure of much the same as the burning bush that was not consumed, and the preservation of Noah and his family in the ark in the time of the flood, and the children of Israel's passing safely through the Red Sea. It also was a figure of Christ's coming forth out of his state of humiliation and suffering, wherein he was as it were in the midst of great waters, to be received by the Gentile church, of which Pharaoh's daughter is the type. See note on Exodus 19:5. See also "Miscellanies," no. 1069, p. 2.In "Miscellanies," no. 1069, "Types of the Messiah." JE parallels the preservation of Moses, "a little helpless infant," with the deliverance of God's people in Egypt, who "were like an helpless infant," from "cruel, bloodthirsty enemies" (*Works, 11*, 195–96).

Exodus 2:11. "He went out unto his brethren," etc.] Moses, though he was brought up among the Egyptians in Pharaoh's court and as the son of Pharaoh's daughter, yet never became as a natural Egyptian. He did not forget his brethren. He chose not to be an Egyptian, but to be one of that people of whom he was by birth. All the pleasures and honors of Pharaoh's court, added to his being brought up among the Egyptians, did not win him over to that people to be willing to be one of them rather than one of Israel. See Hebrews 11:24.

Exodus 3:2–3. "And the angel of the Lord" (i.e. Christ, who is often so called) "appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. And he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. And Moses said," etc.] 1. This bush represents the human nature of Christ, whose name is the Branch. This bush well represents the human nature of Christ because it was the growth of the earth. Though Christ with regard to his divine nature be the Lord from heaven, yet with respect to his human nature he was the growth of the earth. He was of earthly descent, of the race of mortal mankind. And upon the account of its low and humble stature, it was a bush or bramble, as the wordסְנֶה in the original signifies. This well represented Christ's state of humiliation, and also his meekness and lowliness of heart. And also upon the account of its tenderness and liableness to be destroyed, what [is] more easily crushedMS: "Crush." or consumed than a bramble bush? This bush, upon each of these accounts, well represented what is spoken of Christ in the Isaiah 53:2. "He shall grow up before him as a tender plant, as a root out of a dry ground; he hath no form nor comeliness." This bush was "a root out of a dry ground" (See Hosea 13:5, Deuteronomy 8:15.), for it was a bush that grew on Mt. Horeb, as Exodus 3:1, which was so called from the remarkable dryness of the place, for the word "Horeb"חֹרֵב signifies dryness.

"And Moses said, I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." The great sight that Moses here said he would turn aside to see, and that he did turn aside to see as he said, as we have account in the next verse, was not that the bush was not burnt. For this Moses had seen already, which was the occasion of his earnestly desiring to know, and his turning aside to see, something further. But what the great sight he turned aside to see was why the bush was not burnt, or upon what account, or for what reason, as the wordמַדּוּעַ in the original signifies. Moses seems to have spoke these words after he had stood a while with astonishment, beholding the bush burn. And when he after a while perceived that bush, notwithstanding, was not burnt, he then concluded it must be some great and very extraordinary thing that must preserve the bush so in the midst of the flames. By the "sight" is meant the thing to be seen. It is as much as if he had said, I will turn aside, and see this great thing on the account of which the bush was not burnt. This great

<!-- p. 209 -->

thing was that God "dwelt in the bush," as Deuteronomy 33:16. 'Tis probable Moses was sensible that there was something divine in the case. He might probably see some token of divine glory there present, some extraordinary luster or effulgence that had an appearance of exceeding awful majesty, and also surpassing pleasantness and sweetness, like that which Peter describes, 2 Peter 1:16–17, speaking of what he saw in the mount of transfiguration, which Moses saw in the time that the bush was burning, and also saw to continue there after the flame was out, and concluded the bush's being preserved was by reason of that divine thing that he there beheld. This Moses seems to have respect to when he says, "I will turn aside, and see this great sight." This appearance was so divinely excellent and ravishing that it seems to have left an everlasting impression on Moses' mind, and probably made him the more earnestly desirous to see God's glory afterwards (Exodus 33:18). And he remembers it when he blesses Joseph (Deuteronomy 33:16). And Moses had now a mind to come nearer to behold this great, and sweet, and wonderful sight, the glory of God united to and dwelling in the bush. This great sight that Moses speaks of represents two things. 1. The incarnation of Christ, which was represented by God's dwelling in the bush. 2. The death and sufferings of Christ, which was represented by God's appearing and dwelling in the burning bush, or in the bush when all on fire. Which two things were the greatest sight that ever were seen by angels or men.This paragraph is a separate later entry which JE inserted at this point.

The Son of God, the second person of the Trinity, his appearing in this bush, is a type of his being manifest in the flesh. ChristMS: "God ‹X›." is said, Deuteronomy 33:16, to have "dwelt in the bush"; hereby was typified his dwelling in flesh. "As the bush burned with fire, and was not consumed," so Christ in the human nature suffered extremely. He endured the wrath of God, but was not overcome, perished not, was not consumed. He rose again from the dead, and did not see corruption. Though his human nature was but a bush, a tender plant, in itself easily capable of being consumed, and though the fire spent all its force upon it, yet because of the divinity that dwelt in it, it was impossible that it should be consumed. The power of God was made perfect in weakness. Satan could not prevail against Christ; though he cast him into the fire, yet he could not destroy him.

2. This bush represents the church, the mystical body of Christ. As it was with Christ, so it is with his church. It is a tender plant. 'Tis the branch

<!-- p. 210 -->

of the earth, and oftentimes is in the fire. But God will not suffer it to be consumed, but it always survives the flames. The gates of hell never prevail against it; her enemies are not suffered to swallow her up. God has promised that when she goes through the fire, she shall not be burnt; neither shall the flames kindle upon her [Isaiah 43:2].

But doubtless a special respect is herein had to the church, now in her suffering state in Egypt, which her enemies had labored to destroy, but were not able. The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied. God always carried them on eagles' wings out of their enemies' reach; and when they had well nigh swallowed them up at the Red Sea, God delivered them.

Tis probable that each of these three signs represents Christ's humiliation, and even this last. Christ is sometimes in Scripture compared to a river, and particularly a river of water in a dry place, upon which account the river Nilus did fitly represent Christ, it being a river that watered that dry land of Egypt, where it never rained, and which had no other watering but what it had from that river, which by reason of the great benefit they had by it was worshipped by the Egyptians as a god. Christ also, in coming to and communicating his benefits to sinful miserable men, is represented in Scripture as waters poured upon the dry ground. Here the water of this river, in being poured upon the dry ground, became blood, which represents Christ's being made sin for us (for blood is used in Scripture as a type of sinful pollution), and also his undergoing death for us, whereby he shed his blood, and it was poured out upon the earth as water. It was noted of that river that its fountain was not known; it was so far off it never could be discovered, and was therefore the fitter type of Christ, of whom it is said, "Who shall declare his generation?" [Isaiah 53:8], and that his "goings forth were of old, of everlasting" [Micah 5:2].

Exodus 8:28.] Pharaoh, in keeping the children of Israel, kept his sins, for his holding them in bondage was his great iniquity, about which the controversy between God and him was. God would have him part with this sin, but he refused. At last by convictions and fears, he is brought to be willing to let the children of Israel go, but not "Very far away, not so but that he might fetch 'em back again. Thus some sinners, who in a pang of conviction part with their sins, yet are loath they should go very far away, for when the fright is over, they'll return to them again. A mighty struggle here was between Pharaoh's convictions and his corruptions. His convictions said, Let them go; his corruptions said, Yet not very far away," not to be forever gone. "But he sided with his corruptions against his convictions, and it proved his ruin." Henry.Exposition, 1 (1725), 171.

Exodus 9:6.] In this plague also God executed judgments on the gods of Egypt, as in his turning the river Nilus into blood, for they worshipped their cattle. They were called "the abomination of the Egyptians," in the Exodus 8:26.

<!-- p. 218 -->

Exodus 9:10.] The children of Egypt had oppressed Israel in the furnaces in which they burnt their bricks, and now the ashes of these furnaces were made as much of a terror to them as ever they had been to the Israelites. These furnaces were a type of hell. God sends upon the wicked these plagues, that are some participation of the misery and destruction of hell, are as it [were] a sprinkling of the ashes of that furnace upon them. Their consciences are scalded with the hot embers of hell fire. These boils and blisters were exceeding grievous, probably attended with extreme smart, like the continual scalding of the hot embers of a furnace. Therefore 'tis said, "the magicians could not stand before" Exodus 9:11] this plague. This sort of boil is called "the botch of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 28:27).

Exodus 9:11.] Thus the magicians were driven [from] the field. Their power was restrained before (Exodus 8:18); but they continued to confront Moses, and confirm Pharaoh in his unbelief, till now at length, under the smart of God's rod, they were forced to retreat, and "could not stand before Moses," to which the Apostle refers, 2 Timothy 3:9, when he saith that "their folly was manifested unto all men."

Exodus 9:24. "Such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 351.

Exodus 10:21–23.] No. 388.*Works, 15*, 372–73. SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 356–57.

Exodus 10:23. "But all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings."] "Not only in the land of Goshen, where most of them dwelt, but in the particular dwellings, which in other places the Israelites had dispersed among the Egyptians, as it appears that they had by the distinction afterwards appointed to be on their doorposts. When God made this difference between the Israelites and the Egyptians, who would not have preferred the poorest cottage of an Israelite before the finest palace of an Egyptian?" Henry.*Exposition, I* (1725), 176.

Exodus 10:26.] "Note, the terms of reconciliation are so fixed, that though men dispute 'em never so long, they cannot possibly alter them, nor bring 'em lower. We must come up to the demands of God's will, for we cannot expect he should condescend to the provisos of our lusts. God's messengers must always be bound up by that rule, Jeremiah 15:19, 'Let them return

<!-- p. 219 -->

unto thee, but return not thou to them.' Moses gives a very good reason why they must take their cattle with them. They must do sacrifices, and therefore they must take wherewithal. What numbers and kinds of sacrifices would be required, they did not yet know, and therefore they must take all they had. Note, with ourselves and our children, we must devote all our worldly possessions to the service of God, because we know not what use God will make of what we have, nor in what way we may be called upon to honor God with it." Henry.Ibid.

Exodus 11:2–3.] With so high an hand did God bring out the children of Israel, that he did not only set 'em at liberty from their slavery to the Egyptians, but he also took care that they should be well paid by the Egyptians for their past service as they went off. So that after all the Egyptians' obstinacy in refusing to part with their future service, God at last made 'em in effect part with the benefit, both of their future service and past service too. See note on Exodus 12:36.This reference is a later addition.

Exodus 12:2. "This month," etc.]JE deleted "For the same reason that G." As God would have the children of Israel honor the month of their redemption by beginning their year with it, so would [he] have the spiritual Israel begin their week with the day of their redemption. See "Scripture," no. 471.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 563–64.

Exodus 12:3. "In the tenth day of this month."] The lamb was set apart four days before it was slain, which probably represents the four thousand years that Christ was promised to be our Redeemer and sacrifice, and his eternal designation to the office of a mediator revealed, and his beginning to act as a mediator, because he actually came into the world to die for sinners. Christ came to Jerusalem on the tenth day of this month. SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 359.

Exodus 12:5. "Without blemish."] SSS.Ibid.

Exodus 12:7.] See note on Exodus 12:22.

Exodus 12:8. "And with bitter herbs shall they eat it."] This is to teach us that when Christ is truly received and fed upon by faith, faith is accompanied

<!-- p. 220 -->

with repentance, and a sense of sin and godly sorrow for it. Faith and repentance go together, as the eating the paschal lamb was always with bitter herbs.

"And unleavened bread." 1 Corinthians 5:7 notes.This reference is a separate entry.

Exodus 12:10. "And that which remaineth."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 362–63.

Exodus 12:11. "And thus shall ye eat it," etc.] This is to teach us that, however we are saved freely through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ and by faith in him, yet that we are not hereby encouraged in sloth and idleness. But that all those that do truly receive Christ and exercise a right faith in him,JE deleted "their faith is accompanied with wor." they do it as it were with their loins girded, with their shoes on their feet, and their staff in their hand, in a disposition and preparation for activity, labor, and diligence in doing their duty and working the workJE deleted "and going the way." that God hath appointed them, and to be hastening away from the spiritual Egypt, from sin and the service of Satan, towards that Canaan that Christ, our Passover, has purchased for us.

They eat the Passover in haste to be gone out of Egypt. So he that truly receives Christ, he makes haste and delays not to keep God's commandments. He is willing immediately to forsake all sin. Love to no sin, love to the onions and leeks of Egypt, will not detain him; he immediately betakes himself to his duty.

Exodus 12:14.] The Jews anciently had a tradition that this day, even the fifteenth day of the month Nisan, Israel was to be redeemed by the Messiah. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 365.

"Throughout your generations, ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever." This and such like expressions may be explained by Romans 7:1. "Know ye not, brethren (for I speak to them that know the law), how that the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth?" The old testament church died in Christ when his body died, and the ordinances of that dispensation were nailed to his cross. See also notes on Matthew 24.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"By an ordinance forever." Such a phrase sometimes signifies no longer than till the year of jubilee. So Exodus 21:6. But if this phrase is limited by the year of jubilee, which came at the end of every fifty years, no

<!-- p. 221 -->

wonder that should be spoken of as what should be continued "forever," which was to last to the end of the ages of that dispensation till the coming of Christ, and the introduction of the glorious gospel day, the great thing typified by the jubilee.

There were some ordinances which were only for one particular time. So were several in this Exodus 12, such as eating the paschal lamb with their staff in their hand, etc. Exodus 12:11], andThis word is in a different hand, perhaps Grosart's. their sprinkling the blood on the doorposts Exodus 12:7], etc. Many ordinances were only occasional precepts to [be] observed on the occasion of God's appearance at Mt. Sinai, and the occasion of building the tabernacle, the occasion of setting apart the tribe of Levi and the family of Aaron, consecrating the tabernacle altar, etc., the occasion of the destruction of Korah and his company, the occasion of their being plagued with fiery serpents, the occasion of their passing through Jordan, the occasion of the siege of Jericho, etc. Some ordinances were in force only during their continuing in the wilderness, as the ordinances concerning their encampments and marches, their gathering and disposing of the manna, their bringing all the beasts they killed to eat to the door of the tabernacle, etc. It is in contradistinction to these that the ordinances that were to be continued throughout the ages of that dispensation, and of the Jewish state in Canaan, are called perpetual or everlasting statutes. And in this view, and as compared with those transitory and temporary statutes, they might well be so called.JE misidentified this paragraph and the preceding one, which form a separate entry, as "Genesis 12:14."

See SSS on Joshua 8:28.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 952.

Exodus 12:15.] Concerning the leaven as a type of sin, see "Scripture," no. 280,See *Works, 15*, 237. and "Papers on Original Sin," p. 86.These "Papers" are in JE's "'Controversies' Notebook." JE writes, "that LEAVEN is so much made use of in the law of Moses as a type of sin is an argument that sin is an evil nature derived from our parents. For leaven was some of the old lump united and incorporated with the new in the first kneading and making of it.… One lump communicates sourness and fermentation to another, as one generation communicates corruption to the next." See *Works, 15*, 237, n. 8, for further discussion of the parallels between sin and leaven. How the heathen mimicked these divine ceremonies, see SSS.For example, Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 360. "Unleavened bread." No. 280.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 237.

<!-- p. 222 -->

Exodus 12:16. "Seventh day."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 365–66.

Exodus 12:22.] The striking or sprinkling the blood of the lamb with a bunch of hyssop on the two side posts and lintel of the door signifies the cleansing of our conversation by the blood of Christ, which is in the language of Scripture called our "going out and coming in." 1 Samuel 29:6, "Surely, as the Lord liveth, thou hast been upright. And thy going out and thy coming in with me in the host is good in my sight, for I have not found evil in thee since the day of thy coming unto me unto this day." 2 Samuel 3:25, "Thou knowest Abner, the son of Ner, that he came to deceive thee, and to know thy going out and thy coming in, and to know all that thou dost." 2 Kings 19:27, "I know thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me" (and Isaiah 37:28). Psalms 121:8, "The Lord shall preserve thy coming in and going out."KJV: "thy going out and thy coming in." The Holy Spirit probably has respect to this very type of the going and coming, being cleansed by the blood of the paschal lamb, in 1 Peter 1:18–19, where the Apostle speaks of our being redeemed from our "vain *conversation*" by the "precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." The destroying angel passed by none but those who had the blood of the lamb on their door posts, signifying that when God comes to proceed with men as a judge, he will judge everyone according to his works, and will save none but those whose conversation has been cleansed by the blood of Christ (see Exodus 12:7).

Exodus 12:35. "Egyptians jewels."] No. 351.*Works, 15*, 336–38.

Exodus 12:35–36.] "The Hebrew wordשָׁאַל which our translators have rendered 'borrow' is *shaal*, which does not signify to 'borrow,' but to 'ask one to give.' It is the very word used, Psalms 2:8, *sheal-ve ettenah*,וְאֶתְּנָה שְׁאַל 'Ask of me, and I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance,' etc." Shuckford's *Connection*, vol. 2, p. 440.Shuckford, *Sacred and Prophane History* (2nd ed). The same word is used in Exodus 3:22 and Exodus 11:2. That "to ask to give," or "to beg," and not to "borrow," is the proper English of the word, according to the sense it is commonly used in Scripture, is abundantly evident by Buxtorf's *Lexicon*.*Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum*, 725–26. To lend is to give, in 1 Samuel 1:28.This sentence is a later addition.

<!-- p. 223 -->

'Tis probable that "when the Egyptians urged the people to be gone," they mentioned to them their poverty, and the difficulty of undertaking such a journey without such and such supplies, particularly that they should need many things to offer to God and serve him with. The Egyptians were not unacquainted with costliness in worship, and therefore would not think it strange that this great God that had wrought such wonders among them required a costly service. The Egyptians were now made sensible how much it concerned 'em to reconcile themselves to this God, and so to obtain the favor of this people, who were such peculiar favorites of his, and whom they had heretofore so greatly injured, and thereby so much provoked their God. Even Pharaoh himself now is brought to desire their prayers. The wills of the king and people were now broke, and their frame now was to be kind to 'em, as heretofore it had been to afflict and destroy 'em. They were now engaged with vehemence of spirit to counteract their former ill treatment of the people. They were brought as to [be] willing as it were, without hesitation or delay, to yield and resign up anything to save their lives, fearing they should very speedily be all destroyed. They were in a great terror and great commotion of mind, and like the sea, which after a very high and strong flood, when it comes to ebb, returns with the greater impetuosity. Mr. Henry observes the Egyptians by these gifts probably intended "to make atonement, that the plague might be stayed, as the Philistines, when they returned the ark, sent a present with it for a trespass offering, having an eye to this precedent." 1 Samuel 6:6, "Wherefore then do ye harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he had wrought wonderfully among them, did they not let the people go, and they departed?" taken with the context.*Exposition, 1* (1725), 180.

Exodus 12:38. "And a mixed multitude" (or "a great mixture," as it is in the original)רַב     וְגַם־עֵרֶב "went with them."] These mostly were not sincere proselytes, for they afterwards proved a snare to the children of Israel. See Numbers 11:4. In a time of God's doing some great work for his church, 'tis common that a great number of hypocrites are mixed with them.

Exodus 13:2. "Sanctify to me all the first-born, whatsoever openeth the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast; it is mine."] This we are not to understand as a command of anything that was to be done now immediately, that the first-born of the cattle should be immediately

<!-- p. 224 -->

sacrificed to God; nor indeed did God require that the first-born of cattle that were then in being should ever be sacrificed. This was only a precept that should take place with respect to the cattle after the people were settled in Canaan. See Exodus 13:11 and Exodus 13:12. This precept could not conveniently be attended either in Egypt or the wilderness. Nor were the first-born of men now to be either dedicated to the special service of God, or redeemed by the sacrifices of beasts. Nor does it seem to be the intent of the precept that all that were now in being, that had already opened the matrix, should be the Lord's, but all that should be born and open the womb from this time forward throughout their generations should be his. See notes on Numbers 3:39 and Numbers 3:43.

Exodus 13:9. "A sign unto thee upon thine hand."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 373–74.

Exodus 13:18. "Harnessed."] See the same wordחֲמֻשִׁים in the original, in Joshua 1:14.

Exodus 13:19.] Acts 7:16 notes.

Exodus 13:21.] Concerning the pillar of cloud and fire, see no. 463.*Works, 15*, 553.

"And by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light to go by, day and night." Here in the camp of Israel was something of a resemblance and image of what is said of New Jerusalem. Revelation 21:23, "The glory of the Lord did lighten," for here the Shekinah, which was commonly called "the glory of the Lord," gave them light. And in the Revelation 21:25, "There shall be no night there," the light of which was said of Zion, Isaiah 60:20, and of the church in her glorious state (Zechariah 14:6–7). Here is some resemblance, for the camp of Israel had always light, both day and night; nor was it a dim light that they had in the night, but a light sufficiently clear, well to direct that vast multitude in traveling in the wilderness, so thatJE deleted "it was a kind of daylight." night was in a great degree turned into day amongst them. See Numbers 9:21; Deuteronomy 1:33; Nehemiah 9:12, Nehemiah 9:19; Psalms 78:14, and Psalms 105:39.This paragraph is a separate entry.

The congregation of Israel in all their travel were in the form of an army. They went up "by their armies" (Exodus 12:51). And "they went up harnessed," as Exodus 12:18 of this chapter. They were in military order in their camp and in their marches; and the pillar of cloud and fire was their

<!-- p. 225 -->

grand ensign, lifted up in the view of the whole army, as the ensign which they should follow, and the standard by which they should abide. And as this pillar of cloud and fire was the symbol of the presence of Christ, so here was represented that which is spoken in Isaiah 11:10. "And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek. And his rest shall be glorious." As here this ensign, the pillar of cloud and fire, was to lead the people to their rest, so Isaiah 11:12, "And he shall set up an ensign for the nations."This paragraph is a later addition.

Exodus 14:5. "And it was told the king of Egypt that the people fled."] The people, till they turned towards Pihahiroth, went straight forward toward the wilderness, the way that they had asked to go. But now Pharaoh heard that they fled, i.e. that they departed from their course that they all along pretended they would go, and that he had given them leave to go, which made Pharaoh to suspect them of some other design in desiring to be let go from what they pretended, and that they dealt fallaciously with him.

Exodus 14:20. "And it was a cloud and darkness to them, but it gave light by night to these."] In like manner as the gospel and the discoveries God makes of himself in and by Christ are a mere "cloud and darkness," and foolishness, "a stone of stumbling and rock of offense" [1 Peter 2:8], a snare and gin [Psalms 140:5], a "savor of death unto death" [2 Corinthians 2:16] unto some, while it is a most glorious light, the power of God, and wisdom of God, a savor of life unto life unto others.

Exodus 14:22.] The children of Israel's passing through the midst of the sea without the waters overflowing them was a remarkable figure of God's preserving his church when in the most imminent danger, when troubles and enemies are ready to swallow them up. Of which there was at this time also a remarkable instance of delivering them from their enemies, the Egyptians that pursued them, that they seemed to be in immediate danger of their being swallowed up by, when they were just behind them and the wilderness had shut them in. So that here was a remarkable type and a remarkable instance together of the same thing, as the people had been a wonderful instance of it before in Egypt.

Exodus 14:24–25.] See notes on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210, *Corol*. 2.*Works, 15*, 139–40.

<!-- p. 226 -->

Exodus 14:27.] Traditions among the heathen concerning this miracle, see SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 381.

Exodus 14:28.] Pharaoh, who cruelly endeavored the murder of all the males of the children of Israel by drowning, is now himself at last drowned.

Exodus 14:30. "Dead upon the seashore."] "The Egyptians were very nice and curious in embalming and preserving the bodies of their great men" (and creating stately sepulchers and monuments for them), "but here the utmost contempt is poured upon all the grandees of Egypt. See how they lie heaps upon heaps, as dung upon the face of the earth. The beasts and birds of prey are called to eat the flesh of captains and mighty men. Isaiah 66:24, 'They shall go forth, and look on the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me.' Probably the Israelites stripped the slain, and now got arms from them."Henry, *Exposition, I* (1725), 187.

Exodus 15:20.] Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, joining with and following Moses in this song, makes the affair a more lively representation of the communion of the church in the joy and triumph of Christ, and joining with him, and being led by him in eternal songs of praise to God. See Revelation 15:2–3 and Revelation 19:5–6.

Exodus 15:23. "For they were bitter."] "The best heathen writers agree, that there were lakes of bitter waters, in the parts where the Israelites were now traveling. DiodorusDiodorus, Greek historian, 1st century B.C.E. informs us, that there were such waters at some little distance from the city of Arsinoe, Strabo says the same thing, and PlinyPliny the Elder (23–79 C.E.), Roman naturalist and author. carries on Trajan's river from the Nile to the bitter fountains; and these bitter fountains and the bitter lakes mentioned by Strabo and Diodorus, and the bitter waters which the Israelites found at Marah, may easily be conceived to be the same." Shuckford's *Connection*, vol. 3, p. 4, second edition. Strabo says these lakes "were in ancient days bitter, until by a communication of the river, the later inhabitants of the country found out a way to meliorate the taste of them." Ibid., p. 6.*Sacred and Prophane History, 3* (1740).

Exodus 15:25. "There he made them a statute and an ordinance."] I.e. there he made an establishment, came to settled terms with them, upon which

<!-- p. 227 -->

they were to obtain those blessings which he had promised their fathers and them, and should escape the judgments of Egypt, which they had deserved as well as the Egyptians, inasmuch as they had served the gods of Egypt and conformed to their corrupt practices, and now manifested a like corrupt and hard heart. The signification of the word *choİk*,חֹק translated "statute," very well agrees with this interpretation.

See Joshua 24:24. "There he proved them." I.e. there he put them upon their trial. He revealed to them a settled [covenant] with what was to be the proper proof and evidence, whether they were proper and fit persons to have the blessings of Canaan and other blessings promised to their fathers bestowed upon them, or no. See Exodus 20:20. God also proved them by this miracle, whether they would walk in his law, or no, as this was a further evidence of God's worthiness to be obeyed and trusted. "He proved them," whether their hearts were such as might by any means be indued to trust entirely in God, and wholly to follow him, and yield subjection unto him. See the next chapter, Exodus 16:4.This paragraph is a later addition.

Exodus 15:25–26.] See no. 130.*Works, 15*, 87.

Exodus 15:27.] See no. 172.Ibid., 100–101. Here they had fountains to drink at, and palm trees to rest under. As they were for shade, they represented the ministers of the church. And in the number seventy, respect seems to be had to the seventy elders of the congregation. They also represent Christ as giving rest and spiritual refreshment by his ministers.

These twelve fountains and seventy palm trees don't only represent the twelve patriarchs and seventy elders, but the twelve apostles and seventy disciples or elders of the Christian church.

Exodus 16:4. "That I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no."] Though hitherto they had showed themselves perverse, notwithstanding the great things God had done for them, yet he will try them further by doing more for them, to prove whether they by any means may be induced to obey him, or not. See note on Exodus 15:25 and Exodus 20:20.

Exodus 16:5.] By this verse and also the twenty-second and twenty-third, it is evident that the time when the manna first appeared was on the morning

<!-- p. 228 -->

of the first day of the week, the time when Christ arose from the dead, and the day when the Holy Ghost descended on the day of Pentecost, making application of Christ as the food of the soul, and also the day when Christ was born, as Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology* shows to be exceeding probable.*Scripture Chronology*, 449–50.

Exodus 16:10. "The glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud."] The Shekinah that now appeared, and that appeared afterwards in the tabernacle and temple, was called the "glory of the Lord," not only because of that outward brightness that appeared, but especially because that brightness was the symbol of the Son of God as there manifesting himself, who is the brightness of God's glory. The glory of God is spoken of as a person in Isaiah 3:8. See note on Revelation 21:23.

Exodus 16:16–19.] "The Israelites were ordered, every head of a family, to gather as many omers of the manna every morning as he had persons in his family. But as they went out to gather without taking measures with them, it so happened that some gathered more than their quantity, and some less; but they corrected this before they carried their gatherings home, for they measured what they gathered with an omer, and he that had gathered more than his quantity gave to him that had gathered less, so that everyone had his just quantity made up, and no more. The words of the Exodus 16:18, as our English version renders them, seem to imply that God was here pleased miraculously to adjust the several quantities that were gathered. But the words of Moses, if rightly translated, express the fact to have been very different. The wordהֶעְרִּיף לאֹ which we translate "had nothing over," should be rendered, "he made to have nothing over"; and in like manner, the wordהֶחְסִיר לאֹ translated "had no lack," should be translated, "he caused to have no lack." And Moses was the person that thus ordered it.

And the Exodus 16:17–19 should be word for word thus translated.

Exodus 16:17.וְהַמַּמְעִיט הֵמַּרְבֶּה וַיִּלְקְטוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּנֵי וַיַּעֲשׂוּ־כֵן "And the children of Israel did so, and gathered some more, some less."

Exodus 16:18.לָקָטוּ לְפִי־אָכְלו אִישׁ הֶחְסִיר לאֹ וְהַמַּמְעִיט הַמַּרְבֶּה הֶעְדִּיף וְלאֹ בָעֹמֶר וַיָּמֹדּוּ "And they measured with an omer; and Moses caused him that

<!-- p. 229 -->

had more not to abound, and him that had less not to fall short (for they gathered each one according to his eating)." Exodus 16:19.עַד־בֹּקֶר מִמֶּנּוּ אַל־יוֹתֵר אִישׁ אֲלֵהֶם מֹשֶׁה וַיּאֹמֶר "And said, Let no man leave of it till the morning." In the Hebrew, "Moses," the nominative case to the three verses, is put after the last, a construction very common in the ancient languages. So that the fact here was that Moses directed them to give to one another: they that had more than their measure, to make up what was wanting to them that had less, that all might have their full quantity, and no more. The words, "they gathered everyone according to his eating," are a remark by way of parenthesis, to give a reason for what Moses directed. He caused them that had overmuch to give to them that had less than they were to have, because they gathered, as we say, "from hand to mouth"; and it would have been of no service to have laid up what they had to spare." Shuckford's *Connection*, vol. 3, pp. 10–12.

But yet there seems to be so much of a special and wonderful providence in ordering this affair, "that the different quantities of manna were gathered by different persons, yet so much in the whole was always gathered, that on an average there was an omer for each," as Dr. Doddridge observes in note on 2 Corinthians 8:15.This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 4*, 489, n. f.

Exodus 16:19–20.] See no. 59.*Works, 15*, 66–67. See Mather on the *Types*, pp. 140–41.This reference is a later addition. Samuel Mather drew instruction from the manna that bred worms when kept overnight. The worms he viewed as judgment on the Israelites' unbelief, as a lesson that they must "depend upon a daily Providence for daily Bread," and as counsel to be content with present supplies. He also applied this type to Christ, who is the Manna upon which Christians must feed daily, "or else the sweetest Manna will become as rottenness" (*Figures or Types of the Old Testament* [2nd ed.]).

Exodus 16:25–27.] There was no manna to be found on the seventh day, which probably might have respect to Christ (the antitype of the manna), his lying dead on that day.

Exodus 16:33. "Manna therein."] Note on Revelation 2:17, no. 262.*Works, 15*, 208–9.

Exodus 17:6. "And thou shalt smite the rock."] The rock was smitten in order to afford water; so Christ was smitten and suffered in order to afford us his blood, and Holy Spirit, and spiritual supplies. What we have an account

<!-- p. 230 -->

of in this verse is also typical of what is prophesied of in Isaiah 35:6–7, and Isaiah 41:18, and Isaiah 43:19–20, and is also typical of "rivers of living water" flowing out of the heart when it is smitten and broken, which Christ expresses, John 7:38–39. By "rivers of living water" flowing out of the "belly," meaning the heart, see notes on Deuteronomy 32:13. As the rock here represents Christ, the rod of God with which the rock was smitten represents the rod of God's anger. As the rock represents the heart, Moses' rod signifies the word of God, which is called "the rod of God's mouth" (Isaiah 11:4), and is the rod with which God smites and breaks the rocky heart, which is said to be as a fire and "hammer that breaks the rock in pieces" [Jeremiah 23:29].

This water's descending out of Horeb, the mount where God dwelt, signified the same thing as Ezekiel's waters issuing out of the temple (Ezekiel 47:1), and the "river of water of life," in Revelation 22:1, proceeding "out of the throne of God and the Lamb."This and the following paragraph are a later addition.

The rod signifies the word of God; and Moses' rod especially signifies the word of God by Moses, and the law was especially so. The law was given by Moses. Christ, the rock of our salvation, was smitten by the law. He suffered for us the curse of the law; and by this means he shed his blood, and affords us the water of life. The Apostle says this "Rock was Christ" [1 Corinthians 10:4].

"Smite the rock." Dr. Clayton, Bishop of Clogher in Ireland, in his *Vindication of the Histories of the Old and New Testament*,Robert Clayton (1695–1758), author of *A Vindication of the Histories of the Old and New Testament. In Answer to the Objections of the late Lord Bolingbroke. In Two Letters to a Young Nobleman* (Dublin, 1752). in answer to Lord BolingbrokeMS: "Bolinbroke." Henry St. John, Lord Viscount Bolingbroke (1678–1751), in *Letters on the Study and Use of History* (2 vols. This rock, the Apostle tells us, was Christ [1 Corinthians 10:4]. It yielded its refreshing abundant waters by being smitten by the rod of Moses, aptly signifying that we receive the Holy Spirit and all spiritual blessings from Christ through his being smitten by the curse of the law. The law is fitly represented as the rod of Moses, for the law was given by Moses.This paragraph is a later addition.

Exodus 17:8–13.] Presently, after the children of Israel had their songs of deliverance and joy at the Red Sea, they had a great conflict with an enemy that came out against them. So it commonly is with Christians after their first comfort, and other times after times of great spiritual deliverance and rejoicing.

Exodus 17:9. "I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand."] See "Scripture," no. 473.*Works, 15*, 569–71.

Exodus 17:14. "I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven."] For the fulfillment of this, see 1 Samuel 14, and 1 Samuel 27:8, and 1 Samuel 30; 1 Chronicles 4:43; Esther 9:1–10.

Exodus 17:15. "Jehovah Nissi."] See no. 205.Ibid., 128–29.

Exodus 18:2–5.] What is here related, if that clause in the Exodus 18:2, "after he had sent her back," had not been inserted, would have been much such a difficulty as there are in some other parts of the Scripture history through the brevity of the relation. We have an account that Moses, when he went from Jethro into Egypt, took his wife and his children with him. And yet here we have an account of Jethro's bringing of them to him in the wilderness from his own home, as if Moses had not taken them with him when he went away. We should have been ready to suspect that this was a blunder in the historian, had it [not] been here hinted that Moses had at some time sent her back, for we have no account of her sent back anywhere else.

We may here observe the remarkable self-denial Moses subjected himself to, whereby he was fitted for those privileges he afterwards received of God and which was rewarded by those privileges. First, he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. He renounced the wealth, and

<!-- p. 232 -->

glory, and pleasures of the kingdom of Egypt that he might have had as the heir of Pharaoh's crown, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God. All this he forsook for a share with God's people. And then he met with another great trial. He was banished even from them whose company he preferred to all the glory of Egypt. Yet he must not enjoy that, but was driven away alone into the wilderness, wandering in a poor, disconsolate, desolate condition he knew not whither. And now, after he had dwelt forty years in the land of Midian in the family of Jethro, into which he had married, and had a family and a place of rest there, then he was called on God's errand to forsake his wife and children without ever expecting to see them any more, and once more to leave all that he had to follow Christ.This and the following paragraph are a later addition.

*Corol*. Hence we may learn that ministers, in order to fit them for the service of Christ, should be brought to be willing to be cast off even by their own people, by saints, by those to whose good especially they are ministers, as Moses was cast off by his brethren the Israelites.

Exodus 18:12.] This that Jethro did was in pursuance of his office, for he was a priest, and in all probability, a priest of the true God in the land of Midian, as Melchizedek was in Canaan.

Exodus 19-20.] See note on Psalms 68:8–9, being no. 210.*Works, 15*, 135–40.

As there was a trumpet at the giving of the law [Exodus 19:16], so a great trumpet will sound when the law comes to be executed at the day of judgment. Then Mt. Sinai was in a conflagration; but at the day of judgment, the whole earth will be in a conflagration, and the other appearances will be proportionably greater, the trumpet louder, the appearing majesty of God greater, the fire more terrible, the thunders and lightnings more dreadful. How miserable then will those be that then shall feel the almighty vengeance of that [one] whose wrath will be proportionable to those appearances of his dreadfulness.This paragraph is a later addition.

Exodus 19:3. "And Moses went up unto God."] Probably he went up to the place where God had appeared to him before, expecting there to meet with him. And there God spake to him out of the same bush, and so from time to time. And therefore God is said to have "dwelt in the bush" (Deuteronomy 33:16).

<!-- p. 233 -->

Exodus 19:4. "On eagles' wings."] Far out of the reach of all danger, an eagle is very lofty in his flight. See how God did thus towards the children of Israel, in sermon on the verse.JE's sermon on Exodus 19:4, preached Aug. 1731–Dec. 1732, with the doctrine, "God carries his people along through the world towards glory far above the reach of all their enemies, or anything that might hinder their blessedness" (MS, p. 5). See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 397. This is a later addition.

Unto myself." See note on Deuteronomy 33:2.This reference is a separate entry.

Exodus 19:10–11. "Sanctify them today and tomorrow;… and be ready against the third day, for the third day the Lord will come down," etc.] The third day here spoken of, or the day in which God came down on Mt. Sinai, was the first day of the week, as is evident because the feast of Pentecost, which was appointed in commemoration of this, was appointed to be always on the first day of the week, as appears by Leviticus 23:15 ff. So that the days whereon the Jews were to sanctify themselves in order to this day were the sixth and seventh days of the week, but chiefly the seventh, for there was only a part of the sixth remaining when God gave the order, and probably but a little part, considering the antecedent transactions of the day which we have here account of. So that the Jewish sabbath was to be spent in preparing themselves for the day following, viz. the first day of the week, the day on which God descended and gave the law on Mt. Sinai, in honor to this day being the day on which Christ was to rise from the dead, and in which God would descend more gloriously on his apostles to reveal the glorious gospel. Thus this day is by God's own direction set above the day of their sabbath. The day of the Christian [sabbath] is honored above the Jewish sabbath by God's appointing the Jewish sabbath to be a day of preparation for it, as the Jewish dispensation was a preparation for the Christian. The law is an handmaid to the gospel, and is "our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ" [Galatians 3:24].

Exodus 19:15. "Come not at your wives."] See, concerning customs of the heathen agreeable to this, SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 398–99.

Exodus 19:18. "And Mount Sinai."] Called סִינַי, from סְנֶה, a "bush," for it was there that God appeared unto Moses in the bush, which burned with fire and was not consumed. See Buxtorf.The name "Sinai" derives from the Hebrew סְנֶה, which implies all shades of red and is the term for the blackberry bush or the bramble bush (*Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum*, 486).

<!-- p. 234 -->

Exodus 20:3–7.] The three first commandments. The First Commandment respects the object of worship, and does especially forbid those things in worship that are against *God the Father*. The Second Commandment respects the means of worship, and especially forbids those things in worship that are against *God the Son*, that it should not [be] by other lords and mediators instead of Christ, the Lord our God, who is as it were the husband of his people, and is a jealous God, a jealous husband, that will not bear spiritual adultery. This commandHere a "t" has been interlined at the end of the word, perhaps by Grosart, making "commandment." forbids our making use of other images in our worshipping God besides Christ, "who is the image of the invisible God" [Colossians 1:15], "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" [Hebrews 1:3], by which image alone God makes known himself, and sets forth himself, and shows his glory, as the fit object of our worship, for we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" [2 Corinthians 4:6]. The heathen had images that they might have something present with them as representatives of the deity that was absent; but Christ only is our Immanuel, or "God with us." The Third CommandHere again a "t" has been interlined. forbids those things in worship that are especially against *the Holy Ghost*, even the unholy manner of worship. We ought, when we come to God to worship him, to come by the Son, that we may come by right means; and we ought to come by the Holy Spirit, that we may worship with a right spirit and in an holy manner. These sins against the Holy Spirit are represented as peculiarly exposing persons to divine vengeance without forgiveness, agreeable to what we are taught in the New Testament.

Exodus 20:4. "Any likeness of anything that is in heaven above."] I.e. the likeness of sun, moon, or stars, or any bird. "Or that [is] in the earth beneath." I.e. of any man, woman, beast, or creeping thing. "Or that is in the waters under the earth." I.e. any fish. This interpretation is evident from Deuteronomy 4:16–18.

That the Second Commandment has respect to worshipping the true God by images. See note on Deuteronomy 5:7–8.

Exodus 20:5.] That which is said in this verse is not only annexed to the Second Commandment, but has respect to both the preceding commands, and is added to confirm and enforce both.

<!-- p. 235 -->

Exodus 20:8. "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."] This expression, "Remember the sabbath," probably was the rather used because this was not the first institution of the sabbath. It had been too much forgotten, especially while the children of Israel were in Egypt. The sabbath had also been renewedly commanded (Exodus 16). God here charges them to take notice of his institution of the sabbath, and not to forget it, as they formerly had done.

Exodus 20:12. "That thy days may be long," etc.] There is a peculiar suitableness between the command and the enforcement annexed to it. If we honor our parents by whom we came into the world, that is the way to be continued in the world. If we don't honor them who were the second causes of our lives and beings in the world, God will take away our lives that he gave us by them; and our beings that we had from them shall not be continued.

Exodus 20:20. "Fear not, for God is come to prove you."] There was such a terror in the voice that, together with the awful appearances that attended it, gave them such apprehensions of the mighty power of God, and dread-fulness of his majesty, his holiness, and vengeance, which together with a sense of their own guilt made them tremble with apprehensions that God would break forth upon them, and terribly destroy them. Something thus, sometimes persons are ready to be afraid in a time of thunder and lightning. Moses bids them not be afraid, and tells them that God is not come to destroy them, but only to prove them.JE deleted "designing to give them opportunity after this to see whether they would obey before and and to see whether they would obey God or no and to see wait upon them before he destroyed them." This shows that they need not fear being destroyed now, for if God is come to prove them, that implies that he will wait upon them, and that he'll give them time of trial. God came to prove them.

1. As his giving the law, as we have account in the preceding part of the chapter, was to prove them. One principal end of giving the law to fallen man is to prove him, to know what is in his heart, to make it appear whether he will obey God or not, to manifest man, to make his wickedness appear to himself and others. Sin is known by the law. This makes man appear exceeding sinful, and we are hereby shut up to the faith that should afterwards be revealed.

2. They were proved by the awful manner in which the law was given by the manifestations of God's awful majesty, etc., that attended the giving

<!-- p. 236 -->

the law. Persons are proved, or tried, or discovered by incitements to obedience as well as by temptations to disobedience. See Exodus 16:4 and Exodus 15:25 note.This reference is a later addition. If persons have very great incitements to obedience, and it don't influence them to it, this tries them, and shows how great their wickedness, how exceeding their hardness and confirmedness in sin. After the same manner, as when they have great temptations to disobedience, that tries them; and if they resist and overcome them, it shows the sincerity and strength of their grace.

3. Particular commands and duties required are the proper proof of a spirit of submission to God's authority, and a spirit to cleave to God, which was the grand condition of their entering into Canaan. The people might profess this, and appear forward in it, before they knew what God's will was; but when this is particularly revealed, then is the trial. See Exodus 15:25 note.This and the following paragraph are a later addition.

It is our duty to have an heart to devote ourselves absolutely to God, to obey his commands whatever they shall be, to comply with whatever God shall please to prescribe before we know what that shall be, as it were to give God a blank that he may write what he pleases, and with such a disposition and determination of mind to say, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? This is the true spirit of obedience. This was what God required; and this was what the people hadMS: "had been." solemnly proposed to them, and which the people had solemnly promised and appeared very forward [in] it (Exodus 19:3–8). Now is the trial, when the particular commands are given. The man that said to Christ, "Lord, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest" [Luke 9:57], made a forward profession of friendship to Christ. But the trial was when Christ came to tell him particularly what it would be to follow him. "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head" [Luke 9:58].

Exodus 20:24–26.] See "Scripture," no. 474.*Works, 15*, 571.

Exodus 20:25.] Their being forbidden to lift up their tool on the stones of the altar seems to signify to us these two things, viz. 1. That we must not add anything of our own works to Christ, because Christ is sufficient alone without our righteousness. If we go to add our works to make up his deficiencies,

<!-- p. 237 -->

instead of making the altar or the foundation of our acceptance with God better, we shall utterly spoil it. We must depend on Christ as he is, notwithstanding his seeming homeliness.Conjecture for unclear word. 2. We must not add anything of our own works or inventions to polish the worship of God. We must attend as God hath made and appointed in its simplicity. If we add anything of our own to polish and adorn it, we pollute it.

The altar was that which sanctified the gift, and added worth or merit to the sacrifice. We must not add our works to that by which acceptance is merited, must not join our works to Christ to make the merit greater or better in order to the acceptance of the offering. Hewn stone seem to be used as a type of our own righteousness in Isaiah 9:10.This paragraph is a later addition.

Exodus 23:20–23.]. See no. 63.*Works, 15*, 68. God says of this angel, "My name is in him" Exodus 23:21]. God had a little before, from this same Mt. Sinai, declared to Moses with very great solemnity, that he might thereby make him known to the children of Israel (who were become very ignorant of him) what his name was, viz. I AM THAT I AM and JEHOVAH. Exodus 3:13–14, "And Moses said unto God, Behold, when I come unto the children of Israel, and shall say unto them, The God of your fathers hath sent me unto you, and they shall say unto me, What is his name? what shall I say unto them? And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM. And he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you." And again Exodus 6:2–3, "And God spake unto Moses, and said unto him, I am JEHOVAH. And I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac and unto Jacob, by the name of God Almighty, but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known unto them." And again very lately, after the children [of Israel] were come to that Mt. Sinai, where God revealed himself to Moses, and told him his name to declare it to the children [of Israel], and the people heard God speak from thence himself in a most solemn and awful manner, with a great voice declaring the same name (Exodus 20:2), "I am JEHOVAH, thy God," etc., which were the first words of God that they heard from Mt. Sinai, when he spake to 'em from thence, when the mountain burnt with fire, etc. This was at most but a few days before God said this that he does concerning his angel, and perhaps it was the same day. So that when he says,

<!-- p. 239 -->

"My name is in him," they could naturally understand no other than that name that he had lately revealed himself by, which was in an eminent manner his name, even I AM THAT I AM, or JEHOVAH, which being in an eminent manner God's name, above all other names expressing his nature. And it having been a common thing in those days from the beginning of the world to give names to express the nature of things, they naturally must understand it that God's nature was in him, and that so his name "Jehovah" belonged to him. They must naturally understand it, that the thing expressed by that name was in him, and that the children of Israel must understand it is also confirmed by this, that [he] here commits the care of the congregation to this his angel, that he might go before them as their captain, and lead 'em, and bring 'em into the land of Canaan, and fight against them, and possess them of their land. And therefore when this angel appeared to Joshua with a "sword drawn in his hand" (Joshua 5:13), and told him that as the captain of the Lord's host he was come, Joshua seems to understand him to be this angel, and therefore immediately falls on his face. And the angel teaches Joshua to pay him divine respect by taking off his shoe, because the ground was holy Joshua 5:15], as Moses was commanded when Jehovah appeared to him at the bush, and he obeyed. And afterwards in the process of the story this angel is called Jehovah, as in the Exodus 6:2, by the penman of the history.

What is said of the Messiah, Micah 5:4, is parallel with this. "And he shall stand and feed in the strength of JEHOVAH, in the majesty of the name of JEHOVAH his God. "Proverbs 21:24, " Proud and haughty scorner"shall men call him that" dealeth in proud wrath. That is, that is his true nature and character. The saying, "My name is in him," evidently implies as much as that "My divine essence and character is in him."

By God's name is plainly meant his internal name and essence in Proverbs 30:4. "What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?" Why should it be there represented that none can tell what God's name is, when God had so plainly and expressly declared it to Moses, and told him that his name was "Jehovah," and "I am that I am"? Therefore the meaning must be that none could comprehend that infinitely perfect nature signified by that name. None by searching can find out the nature of God. 'Tis high as heaven. What can we do? Deeper than hell. What can we know?
