Exodus 25.] The sacreds of Apollo from among the heathen seem to be derived from those of the true God in the TABERNACLE and TEMPLE. He was called *Ie* and *Ion* in imitation of God's name *Jah*. "As God had his tabernacle, so Apollo had his cortineI.e. curtain. exactly answering thereto. As God had in the tabernacle his ark overlaid with gold, and on his ark a propitiatory seat from whence he gave forth his oracles, so Apollo in his cortine had his *tripos* overlaid with gold, and above that a certain seat called ὅλμον, on which his Pythian she-priest, or prophetess, sat and gave forth oracles from Apollo. Apollo is said to learn his art of divination from Pan, the god of shepherds." (Which Pan is the great God of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians called shepherds, because in so being they were distinguished greatly from the Egyptians. This God revealed himself to Israel in Egypt as he whose name is I AM, "He that is, and there is none else," the Great All or τὸ πάν, as some of the Grecian philosophers called him. And from the Egyptians the Greeks had many of their fables of the gods.) "God had his sacred fire always burning on his altar (Leviticus 6:12–13). So Apollo had his πῦρ ἄσβεσον, which they called Εσία, as 'tis supposed from יה אש, 'the fire of Jah.'" The ark was compassed about with a crown; so was Apollo's *tripos*, as Scholiast, in *Aristoph. Phuto*. So Apollo

<!-- p. 241 -->

was praised with singing *Eleleu Ie*, in imitation of the manner in which God was praised in the tabernacle and temple by singing Hallelujah. (See note on Psalms 106:1.)Gale, *Court of the Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 4, p. 39, 43; Pt. 1, Bk. 3, ch. 1, p. 13.

Exodus 25:10. "An ark of shittim wood."] No. 285.*Works, 15*, 242–46.

Of the ARK. A man's ark, or chest, or cabinet is one of the utensils of his house; and it is there wherein he keeps his treasures, his money, his jewels, and precious things. So God's ark is one of the utensils of his house, typifying that wherein he kept his treasure, his jewels, his precious things, and that which he had laid apart for himself as his portion, that he will keep in the secret of his presence; and this is Christ and his people. Both are typified by the things contained in the ark, viz. the law, or covenant written in tables of stone, representing Christ, the *Word* of God, and also the law written in the hearts of his people. The manna represents Christ, who is God's and men's food, and believers, who are God's food, his first fruits; and the rod that budded represents both also.This paragraph is a separate entry.

See SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 445.

Exodus 25:16. "The testimony which I shall give thee."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 446.

Exodus 25:23–40.] Concerning the showbread table and the candlestick, see no. 475.*Works, 15*, 571–75.

Exodus 25:33.] Concerning the candlestick, and its knops, and flowers, and bowls "like unto almonds." In the candlestick, fruit and flowers are intermixed, as in Aaron's rod were buds, flowers, and almonds. See Numbers 17:8.

Exodus 26:14. "A covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red."] We may suppose that these are skins of rams offered in sacrifice, and this covering to the tabernacle a type of the church. Of the skins of the sacrifices seems to signify the same thing as the skins that God clothed Adam and Eve with, which are also supposed to be skins of sacrifices, which signified the righteousness of Christ, the great sacrifice. These skins were to be

<!-- p. 242 -->

dyed red to denote that Christ's righteousness was wrought out through the pains of death, under which he, in obedience to God, yielded up his life and shed his precious blood. The skin is put for the life, as it is in Job. "Skin for skin, and all that a man has will he give for his life" [Job 2:4]. Our covering of the righteousness of Christ is obtained by laying down his life. He could give us that righteousness no otherwise than by giving us his own life, and as it were giving us his own skin for our covering. See Genesis 3:21.

"And a covering above of badgers' skins." The tabernacle had a rough hairy coat without, an homely covering, but was glorious within. So is the church, and so was Christ in his state of humiliation.

Exodus 32:1–2 ff.] As the travel of the children of Israel from Egypt through the wilderness towards Canaan represents the travel of a visible Christian in seeking salvation, so this golden calf that the children of Israel made to bring 'em to Canaan seems to represent men's own righteousness. The children of Israel made an idol of the work of their own hands and trusted in it, as sinners idolize and trust in their own works. Sinners take their own good qualifications and good works, the supposed ornaments of their souls, and make a god of them, as the children of Israel took their golden earrings and ornaments, and made the golden calf, and set it up for their god, and worshipped it, and trusted in it instead of the God of Israel. Men's own righteousness is a god of their own forming, as the golden calf was, as in the Exodus 32:4; he "fashioned it with a graving tool." They pay that honor to it that is due alone to Jesus Christ. They ascribe to their own righteousness the glory of redemption, as the children of Israel ascribed the glory of their redemption out of Egypt to the golden calf. They said, "These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt" Exodus 32:8]. Sinners trust in their own righteousness to carry them to heaven, as the children of Israel trusted in the golden calf to bring them into Canaan. That was their end in making of it, that they might have a god to go before them to bring them to Canaan, as in the Exodus 32:1. "Up, make us gods, that may go before us." Aaron their priest made it. Sinners, in trusting to their own righteousness, act as being their own priests. Men's own righteousness looks very splendidly in their own eyes, and of great price and value, as the calf of the children of Israel was made of gold. It looked like a god in their eyes, but, indeed,

<!-- p. 244 -->

it was a dumb beast, and that a beast without life. See Hosea 14:3, compared with Hosea 5:13 and Hosea 12:1.This sentence is a later addition.

It was in the camp of Israel, while Moses tarried long in the mount, as it is in the church of God, while Christ delays his coming and stays long in heaven before he returns. Both wise virgins and foolish slumber and sleep; and many say, Where is the promise of his coming? And many a wicked servant encourages and emboldens himself in wickedness, saying, My Lord delayeth his coming.This sentence is a later addition.

Exodus 32:4. "Made it a molten calf."] The children of Israel hadMS: "has." been addicted to this kind of idolatry in the land of Egypt. There they had worshippedMS: "worship." this sort of idol. See note on Exodus 3:13.

Exodus 32:6. "And rose up to play."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 485–86.

Exodus 32:19. "And brake them."] Moses' breaking the tables seems to signify the following things. 1. That sin breaks the law, and particularly that it breaks it as a covenant of works. The tables were the tables of the covenant. The Ten Commandments contained a new revelation of the covenant of works, of which two ways of fulfillment were proposed: one was by mere man; the other was by Christ. These tables of the law were the workmanship of God without any hewing of Moses, as the tables of the heart of man in innocency, wherein the law was written, were already prepared by God, and needed not any work of the law or hewing of legal convictions to prepare it. 2. Another thing signified by Moses' breaking the tables was God's breaking his covenant between him and the people, and so were threatening to cast 'em off from being his covenant people (for these were the tables of the covenant between God and the people), agreeable to God's threatening (Exodus 32:9–10). See note on Exodus 34:1. "He cast the tables out of his hands." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 488.

Exodus 33:18–19.] See sermon on the words, exposition of the text.JE crossed out this sentence. His sermon on Exodus 33:18–19, preached Aug. 1731–Dec. 1732, with the doctrine: "God's goodness is that wherein his glory doth eminently appear to the children of men" (MS, p. 3). The exposition of the text features the ways that God's extraordinary disclosure of his glory to Moses is agreeable to his "manner of discovering himself to the souls of his people." The latter discovery is not face to face, which is "reserved for the heavenly state." Nor is it an abiding view, but rather "passing" or transitory. The discovery is "not by immediate intuition," but rather by the revelation of his name in the Bible and by the "proclamation of his free and sovereign grace to sinners in consistence with his justice." See nos. 267 and 358.These references are a later addition. *Works, 15*, 220–22, and 343–44.

Exodus 33:23. "Shall not be seen."] SSS.Ibid., col. 497.

Exodus 34.] This continuance of Moses forty days and forty nights seems to have been ordered of God to be an image and specimen of the state of the saints in glory. Mount Sinai was a type of heaven; it was the mount of God. It was holy ground. Moses was there with God, and there GodJE deleted "discovered to." showed him his glory. His body was in a degree glorified so as to need neither meat nor drink, and so as to shine.

As here was a specimen on earth of the state of the glorified saints in heaven in the principal prophet of the Old Testament, so we have another in the three chief disciples of the New Testament when they were present at Christ's transfiguration, which was also on a mountain, where they were with Christ, and with this same Moses, and with Elias, who both before had

<!-- p. 246 -->

been with Christ on Mount Sinai, one of which had his body glorified on the mountain, and the other did in his body actually ascend into glory in heaven. See note on 2 Corinthians 12:2–4; also note on Matthew 17:1–5.

Mountains are often made use of in Scripture as types of heaven. Mount Zion and the mount of the temple are often so spoken of; and the Apostle particularly teaches of Mount Sinai, that it was a type of heaven, in Hebrews 8:5.

Exodus 34:1.] See "Miscellanies," no. 1030.*Works, 20*, 367–69.

Moses was commanded to hew two tables of stone like the first that were broken, signifying that after man had broken the law which God wrote at first on the tables of his heart in innocency, which was God's own workmanship, that in order to the law's being written in the table of the heart again after the fall, the heart needs to be first prepared by being hewed by Moses, i.e. hewed by the law of Moses, or by legal convictions. But that the law can go no further than this: it can prepare the heart; but it is Christ's work, and his only, to write the law in the heart. Romans 8:3–4, "What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh. That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." Moses was commanded to prepare these second tables, to bring 'em with him, that he might write the law on them, when he should cause all his goodness to pass before him, and proclaim his sovereign mercy in forgiving iniquity, etc., which should preserve these tables from being broken as the first were, and prevent a final breach of covenant between God and the people. Compare Exodus 33:19; Exodus 34:1–7, Exodus 34:10; Jeremiah 31:31–33 and Jeremiah 32:40. See note on Exodus 32:19.This paragraph is a later addition, and the next eight paragraphs are another later addition.

There is this in the nature of the case that confirms that the breaking of the first tables was a type of the breaking of the first covenant, and the utter impossibility of men's obtaining life by the law. Moses himself in all probability cast away the tables, and broke 'em beneath the mount when he came to see the golden calf, under a strong apprehension that was impressed on his mind by what he then saw, that it was not worth the while to carry this holy law to such a people under any notion of their keeping it, and so attaining God's favor by that means.

<!-- p. 247 -->

The Ten Commandments at first were given with thunder, and lightning, and earthquake, but now the second time with a gracious proclamation of mercy, long-suffering, abundant goodness, and truth, and forgiveness of iniquity, transgression, and sin, yet mercy perfectly consistent with infinite holiness and strict justice, which will by no means clear the guilty.

When the children of Israel had broken this covenant, Moses cast it away and broke the tables in pieces, which represents God's utterly casting away that covenant made at first with mankind as now entirely useless, the obtaining life in that way being now utterly and everlastingly to be despaired of. See note on Exodus 32:19, and Exodus 34:1, and Exodus 32-34 ("Scripture," no. 441).This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 522–24.

God as it were broke the tables in pieces as disannulling all hopes of men's ever obtaining life in that way. Now this second time the tables are made by the ministration and instrumentality of Moses, who herein is a type of the gospel ministry. God commanded that the second tables should be committed to the ark to preserve them, that they might not be broken as the first were (Compare Deuteronomy 9:16–17 with Deuteronomy 10:1–2). Thus the affair of the preservation of the hearts of God's people in holiness is committed to the keeping of Christ.

The delivering of the tables of stone this second time is spoken of as the making of a new covenant (Exodus 34:10).

When Moses came down from the mount with these new tables, it was with his face shining, and not with wrath in his face as before.

It was this covenant that was renewed in Deuteronomy. This was a lively type of what we read of in Jeremiah 31:31–32. "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel," etc., "not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, which my covenant they broke."

See note on Jeremiah 31:32, and Hebrews 8:9. What is said in those places would lead one to think that Moses' breaking these tables signified the breaking, or God's setting aside, not only the covenant of works, but that old federal dispensation by which God was as an husband to that people Israel, because of its proving insufficient through their sins, to make way for a better covenant, a federal dispensation, to be introduced by Christ, and in him to be fulfilled, and confirmed, and made an everlasting covenant, as the second tables made instead of these were secure and kept safe in the ark.

<!-- p. 248 -->

Exodus 34:29. "Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone."] Though it appeared exceeding bright and dazzling to others; so the saints whose souls shine bright with the reflection of God's glory, and appear so to others, yet don't appear bright in their own eyes.

Exodus 34:29–35.] Moses put a veil over his face to relieve their weak sight, that could not bear to behold the glory of his face. So in the revelation that God makes of himself to his people in the old testament, or under the Mosaic dispensation, God hides with a veil those doctrines of the gospel that are the main design and glory of all divine revelation, because the church in that infant state could not bear a direct and plain revelation of these doctrines. The mystery of redemption by Christ is such as mankind stood in need of a great deal of preparation in order to their being fitted to entertain it. Christ tells his disciples that he had many things to tell them, but they could not bear them then [John 16:12]. So it was with the church of old. Christ the Mediator came to the church under the old testament, and made known himself to them, but in merciful compliance with the feebleness of their sight came with a veil over his face, that their eyes might not be dazzled and offended with theJE deleted "glory of his countenance." brightness of it.

Exodus 35:3. "Ye shall kindle no fire," etc.] Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology* gives the most probable account of this that I have seen, viz. that the Jewish sabbath was the day when Christ lay dead, and therefore kindling fires has some image of a resurrection. Kindling fires is, indeed, very much of an image of the giving or renewing of life. The breath or wind with which fire is blown when it is kindled is an image of the spirit of life, or of the Spirit of God that gives and renews life. This institution occasioned that, on Sunday morning, they were kindling fires all over the land that had gone out, which was a lively image of resurrection, and probably pointed at that resurrection of Christ which was on the morning of that day.*Scripture Chronology*, 389.

Exodus 36:8.] 'Tis very common in the Old Testament that in the same sentence there shall be a change of the pronoun, sometimes by the alteration of the number, sometimes by the alteration of the person, or the number and person of the verb is changed, agreeing with different nominative

<!-- p. 249 -->

cases and relating to different things, though they follow one another after such a manner as pronouns, relating to the same antecedents and verbs agreeing with the same nominative cases, are wont to do in English. As here, in the beginning of this verse, 'tis said, "Every wise-hearted man among them," etc., "made ten curtains," where the verb "made" is in the plural number;וַיַּעֲשׂוּ but in the latter part of the verse, 'tis added, "with cherubims and cunning work made he them," in the singular number,עָשָׂה relating to Moses not lately mentioned. So sometimes we find verbs and pronouns when the substantives that they relate to are not expressed.

Exodus 38:8. "Of the looking glasses."] Probably this signifying, viz. that a right sight of ourselves and of our own pollutions is a necessary mean of our being cleansed. The brass was probably so polished and bright, after it was made into the laver, that the priests that came to wash might see their spots in it.This sentence is a later addition.

Leviticus 4:20. "And the priest shall make an atonement for them, and it shall be forgiven them."] It is not meant that the sacrifice, in itself considered, made a true atonement for any sin, or that any iniquity whatsoever should on account of these sacrifices simply considered, without true repentance and faith in the mercy of God, be forgiven. For the Old Testament does sufficiently teach that sacrifices are nothing without sincere prayer or faith, of which prayer is the expression; and that, on the contrary, "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to God." Proverbs 15:8, "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, but the prayer of the upright is his delight." It was not the sacrifice that was the true bread of God and a sweet savor to him, but the offerer became accepted and the object of God's delight through faith, of which prayer was the expression. See what is said of the wicked, and their sacrificing, and taking God's covenant into their mouth, in Psalms 50, and many other places.

Leviticus 5:1.] It is the man himself that is suspected of being guilty of the fact that is adjured, or put upon his oath. If anything was stolen, or other mischief was done, they were wont to put persons that they thought there was reason to suspect upon their oaths, or adjure them. This appears to be the meaning by 1 Kings 8:31 and Proverbs 29:24.

Leviticus 10:1–2.] This awful destruction of two of the priests, the sons of Aaron, happened on the eighth or last day of the consecration of Aaron and his sons, by which the Levitical priesthood was first introduced, or on the first day of Aaron and his sons officiating as priests. That it was on this day appears, because it was on this day they offered the goat (Leviticus 9:3, Leviticus 9:15) which was burnt, because on this day such things had befallen Aaron that he was not fit to eat thereof, as in the Leviticus 10:16–20. Thus the service of the Levitical priesthood was begun with the awful death of two of the priests that were consumed by the divine wrath. Thus it pleased God to show the insufficiency of the Levitical priesthood at the first setting of it up. He showed that they were so insufficient to make atonement for others, that they were liable to the divine wrath themselves for their own sins. See SSS.This reference is a later interpolation. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 534. And this was also so ordered to impress on the minds of the priests a sense of the sacredness of their work, and the infinite holiness and majesty of that Being with whom they had to do in their office, as Leviticus 10:3.

There is no temptation visible that Nadab and Abihu should have to offer strange fire rather than the holy fire that had descended from heaven. But the case with them seems to have been this, that day being

<!-- p. 253 -->

the first day that ever they had officiated in the priests' office, and a day of rejoicing and feasting, wherein they fed on their peace offerings. And it seems that those two young men had in this feast in a measure intoxicated themselves with strong drink, whereby they either became unable to keep exactly to the points of the law in the execution of their office, and to distinguish between holy and profane, or at least made less careful so to do. So that while they were elevated with drink, they did not distinguish between holy fire and common fire, which seems to be the special reason of God's appointing that law which he does in the Leviticus 10:8–11. For that law seems to be given on this occasion. It was given on the same day that Nadab and Abihu died, as appears by comparing the beginning of the Leviticus 9 with the latter end of this; and it was immediately upon it, for it was while the affair of their offering the sacrifices of the day were under consideration, as appears by the Leviticus 9:12 and following verses.

*Corol*. By this it is manifest that persons are responsible before God for those crimes they commit when drunk.

Another thing observable concerning Nadab and Abihu's death is this. We have an account in the Leviticus 9:24 of a fire's coming "out from before the Lord," and consuming the sacrifices on the altar. Here we have an account of fire in like manner coming out "from the Lord," and consuming, not the sacrifices offered, but the persons that offered, because they had not respect to and did not trust in that fire from the Lord consuming the sacrifice, but offered strange fire, fire of men's kindling. Whereby we seem to be taught this: that they that come to God, and don't trust in the atonement for sin made by Christ's being consumed in the fire of God's wrath, shall be consumed by that fire of God's wrath themselves. They that come to God offering strange fire, and dare to appear before him in their own righteousness, he will be a consuming fire to them. They will be exposed to all the fierceness of the flame of God's vindictive justice, having no benefit of the execution of it on Christ, the great sacrifice for sin.This paragraph is a later addition.

Leviticus 14:12–18.] The sacrifice was to be offered to God with oil. They were to be waved together before the Lord. And after the lamb was slain, and his blood shed before the Lord, the priest was to sprinkle of the oil seven times before the Lord. So the sacrifice of Christ was offered up to God with the Spirit, with divine love, love to God and love to men, which sanctified the sacrifice and made it effectual. Both the blood and the oil were first offered to God before they were applied to the leper. SoThis word appears to be in a different hand. not only is Christ's blood first presented to God before 'tis applied to the sinner, but the spirit of love that he has without measure, first flows out to God before it flows out to the sinner and be communicated to him in sanctification. In the application, both the blood and oil are applied to the right ear of him that was to be cleansed, to cleanse the ear by which men hear and listen to the commands and counsels of God, and the offers and invitations of the gospel; and the thumb, the chief part of the right hand, to cleanse the hands by which we work; and to the chief part of the right foot, to cleanse the feet by which we walk. The application of the blood is to cleanse from the guilt of sins of the ear, or heart, and of the hands or works of the hands, and of the feet or the way and walk. The application of the oil which followed signifies the sanctification of them by the Holy Spirit.

The blood and oil were first applied to the ear, hand and foot, and then afterward oil was poured on the head of the leper, to signify that persons are first justified, then sanctified, and then glorified, as pouring oil on the head was used as a token of initiation to some high and honorable office and great dignity, as that of prophet, priest, or king. As the saints when glorified are made kings and priests unto God, and as the

<!-- p. 255 -->

ear is sanctified to hear God's commands, and the hands to do God's will, and the feet to walk in God's ways, before the pouring oil on the head, it shows that a holy conversation is the only way to glory.

Leviticus 14:34.] The leprosy of an house was typical of the corruption of a church or family. A church in Scripture is represented as an house builded. "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up an spiritual house" [1 Peter 2:5]. A family is often called an house.

Leviticus 18:6.] Marriage is forbidden between those that were nearly related, whereby it is the more lively image of the union between Christ and his church, which is between those that were far separated before that union. The Holy Ghost mainly delighting in the marriage union as a representation, or similitude, of the union between Christ and his church, and marriage being instituted to that end, as the Apostle teaches in the latter end of the Ephesians 5, therefore God would order the circumstances of marriage so as to render it the most lively image of this union.

Leviticus 19:14. "But shalt fear thy God."] Though the fear of those deaf and blind won't restrain you because they can't hear or see you, yet God hears and sees.

Leviticus 19:19. "Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind."] Our virtues should not be mingled with vice. We should not go about to make an union between religion and the service of God and the service of our lusts, which never will agree together. We should allow grace and virtue only, without uniting any vice with it. Our eye and our heart should be single and pure, aiming at and allowing nothing but holiness.

"Thou shalt not sow thy fieldMS: "Seed"; KJV: "field." with mingled seed." This signifies the same thing. The field is the heart. The seed that we sow there should be the word of God and the grace of God's Spirit alone. We should not suffer diverse and opposite principles [to] grow in our hearts with grace. It also carries in it instruction to ministers in managing their spiritual husbandry, to preach the pure word of God, to sow that holy seed alone without any mixture of the doctrines and inventions of men, or wild notions of their own.

"Neither shall a garment mingled with linen and woolen come upon thee." Which still seems to signify the same thing, for the qualifications of our minds are often in Scripture compared to [a] garment. Inherent righteousness or holiness is often compared to a garment. This should not be mixed with contrary qualifications. But that which seems especially to be signified is that we should not mingle the righteousness of Christ with our own righteousness, or go about to cover ourselves partly with his righteousness and partly with our own, as though the garment of Christ's righteousness was not sufficient of itself to cover us and adorn us without being patched with our righteousness to eke it out. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 584–85.

"The seventh day is the sabbath of rest, an holy convocation."] By this it appears that although the children of Israel were obliged to meet together at the temple but three times in the year, yet the weekly sabbath among them was from the beginning a day for their meeting together for some sort of religious public worship, which is confirmed from 2 Kings 4:23, and Isaiah 66:23, and Ezekiel 46:3. Whence it may be argued that the people had something like synagogues among them long before the captivity into Babylon, which is confirmed from Psalms 74:8, "They have burnt up all the synagogues of God in the land." The wordמוֹעֵד translated "synagogues" signifies a convention, congregation, or meeting together. See also Psalms 83:9.This biblical citation is an apparent error. Psalms 83:9 does not include a reference to the "congregation" or "meeting together." JE crossed out "Psalms 28:9" before he wrote "Psalms 83:9." Psalms 89:5 contains the phrase, "the congregation of the saints"; Psalms 82:1 contains the phrase, "the congregation of the mighty."

Leviticus 23:10.] This sheaf was to be offered to God on the first day of the week after the Passover, on the same day that Christ arose. It was the first fruits of all the seed sown; so Christ was "the first fruits of them that slept" [1 Corinthians 15:20]. The body that dies and is buried is compared to the seed of bread corn sown in the earth (1 Corinthians 15:36–37), and Christ's resurrection in particular is compared to this. John 12:24, "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." And "the end of the world," the time of the resurrection, is represented by the harvest (Matthew 13:39). Things rising in the spring, after all seemed to be dead in winter, is a lively image of the resurrection. This sheaf was the first fruits of the earth that they had in the spring. And it is to be noted that the time when this sheaf of the first fruits was offered was not only on the same day of the week, but at the same time of year, the first day of the week after the Passover, as that was.

<!-- p. 258 -->

Le23:15–17.] Concerning the feast of Pentecost, see Mather on the *Types*,Samuel Mather's discussion of the Feast of Pentecost, also called the Feast of Weeks, underscored three "mysteries." The feast, kept fifty days after Passover, was a testimony of gratitude for the land of Canaan and for the harvest from the land. Therefore the people were to present the first fruits as an offering. The feast was a memorial to the giving of the law on Sinai, an "inestimable mercy" to be commemorated everlastingly. And the feast was an anticipation of God's pouring forth of the Spirit upon the apostles, making possible the preaching of the gospel (Mather, *Figures or Types of the Old Testament*, 422–24). and also my notes on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210, *Corol*. 1.*Works, 15*, 136–39.

Leviticus 23:17.] These wave loaves were the first fruits of wheat harvest, and typified the first fruits of the Spirit that were given after Christ's resurrection on the same day of Pentecost, and the first fruits of the Christian church brought in then by that pouring out of the Spirit on this day. "The apostles, having received the first fruits of the Spirit, begat three thousand souls, and presented them as the first fruits of the Christian church to God and to the Lamb." Bedford.*Scripture Chronology*, 452.

Leviticus 27:11–25.] The unclean beast, the house, or field that were sanctified,Here and two other places in this entry JE substituted "sanctified" for "devoted." if the owner did desire to redeem 'em, yet were to be estimated, for they might be sold and the money go into the holy treasury. But if the original owner that sanctified them changed his mind, and desired to redeem what he gave, he was to pay dearer than another by a fifth part, which he must add to the priest's estimation. Or if the sanctified thing were not sold, yet it was necessary to estimate, that it might be known what the owner would have to pay with the addition of the fifth part, in case he should desire to redeem it.

### Numbers

Numbers 3.] Concerning the number of the Levites and of the first-born. "As many as there were Levites, *over and above the first-born of the Levites*, who, by being first-born, were before this institution holy to the Lord, so many of the first-born of the other tribes were discharged from attending upon the service of the tabernacle. And accordingly there being twenty and two thousand Levites, these were accepted instead of the firstborn males of the children of Israel. The whole number of the first-born of the Israelites were twenty-two thousand, two hundred, threescore, and thirteen. And the whole number of the Levites were, of the sons of Gershon 7500, of the sons of Kohath 8600, of the sons of Merari 6200; in all 22,300. And yet we are told that there were 273 of the first-born of the children of Israel more than the Levites, i.e. more than there were Levites to be accepted instead of them. But this difficulty is easy to be accounted for, for of the Levites many were the first-born of their families, namely, 300 of them. So that there remained 22,000 only, who were not first-born, and might therefore be accepted instead of the first-born of the other tribes." Shuckford's *Connection*, vol. 3, pp. 163–64.*Sacred and Prophane History*.

Numbers 3:39.] The number of the Levites, according as the number of the particular families are reckoned (Numbers 3:2, Numbers 3:28, and Numbers 3:34), being added together amounts to 22,300; and yet here the whole number is reckoned only 22,000. Concerning this, see SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 626–27. Also see note on Exodus 13:2.This reference is a later addition.

Numbers 3:43.] Concerning the small proportion which the number of the first-born bears to the number of the whole congregation, see SSS on Numbers 3:39, Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 626–27. and also note on Exodus 13:2.

Numbers 6:5.] The Nazarite seems to be forbidden to shave or cut his hair on two accounts. 1. To signify the great degree of their purity. The very hair of their heads was pure, and therefore must not be profaned. It must not be cut off or trodden underfoot. 2. Hair, that is the growth of the head, seems to typify thoughts and contemplation. And that the Nazarite should never cut his hair seems to typify the devoting of the life to divine contemplations, as the ministers of the gospel, who are typified by the Nazarites, ought to do, and, indeed, as the Nazarites themselves were obliged to do. (See my notes on Jephthah's vow.)"Scripture," no. 223, *Works, 15*, 160–69. The growing of the hair seemed to signify increasing in spiritual knowledge. So it seemed to signify in Sampson; as his hair grew, his strength increased [Judges 16:22]. So our strength increases with our knowledge of God.

Numbers 10:10.] The new moons were to be kept as holy times and times of rejoicing, and trumpets were to be blown, which ever signified the declaring of the glad tidings of the gospel. Probably it was because the moon with her new light received was a type of the beginning the new and glorious dispensation introduced by Jesus Christ, wherein the gospel was to be clearly and plainly preached and proclaimed unto all nations. The moon is a lively image of the church; as she borrows all her light from the sun, so doth the church receive light from Christ, the Sun of righteousness. The old moon represents the church under the old testament, which looks to, depends upon, and receives light from Christ yet to come, and is drawing nearer and nearer to the time of Christ's coming, as the old moon, and receives light from it yet to come, whose conjunction with the moon is yet future. The new moon represents the church under the new testament, which receives light from Christ already come, and having already united himself to the human nature, as the new moon looks towards and receives light from the sun as having already been in conjunction with her. The conjunction of the sun and moon in the time of the change seems to represent the coming of Christ, whereby Christ actually united himself to the church by uniting himself to the human nature, the church's nature. Bedford, in his *Scripture Chronology*, supposes and shows it to be very probable that Christ's conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary (who was a type of the church), which was Christ's first assumption of the human nature, the nature of the church, was at the time of the change of the moon. For Christ's being born at the feast of tabernacles (as 'tis exceeding probable that he was), if we from thence reckon back nine months, it will bring it to the time of the change of the moon. If so, it is probable it was much from respect to this that the new moon was appointed to be kept.*Scripture Chronology*, 400–405. See also *Works, 15*, 127–28. See also Mather on the *Types*, p. 443.Samuel Mather's reflections on the new moon underscore the perpetual duties performed on the new moons and also point to the mystery of the incarnation and Christ's conception in the womb of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Ghost. The change of the moon at the conjunction of the sun and moon shadows "the Conjunction or Union of the two Natures of Christ in one Person" (*Figures or Types of the Old Testament*). See nos. 271 and 315This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 225–28, 290–92.

Numbers 10:33. "As the ark went before the congregation of Israel to seek out a resting place for them, so Christ goes before his church to heaven to prepare a place for them. He is entered into his rest as their forerunner; he is entered for them, and to take possession in their name.

Numbers 10:35–36.] The ascending of the ark out of the wilderness in Canaan, the land flowing with milk and honey, typified the same thing with ascending the ark afterwards into Mt. Zion, even the ascension of Christ into heaven. And therefore the same words were uttered by David on that occasion that were uttered by Moses on this. And therefore also David on that occasion speaks of this marching of the ark through the wilderness (Psalms 68:7). See Psalms 68:1. In these words that Moses spoke on occasion of taking up the ark in order to its ascending into Canaan, viz. "Rise up, Lord, and let thine enemies be scattered; and let them that hate thee flee before thee," respect seems to be had to the glorious victory and triumph Christ had over his enemies that he had been conflicting with in his resurrection and ascension, spoken of, Psalms 68:18. And in those words which Moses uttered when the ark rested, "Return, O Lord, unto the many ten thousand thousandsKJV: "many thousands." of Israel," respect is had to Christ returning again to the earth after his ascension by his Spirit (agreeable to his promises, John 14:18–23 and John 16:16), whereby the number of his people was so vastly increased, agreeable to Psalms 110:1–3.

Numbers 12:1.] The Ethiopian woman that Moses had married represents the church, as Solomon's wife did who was an Egyptian. The church is naturally sinful, black, and deformed. Especially does she represent the Gentile church. Aaron and Miriam's murmuring represents the Jewish priests and Jewish church envying the Gentile converts, and self-righteous persons envying great sinners, or very mean persons, when made the subjects of divine grace. Numbers 12:6–8.] See no. 118.*Works, 15*, 83.

This that is mentioned here as an extraordinary privilege, bestowed upon Moses above other prophets, was bestowed on all the disciples in a much greater degree. Christ spoke to them "mouth to mouth," not as to Moses by a voice out of the pillar of cloud and fire, but he dwelt among them in the human [nature], and conversed with them familiarly for several years together. They did not only behold a similitude that was to represent Christ, but they indeed sawJE deleted "him face to face." his face. They saw him, and [he] dwelt with them, and [in] the human nature. And that privilege of speaking to him apparently and not in dark speeches was granted to all the apostles, evangelists, and prophets under the new testament (which were a great part of the Christian church) in a much further and more glorious degree than to Moses. So that herein they were all greater than Moses, for Christ spoke these things to them with great plainness of speech that were revealed of old in visions and dark speeches. This is one instance wherein the new testament church is more highly privileged than the old. God, in that he declared gospel things to the church of old in dark speeches, therein treated them as servants, for the servant knoweth not what his Lord doth. But Christ, in plainly revealing these things to Christians, treats them as friends, for all things he hath heard of the Father, he hath revealed unto us. So God, because he did not speak to Moses in dark speech but apparently, is said to speak with Moses "as a man speaketh with his friend" (Exodus 33:11). But the days are now come wherein Christ grants this privilege to all his people, and in a much higher degree than to Moses. This was one thing wherein Christ distinguished his disciples from others while on earth, that he gave to them to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them that were without, in parables.This paragraph is a later addition.

Numbers 12:8. Moses in this story especially represents Christ mystical under the new dispensation of the gospel and in the Gentile [church], to whom God did not reveal himself as he did of old to the Jewish church and the old testament priests and prophets "in dark speeches," etc., but with "great plainness of speech," and showed himself with "open face" (See 2 Corinthians 3, 2 Corinthians 3:12, 2 Corinthians 3:18].), and as envied by the Jewish priests and scribes and the Jewish church. See note on Numbers 12:1. Deuteronomy 24:9, "Remember what the Lord thy God did to Miriam," etc.This paragraph is another later addition.

Numbers 12:9–10.] This represents the punishment God inflicted on the Jewish church when they were offended in Christ and envied the Christian church. God left his temple in Jerusalem; and the Jewish church was smitten with a curse, and was rejected as unclean for her sins, as Miriam became leprous and was shut out from the camp. Therefore is that charge left in Deuteronomy 24:9. See note on that place.

Numbers 13:23–24.] Concerning the "cluster of grapes," see SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 662.

Numbers 13:27–33.] Concerning the gigantic inhabitants of Canaan that dwelt in Canaan, and opposed the children of Israel's coming in thither, and must be overcome in order to their possessing it. These giants represent the devils who once were the inhabitants of heaven, who set themselves against Israel, against God's people of mankind, whom they understood were to have the possession of that land above them and to have the dominion there, and that one in that nature was to be the absolute lord of the land, and were overcome by the spiritual Joshua, the Lord Jesus Christ, in their rebellion and war in heaven, and were cast out of that land. And they stand in the way to oppose God's people in all ages, having the possession of heaven, and make war with them, as they did with Christ at first. Their war with them is only that first war with Christ continued; and 'tis a war on the same account, and in the exercise of the same spirit, the same envy. And 'tis all one to God's elect people, as if they were still dwelling in heaven and fought there, as once they did. The walls up to heaven, that defended the cities of Canaan, are the lusts of men and the great difficulties that must be surmounted in order to the possession of heaven.

Numbers 13:30.] According to Caleb's faith, so was it done unto him. The people were discouraged with the report of the spies, that there they saw giants, the sons of Anak, and that they were in their "own sight as grasshoppers," and so they "were in their sight" (Numbers 13:28, Numbers 13:33). Caleb was confident that they were "well able to overcome" them; and therefore God gave Caleb Hebron for his possession, which was the chief seat of those giants, as appears by Numbers 13:22, Joshua 11:21, and Joshua 14:12, Joshua 14:15. God enabled Caleb himself to drive the giants thence (Joshua 14:12 and Joshua 15:13–14).

Numbers 13:32–33. "That eateth up the inhabitants thereof," etc.] I.e. by the violence of the giants, as the earth before the flood was filled with violence,

especially through the lawless ravages of the giants. So it was with the land of Canaan. See SSS.Ibid., col. 663.

Numbers 14:11. "For all the signs which I have showed among them."] Here God declares that signs and miracles are good ground, and that they are such arguments as do most reasonably oblige us to receive a message delivered in his name as from him, and that those promises shall be fulfilled which the maker of the miracles makes. Therefore the miracles that Christ wrought were such arguments as oblige our believing in him.

Numbers 14:17. "Let the power of my Lord be great," etc.] Here God's pardoning great, and aggravated, and manifold sin, and showing mercy to the very unworthy, is mentioned as a manifestation of the high and glorious all-sufficiency of the divine nature. Therefore the declared design of the gospel, which is to magnify the infinite riches of free grace, is most worthy of God. Such exceeding goodness to enemies and vipers does greatly show the infinite height, fullness, and glory of the Divine Being, and may well be looked upon as the most exalted manifestation of the divine excellency that ever was. This therefore is a confirmation of the divinity of the gospel of Jesus Christ.

Numbers 14:20–21.] At the same time that God pardons sin, he will take effectual care that his justice and vengeance, with respect to these very sins, should be duly glorified.

"The book of the wars of the Lord."] 'Tis probable "there was among the Hebrews a book, called 'the Book of the Wars of the Lord,' that was a collection of poems, or historical songs, composed on the various most memorable occurrences that befell them through the wilderness. Pious and devout persons might well be supposed to employ their wit and genius in such an useful manner. I apprehend the Book of Jasher, mentioned, Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18, to be the same, which was continued by the addition of odes or songs on remarkable occasions." Dr. Winder, *History of Knowledge*, vol. 2, pp. 46–47. He also there supposes the book of Psalms was collected out of this book.*Critical and Chronological History* (2nd ed.), II, 46–47. I should rather think it was a distinct collection of songs of prophets and inspired persons, as the other was the songs of others uninspired.

Numbers 21:16–18.] See no. 275, latter end of that note.*Works, 15*, 231.

Numbers 21:18.] This waterJE deleted "signifies the." typifies the Holy Spirit, and so all spiritual blessings, graces, comforts, etc., of which he is the spring. This is the fountain at which the church drink and are satisfied, this the living water which is in believers as "a well of water, springing up to everlasting life" [John 4:14]. This is that "river of water of life" [Revelation 22:1] that waters the New Jerusalem.

The princes either represent the church in general, for they were the

<!-- p. 271 -->

representatives of the whole congregation. All the people could not come to work to dig this well, and therefore their princes must come as their representatives. Or else, they typify the elders of the church, or else those of the church that are strong in faith. The nobles of Israel may well typify eminent saints, who are the nobles of the spiritual Israel.

Their staves that they dug the well with typify faith, as seems to me most probable. Faith is to believers as their staff in their journey through the wilderness of this world. They walk by faith; 'tis faith that supports them, as a staff doth a man that goes in [a] rough way and through a wearisome wilderness. I am ready to think that it is taken notice of that Jacob leaned upon the top of his staff when he worshipped, because his staff typified faith. Hebrews 11:21, "By faith Jacob worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff." And that this is the reason why Christ commanded his disciples to take nothing but a staff in their journey (Mark 6:8). Their using their staves in digging typified the church's, or the elders', exercising their faith in prayer.

'Tis thus that the church obtains the spirit of God and spiritual blessings. By faith and prayer thus the apostles and primitive Christians obtained the effusion of the Holy Ghost at Pentecost (Acts 1:14).

And possibly 'twas for this reason that Elijah directed his servant to lay his staff upon the face of the dead child (2 Kings 4:29), for we are taught that 'tis by faith that miracles are performed.

We read that David "took his staff in his hand" [1 Samuel 17:40], when he went against Goliath, which signified faith.

So Jacob says, Genesis 32:10, "With my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I am become two bands." So Moses' rod, or staff, represents faith as well as other things. See latter end of note on Exodus 4:20, no. 195.*Works, 15*, 108. Jacob's lameness, after he had wrestled with the angel [Genesis 32:24–25], made him lean more upon his staff; so the affliction the godly meet with in the world make 'em to live more by faith.This paragraph is a later addition.

Numbers 22:20. "If the men come to call thee," etc.] Balaam's disobedience partly appeared in his being more forward to go than God directed him. God allowed him to go "if the men come to call" him, i.e. if the men come to him early, or some such way showed that they very earnestly insisted on his going, or still continued greatly engaged in the matter, he might go. Balaam, being eager for the reward that Balak promised, and hoping

<!-- p. 272 -->

that he should be allowed to curse the people, catched at this allowance God gave him, and strained his license beyond God's limitation. When he had once from this conditional license entertained hopes of going and getting the reward, and not doubting but that the princes would come to call him, and appear still engaged in that which they had been so earnest in hitherto, he could not bear to be disappointed. And though the appointed conditions failed, he went notwithstanding. The messengers were probably pretty much discouraged by what Balaam had said to them in the Numbers 22:18, for Balaam seemed so very positive in it not to curse them, unless the God who was the God of Israel directed him to. It disheartened them much, and made them that they didn'tMS: "did." Grosart added "t." come so early to know what God had said, nor appear so strenuous in the matter as they had, whereby Balaam was disappointed, and was cut off from liberty to go according to God's direction. But his expectations and hopes being raised, and his eagerness after Balak's reward stimulated him; and he broke over the difficulty, and went contrary to God's order. Thus Balaam ran greedily for a reward (Jude 11).

Numbers 22:22–24 ff.] See note on 2 Peter 2:16.

Numbers 22:23. "And his sword drawn in his hand."] Balaam, in going contrary to God's commands, and acting against God's people, kicked against the pricks, and run upon a drawn sword, as it afterwards proved; for after he had given that wicked advice to the Moabites to tempt the Israelites by their women, he was slain with the swords of the armies of God (Numbers 31:8).

Numbers 22:25.] 2 Peter 2:16.

Numbers 22:28.] Hence probably arose the fable among the heathen, "that Bacchus gave a reward to a certain ass, that he should speak with human voice, with which the giants, which were Bacchus' enemies, were terrified. So Stillingfleet, *Origines Sacrae*." See Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 6, p. 69.Second edition. See concerning the gods and giants, "Scripture," no. 402.*Works, 15*, 405–11.

"And the Lord opened the mouth of the ass," etc. Here Mr. Ainsworth

<!-- p. 273 -->

observes that the devil, when he tempted our first parents to sin, did it by a subtile serpent. But God, when he would convince Balaam, did it by a silly ass, a creature dull and sottish to a proverb. For Satan corrupts men's minds by the craftiness of them that lie in wait to deceive, but Christ "has chosen the foolish things of this world to confound the wise" [1 Corinthians 1:27].This paragraph is a separate entry. Henry Ainsworth (1571–1622 or 1623) was a leader of the Puritan separatist congregation in Amsterdam. His comments on this passage include the judgment that the ass is "the most silly of all beasts." He asserts that "no workes, signes or miracles are able to change the hardnesse of mans hart, but grace from God onely." He also notes "how Satans continual practise is to corrupt mens mindes from the simplicitie that is in Christ" (*Annotations upon the Fourth Book of Moses, called Numbers. Wherein, by Conference of the Scriptures, by Comparing the Greek and Chaldee Versions, and testimonies of Hebrew writers; the Lawes and Ordinances given of old unto Israel in this book, are explained* [London, 1619], n. p.), bound together with several other commentaries by Ainsworth under the title, *Annotations upon the Five Bookes of Moses, and the Booke of the Psalmes* (London, 1622). See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 702.

Numbers 22:29. "And Balaam said unto the ass," etc.] It may appear a difficulty that Balaam heard the ass speak, that he was not too much surprised and astonished to make such answers to the ass. But the difficulty may be resolved thus. Balaam, being a soothsayer or diviner, and a very great and famous heathen prophet or conjurer (though on this occasion he received revelations from God), he was not unused to extraordinary appearances and voices, but doubtless more used to them than less noted magicians. It was not an unusual thing for heathen magicians to converse with spirits and hear their voices, appearing to them in the shape of birds and beasts, and probably sometimes speaking out of such animals, as the devil at first spoke out of the serpent, which might be the cause that Balaam might not be so much frightened at so extraordinary a thing. And if it was yet different on some respects from what he had been used to, no wonder he did not turn that much in his thoughts in the heat of passion. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 702.

Numbers 22:41. "Baal."] SSS.Ibid., col. 704.

Numbers 23:9. "Dwell alone."] John 15:19.

Numbers 23:21. "The shout of a king is among them."] See note on Revelation 19:5.

Numbers 23:22.] Concerning the unicorn, see SSS.Ibid., cols. 710–11.

Numbers 24:7.] Men are wont to water gardens by pouring water out of buckets or some such vessels. So God will take care of his church that is, in the preceding verse, compared to a garden.

Numbers 24:14. "In the latter days."] By this it is evident that by "latter days" in Scripture is sometimes only meant a great while hence, for what this people should do to Balak's people, that is here spoken of, was in David's time. They used the expression "the latter days" for a long time hence, as they then and we now do "former days" for a great while ago or in ancient times. See Deuteronomy 4:30 and Deuteronomy 31:29.

Numbers 24:17. "There shall come a star out of Jacob."] Balaam lived to the east of the land of Jacob, and therefore the star that he speaks of rising "out of Jacob" must appear in that country (contrary to the ordinary course of stars), rising from the western horizon. So the star appeared that rose out of Judea in the sight of the wise men that came from the east at Christ's birth. These things probably note that in the great gospel day religion will begin in the western part of the world, that the light will first rise in America and make progress backwards towards the east, contrary to the course of theJE deleted "lights of heaven." sun and stars. So that when the new heaven and new earth begins, the luminaries of the new heaven will be contrary to the course of the lights of the old world. For the course of Christ and Christians is not according to, but contrary to, the course of this world.

<!-- p. 275 -->

This is confirmed by Isaiah 60:9, together with Isaiah 60:1, and Psalms 19:5–6 with context.The remainder of this entry is a later addition.

The same seems also signified by the sun's going back from west to east when Hezekiah was healed, and God promised to do such great things for his church to deliver it out of the hand of the king of Assyria, which is often used by the prophet Isaiah as a type of the glorious deliverance of the church from her enemies in the latter days. See note on Isaiah 38:5–8. The same seems to be represented by the course of the waters of the sanctuary in Ezekiel 47, which was from west to east, which waters undoubtedly represents the Holy Spirit that shall flow forth from God in the latter age of the world, for 'tis manifest that the whole of these last chapters of Ezekiel is about the glorious state of the church that shall be then.This and the following paragraph are a later addition.

The course of nature will at that time be as it were changed, in answer to the prayers of the church, as the sun and moon were stopped in their course at the prayer of Joshua. The course of God's ordinary providence shall be changed in the exercises of his grace in forgiving great sinners, sinners under such circumstances as don't use to be forgiven, and many other ways.

"Of Sheth." No. 418.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 470–71.

Numbers 24:17. "A star out of Jacob."] SSS.Poole, *Synapsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 715–16.

Numbers 24:23–24. "Alas, who shall live when God doth this? And ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and shall afflict Eber, and shall afflict Asshur."] This is a prophecy of the invasions, both of the Macedonians and Romans, who both were the posterity of Chittim. See "Scripture," no. 419.*Works, 15*, 471–99, particularly 478–79. The remainder of this paragraph and the following two are a later addition. They both came in ships; the Macedonians came over into Asia in ships, as well as the Romans. When it is said, "Alas, who shall live when God doth this?" the words have respect to two things, viz. the calamities these two people of the posterity of Chittim should bring on the nations of the

<!-- p. 276 -->

world, and the calamities they should bring on God's people, both which are spoken of in the next verse: "They shall afflict Asshur, and shall afflict Eber."

1. It is said, "Who shall live when God doth this?" because of the general conquest they should make of the nations, and overthrow of the kingdoms of the earth.JE deleted "None of the nations of the known world should." Scarce any of the nations of the known world should escape, agreeable to the prophecies of the two empires of the Macedonians and Romans in Daniel. Daniel 2:39–40, "And another third kingdom of brass, which shall bear rule over all the earth. And the fourth kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces and subdueth all things; and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise." Daniel 7:7, "After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth. It devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it." Daniel 8:5–7, "And as I was considering, behold, an he goat came from the west on the face of the whole earth, and touched not the ground; and the he goat had a notable horn between his eyes. And he came to the ram that had two horns, which I had seen standing before the river, and ran unto him in the fury of his power. And I saw him come close unto the ram, and he was moved with choler against him, and smote the ram, and brake his two horns. And there was no power in the ram to stand before him, but he cast him down to the ground, and stamped upon him. And there was none that could deliver the ram out of his hand."

2. The Spirit of God in saying, "Alas, who shall live when God doth this?" has respect to these nations afflicting Eber in the great and unparalleled calamities and troubles they should bring both upon the natural and spiritual posterity of Abraham, the son of Eber; and particularly those dreadful calamities that should be brought upon the Jews under the Macedonian empire by Antiochus Epiphanes,Antiochus Epiphanes (d. 164 B.C.E.), king of Syria, who attacked Jerusalem and the temple. so much spoken of in the prophecies of Daniel; and the amazing destruction of the Jews afterwards by the Romans, and the manifold terrible calamities they should suffer during the continuance of their empire until the last kingdom upon earth should succeed it, viz. that of the saints of the most high God; and also the great and unparalleled persecutions the Christian church should suffer both from Rome heathen and antichristian, the latter

<!-- p. 277 -->

of which is the antitype of the kingdom of Antiochus Epiphanes. So that what the Spirit of God has a special respect to in this place is the same that Christ speaks of, Matthew 24:21–22. "Then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved." See notes on that place, "Scripture," no. 292.*Works, 15*, 251–64. "And he also shall perish forever." "Thus saith Dr. Lightfoot,John Lightfoot (1602–75), a noted English biblical critic and divine. 'Balaam, instead of cursing the church, curseth Amalek the first, and Rome the last, enemy of the church.'" Henry.This paragraph is a separate later addition. *Exposition, I* (1725), 395.

Numbers 26:53.] Concerning of dividing the land by lot, see SSS.Ibid., cols. 724–25.

Numbers 27:3. "He died in his own sin."] Hence I would observe that men's temporal death is a fruit and punishment ofJE deleted "their own." sin. And hence I infer original sin, in that infants die. If temporal death be the fruit and punishment of sin, it must be the punishment of sin that he is guilty of that dies, because 'tis contrary to God's declared method of proceeding with mankind to bring death upon them for sin, or as the punishment of sin that they have not the guilt of, as is very evident by the eighteenth of Ezekiel.

Numbers 27:18–19, and Numbers 27:23.] By what is here said it is manifest that it is proper, in ordaining or appointing a person to an office in the name of God, to give a charge with the laying on of hands.

Numbers 31:8. "Balaam also the son of Beor."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 734–35.

Numbers 31:24.] SSS.Ibid., col. 736.

Numbers 31:48–54.] "Here's a great example of piety and devotion in the officers of the army.… They came to Moses as their general and commander in chief, and respectfully addressed themselves to him, calling themselves his servants. The honors they had won did not puff them up so as to make them forget their duty to him. They take a pious notice of God's wonderful goodness to them in this late expedition, in preserving not only their own lives, but the lives of all the men of war that they had under their charge.… 'Tis an evidence of the tenderness these commanders had over their soldiers, and that their lives were very precious to them; they looked upon it a mercy to themselves that none of these under their charge miscarried.… The captains offered their oblation to make an atonement for their souls (Numbers 31:50). Instead of coming to Moses to demand of God a recompense for the good service they had done in avenging the Lord of Midian, or to set up the trophies of their victory for the immortalizing their own names, they bring an oblation to make atonement for their souls, being conscious to themselves, as the best men must be even in their best services, that they had been defective in their duty, not only in that instance for which they were reproved (Numbers 31:14), but in many others." Henry.*Exposition, I* (1725), 408. This is an instance of the piety of this generation.

Numbers 32:21.] They were allowed to leave enough behind to defend their wives, and children, and possessions. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 739.

Numbers 35:6.] The city of REFUGE did not so properly represent Christ, as the church of Christ, of which Christ is the foundation and the wall of defense. Numbers 35:11–15.] These cities of refuge do more immediately and directly typify the church than Christ, though it be by Christ that persons are safe in the church. Isaiah 14:32, "The Lord hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it," or "betake themselves to it," as it is in the margin. Isaiah 26:1–2, "In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah: We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation that keepeth the truth may enter in."
