### Deuteronomy

Deuteronomy 1:1. "Against the Red Sea."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 751–52.

Deuteronomy 1:2.] SSS.Ibid., col. 752.

Deuteronomy 1:20. "Ye are come unto the mountain of the Amorites."] The southern part of the land of Canaan, all that part that was afterward the possession of the tribe of Judah, was possessed chiefly by the Amorites, as appears by Joshua 10:5–6; and it was generally a mountainous country. See note on Deuteronomy 3:25.

Deuteronomy 1:37. "For your sakes."] SSS.Ibid., col. 755.

Deuteronomy 2:10. "Anakims."] SSS.Ibid., col. 757.

Deuteronomy 2:20.] Zamzummims is a wordIn Hebrew, זַמְזֻמִּים; in Arabic, زَمَزَم that in Arabic signifies "thundering fellows," being taken from a word that signifies "a rattling like thunder." Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, pp. 316 and 353.

Deuteronomy 2:21 ff. "And the Lord destroyed them before them."] I.e. he destroyed them by the hand of ChedorlaomerA king of Elam mentioned in Genesis 14. and the other kings of the east, to make room for them. See note on Genesis 14:5–6.

Deuteronomy 2:34. "Men, and the women, and the little ones."] The destruction of these accursed nations by the children of Israel typifies the eternal destruction of the wicked. And "the little ones" being destroyed is an intimation of the doctrine of original sin, and that we deserve eternal damnation as soon as we are born.

<!-- p. 281 -->

Deuteronomy 3:11. "For only Og, king of Bashan, remained of the remnant of the giants."] I.e. after that destruction that had been made of them by Chedorlaomer and the other kings that were with him (See note on Genesis 14:5–6.), which destruction is spoken of in the preceding chapter, vv. 19 ff. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 761.

Deuteronomy 3:25. "That goodly mountain."] Hereby seems to be intended the whole land of Canaan, which, being generally a very mountainous country, is all together called a "mountain" here, and Psalms 78:54, Exodus 15:17, Jeremiah 17:3, Ezekiel 17:23, and Ezekiel 20:40, as the possession of the Amorites in the southern parts of that land, being a mountainous country, was called "the mountain of the Amorites" (Deuteronomy 1:20), and as the whole original possession of the tribe of Ephraim, being a very hilly country, was called "Mount Ephraim," as Joshua 17:15 and Judges 7:3.Judges 7:3 speaks of "Mount Gilead."

Deuteronomy 4:6–8.] Agreeable to what is said in these verses were some traditions found amongst the heathen, which Grotius gives an account of in his book, *De Veritate Religionis Christianae*, Bk. 1, sec. 16, notes.*Truth of the Christian Religion* (2nd ed., 1719), 65. JE marked this entire entry with two large "X" s after deleting the following: "There he says, Strabo, Bk. 14, after the history of Moses, says that his fellows. Justin says thus, Bk. 26, ch. 2, speaking of the kings and priests of the."

Deuteronomy 4:19. "Which the Lord thy God hath divided unto all nations."] This expression, "divided," is here used because men's gods are their portion. That which men worship as god they are to have a supreme respect to, and a dependence on for happiness. So the true God is called "the portion of Jacob" (Jeremiah 10:16). So God divided out to every nation their several portions, which were their gods.

Deuteronomy 4:21–22.] In this Moses was a type of Christ. God was angry with Moses for their sakes; so God was as it were angry with Christ for our sakes. He bore the wrath of God for our sakes. Our iniquities were laid upon Christ; our guilt lay upon him.JE deleted "So the sin of the children of Israel did." And so he in some respect partook of our guilt. So Moses partook of the guilt of the children of Israel when, by their rebellion, they provoked his spirit so that he spoke unadvisedly with his lips. And Moses was as it were a sacrifice for them: he died in the wilderness;

<!-- p. 282 -->

and they lived, and went in to possess the good land,The remainder of this entry is a later addition. as in Deuteronomy 4:22. Moses mentions this as an instance of God's mercy to the people, as is evident by the Deuteronomy 4:21 and by Deuteronomy 4:22. "But ye shall go over, and possess the good land."

God was pleased so greatly to testify his displeasure against Moses' sin, though he but lightly partook of the sin of the congregation, as utterly to refuse to suffer him to go over and possess the good land, and yet to suffer them, the children of that evil generation who partook more largely of their fathers' sin, to go over. God insisted on having a great outwardMS: "out." manifestation of his displeasure against the sin of that congregation. The death of so great a person, and so holy a person as Moses, the head of the congregation (who only was nearly related to them, and lightly partook of the evil of that degenerate time), was so, as God in a time of public judgments is pleased sometimes to slay the righteous with the wicked, whereby there is a so much greater and more awful testimony of his displeasure to the world (Ezekiel 21:3–4). God thus slaying Moses, and not suffering him to go in to the good land, God looked on the outward manifestation of wrath by this means to [be] sufficient, without slaying the congregation. And so the younger generation were spared, and suffered to go in to the good land. Thus Moses' death was a kind of atonement for the congregation as to temporal judgments and manifestations of God's wrath in this world, and so he was an eminent type of Christ.

Deuteronomy 4:24. "A consuming fire."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 766.

Deuteronomy 4:28. "Gods."] SSS.Ibid.

Deuteronomy 4:30. "Even in the latter days."] By this it appears that oftentimes by "the latter days" in Scripture is only meant "many ages hence," for this has respect to their captivity into Babylon. See note on Numbers 24:14. See also Deuteronomy 31:29.This reference is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 4:31–34.] The things here mentioned are mentioned as evidences of that peculiar favor and covenant mercy mentioned in the Deuteronomy 4:31. That they should "hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst

<!-- p. 283 -->

of the fire," as they had heard, and yet live Deuteronomy 4:33], and therein be distinguished from all others, was a great evidence of it. If God had not had a peculiar regard to them, they would have died when they heard and saw such things. And the following things were further testimonies of the same peculiar favor.

Deuteronomy 4:32–34.] That which is here mentioned is spoken of as the wonder of wonders: "That a people should hear God speaking to them out of the midst of the fire," such a devouring fire, that was so terrible to behold, that had such peculiar manifestations of God's awful majesty, and his consuming justice and vengeance (See Deuteronomy 5:25.), "and yet live." 'Tis not to be supposed that God would speak of this as so exceedingly and beyond all parallel wonderful, but that he had in his eye that which is, indeed, the wonder of wonders, and which is often spoken of as such by the Prophets, and which God's people are the subjects of through Jesus Christ. Through him we hear God speaking to us "out of the midst of the fire." God manifests himself to us in all his dreadful majesty, and most terrible and strict justice. And yet we live; we are safe. God appears to us as a strict judge and terrible revenger ofJE deleted "iniquity." all sin, and yet as our Savior and a fountain of life to us. God is just, and yet the justifier of him that believes in Jesus. Although this that the children of Israel were the subjects of at Mt. Sinai is here spoken of as so exceeding wonderful, yet this which is accomplished by Christ is spoken of as so much more wonderful, that these things, which God did for the children of Israel when he brought 'em out of Egypt, are represented as no more worthy to be mentioned or remembered after God had wrought this (Jeremiah 16:14–15, and Jeremiah 23:7–8, and Isaiah 43:18–19). Balaam does, in effect, say that these things that God wrought for Israel, when he brought 'em out of Egypt, are typical of that wonderful astonishing thing which he would work for them in the latter days. Numbers 23:23, "According to this time" (or agreeable to what God had done at this time), "it shall" (hereafter) "be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought?" See also Micah 7:15. The context is a full proof that this was what God had in his eye when God spoke to the children of Israel from Mt. Sinai in so terrible a manner. It was in giving the law. And thus God's people have God speaking to them from Mt. Sinai in all ages, for they all hear God's voice in his holy strict law. God's appearing at that time as a consuming fire, without doubt, was a representation of the thing spoken here in the Deuteronomy 4:24, "The Lord thy

<!-- p. 284 -->

God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God." And the words of the text we are upon are brought in as an evidence of what is spoken of in the immediately preceding verses, viz. God's forbearing to execute justice on the people for their wickedness, and his forgiving their iniquities in the exercise of his great mercy, and his faithfulness to the covenant of grace made with their fathers.

Deuteronomy 4:36.] The voice here is said to be "out of heaven," but the fire on earth, whereas we are often told that the voice was out of the midst of the fire. But ['tis] probable, the Holy Spirit in such a manner of expression has an eye to the antitype of what was seen and heard at Mt. Sinai, viz. what shall be seen and heard at the day of judgment, when the voice will be out of heaven, and the fire on earth.

Deuteronomy 5:5.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 767–68.

Deuteronomy 5:7–8.] That the First Commandment has respect to worshipping other gods, but the second has respect to worshipping the true God by images, is confirmed by Deuteronomy 4:15–18. The people were in danger of representing God by some image of bird, or beast, or some other animal, because the Egyptians, that were a neighboring nation and a people among whom they had dwelt, represented all invisible things by images and hieroglyphics.

Deuteronomy 5:15.] See "Miscellanies," no. 691, § 11.*Works, 18*, 268–69.

Deuteronomy 5:25.] Any very great fire is terrible, but it seems that this fire, which represented the wrath that those were in danger of that violated the law then given, had something peculiarly and inexpressibly terrible in its appearance, so that it greatly affrighted the children of Israel only to look on it, and filled them with awful apprehensions that they should be slain. And so the voice was answerably terrible; whence we may argue the inexpressible dreadfulness of the future misery of the wicked.

Deuteronomy 5:26. "Hath heard the voice of the living God out of the midst of the fire, and hath lived."] These words, with the context, lead [me] to suppose that the apprehension that seemed to be so generally fixed in the minds

<!-- p. 285 -->

of God's people of old arose from a tradition handed down from the ancient patriarchs, that sinful men could not have immediate access to God and intercourse with him, who is a consuming fire, and that the presence of God, and to have to do with him directly without a mediator, would be the sinful creatures' immediate destruction. See Exodus 33:20, Genesis 32:30, Exodus 24:11, Judges 13:22–23. See SSS on Exodus 33:20.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 497. See Deuteronomy 5:24 of this ch., and Deuteronomy 4:33; Judges 6:22–23. From Judges 13:22–23, it appears that this notion was not from an apprehension that death would be the natural consequence of so great and terrible a sight, but that sinful men in such a case would be exposed to be slain by the anger of God.This sentence is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 6:3. "As the Lord God of thy fathers hath promised thee."] This shows that a blessing that was promised before may be given in reward for what is done long after the promise is absolutely made. See my *Treatise on Justification*, pp. 95–96.In *Justification by Faith Alone*, JE writes, "Believers having a Title to Heaven by Faith antecedent to the Obedience, or it's being absolutely promised to them before, don't hinder but that the actual Bestowment of Heaven may also be a Testimony of God's Regard to their Obedience tho' performed afterwards." He cites the promise of multiplying his seed given to Abraham as an example of a reward long after the promise (*Discourses on Various Important Subjects, Nearly concerning the great Affair of the Soul's Eternal Salvation* [Boston, 1738]). See *Works, 19*, 216. See Deuteronomy 6:18–19.

Deuteronomy 6:4. "The Lord our God is one Lord."] "Miscellanies," no. 1105.*Works, 20*, 487–88.

Deuteronomy 6:13. "Swear by his name."] See no. 468.Ibid., *15*, 556–61.

Deuteronomy 6:25. "And it shall be our righteousness."]JE marked the initial six paragraphs of this entry with a vertical line near the left margin. This may be understood either, first, in a legal sense, as declaring the condition of the covenant of works, in the same sense as that, Leviticus 18:5, "Ye shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them," according to the Apostle's own interpretation of them (Romans 10:5). God dealt with his church of old, before Christ came to reveal the glorious gospel, more in a legal manner. The Mosaic dispensation was a legal dispensation of the covenant of grace. God at Mount Sinai did really reveal and propose the covenant of works to Israel (though he did not reveal that only); he proposed it to them for their trial and conviction, and that

<!-- p. 286 -->

they might by the law be shut up to the faith in the grace of God. But this is not the only sense it is to be understood in. But, secondly, it is also doubtless to be understood in an evangelical sense (as I suppose that also in Leviticus 18:5 is). And thus if we keep God's commandments, it shall be our righteousness in two respects.

1. As it is the sign and evidence of our beingJE deleted "justified." accepted of God as righteous. Such a manner of speaking is often used in the Old Testament. Things are said to be this or that, when it is only intended that 'tis a sign or token of it. Yea, obedience is a condition of acceptance with God as righteous, and the condition that was chiefly revealed and insisted on in the law of Moses. See "Miscellanies," no. 659.*Works, 18*, 198–99. This interpretation sufficiently answers Moses' design and drift in this text, which is to excite the people to obedience by showing them the great benefit and advantage of it to them by reason of its connection with their acceptance with God as righteous, and accordingly dealing graciously with them, which Moses was speaking of in the Deuteronomy 6:18–19, and the Deuteronomy 6:17.

2. The sincere obedience of the saints is their righteousness, as 'tis that which God has respect to (beholding of them, as in Christ), as meet to be rewarded upon the account of the loveliness there is in it, in the manner which is explained, "Miscellanies," no. 627.Ibid., 155–56. So that 'tis their righteousness on the account of which God has respect to them in a secondary manner.

The children of Israel were in no danger of being led by this expression (if they duly considered it) to trust in their own righteousness to the prejudice of free grace, for its being in such a manner promised, as it here is, that it should be accepted as their righteousness, plainly shows that in itself it is not a righteousness, and is so only as God is pleased of his grace to promise to accept it, and impute it to 'em as such. If it were in its own nature a righteousness, and could in reason challenge to be accepted of God as such, what need of making such a particular promise, that "it shall be our righteousness," as though it was our righteousness, because God would make it to be so, or would by his grace put the value of a righteousness upon it? Galatians 3:18, "For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise; but [God] gave it to Abraham by promise." Also Romans 4:14. This promise here, that if they would obey God's commands,

<!-- p. 287 -->

it should be their righteousness, is plainly as much as if it had been said that it should be counted to 'em for righteousness, which shows plainly that 'tis of grace, as Romans 4:2–5. And besides, reason would tell 'em that nothing else but perfect obedience was a righteousness in itself, or could be accepted as such any otherwise than by grace. The contrary is absurd. They could not think that the breaches of the law could be forgiven without grace, or that that partial obedience that there was could be accepted as a conformity without grace, and the many severe threatenings and declarations of God's strict justice and jealousy that were contained elsewhere in the law sufficiently guarded against any such interpretation. So that, though the particular ground or reason of the acceptance of a sincere obedience as a righteousness was not explained, viz. that Christ has covered the defects, or done them away in his blood, and put a value upon our good works by his merits, yet it was revealedJE deleted "sufficiently." in the general that it was of mere grace.

And this is not inconsistent with what I have written in "Miscellanies," no. 647,*Works, 18*, 187–88. viz. that to suppose obedience the condition of being in Christ, as a moral fitness for it, is contrary to the doctrine of justification by faith alone.JE crossed out the following: "because that doctrine either derogates from the freedom of grace or our dependence on Christ, for if it be a condition of being in Christ as a moral fitness, then either 'tis not of grace."

Because what is here said of obedience being accepted as a righteousness is only general, of which the doctrine of justification by Christ in the New Testament is a particular explication, it explains the reason and manner of what is here generally revealed. But the doctrine opposed in the forementioned 647th "Reflection" is directly contrary to that gospel explication.JE's vertical "use line" ends with this paragraph; "Reflections" was JE's early title for the "Miscellanies."

In the originalתִּהְיֶה־לָּנוּ צְדָקָה it is, "Righteousness shall be to us," or "with us." In the Septuagintἐλεημοσύνη ἔσται ἡμῖν. it is, "Mercy shall be to us," which rendering of the Septuagint seems to be the true meaning. "For as the Hebrew word rendered 'righteousness' is very often put for mercy (Psalms 24:5, and Psalms 36:10, and Psalms 51:14; Proverbs 10:2, and Proverbs 11:4; Daniel 9:16, etc.), so this sense seems best to agree with the Scripture use of this phrase, in which 'righteousness' seldom or never, but grace and mercy frequently, are said to be 'to us' or

<!-- p. 288 -->

'with us,' as 2 Samuel 15:20, Psalms 89:24, Proverbs 14:22, Galatians 6:16, 2 John 3. And with the foregoing verse and argument, God, saith he, 'commanded us these things, for our good, that he might preserve us alive, as it is this day' [Deuteronomy 6:24]. And, saith he in this verse, This is not all, for as he hath done us good, so he will go on to do us more and more good; and God's mercy shall be to us, or with us, the remainder of our lives, and forever, 'if we observe,' etc." See Poole's *Annotations*.*Annotations, I*, no pagination. A great confirmation of this explanation is Jeremiah 51:10, where the Prophet, speaking of the deliverance of the Jews out of Babylon, says, "The Lord hath brought forth our righteousness. Come, and let us declare in Zion the work of the Lord our God"; especially if we consider this verse with other parts of this prophecy that are so inconsistent with our understanding [of] it, that they were delivered out of captivity upon the account of their good works.

The righteousness of God, as his holiness, is in the Old Testament put for his moral perfection in general, which is principally displayed to the children of men in works of mercy to his people. It is to be considered that the grand objection in all the ages of the Old Testament against the moral perfection of God was the affliction and sufferings of the righteous. Therefore often is God's goodness to them, especially in bestowing their most peculiar privileges and highest rewards, called his righteousness, as being that which especially vindicates his moral character from this objection. See Psalms 92:15, with preceding verses. 'Tis to be observed that where God is spoken of as a rock and the proper object of the trust of his people, his righteousness, or moral perfection, is chiefly insisted as what, on the account of which, he is especially called a rock, as in that Psalms 92:15, and Deuteronomy 32:4, 1 Samuel 2:2.This paragraph is a later addition.

But upon further consideration, I think this is the true meaning. In the original it is, "It shall be righteousness unto us." It signifies as much as that God will remember it, and reward it, and give thee a blessing for it, for whatsoever is rewarded is rewarded as righteous. It seems plainly to signify the contrary of that expression, Deuteronomy 15:9, "and it be sin unto thee," i.e. I will remember it against thee, and punish it, and bring a curse on thee for it. The manner [of] expression in the original is the same. So Deuteronomy 24:15 and 1 Kings 13:34. This is confirmed by Deuteronomy 24:13, compared with Deuteronomy 24:15, and Psalms 106:31.This paragraph is another later addition.

When it is said, 1 Kings 13:34, "And this thing became sin to the house

<!-- p. 289 -->

of Jeroboam, to cut it off," etc., the meaning is not that this thing was looked up [on] asJE deleted "a deserving cause. what properly merited punishment, for so does all sin deserve to be punished as sin. But the meaning is that this should be remembered against Jeroboam and his family by God in his providence as therein appearing sinners, wicked men, and God's enemies, and shall be treated accordingly. So here when it is said, this "shall be our righteousness," 'tis not meant this shall be esteemed as the thing which properly merits or recommends to God's favor and a title to happiness, but that this God shall as it were remember and set before his eyes in his providence as an evidence of our being righteous, and his treating us accordingly as good men, God's friends. When God takes occasion from men's works, which manifest 'em to be good men, to treat 'em accordingly, then their good works, in the sense of this text, prove to be righteousness unto them. But that is not the same thing as to be the price that recommends and gives title to God's favor, and that happiness which is the fruit of it.

See "Controversial Papers," p. 153b.This reference is a later addition. JE's reference is to a discussion of the words צֶדֶק and צְדָקָה, translated "righteous" and "righteousness," as properly forensic terms, in a subsection of the notebook entitled "Of the Meaning of the Words 'Righteous,' 'Righteousness,' etc. in the Old Testament." He notes that these are sometimes "put for that reward which the good judge assigns to the good," as in Deuteronomy 6:25. Other times they are "put for that in the person judged, to which the judge annexes the reward of righteousness." JE's discussion in the "Controversies" Notebook cross-references this location in the "Blank Bible" ("'Controversies' Notebook: Justification," *Works, 21*, 347).

It is evident it was the manner of the Hebrews, with regard to many things of a moral nature, to call the fruit, consequence, or recompense of a thing by the same name with the thing itself. So the punishment of sin, or that misery that is the consequence of it, is often called by the same [name] of sin. Besides the places which have been already mentioned, we may to the purpose observe Job 4:8. "They that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, shall reap the same." Psalms 7:14, "Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood." Proverbs 22:8, "He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity." Hosea 10:13, "Ye have plowed wickedness; ye have reaped iniquity." 1 Samuel 24:12–13, "The Lord shall avenge me of thee, but mine hand shall not be upon thee. As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked, but mine hand shall not be upon thee," i.e. misery proceedeth from the wicked, is the fruit produced by their wickedness. Proverbs 16:5, "Though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished." In the

<!-- p. 290 -->

originalיִנָּקֶה לאֹ it is, "shall not be held innocent." Proverbs 28:20, "A faithful man shall abound with blessings, but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent," shall not be unpunished. That is much the most probable and natural sense. Proverbs 10:16, "The labor of the righteous tendeth to life, the fruit of the wicked to sin."This paragraph is another later addition. The next four paragraphs are another later addition.

So the verbs "sin," "err," etc., are often used to incur or suffer punishment, calamity, or misery. Proverbs 10:17, "He is in the way of life that keepeth instruction, but he that refuseth reproof erreth." See the foregoing verse. Proverbs 14:21–22, "He that despiseth his neighbor sinneth; but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he. Do they not err that devise evil? But mercy and truth shall be to them that devise good." Proverbs 19:2, "Also, that the soul be without knowledge is not good, and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth." See Job 5:24.JE crossed out a cue sign here pointing to "The words *aven*…"

So the word "folly" is put for that confusion and misery that is the fruit and end of folly. Proverbs 16:22, "Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it, but the instruction of fools is folly." But see not.JE interlined these last three words. He marked the paragraph with a vertical line in the middle of the entry.

TheJE crossed out a cue sign at the front of this word, pointing back to the end of the second last paragraph. words *aven*אָוֶן and *gnauvel*,עָוֶל etc., which properly signify iniquity, are often put for calamity in the Hebrew Bible, as Proverbs 22:8, Job 5:6 and Job 15:35, Isaiah 59:4–5. Proverbs 12:21, "There shall no evil happen to the just" (no iniquity, *aven*), "but the wicked shall be filled with mischief." Jeremiah 4:15; Psalms 55:10; Psalms 90:10, "labor and *sorrow*" (*aven*); Habakkuk 1:3 and Habakkuk 3:7.

So the words translated "vanity," they seem indifferently to signify both sin and misery.

"And it shall be our righteousness." No more can be understood by it than that it shall be a sign and evidence of our righteousness. All that Moses intended by it was that it would be sure sign and token that we are accepted and justified of God. Such a manner of expression is often used in Scripture. Things are said to be this or that, when it is only intended that it is a sign or token of it.This paragraph is a separate entry. JE marked it with two large "X" s, perhaps because of its close parallel with materials in the second paragraph at the beginning of the Deuteronomy 6:25 entry.

<!-- p. 291 -->

Deuteronomy 7:2.] See SSS on Joshua 9:15.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 957–58.

Deuteronomy 8:4. "Thy raiment waxed not old upon thee."] Which probably was a type of the durableness of the spiritual clothing of the spiritual Israel in their journey through the wilderness of this world towards the heavenly Canaan. The saints' grace or righteousness is often represented as their clothing. "Neither did thy foot swell." If their feet had swelled, they would not have been able to go any further. But the righteous shall be enabled to hold on his way; and God will keep the feet of his saints, and establish their goings. This seems to be the chief reason why this is remarked, viz. because it was a type. For in itself it seems no very remarkable thing that their foot did not swell, for they lay still most of the time, and did not travel at all; and when they did, it is probable it was not by long journeys, but as the women and children could bear. 'Tis not likely that they traveled more in that forty [years] than is common for men of settled habitations to travel in such a space of time. It was in itself remarkable on no other account than this, that the ways were exceeding rough, representing the way of the saints towards heaven. Their way is full of difficulties and obstacles, but God will enable 'em to go through 'em all.

Deuteronomy 8:17.] If it was so dangerous, and a thing so much to be guarded against, then undoubtedly it is very ill and very dangerous for persons to ascribe their title to the blessings of the heavenly Canaan to their own strength. God led the people through the great and terrible wilderness before he brought 'em to Canaan, to show 'em their own weakness and impotency, to fit ['em] for the comforts of that good land. They that ascribed their possession of Canaan to their own strength, it was a sign that their hearts were lifted up, and that they did not humbly rely on God (Deuteronomy 8:14). And so it was a sign that their hearts were not upright in them, and so if they ascribed it to their own righteousness, as Deuteronomy 9:4–6. See Habakkuk 2:4.

Deuteronomy 9:5. "And that he may perform the word which the Lord sware unto thy fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."] Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob herein are types of Christ. God saves us, not for our righteousness, but that he may perform the promise which he made to Christ, our spiritual father, in the covenant of redemption.

Deuteronomy 9:21. "And I cast the dust thereof into the brook that descended out of the mount."] This brook in all probability was the water out of the rock,

<!-- p. 292 -->

for that rock was in Mount Horeb (Exodus 17:1–8), the mount that is here spoken of, as in Deuteronomy 9:8. If there had been any other brook there before, it would not be said that "there was no water for the people to drink," as Exodus 17:1. There would have been no such murmuring for want of water, nor would there have been occasion to fetch water out of the rock. From the dryness of the place, the mountain was called Horeb, which signifies dryness. This brook that came forth out of the rock, and that descended out of the mount of God, was a type of the Holy Spirit, the same with Ezekiel's waters that come out of the temple [Ezekiel 47:1–12], and the same with the "pure river of water of life that proceeded out of the throne of God and the Lamb" [Revelation 22:1], and the same with those "rivers of living water," spoken of, John 7:38–39, which we are there told is meant of the Holy Spirit. The idol of the children of Israel is ground to powder, and the dust of it cast into this brook, to signify that 'tis by God's Spirit that God consumes idols, and destroys the kingdom of Satan. The same seems to be signified by Hezekiah's casting idolatrous altars into the brook that watered Jerusalem, God's holy city. 2 Chronicles 30:14, "And they arose and took away the altars that were in Jerusalem, and all the altars for incense took they away, and cast them into the brook Kidron." See also 2 Chronicles 29:16.This reference is a later addition. We are told, Exodus 32:20, that Moses "made the children of Israel drink" of the water, but that was no otherwise than as he strewed the dust on that brook, which the congregation wholly depended on for drink, and so were obliged to drink of it. Their drinking that water in which their idol was consumed was a type of repentance, in which men are made partakers of and have the influences of that Spirit that destroys those sins, and consumes those idols that they formerly were devoted and addicted to.

There is another thing also that perhaps is more especially intended by that which we have here an account of. There seems to be a special respect to this, Psalms 99:8, speaking of Moses and Aaron." Thou answeredst them, O Lord our God. Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions, "which is agreeable to the history of this affair in the Exodus 32, where we have an account of God's pardoning the people on Moses' intercession, but vengeance was taken on the calf they had made. The idols of the people are called their" inventions. "So Psalms 106:28–29." They joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead. Thus they provoked him to anger with their inventions." And Psalms 106:38–39, " They sacrificed

<!-- p. 293 -->

unto the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood. Thus they were defiled with their own works, and went a-whoring with their own inventions." God's fierce wrath and vengeance was typically executed to the full on the golden calf. Those things were done to it that are made use of to signify the merciless executions of God's wrath in the perfect destruction of him that is under guilt. Moses "burnt it with fire, and stamped it, and ground it" to powder, beat it "very small, even till it was as small as dust." And that brook that this dust was mixed with signified the blood of Christ, for it was as it were the bleeding of that rock that had been wounded by the rod that smote it; and that rock was Christ. The calf, in thus having vengeance executed upon it, being cast in its utter destruction into this brook, signifying that the sin of those who are pardoned of God has full vengeance taken on it in the blood of Christ, their calf is here called *their sin*. The water of this brook was the drink of the children of Israel with this destroyed and ruined calf in it. And thus it is that believers do by faith drink the blood of Christ, viz. as an atonement for their sins, or as that in which their sin is fully punished, and perfectly destroyed, and justice fully satisfied.This paragraph is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 10:6. "The children of Jaakan."] Who this Jaakan was, see SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 778–79.

Deuteronomy 10:14–15.] See "Miscellanies," no. 1116.*Works, 20*, 492.

Deuteronomy 10:18. "The fatherless and the widow, and loveth the strangers."] From the many things in the law of Moses to this purpose, the heathen nations seem to have received the same notion. "So speaks EumaeusThe faithful swineherd of Odysseus in Homer's *Odyssey*. unto Ulysses, when he entertained him as a poor stranger. 'O stranger! It is not lawful for me, though one should come more miserable than thou art, to dishonor or disregard a stranger; for strangers and poor belong to the care of God.'" Deuteronomy 11:10.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 782–83.

Deuteronomy 11:24.] The land was not given in this extent, but a small part of it, till David's time. Then first the people had given 'em the promised land fully, though the people probably expected immediately upon their entering into the land. This is an instance of the gradual fulfillment of the promises that God makes to his church. So the promises made toJE deleted "the Jews." God's people when they should return from Babylon, in the main things contained in them, were not fulfilled till Christ came, and will not have their fullest accomplishment till the last calling of the Jews. Deuteronomy 12:5.] God forbore to choose him a place in Israel for his settled habitation to place his name there till the days of David, which was a manifestation of the displeasure of God against that people for their frequent transgressions and apostasies. HeI.e. God. refused to settle his abode among them as long as they remained soMS: "to." unsteady in his service and so perverse in their ways, but walked in a tent and in a tabernacle, as ready to depart, or at least undetermined whether to stay with them or not, and yet in his great goodness loath to leave them, but at last did actually depart from them when he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh. But remembering his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he returned again, but then stayed in the border of the land, as though it was to see whether they would reform or no before he would again enter in amongst them. But when on long trial it proved that they never were like to appear worthy that he should be with them, at length David, a great typical mediator, appeared. God for his sake came into the midst of the land, and chose him a place in Israel "to put his name there," and took up his settled abode there, and instead of a tent dwelt in a temple. God speaks of it to David as an instance of his peculiar favor to him that he now at length consented to settle his abode, that he had never moved any such thing before, andGrosart overwrote this word with "David." had spoken of having an house built for him (2 Samuel 7).

<!-- p. 295 -->

And [God]This is Grosart's interpolation. there declares that for his sake heHere Grosart overwrote an illegible word with "he." would show favor to Israel, "and would plant 'em, that they might dwell in a place of their own," etc. Deuteronomy 12:10]; and it is often mentioned afterwards as the reason why he did not cast off Israel.

This is another instance of God's deferring the accomplishment of that which, by the manner of prediction, was expected to be accomplished immediately upon their being settled in their own land. (See note on Deuteronomy 11:24.) So Daniel seemed to expect an immediate accomplishment of the glorious things that were to be brought in by the Messiah on the return of the Jews from Babylon. See note on Daniel 9:23–24. So the primitive Christians seemed to expect Christ's last coming to accompany the destruction of Jerusalem.

Deuteronomy 15:9. "And it be sin unto thee."] Sin here is put for calamity, misery, or ruin, because that is the consequence of sin. Thus the word sin is often used in Scripture. So Deuteronomy 24:15. "Lest he cry against thee unto the Lord, and it be sin unto thee." So Deuteronomy 23:21–22. "For the Lord thy God will surely require it of thee, and it would be sin in thee." 1 Kings 12:30, "And this thing became sin, for the people went to worship the one, even unto Dan." 1 Kings 13:34, "And this thing became sin unto the house of Jeroboam, even to cut it off, and to destroy it from the face of the earth." righteous tendeth to life; the fruit of the wicked to sin." So probably it is to be understood. Proverbs 24:9, "The thought of foolishness is sin." (See note on that place.) See also Hosea 8:11.

So "iniquity" is a word often used in like manner in Scripture to signify both sin and its punishment, both moral evil and natural evil, or misery and destruction.

Deuteronomy 18:15. "The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a prophet," etc.] Let us understand this which way we will, either of Christ the great prophet

or of those prophets that were successively raised up in Israel, 'tis a great confirmation of the true religion. If we understand it of the latter, it confirms that those prophets that were raised up from time to time and spoke in the name of the Lord, whose writings we have delivered down to us, were true prophets. For it was promised by God by Moses that such there should be; and if there were any, these were they. I believe that respect is here had both to Christ and to the successive prophets in Israel, though the former principally. If it be not here foretold that there should be prophets from time to time in Israel, yet undoubtedly 'tis implicitly foretold in the Deuteronomy 18:22, and in the beginning of the Deuteronomy 30, where the children had rules given to distinguish true prophets from false in all generations, which further confirms that these prophets, whose writings are transmitted to us, were true prophets, and proved so by these rules.

Numbers 12:6–8, "If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream. My servant Moses is not so.… With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches," in the Hebrew,בְחִידֹת וְלאֹ "not in enigmas." Deuteronomy 20:19. "For the tree of the field is man's life."] It might have been rendered much more agreeable to the original,הַשֶּׂרֶה עֵץ הָאָדָם כִּי "for man is a tree of the field." It was God's will that a fruitful tree should not be cut down, but only trees that yielded no meat, because trees with respect to their barrenness or fruitfulness represented man. And therefore he would men deal with them as he deals with men. This is an argument in the law of Moses itself that its commands were given from some typical respect.

Deuteronomy 21:22–23.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 829–31.

Deuteronomy 21:23.] See no. 121.*Works, 15*, 84–85. The manner of the Israelites in pursuance of this institution used to be to let them hang till the sun was down, and then to take the bodies down and bury them, as is evident by Joshua 8:29 and Joshua 10:26–27. God did not see meet that [that] which was a curse and execration should remain in open sight for an abomination to the pure eyes of the God that dwelt in that holy land.JE deleted "all night." They were therefore to remove such abominable things out of God's sight, that God might dwell and walk in the land, and not withdraw from it. See Deuteronomy 23:13–14. But 'tis very probable that one reason why those that were hanged and accursed were to be taken down and buried as soon as the sun was down was that the sun was a type of Christ, and in setting was a type of the death of Christ. See note on Luke 23:44. The bodyMS: "Curse." was to be removed and buried as soon as the sun was set, to signify that the curse is removed by the death of Christ, for he in dying was made a curse for us. And the curse, by his death, is taken from the earth, or at least from the land of Israel, or the

<!-- p. 299 -->

land of the church, so that that land is not defiled. God's people have not the curse remaining amongst them to render them abominable to God, and to cause him to depart from them. Their sins and abominations are buried forever out of his sight by Christ's death. Indeed, it was so ordered that the body of Christ, though it was hanged on a tree, was taken down and buried before sun setting. The Jews took it down before, that it might not remain in the open air on the sabbath day (John 19:31). This seems to be so ordered because Christ, though made a curse, was not such a curse as was removed by what was typified by the setting of the sun; but he was the antitype itself.

"Remember," etc.] Doubtless what God here says supposes that they had special need to beware of sin of that kind, and that such sin as that of Miriam was what God knew they were in peculiar danger of, and in danger of suffering the awful effects of God's sore displeasure by; and so it has proved. Miriam was one that had been highly privileged. She was a prophetess, and was Moses' sister. And from pride of her high privileges and favors she had received of God and her sacred distinction, [she] envied Moses, and was displeased with him, and openly opposed him because of the Ethiopian woman that he had married. <!-- p. 300 -->

or Jewish church or people, rose in open opposition to Jesus Christ, though he was one of themselves, was their brother, from pride of their privileges as a holy people near to God, a people that God had distinguished by revealing himself to them so that to them belonged the oracles of God. From this root of spiritual pride they envied Christ the peculiar honors which he appeared to have above them, and because he professed to be the Son of God, and far above them in divine privilege as the peculiar friend and favorite of God. They found fault with him for conversing with publicans, and sinners, and Gentiles, and [for] intimacy as it were with Ethiopians. And after his ascension to heaven, [they] were enraged at the calling of the Gentiles, and admission of the Gentile church to such a high privilege of being the spouse of God. On this account especially they persecuted Christ in his members. Miriam's sin especially represents the sin of the Jewish priests and scribes, who were proud of their peculiar sacred privileges, and were in a peculiar manner the bitter persecutors of Christ on the forementioned accounts.

Moses was a type of Christ in a peculiar manner in those things which God said of him on that occasion, Numbers 12:5–8: [he was] more than a prophet, the friend and servant of God, who was "faithful in all his house," with whom God spake "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches," etc. And the punishment of Miriam well represented the punishment of the Jews for their opposing Christ. Deuteronomy 25:12–13.] This rule, besides what it literally forbids, seems also to have a mystical signification, and to be equivalent to that great rule of equity that Christ says is "the Law and the Prophets" [Matthew 7:12], of doing to others as we would that he should do to us, for that is to measure to others in the same measure in which we would have them to measure to us.

<!-- p. 301 -->

For persons not to do to others as we would that they should do to us is to have diverse measures, one for us to give to our neighbor in, and another for us to receive from our neighbor. When persons conform to this rule, their work is said to be pure and right, and is compared to his not having "diverse weights and diverse measures" (Proverbs 20:10).

Deuteronomy 28:45–68.] Mr. Henry supposes that "the former part of the commination," in this chapter in the verses foregoing, "foretells the Jews' captivity in Babylon, and the calamities which introduced and attended that, by which even after their return they were brought to that low and poor condition described, Deuteronomy 28:44. But that here in this latter part, he foretells their last destruction by the Romans, and their dispersion thereupon.

And," says he, "the present deplorable state of the Jewish nation, and of all that have incorporated themselves with them by embracing their religion, doth so fully and exactly answer this prediction here in these verses, that it serves for an uncontestable proof of the truth of the prophecy, and consequently of the divine authority of the Scripture. And this last destruction, being represented more dreadful than the former, it shows that their sin in rejecting Christ and his gospel was more heinous and more provoking to God than idolatry itself, and left them more under the power of Satan. For their captivity in Babylon cured them effectually of their idolatry in seventy years' time, but under this last destruction now above 1600 years, they continue incurably averse to the Lord Jesus. Deuteronomy 28:46, it is said, these curses 'shall be upon thee for a sign and a wonder.' It is amazing to think, that a people so long the favorites of heaven should be so perfectly abandoned and cast off; that a people so closely incorporated should be so universally dispersed; and yet that a people so scattered in all nations should preserve themselves distinct, and not mix with any, but like Cain be fugitives and vagabonds, and yet marked to be known. Deuteronomy 28:49, 'The Lord shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the ends of the earth, as swift as the eagle flieth.' Our Savior makes use of this similitude in foretelling this destruction: that 'where the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together' (Matthew 24:28). And Bp. PatrickSimon Patrick (1625–1707), Bishop of Ely, wrote numerous commentaries on the books of the Old Testament. observes, that to make the accomplishment the more remarkable, the ensign of the Roman armies was an eagle. Deuteronomy 32:2. "My doctrine shall drop as the rain; my speech shall distill as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, as the showers upon the grass."] God here speaks to the peopleJE deleted "instructs, warns, and counsels them quite in a." quite in a different manner from what he did at Mount Sinai, when he spake to them out of the midst of the fire with a great and terrible [voice] that was not suited to their tender frame, and that exceedingly [did] terrify them, and was ready to destroy them. God's word then was like thunder, and lightning, and devouring fire, overbearing and consuming so frail and tender a creature as man, who is like the grass and flower of the field. God's voice now is gentle, delivered in a pleasant song, and instead of being like lightning to destroy and consume, is like the gentle showers and refreshing dew to the tender grass, instructing, reproving, warning, revealing, not only his wrath but his great mercy, in a manner adapted to man's tender frame. Here is much of the glorious gospel in this song; and even the warnings and threatenings that are in it are delivered in an evangelical manner, much in the same way that they were delivered by the gentle voice of the glorious Messiah. All the songs of Scripture are the voice of the gospel. The glorious things of the gospel are their foundation and subject matter; and therefore in them God's word "drops as the rain," etc.

Deuteronomy 32:4.] A rock for "strength," for sure "defense" (Psalms 18:2, Isaiah 33:16). A rock for lastingness, durableness. God is "everlasting" (Isaiah 26:4). A rock for faithfulness and immutability, as a rock is stable and immovable, which seems more especially to be aimed at in this verse. See Job 18:4. A rock for a sure foundation (Matthew 7:24). As a rock is solid, sound, and weighty, so is God "perfect" and no way defective in his nature or any of his ways, as it follows in the next clause.

The rock is the more fitly made use of to represent God because of its height, for they were wont to call the rocky mountains rocks whose sides

<!-- p. 305 -->

were high, steep rocks. Psalms 61:2, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." Job 14:18, "Shall the rock be removed out of its place," meaning one of these high mountains of rock. And so Nahum 1:6, "The rocks are thrown down by him." Tis manifest that rocky mountains were called rocks, by 1 Samuel 23:26–28. There we find that the mountain that divided between Saul and David is called *sela hammah lekoth*,הַמַּהְלְקְוֹת סֶלַע i.e. "the rock of divisions."These last two sentences are a later addition to this paragraph. God may be compared to these great rocks, for the reason as he was represented by a cloud, viz. their majesty. And by reason of the safety and inaccessibleness of these high rocks, he that dwells on them dwells on high out of the reach of trouble and danger. Isaiah 33:16, "He shall dwell on high; his place of defense shall be the munitions of rocks." They were commonly wont to build their fortresses upon such high rocks. See Deuteronomy 33:29. God is said to be "an high place" (Psalms 9:9, Psalms 46:7). The mountain that divided David from Saul is called a rock (1 Samuel 23:26–28). 'Tis called *sela hammah lekoth*, i.e. "the rock of divisions."This paragraph is a later addition.

'he hath corrupted to himself,' or, 'that they are not his children,' that is, 'their blot.'" Glas translates the words thus: "The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are judgment. God of Truth, and without iniquity, just and upright is he. A perverse and froward generation hath destroyed him; their spot is not of his children. Deuteronomy 32:5. "Their spot is not the spot of his children."] In all probability here is a reference had to those spots mentioned in the thirteenth ch. of Leviticus, where are rules for the trial of spots, whether they were leprous spots or no. There are many spots there mentioned that somethingI.e. somehow. resembled the leprosy, notwithstanding which the diseased person was to be pronounced clean, and might still be looked upon as of the congregation of Israel, and allowed the privileges of such. But if the spot was, upon trial, found to be a leprosy, he was to be separated from the congregation.

<!-- p. 306 -->

His spot was not the spot of God's people, and he was not to be looked upon as one of 'em.

Deuteronomy 32:8. "He set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel."] It is observable that the number of nations by which the earth was peopled (Genesis 10) was just the same with the number of the children of Israel that went down into Egypt (Exodus 1:5 and Genesis 46:27), as Henry observes in his notes on Exodus 1:5. "When the earth was divided among the sons of men, in the days of Peleg after the flood [Genesis 10:25], and each family had its lot, in which it must settle and by degrees grow up into a nation, then God had Israel in his thoughts and in his eye, for designing this good land into which they were now going, to be in due time an inheritance for them. He ordered that the posterity of Canaan, rather than any other of the families then in being, should be planted there in the meantime, to keep possession as it were till Israel was ready for it, because those families were under the curse of Noah, by which they were condemned to servitude and ruin (Genesis 9:25), and therefore would be the more justly, honorably, easily, and effectually rooted out, when the fullness of time was come that Israel should take possession. Thus he set the bounds of that people with an eye to the designed number of the children of Israel, that they might have just as much as would serve their turn. And some observe that Canaan himself, with his eleven sons (Genesis 10:15), make up just the number of the twelve tribes of Israel.… The early designation of the land of Canaan for the inheritance" of the children of Israel rendered it "a type of our heavenly inheritance, that it was of old ordained and prepared." Henry, *in loc*.*Exposition, 1* (1725), 498.

Deuteronomy 32:11. "As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings."] "Eagles are observed to have a strong affection to their young, and to show it not only as other creatures, by protecting them, and making provision for them, but by educating them, and teaching them to fly. For that purpose she stirs them up out of her nest, where they lie dozing, flutters over them to show them how they must use their wings, and then useth them to fly upon her wings, till they have learned to fly upon their own." Henry.Ibid., 498–99.
