Deuteronomy 32:13. "On the high places."] I.e. fortresses of their enemies. See note on Deuteronomy 32:4 and Ezekiel 36:2.This opening paragraph is a later addition.

"He made him to suck honey out of the rock," etc. This is signified by it in the general, that God is wont to bring good to his people out of those things that have no good in 'em in their own nature, seem the most unlikely to yield it, things that men would be ready to imagine such good could not come from. AndJE deleted "particularly." hereby is signified the great good God's people have from Christ, a poor, obscure, despised man, in whom they saw" no form, or comeliness, "or beauty, that they should desire" [Isaiah 53:2]. They esteemed him not. He was "a root out of a dry ground" that seemed most unlikely to yield such excellent fruit. The people could not imagine that they were to receive the glorious blessings spoken of in the prophecies from a person of such a form and appearance. For other reasons, likewise, is Christ compared to a rock here, as he is in the Deuteronomy 32:4 and other places of the chapter. This also is signified by the verse, that God causes good to arise to 'em when in a state wherein they are very remote from it, and one would think it impossible that they should receive it. God gives them oil and honey in the wilderness, where there is nothing but dry sands and barren rocks, which is represented by the rock's yielding it to them, by an elegant metaphor not unlike to Scripture metaphors. Thus God did by Israel, for "he found him in a desert land," as in Deuteronomy 32:10. See Isaiah 35:6, Deuteronomy 8:15.

And as God's supplying Israel with such excellent provision in a dry, barren, desolate wilderness represents the excellent spiritual provision that God makes for and bestows upon sinners who, as sinners or as they are in a natural condition without that provision, are in a most wretched, destitute, famishing, lost condition, and as it were in a vast howling wilderness, so God's making them "to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock," represents God's causing the grace and excellent consolations, like oil and honey, to flow out of their hearts that are naturally as a flinty rock.See JE's sermon on Deuteronomy 32:13, entitled *Honey from the Rock*, preached fall 1730, with one of its three doctrines as, "By causing his people to receive such great blessings from Jesus Christ, he does, as it were, cause them to suck honey out of a rock" (*Works, 17*, 132–36). As Christ says, "Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" [John 7:38]. See note on Exodus 17:6.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 873.

<!-- p. 308 -->

Deuteronomy 32:14. "Fat of the kidneys of wheat… pure blood of the grape."] See "Shadows of Divine Things," nos. 68 and 149.*Works, 11*, 73, 102–3.

"And thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape." 'Tis a further evidence that God intended wine, which is the juice squeezed or pressed out of grapes, to be a type of the blood of Christ shed under his extreme sufferings as a sacrifice, that the word used in Genesis 40:11 for pressing grapes in order to get thence wine is the same that is used for killing or sacrificing. When the chief butler, relating his dream, says, he sweeted or "pressed the grapes into Pharaoh's cup," the words are *vaeshchat otham*.אֹתָם וָאֶשְׂחַט Now the word *shachat*שָׂחַט signifies "to sacrifice" or "to cut the throat," as they did in sacrificing, and is everywhere so used, as appears by the Hebrew concordance.Buxtorf defines שָׂחַט in a primary way with *macto* and *jugulo*, "to sacrifice" and "to kill or cut the throat," respectively. The use in Genesis 40:11 he associates with *exprimo*, "to press or squeeze out" (*Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum* [6th ed.], p. 760). See also John Taylor, *Hebrew Concordance*. It is not known if JE owned Taylor's volume, which is not mentioned in the "Catalogue." The same information found in Buxtorf appears in Taylor's entries nos. 1913–14 in vol. 2 under שחט, with the contrast drawn between *mactare/jugulare* and *exprimere*. And this text is mentioned as the only exception where it is used to squeeze or press grapes, which is a great argument that the pressing of grapes was a type of the sufferings of Christ, the antitype of the sufferings and death of their sacrifices of old.This paragraph is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 32:15. "Jeshurun."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 874.

Deuteronomy 32:20, Deuteronomy 32:29.] The end of the children of Israel spoken of in these verses, so far as hereby is intended their end as a people, respect is chiefly had to their destruction by the Romans, which was properly their end as a people. It was their end as the peculiar people of God, and the end of the Jewish state and church, and as it were the end of the world. In the Deuteronomy 32:20 it is said, "I will hide my face from them. I will see what their end shall be, for they are a very froward generation, children in whom is no faith." Thus God hid himself from the Jews before their destruction. Then in a remarkable manner he blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes. And that threatening of Christ was fulfilled, "Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me" [John 7:34, John 7:36]. Then were the things that belonged to their peace hid from

<!-- p. 309 -->

their eyes. And then, above all other times in the world, did they show themselves to be a "froward generation." And their great condemnation was that they had no faith. Christ tells 'em, "He that does not believe is condemned already, because he hath not believed on the only begotten Son of God" [John 3:18]. In the Deuteronomy 32:29, it is said, "O that they were wise, that they would consider their latter end," which is much like the exclamations of Christ over Jerusalem when he speaks of her approaching destruction by the Romans. "O that thou hadst known, at least in this thy day the things that belong to thy peace; but now they are hid from thine eyes," etc. [Luke 19:42].

Deuteronomy 32:21. "I will move them to jealousy with those that are not a people," etc.] This is a prediction of the rejecting the Jews, and calling the Gentiles. See Romans 10:19.

Deuteronomy 32:22.] The same word in the originalשְׁאוֹל signifies both the grave and hell. So the same wordמָוֶת which we translate "death" signifies both temporal death and damnation; one is the image of the other. The horrors of the grave, they are an image of the doleful, horrible darkness and misery of hell. The dolors and agonies of death are an image of the amazing dolors of the damned.

'Tis an awful description of the terribleness of the wrath of God against ungodly men, especially such as live under means of grace, that we have in this verse. "A fire is kindled in mine anger, and it shall burn to the lowest hell." That is, the fire is so great, and the heat of it so intense, that it shall heat and burn the earth, even to its most inward and lowest parts. This is meant, as is evident by what follows. It shall "set on fire the foundations of the mountains." How great and intense must that fire be which burns the earth to its center.

"Unto the lowest hell." SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 875.

Deuteronomy 32:33.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 877–78.

Deuteronomy 32:35.] Here God begins on a new subject. Before he spoke of punishing his professing people by the cruelty of their enemies; now he speaks

<!-- p. 310 -->

of vengeance on their enemies for that cruelty as upon their enemies, when he shall be about gloriously to deliver his people from their hands. The same thing is further insisted on, the Deuteronomy 32:40 and following verses; and then the consequent joy and prosperity of his church is spoken of Deuteronomy 32:41. This vengeance and this mercy shall be fulfilled, especially at the calling of the Jews and fall of Antichrist.

Deuteronomy 32:50.] See no. 113.*Works, 15*, 82–83.

"And die in the mount whither thou goest up." See Deuteronomy 34:5 note.This reference is a separate entry.

Deuteronomy 33:2. "The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them."] What was called Mt. Seir included all that mountainous part of Arabia that was the country of Edom, of which Mt. Sinai was a part. See notes on Jeremiah 17:3. When the children of Israel were in that wilderness, they were within the bounds of the country of the Edomites, which made the Amalekites, which were Edomites, come forth against them to battle, as they did soon after they came into that wilderness (Exodus 17). Mt. Sinai is here represented as that which was God's dwelling place. It was the holy mountain; it was called the mount of God. There God appeared to Moses in the bush; and God in Deuteronomy 33:16, is said to have dwelt in that bush. And therefore whenever God appeared to the children of Israel in the wilderness, when he first came to them in the pillar of cloud and fire, when he fought for them at the Red Sea, when the cloud came and abode on the tabernacle and the glory of the Lord filled it, and whenever he remarkably appeared, it is represented as rising up or coming forth from thence. Because that was represented as God's dwelling place, therefore when God had brought them, 'tis represented that God had brought them to himself (Exodus 19:4).

"From his right hand *went* a fiery law for them." The words seem to be something wronged in the translation. The word "went" is not in the original but is supplied. And if the word "proceeded" or "came" had been supplied, it might more naturally have led us to what Moses had respect [to], which seems to be God's writing the law with his right hand on the two tables of stone, and then delivering them with his right hand, thus engraven to be for the people, as he did the two first tables that were the workmanship of God. And also the other two that Moses had made were delivered to Moses out of God's hand, after he had written the law on

<!-- p. 311 -->

them. But the sense seems to be wronged in the translation more in rendering the words "a fiery law for them." The words in the originalלָמוֹ אֵשׁדָּת are "a fire of law for them," i.e. to be for a light to them, or for a fire to enlighten, as the pillar of fire was for a light to them in the night; for the commandment is a lamp, and the law is a light. The same seems to be meant here as is expressed, Isaiah 51:4. "For a law shall proceed from me, and I will make my judgment to rest for a *light* of the people." This best agrees with the foregoing words, wherein it is said that God "shined forth from Mt. Paran." And 'tis more natural to understand it thus, for 'tis said to be "for them." If it was a light to enlighten them, it is more natural to say 'tis for them than if it were a fire threatening to consume them. And this sense much best agrees with the following verses and their evident connection with these words, which speak of God's great love and grace in giving them this law, and how it was given as an inheritance to them, and with what pleasure and delight they received it. "Yea, he loved the people; all his saints are in thy hand. And they sat down at thy feet; everyone shall receive of thy words. Moses commanded us a law, even the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob" Deuteronomy 33:3–4].This paragraph is a separate entry. See note on Job 28:5.This sentence is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 33:5. "Jesurun."] The nameיְשֻרוּן by which Israel is here called is the "upright one," signifying that they only are truly God's Israel or Israelites indeed, but those that are upright or without guile, as Christ says of Nathanael, "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile" [John 1:47].

Deuteronomy 33:7.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 884–85.

"Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people." So David was brought to his people as their prince, after being driven out and banished by Saul, and again after he was driven out by Absalom. Solomon was brought to his people, after he was excluded by Adonijah. Christ was brought to his people to be their king, after the family of David had long been excluded from the throne by powers of the four monarchies and by other enemies. Christ, after he was thrown away by the Jews, was brought to have a place in the building, and to be the head of the corner. He will be brought to his people again, after he has been long as

<!-- p. 312 -->

it were driven away by Antichrist. And he will come to his people at the end of the world for their most complete and eternal salvation, after driven out by Satan operating in Gog and Magog, and after all the instances of his expulsion and exclusion by all his enemies through all ages of the world.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Deuteronomy 33:8. "And of Levi he said, Let thy Thummim and thy Urim be with thy holy one, whom thou didst prove at Massah, and with whom thou didst strive at the waters of Meribah."] Here Christ is evidently called Levi's "holy one." Aaron, the high priest of that tribe, was Levi's "holy one" in some sense. But it was not Aaron, but Christ that was tempted at Massah and Meribah (1 Corinthians 10:9). Moses was of that tribe, and might also be called their "holy one"; but neither was he the person there tempted. Yea, both Moses and Aaron there rather concurred in the temptation (Numbers 20:10–13). Christ, the great antitype of Moses and Aaron, the true high priest that was the substance and end of all the ancient sacrifices, and offerings, and of all the peculiar ministrations of the high priest of the tribe of Levi, according to Jeremiah 33:17–22, Christ may well be called Levi's "holy one," for it is there represented as though the great honor and privilege of Levi in its having the office of the priesthoodJE deleted "should." be upheld and completed in Christ. For all the honor and privilege which there ever was in having the priesthood of their tribe arose from the relation of that priesthood to Christ, and the glorious things which he should accomplish in his sacrifice and intercession, and the eternal benefits he should procure. And therefore the actually existing and appearing of Christ, the great and true high priest, and actually accomplishing these glorious things, and procuring these eternal benefits, are the sure substance and perfection of all the honor and privilege which belonged to their office. And therefore this is properly mentioned in Moses' blessing of this tribe, for it shows their privilege above all other things inasmuch as herein it appears that their priesthood was no vain thing. It was unspeakably valuable, and of infinitely good effect as it stood in relation to the priesthood of Christ, and should be brought to its glorious and infinitely blessed effect in him. It was by the Thummim and Urim that the high priest was especially furnished to enter into the holy of holies to make atonement and intercession for the people there once a year, and was enabled to teach the people, and reveal the mind and

<!-- p. 313 -->

will of God to them. But this typical Thummim and Urim were nothing but as they relate to and were typical of the perfection, merits, light, and glory that was in Christ. In Christ having this perfection, glory, and merit, and this sufficiency to be the light of the world, Levi's Thummim and Urim were fulfilled, and so honored and magnified. That spoken of and promised concerning the priests, the Levites, in that, Jeremiah 33:17–22, is manifestly the chief of all blessings of God's covenant with that tribe, as that which promised in the same place concerning the house of David is the chief thing promised in God's covenant with David, which is a thing that much confirms that this is the great thing here intended in Moses', blessing of this tribe.

Deuteronomy 33:12. "The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in safety by him."] I.e. Benjamin, being "the beloved of the Lord, shall dwell in safety" by the Lord. Paul, the great apostle, was of this tribe, who perhaps above all mere men was "the beloved of the Lord."

"And he shall dwell between his shoulders." Which seems to allude to a custom of parents carrying their children on their backs or between their shoulders, agreeable to the custom of the Indians here in America. The same thing seems to be alluded to again in Isaiah 49:22, and perhaps also in the parable of the lost sheep in Luke 15:5.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Deuteronomy 33:14. "The moon."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 888.

Deuteronomy 33:16. "And for the good will of him that dwelt in the bush."] *Ques*. Why is God here mentioned under this appellation, "of him that dwelt in the bush," when speaking of his good will? *Arts*. Because by his dwelling in the bush was typified his incarnation. He "that dwelt in the bush" was Christ. And by the grace and love of Christ Jesus, God-man, it is that Joseph and all God's people are blessed. See note on Exodus 3:2–3. See note on Exodus 19:3.

Deuteronomy 33:17. "With them shall he push the people together to the ends of the earth."] This was fulfilled in Joshua and Gideon that were of this tribe. Joshua drove the nations away "to the ends of the earth," and drove 'em together there to make room in the middle for God's people. And there was a great gathering of innumerable multitudes from "the ends of the earth" that were destroyed by Gideon.

<!-- p. 314 -->

Deuteronomy 33:18–19. "And of Zebulun he said, And they shall call the people unto the mountain. There they shall offer the sacrifices of righteousness. For they shall suck the abundance of the seas, and of treasures hid in the sands."] This seems to have respect to the calling of the Gentiles by the preaching of the apostles, who were of Galilee and probably chiefly of the tribe of Zebulun, which was that part of Galilee where Christ was chiefly conversant. 'Tis evident the mountain here meant is the mountain of the house of the Lord, the place of offering sacrifice. And the event referred to by their calling "the people to the mountain" seems to be that prophesied of, Isaiah 2:2. And Isaiah 27:13, "The great trumpet shall be blown." And the offering "sacrifices of righteousness," etc., is the same with that spoken of, Isaiah 60:7 and Isaiah 66:20. And their sucking "the abundance of the sea, and treasures hid in the sand," seems to have reference to what is foretold in Isaiah 60:5, Isaiah 60:9, Isaiah 60:16, and Isaiah 66:12. The success of the apostles was chiefly in gathering the people that dwelt in the sea or beyond the sea, called in prophecy "the islands of the sea." And therefore, as they were fishermen before their calling, and gathered the fullness of the sea for their food, so Christ, when he called them, told them he would make them "fishers of men" [Matthew 4:19], to gather the multitudes of men that were as it were the inhabitants of the sea.

Deuteronomy 33:20. "Blessed be he that enlargeth Gad."] See 1 Chronicles 5:18–22.

Deuteronomy 33:21. "And he provided the first part for himself, because there, in a portion of the lawgiver, was he seated. And he came with the heads of the people, and he executed the justice of the Lord, and his judgments with Israel."] "They chose their lot with the first, in a country already conquered.… Though he had a concern for his brethren, yet his charity began at home. He was willing to see himself first served, first settled. The Gadites were the first and most active movers for an allotment on that side Jordan, and therefore are still mentioned before the Reubenites in the history of that affair (Numbers 32:2). And thus while the other tribes had their portion assigned them by Joshua the conqueror, Gad and his companions had theirs from Moses the lawgiver. And in it they were 'seated' by law, or (as the wordסָפַן is) 'covered,' or protected by a special providence which watched over them that were left behind, while the men of war went forward with their brethren.… They came with the heads of the people, before whom they went armed over Jordan, to

<!-- p. 315 -->

execute the justice of the Lord upon the Canaanites, under the conduct of Joshua to whom, we afterwards find, they solemnly vowed obedience (Joshua 1:12, Joshua 1:16). This was what they undertook to do when they had their lot assigned them (Numbers 32:27). This they did (Joshua 4:12). And when the wars of Canaan were ended, Joshua dismissed them with a blessing (Joshua 22:7)." Henry.*Exposition, 1* (1725), 508.

Deuteronomy 33:23. "O Naphtali, satisfied with favor, and full with the blessing of the Lord."] This probably has respect to Christ's dwelling in this tribe. Capernaum and Bethsaida were in this tribe. And though the greater part of the people rejected Christ, yet many of the Galileans believed on him, and were made happy in him; and the privileges that only some particular persons of a tribe were the subjects of are in divers instances mentioned in Moses' and Jacob's benedictions of the tribes.

"Possess thou the west and the south." "It may be read 'the sea and the south," i.e. of that sea which shall lie south of thy lot, that was the sea of Galilee, which we so often read of in the gospels, directly north of which the lot of this tribe lay, and which was of great advantage to this tribe. Witness the wealth of Capernaum and Bethsaida, which lay within this tribe, and upon the shore of that sea." Henry.Ibid.

Deuteronomy 33:25. "Iron and brass."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 893.

Deuteronomy 33:26. "Who rideth on the heavens in thine help, and in his excellency on the sky."] The universe is the chariot in which God rides, and makes progress towards the last end of all things on the wheels of his providence; and the place of the chariot, in which God has his seat, is the highest heavens, as in Psalms 68:33 and also Psalms 68:4. The pavement of the chariot, above which God's throne is, is the firmament or the sky, as Ezekiel 1:25–26. (See notes on the Ezekiel 1 concerning Ezekiel's wheels.) Therefore this verse signifies as much as that God governs the whole world for the good of his church; the wheels of the chariot of the universe move for them; and the progress that God makes therein in his throne above the firmament, the pavement of this chariot, is for them; and every event in the universe is in subserviency to their help and benefit.See *Concerning the End for Which God Created the World, Works, 8*, 508.

<!-- p. 316 -->

*Corol*. Hence it was meet that Christ, when he came to be invested with the government of the universe as head over all things to the church, to govern the motions of this chariot, and make progress in it for their help and salvation, should ascend into the highest heavens above its pavement, to sit on the throne of this chariot. And therefore in the Psalms 68, which is on the subject of Christ's ascension, mention is made once and again of God's riding on the heavens, as Psalms 68:4 and also Psalms 68:33.

The under part of the wheel of a chariot seems to run backward, but it is not so. The whole machine is constantly moving forward toward the journey's end. So when the church of God is brought low in the world, 'tis like that part of the wheel that is brought next the ground. The course of things seems to be backward, away from the proposed and promised end; but 'tis a mistake. God is still constantly making progress towards the church's promised glory.This paragraph is a later addition.

"There is none like the God of Jeshurun, who rideth," etc. Jeshurun, *from jasher*,יָשָׁר "upright." See Wilson's *Christian Dictionary*.In an entry entitled "Jesurun, or Jeshurun," Thomas Wilson writes, "That is, (as the *Chaldee* explains it) *Israel*; the *Greek, beloved*.… It hath the name of *Jasher*, righteousness, as being a righteous people by calling, having Laws right and equall, if they had walked in them" (*Complete Christian Dictionary*, p. 308). Israel is here properly called by this name here, for what in account is the spiritual Israel, the congregation of the upright, as the true church of God is called (Psalms 111:1).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Deuteronomy 33:29. "Thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee."] I.e. liars in theirJE deleted "threatenings." boastings and menaces.JE added this paragraph as a later addition.

"And thou shalt tread upon their high places." I.e. their fortresses built upon high rocks and steep. That is, thou shalt conquer and take their strongest places, and take possession of them. God is said to be "an high place" (Psalms 9:9 and Psalms 46:7), that is, a fortress or refuge.

Deuteronomy 34:5. "So Moses, the servant of the Lord, died there," etc.] Moses brought the children of Israel into the wilderness and to the very borders of Canaan, but carried them no further. There he left them. And it was not Moses, but Joshua, or Jesus, that carried them over Jordan, and brought them into Canaan to the promised rest, and gave them possession

<!-- p. 317 -->

of the land flowing with milk and honey, which seems to signify to us that we can never obtain heaven or saving blessings by the law. Moses, who gave the law, seems here to signify the law. The law brings persons into the wilderness, that is, can bring souls under convictions, and leads 'em on in [to]Grosart's interpolation. the wilderness. It carries along in that work that is preparatory to saving grace and comfort, even till they are brought to the very borders of Canaan, till they are brought to a next preparation for conversion and comfort; but there it leaves them. It can carry them no further. It cannot bring them over Jordan into a state of salvation; that must be done by Jesus, or the spiritual Joshua. All the use of the law is to lead men on in their wilderness travel, and when it has done that, and brought them to the borders of Canaan, or to a next preparedness for a state of salvation, there it dies. John 1:17, "The law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ." Hebrews 7:19, "For the law made nothing perfect, but the bringing in of a better hope did, by the which we draw nigh unto God." See note on Joshua 1:2.This reference is a later addition.

Deuteronomy 34:10–12.] Thus the book of the law concludes with something that leads to Christ, what is here said naturally tending to lead all to wait for the fulfillment of that great promise which God made to the congregation of Israel at Mt. Sinai, when they were in trembling fear through the awful manifestations of God's holy majesty that we read of, Deuteronomy 18:15–18, which there seems to be a reference to in these words. And thus the Old Testament concludes in the Malachi 4, and thus the prayers of David conclude (Psalms 72), and thus David ends all his sayings in his last words (2 Samuel 23).

<!-- p. 318 -->

### Joshua

Joshua 1:2.] As soon as ever Moses is dead, God commands Joshua, or Jesus, to lead the people over Jordan. So as soon as ever men through the law are dead to the law, they are fitted for the comforts of Canaan. When Moses, or the law our first husband, is dead, we are at liberty to be married to a risen Savior, and so to [be] brought to the possession of Canaan that is his inheritance. See note on Deuteronomy 34:5, above.

Joshua 2:1.] Joshua, just after God had encouraged him and promised to give him Canaan, and that no man should be able to stand before him all the days of his life [Joshua 1:5], proceeds with great caution, and sendsMS: "send." messengers to spy out Jericho, that he might know the better how to enter into the land and attack the city.

Joshua 2:18–19.] Faith is made the condition of Rahab's kindred as well as her own. They were to retire to Rahab's house and not stir out, which they would not do unless they believed that God would indeed deliver that city and land into the hand of the children of Israel, as he had said, and would destroy their enemies and save their friends. As in the old world, they that believed that God would destroy the world as he had said, fled to the ark. And in Egypt, they that believed that God would accomplish what he had said concerning the hail and fire, retired to their houses beforehand and were saved. And in Jerusalem, they that believed what Christ had said about Jerusalem's destruction, fled out at the signal that Christ gave them and were saved. And in Jerusalem's first destruction, they that believed that God would destroy the city as he had said by the prophet Jeremiah, went and submitted themselves to the king of Babylon and were saved. Rahab, as she was the mother of Christ, so her house in this case was a type of the church, or of the house, the habitation, and fortress of the church, Christ Jesus, where the righteous dwell in safety, and where they must hide themselves till the indignation be overpast,

<!-- p. 319 -->

and from whence they must not depart, but must be found in him at the hour when judgment comes in order to their being saved.

Joshua 2:20.] It was needful that Rahab should keep counsel in this matter, lest they should be betrayed when they were gone, or lest others should tie scarlet lines in their windows.

Joshua 3:3–4.] Christ shows us the way to heaven by his example. He is gone before us to heaven. We must go our journey, run our race, "looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith" [Hebrews 12:2]. Christ's word and example is to be exhibited to the view of the church by ministers, as the priests and Levites exhibited the ark to the view of the congregation of Israel (that they might follow it) when they were going through Jordan to Canaan.

Joshua 3:15–16.] God brought his church out of the wilderness into Canaan at a time when the waters of Jordan, that were in the way to keep them out, were at their greatest height. So when God shall bring his church out of its low, obscure, afflicted state to its latter-day rest and prosperity, the obstacles in the way of it will be at their greatest height and in their greatest strength, such as infidelity, libertinism, contempt of the true gospel of Christ, and luxury, and profaneness, and contempt of vital piety. These things shall be greatly advanced, carried with an high hand, and shall prevail like a flood that scorns all control.

Joshua 3:15–17.] Israel's passing over Jordan was not like their passing the Red Sea: that was in a dark night with thunder, lightning, and rain; thisMS: "that." was in the daylight. So the last conflict of the church with her enemies, just before the church enters into her state of peace and rest, will not be like some preceding conflicts, though her enemies shall be like Jordan overflowing all its banks [Joshua 3:15]. In this last conflict the church shall fight in white garments. In the former, the witnesses are clothed in sackcloth, etc. See "Revelation," my exposition concerning "The Slaying of the Witnesses."*Works, 5*, 201–8, 210–17.

Joshua 3:16.] The lake of Sodom into which Jordan emptied itself was a type of hell. It was a lively type of hell on many accounts. The fire by which

<!-- p. 320 -->

Sodom and the neighbor cities were destroyed is expressly called eternal fire. The river Jordan (that was a swift river), whose waters were constantly and swiftly flowing into that lake, represents the continued flowing of multitudes (that are in Scripture often called "waters") into hell. The lake of Sodom was never full, though these waters incessantly flowed into it; so hell is never satisfied. The waters must be supposed to have some subterraneous passage from that lake by which they were as it were sucked down into the lower parts of the earth and as it were into hell, which makes the type the more lively. These waters shall be in a great measure cut off when our Jesus, or Joshua, comes to bring his spiritual Israel into Canaan at the latter day by that work which was an antitype of this work of Joshua that we have an account of in this book. Then shall the great stream that constantly flowed down to hell fail. This shall [be] at the time of God's spiritual harvest, spoken of, Revelation 14, as Joshua's bringing the people through Jordan was at the time of harvest. Just before the waters were then cut off by Joshua, they flowed in more than ordinary plenty, it being a time when Jordan overflowed all his banks; so just before Christ shall do this for his church in the latter day, it will be a time of great wickedness and degeneracy.

Secondly, these sweet waters of Jordan represent the means of grace, which was one thing represented by Ezekiel's waters of life [Ezekiel 47]; so the waters of Jordan represented in healing Naaman's leprosy [2 Kings 5:14]. And the lake of Sodom in this case represents the same as those miry places and marishes in Ezekiel's vision that were given to salt, never to be healed by the living waters however constantly and plentifully flowing by them. Therefore the waters being cut off when Joshua comes represents the awful judgment of God on reprobates who had long abused means of grace. When Christ shall come, these means they have enjoyed shall be taken from them. They shall be miserably destroyed, and all streams of mercy shall be cut off from them.

Lastly, this river flowing into the lake of Sodom represents the supplies of the kingdom of Satan, and especially the Church of Rome that is spiritually called Sodom, and so represents the same that the river Euphrates did in old Babylon. These shall be dried up when the spiritual Joshua shall come. Thus the sixth vial was poured out "on the great river Euphrates, and the waters thereof were dried, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared" [Revelation 16:12]. As there the river Euphrates represents two things that the literal river Euphrates was to old Babylon, viz. its supply and its defense, so here Jordan, to Sodom and the land about, used formerly to be a supply when it was well watered everywhere

<!-- p. 321 -->

as the garden of the Lord, and now was a supply to the lake of Sodom. But to Jericho, another type of the kingdom of Satan, it was a defense. It is evident that the destruction of Jericho was a remarkable type of the destruction of Satan's kingdom by the spiritual coming of Christ in the latter days. The dividing Jordan therefore, to make way for the enemies of Jericho to come from the east and destroy, was evidently a type of the same thing that is accomplished by pouring out the sixth vial.See "Apocalypse," *Works, 5*, 184–91, 200–201, 253–84, 298–305, for JE's detailed observations on the Sixth Vial.

Joshua 5:1–9.] "A mighty show, no doubt, the numerous camp of Israel made in the plains of Jericho where they now had pitched their tents. Who can count the dust of Jacob? That which had long been the church in the wilderness is now come up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved, and 'looks forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners' [Canticles 6:10]. How terrible she was in the eyes of her enemies, we are told, Canticles 6:1. How fair and clear she was made in the eyes of her friends, we are told in the following verses, by rolling away the reproach of Egypt." (Henry.)*Exposition, 2* (1725), 19. See Canticles 6:10 and Canticles 8:5.

Joshua 5:2. "Circumcise the children of Israel again the second time."] This was the second general circumcising of the congregation. The first was probably before the Passover they kept in Egypt. "While they had peace in Egypt" (as Mr. Henry says), "they doubtless circumcised their children the eighth day, according to the law. But after they began to be oppressed, especially when the edict was made for the destruction of their male infants, the administration of this ordinance was interrupted."Ibid., 20. But before the Passover, the night before they came out of Egypt, they were doubtless generally circumcised because it was then most strictly commanded that no uncircumcised person should eat the Passover. As now, this general circumcision in Gilgal was at the same time of year, just before they kept the Passover. See Joshua 4:19, and the Joshua 5:10. See SSS on Genesis 10:21 and on this place.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 133–34, 924–26.

Joshua 5:4, Joshua 5:6–7. "Them they had not circumcised."] Concerning their not circumcising the children that were born in the wilderness. Considering

<!-- p. 322 -->

the plainness of the precept of circumcision, and the strictness of the injunction, and that so great stress was laid upon [it], and that it was so expressly commanded that no uncircumcised person should eat of the Passover, which was with great strictness and often commands required most watchfully and diligently and without fail to be kept every year, and considering that the congregation in the wilderness was under Moses' government; I say, considering these things, 'tis unaccountable that all the children that were born for thirty-eight years together should not be circumcised, unless it was omitted by divine direction. "Some think God favorably dispensed with the omission, on consideration of the unsettledness of their state, and their frequent removes, and that stirring the children might be dangerous to them while they were sore. This reason is generally acquiesced in, but does not seem to be satisfactory, for sometimes they stayed a year in a place (Numbers 9:22), if not much longer, and in their removes their little children, though sore, might be wrapped so warm, and carried so easy as to receive no damage, and might certainly be much better accommodated than the mothers in travail or lying in. Therefore it rather seems to have been a continued token of God's displeasure against them. Circumcision was originally a seal of the promise of the land of Canaan. But when God had sworn in his wrath concerning the men of war that came out of Egypt, that they should be consumed in the wilderness, and never enter into Canaan, as that sentence is here repeated, Joshua 5:6, relation being thereunto had (and it seems to be here brought in as giving the reason of the omission), as a further ratification of that sentence, and to be a constant memorandum of it to them, all that fell under that sentence, and were to fall by it, were forbidden to circumcise their children." (Or rather, as I should think, Moses as the prophet of God, immediately under the divine direction, was restrained from putting them upon it, was ordered to let them alone, and leave 'em to their own negligent and disobedient hearts in this affair.) "This was such a significant indication of God's wrath, as the breaking of the tables of the covenant was, when Israel had broke covenant by making the golden calf." (Henry.)*Exposition, 2* (1725), 20. 'Tis probably they also generally omitted keeping the Passover, from the pronouncing of the sentence in Numbers 14, until now, for they never would have been tolerated in keeping the Passover from year to year in uncircumcision. The keeping of the Passover here seems to be mentioned as being now a new thing among 'em, as well as circumcision. This gives light into what is said, Joshua 5:9. God's suffering them

<!-- p. 323 -->

judicially to continue in uncircumcision for so long a time like the Egyptians, where their fathers for a long time had many of 'em lived in uncircumcision, for their hankering after Egypt and going about to make them a captain to return to Egypt, was a continuing of them under the "reproach of Egypt," which reproach was now "rolled away." Moses had told 'em while they were in the plains of Moab, Deuteronomy 12:8, that when they came into the land of Canaan they should not do as they did then, "every man what was right in his own eyes," which confirms that the omission of circumcision, the Passover, and other divine institutions was not from a divine prohibition, but rather from a judicial leaving them to themselves. See note on Amos 5:25.

Joshua 5:9. "And the Lord said unto Joshua, This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you."] This circumcision and rolling away "the reproach of Egypt" from the children of Israel at their first entrance into Canaan, as soon as ever they have passed Jordan, seems to denote the perfectly cleansing of their souls from all remainders of sin as soon as they have passed through death and at their first entrance into the heavenly Canaan. The saints have their hearts circumcised the first time at regeneration. The reproach of Egypt is partly rolled away at first going out of Egypt. Sin is then mortified, but not fully removed till they enter into the holy land by that second circumcision. "Reproach of Egypt." SSS on Exodus 10:21.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 356.

Joshua 5:11. "Did eat of the old corn."] The "country people" round about Jericho, when they saw this mighty company come over Jordan after such a manner, being exceedingly surprised, fled in the utmost haste and confusion into Jericho, and "left their barns and fields, and all that was [in] them, and their country houses, which served for the supply of this great army. "On the morrow after the Passover," they eat unleavened cakes and parched corn. This they could not do according to the appointment when they had nothing but manna to live upon. "They did eat the fruit of the land of Canaan that year" [Joshua 5:12]. "On the morrow after the Passover sabbath, they were to wave the sheaf of the first fruits before the Lord (Leviticus 23:10–11). And this they were particularly ordered to do when they were come into the land which God would give them; and they were furnished for this with the fruit of the land that year." Henry.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 21.

The elements, and the sun, and moon, and lights of heaven, were the deities at this time worshipped by the inhabitants of Canaan. But the Israelites were the servants of a truer God, by whose command, and under whoseJE deleted "direction." protection they were to war against these nations and their gods. And what greater demonstration could be given

of the power of their God to support 'em, or of the inability of the false deities of the Canaanites to assist their worshippers, than to see, that the God of Israel could cause these to contribute to, instead of preventing the ruin that [was] coming on those who served them?" Joshua 10:12. "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon, and thou, moon, in the valley of Aijalon."] Gibeon was the place that the sun appeared to stand over at that time, in the place where Joshua then was, and the valley of Aijalon, the place which the moon, which was also then visible, appeared standing over.

Joshua 10:12–13. "Thou, moon." The moon's standing still. This proves the truth of the history, for a circumstance of the sun's standing still being caused by staying the earth's diurnal revolution is mentioned, though the occasion of such a circumstance must be wholly unknown in those days to the Jews, which argues the truth of the fact. For nothing but the real fact, the means of which was wholly unknown, could have put this into the head of the historian.This entry was written later than the preceding entry. There is some ambiguity in JE's intention with the canonical citation. He referenced the entry from Joshua 10:12.

Joshua 10:13.] See nos. 117, 167, 207, and 209.*Works, 15*, 83, 98, 129–31, 134–35.

Now was a remarkable fulfillment of those words of Job 9:7, "Which commandeth the sun, and it riseth not, and sealeth up the stars," which words are a confirmation that the sun, moon, and stars all stopped as to their diurnal motion by the staying the revolution of the earth about its axis.This and the following paragraph are a separate entry.

In the song of Deborah it is said, "The stars in their courses fought against Sisera" [Judges 5:20]. The angels are called stars. Christ is often compared to the sun. Here we have all the heavenly hosts—the sun, moon, and all the stars—standing still to fight against the enemies of God's people, representing that Christ and all the heavenly hosts of saints (constituting the heavenly church, represented by the moon), and all the angels, are fighting against the enemies of the church. Hereby is typified that which is represented in prophecy in Revelation 19.

This was to render this great victory a more remarkable type of that

<!-- p. 327 -->

glorious victory that the church shall obtain over her enemies, which is spoken of in the latter end of the Revelation 16 and Revelation 19, which shall be attended with great hail (in a spiritual sense) as this was, when that time of the church's light and glory shall begin, spoken of, Isaiah 60:20, "Thy sun shall no more go down; neither shall thy moon withdraw itself," and Zechariah 14:6–7. See note on Zechariah 14:4–5 ff., especially at the latter end.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Moladah, 3. Hazarshual, 4. Azem, 5. Eltolad, 6. Hormah, 7. Ziklag, 8. Rimmon, and 9. Eder or Ether.

Joshua 18:28. "Which is Jerusalem."] The word is evidently compounded, the latter part being the name of the city in Melchizedek's time. The former part, "Jeru," signifies "they shall see," and is of the same radix with Moriah, and with Jireh in Genesis 22:8, where Abraham tells Isaac that "God will provide himself a lamb," and in the Genesis 22:14, where Abraham calls part of the ground of this city, or it may be the whole, Jehovah Jireh. The signification of the word "Jerusalem"יְרְוּשָׁלַם is "they shall see peace," agreeable to that in that Genesis 22:14 of the same place, "in the mount of the Lord it shall be seen."

Judges 2:7.] Agreeable to this are some traditions preserved concerning the Jews among the heathen, mentioned by Grotius, *de verit*., Bk. 1, Sect. 16. As he observes in his notes, "Strabo, in his fourteenth Bk., after the history of Moses, says, 'That his followers for a considerable time kept his precepts, and were truly righteous and godly.' And a little after he says, those who believed in Moses worshipped God, and were lovers of equity."*Truth of Christian Religion*, 63.

Judges 2:13.] Of this Ashtaroth, see Bedford's *Scripture Chronology*, p. 234.Bedford links Naamah, identified as the wife of Ham, who survived on the ark, called Ashtaroth (in Hebrew) or Astarte (in Greek), with Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, identified as Venus by the Romans.

Dr. Winder in his *History of Knowledge*, pp. 192 ff., observes that Ashtaroth is a wordעַשְׁתָּרוֹת that in the Hebrew signifies "flocks," and is so from time

<!-- p. 330 -->

to time translated, and supposes that the moon was the deity that was called "Ashtaroth, a name of office with regard to some particular expectations, which they had from that luminary, with regard to their flocks, they having a notion, that the moon especially presided over the night and governed its affairs. And that, in that season wolves and other beasts of prey range about, and robbers and spoilers often march forth to plunder and destroy, so in this time of danger their flocks will be especially exposed. And as a principal part of the wealth of those early ages consisted in their flocks, for these reasons they might particularly address themselves to the moon, who ruled the night, for protection, and worship this luminary under the name of Ashtaroth, or the guardian, των Ashtaroth, of their flocks."This paragraph is a later addition. *Critical and Chronological History* (2nd ed.), I, 192–94.

Judges 4:2. "Of the Gentiles."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1082–83.

Judges 5:10. "White asses."] The wordאֲתֹנוֹת signifies white "she-asses." "The judges in Israel were types of Christ," who came with great labor and doing a hard service, of which an ass was the hieroglyphic. They rode on she-asses, it being "the nature of those creatures to bring forth their young only in the dark, as Christ, by lying in darkness and the grave for a while, was to bring us forth to light and glory, viz. at his resurrection. And so we are called, Luke 20:36, 'the children of the resurrection.' And God is said 'to have begotten us again to a lively hope, by the resurrection of Christ from the dead' [1 Peter 1:3]; who, according to the promise, was to 'see of the travail of his soul, and be satisfied' [Isaiah 53:11]. And therefore he exults in spirit, and says, 'Behold I and the children, which God hath given me' [Hebrews 2:13]." (See Merrick's sermon on *Christ the True Vine*, p. 14.)Merrick, *Parable of the Vineyard and Christ*. Marshal Montagu Merrick (1719–82), an Anglican divine. The church also, who may be represented by the she-ass, brings forth when subject of much toil and labor, and when brought into great darkness.

<!-- p. 331 -->

Judges 5:11. "Righteous acts."] We find God's goodness often in Scripture called his "righteousness," the true reason of which seems to be that righteousness is a word of extensive meaning in Scripture, including all moral perfection. This is confirmed by Psalms 25:8, "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore will he teach sinners the way." See also Psalms 30:4.

Judges 5:14. "They that handle the pen of the writer."] This shadows forth the great hand that authors shall have in the great and last battle that the church shall have with her enemies, of which that, about which is this song, was a type.

Judges 5:15. "He was sent on foot into the valley."] Without chariots or horses, in which his enemies abounded.

Judges 5:15–16. "For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart."] I.e. for their division from the rest of Israel in this affair, that they did not come and join themselves with the rest of God's people in fighting against their enemies, it was much wondered. And therefore 'tis said of Reuben in the Judges 5:16, "Why abodest thou among the sheep-folds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks?" Ephraim, and Issachar, and Zebulun, and Naphtali are here commended for the hand that they had in this matter, but 'tis complained of Reuben, Gilead, and Dan, and Asher, that they stayed at home.

Judges 5:20.] When God is doing some great thing for his church on earth, the hosts of heaven are engaged with the church on earth; and hence God's army is a company of two armies. So when Jacob was going against Esau with his host, the host of heaven appeared with him at Mahanaim [Genesis 32:2]. Thus heaven is concerned in what is done for the church on earth. So when Christ goes forth to battle against Antichrist (of which this battle is a type), it is said the armies of heaven "followed him on white horses" [Revelation 19:14].

"They fought from heaven." See no. 211.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 140–42.

Judges 5:21. "That ancient river."] The river Kishon was probably so called because it was designed of old in the council of God to serve his purpose against Sisera at this time, and did so as if it had been made on purpose.

<!-- p. 332 -->

Thus the water of the old pool God is said to have fashioned long ago for that use to which it was put (Isaiah 22:11).

Judges 7:20.] Gideon and his company represents the church, and the army of the Midianites represents the host of the enemies of the church. The

<!-- p. 333 -->

earthen pitchers represent two things, viz. the frail human nature of Christ and also the ministers of Christ. The lamps that were in the pitchers representMS: "Represents." gospel truth and grace. Christ had this treasure in him when on earth, and the ministers of the gospel have this treasure in earthen vessels. By the breaking of the frail nature of Christ, the light of the gospel shone forth in the world; and the grace of God appeared to the salvation of his people, and the confusion of Satan and the enemies of his church. And the martyrdom of the ministers and saints of Christ has been made a means of propagating the gospel and confounding the enemies of the church. The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.This saying in various translations is identified with the African church father Tertullian (c. 160–c. 225 C.E.). B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, 1980), *III*, 55. The blowing with trumpets signifies the preaching the gospel.

that they devoted the place thus sowed with salt to everlasting desolation and emptiness. Probably it came to [be] thus used from what was observed of the providence of God with respect to Sodom, and the cities and country round about, that was effectually devoted to perpetual desolation by being covered with the salt sea. Judges 12:1–4.] "The Ephraimites had the same quarrel with Gideon (Judges 8:1), who was of Manasseh, on their side Jordan, as Jephthah was of Manasseh, on the other side Jordan. Ephraim and Manasseh were nearer akin than any of the other tribes, being both the sons of Joseph; and yet

<!-- p. 335 -->

they were more jealous one of another than any of the other tribes, Jacob having crossed hands, and given Ephraim the preference, looking as far forward as the kingdom of the Ten Tribes, which Ephraim was the head of, after the revolt from the house of David" (and that tribe having been preferred in the wilderness as the standard-bearing tribe, and Joshua being of that tribe). [Ephraim], "not content with that honor in the promise, was displeased, if Manasseh had any honor done it in the meantime. It is pity that kindred and relation, which should be an inducement to love and peace, should be ever an occasion (as often it proves) of strife and discord. A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and their contentions are as the bars of a castle." Henry.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 116.

Judges 12:4–6.] "Let us observe the righteousness of God in the punishment of these proud, passionate Ephraimites, which in several instances answered their sin. 1. They were proud of the honor of their tribe, gloried in this, that they were Ephraimites; but how soon are they brought to be ashamed or afraid to own their country. 'Art thou an Ephraimite?' No, now rather any tribe than that. 2. They had gone in a rage over Jordan to burn Jephthah's house with fire; but now they come back to Jordan as sneakingly as they had passed it furiously, and were cut off from ever returning to their own houses. 3. They had upbraided the Gileadites with the infelicity of their country, lying at such a distance, and now they suffer by an infirmity peculiar to their own country in not being able to pronounce 'Shibboleth.' 4. They had called the Gileadites unjustly 'fugitives,' and now they are really and in good earnest become fugitives themselves. And in the Hebrew, it is the same wordפְּלִיטֵי (Judges 12:5) that is used of the Ephraimites that escaped, or that fled, which they had used in scorn of the Gileadites, calling them 'fugitives.' He that rolleth the stone, or reproach unjustly upon another, let him expect that it will justly return upon himself." Henry.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 117.

"Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?"] This argues that this is the same person spoken of in the Isaiah 9:6, "To us a child is born," etc., "and his name shall be called Wonderful," which is the same word in the originalפֶּלֶא that is here rendered "secret." And what is said in the Judges 13:20 further argues it. See note on Isaiah 9:6. What is here said about the name of this person, compared with Proverbs 30:4, argues that it was the Son of God. See also Revelation 19:12.

Judges 13:19. "And offered it upon a rock."] That rock doubtless represented Christ, who is the rock of Israel, and is so often called a rock. Hence we may infer that the altars on which the legal sacrifices were offered were doubtless typical of Christ, especially the divine nature of Christ that sanctifies the gift and renders it satisfactory and meritorious, so that Christ is both priest, sacrifice, and altar. See note on Genesis 28:11–12. See Judges 6:20.

Judges 13:20. "For it came to pass, when the flame went up toward heaven."] See no. 139.*Works, 15*, 90.

Judges 13:25. "Camp of Dan."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1162.

Judges 14-16.] The history of Sampson, see no. 377.*Works, 15*, 361–62. Concerning his cleaving to the daughters of the Philistines and their proving his ruin.

Judges 14:5–6. "And, behold, a young lion roared against him. And the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him, and he rent him as he would a kid."] Thus it was to the lion's cost that he roared upon Sampson, though [he] roared upon him as his prey, and thought to have a sweet repast of him, and to satisfy his appetite on him; but when he expected to have rent Sampson, Sampson "rent him as [he] would a kid." Herein Sampson was a type of Christ who most effectually destroyed Satan in his last sufferings, when Satan did so dreadfully roar upon him as his prey. And Christ, by thus destroying him, caused that out of the eater should come forth meat, and sweetness out of the strong [Judges 14:14], agreeable to

<!-- p. 337 -->

the riddle Sampson put forth on occasion of his finding honey in the carcass of the lion that before roared upon him and that he had slain.

Judges 14:9.] Sampson's father and mother here seems to represent the old testament church that is often called hisI.e. Christ's. mother. The patriarchs, kings, prophets, and elders of the church were as it were his father. Many of these were his progenitors, as Adam, Seth, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, etc.; these were his fathers. Christ imparted to the people of God under the old testament the benefits of his conflict with the roaring lion and conquest of him in his death and resurrection, but did not particularly and clearly reveal to 'em the manner how these benefits were procured, as Sampson gave his father and mother the honey he took out of the carcass of the lion, but told 'em not that he took the honey out of the carcass of the lion. See note on Judges 14:17–18.

Judges 14:14. "Out of the strong came forth sweetness."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1165–66.

Judges 14:17–18.] Sampson's wife in this case represents the church, the spouse of Christ. Sampson, after a long time of his wife's weeping and sorrowing and earnest supplication to him, explained to her his riddle, which he had never explained to his father or his mother. So Christ revealed to his church in the gospel day the mystery of the gospel, which had been kept hid from ages and generations, after his church had long sorrowed and wept under her legal dispensation that bringsMS: "bring." sorrow and conviction of conscience. The law also stirs up earnest desires after the gospel, and moves to seek to Christ for his salvation.

On the seventh day Sampson told his wife the riddle. So Christ revealed the mystery of the glorious gospel to his church in the fullness of time in the latter day, and will most fully reveal it in the seventh thousand year of the world. The people learned the riddle by plowing with Sampson's heifer, or conversing with his wife. So it is in the church of Christ, by the teachings given in the church and by conversing with the saints, that persons come to a saving acquaintance with the mystery of gospel salvation. Sampson's companions won change of raiment by explaining the riddle. So do believers obtain spiritual change of raiment—by a saving knowledge of the mystery of the gospel.

<!-- p. 338 -->

Judges 14:20. "But Sampson's wife was given to his companion, whom he had used as his friend."] Sampson was a type of his wife. By nature a Philistine, of that people that were his great enemies, signifies Christ's church, naturally sinful, an alien and an enemy. Sampson's wife forsook him, and became an whore, and committed adultery with him who had stood in the place of groomsman, or the friend of the bridegroom at the wedding, this typifying the apostasy under Antichrist, the church of Christ forsaking him, yielding to the usurpation ofJE deleted "the man of sin, or the Romish clergy who." the clergy, and especially the bishop of Rome, and committing adultery with him, and so becoming the great whore. Ministers of Christ are, with respect to him as the bridegroom of his church, expressly compared to the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29). This may also refer to the apostasy of the Jewish church, and her forsaking Christ, and yielding to the usurpations of her false teacher, the scribes and Pharisees.

Judges 15:4–5.] Foxes represent heretics and heretical doctrines (See note on Canticles 2:15, and also Mr. Hellenbroek's sermon on that text, pp. 4 ff.).Abraham Hellenbroek, *A Sermon. From Canticks*, 4–12. Hellenbroek (1658–1731), a minister at Rotterdam, provided an extended comparison between foxes and heretics. In his sermon, preached in 1717 and translated in this edition, he sounded the theme that "if ever there was a time since the Creation, in which it might be said the Church *crawls* with all Kinds of Foxes, we must confess it is even in our Day" (p. 25). The sermon was translated and published in 1742. See *Works, II*, 43, 102. Christ will destroy the food and support of the enemies of his church by showing the inconsistency of false doctrines, by bringing them and comparing one with another to show that they can have no union, but have as it were a firebrand between. Then the great number of foxes represents the multitude of heresies that infect the church. Foxes also represent the crafty enemies of the church in general. Christ will destroy the food of the Philistines by setting the enemies of the church at variance one with another by causing them, against their wills, to counterwork each other, as he set the builders of Babel at variance, and as he often made the enemies of his people to kill one another, and so delivered Israel, as the Midianites before Gideon and other instances.

See SSS on the verse, and also see ibid., concerning the fables of the heathen derived from hence, this double mark || in the margin.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1169–72.

<!-- p. 339 -->

Judges 15:8. "And thigh."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, col. 1173.

Judges 15:15.] Sampson slays the Philistines with a jawbone, a despicable instrument. He triumphs over them in this, which typifies Christ's victory over Satan and his enemies by despicable means. He triumphed over principalities and powers in the cross (See note on Colossians 2:15.), and chooses "the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things of the world to confound the things that are mighty, and the base things of the world, and things that are despised, and things that are not, to bring to naught the things that are" [1 Corinthians 1:27–28].The remainder of this paragraph is a later entry. But especially by the "jawbone of an ass" here is meant the mouth or preaching of ministers, who are often compared to oxen, and here to the ass for its foolishness, ministers being in themselves weak, insufficient, blind, and foolish. And their preaching, which is the main instrument by which Christ destroys his enemies, is called "the foolishness of preaching" [1 Corinthians 1:21].

Judges 15:18. "And called on the Lord, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant; and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?"] As Sampson in most of his wonderful acts was certainly intended as a type of Christ, and his miraculous conflicts with and victories over his enemies shadows of Christ's great conflict with the powers of darkness and victory over them, so this that we have here an account of is probably a representation of Christ's intercession, by which he obtained the Holy Spirit after his sufferings, pleading those sufferings, that great battle and victory, and also the prayer of believers who are the members of Christ, or the church, which is as it were Christ, using that argument with God, that seeing God hath wrought that great redemption for us by that conflict and victory of Christ, may they not well think his mercy sufficient to give them the Holy Spirit, that living water, that they may not die for thirst and fall into the hands of the mortal enemies of their souls, which is the same argument which is mentioned, Romans 5:6–10 and Romans 8:32. Christ pleads this argument in heaven, for if his elect people perish with thirst, 'tis all one in his view and God's view, as if he perished with thirst. And he pleads this argument by his spirit (the spirit of faith and prayer in his saints). The Israelites'

<!-- p. 340 -->

binding and delivering up Sampson (as we have account in the foregoing part of the chapter) into the hands of the Philistines represents the Jews' binding, delivering up, Christ unto the heathen, and as it were to Satan and to death, in the time of his last sufferings. His bursting their bonds represents Christ's bursting the bonds of death when he rose from the dead. The victory he obtained afterwards represents the glorious victory of Christ by the preaching of the gospel consequent on his resurrection (see note on Judges 15:15). The great thirst that followed represents the exceeding low state of the church after that first victory whereby Christ conquered the Roman Empire, in the great withdrawings of the Spirit, especially in the times of Antichrist and in the present time. Sampson's crying to God for relief from his thirst represents the prayers and cries of the church of God for the outpourings of the Spirit with Christ's intercession. The abundance of waters from the jawbone represents the glorious and abundant outpouring of the Spirit with the foolishness of preaching that shall be in the latter days.

Judges 15:19. God's causing water to flow out of the jawbone of the ass to refresh and revive Sampson when thirsty.] The jawbone, I have observed (note on Judges 15:15), signifies the mouth of ministers. The water flowing thence is the word of God, and the blessed spirit of and grace of God which accompanies the word preached, which things are very often in Scripture compared to water. And particularly the words of wisdom in a man's mouth are compared to a flowing brook. Proverbs 18:4, "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook." Proverbs 10:11, "The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life." And Proverbs 13:14, "The law of the wise is a fountain of life." This flowing stream of the word of God is that which refreshesJE deleted "the heart." the church of Christ, and satisfies the thirst of the people of Christ, which is Christ mystical, and also refreshes the soul of Christ, as hereby he reaps his fruit and obtainsMS: "obtain." the success of his great labors. The success of the gospel in the salvation of souls is the joy that was set before Christ [Hebrews 12:2]. Jesus rejoiced in spirit when the disciples returned and told him the success of their preaching.

Judges 16.] Delilah in this chapter seems to represent beloved sin, or lust, or sinful pleasure. Sampson's love to her and cleaving to her became his

<!-- p. 341 -->

ruin. Sampson resists her awhile, but he was wedded to her, and had such a love to her that by her continual solicitations she at length overcame him. Much so it is oftentimes with men with respect to their lusts. If they ben't divorced in their hearts from them, they may resist them a while, but their importunate solicitations will at length overcome them. Such men's righteousness is but short-lived; they can't hold out always against the enticements of their lusts. "It happens to them according to the true proverb: The dog is returned to his vomit again, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire" [2 Peter 2:22]. The mighty power of sin in the hearts of those that harbor it is well represented by her overcoming Sampson whoJE deleted "was so backward and." resisted her so much; and in that she overcame and weakened him that was of such mighty strength, it was because God was departed from him. Sin will overcome the strongest man in the world when God leaves him, and he stands only in his own strength.JE deleted "Sampson disobeyed God in suffering." Delilah robbed Sampson of his strength, and betrayed and ruined him when she had lulled him asleep. So men's lusts stupefy them, and lull them asleep, and then have fair opportunity to rob them of their strength, of all that is good in them, and utterly to ruin them. Delilah, under a show and pretense ofJE deleted "great." love, and with enticing, bewitching behavior of a lover, became his traitor; while she lulled him asleep in her bosom, she betrayed and ruined him. So men's lusts, under a show of friendship, of entertaining and delighting 'em, do indeed destroy them.

Judges 16:17.] The Nazarite's hair represented the contemplation, consideration, sense, and watchfulness of the mind. When these things are gone, men's strength is soon gone; and they are an easy prey to their enemies. See, of the hair of the Nazarite, Numbers 6:5. See fables of the heathen from hence, SSS.This sentence is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 1181, 1183.

Judges 16:21.] Which is a very lively image of the miserable bondage and slavery that men are brought into by the spiritual Delilah, their lusts and sinful pleasures. These betray men into the hands of devils while they are lulled asleep in their lap, as Delilah betrayed Sampson into the hands of the Philistines; and they serve them as the Philistines did him. They keep them close prisoners, as it were shut up in prison and bound with fetters

<!-- p. 342 -->

of brass, so that they can by no means deliver themselves. And not only so, but they make them do their drudgery in the prison. They grind in the prison house their bread to feed them, and satiate their pride and cruelty. And besides that, they put out their eyes, and make 'em serve blindfold. And more than that, all the wages they intend for them is to kill them when they have done, and all to make themselves sport in their calamity.

1 Samuel 2:1–10.] THE SONG OF HANNAH. This song of Hannah (as 'tis with some parts of the song of Moses at the Red Sea, and the song of Deborah) is not so much accommodated to the event that is the immediate occasion of the song as that much greater event of which it was a type. Hannah's having a child, who had been barren, especially her having a child that was so great a prophet, and so her being exalted above her adversary Peninnah, was an undoubted type of [the] event foretold, Isaiah 54, and events of that kind. And therefore Hannah's song is a kind of prophecy of these great events with their circumstances. This observation is much confirmed by Psalms 113:7–9.

Psalms 2:2. "There is none holy as the Lord."] God's holiness here, as in many other places, is to be understood in the most extensive sense for all his moral perfection, and including his goodness and grace. See Psalms 97:12.

So God's righteousness is commonly to be understood.

1 Samuel 2:8. "The throne of glory."]'Tis probable that what was especially called "the throne of glory" was the throne of God in the tabernacle and temple, on which the "glory" of the Lord abode, and where it appeared. Christ, who dwelt there, was the glory of the Lord, and was called simply "glory." 1 Samuel 4:21–22, "The glory is departed.… The glory is departed."

1 Samuel 5:2.] So the Papists set the ark of God and Dagon together in the house of Dagon. They mingle heathenism and Christianity together. The beast has horns like a lamb, and speaks as a dragon [Revelation 13:11].

1 Samuel 5:3. "And they took Dagon, and set him in his place again."] So when Dagon was fallen in the overthrow of the heathen empire, they took him, and set him in his place again by setting up the popish hierarchy and idolatry.

1 Samuel 5:4.] The Bible and other remains of the true religion that were kept in the Church of Rome, the antichristian church, will at length be the occasion of the fall of their Dagon, and of breaking off his head and hands. When Antichrist falls, there will be a remainder of him yet, but he shall be utterly despoiled of strength and glory. He will be like a stump without head or hands.

This is a type of the same thing as Sampson's overthrowing Dagon's temple and killing the Philistines at his death, and of Jonah's being vomited out after swallowed by the whale. The ark of God being taken captive by its enemies represents the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, who therein was taken captive by his enemies. The ark of God was brought by Dagon's people into Dagon's temple, was by the Philistines presented to Dagon as his captive. So Christ for a time was as it were Satan's prisoner and captive. It was to Dagon's cost that he had such a captive, for

<!-- p. 348 -->

he fell and lost his head and hands before it. The bringing this captive into Dagon's temple proved the ruin of Dagon; the ark ruined him in his own temple. So when Satan had taken Christ captive, and had procured his death, and held him his prisoner, it was to his cost. This very thing was what ruined him; Christ in dying bruised Satan's head. Dagon and the Philistines were sick of their captive, and were forced to send it back, as the whale was sick of Jonah that he had swallowed, and was forced to vomit him up again on the dry land. The ark's entering into Dagon's temple, and the effects of it in Dagon's falling and losing his head and hands, and nothing being left but the stump of Dagon, represents Christ's entering into the soul in conversion, which before was the temple of sin and Satan, and making it his own temple, and the mortification of sin that attends it.

"There is a Grecian fable of BacchusGreek god of wine. being angry with the Athenians, because they dishonored his sacreds, neither received them with that solemnity, when they were first brought from Baeotia into Attica by Pegasus.The winged steed of the Muses. Wherefore he afflicted them with a grievous disease in their privy parts, from which they could find no remedy, until, being admonished by the oracle, they yielded themselves more obsequious to the god, and created *Phallos*, i.e. certain images of those privy parts he had afflicted, for his honor. An egg is not more like another, says Bochart, than this comment to the history of the Philistines." See Gale's *Court of Gentiles*, Pt. 1, Bk. 2, ch. 3, p. 33.Second edition.

1 Samuel 15:32–33.] When Samuel was about to kill Agag, the king of the Amalekites, Agag came to him delicately; he came in his best hue, put on the most taking and pleasing appearance that he could, that he might appear innocent, and desirable, and as one that was worthy to be saved alive, and that it was a thousand pities to kill. Thus do those lusts that are most beloved, and are chief in our affection, and are among our lusts as the king among the Amalekites, when we go about to slay them or do anything in order to it. Thus do they plead for their lives. They represent themselves to us in their most innocent and taking hue, and come to us delicately, pleading that they are not worthy to be slain, but worthy to be well entertained. "Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal," in the place where the congregation of Israel was circumcised, and their reproach rolled away. Thus our most beloved lusts must be served. They must be utterly destroyed without mercy in order to our being delivered from the bondage of sin, and the rolling away our reproach; and thus do men treat their beloved lusts before the Lord in true circumcision of heart. They serve sin as Saul did Agag, and as the children of Israel did Achan. See notes on the story of Achan."Scripture," no. 360, *Works, 15*, 344–47.

Samuel declared to Agag that he would make his mother childless. Many in their pretended repentance and conversion slay some of the children of original corruption, but save some one of the children alive, that which is dearest and chief in their esteem, or has the highest place in their hearts. Samuel gave that reason why his mother should be made childless, that his "sword had made women childless." So the beloved lust, the sin that is chief in affection and esteem, has destroyed multitudes of souls, and made many women childless. This work was done by Samuel, the prophet of the Lord. So when such a mortification is wrought in the heart, it is by the word of the Lord.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Samuel 16.] Warburton, vol. 2, p. 318.Warburton writes a long footnote about the difficulties in the history of David as related in 1 Samuel 16-17. He notes that 1 Samuel 16:14–23 is out of historical order, being an anticipation of a later account, an episode that correctly follows David's defeat of Goliath. Warburton adds that such literary anticipation is common in sacred history (*Divine Legation of Moses Demonstrated* [2nd ed. London, 1742], pp. 313–17). The principal text on these same pages contrasts the character of Saul the king and the youthful David as well as their "different Acceptation with the God of *Israel*." David's successes came when he was armed "with no other Power but of Miracles… and with no other Wisdom but of Truth," which is characteristic of all of God's dispensations (p. 318).

Therefore 'the elders of the town trembled at his coming' 1 Samuel 16:4], fearing it was an indication of God's displeasure against them, and that he was come to denounce some judgment for the iniquities of the place. 1 Samuel 17:4–7.] Concerning the stature of Goliath, Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 535. "His height is described to be 'six cubits and a span' 1 Samuel 17:4], so that as a cubit is reckoned to be 21.888 inches" (See note on Genesis 6:15, concerning the dimensions of the ark.), "and a span ten inches, he was 11 feet and 9 inches high. The Anakims who fled to Gath (Joshua 11:22–23) were a race of giants (Numbers 13:28, Numbers 13:32–33; Deuteronomy 9:1–2), and this Goliath of Gath exceeded them all in stature. And as the common size of men is but half so high" (i.e. 5 feet, 10 inches, and an half), "so if every part was proportionable to his height, as probably it was, the weight of his whole body, or of each limb, must be to others, as the cube of two to the cube of one, or eight times as much; and consequently his head was a sufficient burden for a man to carry. The weight of his armor seems proportionable to his bulk. The weight of his coat of mail, 1 Samuel 17:5, 'was 5000 shekels of brass,' so that as a shekel weighed about half an ounce of our common weights, sixteen of which goes to the pound, it weighed about 156 pound and a quarter. 'The staff of his spear (1 Samuel 17:7) was like a weaver's beam.' The 'spear's head' (ibid.) 'weighed 600 shekels,' or eighteen pound and three quarters. Hence the weight of his whole armor hath been thus computed. The spear's head 18 lb. ¾, the staff of

<!-- p. 355 -->

the spear 18 lb. ¾, the helmet 15 lb., the shield 30 lb., the coat of mail 156 lb. ¼, the sword 4 lb. ¼, total 243 lb. So that his proportion of strength and stature being as eight to one, it would be equivalent to a coat of mail thirty-two weight for a common person in his age."*Scripture Chronology*, 535, n. t.
