1 Samuel 17:40. "And he took his staff in his hand" (See Numbers 21:18), "and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook."] This brook and the stones that he chose out of it were doubtless typical of something. The brook seems to be a type of the Spirit of God, the same with Ezekiel's waters of the sanctuary [Ezekiel 47], and the "pure river of water of life that proceeded out of the throne of God and of the Lamb" [Revelation 22:1]; and the same with those "rivers of living water" spoken of, John 7:38–39, which we are there told is meant of the Holy Spirit; and the same with the brook that descended out of Mt. Sinai, spoken of, Deuteronomy 9:21 (See notes on the place.); and the same with the well spoken of, Numbers 21:18. As the princes of Israel obtained the water of that well by their staves, so David comes to gather those stones out of the brook with his staff. The stones that David chose out of the brook seem to denote words of the Lord, or passages of his word, which weapon is from the Spirit of God, and therefore is called "the sword of the Spirit" [Ephesians 6:17]. WithMS: "which." such weapons, Christ the true David, fought with Satan, the spiritual Goliath, as in the account of his temptation in the wilderness. This, viz. the word of God, is the great and only offensive weapon of the Christian that the Apostle mentions in his description of the Christian armor (Ephesians 6:13–16), but these stones are David's offensive weapons by which Goliath was to be slain. As the word is called there "the sword of the Spirit," so those stones are out of the brook, which represents the Spirit of God. The stone with which Goliath was slain signifies the same with Daniel's stone "cut out of the mountains without hands" [Daniel 2:45], which smote the great image

<!-- p. 356 -->

and destroyed [it], which signifies the word of God. David chose smooth stones, a variety of them, as a Christian may find a variety of apt passages in the Holy Scripture wherewith to resist and fight against Satan in all his temptations and against all his spiritual enemies.

1 Samuel 17:50.] The stone with which Goliath was slain typifies the word of God, the same that was typified by the stone that smote Nebuchadnezzar's image [Daniel 2:35]. The stone is taken out of the brook, which brook is the Holy Ghost. See Psalms 110:7. The sling is the gospel ministry. Ministers are instruments in the hand of Christ. They are but slings in his hand wherewith the stone of his word is cast.

1 Samuel 17:55–58.] Concerning Saul's not knowing David, and Abner's not being able to tell who he was. 'Tis probable that Saul never had seen him but once before. He once was sent to him by his father Jesse to try the experiment of relieving Saul by his music, and then returned again to his father's house. And what is said in the 1 Samuel 16:21–23's standing before Saul, or continuing in his presence, and his loving him greatly, and his becoming his armor-bearer, and Saul's sending to Jesse to let him continue with him because he had favor in his sight, is evidently anticipated. 'Tis an account of what came to pass after David's killing Goliath, as is evident by the 1 Samuel 18:2. "And Saul took him that day, and would let him go no more home to his father's house." 'Tis very common that when the Scripture begins the history of any affair, some things that are most remarkable in the affair are first generally and briefly mentioned, and then a more particular account is begun. So here when David's being sent for to relieve Saul by his music is mentioned, the historian then generally mentions the consequences of it, though they happened some considerable time after his being first sent for, and after some particulars that are related afterwards. It was after David's killing the Philistine that Saul loved David. He set his heart on him at the same time that his son Jonathan did. And it was after that that he became his armor-bearer, as is evident by 1 Samuel 18:5; he "set him over the men of war," for he appeared only a musician, and not a military man, before that. If he had been his armor-bearer before, he would have been then in the army with Saul.

And it was after that that Saul sent to Jesse to let David stand before him, as is evident by 1 Samuel 18:2. There was some time, after David came from the slaughter of the Philistine, that David was in great favor with

<!-- p. 357 -->

Saul, before his falling out with him on occasion of the songs of the women ascribing to Saul but thousands and to David ten thousands, as is evident by the beginning of the 1 Samuel 18. David had gained the love of Israel by his discreet behavior before that, as 1 Samuel 18:5.

And therefore 'tis not much to be wondered at that Saul did not know David, seeing he had never seen him but once before. In such a multitude of business as kings have, and among so many new faces which they see every day, it was easy to forget a man. David also now came in another kind of habit than when he was sent to wait on Saul at court, for he was clothed as a shepherd in a rustic dress. He appeared then in the soft airs of a musician, and therefore was the less suspected to come now as a champion. And as for Abner, he, being a military man and much abroad, might not have seen David when he was at court, or perhaps knowing that his three eldest brethren were in the army, and that David was not among the number, though they might both know his face, yet they could not call him to mind as not expecting to see him at that time.Conjecture for illegible word. Here compare Ruth 3:16.This sentence is a later addition.

1 Samuel 23:26–28.] It seems as though this mountain that divided between Saul and David was a very steep rocky mountain, and at or near that place impassable, and so was a defense to David, kept Saul from coming at him. And therefore, in remembrance of the great benefit David had by it, it was thenceforward called by a name taken from the benefit, "the rock of divisions." This mountain or rock, as it is called, was a type of Christ, the Rock of Israel and the Rock of Ages, who is the rock of their defense. Christ is the true *Sela-Hammah-Lekoth*.הַמַּחְלְקְוֹת סֶלַע He is between his people and their enemies as an impassable mountain. He was so all along between Saul and David. David often calls God his "rock of defense" in the Psalms. And probably the defense that he had by this mountain led him to the consideration of the defense he had by God; and that it [was], with a pious and grateful respect to God, and that he might keep the remembrance of his mercy in defending him, that he thus named the mountain.

2 Samuel 1:17.] See 2 Samuel 1:11–12. David's behavior on occasion of the death of Saul, his grand persecutor, who long sought his life, and whose death was so much to his advantage, together with the spirit he showed on other occasions of love, meekness, and forgiveness towards those that injured him, do greatly confirm that the imprecations we have in his psalms on his persecutors, of which Saul was the chief, are not the expressions of a spirit of private revenge, but imprecations he put up in the name of Christ as head of the church against his and his church's enemies, and what he spake as a prophet in the name of the Lord. 2 Samuel 7:10.] God's ceasing to walk in a tent and tabernacle, and dwelling in a temple, was a great token of mercy to the children of Israel, for while God dwelt in a movable tabernacle he dwelt as a wayfaring man, as one that was not fixed in his abode, was ready to depart, that is to stay but a little while, or that is undetermined whether to stay or no. But when he came to dwell in a temple, that [was] a fixed habitation, it was a token for good several ways. It was a token that God would dwell among them, and make his settled abode among them, and that he would not lead them forth out of the land, but continue them in the possession of it. For they were to go where the tabernacle went before them, but now God dwelled in an immovable temple. It was a token that they should no more be removed. It was a token that God would not cast them off from being his people, for if he should so do, he would remove 'em out of that land, for that land was his land, a land that he had chosen to be a holy land.

2 Samuel 11:4. "For she was purified from her uncleanness."] When David saw her washing herself, she was then washing herself at the end of the seven days of her uncleanness (Leviticus 15:19). The time being come that she should be clean, she was, as usual at the time of her cleansing, washing her body from all remaining stain or pollution from her issue of blood. And therefore we are told that David saw her washing herself "in an eveningtide" (2 Samuel 11:2). It was probably just about sun setting", which was the time of day when those that were legally unclean were cleansed. The case being thus, it greatly increased David's temptation, for when a woman was thus cleansed from her uncleanness, then it was lawful for her husband to lie with her, so that it put David in mind of that act, and stirred his lust.

2 Samuel 15-18.] ABSALOM seems to be a type of Antichrist. He was a son of David, as the man of sin was originally a Christian bishop, one of the ministers of the gospel who in a peculiar manner are as it were Christ's sons. Absalom was David's son by Maachah, the daughter of the king of Geshur, the only wife he had that was a Gentile. So popery is a mixture of Christianity with heathenism. Absalom was the son of a heathen mother, or one that had been a heathen; so the Church of Rome is the daughter of old heathen Rome. Absalom usurped his father's authority over his kingdom, and his city Jerusalem, and over his house, as the pope usurps the authority of Christ, sets himself up to be king in his kingdom, and takes possession of the church, the spiritual Jerusalem, and sits in the house of Christ as lord of that. Sitting in the temple of God, he showeth himself that he is God. Absalom was a person of great beauty, and was exceedingly admired and praised by the people for his beauty. So it has been with the pope, whereas Christ himself appeared in a mean and low condition, without form or comeliness, without any external

<!-- p. 366 -->

magnificence; and when the people saw him, there was no beauty wherefore they should desire him [Isaiah 53:2]. On the contrary, Antichrist appears in exceeding external pomp and glory, decked with gold, and silver, and precious stones,MS: "Stone." fine linen, and scarlet, which all the world has admired, and all wondered after the beast, saying, "Who is like unto the beast?" [Revelation 13:4]. Absalom's head was exceeding fruitful in hair, representing the exceeding policy and subtilty of Antichrist. See note on Numbers 6:5. Absalom cloaked his rebellion and usurpation with a pretense of religion and the service of God, like Antichrist. He said to his father, 2 Samuel 15:7–8, "Let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed. For thy servant vowed a vow while I abode at Geshur in Syria, saying, If the Lord will bring me again indeed to Jerusalem, then will I serve the Lord." Absalom drove David and those that adhered to him out of Jerusalem; so Antichrist casts out of the church all the true and faithful followers of Christ. David went away into the wilderness, and his faithful subjects went with him wherever he went (1 Samuel 15 ff.). "And David said unto all his servants that were with him at Jerusalem, Arise let us flee.… And the king's servants said unto the king, Behold, thy servants are ready to do whatsoever my Lord the king shall appoint. And the king went forth, and all his household after him" 2 Samuel 14:14–16]. 2 Samuel 14:17, "And the king went forth, and all the people after him, and tarried in a place that was far off." Ittai the Gittite expressed the spirit of his true followers on this occasion. 2 Samuel 15:21, "As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be," which is agreeable to what is described to be the spirit of the true followers of Christ in the time of Antichrist. Revelation 14:4, "These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth." Revelation 17:14, "They that are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful."

Jerusalem was left, and as it were given up to Absalom and his multitude; and it was as it were trodden down by them, which is agreeable to the description of the time of the reign of Antichrist. Revelation 11:2, "It is given to the Gentiles, and the holy city shall they tread under foot."

Absalom committed whoredom with his father's concubines, and that openly in the sight of the sun. Thus Antichrist defiles the church that by profession is bound to be faithful to Christ as his spouse. He claims the peculiar prerogatives of the husband and lord of the church, and usurps these prerogatives in the most open manner.

But they that were defiled by Absalom were not any of hisI.e. David's. true wives

<!-- p. 367 -->

who went with David, but only his concubines. So Christ's true followers during the reign of Antichrist are not defiled when other women are defiled. Revelation 14:4, "These are they which were not defiled with women, for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth."

The place where David and his men went was the wilderness (2 Samuel 15:28). So David in the Psalms 42, which probably was penned on this occasion, speaks of himself as an exile in the wilderness of Mt. Hermon, a place noted for beasts of prey. (See Canticles 4:8, "Look from Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards.") So the church is represented as flying away into the wilderness to reside there during the reign of Antichrist (Revelation 12:14).

The time of Absalom's usurpation is represented as a time of great affliction with David and his followers. 'Tis said, 2 Samuel 15:23, "And all the country wept with a loud voice." And 2 Samuel 15:30, "And David went up by the ascent of Mt. Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and went barefoot. "And all the people that was with him covered every man his head; and they went up, weeping as they went up." And David, in the book of Psalms, speaks of himself as then in great affliction (Psalms 3 and Psalms 42). So the time of the reign of Antichrist is represented as a time of great affliction and sorrow to the church of God, wherein the witnesses prophesied in sackcloth, etc. [Revelation 11:3].

The time of Absalom's usurpation was a time wherein David was greatly reproached and persecuted, as when Shimei cursed him [2 Samuel 16:7–8], aptly representing the great blasphemies of Antichrist that we read of, Daniel 7:8, Daniel 7:11, Daniel 7:25; Revelation 13:1, Revelation 13:5–6, and the cruel persecutions of Antichrist.

David, when bitterly reviled and persecuted by Shimei, reviled not again, nor took any revenge, but bore all with great patience and meekness, representing the spirit and practice of God's true saints under antichristian persecutions, as that is represented in Revelation 13:10 and Revelation 14:12.

Ahithophel well represents the Jesuits and other subtile, crafty counselors of Antichrist. God's defeating the counsels of Ahithophel to his own exceeding and intolerable vexation livelily represents the same thing that is prophesied of, Revelation 16:10. "And his kingdom was full of darkness, and they gnawed their tongues for pain."

The battle that was fought in Gilead between David's men and the great multitude that followed Absalom, wherein the latter were overthrown, represents that great battle between Christ and his true church, and Antichrist and his adherents, which we read of, Revelation 16:14 ff. and Revelation 19.

<!-- p. 368 -->

This battle was fought when David and his friends were come to Mahanaim, which wordמַהֲנַיִם signifies two armies, and was the place where the army or host of angels met himI.e. not David, but Jacob. to encourage and defend when the host of Esau, his false, persecuting, and murderous brother was coming against him, thirsting for his blood. David's company was truly the company of Mahanaim, as the church of Christ is called, Canticles 6:13. And that battle, which this company had with Absalom and his followers, was the more fit representation of the great and last battle of Christ and his church with Antichrist and his followers, in which "the armies which were in heaven" are represented as following Christ (Revelation 19:14), and which is said to be fought at Armageddon, or at the mountain of Megiddo, where the battle of Deborah and Barak with Sisera and his host was fought, wherein it is said that "the stars in their courses," or the glorious angels and hosts of heaven, "fought against Sisera" [Judges 5:20].

In the end, Absalom's hair, that he so much gloried in, proved his destruction, representing that Antichrist, though so exceeding subtile and crafty, shall finally be ruined by his own craftiness, shall be taken in his own snare. The same thing is also represented by Ahithophel's hanging himself [2 Samuel 17:23].

Absalom was "cast into a *great pit* in the wood" [2 Samuel 18:17]. This "great pit" represents that bottomless pit into which it is said the beast and false prophet were cast (Revelation 19:20 and Revelation 20:10). Absalom had a "great heap of stones" raised upon [him], a most conspicuous and lasting monument of his wickedness and ruin, representing the same thing as that smoke of Babylon's torment which is said to rise up forever and ever (Revelation 19:3 and Revelation 14:11). Soon after this was that joyful triumphant song of praise which we are told, 2 Samuel 22:1, he "spake unto the Lord in the day that he had delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies," which song agrees much better with the description of the great things God did for his church in and upon the destruction of Antichrist than to anything David himself was the immediate subject of. As that in the 2 Samuel 22:8 ff., "Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of heaven moved and shook because he was wroth," which agrees with the account of the great earthquake that accompanied Antichrist's destruction. "There went up a smoke out of his nostrils, and fire out of his mouth devoured: coals were kindled by it." 2 Samuel 22:13–15, "Through the brightness before him were coals of fire kindled. The Lord thundered from heaven; the Most

<!-- p. 369 -->

High uttered his voice. He sent out arrows, and scattered them; lightning, and discomfited them. And the channels of the sea appeared; the foundations of the world were discovered" 2 Samuel 22:16]. In the same song, as we have it, Psalms 18, we have these words, Psalms 18:12–13, "At the brightness that was before him his thick clouds passed, hailstones, and coals of fire. The Lord also thundered in the heavens, and the Highest gave his voice, hailstones and coals of fire." These things agree with Revelation 11:19. "And there were lightnings, and voices, and thunderings, and an earthquake, and great hail." And Revelation 16:18, "And there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great. "Revelation 16:20–21, " And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found. "And there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent." There are also other passages in that song of David that agree much better with the time of Antichrist's destruction than the times wherein David sang it, as 2 Samuel 22:28. "And the afflicted people thou wilt save; but thine eyes are upon the haughty, that thou mayst bring them down." And 2 Samuel 22:44–46, "Thou hast kept me to be the head of the heathen; a people which I knew not shall serve me. As soon as they hear, they shall be obedient unto me. Strangers shall fade away, and they shall be afraid out of their close places." Thus Christ will lead the way in the joyful songs of the church after Antichrist's destruction (Revelation 19:1–7). Soon after this great victory of David and his company, and this joyful song, succeeds the peaceable, joyful, and glorious reign of Solomon, which undoubtedly was a type of the glorious day of the church after the fall of Antichrist.

David's sake. He cleaves to his master David in the time of his affliction and adversity, when his affairs ran very low, and it looked dark on his side, and it seemed very doubtful what would be the issue, and David's party seemed to be the underling party, and were fleeing before their enemies. Yet Ittai resolves to cleave to him whether in life or death, as true Christians "follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth" [Revelation 14:4].

2 Samuel 20:15–22.] It is probably the design of the Holy Ghost to represent something spiritual in this story. The city of Abel of Beth-maachah may here

<!-- p. 372 -->

fitly represent a people or the heart of a particular person. Sheba, the son of Bichri, the rebel against the lawful rightful sovereign that that city harbored, represents sin. Joab, the captain of the king's host that besieged the city with all his army, and battered the wall to throw it down, represents the wrath of God. Joab requires that the head of Sheba be thrown over the wall in order to his leaving the city. So the wrath of God will stand against us with all its army, and seek our destruction, till we destroy and give up sin. The wise woman in the city represents either the church or God's saints among a people, or a principle of true wisdom and grace in the heart of a particular person. She makes the city willing to cut off the head of Sheba, and throws it to Joab over the wall, whereupon Joab blew a trumpet, and his army retired from the city. So when once we have given up sin, God proclaims liberty and peace to us. Repentance is the condition of the remission of sins.

2 Samuel 23:39. "Thirty and seven in all."] The Historian first gives an account of the first and the second three, which makes six, and then reckons up after

<!-- p. 374 -->

them the thirty, which makes thirty-six. And in order to make the number thirty-seven, we must reckon in Joab, who had always the chief place of dignity and office among all David's men of war, but yet seems to [be] mentioned here in this catalogue only occasionally, in the 2 Samuel 23:37 on occasion of the mention of his armorbearer, and again in the 2 Samuel 23:18 on occasion of the mention of his brother Abishai. The reason why he is not inserted in this catalogue seems to be either that the design of the catalogue was only to mention those that were then called of the first and second three, and of the thirty, for David's mighty men were wont, it seems, so to be reckoned by parcels in Israel. But Joab, though a very mighty man, yet was not wont to be reckoned to any of these parcels, for he did not stand as mate with any of them, but was one by himself alone, distinguished from all as the captain general of the whole host. And there was not that occasion to mention him now, or relate what he had done in this catalogue, he and his acts having been so particularly enlarged on in the foregoing history. But yet the Historian shows that he was not forgotten, he being twice occasionally mentioned in this catalogue. The reason why he is not mentioned can't be because he was not one of David's mighty men, for by all the history 'tis evident he was one of the greatest warriors. Asahel is here mentioned among the mighty men [2 Samuel 23:24], who is represented in the history as a child to Abner, when he was killed by him by the hinder end of his spear. But Abner don't appear to be more than Joab's match; and here the armor-bearer of Joab is mentioned, who can't be supposed to be a greater warrior than Joab himself. Or secondly, it might be because of Joab's infamous carriage in murdering Abner and Amasa. He therefore deserved that his name should be blotted out of the roll of David's worthies, noble warriors. That seems to be typical of the book of the Lamb, or the true David, wherein are enrolled the names of his faithful valiant soldiers, or those that overcome, to whom 'tis promised that they shall not be blotted out of the book of life, and that his name shall be confessed before his Father, and before his angels (Revelation 3:5). 'Tis unreasonable to suppose that its being said that David's mighty men were "thirty and seven in all" was a blunder in the Historian, for it cannot be supposed that the Historian should mistake so as to mention over thirty-six names, and expressly divide them into the lesser sums of thirty and twice three, and then not know that these three sums added together made thirty-six, and that such a mistake should stand in the public records of the Jews from age to age. The Historian mentions those mighty men that were wont to [be] reckoned by parcels amongst their fellows, mentioning

<!-- p. 375 -->

first the two threes, and then the thirty, not mentioning Joab, he belonging to none of these parcels, and supposing the reader would not want to have him mentioned,MS: "mention." so great a part of the foregoing history being about him. Yet when at the end he goes to tell how many David's mighty men are in all, Joab, the one by himself, must not be left out of the sum; and therefore the Historian declares it to be thirty-seven. This being so plain a case, it may ease us with respect to other difficulties of the Scripture of this nature that look like blunders, and may well make us think they are not so, but that there is some good reason for the seeming inconsistence, though we don't know what it is. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 402.

When Solomon thus threatened Shimei, we can't rationally understand any more by it than that death should be certain to him. He should stand guilty of death, obliged to die, by a fixed unalterable establishment from that day. 1 Kings 10:1–14. Concerning the story of the queen of Sheba who came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. She (as well as Pharaoh's daughter that Solomon married) was a remarkable type of the Gentile church and of the church of Christ in general, for she was a Gentile queen. Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology*, p. 608, says that, "She lived in the southern parts of Arabia near the Red Sea, which was therefore called 'the uttermost parts of the earth' [Matthew 12:42], because there was no traveling any further that way by land"; and observes that, "'Tis probable that she came to hear of Solomon's character by the ships that went to Ophir. For they sailed by her coast, and spread his fame there, as they did in all other places where they touched, proclaiming his magnificence, and especially his wisdom, and the glorious temple which he had built for the worship of God"; and says that, "The questions that she asked seemed to be about things pertaining to piety and the service of God. For our Savior saith, that she came 'to hear the wisdom of Solomon,' and should therefore 'rise up in judgment' [Matthew 12:42] against that generation, who would not learn of him. And it is said (1 Kings 10:1 of this

<!-- p. 380 -->

ch.) that the particular fame, that she heard of Solomon, was 'concerning the name of the Lord,' and this most probably was the occasion of her journey." Herein she is a type of the church of Christ, which is made up of those that are naturally far off, that have as it were wandered from God to the ends of the earth, and are aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and have their souls black with sin, as the people of Sheba, who were Ethiopians, were black, and could not change their skin, or wash off their dark color. The queen of Sheba comes to hear the wisdom of Solomon, as those that are of the church of Christ come to hear his wisdom, and learn of him who is the wisdom of God and the light of the world. She came with spices and precious things to present to Solomon, which are a type of the graces of the church and her good works. Solomon instructed her and told her all her questions, which is a type of Christ's instructing and enlightening the souls of believers, and satisfying their doubts, and extricating them out of their difficulties by his divine teaching.

She says, "It was a true report that I heard in mine own land of thy acts and of thy wisdom. Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it. And, behold, the half was not told me. Thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard" 1 Kings 10:6–7]. So when persons come to Christ, they are never disappointed in him by finding less in him than ministers told them of while they were in a natural condition.

But the queen of Sheba is especially a type of the Gentile church, for she was a Gentile, and as she came from the uttermost parts of the earth. So in the calling of the Gentiles, they that "were far off were made nigh," as in Ephesians 2:13, Ephesians 2:17. 'Tis said that "she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones" 1 Kings 10:2], which is very agreeable to the prophecies of the Gentiles coming to the spiritual Jerusalem. Isaiah 60:5–6, "The forces of the Gentiles shall come unto thee. The multitude of camels shall cover thee, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from SHEBA shall come. They shall bring gold and incense; and they shall show forth the praises of the Lord." And Isaiah 60:9, "Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the Lord thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee." Isaiah 66:20, "And they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the Lord out of all nations upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift

<!-- p. 381 -->

beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem," saith the Lord, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.

1 Kings 11:3.] David is a type of Christ in his suffering state, and of the church in that militant state it is in before the glorious times. Solomon is a type of Christ in his exalted state, and especially in his glorious dominion in the latter days, the days of the church's peace and prosperity. And the multitude of his wives is probably typical of the largeness of Christ's church, the multitude of souls and multitude of nations espoused to him at that time, the multitude of national churches.

"And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines." See no. 249.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 200–201.

1 Kings 11:4.] 'Tis very observable that when persons are old, they are more yieldable, and more easily prevailed upon by those that they have long had a fondness for, and persuaded to this or that.

1 Kings 11:5–7.] It does not appear that Solomon did himself worship these strange gods, but what his wives persuaded him to was to build high places for them to worship their gods in. He probably went after other gods, only as he honored them so far as to build places for their public worship in the land of Israel, wherein his wives and their attendants might worship them. For 'tis said in the 1 Kings 11:8, that he did this "for his wives, which sacrificed and burnt incense unto their gods" in them. He might possibly think it but reasonable that his wives should be allowed the exercise of their own religion, and the worship of their own gods, and might think it hard, seeing he had brought 'em out of their own country, to deny 'em high places and altars at which they might worship them in his country.

1 Kings 14:14–15.] 'Tis God's manner in Scripture, when threatening the wicked for their sins, to pass from those judgments that are soon to be inflicted and are the more immediateJE deleted "fruits of the punishment of their sins." occasion of God's sending a messenger to threaten them, to some great remote judgments, of which perhaps the judgments more immediately threatened are images or forerunners. Thus when God first sent Moses to Pharaoh, he sent him with a threatening of the last and greatest plague; and the other foregoing plagues are all omitted. Exodus 4:22–23, "And thou shalt say unto Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord. Israel is my son, even my first-born. And I say unto thee, Let my son go, that he may serve me. And if thou refuse to let him go, behold, I will slay thy son, even thy first-born." So in the Exodus 9:15, God again threatens the last plague, and Pharaoh's own destruction that was accomplished in the Red Sea: "For now I will stretch out mine hand, and I will smite thee and thy people with pestilence; and thou shalt be cut off from the earth," though there was the plague of hail, and locusts, and darkness afterwards before the plague of pestilence. So when the wife of Jeroboam comes to the prophet to inquire whether her son shall live, the prophet passes from a threatening of his

<!-- p. 383 -->

death and judgments suddenly to be inflicted on his family to the captivity of the Ten Tribes, though it was to be long after Jeroboam's death.JE deleted "So also it is God's manner when promising blessings to his people." So also it is the manner of the prophets, when sent on some particular occasion to promise some mercy to God's people, to insist on some greater mercy that is remote, and that is to be bestowed on God's people in after generations. Thus when Isaiah was sent to Ahaz, when Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, were combined against him, to comfort him by foretellingJE deleted "the frustration of his design." the disappointment of their enemies and deliverance of Judah, he comes to Ahaz with Shearjashubיָשׁוּב שְׁאֶר his son, that signifies "the remnant shall return," to foretell the return from the captivity to Babylon, as in the Isaiah 7. And it is very frequent with the prophets, when foretelling lesser mercies that God has to bestow on his people, to pass to and insist upon that greatest of all mercies, the coming of Christ. So did Isaiah when he came to Ahaz on the forementioned occasion (Isaiah 7:14). So the prophets, when foretelling the return from the Babylonish captivity, often insist on the redemption of Christ, of which this is a type. So do the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, when sent to encourage the people to build the temple with promises of success therein, insist chiefly on the prosperity that God will give the church in times of the gospel.

1 Kings 18:30. "Repaired," etc.] Not that this was the same individual altar that had before been used in the service of God, which was now built up again of the same materials. But it was as it were a repairing the altar of the Lord, as it was a restoring the worship of God, in this way of offering sacrifices to him according to his own appointment.

1 Kings 18:33–35.] Elijah's sacrifice, in the time wherein it was offered, was attended with the greatest obstacles to its being consumed by fire. God, who has more ends than one in what he does, probably did not only intend by this to show his power beyond that of Baal, but to represent what came to pass with respect to the sacrifice of Christ, the great antitype of all the ancient sacrifices, whose last suffering were attended with such circumstances as seemed to tend in the highest degree to hinder his going on to offer himself in the heavenly flames of divine charity, and voluntarily presenting himself to suffer the flames of divine wrath. Such was God's hiding his face from him, and dealing with him in some respect as if he had been an enemy, which was a great trial of his love to the Father, and tending like floods of water to quench the fire of divine love in his soul, and to prevent that great degree of it which was necessary to carry him through the extreme sufferings that were before him. And also the extraordinary view which Christ had then given him of the unworthiness

<!-- p. 385 -->

of mankind for whom he died, the hateful nature of their sin that he was about to expiate by his extreme sufferings, and their great enmity against him, which was then set before him and exercised towards him in the contempt and cruelty of his enemies, and some of them the very persons that he was about to die for, and the ingratitude of his own disciples that had already received saving benefits of his death, in their coldness toward him in the time of his agony, their being unwilling to watch with him one hour, their all forsaking him when he was apprehended, Peter's denying him with oaths and curses—these were like floods of great waters that were then thrown upon him to quench his love and to prevent his going on to endure those extreme torments in the fire of God's wrath, as was also that extraordinary view he had given him beforehand of the cup he was to drink, which made his soul exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. But many waters could not quench his love, neither could the floods drown it.

1 Kings 18:42. "He cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees."] The posture of most humble and earnest prayer, agreeable to what the apostle James says, James 5:18, "Elias… prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit."

1 Kings 18:44 ff.] The rain, after the great drought, came on Israel from a little cloud that came out of the west from beyond the sea. So probably that great outpouring of the Spirit that shall be in the latter days, so often compared to plentiful showers of rain on the dry [land], will arise in and from America.

That drought continued three years and six months, or a time, times, and an half [Revelation 12:14], answerable to the time of the continuance of the church's trouble and spiritual drought before the glorious times. See Luke 4:25 and James 5:17. The king of Israel also at that time came in his chariot from Carmel to Jezreel, which was from the west to the east. See note on 1 Kings 18:46. So the materials of which the temple was built were brought by sea (1 Kings 5:9). See note on Psalms 19:3.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Kings 18:46.] Elijah here, in this case of the approach of this plentiful shower, is the forerunner of the king of Israel in his speedy and swift entrance in Jezreel, as John the Baptist, the New Testament Elijah, was the forerunner of Christ, the great king of Israel.

The truth with respect to what is related in these verses probably was thus. Elijah was directed by the Spirit of God to cast his mantle on Elisha. But Elijah had not the design of God in it fully made known to him, supposing it to be intended as a sign that Elisha should be prophet after him, agreeable to what God had said to him at Mt. Sinai. But God [had] a further meaning in it, which was intimated by his spirit which went with Elijah's mantle to Elisha, viz. that he should immediately forsake all, and follow him, and devote himself to the work of the ministry in the business of a prophet. Elisha, supposing Elijah had this design of God made known to him, and had been directed to cast his mantle on him with this view, and finding at first a reluctance, desires of Elijah that he by his prayers would obtain leave of God that he should first kiss his father and mother. Elijah, surprised at this request, as is natural, supposing him thus ignorant, says, "Go back; for what have I done" 1 Kings 19:20] that should hinder it? However, Elisha, who understood the mind of God, soon recovered from his reluctance, and went no further back than to his oxen, and took them and the instruments, and offered up all to God, signifying by this action his full consent to forsake all, and make a sacrifice of all this world's possessions and concerns to the great and infinitely important designs of his ministry.This paragraph is a later addition.

### II Kings

2 Kings 2:1–6.] Elisha obtained the great blessing of such a measure of the spirit of God as he inherited from Elijah in a way of constant seeking of it. He constantly and resolutely followed and clove to Elijah. His constancy was tried three times, and three times he declared his resolution, that as the Lord lived, and as his soul lived, he would not leave him. "As soon as Elijah had prophesied against Ahaziah, king of Israel, and sent the letter to Jehoram, king of Judah, he departed from Samaria, and went with Elisha to Gilgal, a place near Jordan about five and twenty miles from Samaria. And to try Elisha's constancy, he proposes to go back again to Bethel, a journey of about twenty miles, not far from the road to Samaria." And then further to try his constancy, he goes back again to Jericho, which was near Gilgal, and to try him further goes again to Jordan by Gilgal. And Elijah had thoroughly proved the constancy of Elisha's resolution. He ceased to speak to him any more. Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 626.

Elisha's following Elijah so closely hither and thither, and following him to and through Jordan, and after that seeing him ascend, and receiving his blessing and a double portion of his spirit, signifies that the way to pass safely through death, and to receive the portion of the firstborn is to "follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth" [Revelation 14:4], and to follow him even unto death, and to be "made conformable to his death" [Philippians 3:10].This paragraph is a later addition.

2 Kings 2:3. "Hold you your peace."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 593.

2 Kings 2:7.] SSS.Ibid.

2 Kings 2:8.] Elijah's passing through Jordan, when going out of the world, on dry ground without passing through water, represented his passing out of the world without dying. Jordan's being divided by his mantle signifies

<!-- p. 390 -->

that believers in general pass through death without being overwhelmed or hurt by death, so that Christ says, They die not [John 11:25–26]. Jordan's being divided by Elijah's mantle signifies believers' having this privilege by the righteousness of Christ, and it signifies Christ not being overwhelmed and destroyed in death through his own righteousness.

2 Kings 2:9.] Elijah was now about to leave the world; and as parents, when they are leaving the world, are wont to bequeath portions to their children, so Elijah asks Elisha what he shall bequeath to him. Elisha was as it were his child, and Elisha calls him his father (2 Kings 2:12). That portion that he desires to inherit from his father is his spirit; and he desires a double portion of it, i.e. a much larger portion than the rest of his children, as it was ordained that the eldest son should inherit a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). It was his birthright to have the best share of his father's estate.JE deleted "So Elisha desires that his father Elijah would now in his last will and testament bequ." Elijah had many other children besides Elisha. There were many sons of the prophets that were under Elijah's care and instruction, so that he was as it were a father among them, as afterwards Elisha was, as is evident by 2 Kings 4:38 ff. and 2 Kings 6:1–2. Now what Elisha desires is that he may be distinguished from all the rest of the children by having a double portion of his spirit bequeathed to him, for Elijah's estate did not consist in silver and gold, but in those gifts of the spirit which he possessed. So that he was about to give something he might say as Peter, Acts 3:6, "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have, give I unto thee." Elisha desires that he might inheritJE deleted "the principal part." a double portion of this, and beGrosart inserted this word and deleted the following two words on the MS. made therein the main heir of those blessed spiritual gifts which he had, which was accordingly granted him.

2 Kings 2:9–13.] How Elijah's ascension [was] a type of Christ's, see no. 283.*Works, 15*, 240.

2 Kings 2:11.] Note on Genesis 5:24.

2 Kings 2:12. "Chariot of Israel, and horsemen thereof."] See Hervey's *Dialogues*, vol. 3, p. 365, margin.Hervey writes, "There is a peculiar Beauty, and most apposite Significance in this *proverbial* Saying, as used by the antient *Israelites. Horses* and *Chariots* were deemed, in those Ages, the principal Strength of the Battle, the most formidable Apparatus of War. Of these the *Israelites* were intirely destitute. Their GOD had expressly forbidden them to multiply Horses; and We never read of their bringing any considerable Number of Cavalry into the Field.—But, so long as they enjoyed the Presence of their Prophets, they wanted not this Arm of Flesh. They had more than an Equivalent for Chariots and Horses, in the *fervent*, the *effectual* Prayers of those holy Men of GOD (*Dialogues, 3*, 365–66, note).

<!-- p. 391 -->

2 Kings 2:14.] Elisha's passing through Jordan by the mantle of Elijah signifies believers' being preserved by the righteousness of Christ from being overwhelmed or overcome by any evil whatsoever, and particularly by death. Isaiah 43:2, "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee."

2 Kings 2:23–24.] Bethel was the place where one of Jeroboam's golden calves was set, and it was the chief seat of Israel's idolatry. And therefore instead of Bethel, the house of God is called Beth-aven,אָוֶן בֵּית "the house of iniquity," by the prophet Hosea [Hosea 10:5]. The inhabitants were probably chiefly idolaters. Hence their very children manifested such contempt of the prophet of the Lord. They seem "to mock both at him as an imposter, and at the miracle of Elijah's ascension as a fiction. They laughed at him, and called him 'baldhead' as a term of reproach (Jeremiah 16:6, and Jeremiah 48:37; Ezekiel 27:31, and Ezekiel 29:18; Micah 1:16; 2 Samuel 10:3–6; Isaiah 3:24), and bad him, Go up to heaven, as Elijah was reported to do, that they might see it, and believe it, and be troubled with him no longer." Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 626.

2 Kings 3:15. "But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the Lord came upon him."] The prophet composed himself to receive instructions from God. His mind was somewhat ruffled and disturbed at the sight of Jehoram, though he was not put into a sinful heat or passion, nor had spoke unadvisedly. Yet to be in the fittest frame for divine contemplation and the operations of his spirit, he needed the greatest calmness, and sedateness of spirit, and a mind more disengaged from temporal objects than that fervor of zeal against

<!-- p. 392 -->

Jehoram's sin did well admit of. He therefore called for a devout musician, one that used to play upon his harp and sing psalms to it. Probably it was some hours after his conversation with the kings, possibly in the evening. To hear God's praises sweetly sung, as DavidJE deleted "used to do it." had appointed, would settle and compose his mind, and help to put him into a right frame, both to speak to God and to hear from him. We find a company of prophets prophesying "with a psaltery and a tabret before them" (1 Samuel 10:5). See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, cols. 601–2.

2 Kings 3:16–26.] They were now in the deserts of Arabia, a dry country, where were no fountains nor streams of water; and it was a time of drought. "The Moabites knew that they were in those difficulties, which they expected before that they would be in, and therefore advanced with their whole army to take the advantage, resolving to attack them early in the morning. Their enemies, being in a valley, as 2 Kings 3:16–17, and themselves on an advanced ground, when the sun was risen in the east, on which side their enemies were, the angle of incidence with the rays upon the water coming directly into their faces, made it look red like blood. They, knowing that there was no water in those parts, and that there had been no rain, concluded that it was blood indeed, and that their enemies had quarreled among themselves, and destroyed one another, so that there was nothing to do but to take the plunder. This made them run thither without any military order, expecting that they who came first should enrich themselves most, and so they tired themselves before they came to the camp." So that the Israelites, when they came up, "gained an easy and entire victory over them, and pursued them into their own country, and there made a greater havoc of them, plundering their cities, destroying their fields, stopping up their wells, and cutting down their trees." Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, pp. 629–30.

2 Kings 3:25. "Only in Kirharaseth," etc.] It seems they demolished the walls of other cities, and scattered the stones into the gardens, vineyards, and

choicest fields near the city; but Kirharaseth, the royal city (on the walls of which that horrid human sacrifice was offered, 2 Kings 3:27), they never wholly subdued. And therefore it does not appear that the rebellion was suppressed, and the king of Moab ever reduced to subjection to the king of Israel any more.

2 Kings 4:23. 2 Kings 4:29.] See Numbers 21:18.

2 Kings 4:34. "And put his mouth upon his mouth," etc.] Elisha's doing thus is doubtless typical. The prophet here represents Christ, and the raising of the child to life represents the regeneration of a sinner. And by its being done in such a manner, several things are signified.

First. Hereby is signified the universality of the change in conversion. They are renewed in the whole man, sanctified throughout in every part and member. They put off the old man, and put on the new man. They have new eyes, new tongues, new hands, and new feet. Every part was before dead, but every part has new life put into it.

Secondly. Hereby is signified the universal conformity of the new man to Christ. As the parts of the body of the child corresponded with the parts of the body of the prophet, so doth every member of the new man to Christ. There, grace for grace, part for part, the new man is created after God. 'Tis after the image of him that created it. A man, when he is converted, he puts on Christ. Every feature, every part of the body, corresponds exactly with theJE deleted "answerable." parts of Christ's body.

Thirdly. Hereby is signified that the life of every part of the new man is by communication of Christ's life to us. Christ unites himself to us. He

<!-- p. 394 -->

stretcheth himself upon the dead child to impart of his warmth and his life to it. Christ doth as it were put his hands upon our dead hands to impart the life and virtue of his hands to ours, that our hands may be disposed and fitted to the same work that his hands doth. He puts his eyes to our blind eyes to impart the life and powers of his eyes to ours, that we may see the same spiritual objects that his eyes see, and so of the other parts.

2 Kings 4:41.] This meal that healed the poisoned pottage, and took death away from the pot,JE deleted "was a type of the same." signified the same with the tree that healed the bitter waters (Exodus 15:25). Wheat and other corn is often made use as a type of Christ. It was so in the sheaf of the first fruits, and in the first fruits of wheat harvest, in the wave loaves offered at Pentecost, and in all their meat offerings. Christ compares himself to a corn of wheat which,JE deleted "is not quickened." except it die, abideth alone [John 12:24]. And how often is Christ compared to bread. This meal was corn ground to powder; so Christ, before we can be healed by him, must suffer to the greatest extremity. See no. 217.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15* 150–51.

2 Kings 18:5. "So that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that was before him."] The same is said of Josiah (2 Kings 23:25). And yet we observe the words annexed and the manner of expression in each place; there is no inconsistence. Hezekiah exceeded all before and after in the manifestation and exercises of piety, fortitude, resolution, and steadfastness, with which he carried on the work of reformation, "trusting in the Lord God of Israel, departing not from him, but keeping his commandments," as is here said 2 Kings 23:5–6], manifesting this confidence

<!-- p. 398 -->

in God and steadfastness under very great temptation. Having taken the kingdom under the power of that great king of Assyria, he ventured to rebel against him, and continued steadfast under the great trial he had when his kingdom was, most of it, subdued, and he was besieged, and so proudly and terribly threatened in his royal city by Sennacherib's great army. But Josiah exceeded him in the degree to which he carried his reformation, his care and earnest endeavor that everything should be brought up exactly to the law of Moses. See the manner of expression, 2 Kings 23:25. See also 2 Kings 23:22 and 2 Chronicles 35:18.

Therefore this is as much as to say that he smote every fortification, took or destroyed everything that they had built for their own defense. Therefore this is a phrase that signifies emphatically his totally subduing the whole country.

2 Kings 20:12.] The special reasons of the king of Babylon's putting so much respect upon Hezekiah on this occasion were probably these. First, God gave Hezekiah exceeding great temporal prosperity in reward for his piety, as he had David and Solomon before. This appears by the next verse and 2 Chronicles 32:27 ff. These messengers probably showed this by applauding his prosperity, which probably was Hezekiah's temptation. 2. Hezekiah had been raised high in his reputation with the Babylonians by God's so wonderfully weakening the kingdom of Assyria (with whom the Babylonians were at war, as Mr. Henry observes) for Hezekiah's sake, as he did by the destruction of Sennacherib's army by the angel. See 2 Chronicles 32:21-23:3. By reason of that wonderful sign that God had given Hezekiah of the sun's going back ten degrees (2 Chronicles 32:31). This was the more taken notice of because the sun (as says Mr. Henry) was the Babylonian god, so that on their apprehension their god did very greatly favor, or was a great friend of Hezekiah's, which the more induced them to show themselves friendly to him.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 464–65.

<!-- p. 400 -->

2 Kings 20:13.] It is an hard matter, says Mr. Henry on the place, to keep the spirit low in the midst of great advancements. God had given Hezekiah great outward wealth and prosperity, and had wrought one great miracle after another for him: first, overthrew the mighty army of Sennacherib, that great and proud potentate, by an angel; and now even caused the sun to go back ten degrees. And he saw him greatly famed and honored in distant lands by these things, and now was receiving the compliments of a great prince on this occasion.Ibid., 465–66.

2 Kings 21:10–15.] 'Tis evident by this and many other passages of Scripture that the first destruction of Jerusalem was principally for the sins of Manasseh and the wickedness that the people were guilty of in his reign (2 Kings 23:26–27, and 2 Kings 24:3–4, and Jeremiah 15:4). And yet the first captivity in Jehoiachin's time was not till about forty-four years after Manasseh's death, and the total destruction of Jerusalem in Zedekiah's time not till about fifty-five years after his death. Hence I would observe that 'tis no argument against the dreadful destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, its being an evident token of God's wrath against the people for their rejecting and crucifying Christ, that that destruction happened about forty years after Christ's crucifixion.

1 Chronicles 2:6.] "Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara."] "Which were not perhaps the immediate sons of Zerah, but descendants from him, because they were the glory of their father's house; for when the Holy Ghost would magnify the wisdom of Solomon, he saith, 'He wasMS: "they were." wiser than' those four men, who, though 'the sons of Mahol,' are called Ezrahites, from Zerah (1 Kings 4:31)."*Exposition, 2* (1725), 483.

1 Chronicles 4:9–10.] Jabez's mother was probably a type of the church, and Jabez a type of that man-child which the church brings forth with the sorrow and travail of persecution, that we read of John 16:19–22, Revelation 12:2, Revelation 12:5, which shall be born especially at the commencement of the promised glory and enlargement of the church, which shall be given in answer to the prayers of the saints and especially of godly ministers, when God shall "bless his people indeed, and enlarge their coast, and his hand shall be with them, and when God shall keep 'em from evil, that it may not grieve 'em" (as is here said of God for Jabez, in answer to his prayer). See Ezekiel 36:33–38; Isaiah 40:1–2; Isaiah 54:1–4, and Isaiah 54:9, Isaiah 54:11–17; Psalms 102:13–22; Isaiah 26:15–17. 'Tis probable that it is for this very reason that these things concerning Jabez are inserted in this place.

One thing more may be worthy to be noted concerning Jabez, viz. that he was probably a scribe or divine, and that he "was more honorable than his brethren" 1 Chronicles 4:9], especially in "learning and piety," because we find "that the families of the scribes dwelt at Jabez (1 Chronicles 2:55), a city which it is likely took its name from his name," as Mr. Henry observes.Ibid., 486. So that

<!-- p. 404 -->

he is especially a type of the Christian ministry, and what is here said of him represents God's comforting and enlarging the church in answer to the prayers of gospel ministers.

1 Chronicles 4:22–23.] "It was found among the 'ancient things' that they had the dominion in Moab; probably in David's time, when that country was conquered, they transplanted themselves thither, and were put in places of power there, which they held for several generations. But this was a great while ago, time out of mind. Their posterity were now potters and gardeners, 'and those that dwelt among plants and hedges' 1 Chronicles 4:23], as is supposed in Babylon, where they dwelt with the king for his work." 1 Chronicles 4:24–43.] "Here is 1. The cities allotted the Simeonites, of which see Joshua 19:1–8. When it is said, they were theirs 'unto the reign of David' 1 Chronicles 4:31], it intimates that when the Ten Tribes revolted from the house of David, many of the Simeonites quitted these cities, because they lay within Judah, and seated themselves elsewhere. 2. The ground they got elsewhere. When those of this tribe that revolted from the house of David were carried captive with the rest into Assyria, those that adhered to Judah were remarkably owned of God, and prospered in their endeavors to enlarge their coasts. It was in the days of Hezekiah" (after the Ten Tribes were carried captive) "that a generation of Simeonites, whose tribe had long sneaked and truckled, was spirited to make these bold efforts." (It is said of the land they conquered, that it was "quiet and peaceable" 1 Chronicles 4:40]). "Even then, when the king of Assyria was giving disturbance to all their neighbors, this land escaped their alarms." In their conquering the Amalekites, "the curses on Ham and Amalek had a further accomplishment, as also the curse on Simeon, that he should be divided and scattered." (They were before scattered in Israel by many of 'em removing into the kingdom of Ephraim in Jeroboam's time.) "Yet to him it was turned into a blessing, for the families of Simeon, that thus transplanted themselves into those distant countries, are said to dwell 'there unto this day' (1 Chronicles 4:43), by which it should seem they escaped the calamities of the captivity." Henry.Ibid., 487.

1 Chronicles 11:39. "Zelek the Ammonite."] Here one of David's worthies is said to [be] an Ammonite, and another of 'em, 1 Chronicles 11:46, a Moabite. And yet in Deuteronomy 23:3, 'tis forbidden in the law of Moses that an Ammonite or Moabite should ever "enter into the congregation of the Lord." So Ruth was a Moabitess, but yet was received. By this it appears that evident piety prevailed for persons' admission, notwithstanding this law. When the case

<!-- p. 406 -->

was so, they were no longer Ammonites or Moabites in the eye of the law. By these things and many others it appears that evangelical qualifications always prevailed over legal ones. 1 Chronicles 19:18. "And forty thousand footmen."] In 2 Samuel 10:18, 'tis "horsemen." By "footmen" here is probably meant all that did not ride in chariots, who might be some horsemen and some footmen, most strictly so called. The whole forty thousand are here called footmen because they did not ride in chariots, and they are all called horsemen in Samuel because the bulk of the army were horsemen. It was the manner of the Syrians to use horses very much in war; and therefore all their warriors were called horsemen, as now valiant men by the French are called *cavalier*.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. See SSS on 2 Samuel 10:18.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 309. In this place all are called "men of feet," as it is in the

1 Chronicles 21:12. "Either three years of famine."] In 2 Samuel 24:13, it is, "Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land?," "which could not begin from this time, for David did not live so long after." But the case was thus. "There had been already three years of famine for the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1), and this year of numbering the people was almost ended. So that the question was," Shall I still further afflict the land with famine, and lengthen out the calamity that you have suffered already, even until seven years? Will you choose to have it made up a seven-years famine? "Shall three years of famine come, to begin with the following year, and so to be added to the three years already passed, and the present year, and make up the number seven in all?" Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*.*Scripture Chronology*, 559–60. The prophet thus refers to the famine that had been already, the calamities of which were fresh in memory.JE deleted "and not yet fully got over, by destroying the crop that was then growing, which was in." Because David by that knew what a three-years famine was, he might judge whether to choose three years more so as to make it up seven years, or no.At the beginning of the next paragraph, JE deleted "In the present year the drought was not continued that occasioned the famine in the three years past."

The famine for the Gibeonites was longer than of three years' continuance. The drought had continued three full years before the seven sons of Saul were hanged, which was done in theJE deleted "beginning of the year or spring." usual time of harvest on the same year that David numbered the people, and Rizpah watched them, "till water dropped upon them out of heaven" [2 Samuel 21:10]. And they had not as yet had any benefit of the rain by receiving the fruits of the earth produced by it, so that if three complete years of famine should come after this, it would make it up seven years of famine.

"Three years' famine." See note on 2 Samuel 24:13.This marginal reference, which is a separate entry, has an "X" through it. The only 2 Samuel 24:13 note is a reference to 1 Chronicles 21:12.

1 Chronicles 21:18-22:2.] Though there was so much land possessed by the children of Israel, yet God chose the land of Ornan the Jebusite, a Gentile proselyte, for the place where his temple should be built, which seems to be to signify two things, viz. 1. the calling of the Gentiles, and that when the gospel church should be erected by Christ, the true Solomon, of which this temple was a type, it should be erected on Gentile ground; and 2. his being a Jebusite, one of the accursed nations of Canaan, which seems to be to signify that Christ's church in all ages is made up of those that are naturally sinners and under the curse, and Christ's kingdom erected in the hearts of such. The church of Christ, in being set up here in this fallen sinful world, is set up on accursed ground, on the possession of those that were as it were Amorites, Hittites, and Jebusites. The corruption of nature that derive by natural generation is compared to our father's being an Amorite, and our mother an Hittite, and our births' being of the land of Canaan (Ezekiel 16:3). The children of Israel's settling in the land of those accursed nations seems to signify the same thing, for the children of Israel were the visible and typical church of God. And both these things seem also to be signified in the 1 Chronicles 22:2. They were strangers that were improved to hew stones for the temple, and this temple was therein the more fit type of the Christian church that was built up by the Gentiles. Isaiah 60:10, "And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls." Zechariah 6:12–13, Zechariah 6:15, "Behold the man whose name is the Branch, and he shall grow up out of his place. And he shall build the temple of the Lord. Even he shall build the temple of the Lord, and he shall bear the glory," etc. "And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord." And 'tis herein a more fit type of the church or spiritual temple in all ages, that is built up of those that are naturally strangers and aliens from the commonwealth of Israel.

Oman's giving freely the possession he had there for a place for God's altar, and the oxen for a burnt offering, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for a meat offering—his thus freely and readily giving everything that he had there, signifies to us how the true convert consecrates all to God, is ready to sacrifice all to the interest of religion, and is ready to part with all for Christ. See no. 217.*Works, 15*, 150–51.

1 Chronicles 22:13. "Dread not, nor be dismayed."] Persons need a great deal of courage that undertake any great enterprise for the church of God and the advancement of Christ's kingdom. Not only did Joshua need courage to conquer the land of Canaan, but Solomon to build the temple when all was in peace.

1 Chronicles 22:18–19.] So when persons are converted and have got through the great opposition that stood in the way of their safety, and God has given 'em rest, and given them the possession of the good, it is so far from being a just reason for slothfulness that it should, on the contrary, be improved as a reason why now they should set their heart and soul to seek the Lord their God, and to build the house of God.

1 Chronicles 23:26. "They shall no more carry the tabernacle," etc.] Thus the ceremonial law was in part altered before Christ's time. The service of the Levites, by the law of Moses, consisted much in carrying the tabernacle, and vessels, and instruments of it (Numbers 3-4). But when the temple was built, this service ceased, and was abrogated by David, there then ceasing to be occasion any longer for that work. And therefore David gave 'em new ordinances, and appointed them new work, which shows that the ceremonial law was alterable. If it may be altered in part, it may be altered in the whole. If David might abrogate some ordinances, Christ, the true David, might abrogate all. See note on Jeremiah 3:16–17 and Isaiah 56:3–4. InMS: "in the." 2 Chronicles 23:18, the ordinances of David are mentioned as of parallel validity with those of Moses as a rule for their public worship. See note on Isaiah 51:4. See "Miscellanies," no. 1027.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 20*, 358–65.

1 Chronicles 25:9–31.] The company of singers in the temple, in their several ranks and exact number and order, were a lively type of the triumphant church. And therefore there is, undoubtedly, something mystical and significant in this number and order that we have here an account of: twenty-four wards with twelve persons in each ward, so that the whole number was twice twelve times twelve, which is agreeable to the numbers by which things are reckoned that appertain to the church of God and the New

<!-- p. 410 -->

Jerusalem in the Revelation, where we find the number twelve in these things are always made use of. And the leaders or heads of these twenty-four wards do probably represent or typify the same thing that is signified by twenty-four elders in Revelation.

1 Chronicles 28:19.] The Spirit of God acted and guided the prophets "as to the very organs of their bodies, whereby they expressed the revelation which they had received by inspiration from him. They spake as they were acted by the Holy Ghost.… So when David had received the pattern of the temple, and the manner of the whole worship of God therein by the Spirit, he says, 'All this the Lord made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the work of this pattern.' The Spirit of God not only revealed it unto him, but so guided him in writing of it down, as that he might understand the mind of God out of what himself had written; or he gave it him so plainly and evidently, as if every particular had been expressed in writing by the finger of God." Owen, *On the Spirit*, Bk. 2, ch. 1, §10.*ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΟΛΟΓΙΑ*, p. 105.

1 Chronicles 29:2 ff.] David did not lay up those vast treasures he obtained in his wars for the enriching his family, and to leave to his son that should be the heir of his sin, but gave it to God. But God rewarded him in the exceeding great wealth of his son. He had not less then, but doubtless much more than if David had laid up all that he had gotten for him. So the princes of Israel and the people in general gave most liberally to the house of God, and how was the whole land enriched soon after. There appeared a wonderfully liberal, bountiful spirit amongst the people, and what riches soon ensued throughout the whole land.

1 Chronicles 29:8–9.] God greatly rewarded this extraordinary liberality of the people by exceedingly enriching them afterwards in the days of Solomon, as well as rewarded David's liberality, in giving that which he might have laid up for his son and successor, by bestowing such vast riches and honor on Solomon.

1 Chronicles 29:15. "For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers."] These words are exegetical of the last words in the foregoing verse: "of thine own have we given thee." They that only sojourn with another, the habitation they live in and the things they use are not their

<!-- p. 411 -->

own, but their landlord's. They are but lent to them. And this is added, "as were all our fathers," perhaps as a further evidence that what we have is not our own, for though we have it from our fathers, come by it by inheritance, yet our fathers themselves had it not of their own, but only lent to them by God.

So when it shall come to that in the latter days, that the ministers of the gospel shall generally be united in preaching the true doctrine of the gospel of God's glorious grace, those doctrines especially that are in a peculiar manner evangelical, by which especially is manifested the glory of God's eternal mercy, and free and sovereign immutable grace through Christ Jesus, by which especially the preached gospel is like a song of praise to the Most High: I say, when once it comes to this, and when, withal, ministers shall be united in affection and act in union as fellow laborers and fellow helpers to the grace of God, then shall the glory of God remarkably appear in his church and fill the world. Then shall the Spirit of God, as a spirit of light, holiness, and joy, descend from heaven in a very new and glorious manner; and remarkable success shall attend the preaching of the gospel everywhere; and then shall be the proper commencement of the day of the church'sJE deleted "letter glory." rest, glory, and triumph on earth.

The peaceful reign of Solomon in his wisdom, wealth, and glory, after the militant troublesome reign of David, is evidently typical of the peaceful, joyful, and glorious reign of Christ in the latter days; and God's dwelling in the magnificent temple as the settled place of his rest, after removing to and froMS: "from." in a tent and tabernacle, is typical of the glorious manner of his dwelling with his church in the latter days, as compared with preceding times.

Nehemiah 8:17.] This is a remarkable instance how some of God's institutions are sometimes long neglected in his church, even in the church's flourishing times, and how God winks at such a neglect. 'Tis remarkable that this ordinance had been neglected in David's, and Solomon's, and Hezekiah's, and Josiah's times; and we have no account of the people's being particularly reproved for it by any of the prophets. This ordinance never

<!-- p. 421 -->

was observed in the Israelitish church from about the time of its being first settled in Joshua's time till after the captivity when it was drawing to an end. So the due keeping the Passover seems to have been neglected from the days of the judges till Josiah's time (2 Kings 23:22, 2 Chronicles 35:1). So the law against polygamy, Leviticus 18:18, seems even to have been neglected and not understood, nor the contrary practice reproved, till Malachi's time. So in the Christian church, some Christian institutions have been perverted, and others neglected, almost from the days of the apostles till these latter ages since the Reformation. So the right order of the minister, Christ's institution of the two orders of bishops and deacons, and the purity of ministers, seems to have been set aside from near the apostolic age till the Reformation, which well answers to the Jewish return from the captivity into Babylon, for the Reformation is the church's return out of the spiritual Babylon. So how long has that very great and essential part of the stated public service of the Christian church been neglected, viz. charity.JE deleted "which is an essential part of the public service of the Christian churches."

*Corol*. 1. The Scripture only is our rule to direct us in matters of faith and worship, and not fathers, or councils, or ecclesiastical history, or the practice of the church in former times or in its flourishing times.

*Corol*. 2. Hence no argument can be drawn against infant baptism from the practice of the Waldenses, if it should really appear that they did not baptize infants.
