### Esther

THE BOOK OF ESTHER. See no. 46; *Works, 15*, 60–63. and "Miscellanies," no. 702, third last paragraph in *Corol*. 3.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 18*, 305–6.

Esther 1:8. "None did compel."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, cols. 992–93.

Esther 1:14.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 255.The seven princes were seven privileged counselors to the king of Persia (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 255).

Esther 3:2.] The probable reason why Mordecai refused to bow to Haman was because he was an Amalekite, as he is called an Agagite (Esther 3:1), that is, of the posterity of Agag, or of the royal race of Amalek. The kings of Amalek used to be called Agag, as the kings of Egypt were called Pharaoh (Numbers 24:7), so that he was probably, before his advancement in Ahasuerus's court, looked upon as the head of the remains of that nation. As Mordecai was the chief [of] the Jews in those parts, his bowing to HamanMS: "Mordecai." would therefore look like the Jewish nation's bowing and submitting to the nation of Amalek, which MordecaiMS: "Haman." refused out of a conscientious regard to what God had declared and commanded Israel concerning that nation, in Exodus 17:8, Exodus 17:13–14, Exodus 17:16, and 1 Samuel 15:2–3, God probably by his Spirit influencing him,MS: "of him." and giving him some intimations of his being supported in his resolution of refusing to bow to him. For the extraordinary and prophetical influences of God's Spirit had not as yet ceased on Israel, and probably Mordecai himself was inspired and divinely directed in writing this history. God, in Exodus 17:16, had declared that he would "have war with Amalek from generation to generation," i.e. that his people should have war with them, which was an implicit command never to be at peace with them. But submitting or bowing to them would

<!-- p. 424 -->

have been inconsistent with upholding a state of war with them. Those would have been manifestations of peace.

Esther 3:7.] "Haman consults the soothsayers to find out a lucky day for the designed massacre. The resolve was taken up 'in the first month, in the twelfth year' of the king, when Esther had been his wife about five years. Some day or other in that year must be pitched upon. As if he doubted not, but that heaven would favor his design, he refers it to a lot." (So the lot was cast for each month, and for the days of the month that the lot fell upon from day to day, till they came to the day that the lot favored.) "And the lot fell upon the twelfth day of that month, so that Mordecai and Esther [had eleven months] to turn them in, for the defeating the design." Henry.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 651. Henry reads "for the Lot fell upon *the twelfth Month*, so that *Mordecai* and *Esther* had eleven Months to turn them in, for the defeating of the Design." See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 1005.

See Esther 9:1 ff.

Esther 3:9. "And I will pay ten thousand talents of silver."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 1006.

Esther 3:15.] See Proverbs 11:10.

Esther 5:2. "So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the scepter."] Favor was offered by the king by holding out to her the golden scepter; but it was expected that she, in order to a title and interest in the offered favor, should draw near and touch the top of the scepter as an expression of her joyful acceptance of the favor, submission to the royal dominion and power of which the scepter was the ensign, and her dependence on the king's free, sovereign, but offered, favor. The act and benefit of saving faith in Christ may be compared to this act of Esther towards Ahasuerus her king, her husband, and in this affair and in what followed, her savior.

Esther 7:8. "Will he force the queen also?"] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1020–21.

Esther 8:2. "And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman."] Here is a second fulfillment of Balaam's prophecy, Numbers 24:7, "His king shall be

<!-- p. 425 -->

higher than Agag." Mordecai herein is a type of Christ, the king of the spiritual Israel, who shall be higher than Antichrist, the spiritual Agag.JE deleted "and Haman."

Esther 8:11. "Little ones and women."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 1022.

Esther 8:15. "And the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad."] See Proverbs 11:10.

Esther 9:5–16.] Probably at this time the Jews slew, with Haman and his ten sons, all that were found anywhere of the nation of Amalek that they belonged to; and this seems to have been the last that was done by the nation of Israel in fulfillment of God's curse and command in Exodus 17:14, Exodus 17:16. There were three remarkable destructions that Israel made of that nation. There were several remarkable destructions that Israel made of that nation in fulfillment of what God had said to 'em in the wilderness: one by Saul (1 Samuel 14), and [an]other by David (1 Samuel 27:8, and 1 Samuel 30), and the last before this was that which we have account of in 1 Chronicles 4:43.

Esther 9:13.] The reason why Esther desired that Haman's ten sons might be hanged probably was not from a revengeful spirit, desiring to revenge Hanan's injury on his sons, but that she might fulfill the will of God concerning the Amalekitish nation declared in Exodus 17:14, Exodus 17:16. And probably she did it by Mordecai's direction, that he gave by the direction of the Spirit of God. See note on Esther 3:2.

Esther 9:30. "With words of peace and truth."] I.e. wishing them "peace and truth," saying, Peace and truth be with you, or the like, as the Apostle in his epistles, "Grace, mercy, and peace" [Titus 1:2] be with you, and the like.

### Job

The Book of Job.] See no. 145, concerning the manner of wise men's discoursing in those times by taking up their parable.*Works, 15*, 91. Concerning the place where Job dwelt, and the penman of this book, see no. 202.Ibid., 122–26. Concerning the reason why such a book as this was inserted into the canon of the Old Testament, and why this book itself is so constituted as it is, see "Miscellanies," no. 810.Each sentence in this paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 18*, 516–19.

The sayings of Job's three friends (though they were wrong in the application) are justly cited as canonical scripture. See note on 1 Corinthians 3:19.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 2:4.] Or "skin even unto skin." See Hervey's *Dialogues*, vol. 2, p. 157e.Hervey explains this expression as reference to "the very inmost Skin, which cannot be taken away, without the greatest Loss, and severest Pain. Yet, even this *Loss* a Man would suffer, this *Pain* He would endure, in order to preserve *precious* Life" (*Dialogues, 2*, 157, note).

Job 2:9. "Curse God, and die."] "Some of the heathens used to reproach their gods when any great adversity befell them. The Idumeans, it is probable, did so, among whom Job's wife might have her education. The ancient Persians, who are said to have worshipped fire as a god, used to threaten to extinguish it by water, when enraged by any grievous calamity. And it may be, to some such irreligious temper, the Prophet at least alludes, Isaiah 8:21. 'They shall fret themselves, and curse their king, and their God, and look upward.' Job's wife, if she had not the principles of these enemies of true religion, it seems, on this occasion, falls into their disposition and language." Bennet, *Christian Oratory*, vol. 2, p. 207.*Second Part of the Christian Oratory*. This selection is from a sermon on Job 2:10 by Benjamin Bennet (1674–1726), a Nonconforming divine of evangelical orientation, entitled "Of Receiving Evil, as well as Good at the Hand of God" (pp. 204–32). This volume is not a "second volume." Edwards apparently designated it as such because it is titled "Second Part." It is a posthumous publication edited by Latham.

<!-- p. 427 -->

Job 2:9–10. "Dost thou still retain thine integrity," etc.?] Job did not only retain his integrity just now for a little while while his calamity was new, but he held it to the end. And theJE deleted "long." continuance of his affliction did wear out his integrity, but he persevered and held out to the end; and so Satan was confounded. Though his weakness appeared under the strength and continuance of his temptations and sufferings, so that he spoke many things very wrong, and God rebuked him sharply, yet he did not curse God and cast him off, as Satan supposed he would, but all along resolves to cleave to him, as appears by Job 13:15 and Job 27:2–10.

Job 3:6. "Let it not be joined to the days of the year," etc.] It seems to have been the opinion of the church of God of old, even in the most ancient times and all nations, that it was proper that those days wherein anything remarkably sorrowful happened should periodically be looked upon and observed as sorrowful days, and that those wherein anything very remarkably joyful [happened] should periodically be observed as joyful days. But if Job thought his birth so sorrowful an event that it was worthy that that day should periodically be distinguished as a day of sorrow and mourning, how much more may the day of Christ's resurrection, the birth day of the whole church of God to eternal glory, be periodically kept as a joyful day.

Job 3:8. "Who are ready to raise up their mourning."] In the original,לִוְיָתָן עֹרֵר "raise up leviathan," i.e. the devil, alluding probably to some custom of the heathen who in their cursings used to raise the devil.

Balaam was a magician of those eastern parts. And by what we are told concerning him, it seems to have long been a custom for such magicians, by their enchantments or concern with the devil, to curse and bring evil upon persons and people. And so probably they might from malice curse particular seasons and days on which certain affairs were to be managed. The word "leviathan" is never used for mourning. See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. Poole, *Synapsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 21–23.

Job 3:23. "Whose way is hid."] I.e. from him, that he knows not where to go, what to do, or which way to turn himself for relief or rest, etc.

<!-- p. 428 -->

Job 3:24. "Before I eat," or "before my meat," or "in the presence of my meat," as in the Hebrew.]לַחְמַי לִפְנַי I.e. while I am eating, when others used to be merry. "Eat, drink, and be merry."

Job 4:8. "Reap the same."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 4:9. "Blast of God."] In this figure, whereby the curse of God is called the "blast of God," allusion is had to some sorts of winds in those countries that caused the fruits of the earth to fade and wither away, especially east winds.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. Or else in allusion to those pestilential blasts of wind that sometimes there were in those parts. See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 35.*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 35.

Job 4:18. "Behold, he put no trust in his servants," etc.] The love and faithfulness of the saints, or of innocent men, or angels, is not at all to be depended on if God should leave them. It was God's pleasure to let both men and angels see their insufficiency and dependence on him, and therefore he suffered a fall of both.

Job 4:21. "Die without wisdom."] See "Old Testament Intimations of a Future State," p. 21e.The extant portion of JE's "Intimations" manuscript contains only ten pages. The section referred to here has not been located.

Job 5:5.] Here it seems to beJE deleted "supposed." implied that they sow among thorns, as in Job 8:17 it is implied that the wicked sow in stony places. The prosperity and substance of oppressors is an harvest among the thorns of worldliness, and envy, and malice, etc. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 41–42.

Job 5:7.] In the Hebrewעְוּף יַגְבִּיהוּ וּבְנֵ־רֶשֶׁף it is, "as the sons of the burning coal lift up to fly." No wonder that coals that are full of fire send forth sparks. No more is it any wonder that trouble proceeds from that fountain of sin that is in man. Sinful man is like a burning coal, full of sin, as fuel that is full of fire, from which affliction proceeds as necessarily as sparks proceed from a fire.

<!-- p. 429 -->

Or the meaning may be that man, that is born of corrupt fallen man, does as naturally and necessarily live a life of sorrow as the sparks that are sons of the burning coal fly upward. As soon as these sons of the coal are born of the burning coal, they begin to fly upward, and continue to do so till they go out, which is very soon. So man, as soon as born, begins to suffer affliction, and so goes on as long as he lives, hastening to his end till his life quickly goes out, like the light of a spark. This seems the more probable meaning. The sparks are driven upwards by a hot blast of wind. A being followed with affliction isJE deleted "often." compared to a being lifted up and made to ride on the wind (Job 30:22). So the wind is put for trouble (Proverbs 11:29); so Ecclesiastes 5:16, Isaiah 27:8 and Isaiah 32:2, Hosea 8:7. See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. This reference was added even later. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 42–43.

Job 5:10–11.] See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 44.

Job 5:12–16.] By these and many other parallel passages in this book it seems that it was a thing noted and commonly observed in the church of God of old, before Moses' time in the age of the patriarchs, that the wicked of the world used to persecute God's saints.

Job 5:24.] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 6:5.] Job was become so poor that he had nothing to eat, and that made him complain. See the two next verses.

Job 6:10. "For I have not concealed the words of the Holy One."] As a teacher, ruler, and judge, the things which I have spoken, the instructions, and counsels, and commands I have given, and the sentence I have pronounced, has been right agreeable to God's mind, agreeable to his revealed will.

Job 6:11. "What is my strength, that I should have hope? What is my end, that I should prolong my life?"] I.e. Job 6:16. "Blackish by reason of the ice."] Or as the wordsמִנִּי־קַדַח הַקֹּדְרִים are literally, "before the frost," i.e. under the ice they appear black, as though there was much water there.

Job 6:19. "The troops of Tema looked."] In the winter when they did not want water, then there was enough. But in summer when they needed, there was none. So Job would intimate it was with his friends. They were friendly in time of his prosperity, but failed in adversity.

Job 6:24–25.] Eliphaz had charged him with being a wicked man, but had not told him wherein. He had mentioned no crime or wicked practice of his. Job challenges him to show on particular instances wherein he had been wicked. He charged and reproved, but what was the thing that he reproved? It was in general his supposed wickedness, but he could fix upon nothing.

Job 6:26.] I.e. do ye imagineJE deleted "to force." by your rebukes to oblige me to hold my peace and not utter my complaint, as though it were causeless? Do you think

toJE deleted "prevent." deny me even the small relief of venting my sorrow, whose desperate case forces me to complain? You had as good think to hinder the wind from blowing, as to hinder me in my extreme sorrow from complaining (Job 10:1, and Job 13:13, and 2:19).

Job 6:28.] This refers to what Job had said in the Job 6:26. (See note.) As much as to say,MS: "See." Look upon me, and behold my case. Consider it in its circumstances, and see if you can think any other than that the extremity of my case is not enough to extort these complaints. The Job 6:27 comes in as a parenthesis. Job 8:9. "For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow."] Bildad here has respect to the much longer lives of preceding generations, whereby they had much greater opportunity to gain wisdom and experience. In Job's time the age of men was shortened very much from what it was a few generations before.

Job 8:11. "Can the rush grow up without mire," etc.?] It seems that there was a sort of weeds in those parts of Arabia, that used to spring up in the spring in the puddles and places moistened with snow water, that died when the sun advanced, and the weather grew hotter and dried up the moisture. To these Bildad here compares Job'sMS: "Bildads." hope and prosperity.

Job 8:14.] See Spencer's *Similies and Sentences*, p. 99.Under the heading, "*The Vanity of* heaping up Riches," John Spencer (d. 1680) writes, "It is a great deal of care and pains that the *Spider* takes in weaving her *web*, she *runneth* much, and often up and down, she *fetcheth a compass* this way and that way, and *returneth* often to the same point, she *spendeth* her self in multitudes of fine threads, to make her self a round Cabinet, she *exenterateth* her self, and *worketh* out her own *bowels*, to make an artificial and curious piece of work; which when it is *made*, is apt to be *blown* away with every *puffe of wind*; she *hangeth* it up aloft, she *fastneth* it to the roof of the house, she *strengthneth* it with many a thread, *wheeling* often round about, not *sparing* her own *bowels*, but spending them willingly upon her *work*; And when she hath done all this, spun her fine threads, *weaved* them one within another, *wrought* her self a fine Canopy, *hanged* it aloft, and thinks all's sure; on a *sudden*, in the *twinckling of an eye*, with a little sweep of a *Beesom*, all falls to the ground, and so her labour perisheth: But here is not all; a Poor *Spider*, she is *killed* either in her *own web*, or else she is *taken* in her *own snare*, haled to *death*, and trodden under *foot*; Thus the *silly Animal* may be truly said either to *weave* her own *winding sheet*, or to make a *snare* to hang her self. Just so do *many Men* wast and consume themselves to get *preferment*, to enjoy *pleasures*, to heap *up riches*, and *encrease them*; and to that end they *spend* all their wit, and oftentimes the *health* of their bodies, *running* up and down, *labouring* and *sweating, carking* and *caring*; And when they have done all this, they have but *weaved the Spiders web* to catch flyes, yes, oftentimes are *caught* in their own *nets*, are made *instruments* of their *own destruction*, they take a great deal of *pains* with little *success*, to no *end* or *purpose*" (ΚΑΙΝΑ ΚΑΙ ΠΑΔΑΙΑ. *Things New and Old. Or, a Store-house of Similies, Sentences, Allegories, Apophthegms, Adagies, Apologues, Divine, Morall, Politicall, &c. With their several Applications. Collected and observed from the Writings and Sayings of the Learned in all Ages to this present* [London, 1658]).

Job 8:17.] This verse implies that they grow in stony places where they have no deepness of earth. Their "roots are wrapped about the heap," but don't penetrate into the ground, and so are withered before the scorching sun. See Matthew 13 concerning them that grew in stony places.

Job 8:18.] "His place will deny him, saying, I have not seen thee."] I.e. he shall be totally destroyed from his place; neither root nor branch shall

be found there. There shall be no remnant. The place shall be as though he had never stood there.

Job 9:7.] See note on Job 34:20.

Job 9:8. "And treadeth upon the waves of the sea."] See note on Matthew 14:24–25.

Job 9:24. "He covereth the faces of the judges thereof."] I.e. covers their eyes, blindfolds them so that they cannot see to [do] justice, so that the wicked are justified, and the righteous suffer.

Job 9:26. "They are passed away as the swift ships, as the eagle that hasteth to the prey."] A most lively and beautiful comparison. When we stand upon the brink of an harbor as a ship sets sail under a full gale, and we look after, or see an eagle aloft in the air upon the wing, swiftly hasting to some distant prey, how fast do they lessen and grow dim, and how soon do they totally disappear and appear no more. We can see nothing of them.

Job 9:29.] I.e. if I am wicked after I have used such care to avoid sin, and taken so much pains to wash myself, if still thou holdest me as a wicked man and treatest me as such, it is not worth the while to strive to be clean and pure, for I have done my utmost. See the two next verses. See also Job 9:1–2, and Job 9:15, and Job 9:20–21, and Job 9:23.

"And mine own clothes should abhor me."] The marginal readingI.e. margin of the KJV. seems preferable: "make me to be abhorred," i.e. my clothes, which hide my deformity and be my ornaments to recommend me, shall instead of that make me appear the more deformed and loathsome, being as filthy rags, as a man's garment would be if he were plunged in a ditch and rolled in mire and filth.

Job 12:7–25.] The discourse that is begun in this verse and continued to the end of the chapter is connected with Job 12:3, "But I have understanding as well as you: I am not inferior to you; yea, who knoweth not such things as these?" as is confirmed by the conclusion of this discourse in the Job 13:1–2, where the same thing in sense is repeated that was said in that Job 12:3. And it appears that what Job has special reference to in the preceding discourses of his three friends, when he thus asserts that he knows as much as they, is what they had said of the greatness, perfections, works, and dominion of God, as Eliphaz (Job 5:9–18) and Zophar, in the Job 11:7–10.

Job 12:18. "The bond of kings."] I.e. the bond that kings bind with, as Psalms 68:6, "He bringeth out those which were bound with chains"; Psalms 146:7, "Which executeth judgment for the oppressed, which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners." "And girdeth their loins with a girdle." I.e. he girdeth those with strength and beauty that before were bound by the strength of others, as 1 Samuel 2:4. "The bows of the mighty men are broken, and they that stumbled are girt with strength." So a girdle was an ornament. Isaiah 3:24, "Instead of a girdle a rent."

Job 13:8. "Will ye accept his person? Will ye contend for God?"] A true respect to God, which primarily consists in a love to his moral perfections, don't tend to any immorality, for surely a true love to moral virtue and excellency don't tend to a regard to moral evil and deformity. A love to God for his justice don't incline to injustice. A love to God for the mercifulness of his nature don't incline to harshness and cruelty. But a false respect to God is very commonly exercised in the vilest and most unrighteous actions. So a false zeal for God commonly is shown in hating men and in the greatest injustice, persecution, and cruelty. This is accepting God's person, which the righteous God will thank no man for, but infinitely abhors and is greatly provoked by, as it follows in the Job 13:10. "He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons."

Job 13:9. "Is it good?"] Would it prove well for you?

"As one man mocketh another, do ye so mock him?" I.e. do ye think to impose upon God and cheat him with your hypocritical pretenses of zeal for him by speaking wickedly for him? Do you think you can deceive him as one man deceives another?This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 13:14.] I.e. though I say, I will speak, let come on me what will, yet I run no dreadful venture. There is no reason for you to imagine that in so expressing myself and solemnly appealing to God, I am devouring my own flesh with my own teeth, or destroying my life with my own hand, for though I boldly refer myself to God's judgment, yet I shall be justified. Yet I am safe; I know I shall be justified. The wordsבְשִׁנּי בְשָׂרִי אֶשֶּׂא עַל־מָה might have been translated most properly, "Wherefore should I take my flesh in my teeth," etc., signifying that he should do so in thus solemnly appealing to God, if his own conscience did testify to his integrity. Job expresses himself thus to confirm his friends that he did not speak against his conscience, as much as to say, Why should I be so foolish as to appeal thus to God, and to go to "take my flesh in my teeth," etc., as I should do if I made such an appeal, and was not conscious to my integrity?

Job 14:4. "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?"] No. 334.*Works, 15*, 318–19.

Job 14:13–15.] See Dr. Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, pp. 240 ff.In Dissertation II, "The Sense of the Antients before Christ upon the Circumstances and Consequences of the Fall," Thomas Sherlock declares that Job, despite his present distress, expected "another Time for Justice" from God based on his hope and expectation "to be called from the Grave." His friends did not share that expectation (*Use and Intent of Prophecy*, 5th ed., pp. 240–41).

Job 14:18–20.] See Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, p. 241.Sherlock describes the responses of Job's friends to his declaration that "all Things were drawing to an End, the Earth, and the Inhabitants thereof" (5th ed., pp. 241–42).

Job 14:22.] 'Tis not unlikely that the Spirit of God in this has some respect to the misery of wicked men inJE deleted "another world." a future state, when both soul and body shall be cast into hell. See Ecclesiastes 11:10.

Job 15:20. "The number of years is hidden to the oppressor."] That is the wicked man spoken of who is an oppressor (Job 15:28, Job 15:34–35). The number of the years of his prosperity and life is hidden to him. The continuance of it is exceeding uncertain, which causes him to be full of fears and suspicions, and have "a dreadful sound in his ears." Oftentimes in the midst of his prosperity, when he seems to be most safe, destruction

<!-- p. 437 -->

comes upon him, as it follows in the next verse. He is in constant fear of sudden destruction, and this makes him travail in pain.

Probably Eliphaz here has reference to what Job had said before concerning himself in his prosperity. Job 3:25–26, "The thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came." And when Eliphaz in the next verse speaks of the destroyer's coming upon him, he probably [has] reference to the Sabeans and Chaldeans, which came suddenly and destroyed Job's substance. And when he says, Job 15:22, "He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness," he seems to have respect to the desponding thoughts which Job had expressed. Job 9:21, "Though I were perfect, yet would I not know my soul. I would despise my life." And Job 9:16, "If I had called, and he had answered me, yet would I not believe that he had hearkened to my voice." And when in the Job 15:23 he speaks of the wicked's wandering "abroad for bread," he probably has reference to Job's poverty.

Job 15:22. "The sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Job 15:26.] "He runneth" boldly on God, even when clad in dreadful armor.

Job 15:32. "His branch shall not be green."] While the branch is only in the bud, before it is leaved out.

Job 15:35. "Bring forth vanity."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Job 16:11.] Thus these good men censured one another as ungodly.

Job 16:18.] I.e. if I have shed any blood wrongfully, sitting an judge, let not the earth cover the blood that I have shed; and if I have done so, let my prayer not be accepted.

Job 17:5.] His friends, he supposed, had flattered before his calamity; and that now it was evident that in times past, when he was "as a tabret" (as he says in the next verse), when they appeared so fair and friendly when he was in his prosperity, it was all nothing but flattery, and that now it evidently proved so when he was come to be in adversity, he being now their byword.

Job 17:12. They change the night into day; the light is short because of darkness."] The words seem evidently to be wrong translated. Most literally rendered, the wordsיָשִׂימוּ לְיוֹם לַיְלָה are thus: "They put the nightJE mistakenly writes "light." into the day," i.e. they bring the night or darkness into the time that, according to the ordinary course of things,MS: "thing." is the time of day, and so shorten the day, make it much shorter than its natural period. Thus the former part of the verse agrees with the latter part, and with the content, and with Job's plain drift and design, which is to represent how his day of prosperity and life is shortened, and suddenly cut off, and all his purposes and hopes broken.

As for that manner of speaking, "They put the night into the day," see note on Lamentations 4:15.

Job 17:13–14.] The grave is the house that is my home; and corruption and worms are the rest of the family that is of the same house, and [that] I am to dwell with in the house of my near relatives of the same family. I desire the grave as a child desires to go home, and desire worms and corruption as the child desires to dwell with its father, mother, etc.

Job 17:15–16. "Where is now my hope? As for my hope, who shall see it? They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust."] The more literal translation of the last of these versesנָחַת עַל־עָפָר אִם־נַחַד תֵּרַדְנָה שְׁאֹל בַּדֵּי is thus: "The bars of the pit descend, when our rest together is in the dust," which seems to be a better translation. The expression signifies as much as that when Job was gone to the grave as his house, and had there took up his settled abode with corruption as his father and with worms as his mother and sister, and was dwelling together in that house with such a family, the door of the pit should be everlastingly shut and barred upon him so that he never should come out again. This he gives as a reason why death would be an end to all his hope. A phrase for a door's being open is its being "lifted up," as in the end of the Psalms 24: "Lift up, ye gates; and be ye lift, ye everlasting door." See SSS on Psalms 24:7.This reference is a later addition. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 703–4. So a door's descending seems to be a phrase for its being fast shut, and the bars' descending, their being thrust down or thrust in for the fastening of the door.

Job 18:2. "Mark, and afterwards," etc.] I.e. mark out some limits to your talk. Set some bounds to your words. Let us know when you have done, and then we will speak.

Job 18:4. "Shall the earth be forsaken?"] I.e. shall God forsake the earth, and cease to take care of mankind, and to exercise his moral government over them, that you may escape punishment? In this sense the phrase of God's "forsaking the earth" is used, Ezekiel 8:12. "The Lord seeth us not; the Lord hath forsaken the earth." "Shall the rock be removed out of its place?" Must the fixed order of the divine government be changed for thee?

Job 18:13–14.] By the "first-born of death" here is probably meant the devil, or the prince of the devils. One that is subject to death, or liable to death or destruction, is called a son of death or destruction, as 1 Samuel 26:16 and Proverbs 31:8. And therefore the devil, that was the first being that ever became subject to death, or the leader of the devils, who first became liable to death, may be called the "first-born of death." The same is probably meant by the "king of *terrors*," in the Job 18:14.

Job 18:14. "His confidence shall be rooted out of his tabernacle."] I.e. that which he set his heart upon, and placed his happiness [in], and depended upon for safety, comfort, honor, or any good that his heart had dependence upon.

Job 19:4. "Mine error remaineth with myself."] It hurts me, and not you. I must bear the punishment alone. I am punished enough by God, and you need not add to my affliction lest I should not suffer enough. This agrees best withMS: "which." what follows.

Job 19:25. "For I know that my redeemer lives."] Job mentions this because he is about to express his hope of what would be after he was dead. He should die, and the worms should destroy his body, but his redeemer lived. And hence he hoped that he would redeem his body from the power of the grave. The resurrection of the body, and that glorification of the whole person that will then be, is especially called "redemption" in the New Testament. And because his redeemer lived, he hoped that though he died, he should live again by his redemption, for in that he lives, we shall live also.

<!-- p. 441 -->

"I know that my redeemer liveth." Though I shall die, and my flesh shall be destroyed with worms. "And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." In the original, it is, "he shall stand over the dust," עָפָר עַל. The word "earth" is very often used in the book of Job, and the word is everywhere *eretz*,אֶרֶץ and nowhere this word that properly signifies "dust." And it is not true that at the day of judgment Christ will properly stand on the earth. The meaning is that Christ will stand over the dust of the dead saints.This and the following paragraph are a separate entry.

"My redeemer," גֹּאֲלִי. The word also, as it was used among the Hebrews, signified near kinsman, as in Ruth 3:12. "And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman, *goeēl*; howbeit there is a kinsman, *goeēl*, nearer than I." Ruth 3:13, "Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, or if he will redeem thee, יִגְאָלֵךְ, well; let him do the kinsman's part, יִגְאָֹל. But if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, לְגָאֳלֵךְ, then I will do the part of a kinsman to thee, וגְאַלְתִּיךְ." So the word is the same, 1 Kings 16:11. "As soon as he began to reign, he slew all the house of Baasha; he left none of his kinsfolks, וְגֹּאֲֹלָיו.

There were four things the *goeēl* was to do for his kinsman unable to act for himself. 1. He was to marry the widow of the deceased kinsman to raise up seed to his brother, as Christ marries the elect church that was left a widow by the first Adam, the first surety, and by the law or first covenant, the first husband having no seed (Romans 7:3–4). 2. He was [to] redeem the inheritance of his poor kinsman (Leviticus 25:25). So Christ redeems the inheritance which we sold. 3. He was to ransom his poor kinsman in bondage, paying the price of his redemption. Leviticus 25:47, "If thy brother wax poor, and sell himself," Leviticus 25:48, "after that he is sold, he may be redeemed again; one of his brethren may redeem him." Leviticus 25:52, "According unto his years shall he give him again the price of his redemption." Thus does Christ redeem us from bondage after we have sold ourselves. 4. He was to avenge the blood of his slain kinsman on the slayer. Thus does Christ avenge our blood on Satan.This paragraph is a later addition.

See Dr. Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, pp. 225 ff.This reference is a later addition. Sherlock argues that Job's declaration in this verse contains "a degree of Knowledge" of the "great Mystery" of the future resurrection "beyond the Proportion of Light communicated to the Age in which he lived." Neither Moses nor Jewish interpreters had such knowledge, which was not available until the time of the New Testament (5th ed., pp. 225–28).

"And that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth." In the original,יָקְוּם עַל־עָפָר וְאַחֲרֹוֹן

it is, "And that at last he shall stand over (or rise above) the dust," concerning which, see SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 191–94.

Job 19:26. "And though after my skin."] Job says thus because his skin was destroyed already by the sore boils that he was smitten with from head to foot, and the worms had destroyed that, as he says, Job 7:5. "My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome." The literal translationנִקְּפוּ־זאֹת עעוֹרִי וְאַחַר is, "Though after my skin, they shall destroy this," probably putting his hand on his flesh and bones. The expression is such a kind of impersonal phrase as is used, as Job 18:19, and Daniel 2:30, and many other places.

The proper meaning of the expression, according to the idiom of the language, is no more than this: "Though after my skin, this is destroyed." See SSS.This paragraph is a later entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 194–95.

Job 19:27. "Be consumed within me."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 196–97.

In the same context JE inserted a second "Job 35:8, " duplicating the Ezekiel reference in the following sentence. So Ezekiel 31:17, and Ezekiel 32:28, Ezekiel 32:32, and Ezekiel 35:8; Psalms 63:10–11. See "Old Testament Intimations of a Future State," pp. 22–23.This sentence is a later addition. Job 20:11. "His bones are full of the sins of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust."] Both these expressions impart the same thing,

<!-- p. 443 -->

and are as much as to say, The sins of his youth remain with him after he is dead;MS: "death." his sin shall lie down with him in his grave, and shall remain on his dead corpse there. When his flesh is putrefied and turned to dust, then his iniquity shall still remain on his bones. His bones shall be full of them, which signifies that his sin shall forever remain with him after he is dead. He shall never get rid of them, but they shall to all eternity lie upon him. See Ezekiel 32:27.

Job 20:16. "He shall suck."] See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 206.

Job 20:17. "He shall not see the rivers."] Which there are in the heavenly Canaan, which is a land flowing with milk and honey.

Job 21:2. "Let this be your consolations."] I.e. if you have no other comforts to administer to me, deny me not this, of suffering me to speak, and hearing me diligently.

Job 21:29. "Have ye not asked them that go by the way? Do ye not know their tokens?"] By "them that go by the way" seems to be meant the angels that were wont often to appear to godly persons before there was any written revelation. Job probably refers to what Eliphaz had said of the vision he had of an angel, and what they had said to 'em (Job 4:12–21). Elihu speaks of such things as common (Job 33:14 ff.). The angels may fitly be called these "that go by the way," being constantly employed as God's messengers and posts as it were, sent forth by the great king into the various parts of his kingdom, and constantly ascending and descending in the way between heaven and earth (Genesis 28:12), and are also continually going to and fro on the earth on messages on which God sends 'em. As evil angels are continually walking about, seeking whom they may devour, and "going to and fro in the earth, and walking up and down in it" (Job 1:7 and Job 2:2), so the good angels walk "to and fro through the earth" (Zechariah 1:10). And the angels frequently appeared to holy men of old before Moses' time as wayfaring men. So they appeared to Abraham as "he sat in the tent door" (Genesis 18:1). So they appeared to Lot, who found 'em "in the street" [Genesis 19:2]. So 'tis probable the angel of God appeared to Jacob that night that he wrestled with him [Genesis 32:24]; so to Hagar (Genesis 16:7). So the angels appeared to Jacob (Genesis 32:2).

<!-- p. 444 -->

Job 21:30.] I.e. that this present life is not the time of their punishment. Here they often prosper, but they are reserved to a future state, which is the proper state of retribution.

Job 21:32–33. "Yet shall he be brought to the grave. He shall remain in the tomb. The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him; and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him."] The proper translation of these wordsיִשְׁקְוֹד וְעַל־גָדִישׁ יוּבֶל לִקְבָרוֹת וְהוּא Job 21:32מִסְפָּר אֵין וּלְפָנָיו יִמְשׁוֹךְ כָּל־אָדָם וְאַחֲרָיו נָחַל רִגְבֵי מָתְקוּ־לֹוֹ Job 21:33 seems to be thus. "And he shall be brought to the grave; and he that is over the heap" (i.e. the heap of dust over the grave, meaning the devil, who has the power of death) "shall watch" (for him), or "he shall watch for him at the heap or grave. The clods of the grave shall sweetly devour him, and shall draw every man after him. And there is no number of those that are before its face," that is before the face of death or the grave, whom it is about to devour and swallow down as its sweet morsels. So the last expression is but an amplificationOr: "ampliation." MS: "amplication." of what is said in the foregoing words, that "the grave shall draw every man into it." The same verb in the same conjugation, which is here rendered by our translators neutrally, "shall be sweet unto him," is rendered actively in Job 24:20, "The worm shall feed sweetly on him." Here it is לוֹ מָתְקוּ; there it is מְתָקוֹ. The true sense is undoubtedly much the same in both places; and this rendering well agrees with the context, and makes the sense plain, which otherwise is exceeding intricate and wholly unintelligible. And this not only makes the words plain, but in this sense they are exceeding significant, and elegant, and agreeable to figures of speech used elsewhere in Scripture, which elsewhere represent death, the grave, and hell as waiting for the wicked, making them welcome when they come, very gladly receiving them as proper inhabitants, as those that are most suitable for it. So in Job 24:20 and Isaiah 14:9. The saints are not the proper food of death; and therefore, though they are devoured by it, yet it shall vomit 'em up again as not suiting its stomach, as the whale vomited up Jonah. When it is said, "He that is over the grave shall watch for him," or "He shall watch for him over the grave," it may well be understood of him who is called, in Job 18:13–14, the "first-born of death" and the "king of terrors," whether by the "king of terrors" we understand the devil or death itself. That this should be understood and not expressed is not strange; such kind of ellipses,JE deleted "a relative without an antecedent." a verb without a nominative case

<!-- p. 445 -->

expressed, is very common in Scripture and in this book.JE deleted "Then the pronoun 'he' is in this book often used." A verb of the third person singular without a nominative case expressed is often used in this book when sometimes theJE deleted "antecedent." nominative case understood is God, sometimes Job.JE deleted "and yet the antecedent is not expressed." (Here see my note on Lamentations 4:15.)This is a later interlineation. See Job 35:15. Or the words might be well rendered thus. "He is watched for at the grave." For as Bp. Kidder observes (*Demonstration of the Messiah*, Pt. II, pp. 28–29), "It is common among the sacred writers, that an active verb, that hath no person going before it, is to be understood as a passive or impersonal," as Luke 12:20, "This night do they require thy soul."*Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 28–29.

Job 22:2.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 231–32.

Job 22:4. "Will he enter with thee into judgment?"] SSS.Ibid., col. 233.

Job 22:12.] This verse shows that the heaven of the blessed, the heaven that is the dwelling place, or house, or temple of God, is the highest of the heavens. God is "in the height of heaven," i.e. according to the idiom of the language, in the highest part of heaven, and that this heaven is above the stars, and yet in the upper parts of our atmosphere, as some have supposed.

Job 22:16.] Their foundation is mentioned because they were in great outward prosperity, as Job once had been (See Job 22:18.), and they trusted that their foundation stood strong. They blessed themselves in their hearts that they should never be in adversity, but the destruction God brought upon them showed the foundation of their prosperity to be sandy. And what then happened to them was a representation of that which is spoken of, Matthew 7:26–27.

"Foundation." SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 238–39.

Job 22:19.] See Revelation 18:20.

<!-- p. 446 -->

Job 22:20. "The remnant of them the fire consumeth."] Here may probably be some reference to the destruction of Sodom and the neighbor cities, the next remarkable judgment that followed the flood, destroying the ungodly.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 240–41.

Job 22:24. "Ophir."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 243.

Job 23:8–9.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 249–50.

Job 23:12.] By this it appears that the people of God had the word of God, or the mind and will of God, made known by revelation for their rule before the church enjoyed a written revelation for their standing rule.

Job 23:14. "And many such things."] SSS.Ibid., col. 252.

Job 24:1. "Times are not hidden."] I.e. seeing he knows the state of things. So the phrase, "knowing the times," is used (Daniel 2:21, and Daniel 7:25; 1 Chronicles 12:32; and Esther 1:13; Psalms 31:15). "Not see his days." I.e. days wherein God shall manifest himself in behalf of his people, days of the divine favor, or days wherein God shall interpose in a visible manner as ruler and judge, days of his kingdom wherein the state of things shall visibly be under him and ordered for him. Psalms 77:10, "I will remember the years of the right hand of the Most High."

Job 24:2–8.] Job here has respect to two sorts of unrighteous ones. 1. Tyrants, or those that do wrong under pretense of authority (Job 24:1–4). 2. He speaks of robbers, and rapparees, and those that do wrong by downright force, as the bands of the Sabeans and Chaldeans which had lately plundered him. Among the Arabians, children of the East, Job's country, there were those that lived by spoil and rapine, making incursions upon their neighbors, and robbing travelers. "Behold, as the wild asses in the desert" Job 24:5]. These robbers were like wild asses, untamed, untractable, unreasonable—Ishmael's character. Genesis 16:12, "He shall be a wild man." The word properly signifies a wild ass-man. They choose the desert that

<!-- p. 447 -->

they may be lawless and unsociable, and that they may have opportunity of doing the more mischief. "They go forth to their work, rising betimes for a prey." Robbing is their trade which they follow, as the husbandman does his labor; and therefore they get up early, and go forth to it as their work. "The wilderness yieldeth food for them and their children." Not the fields, but the wilderness, i.e. the roads through the wilderness. "They reap every one his corn," etc. Job 24:6]. They not only rob travelers, but make incursions upon their neighbors' fields and vineyards, and rob them. "They cause the naked" Job 24:7], travelers whom they have stripped, to lodge without clothing, etc.

Or perhaps in these words, Job 24:5, "The wilderness yieldeth food for them and their children," the relative may belong to the remote antecedent, viz. the poor and needy, spoken of in the foregoing verse, who, being robbed of their food, are forced to seek it in the wilderness, to live on herbs, roots, etc. See Job 30:3–4.

Job 24:5.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 256–57.

Job 24:14. "The murderer rising with the light killeth the poor and needy."] The poor, who are obliged to get up and go about their business very early to get a livelihood, the murderer watches and kills 'em as soon as they come abroad, that he may do with the greater secrecy, being concealed in the twilight.

Job 24:18. "He is swift as the waters."] I.e. as the waters swiftly hasten to the sea, so he is making haste to destruction. "He beholdeth not the way of the vineyards." I.e. the way to life, comfort, and joy. Here the broad way that leads to destruction is fitly compared to the course of the waters which is descending to the great abyss, and the narrow way that leads to life to the way of the vineyards which were wont to be upon hills, and where were their pleasantest and most reviving fruits which made glad the heart. Spiritual blessings are often compared to wine, andJE deleted "clusters of grapes." God's church to a vineyard, in Canticles and elsewhere. Compare Job 20:17, Proverbs 2:18–19, and Proverbs 5:5–6.

"He is swift as the waters." The instability of this present life, and of all earthly enjoyments, and of all the welfare of wicked men is fitly and elegantly compared to running waters that pass away, and particularly to the

<!-- p. 448 -->

waters of the streams of Arabia (which Job and his friends were well acquainted with), that soon all run off, having no steady fountain to supply them, and therefore quickly left their channels dry. The instability and short continuance of this life is compared to this very thing in Job 14:10–12. "But man lieth down, and wasteth away. Yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? As the waters fail from the sea, and as the flood decayeth and drieth up, so man lieth down," etc. So Zophar, speaking how soon Job's misery would be at an end if he would turn from his sin, represents it thus. Job 11:16, "Thou shalt forget thy misery, and remember it as waters that pass away." This interpretation is greatly confirmed by the next verse. "Drought and heat consume the snow waters; so doth the grave them that have sinned" Job 24:19]. Those brooks of Arabia that so soon run off and dried up were mostly streams of snow water that flowed in the spring, but when the sun rose higher and shone with greater heat, they dried up, as is particularly observed in Job 6:15–18. Therefore when it is said, They are swifter than the waters, the meaning is their life and prosperity is more fleeting than the water, i.e. the waters of the brooks of Arabia, which is also confirmed by the last part of the same sentence, "their portion is cursed in the earth."This paragraph is a later addition.

Job 24:19. "Drought and heat," etc.] There is a like difference between the life and happiness of the wicked and the godly, as there is between the streams and puddles of snow water when the spring approaches and those streams that are maintained by living springs.

Job 24:20. "The worm shall feed sweetly on him."] The wicked are the proper food of death, which is well represented by death's feeding sweetly on them. See note on Job 21:32–33. See Psalms 49:14.

"The womb shall forget him." I.e. his nearest relations, his mother and brethren who were from the same womb. And his destruction shall be so total and perfect that it shall be as though he never had been brought forth or conceived in the womb. (See note on Job 8:18.) It is said in the latter part of the verse, "He shall be no more remembered." The womb shall forget him, from whence he had his life. It shall as it were reject him after it has given him life, as one to whom life don't belong, being unworthy of life. "The worm, or death, shall feed sweetly on him," as its proper food; or death shall embrace him as one that properly belongs to death.This paragraph is a separate entry.

<!-- p. 449 -->

Job 24:23.] The wordsעַל־דַּרְכֵיהֶם וְעֵינֵיהוּ וְישָּׁעֵן לָבֶטַח יִתֶּן־לוֹ more literally translated are, "Though it be given him to be in safety, and he depends upon it, yet his eyes are upon their ways." I.e. though God gives these wicked [ones] that are so unjust to be in safety, and they, because God protects and preserves 'em for the present, depend on future safety, as though God took no notice of their wickedness, and would never punish it, yet God's eyes are upon their ways.

Job 25:1.] Concerning Bildad's aim in what he says in this short speech of his, see SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 267.

Job 25:2. "He maketh peace in his high places."] I.e. in heavenly places where he dwells in the midst of those numberless armies spoken of in the next verse. He causeth and maintaineth perfect peace there, and thither shall he gather together in perfect unity all things in Christ. And thence he commands peace for his people here below. He is the author of that perfect peace and happy love that is in that glorious numerous society above, and from thence he sends peace on earth.This sentence is a later addition.

Job 25:3. "Upon whom doth not his light arise?"] His providenceJE deleted "extends." and influence, his knowledge and his goodness, are universal; and the light of his gospel, the light of the Sun of righteousness, shall be upon all nations. (See Psalms 19.) And the light of his glory and love arises on all his heavenly armies. These things are shadowed forth by the universal shining of the sun.

Job 25:4. "Or how can he be clean that is born of a woman?"] No. 334.*Works, 15*, 318–19.

Job 25:5–6. "The stars are not pure in his sight. How much less man, that is a worm, and the son of man that is a worm?"] Which is not only small, weak, and impotent, but a filthy creature, bred in putrefaction, and fed by putrefaction.

Job 26:2–3. "How hast thou helped him that is without power," etc.?] As much as to say, You and your friends have been abundantly insisting in

<!-- p. 450 -->

your speeches on the duty of pitying and relieving the poor and afflicted, and the great sin and dreadful punishment of those that oppress them, but is this your way of relieving the indigent and helpless? See note on Job 27:12.

Job 26:5. "Dead things."] Or the *rephaim*, which seems to [be] a word by which they signified the inhabitants of the infernal world, which, indeed, only are dead; and especially devils are meant. Giants in the Hebrew tongue are called *rephaim*,רְפֶאִים from *rephau*,רָפה which signifies to make weak, or to cause to faint or fail, because they were so terrible that they caused the hearts and hands of those that saw them to fail. For the same reason, the inhabitants of the infernal world are called by the same name because when men see apparitions of them, they are very frightful and terrifying. These are the same that are called "the destroyers" (Job 33:22). The place of their abode is called "destruction," here in the next verse Job 26:6]. They had this notion of old, that down in the lower parts of the earth was the place of these *rephaim*. To this abode, they supposed, descended the uncircumcised heathen and the wicked when they died, as Ezekiel 32:17 ff. And this is the place that is frequently meant by "hell" in the Old Testament as well as New. It may be special reference is had to the sinners of the old world that were drowned by the flood, the leaders of which were giants, whose spirits are now in prison. The same word is used Proverbs 2:18, and Proverbs 9:18, Proverbs 21:16.

There may be respect to whales, and crocodiles, and other water monsters which God forms from under the waters, which were, according to the signification of the word *rephaim*, terrible huge monsters.This paragraph is a later addition.

"Dead things are formed from under the waters, and the inhabitants thereof." Mr. Henry observes that "some ancient versions" render the word thus." Behold, the giants groan under the waters, and those that dwell with them."*Exposition, 3* (1725), 85. Or the words might have been rendered, "*Raphaim* are wounded or pierced through under the waters," agreeable to the original.וְשֹׁכְנֵיהֶם מַיִם מִתַּחַת יְחוֹלָלוּ הָרְפָאִים (See Buxtorf.)*Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum* (6th ed. London, 1646), 712–13. "From under the waters" seems to allude to the waters of the flood under which the giants were destroyed in God's terrible wrath, which deluge of waters was a remarkable type of the deluge

<!-- p. 451 -->

of God's wrath which comes on the ungodly in another world. The observing this is to Job's purpose, for as Mr. Henry says, "Is there anything in which the majesty of God appears more dreadful than in the eternal ruin of the ungodly, and the groans of the inhabitants of the land of darkness?"*Exposition, 2* (1725), 85. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 270–72. The Job 26:12 confirms this interpretation, and also Job 26:13. See note on that v.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 26:7.] See no. 101.*Works, 15*, 79. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. For Job 26:12–13, see Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 275–76.

Job 26:12. "By his understanding he smiteth through the proud."] That is the way that God chooses for the baffling, bringing down, his proud enemies, to do it by his wisdom, foiling them, and confounding them in their own devices, etc., rather than a mere exercise of his omnipotent power by which he could, if he please, immediately and in a moment, destroy Satan and all the powers of hell without lengthening out the war against them any further.

Note on Job 34:20.This reference is a separate entry.

Job 26:13.] "By the 'crooked serpent,' the Hebrews understand the Galaxy or Milky Way." Dr. Owen, *On the Spirit*, Bk. 1, ch. 4, §7.*ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΟΛΟΓΙΑ*, p. 72. Owen's observation follows his declaration, "Now the Forming and Perfecting of this Host of Heaven and Earth, is that which is assigned peculiarly to the Spirit of God." The Spirit "garnishes" the heavens, making them "glorious and beautiful" (p. 71). See Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, pp. 213 ff.This reference is a later addition. Fifth ed., pp. 213–17.

"His hands have formed the crooked serpent." Itבּרִיחַ נָחָשׁ יָדוֹ חלֲלָה might have been translated, "His hands have wounded or tormented the crooked serpent," that is, the devil. The wordחָלַל translated "formed" is the same that is used Job 26:5. "Dead things are 'formed' from under the waters." (See notes on that v.) That the devil, that old serpent, that great leviathan, should be meant agrees with the foregoing verse. "He divideth the sea with his power; by his understanding he smiteth through the proud," which was remarkably fulfilled in dividing the sea, and destroying Pharaoh, compared

<!-- p. 452 -->

to leviathan, the water monsters that are especially to be found in the waters of Egypt. Psalms 74:13–14, "Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength; thou breakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou breakest the heads of leviathan in pieces," where he is spoken of as the image of the devil. And this leviathanJE deleted "as compared to the water monsters of Egypt." is called the "crooked serpent" in Isaiah 27:1. "In that day [the Lord] with his sore, and great, and strong sword shall punish leviathan, the piercing serpent" (or "the serpent lying across like a bar," *nahash bariach*,בָּרְחַ נָחָשׁ the very same name used here) "even leviathan, that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea."

This is fitly subjoined to the former part of the verse, "By his spirit he hath garnished, or beautified, the heavens." For at the same time that God cast Satan down to hell, he purged and also beautified heaven, increasing the holiness and happiness of his elect angels, and at every time of Christ's remarkably overcoming Satan, and bruising his head, and beautifying heaven, and advancing his holiness and happiness, as when [he] rose from the dead, and ascended into heaven, and when he shall destroy Antichrist, and at the end of the world. And 'tis not incredible that Job should here speak of such mysteries, for 'tis evident he now spake under the influence of the spirit of prophecy by what he says in the preceding verse concerning the dividing of the sea, etc., fulfilled afterwards. This interpretation is confirmed by Job 26:5. See note on that verse.This and the preceding paragraph are separate entries. This paragraph is a later addition.

Job 26:14. "Lo, these are parts of his ways."] "Or, as the original word more literally signifies; and may, I think, be more elegantly rendered; These are only 'the skirts,' the 'very outermost borders,' of his works. No more than a small preface, to the immense volume of the creation. From the Hebrew mar;?—*extremitates*. I cannot forbear thinking, on the extreme and very attenuated fibers of the root, when compared with the whole substance of the trunk; or on the exquisitely small size of the capillary vessels, when compared with the whole structure of the body." Hervey's *Meditations*, p. 129.Hervey, *Meditations and Contemplations* (4th ed.), *II*, 129, note. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 276–77.

"But how little a portion." Literally translated, it is, "how very very small a word."This sentence is a separate entry.

<!-- p. 453 -->

"But how little a portion is heard of him? But the thunder of his power, who can understand?" The former wordsנִשְׁמַע־בּוֹ דָּבָר וּמַה־שֵמֶץ are literally translated, "How very small a word is heard of him?", as it were a small whisper. "But the thunder of his power, who [can] understand?" Itיִתְבּוֹנָן מִי גְּבוּרֹתָו וְרַעַם might have been translated, the "thunder of his greatness," or "glory," or "sufficiency." The word sometimes seems to signify as much as "glory," as Judges 5:31. "Let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his strength." But especially "greatness" and "glory," as appearing in a sufficiency for great and glorious "effects," as 'tis these that Job is here speaking [of], called God's "ways." In this sense we often read of the might of princes, as 1 Kings 15:23; 2 Kings 10:34, and 2 Kings 13:12, and 2 Kings 14:15, 2 Kings 14:28; and 1 Kings 16:5, 1 Kings 16:27; and 2 Kings 20:20; and 1 Kings 22:45; 1 Chronicles 29:30; Esther 10:2. What we hear of God's greatness is but a very little word, as a small whisper. Whereas if all God's greatness, power, and glory as appearing in all his works should be fully declared, it would be in comparison of what we actually hear as a mighty incomprehensible thunder to the smallest whisper. We are not able to understand the language of that thunder. See SSS.This paragraph is a later entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 276–77.

Job 27:5. "God forbid that I should justify you."] I.e. by doing as you do, that I should this way manifest my approbation of such evil ways, by speaking wickedness and uttering falsehood as you do.

Job 27:7. "Let mine enemy be as the wicked," etc.] Hereby Job expresses his sense of the miserableness of the state of an ungodly man, however he may seem to prosper, so that he could desire no worse misery to his worst enemy than to be as they. He don't mean that he wished his enemy such misery, for that is contrary to what he solemnly and expressly professes and swears in the same discourse (Job 31:29).This sentence is a later addition.

Job 27:12. "Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it. Why then are ye thus altogether vain?"] "Ye all have seen it," i.e. the things which I am about to declare of the punishment of wicked men and oppressors." You have all you in your speeches much insisted on this very thing as what you have clearly seen and been fully assured. Why therefore are you so very wicked,

<!-- p. 454 -->

and why are you yourselves guilty of so great a degree of oppression of the poor and afflicted as you now see me to be? See in the beginning of this speech of Job in Job 26:2–3, and the note on Job 26:2–3.

Job 27:14–15.] Here is mention of three calamities which shall come on the posterity of the wicked: sword, famine, and death, i.e. pestilence. Buried in death, buried privately, and in haste, and without any solemnity, without being attended by their friends, as is common in the time of the pestilence and other great calamities. See Ezekiel 24:16, Ezekiel 24:23.

Job 27:19. "Gathered."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 282.

Job 27:20.] 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Job 34:20, Job 34:25; Matthew 25:6.

Job 28.] In the Job 27:11, Job had said, "I will teach you by the hand of God: that which is with the Almighty will I not conceal," which was an introduction to what he intended to speak on two things. First, the dreadful nature of sin, and the misery of the wicked, of this he spoke in that chapter, Job 27:12–23. Secondly, the preciousness of wisdom or true godliness, he proceeds to treat of this in this chapter.

See note on Ecclesiastes 7:24.This reference is a separate entry.

Job 28:4. "The flood breaketh out from the inhabitant." (In the Hebrew,מֵעִם־גָּד "from with the inhabitant.") "They are dried up. They are gone away from men."] Here seems to be reference to some of the brooks of Arabia, which at some time of the year brake out in some parts of that vast wilderness, where none dwelt to make any use of the water, and were "forgotten by the foot," that is, were neglected by the foot. Men came not to them, sought not after the water; and this were neglected and never made use of by men till that time of year came when they dried up. And if any came to the place where their channels were, they would find them dry, and the waters gone away. He mentions this as a mysterious work of God whose wisdom in his works is unsearchable, to the like purpose with Job 38:25–26. "Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of the waters, and a way for the lightning of the thunder; to cause it to rain

<!-- p. 455 -->

on the earth where no man is, on the wilderness wherein there is no man?" This place is illustrated by Job 6:15–20.

Job 28:5. "Under it is turned up as it were fire."] I.e. that which shines like fire, as in Deuteronomy 33:2. The law of God, because it as it were shines and gives light, is called "a fiery law." See note *in loc*.

Job 29:25. "And dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners."] A king in army has very great power. A captain over soldiers says to one, Go, and he goes; to another, Come, and he comes; to another, Do this, and he doth it. They are all near him and about him, constantly attending on him, drawn up in order to be in constant preparation to observe his words of command without dispute or delay; and disobedience is attended with immediate execution. And a king in an army is peculiarly terrible, terrible to his enemies, and terrible to the disobedient soldiers. "As he that comforteth the mourners." By this contrast Job would set forth how great a terror he was to evildoers, to those that needed [terror], and at the same time how great a comfort he was to such as needed comfort. The literal translationיְנַחֵם אֲבֵלִים כַּאֲשֶׁר is, "As he comforteth them when mourning," or when sorrowful, i.e. as the king comforting his sorrowful soldiers. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 306.

Job 30:1. "I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock."] I.e. to have taken among the lowest of my servants, to have attended the sheep as the servants of my shepherds with the dogs. They were so vile, and barbarous, and immoral that they were not fit to be seen among my servants, nor fit to be trusted with any, even the meanest service, so lazy, awkward, raw, and brutish that they had not sense enough to do anything to purpose.

Job 30:2. "Old age was perished."] I.e. their old age was lost, had gained no knowledge or experience by living long in the world, were as raw and ignorant as children, and had now got past the age of learning. See SSS.Ibid., col. 307.

Job 30:4. "Mallows."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 308–9.

<!-- p. 456 -->

Job 30:9–10 ff.] Vagabonds and others of the worst and vilest of men that infested human society now insulted Job, because as a good governor he had put the laws in execution against such.

Job 30:11.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 310–11.

Job 30:12. "They push away my feet."] I.e. they push me away as I go. They roughly turn me aside out of my way to make me give place to them. See Isaiah 32:20. That expression, "Turn our feet into the way of peace," is parallel.See Luke 1:79. This sentence and the preceding reference are a later interlineation. "They raise up against me the ways of their destruction." I.e. they rise up again and come against me in a way of malignancy and enmity, seeking mischief or destruction.

Job 30:13. "They mar my path."] I.e. by laying snares or stumbling blocks in my way, or something that entangle or incommode me as I go, and bring me into difficulty, that from thence they may take occasion to ridicule and insult me.

"They have no helper." I.e. I am so contemptible and so helpless, and little able to defend myself from them, that they are not afraid, any of them singly, to assault me that before was so much feared by a multitude. I am an easy prey to 'em. Nor are they ashamed to abuse me openly without anyone to appear to lead or defend them in it. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 312.

Job 30:14. "The desolation they rolled themselves upon me."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 312–13.

Job 30:15. "Terrors are turned upon me."] SSS.Ibid., col. 313.

Job 30:18. "By the great force of my disease is my garment changed; it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat."] The first part in the Hebrewלְבוּשִׁי יִתְחַפֵּשׂ בְרָב־כֹּחַ is thus: "By the greatness of power is my garment changed," i.e. God by his great power has stripped me of my glory and of my garments of joy, and has clothed me with grief, sorrow, and vexation as a garment. My extreme misery binds me about as the collar of my coat. The Job 30:21 confirms this sense. "With thy strong hand thou opposest thyself

<!-- p. 457 -->

against me." The figure here used is much like that in the Job 30:31.

Job 30:24. "Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave."] I.e. to rescue men from death. Every man must die and be retained in the grave. The redemption of the life is precious, and it ceaseth forever. God will recover men from thence to live again in this world. "Though they cry in his destruction." Though they dread death never so much, when death comes, and would never so earnestly cry to be delivered from the grave.

Job 30:27. "Prevented me."] I.e. came unexpected. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 318.

Job 30:29.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 318–19.

Job 31:11. "An iniquity to be punished by the judges."] See note on Job 31:28.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 323–24.

Job 31:12.] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 324.

Job 31:13–14.] If I despise the cause of my man or maidservant when they plead with me, and when they stand before me to be judged by me, what then shall I do when I come to stand before God to be judged by him? God may justly do by me as I do by my servant. If I despise my servant's cause, how much more may God despise my cause. I am God's servant as they are mine, and much more inferior to God than my servant is to me.

Job 31:15.] This is a good reason why servants should not be trampled on for their mean condition, because the difference of condition between master and servant is not owing to themselves, but to God. 'Tis he that makes 'em to differ in their birth and circumstances of life.

"Did not he that made me in the womb make him, and did not one fashion us in the womb?"JE deleted "What Job probably has chief." And therefore I may be sure he will have respect to his interest as well as mine, will see to it that justice be done to

<!-- p. 458 -->

him as well as to me, and take care that he ben't wronged. For he will have respect to the work of his own hands, and he looks upon it to be what belongs to him, to take care to maintain the rights of his own creatures and uphold justice among them. As we both have one Maker, so we both have one Judge. As he that made him made me, so we must stand before the Judge together, who will do impartial justice between us.

The last clauseאֶחָד בֶּרֶחֶם וַיְכֻנֶנּוּ of the verse might more literally be translated, "Did not he fashion us in one womb," or "in the womb alike?" I.e. he fashioned both in an human womb. We are made of the same human race, and [God] hasMS: "have." given us the same human nature, which more clearly shows the reason why Job should not despise and abuse his servant. In these two things are contained the most forceable reasons against the master's abuse of his servant, viz. that both have one Maker, and that their Maker made 'em alike or with the same nature.This and the preceding paragraph are later additions.

Job 31:27. "Kissed my hand."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 329–30.

Job 31:28. "An iniquity to be punished by the judge."] In the Hebrew,פְּלִילִי עוֹן a "judicial," or "judiciary," or "judged punishment." This phrase used here and Job 31:11 seems to have been a phrase used to signify a very horrid and capital crime. For in the sense of our translation, it seems nothing to Job's purpose. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 330. Probably the word has no reference to the judgment of men, but of God, and means as much as a sin that peculiarly brings judgment or cries for vengeance, a phrase equivalent to our phrase of "crying sin." See Hebrews 13:4.

Job 31:30.] By this it appears that it belonged to the religion of the Old Testament as well as of the New that men should not wish evil to those that injure and hate them, and that it was agreeable to the known and professed principles of the saints of those times, which with many otherJE deleted "parallel texts." things is a very great evidences that the imprecations of curses to enemies we have in the Psalms and some other places are not of private interpretation, and are not to be understood as the expressions of personal

<!-- p. 459 -->

resentments, or the penmen's expressing the desires and wishes of their own spirit. See "Miscellanies," under the word "Imprecations."This is a reference to JE's "Table" to the "Miscellanies," *Works, 13*, 137–38. See also note on 2 Samuel 1:17.

Job 31:31.] The "men of my tabernacle" were enraged at those that injured me. They longed to revenge the wrong. I had difficulty to restrain 'em, as David restrained Abishai from revenge when Shimei cursed him [2 Samuel 16:11.]

Job 31:34. "Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me?"] In those early days great account was made of men's pedigree, and they were kept with care. And when men's lives were so long, great numbers of the descendants of one living ancestor were alive at once, so that those that were called a family were commonly a great multitude. Job declares that he was not deterred from doing justice in his office of a judge through fear of the great multitude that were of the family of him that was to be condemned or displeased in the judgment.

Job 31:37. "As a prince."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, col. 335.

Job 31:39. "Lose their life."] SSS.Ibid.

Job 32:8.] By the spirit that is in man, Elihu seems not to intend the soul of man, but the spirit. And the words might as well have been rendered, "But the spirit is in man."

Job 33:21. "Neither let me give flattering titles unto men."] I.e. let me not from fear or from respect of your persons, because you are my superiors, flatter or compliment you as though I approved of what you say or do, though I know it to be utterly wrong and unjust. There is much of this sort of flattery of great men in the world, which, Elihu expresses his sense, how provoking it is to God.

Job 33:6–7.] God, being about to appear to speak to Job in his awful majesty, in the first place sent Elihu, a man as he was, according to his wish that there might be no appearance, as though God would overwhelm Job by

<!-- p. 460 -->

majesty and terror without giving him fair opportunity, as he desired to plead his cause with one that he need not be afraid of.

Job 33:14–16.] See no. 115.*Works, 15*, 83.

Elihu endeavors to adapt his discourse to the present case. He supposes that God might have thus spoken to Job in a dream, or vision, or some other way, that he did take due notice to reclaim from something displeasing and offensive to him. And therefore God now exercised him with sore affliction to open his ears, and bring him to consider and take notice of his mind and will signified to him. And he hoped he might now do the part of such a messenger or interpreter as that which he speaks of, Job 33:23, to lead into proper reflections, and a right understanding and improvement of the hand of God. And then he hoped that would be fulfilled concerning him spoken of in the Job 33:24 and following verses. And, indeed, so it proved. Elihu thus did the part of a messenger or interpreter first, and the Son of God after him, whereby Job was brought to himself, and so was delivered.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 33:18. "Perishing by the sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Job 33:22. "To the destroyers."] See Job 26:5.

"Destroyers." Psalms 17:4, no. 298.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 272.

Job 33:23.] By the "messenger" and "interpreter" here Mr. Boston understands Christ, who is "the messenger of the covenant of peace, the great interpreter of God's counsels of love to sinners, 'one among a thousand' [Ecclesiastes 7:28], 'one chosen out of the people' (Psalms 89:19), 'the chief among ten thousands'" [Canticles 5:10]. The wordמֵליץ translated "interpreter" might have been rendered "orator" or "an eloquent person," and this especially as the word is here brought in well agrees with Isaiah 50:4–6. He "hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary." "To show unto man his uprightness," Mr. Boston interprets of Christ's showing unto man his righteousness.Thomas Boston, *Human Nature in its Fourfold State* (4th ed., Edinburgh, 1744), 245. Boston (1677–1732) was a Scottish Calvinist divine trained at Edinburgh University. The wordיָשְׁרְוֹ here translated "uprightness" is very much of the

<!-- p. 461 -->

same signification with that which is commonly translated "righteousness." Christ's work is to show his righteousness, and so to comfort the sinner after the sinner is convinced of sin and humbled, as he is here represented. The next verse confirms this interpretation. "Then he is gracious to him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit. I have found a ransom," or "an atonement" (as in the margin).I.e. margin of the KJV. Christ is that messenger in whom God finds an atonement, and that righteousness for the sake of which he delivers from going down to the pit.This remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. See Hervey's *Dialogues*, vol. 2, p. 335, margin.Hervey's reflections on the book of Job identify Christ as the "Messenger of the Covenant," that one of "most meritorious *Uprightness*, on which alone a Sinner may depend, both for temporal and eternal Salvation," who is responsible for "Deliverance from the Pit of Perdition" (*Dialogues, 2*, 335–36). This messenger had Abimelech when he was chastised (Genesis 20:3 ff.). See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 353–55.

Job 33:26. "Render unto man his righteousness."] SSS.Ibid., col. 356.

Job 33:29.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 357–58.

Job 34:12–13. See note on Genesis 18:25.

Job 34:17.] See note on Genesis 18:25.
