Job 35:4.] Elihu, in the Job 34:8–9, had charged Job with "going in company," or making himself a companion with "wicked [men]," in such saying that it is no profit to a man that he is righteous, etc., as here, Job 35:3. 'Tis these companions that Elihu means that he "will answer" with Job, those that said thus as he did, and that he went in company with.

"I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee." 'Tis as much as to say, In what I shall say in answer, I shall direct myself to thee, and also to thy companions, as proper to be taken notice of by you both, and what may be matter of satisfaction to both [of] you, as to those things you have been disputing hitherto without satisfaction to either. See SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 376–77.

Job 35:5–8 ff.] Elihu's argument with Job is that Job said it was no advantage to him that he was righteous. God required him to [do] such and such things without any benefit to him. He dealt no better by him than he did by others that neglected to obey him. But Elihu argues that it must be men's benefit that God aims at in his commands, because it must be either the creature's or his own. But it can't be his own, for he can receive no benefit by the creature's righteousness, nor damage by his sin. And so it is impossible God should be under any temptation to do the creature wrong, as he must aim at some benefit either to himself or men. It must be men's benefit, and not his own, that he aims at.

Job 35:9–10.] In these two verses Elihu seems to have respect to two things. 1. In Job 35:9 he has respect to what he himself had just now said in the foregoing verse, that man's "wickedness may hurt man," as the wickedness of oppressors. But then his mentioning the wickedness and cruelty of oppressors puts him in mind of something that Job had said of the cruelty of oppressing the innocent, and God's letting them alone, and not appearing either to punish the oppressor or relieve the oppressed when they cry to him, as particularly, Job 24:12. "Men groan from out of the city, and the soul of the wounded crieth out. Yet God layeth not folly to them." And therefore,

2. Elihu in the Job 24:10 has respect to this objection JobMS: "God." had made

<!-- p. 463 -->

against divine providence, and answers. His answer is that it is true the oppressed cry out of oppression, but they don't inquire after God. Their affliction don't drive [them] to God, etc.

Job 35:15. "Yet he knoweth it not in great extremity."] The literal translationמְאֹד בַּפַּשׁ וְלְאֹ־יָדַע is, "Yet he knoweth not in great abundance," or "fullness." The meaning seems rather to be that although God has visited Job in his anger for not trusting in him, as in the foregoing verse, yet Job did not know, did not receive instruction by the divine chastisement, was not corrected by it in his great self-sufficiency, or in his confidence of his own abundance, i.e. of righteousness, wherein he was in his own eyes rich and increased with goods, etc. The wordמְאֹד translated "extremity" is a Chaldaic word that properly signifies health, fatness, and good habitude. See SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 381–82.

Job 36:3. "I will fetch my knowledge from afar."] I.e. I won't speak from a slighty overly view of things, but from a deep and thorough consideration, looking to the bottom of things, not judging of things from the next and most outward appearance.

Job 36:4. "He that is perfect in knowledge is with thee."] I.e. he that now had to deal with thee to instruct thee, and reprove thee, is not a poor, imperfect, ignorant, raw, young man, as you may look upon me, but he that is perfect in knowledge, inasmuch as I speak by the inspiration of God. Therefore in my reasoning with thee, thou art to look upon that God, who is perfect in knowledge in reasoning with thee.

<!-- p. 464 -->

act as if you desired it. Don't bring it upon you. Wicked men are represented as choosing and loving death.

Job 36:22. "Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him?"] In order to our being led to the sense of the words, they ought to have been translated, "Behold, God exalteth himself in his power," etc. The design of the words is to signify that God is absolutely perfect in power and wisdom, and is both supreme and independent, not needing the help of any, nor the instruction of any; but that he is the fountain of all power and wisdom. This agrees with the context.

The former part of the verse might as well have been translated, "He is exalted in his power." And the import of the phrase in the latter part of the verse seems to be only this, that "God is above all in wisdom."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Job 36:27. "According to the vapor thereof."] SSS.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 1, cols. 395–96.

Job 36:27–28 ff., from hence to the end of the Job 37.] Elihu concludes his discourse with Job with observations and improvements of God's wondrous works on the clouds, rain, lightning, and thunder. It appears to me probable that the occasion of it was the appearance at a distance of the clouds, and lightning, and thunder of the storm that was then approaching, out of which God spake to Job. There was nothing in Elihu's foregoing discourse that seemed to lead him to it. 'Tis true that he was in the foregoing verses speaking of the greatness of God and his works, but there seems nothing that led him thus suddenly to begin about the clouds and rain in this Job 36:27. But if there then appeared to them a thunderstorm arising, that will easily account for it why he, when speaking of God's greatness, should insist on this rather than any other of God's works. The Job 36:30 seemsMS: "Seem." to confirm this. "Behold, he spreadeth light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea." The manner of expression, his calling on Job to behold, agrees with the supposition that the thing was then appearing that he was speaking [of]. And the description here given, "He spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the roots of the sea," as it is in the original,כִּסָה הַיָּם וְשָׁרְשֵׁי אוֹרוֹ עָלָיו פָּרַשׂ agrees exactly with the appearance of a thunderstorm's appearing as arising above the horizon, for the top of the clouds in such

<!-- p. 465 -->

cases are commonly all spread over with an exceeding brightJE deleted "and majestical." light. Thus God spreads his light upon it. And the lower part of a storm that appears thus rising seems to cover the utmost confines and extreme parts of the sea that are next the horizon, that are here called the roots of the sea, which may elegantly be so called according to the notion they then had of the world as being a flat, and that there was first the land, and after that the sea, which they supposed bounded by the horizon, or the meeting of the firmament with the waters. See no. 149.*Works, 15*, 93. He certainly here speaks of a thunderstorm as it is when rising and approaching, whether there was then one approaching, or no. By the Job 36:30 and also the Job 36:32 and Job 36:33, having first observed how the cloud appears on the top of it, covered with light, and how the bottom covers the roots of the sea, he next observes how it is as it advances higher and comes nearer, how the cloud interposes between the sun and the earth, and hides its light, and how the thunder grows louder, and the notice the cattle seem to show of it. And in the beginning of the Job 37, Elihu seems to speak of what then appeared. "At this also my heart trembleth, and is moved out of its place. Hear attentively the noise of his voice," etc. And it was not the only instance of God's speaking out of a storm of rain and thunder, for so he did at Mt. Sinai. See notes on Psalms 68:8. See SSS on Job 38:1.

Job 36:29–30.] Here the clouds are represented as being spread out over the concave of the heavens, as the covering of a tabernacle, which come down as curtains and cover the utmost edge of the sea, which is the uttermost part of the pavement or ground of the tabernacle. Here the clouds are represented as one covering, and the light another, spread out upon it. As in the tabernacle built in the wilderness, there were various coverings, one without another.

Elihu probably has respect to the cloud as it now appeared. The clouds of a thunderstorm, when rising, appear at top spread over with a bright light, and at the bottom covering the utmost ends of the earth or sea.

Job 36:30.] See no. 149.Ibid.

Job 37:18. "Hast thou with him spread out the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass?"] The sky is in effect solid and firm. The ends and effects are the same as if the sky were a vault of irrefragable and impenetrable strength. It remains the same, unaltered with its beautiful azure undecayed, and with the same golden studs unaltered from age to age, through all changes and revolutions whatever—mighty storms, whirlwinds, hurricanes, thunders, and lightnings. There are all the mighty changes of heat and cold, earthquakes, volcanos, etc.

He saw the cloud with a whirlwind in the bosom of it, coming out of the south [Job 37:9], but now it hung so thick, so black over their heads, that they could none of them see the bright light, which just before was in the clouds. The light of the sun was now eclipsed; this minded him of the darkness, by reason of which he could not speak (Job 37:19), and made him afraid to go on (Job 37:20). Thus the disciples feared when 'they entered into the cloud' (Luke 9:34). Yet he looks to the north, and sees it clear that way [Job 37:22]. And he expects that the wind will pass and cleanse them Job 37:21]. And then 'fair weather will come out of the north' Job 37:22], and all will be well. Job 38:13. "That the wicked might be shaken out of it."] 'Tis probable that one reason why God says this of the morning is because he has in his eye that glorious morning of the light and prosperity of the Christian church, when "the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings" [Malachi 4:2], and God shall say to his church, "Arise, shine, for thy light is come, for the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee" [Isaiah 60:1]; which morning will be accompanied with that earthquake that we read of, Revelation 16:18, by which the wicked shall be shaken, of which morning the morning of the natural day is a type. What is said in the next verse is applicable to the morning of that glorious day more aptly than to the morning of the natural day, for though the face of the earth and the visible objects upon it are as it were turned, and changed, and put on a beautiful form at the rising of the natural sun, so that the sun is as it were the seal and they the clay, and they stand or appear as a beautiful garment that covers the earth, yet in the morning of that glorious day of the church when "the Sun of righteousness shall arise," the world of mankind, the inhabitants of the earth (which seem especially to be intended by the pronoun "they" in the verse), shall be turned or changed by the appearance of that Sun much more properly, as clay to the seal. They shall receive impression from him, as clay from the seal, and shall be changed into the same image, asMS: "as X." [the] 2 Corinthians 3:18. And Christ shall then put them on as a garment, as [the church] is often represented as Christ's garment. And the church shall then clothe herself with new converts, "as with a garment" (Isaiah 49:18). And what is said in the Job 38:15 is not properly applicable to the morning in any other sense than this spiritual sense, or to the morning of the church's day. 'Tis a confirmation of this explanation of these words that God, in other parts of this discourse with Job, has an eye to the future great and good things that he will do for his church. See Job 38:23 with notes.

"From the wicked their light is withholden" Job 38:15]. So it will be in the morning of the glorious day of the Christian church that light, that shall then shine forth, shall be withholden from the wicked. It will be darkness unto them. They will stumble, and fall, and won't acknowledge the work of God, or rather their light, i.e. the light of the godly that stand as a garment. The glorious light and prosperity of that day which the godly shall enjoy shall be withholden from the wicked, for they shall be slain early in that morning at the dawning of the day when the light takes hold of the ends of the earth. Then "the wicked shall be shaken out of it" (Job 38:13).

Job 40-41.] In these chapters BEHEMOTH [Job 40:15], signifying land monsters or monstrous four-footed beasts, and LEVIATHAN [Job 41:1], signifying water monsters, are particularly insisted the rather, because they are images or types of the devil and perhaps of Antichrist, the chief of God's proud and haughty enemies, which are referred to in Job 40:11–12. "Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath; and behold everyone that is proud, and abase him. Look on everyone that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place." This is confirmed by what God says of leviathan in the Job 41:34. "He beholdeth all high things; he is king over all the children of pride." Behemoth is also spoken of as a beast of great self-sufficiency and self-confidence, in the Job 40:23–24. And that these mighty, terrible, and haughty beasts are mentioned to confirm what God had said of Job's insufficiency to subdue his proud and lofty enemies appears the more probable, because concerning each of these Job is put in mind how insufficient he is to subdue them. Job is put in mind of this concerning Behemoth. Job 40:19, "He that made him can make his sword to approach to him," implying that there are not sufficient for this. So concerning the leviathan, in the Job 41:11. So Job 41:25–30. See SSS on Job 40:9, as

Job 41.] By "leviathan" Job 41:1] is meant any water monster. It is a general term that includes various species. The crocodile is one species; the several sorts of whales are other species. The word "whale" in English is a general [term] that includes various sorts of creatures. The word "leviathan" in Hebrewלִוְיָתָן is yet of greater extent, and includes more species. Job 42:7.] Job's three friends were exceeding confident that they were in the right and Job altogether in the wrong. They were confident that they had truth and justice onMS: "of." their side, and that they were pleading the cause of God, and stood up in his vindication. They thought they had great evidence of it, and that God's saints of old were with them on their side in this dispute. And yet we see when God appears and comes to pass sentence, he chiefly condemns them, and in the controversy between them and Job mainly justifies Job. So now in controversies that are managed in religious matters, doubtless many may be very confident that they are in the right, and think they are strenuously pleading the cause of God, that yet will be condemned when God comes to judge. And yet those that God in the main will justify may much miss it in many things in their spirit, and temper, and talk, and behavior, and be truly unreasonable as Job was.

"My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." "They had wronged God in making prosperity a mark of the true church, and affliction a certain indication of God's wrath (Ecclesiastes 9:1). They had censured and condemned Job upon a false hypothesis, had represented God fighting against Job as an enemy, when really he was only trying him as a friend; and this was not right. It is a dangerous thing to judge uncharitably of the spiritual and eternal state of others, for in so doing we may perhaps condemn those whom God has accepted, which is a great provocation to him. It is offending his little ones, and he takes himself to be wronged in all the wrongs that are done to them.… God is very angry with those who despise and reproach their brethren, who insult over them, and judge hardly of them, either for their calamities or for their infirmities." Henry.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Exposition, 3* (1725), 133–34.

Job 42:8.] See note on Hebrews 5:7.

Job 42:10. "And the Lord turned again the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends."] When he forgave their trespass that had injured him and called him an hypocrite, then God forgave him those sins he had been correcting him for. When he exercised charity to them in heartily praying for their good, then God opened his bountiful hand to him. Job was brought to this spirit by being humbled by what Elihu first, and afterwards God, had said to him. A deep humiliation for our own offenses

<!-- p. 474 -->

against God will bring us to a disposition to forgive the trespasses of others against us, and our forgiveness of them is a proper expression of our own repentance which God waits for.

Job 42:11.] Probably the remarkable alteration that appeared in his spirit and behavior after God had humbled him, his amiable lowliness, submission, patience, meek and quiet and charitable spirit, was the means by the concurrence of a divine influence on their minds wonderfully to melt and draw their hearts towards Job, together with what his three friends might say to himMS: "them." after they were convinced to alter their minds about Job's affliction, which might cause them to repent their having so slighted his affliction heretofore. A conviction of their error might have influence to cause their hearts to be in the more tender frame now, and to be opened the wider towards Job.

Hence we may note, that makes the virtue itself a means of that which God intends as its rewards. Note also, that it is proper in doing deeds of charity not only to have respect to men's poverty, but to have respect to the greatness of their losses. Thus a rich man that has met with great losses may be more an object of charity than those that are as poor as he, that han't been brought to poverty by such losses. Job doubtless had much more given then, enough to make him equal with many of his poor neighbors.This paragraph is a later addition.

### Psalms

Concerning the BOOK OF PSALMS, see nos. 434, and 440, and 506.The last two references are later additions. See also "Prophecies of the Messiah," "Miscellanies," no. 1067, §87.Section 87 opens, "This is a great argument the book of Psalms is a great part of it prophetical, and also that very much of it relates to the times of the Messiah, even in those parts of it where the speech is in the present or prefer tense" (MS, Andover coll.), p. 86. SeeJE deleted "Note on Psalms 25:22." "Supplement to Prophecies of the Messiah," at the beginning of "Miscellanies," no. 1068, pp. 1 ff.The "Supplement" (MS, Andover coll.) opens as follows: "The book of Psalms in general the Psalmist speaks either in the name of Christ, or in the name of the church. And this is to be observed concerning a very great part of this book, that the Psalmist speaks in the name of Christ most comprehensively taken, viz. as including his body or members, or in the name of Christ mystical, and even in some of those psalms that seem to be the most direct and plain prophecies of Christ, some parts of which are most applicable to the head or Christ, other parts to the body or the church" (p. 1). Both references to the "Miscellanies" in JE's entry are later additions.

Psalms 1:6. "The way of the ungodly shall perish."] I.e. they lead to perdition. He shall perish that walks in them, the "way" being put for him that walks in that way, by such a metonymy as is used, Psalms 17:5. "Hold up my goings in thy paths," i.e. hold me up in my goings, and keep me from falling.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. Psalms 37:38, "The end of the wicked shall be cut off," i.e. the wicked at their end shall be cut off. Psalms 140:4, "Who have purposed to overthrow my goings," i.e. to overthrow me in my goings. This sense is confirmed by the next verse, "They have spread a net by the wayside." 2 Samuel 1:27, "And the weapons of war perished," i.e. by their perishing who use the weapons of war. Or this verse may very naturally and probably be interpreted thus. God in the judgment will own the way or works of the righteous. They shall be approved of by him, and found to glory and honor to be true gold; but the way and work of the wicked shall perish in the judgment, however fair it might appear. It shall vanish away, and all its seeming goldness disappear when it comes to be tried. Like shining dross, it shall perish when tried by the fire. 'Tis said, Psalms 1:5, the wicked "shall not stand in

<!-- p. 476 -->

the judgment," and the reason is here given, viz. that their way will not stand in the judgment. His work shall be destroyed: the building that he hath built on a sandy foundation shall fall and perish, and he shall perish in it.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 508.

Psalms 2.] See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 509–25.

Psalms 2:1. "And the people imagine a vain thing."] By "the people" is often meant the nation of the Jews, in distinction from other nations. So the apostle Peter seems to understand it here. See Acts 4:25–27.

Psalms 2:6. "Holy hill of Zion."] See note on 2 Samuel 5:7.

Psalms 2:11.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 522–23.

Psalms 2:12. "Kiss the son."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 523–24.

"From the way." [See] Matthew 5:25.This line is a separate entry.

Psalms 3:8. "Salvation belongeth unto the Lord."] Salvation is spoken of throughout the Old Testament as a peculiarly glorious work, and is celebrated as one of the principal glories of the God of Israel, as may be seen under the word "salvation" in the concordance.Alexander Cruden's entry under "Salvation" describes the Hebrew pattern of expression as involving the use of abstractions rather than "concrete terms." "Thus, instead of saying that God saves them, and protects them; they say, that God is their salvation." In this context Cruden underscores their celebration of the joy of salvation (*Complete Concordance*, n.p.).

Psalms 4:8. "Thou only."] I.e. thou alone, without needing a multitude, an army, or any other to assist thee in defending thy people, though there be an army, a great multitude, against me. See Psalms 3:1–3, Psalms 3:5–6, Psalms 3:8. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 536–37.

Psalms 6:5. "In death."] 1. "In death," as it is, without God's salvation. 'Tis God's mercy and salvation which the Psalmist is praying for when in danger of death, and it is proper that all God's saints should pray for this when sick. Or 2. In temporal death, the saints han't that opportunity to bring forth

<!-- p. 477 -->

fruits to God's praise as in life, which made the apostle Paul say, "For me to live is Christ, but to die is gain" [Philippians 1:21]. And therefore in the issue of the conflict he had in his own mind which to choose, he chose life. The fruits the saints bring forth for the enlargement and advancement of Christ's kingdom here enlarge and advance his kingdom and God's praise in heaven to all eternity. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 546–47.

Psalms 6:8.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 548–49.

Psalms 7:3. "If I have done this."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 551–52.

Psalms 7:14. "And brought forth falsehood."] I.e. "a cheat upon himself, a lie in his right hand. He cannot compass what he intended; nor if he gain his point, will he gain that satisfaction which he promised him. He brings forth 'wind' (Isaiah 26:18), 'stubble' (Isaiah 33:11), 'death' (James 1:15), that is, 'falsehood.'" Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 154.

Psalms 8:1. "Who has set thy glory above the heavens."] In this I believe the Holy Spirit has some reference to Christ's ascension; for he is the brightness of God's glory [Hebrews 1:3], and was he that manifested himself in the Shekinah, which was the shining of God's glory, and was called the glory of the Lord. See Psalms 113:4–5.

"Above the heavens." SSS.This line is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 561–62.

Psalms 8:2.] See no. 95a.*Works, 15*, 77.

"Because of thine enemies, that thou mightest still the enemy and the avenger." 'Tis pretty manifest that "the enemy and the avenger" here spoken [of] must be the devil, for 'tis evident the "babes and sucklings" here spoken [of] are mankind that God had put such great honor upon in and after his creation. And thereforeJE deleted "the scope and argument of the Psalmist requires." the import of what the Psalmist here declares of God's end in thus exalting mankind, requires that we understand "the enemy and the avenger" to be someone in natural capacity and strength vastly superior to mankind, and in comparison of

<!-- p. 478 -->

whom men are but "babes and sucklings." For God's ordaining strength "out of the mouths of babes and sucklings" is to pour contempt upon the great and proud enemy and avenger, to conquer him and obtain a glorious triumph by so weak and despicable an instrument, and thrusting him down below babes and sucklings, and subduing him under their feet, and so causing his glorying to cease.

See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 562–63. Each of the three paragraphs is a separate entry.

Psalms 8:4.] Poor, worthless, weak man is the babe that God has chosen to still these mighty and proud enemies, the devils. See Psalms 8:2.

Psalms 8:5.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 566–67.

Psalms 8:5–9. "For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels." The Psalmist is here admiring and praising the wonderful goodness and condescension of God to man in advancing the human nature to such dignity and honor. Now the advancement of the human nature, or crowning of it with glory and honor, is twofold. There was that that was done at God's first work, when God first created man, whereby God gave him dominion over this lower world and the other creatures in it, herein making man but a little lower than the angels, those thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers above [Colossians 1:16]. And as man was made in the image of God, so hereby he had given him an image of God's authority and dominion. He was placed here as God's vicegerent, and hereby there was given a specimen and shadow of the second and greatest exaltation, which God designed the human nature for; which design of God probably had been declared in heaven among the angels before now, then now saw a specimen of it in man's dominion over the creatures. And

Secondly, the second exaltation, or crowning with glory and honor, of which this was but a shadow, is that which is performed in God's second work in actual uniting the human nature to the divine, whereby the human nature was exalted not only to an honor and dominion that was an image of God's, but actually toMS: divine ‹Gods›. God's honor and dominion, whereby he

<!-- p. 479 -->

had indeed in the most extensive sense dominion over all the works of God's hands, and had all things put under his feet. That person in the human nature, that is the head and representative of the rest, is thus exalted; and the rest that are his members, and are united to him, are partakers with him in this exaltation.

Now the Holy Ghost in this place has respect to both these exaltations of the human nature, as it is exceeding common for the Holy Ghost to speak of the shadow and the thing shadowed forth, of the lesser and the greater, of the same kind both under one. He speaks most directly and expressly of the first, but he has an ultimate and perhaps a principal respect to the latter. I believe he has a principal respect to the latter in the Psalms 8:2, "Out of the mouth," etc., and that "the enemy and avenger" there spoken of is the devil, who can't bear to see the human nature so exalted.

These words in the Psalms 8:5, "Thou madest him a little lower than the angels," are spoken in different senses as they relate to man in his first creation and to the man Christ Jesus, but yet in both as a great work of bounty and condescension to the human nature or mankind.

Hence we may understand why the Apostle applies this place as he does, Hebrews 2:6 ff.

The first words in the Psalms 8:5 are spoken with a more special reference to man's first exaltation, and best agrees with that as where Christ, in the Matthew 24, prophesies of the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the world under one. There are some expressions do much best agree with the one, others with the other. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, sec. 2, (3), 2.*Works, 18*, 286–89. In no. 702 JE provides numerous examples in which the "creation of man" shadows forth "his new creation."

Psalms 9:10. "And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee."] I.e. they that know the name and fame which thou hast gotten to thyself by thy faithfulness to thy people that have trusted; they that know and rightly consider the report of thy saints concerning the success of trusting in thee, and the records of thy wonderful works for them that seek thee. The latter part of the verse confirms this. This is sometimes meant by God's name, as Psalms 48:8. "As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts." And Psalms 48:10, "According to thy name, so is thy praise."

<!-- p. 480 -->

Psalms 9:17. "The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God."] If we translate this wordשְׁאוֹל "hell" or "the grave," it will come to the same thing. If we interpret it, "the wicked shall be turned into the grave, or a state of death,"JE deleted "or that they shall die it must be meant of some." by this death must be meant something not common to the righteous and the wicked, to those that forget God and those that do not forget him.

"Hell." SSS.This line is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 577.

Psalms 10:10. "He croucheth, and humbleth himself."] "The sordid spirit of persecutors will stoop to anything, though never so mean, to compass their wicked designs." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 159.

Psalms 10:15. "Seek out his wickedness till thou find none."] See Matthew 5:26.

Psalms 11:5–6.] God "trieth the righteous" oftentimes by sore affliction and persecution (as Psalms 11:1–3). But he destroyeth the wicked; he will rain on them "snares, fire and brimstone," etc.

Psalms 11:6. "Snares."] I.e. this destruction shall come suddenly and unexpectedly upon them, while they are saying, Peace and safety; while they are eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, and gratifying their lusts, as a bird that is securely feeding on the sweet bait, suspecting no harm nigh, and is suddenly caught in the snare. Luke 21:34–35, "And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares. For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the earth." See also Matthew 24:36–39 and 1 Thessalonians 5:6. Ecclesiastes 9:12, "For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them."

Psalms 14:6.] I.e. you have ridiculed his counsel, as though he were very unwise for making God his refuge. See Matthew 27:43, and Psalms 22:7–8; Micah 7:10; Psalms 42:3, Psalms 42:10, and Psalms 79:10; Joel 2:17.

<!-- p. 481 -->

Psalms 16.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 617–29.

Psalms 16:3. "But to the saints that are in the earth."] Their being "in the earth" is mentioned, because hereby they were within the reach of his goodness. God was in heaven, and so far out of the reach of his goodness; his goodness extended not to him.

Psalms 16:4. "Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god. Their drink offerings of blood will I not offer."] Here is respect [had] to the customs of idolaters in offering "drink offerings of blood," and sometimes offering and drinking human blood. But as the psalm is prophetical, and as the Psalmist speaks in the name of Christ, the Spirit of God here probably has in view the cruel religion of the false, idolatrous, self-righteous church, which drinks and offers to God the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus, supposing or at least pretending that they do God service by killing their fellow creature, and shedding Christ's own blood, and the blood of those that are truly Christ's followers, as it was with the corrupt church of the Jews and the Church of Rome. The description of the persons here spoken of agrees with both those, viz. that they are those "that hasten after another," which the Jews did when they rejected Christ, and so rejected God as their Savior, and were set in their own way of trusting in other saviors, and sought another portion, had confidence in the flesh, trusted in their own righteousness, trusted in their false teachers, and were in earnest expectation of another messiah, and were in eager expectation of great earthly prosperity and glory under the messiah which they chose for their portion. The multiplying of the sorrows of these was remarkably fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem. All their sacrifices of beasts, and all their legal services, and legal righteousness, which they trusted so much in, which they offered with a libation of Christ's blood and the blood of his saints, could not save 'em from God's wrath which then came upon them to the uttermost.

'Tis evident that the psalm has reference to the persecution of enemies exercised against him in whose name the psalm is uttered.

Psalms 16:5. "And of my cup."] "It was customary among the ancients, to assign to each guest at a feast a particular cup, as well as dish; and by the kind and quantity of the liquor contained in it, the respect of the entertainer

<!-- p. 482 -->

was expressed. Hence 'cup' came in general to signify a portion assigned, whether of pleasure or sorrow. Compare Psalms 23:5, and Psalms 11:6, and Psalms 73:10; Isaiah 51:17, Isaiah 51:22; Jeremiah 25:15, Jeremiah 25:17; Zechariah 12:2; John 18:11; Matthew 26:39, Matthew 26:42, and Matthew 20:22–23." See Doddridge's note on Matthew 20:22.*Family Expositor, 2*, 266–67. See SSS on this verse.This sentence is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 622–23.

"The Lord is the portion of mine inheritance," etc. As this psalm is concerning Christ,JE deleted "our great high priest." the Psalmist speaks in his name. So this is the more properly said, that which was said of the priests and Levites of old, "The Lord is their inheritance" [Deuteronomy 10:9], being true in a sense the most eminent and highest possible.

"Thou maintainest my lot." This is the most fitly mentioned because, as was observed before (Note on Psalms 16:4.), the psalm has reference to the persecution of Christ's enemies, who endeavored to deprive him of happiness, and make him miserable.These last two paragraphs are a later separate entry.

Psalms 16:9. "My glory rejoiceth."] The following reasons may be given why by "glory" here and in Psalms 57:8 and Psalms 108:1 is meant the soul. 1. This seems agreeable to the use of the same word in the originalכָּבוֹד in Genesis 49:6. "O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, my honor" (or "glory"), "be not thou united." Here the words "soul" and "glory" seem only two different words used to signify the same thing for eloquence sake, as is very frequent in the Old Testament. And so in Psalms 7:5, "Let the enemy persecute my soul, and take it; yea, let him tread down my life, and lay mine honor" (or "my glory") "in the dust." Here those three words, "soul," "life," and "glory" seem all to signify much the same thing. 2. So here in Psalms 16:9, "heart" and "glory" seem to be two words that are of like signification, as "heart" and "soul" are. And so again in Psalms 108:1, "O God, my *heart* is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my *glory*." In the originalאַף־כְּבוֹדִי וַאֲזַמְּרָה אָשִׁירָה the words are, "I will sing and give praise, even my glory," or "also my glory," which manner of expression are much moreJE deleted "emphatical." elegant and forceable, if we understand "even my soul" than "even my tongue." 3. The soul of man is much more properly his glory than his tongue. It was by his soul, that breath of life that God breathed into him, whereby he became a living soul, that he was set in honor above the

<!-- p. 483 -->

beasts that perish. And he becomes "like the beasts that perish" because he understands not (Psalms 49:20). He don't improve the faculties of his rational soul, by which God made man wiser than the beasts of the earth and gave him more understanding than the fowls of heaven. God crowned Adam with glory and honor by setting him above the beasts in understanding and dominion. See Psalms 8:4. As Christ, the wisdom and reason of God, is called his "glory," so is the rational soul of man called his "glory."

But yet Acts 2:26 seems to show that by "glory" here is meant the tongue. I would therefore rather conclude that by man's glory is meant his *logos*, including both the internal and external *logos*, his reason or understanding and his word, as the *Logos* of God is his glory, the brightness of his glory. And sometimes man's glory is put chiefly for his inward *logos*, and sometimes for his outward.This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 16:10.] What came to pass with respect to the real body of Christ is what likewise comes to pass with respect to the church, the mystical body of Christ. It sometimes seems to be dead; it is brought so low that [it] is as it were hid in the grave. It is buried out of sight as if dead, but yet never will suffer it to be wholly destroyed. It shall not see corruption, and it shall come to life again. So it was with the church in the time of Antchrist. God's two witnesses were as it were slain, and their bodies lay dead in the street of the great city three days, and then came to life, and stood on their feet, and ascended into heaven, as in the eleventh of Revelation.

Psalms 16:11. "Show me the path of life."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 628–29.

Psalms 17:3. "Thou hast visited me in the night."] To see how I behave myself in secret, which is a much greater discovery of the heart than the behavior before men. "I have purposed my mouth shall not transgress." This confirms what the apostle James says, that he [that] bridles the tongue "is a perfect man" [James 3:2], and it is a good sign of his sincerity; and what Christ says, "By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" [Matthew 12:37].

Psalms 17:4. "The destroyer."] No. 298.*Works, 15*, 272.

<!-- p. 484 -->

Psalms 17:8.] By "shadow" here is not meant the same as is signified by shadow or shade, according to the common use of the word in English, but thereby is intended no other than covert; as Isaiah 34:15, "Lay, and hatch, and gather under her shadow." So an arrow, or instrument, is said to be hid "in the shadow of the hand," i.e. 'tis held or grasped in the hand (Isaiah 49:2 and Isaiah 51:16). So we read of coming under the shadow of a roof (Genesis 19:8).

Psalms 18:7–15.] The things here spoken of, God probably had at some time or times literally accomplished for David and against his enemies. He had at some time wondrously appeared on David's side in the time of battle, and fought against his enemies, when they were too strong for him and he cried unto him, with mighty thunder [and] lightning, as he did against the Philistines (1 Samuel 2:10), and as he did against the Egyptians at the Red Sea (Psalms 77:16–18), and as he did against the Amorites when Joshua was fighting with them. See note on Habakkuk 3:11, no. 208.Ibid., 131–34. And as he probably did against Sisera when Deborah and Barak fought with him. See note on Judges 5:20.Ibid., 140–42. And as Hannah prophesies that God would do for his people and "his anointed" [1 Samuel 2:10]. But David was God's anointed, the most eminently of all the temporal princes of Israel. It seems also that God had fought against his enemies with hailstones, with thunder and lightning, as he did against the Amorites when the sun and moon stood still. And particularly it is probable that God thus appeared and fought for David against the Philistines at Baal Perazim, in one or both those battles that he fought with them there, that we read in the latter end of the 2 Samuel 5. For both those battles seem to be fought in the same place, and the history gives us an account that God did miraculously there appear for David against his enemies (2 Samuel 5:20, 2 Samuel 5:24). And it appears very probable that God appeared for him with thunder, lightning, and hail, by Isaiah 28:21, where this instance of God's appearing against David's enemies at Perazim is mentioned as parallel with what he did against the enemies of Joshua at Gibeon: "For the Lord shall rise up as in mount Perazim; he shall be wroth as in the valley of Gibeon, that he may do his work, his strange work, and bring to pass his act, his strange act."

Psalms 18:33. "My high places."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 648–49.

<!-- p. 485 -->

Psalms 18:35.] "Thy gentleness," or thy humiliation or affliction. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 649–50. This teaches that the exaltation of God's people is by the humiliation and suffering of their Savior.

Psalms 19:4–6.] See no. 328.*Works, 15*, 311–13.

Psalms 19:5. "As a bridegroom coming out of his chamber."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 658–61.

Psalms 22.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 676–95.

Psalms 22:6. "I am a worm."] "The word,"תּוֹלַעֵת as Mr. Henry observes, "signifies a worm used in dyeing scarlet," which more livel[il]y signifies his suffering and dying state.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 180.

Psalms 22:9–10.] In this verse there is probably a reference to the manner of Christ's birth being in a stable, where the blessed Virgin was alone without the help that is usual in time of travail. There she committed herself and the fruit of her womb to God, and received strength to bring forth by faith, as it had been by faith that she conceived, though she knew not a man. And also to the blessed Virgin's committing him to God, when Herod persecuted him and sought to destroy him, and God's wonderful preserving him on that occasion.

Psalms 22:10.] By this it appears that 'tis fit that God's people should give up their children to God in infancy, and also that by such an act of the parents God becomes the child's covenant God. Whence I would argue that these things ought to be visible: that which should be really by all God's people, should be visibly among them. It should be visible to the public that they do give 'em up to God. And then the public should look upon those infants as some of the covenant people of God; or which is the same thing, those children are actually some of the visible church. Nothing seems more reasonable: that a people that are devoted to the worship of a God should visibly give up their children to their God. This is what the heathen nations do, and certainly it is very manifest by the Scripture that

<!-- p. 486 -->

'tis agreeable to God's will that his people should do so. And if so, then it follows from this text that when parents have visibly given up their children to God, they ought to be looked upon by the public as God's, or some of God's covenant people, or which is the same thing (as the Apostle expresses it), they are holy [1 Corinthians 7:14]

Psalms 22:14. "All my bones are out of joint."] This seems to be spoken of Christ in the time of his crucifixion, by the Psalms 22:16 and Psalms 22:18, and probably at that time literally fulfilled of Christ, his limbs being so stretched forth, and bearing all his weight on them so long, and his nerves and other ligatures so weakened and relaxed with extremity of pain, that it probably drew his bones out of joint. See how the rest of the verse was fulfilled, in notes on John 19:34.

Psalms 22:15. "My strength is dried up like a potsherd."] This was remarkably fulfilled in Christ, whose body was drained of its moisture and animal spirits by a gradual shedding of blood, and want of sleep, and continual pains of body and agonies of mind, from the beginning of his agony in the garden till he expired on the cross.

"My tongue cleaveth to my jaws." "The clamminess of the mouth is an usual symptom of approaching death. This was fulfilled both in Christ's thirst upon the cross (John 19:28), and in his silence under his sufferings." Henry.This paragraph is a later entry. *Exposition, 3* (1725), 181.

Psalms 22:17. "I may tell all my bones: they look and stare upon me."] We must understand the person here speaking as stripped of his garments so that naked body appeared, as it follows in the next verse. "They part my garments among them." "His blessed body was lean and emaciated with labor, grief, and fasting, during the whole course of his ministry, which made him look as if he were near fifty years old (John 8:57)." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 181.

Psalms 22:20. "My darling" (or, "my only one," as in the original)יְחִידָתִי "from the power of the dog."] As these are meant by the Holy Ghost to be the words of Christ, by his "only one" here is doubtless meant the church. In Christ's soul's being delivered, the church was delivered, for he was not delivered as a private person.

<!-- p. 487 -->

Psalms 22:26. "The meek shall eat."] I.e. of "my vows," or sacrifices that I have vowed, spoken of in the foregoing verse.

Psalms 22:29. "All they that go down to the dust shall bow before him."] Christ came to save from death, and he does as it were bring his people up out of their graves (Isaiah 26, Isaiah 29; Ezekiel 37). They are saved from a state of spiritual death and from eternal death, which they are condemned to; and he actually brings 'em out of their graves at the resurrection. Those that are thus saved shall worship Christ as their Savior from death, without whom they must have forever died; and therefore it is added, "and none can keep alive his own soul." And others "that go down to the dust," that are not saved, shall bow before Christ, as he will be their judge (Philippians 2:10). They shall bow before [him], as they shall be forced to be subject to his condemnation and almighty power in executing the sentence. He'll destroy them; they must "go down to the dust," for none of 'em shall be able to keep alive his own soul.

"Eat and worship." I.e. shall eat sacrifices; that was that eating, that worshipping.

Mr. Henry thus. "Even they that live in pomp and fare deliciously, when they have eaten and are full, shall bless the Lord their God for their plenty and prosperity."All three paragraphs are separate entries. *Exposition, 3* (1725), 182.

Psalms 23:2. "He leadeth me beside the still waters."] In the original,מְנֻחוֹת עַל־מֵי "the waters of rest, or quietness." This seems not to have reference so much to the stillness of the waters as to the rest, comfort, and satisfaction which is found in drinking the waters, being such as greatly refresh and give satisfying delight. As Christ says, "He that drinketh the water that I shall give him shall never thirst" [John 4:14]. The word "rest" is sometimes used to signify such refreshment as one has in food or drink, and in gratifying the taste or smell. So in Job 36:16, "That which should have been set on thy table should have been full of fatness"; in the original,דָשֶׁן מָלֵא שֻׁלְחָנְךָָ "the 'rest' of thy table." The word is of the same root as in this place. So in places innumerable, the sacrifices which are called the "bread of God" are said to be "a savor of rest." See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 696.

<!-- p. 488 -->

Psalms 23:4. "Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."] By God's "rod and staff" in this place seems to be meant two things. 1. The rod with which he that is here said to be comforted walks, the staff on which he leans and supports him in walking through this dark, difficult, and terrible valley, and comforts him as it supports him, and keeps him from stumbling and falling, which is "faith." The same that is often represented by a staff was typified of old by Jacob's staff and Elisha's staff. See note on Numbers 21:18. This may be called "God's staff," as it is a staff given by God; and so when it is said, "thy rod and staff comfort me," 'tis as much as to say, "the staff which thou hast given me comforts me."

2. Another thing meant is the rod in the hand of Christ, which he uses as a shepherd. Both these things are signified by Moses' rod. See "Notes on Scripture," nos. 195 and 442.*Works, 15*, 106–8, 524–25. Moses' rod was a shepherd's rod. It was the rod he was found with, or that he had in his hand, as he was feeding the flock of Jethro [Exodus 3].

Or as here are two words, "rod" and "staff." The first may signify the rod of the shepherd; the second may signify a walking staff, or faith. It favors this interpretation, that a plural pronoun and plural verb agree with rod and staff, which seems to suppose 'em to be two things.

Psalms 23:5. "Thou anointest my head with oil."] This may probably not only signify God's exalting him to glorious dignity, as God's saints are made kings and priests, but his testifying his love to him by giving a most friendly entertainment in his house, as this was one way in which they used of old to bid their friends welcome, to anoint 'em with oil (Luke 7:46), as well as spread a table before 'em, and give 'em a full cup.

"Anointest my head with oil." SSS.This line is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 697–98.

Psalms 23:6. "I will dwell in the house of the Lord forever."] "Being there not merely as a servant, or as a guest kindly entertained for a little while (see note on foregoing verse), but as a child adopted into the family. For as Christ says, "The Son abideth in the house forever" [John 8:35].

Psalms 24:5. "And righteousness."] I.e. the reward of righteousness, or a being treated as righteous. He shall be justified, accepted of God, and acknowledged and rewarded by him as righteous. See Psalms 37:6.

<!-- p. 489 -->

Psalms 24:6. "This is the generation of them that seek him."] Therefore the promises that are made to them that seek in Scripture are to such as seek thus, viz. graciously.

Psalms 24:7–10. "Lift up your heads, O ye gates."] This is the will or command of God the Father. God the Father himself opened the gates of heaven to receive his Son after his passion in token of his great acceptance of what he had done.

"Be ye lift up." This has respect to God's, or Christ's, triumphant ascension into heaven after a battle and victory over his enemies here on earth, agreeable to the representation, Psalms 47:5. The representation is of an entrance into heaven from the earth through that vault which is conceived as the pavement of heaven. And the doors are represented as opening upwards, raised or lifted up, when they are opened. And they are called upon to open as of themselves, or to lift up themselves, when the King of Glory [approaches], as most readily receiving the King of Glory as a most proper inhabitant, the rightful owner of the house, one infinitely worthy to be received. The very stones will as it were cry out, and a dumb ass speak, when there is great occasion. So the doors of heaven will open of themselves, when the King of Glory approaches.This paragraph is a later addition.

See no. 308.*Works, 15*, 281–83. SSS.Both references on this line are separate entries. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 703–4.

Psalms 25:9. "The meek," etc.] This was remarkably exemplified in Moses. See Numbers 12. Compare Numbers 12:3 with Numbers 12:6–8.

"He will guide in judgment."] I.e. into righteousness, or into the right way. This is agreeable to the use of the word *mispat*מִשְׁפָּט in the Hebrew Bible.This paragraph is a later entry. See *Works, 21*, 349–50.

Psalms 25:11.] His iniquity's being "great" is here mentioned as a reason why the Psalmist asks God to pardon him only for his "name's sake," and not for any worthiness in him.

Psalms 25:22. "Redeem Israel," etc.] Such passages as these in many of the psalms show that although the Psalmist speaks in the first person singular, yet he speaks in the name of Christ or his church, or rather in the

<!-- p. 490 -->

name of Christ mystical. See Psalms 44:15, JE deleted "Psalms 22:26, Psalms 9:6, Psalms 9:8, Psalms 7:7–8, Psalms 11, and Psalms 11:38, and Psalms 28:9, and Psalms 40:16. Psalms 44:15." compared with the foregoing and following parts of the psalm. Compare Psalms 60:12MS: "Psalms 66:12." with the rest of the psalm.JE deleted "Psalms 10:17, and Psalms 12:7, and Psalms 32:6–11, Psalms 40:5."

For this reason David in many psalms, speaking of hisJE deleted "enemies." persecutors, represents 'em as heathen and aliens. So Psalms 54:3, Psalms 59:5, Psalms 32:8, and Psalms 9:5, Psalms 9:15, Psalms 9:19–20, and Psalms 10:16.

So David speaks of God's making known his dominion to the ends of the earth, or over all nations, by avenging him (Psalms 59:17).MS: "Psalms 59:17." JE marked this entire entry with a vertical line on the left side. The last two paragraphs of this entry are a later addition.

Psalms 26:12. "An even place."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 717.

Psalms 27:13. "Land of the living."] See note on Ezekiel 26:20.

Psalms 29:3.] Lightning and thunder is a very lively image of the word of God upon many accounts. 'Tis exceeding quick, and exceeding piercing, and powerful to break in pieces, and scorch, and dissolve, and is full of majesty.

"The voice of the Lord is upon the waters." Thunderstorms in Canaan generally come out of the west, from off the Mediterranean Sea. So perhaps the voice of God in his word in the latter days, of which this psalm seems to be a prophecy (see Psalms 29:1–2, Psalms 29:10–11), will probably come from the west and over the sea. See 1 Kings 18:41–46.This paragraph is a later addition.

Psalms 29:7.] The "voice of the Lord" here probably includes both thunder and earthquakes.

Psalms 29:10. "The Lord sitteth upon the flood."] There may probably be here an eye to Noah's flood, and things typified by it (not exclusive of the ocean and other floods). Mr. Henry observes that the wordמַבּוּל "is never used but concerning Noah's flood."*Exposition, 3* (1725), 196. In the time of that flood probably were extraordinary thunders and lightnings.

<!-- p. 491 -->

Psalms 30. Title.] David's entering into his house, where was his throne and where he reigned over Israel, was a type of hisI.e. Christ's. entering into heaven, and entering into his spiritual house, the Christian church, after his sufferings. And the dedication of David's house is a type of the new glory added to heaven by Christ's entering into it, and establishing and dedicating the Christian church. And therefore the psalm is accommodated to the latter event rather than the former.

Psalms 31:20. "In the secret of thy presence."] As it were in the holy of holies. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 741–42.

Psalms 31:22.] For the import of the wordחָפַז here translated "haste," see note on Psalms 116:10–11.

Psalms 33:18.] Psalms 119:166, Psalms 147:11, Psalms 40:3; Isaiah 50:10–11.

Psalms 34.] This psalm remarkably shows that a dependence on God for his protection and help should not cause us to neglect any proper endeavors, or the utmost use of our own strength and wisdom for our own preservation, deliverance, or any benefit we stand in need of. This psalm shows that David looked to God and trusted in him, when he was in such great danger in the land of the Philistines, and that God accepted his trust in him, and accordingly remarkably interposed and delivered him. "The angel of the Lord encamped round about him" Psalms 34:7]. And yet David made use of the utmost of his own contrivance and cunning for his own deliverance. "He changed his behavior," and "let his spittle fall down on his beard," and feigned himself distracted [1 Samuel 21:13]; and God made use of this as the means of his deliverance.

Psalms 35:13 "When they were sick."] "When Saul was ill and melancholy," David was his physician to relieve him, and probably not only made use of "his harp, but his prayers." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 209.

Psalms 35:16.] An hypocritical mocker is one that pretends respect out of mockery. Thus they that bowed the knee to Christ, and cried, "Hail, King of the Jews" [Matthew 27:29], were "hypocritical mockers."

<!-- p. 492 -->

Psalms 36:7–9.] See "Discourse on the Doctrine of the Trinity," third sheet this mark ♀, p. 9.JE declares that God's lovingkindness (Psalms 36:7) "is the same with the Holy Ghost," which he also links with "the fatness of God's house and the river of his pleasures" (Psalms 36:8) as well as with "the fountain of life" (Psalms 36:9). He ties these verses to similar images in Ezekiel, John, and Revelation (*Works, 21*, 128). Compare these verses with Revelation 21:23–24, and Revelation 22:1, Revelation 22:5; and see note on Revelation 21:23–24. See note on Psalms 36:8.JE wrote the three sentences in this paragraph at different times.

Psalms 36:8.] By partaking of God's "pleasures," here is meant the pleasures which God enjoys, even in like manner as by entering into God's rest in Psalms 95:11, is meant entering into the rest which God enjoys, as the Apostle explains it. See note on Hebrews 4:5.

Psalms 36:8–9.] See Revelation 21:23 and Revelation 22:1, Revelation 22:5.

Psalms 36:9 "In thy light we shall see light."] We shall not only enjoy light, but thou thyself wilt be our light, as 'tis said, Revelation 21:23, "The city had no need of the sun, nor the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof." And Revelation 22:5, "And they need no candle, neither light of the sun, for the Lord God giveth them light." We shall see light, and not only so, but the light that we shall see and dwell in is thy light, the light of thine own glory that shines round about thee, which was represented by the light of the Shekinah. The Psalmist seems to have the light of the Shekinah in the temple in his eye, for he is speaking here of the pleasures and good things of God's house, as in the foregoing verse, the river of God's pleasure spoken of there is the same that in Ezekiel's visions is represented as proceeding forth from the temple (Ezekiel 47), and in the twenty-second of Revelation as "proceeding out of the throne of God and the Lamb" Revelation 22:1].The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. 'Tis God's light in two respects. 1. As 'tis the light of the glory that shines forth from God, 'tis the light of God's glory. And 2. 'Tis the light that God enjoys, the light in which he is happy. So the saints have fellowship with God in his happiness. The same is meant by the other expression in the verse foregoing, "thou shalt make them to drink of the river of thy pleasures" [Psalms 36:8].JE mistakenly linked an additional paragraph to this entry which belongs with comments on Psalms 72:6. It has been transferred to that location.

Psalms 37:6. "Thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment," etc.] I.e. he, by his treatment of them, shall openly and plainly declare his acknowledgment

<!-- p. 493 -->

of that as righteous, and that in judging he justifies and accepts thee. See Psalms 24:5. "Thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noon day." I.e. though now it be a time of darkness and trouble, and be as it were a time of night with thee, as the foregoing verses imply, yet God will judge righteously between you and your enemies, and bring forth of his righteous judgment, or the fruit of his judgment agreeable to thy righteous cause (And this is frequently the meaning of the word "righteousness" as used in the Old Testament, and called "their righteousness." It signifies the righteousness of their cause in that strife their enemies have with him, as pleaded and manifested by God, their righteous judge.),This parenthesis is a later addition. as the light of the morning after your dark night that has seemed long to continue, yea, and shall at last bring the light to the brightness of noon day. See Psalms 46 and Isaiah 58:8.

Psalms 37:11.] The "meek" spoken of in this verse are those that don't fret themselves, that "rest in the Lord and wait patiently for him" Psalms 37:7], that "cease from anger and forsake wrath," that "fret not themselves in any wise to do evil" Psalms 37:8], spoken of in the foregoing verses. "The meek shall inherit the earth." This [is] accomplished in the glorious times of the church on earth, and proves that departed saints shall have the benefit and enjoy the glory of these times. See "Miscellanies," no. 811.*Works, 18*, 520–22. That which is spoken of in this and the two foregoing verses had its more immediateMS: "immediately." accomplishment in Solomon's reign, a type of the glorious day of the gospel church, when all David's enemies and all the enemies of the church were cut off, and were no more found. But the righteous inherited the land and the earth in a sense, as Solomon reigned over great part of the earth, and was honored and sought to by the whole earth. This was indeed to be in a "little time." See Psalms 72:7, and "Miscellanies," no. 871.*Works, 20*, 110–11. From hence we may infer that when those glorious times shall begin, God's people shall be brought off from censoriousness and bitter complaint of persecution, and other things inconsistent with meekness, that do now too much prevail amongst godly people and ministers. See Proverbs 10:30.The remainder of this entry is a later addition. "Abundance of peace." See Psalms 72:7 and Jeremiah 33:6.

Psalms 38.] By this psalm it seems evident that David labored under some very painful and loathsome disease in his loins, that was brought upon

<!-- p. 494 -->

[him] as a punishment of his sin with Bathsheba, at the same [time] that Absalom rebelled against him, and he fled from him, and Shimei cursed him (which he seems to have respect to, Psalms 38:13–14), and Absalom defiled his concubines. This psalm, according to the title, is to bring that sin "to remembrance."

Psalms 39:7. "And now, Lord, what wait I for?"] I.e. I don't wait for any earthly happiness, for such things as are mentioned in the preceding verse, for which men are disquieted in vain. I don't wait for riches, which men heap up and know not who shall gather them. I don't expect happiness in those things that death will soon separate all men from, but "my hope is in thee."

Psalms 39:12. David asks mercy as a stranger, having reference to the law, often repeated in the Pentateuch, of showing mercy to strangers (a sojourner with thee), alluding to that which is said, Leviticus 25:23, "The land is mine, and ye are strangers and sojourners with me." See SSS.*Synapsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 799–800.

Psalms 40:6.] See nos. 62 and 171.*Works, 15*, 67, 99–100.

"Mine ear hast thou opened." Rawlin on *Justification*, p. 87, observes that the word כָרָה, translated "opened," "signifies not only to dig or bore, but alsoMS: "more generally ‹also›." Rawlin reads "more generally." to adapt, fit, or make ready," which also appears both by the Hebrew lexicon and concordance.See Buxtorf, *Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum* (6th ed.), pp. 354–55. See also Taylor, *Hebrew Concordance, I*, entry 890 on כרךְ. So that if we suppose the word is here used so as to imply both these significations, they do the more naturally signify Christ's incarnation or taking on him the human nature, of which the Apostle interprets; for by that he willingly "took on him the form of a servant" [Philippians 2:7], and has his ear bored as such, and by that he had an ear prepared or fitted, by preparing a proper nature for him to receive and obey God's commandments in.This paragraph is a later entry. Richard Rawlin, *Christ the Righteousness of his People; or, The Doctrine of Justification by Faith in Him. Represented in several Sermons, Preached at the Merchants Lecture at Pinner's-Hall* (London, 1741), p. 87, note. The interpretation of Rawlin (1687–1757), an Independent minister at Fetter Lane, London, rests on the "easy and common figure of a part for the whole, by Christ's having his ear *hollowed* or framed, we are to understand his having a proper human body given him."

<!-- p. 495 -->

Psalms 40:6–8.] See Isaiah 50:5–6.

Psalms 40:7. "In the volume of the book it is written of me."] See Matthew 26:54.

Psalms 45.] See the evidence there is that this psalm is no epithalamium relating to any marriage of David or Solomon, §46 of the "Prophecies of the Messiah," "Miscellanies," no. 1067.JE offers a detailed refutation of the notion that the person spoken of in this psalm is either David or Solomon. The account is "inconsistent" with David's marital history, and Solomon was never "a mighty hero in the field of battle and a great conqueror," as the object of this song is described. Furthermore, "the person here principally intended… is spoken of as one above mere men" ("Miscellanies," no. 1067, pp. 16–17).

Psalms 45:1. "My tongue is as the pen of a ready writer."] I.e. I am not any more at a loss for words and expressions than a ready scribe who writes from a copy, where all the words are already set before his eyes.

Psalms 45:7.] See no. 163.*Works, 15*, 97.

Psalms 45:8.] Ivory is a white substance, and these spices coming "out of ivory palaces" representMS: "represents." the same as Mary's precious ointment, perfumed with spices, out of an alabaster box. See note on Mark 14:3. Ivory is evidently used in Scripture as a type of spiritual purity by reason of its whiteness. So Solomon's throne of judgment was of ivory (1 Kings 10:18), to signify the righteousness and purity of his judgment, and righteousness of his government, as Christ is represented at the day of judgment as sitting on a great white throne (Revelation 20). The same may be argued from Canticles 5:14, "His belly is as bright ivory." And Canticles 7:4, "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory." By the "ivory palaces" is probably meant heaven. So SSS.This reference and the preceding sentence are a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 841–42.

Psalms 45:10. "Forget also thine own people, and thy father's house."] By which may be intended sin, and the pleasures and profits thereof, the objects of our lusts; which may well be compared to our father's house and natural kindred, both because sin and corruption is what we have naturally, that which we are born with, and that we derive from our parents. 'Tis that which we have by the first birth, whereby we are born of earthly parents, for "that which is born of the flesh is flesh" [John 3:6], and also because

<!-- p. 496 -->

sin is naturally dear to us, as those relations that we are akin to by birth, that we are born of or amongst, and are nourished and brought up by and with.

By her "father's house" may be intended also this world, which is our native country. We are naturally, and by our first birth, of the earth, earthly. We must forsake this country in our hearts for Christ. See Ephesians 5:30–32.This reference is a later addition.

Psalms 45:13. "The king's daughter is all glorious within: her clothing is of wrought gold."] So it was with the tabernacle that Moses erected. Its inward clothing or curtains were of fine linen, embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet, coupled together with taches of gold; but its outward coverings were plain, of rams' skins and badgers' skins [Exodus 25:4–5]. The church is "black, but comely," outwardly of a mean appearance, "as the tents of Kedar," and inwardly beautiful and glorious, "as the curtains of Solomon" [Canticles 1:5].

Psalms 46:9. "He maketh wars to cease unto the ends of the earth. He breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder. He burneth the chariot in the fire."] We have a more particular prophecy of this, and of what is spoken of in that parallel text, Psalms 76:3–6, in Ezekiel 39:8–10.

Psalms 47:4. "The excellency of Jacob."] It seems as though the tabernacle and temple used sometimes to be so called (See Amos 6:8.), but more eminently that divine person who dwelt in the tabernacle and temple. See "Controversies Book."JE identifies the "excellency of Jacob" with the person "elsewhere called the excellency and beauty and glory of the Lord, and the glory of Israel." Then he adds, "But that which was eminently the glory and excellency of Israel, was that divine person who dwelt in the temple over the ark" ("'Controversies' Notebook: Justification," *Works, 21*, 386).

Psalms 47:9.] The angels, those principalities and powers, were "gathered together" to attend on Christ at his ascension and entrance into heaven. They were as it were his royal guard who as it were bore "the shields of the earth." As at a king's coronation in Israel, "the princes of the people," and their chief captains, and men of war used to be gathered together to attend upon the king to his palace and to the temple, probably bearing before him the public shields (1 Kings 14:27–28).

<!-- p. 497 -->

Psalms 48:7.] See no. 16.*Works, 15*, 52.

Psalms 49:3–4.] See no. 17.Ibid., 52–53.

Psalms 49:4.] This psalm may be called a parable, and what it contains a "dark saying," because the main subject of it is a future state of rewards and punishments after death. This doctrine under the old testament was enveloped in parables and dark sayings. But Jesus Christ has "brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" [2 Timothy 1:10]; and the New Testament speaks of these great things not in dark speeches, but it uses great plainness of speech. SSS.This reference, which JE repeated on the margin of the Bible, is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 859.

Psalms 49:5.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 859–60.

Psalms 49:8.] SSS.Ibid., col. 862.

Psalms 49:14. "Dominion over them in the morning."] See no. 366.*Works, 15*, 356–57.

"Death shall feed upon them." See note on Job 24:20, and Job 21:32–33, and Isaiah 14:9.

"In the morning." SSS.Each of these paragraphs is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 866–67.

Psalms 49:15. "But God shall redeem my soul from the power of the grave, for he shall *receive me*."] The wordלָקַח "receive" here is the same with that translated "took" (Genesis 5:24). "And Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him," which confirms two things, viz. 1. That the souls of the saints do not die when their bodies die, but are received to a state of happiness in more perfect union and communion with God. 2. That the souls of saints at death are received to heaven, the abode to which Enoch, and Elijah,The following three words are a later addition. and Jesus Christ are gone.

<!-- p. 498 -->

Psalms 49:18. "And men will praise thee."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 869.

Psalms 49:19. "Never see light."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 869–70.

Psalms 50.] This psalm is a prophetical description of the nature of that new dispensation that is in the New Testament so often called the "kingdom of heaven," including the whole of it from Christ's coming in the pouring of his Spirit after his ascension till the consummation of all things after his coming to the last judgment. This dispensation is a dispensation wherein the word of God is not confined to one nation only, but the law goes forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. From thence the light of the gospel shines forth to the Gentile nations into all the earth, "from the rising of the sun to the going down" of the same, which is prophesied of, Psalms 50:1–2.

Under this dispensation the Son of God comes to set up his kingdom on the world, and to reign and judge amongst all nations, which is prophesied of, Psalms 50:3–6. From the Psalms 50:7–16 there is a description of this gospel dispensation with respect to God's church and people, showing that the worship of God's church shall not consist in legal ceremonies and external forms, but in a spiritual service, as Christ says, John 4:21, John 4:23. "But the hour is coming, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.… But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth; for the Father seeketh such to worship him."

And nextly, the nature of this dispensation is described as it respects wicked men, when the church of God would be so constituted that visibly wicked persons should more effectually be shut out from that people that are called the Israel of God, that come and join in his visible worship (Psalms 50:16–20), and when God should bring more terrible wrath against wicked men (Psalms 50:21–22), and lastly, in the Psalms 50:23, what those things are that God looks at in order to acceptance. See SSS.This reference, which JE duplicated on the margin, is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 871–79.

Psalms 50:1. "Mighty God."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 872.

Psalms 50:2. "Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, hath God shined."] This is mentioned as a great distinction between the glorious new dispensation

<!-- p. 499 -->

or revelation given in the days of the gospel of Jesus Christ, from that delivered from Mt. Sinai when God gave the Law in the wilderness. It is said, Deuteronomy 33:2, "He came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir, and shined forth from Mt. Paran, and came with ten thousands of his saints; and then from his right hand went a fiery law." But in the days of the gospel we are not come to Mt. Sinai, but we "are come to Mt. Zion, the city of the living God, to the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:18–22). Compare Galatians 4:26–27 with the context. See Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:1, Psalms 80:1.

Psalms 50:3.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 872–73.

Psalms 50:5. "By sacrifice."] SSS.Ibid., col. 874.

Psalms 50:16–22.] The Spirit of God, in what is said in these verses, seems to have a special regard to the scribes and Pharisees in Christ's time, and to the popish priests afterwards.

Psalms 50:21.] I won't let thy sins pass as little things not worthy to be taken notice of, as thou thyself didst, and was ready to think that I did, because "I kept silence." But I will by no means clear the guilty, or acquit the wicked. I am an "holy God" and "a jealous God"; I "will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins" (Joshua 24:19).

Psalms 51:4. "That thou mayest be justified when thou speakest," etc.] "Justified" in that "sentence passed upon him: 'The sword shall never depart from thine house,' etc. (2 Samuel 12:10–11)." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 248.

Psalms 51:7. "Purge me with hyssop."] "The expression alludes to the ceremony of cleansing the leper, or those that were unclean by a dead body, by sprinkling water, and blood, or both, upon them with a bunch of hyssop, by which they were at length discharged from the restraints they were laid under by their pollution. 'Purge me with hyssop,' i.e. with the blood of Christ applied to my soul." Henry.Ibid., 249.

Psalms 51:12. "Uphold me by thy free spirit."] The same that in the New Testament is called the "Spirit of adoption," and set in opposition to a "spirit of bondage" [Romans 8:15], which David's sin had brought him under.

<!-- p. 500 -->

"By thy free spirit." The word rendered "free"JE deleted "in the original." נְדִיבָה signifies "voluntary, ingenuous, generous." The Spirit of God is a spirit of love and not of fear, and therefore disposes to an ingenuous, free obedience. Therefore the Apostle says, "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" [2 Corinthians 3:17].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Psalms 51:16.] The law of Moses made no provision of any sacrifices for such sins as David committed, nor accepted any sacrifice of beasts for them.

Psalms 51:18.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 888–89.

Psalms 51:18–19. "Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion. Build thou the walls of Jerusalem," etc.] Here the Spirit of GodMS: "David ‹the Sp. of G›." has respect to the accomplishing the work of redemption by Jesus Christ, which shall be accomplished for such vile rebels as David, not for any sacrifice, but of sovereign mercy and of God's good pleasure. When that time should come, then should a sacrifice be offered to God, which was the antitype of the sacrifice of bullocks, which indeed should be pleasing to God, and sufficient to atone for such sins as David's. And therefore it follows, Psalms 51:19, "Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices," etc. Note there was a typical accomplishment of this, which David prays for, when the temple was built in Jerusalem with its courts, and dedicated with such a vast number of whole burnt offerings, and God manifested his acceptance of the sacrifice by fire coming down from heaven in so wonderful a manner in the sight of all the people—and at the same time the city of Jerusalem [was] so fortified and beautified with many magnificent buildings by Solomon—which abundance of sacrifices at the building of the temple was a type of the greatness, preciousness, sufficiency, and infinite fullness of the sacrifice that was offered, when Christ was incarnate, and the temple of his body built (1 Kings 8:5, 2 Chronicles 7:4–5), and which the spiritual Solomon offered to God, whenMS: "which." the church, the spiritual temple of God that he built, was sanctified and dedicated to God. But this has its ultimate and proper accomplishment in the redemption of Christ, which so often [was] prophesied of under such figures as "building up Zion" [Micah 3:10], "building the old wastes" [Isaiah 61:4], etc.

<!-- p. 501 -->

Psalms 52:8. "Olive tree in the house of God."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 893.

Psalms 58:1. "O congregation."] See Numbers 35:12 and Joshua 20:6.

Psalms 58:5.] I.e. that "will not be charmed," but will bite, notwithstanding any enchantment that can be used. See Jeremiah 8:17 and Ecclesiastes 10:11. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 916–17.

Psalms 58:9.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 918.

Psalms 59.] Concerning David's PRAYING AGAINST HIS ENEMIES. 'Tis evident by this psalm and several others that when DavidJE deleted "prays against his enemies." seems to pray against his enemies, the enemies that he speaks [of] are not his personal enemies. That however he takes occasion to pray, as he does from the malice of his personal enemies, yet that the enemies he has respect to in his prayer are principally not those personal enemies that give the occasion of his prayer, but they are the enemies of the church of Christ. He speaks as the head of the church and in the person of Christ, of whom he was the great type. Thus in this psalm the occasion of this prayer was Saul's sending to watch the house to kill him, as the title declares; but 'tis evident that the enemies that he prays against are not Saul and others in Israel that were his personal enemies, but the heathen, as Psalms 59:5 and Psalms 59:8. See "Miscellanies," nos. 600, 640.*Works, 18*, 141–42; 173–75.
