Psalms 132:10 especially renders it probable that it was written on this occasion, and not on occasion of David's bringing the ark into Zion.

Psalms 132:6. "We found it in the field of the wood."] "I.e. *kirjath-jearim*,עָרִים קִרְיַת This was the city of Baal (Joshua 15:60). Henry was not citing this transliteration from Psalms 132:6. which signifies a 'city of woods.'" Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 429.

Psalms 132:15–16. "I will satisfy her poor with bread. I will also clothe her priests with salvation."] This, with the context, is a prophecy of the gospel state of the church, when God shall have accomplished that promise to David, spoken of, Psalms 132:11–12, Psalms 132:17–18. And these two things here mentioned have a remarkable accomplishment in the institution of those two kinds of officers in the church, deacons to satisfy her poor with bread, and bishops to be the instruments of the salvation of men's souls; and in that remarkable success of these two kinds of officers that there was in the apostles' times, when there [was] such an abounding spirit of charity to the poor, as in the church where they had all things common, and also in other churches, and such glorious success of the office of elders in the salvation of multitudes. So were the priests clothed with salvation, and

<!-- p. 536 -->

both these things will yet have a more glorious fulfillment in the future glorious times of the church. See sermon on Romans 12:4 ff.JE's sermon on Romans 12:4–8, preached Aug. 19, 1739, with the doctrine, "The offices that Christ has appointed in his church do respect either the souls or bodies of men" (MS, p. 6). This sermon was "On occasion of the ordination of the deacons." Published in *The Salvation of Souls: Nine Previously Unpublished Sermons on the Call of Ministry and the Gospel by Jonathan Edwards*, ed. Richard A. Bailey and Gregory A. Wills (Wheaton, III., Crossway Books, 2002), 93–110.

Psalms 132:17. "To bud."] See note on Zechariah 6:12.

Psalms 133:2.] The Spirit was poured forth upon Christ, the head of the church, in abundant measure, in great fullness. He was anointed with the Holy Ghost. From this head this ointment goes down to the church, which is Christ's body. We receive of his fullness, and "grace for grace" [John 1:16].

Psalms 133:3. "As the dew," etc.] By "the dew that descends on the mountains of Zion," 'tis plain must be meant a spiritual dew and not a natural, for Zion was a dry place, as the wordצִיּוֹן signifies. Neither on that which was first called Zion, nor the mountain of the temple, nor any hill in Jerusalem, were pastures or fields; nor was their excellency any fruitfulness in the produce of the earth by rains or dews. By "the dews that descend on the mountains of Zion" therefore is doubtless meant spiritual and divine influences, communications of the Holy Spirit from above. In the originalצִיּוֹן עַל־הַרְרֵי שֶׁיּרֵד כְּטֵל־חֶרְמוֹן the words are, "As the dew of Hermon, which descended on the mountains of Zion," which probably is as much as to say, "plentiful, abundant, and most fruitful dews descending on the mountains of Zion," causing them "of the city to flourish as the grass of the earth," as the expression is (Psalms 72:16), and making converts to be as spires of grass with drops of dew (Psalms 110:3). Hermon was an high mountain, and in such places the dews are in great plenty, and perhaps in some parts of it, full of it, very fertile as to this. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. II, cols. 1354–56.

Psalms 135:6. "Whatsoever the Lord pleased, that he did in heaven, and in earth, in the seas, and in all deep places."] I.e. when he brought the children of Israel out of Egypt into Canaan, in the wonders which he wrought then, he did what he would in heaven and earth. He did what he would in the sea and deeps, by dividing the Red Sea and Jordan, and turning

<!-- p. 537 -->

the waters of Egypt into blood; in heaven, in stopping the sun and moon. These things he did without control from the gods of Egypt, or Canaan, or any other gods, which shows him to be above all gods, as is said in the preceding verse, and that his dominion is not limited to a particular people or country, and that he is not God only of a particular part of the world, but that he is supreme and absolute Lord of the whole universe.

Psalms 136.] This psalm confirms me that an ultimate end of the creation of the world and of all God's works is his goodness, or the communication of his good, to hisJE deleted "people." creatures. For this psalm sufficiently teaches that all God's works, from the beginning of the world to the end of it, are works of mercy to his people, yea, even the works of his vindictive justice and wrath, as appears by the Psalms 136:10, Psalms 136:15, Psalms 136:17–22. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, §6.*Works, 18*, 292–94.

Psalms 137:8–9. "Happy shall be he," etc.] Fulfilled in Cyrus's great prosperity.

Psalms 137:9.] The dashing the "little ones" of Babylon "against the stones" probably was fulfilled in some degree when Cyrus took the city, but it had its greatest fulfillment afterwards, when that prophecy was fulfilled (Isaiah 47:9). See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 265.Prideaux describes the steps taken by the defenders of Babylon during the siege by Darius, including the killing of their own women and children (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 265). It was God's pleasure to show the event to be agreeable to his will by giving those that did it external prosperity. But the prophecy seems to look beyond the destruction of the literal Babylon to that of the spiritual Babylon. They indeed will do God's work, and will perform a good work, who shall be God's instruments of theThis word is partially blocked by a hole created by the binding process. utter overthrow of the Church of Rome with all her superstitions,JE deleted "idolatries." and heathenish ceremonies, and other cursed fruits of her spiritual whoredoms, as it were without having any mercy upon them.

See Jeremiah 48:10.This reference is a separate entry.

Psalms 138:1. "Before the gods will sing praise unto thee."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. II, col. 1366.

<!-- p. 538 -->

Psalms 138:2. "Thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name."] In the Psalms 49:10, it is said, "According to thy name, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth," i.e. according to the great fame the nations abroad in the world have heard of thee, so are their praises of thee, when they come to be acquainted with thee. They find thee as they have heard, and therefore now themselves report of thee in their praises according to the report, name, and fame they heard of thee before. And here when it is said, "Thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name," the meaning is, Thou hast done far greater things in thy faithfulness and truth towards thy people, and in fulfillment of thy promise and word to them, than all that we have heard thou didst of old. Thy word and promise to us of what thou wouldst do has been beyond all thy name, or all the fame that we heard of thy great acts of old. And thou hast fulfilled those great promises to us, and so hast set thy word, and truth, and loving kindness to us beyond all that has been reported of thy deeds of old.

Psalms 139:9. "If I take the wings of the morning."] I.e. if I could fly as swiftly as the morning, which so suddenly flies from one end of the earth or one uttermost bound of the sea to the other, beginning first in the extreme parts of the east and suddenly flying to utmost parts of the west.

Psalms 139:13. "Thou hast covered me."] Covered me with flesh and skin, or secundine, or with the womb and body of my mother. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 1374–75.

Psalms 139:24. "And lead me in the way everlasting."] 'Tis said, Psalms 1:6, "The way of the ungodly shall perish," i.e. their way is said to perish metonymically, intending that they that walk in it shall perish. And so the way of holiness and uprightness is here called "the way everlasting," meaning that those that walk in it shall never perish. Their life, and peace, and happiness in this way shall be everlasting. By a like figure of speech it is said, Proverbs 2:8, "He keepeth the paths of judgment, and preserveth the way of his saints." And Jeremiah 12:1, "Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? Wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?" Isaiah 1:12, "O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths." In the Hebrew,בִּלֵּעוּ אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ וְדֶרךְ it is "swallow up the way," etc.

Psalms 141:2. "As the evening sacrifice."] This is mentioned probably in opposition to the setting [of] incense before God, the time of which was more

<!-- p. 539 -->

especially in the morning. Incense was set on the showbread every sabbath in the morning (Leviticus 24:7–8). And it must be in the time of the morning sacrifice that the high priest entered into the holiest of all on the day of atonement, for there could be time after the evening sacrifice for all the service that was to follow. See Exodus 16.

Psalms 141:5. "An excellent oil that shall not break my head."] Anointing the head of a friend with oil was used of old as a peculiar testimony of respect and kindness, as is evident by Luke 7:46, Matthew 26:7, and parallel places in the other evangelists. The Psalmist was ready to take the reproof of the righteous thus, and not as a contempt or disgrace. Oil was used to heal wounds. The Psalmist would take reproof as a balsam to heal his wound, viz. the sin reproved, and not as what gave a wound.

Psalms 141:6. "Stony places."] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1391–92.

Psalms 142:5. "In the land of the living."] See note on Ezekiel 26:20.

Psalms 143:2. "Enter not into judgment with thy servant," etc.] "With thy servant," not with thine enemy. By this it is evident that the true saints are not perfectly free from sin. This verse is cited by the [Apostle], Romans 3:20, as true, not only in Old Testament times, but in all ages and all over the world.

Psalms 144:3–4.] See "Old Testament Intimations of a Future State," p. 27.See footnote on Job 4:21 entry.

Psalms 144:5. "Bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down."] This was never so remarkably fulfilled as in the incarnation of Jesus Christ, when heaven and earth were as it were brought together. Heaven itself was as it were made to bow that it might be united to the earth. God did as it were come down and bring heaven with him. He not only came down to the earth, but he brought heaven down with him to men and for men. It was a more strange and wonderful thing. But this will be more remarkably fulfilled still by Christ's second coming, when he will indeed bring all heaven down with him, viz. all the inhabitants of heaven. Heaven shall be left empty of its inhabitants to come down to the earth. And then the mountains shall smoke, and shall indeed "flow down at his presence," as in Isaiah 64:1

<!-- p. 540 -->

Isaiah 64:1. "O that thou wouldst rent the heavens and come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence."

Psalms 144:8. "Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood."] When they speak fair, and promise friendship, their mouth is false; and if they give their right hand (as they were wont to give their right hand, to confirm covenants and promises, as appears by several texts), their right hand was as false as their mouth.

Psalms 144:12. "And our daughters as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace."] I.e. that they may be excellent mothers of desirable and prosperous families. Such a mother is in a family as a corner stone in a building. And an amiable wife and mother in a family is like a corner stone, polished as the corner stones of palaces used to be; and when her family is excellent like herself, she is the corner stone of a palace. And daughters in a family, even while they are only daughters, yet if they are virtuous and wise, may be such great blessings and of so great importance in the family that they may be as corner stones in the house.

"That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth." That is, that they may be plants so flourishing in virtue and religion that in spiritual respects they may be given up, or come to a full grown state, while they are yet children. As 'tis said in Isaiah, "the child shall die an hundred years old" [Isaiah 65:20].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Psalms 144:14. "That there be no breaking in, nor going out."] "No distressing wars, no breaking in of invaders, no going out of deserters. 'No complaining in our streets.' No oppression" at home. Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 447.

Psalms 145 and Psalms 146, to the end of the book of Psalms.] The title prefixed to this psalm, "David's Psalm of Praise," seems to belong to this and all the following psalms; and therefore the psalms that follow have no title. The matter of all these psalms seems to confirm that this title belongs to 'em all as one continued song. The frequent repetition of the word that is prefixed to this psalm as the title, viz. תְהִלָּה, or words of the same radix through all these psalms, confirms that the title belongs to 'em all, and, that however this Psalms 145, being an alphabetical psalm, and the alphabet's being finished in the initial letters of the verses

<!-- p. 541 -->

of this psalm, seems to look as if it were a distinct psalm by itself.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. And this indeed is ground of some distinction, but yet this psalm seems only to be an introduction to the following, or rather the argument and summary of the great things that he praises God more largely for in what follows to the end of the book, or the things that excited him thus to praises laid down in alphabetical order for the help of the memory.

Psalms 146:9. "The Lord preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and the widow."] See a citation from Homer agreeable to this, in note on Deuteronomy 10:18.

Psalms 147:4. "He telleth the number of the stars," etc.] There is probably some allusion here to what is done by a captain of an army, who numbers them, and marshals and arranges them in exact order.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. What is chiefly meant by "stars" by the Spirit of God in this place [is] probably God's saints. This agrees with what is said in the foregoing and following verses, and other scriptures. "He gathers the outcasts of Israel" Psalms 147:2], and not one shall be lost. Though they may be sorely oppressed by their enemies, yet "the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth those that are his" [2 Timothy 2:19]. He knoweth them by name, and will make up their number. None can be overlooked, for his understanding is infinite. He will deliver them, and lift them up, and cast down their oppressors to the ground, for he is great and of great power.

Psalms 147:11. "That fear him, in those that hope in his mercy."] See Psalms 33:18, Psalms 40:3, Psalms 119:166; Isaiah 58:10–11.

Psalms 148.] This psalm represents the joy of all creatures in heaven and earth on occasion of the universal establishment of the kingdom of the Messiah through the earth, and the glorious victory of his church over her enemies, as appears by the conclusion of the psalm, which is agreeable to Psalms 96 and Psalms 98, Isaiah 44:23, Isaiah 49:13, and many other places. And seems to have respect chiefly to the time prophesied of in Revelation 19 and the Revelation 19:1–9, which is a time wherein the creation that now groans and travails in pain, being made subject to vanity, will be remarkably delivered. The Psalms 97-98 seem to be only a continuation of praise on the same occasion.

<!-- p. 542 -->

Psalms 148:4.] See no. 56.*Works, 15*, 66.

Psalms 149:5. "Let the saints," etc.] In these Psalms 149:1–6 is a prophecy of what shall be when God shall gloriously appear for his church in the latter days, in the times foretold in the Revelation 18-19. And those that are spoken of in this verse seem to be the souls of departed saints, and the Spirit of God seems to have respect to the same thing here as in Revelation 18:20 and Revelation 19:1–7. By "glory" here is probably meant the state of the saints' blessedness in another world, as in Psalms 73:24. "Thou shalt guide me by thy counsel, and afterwards receive me to glory." And what especially confirms it is the expression in the latter part of the verse, "Let them sing aloud upon their beds." Those that are departed, and their souls in the invisible world, are in the language of the Old Testament represented as being "in beds," which seems to have arisen from a custom of laying dead corpses on beds in their graves. See Ezekiel 32:25. And particularly the happiness of the departed souls of the righteous is represented by that, that "they rest in their beds." Isaiah 57:2, "He shall enter into peace; they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness."

Psalms 149:9. "This honor have all his saints."] See Revelation 2:26–27 and Joshua 10:24.

<!-- p. 543 -->

### Proverbs

Proverbs 1:8. "My son."] See Proverbs 24:21.

Proverbs 2:1–5.] These and such like promises made to seekers, if they are understood of true seekers, that is, those that seek from love and sense of the value of [the] thing sought, and with longing desire after the thing for its own sake (for gracious seekers are the only true seekers, Psalms 24:6), then they are to be understood as absolute promises. But if they are understood of those that seek only from fear and self-love, as natural men may do, then they are to be taken only thus: that this is the way of finding which is fixed and established, and that ordinarily success follows, as sometimes things spoken absolutely are so to be understood, as Proverbs 22:6. "Train up a child in the way he should go; and when he is old, he shall not depart from it." And Proverbs 13:20, "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise." And so those things that are said of the diligent in this book, as that "the diligent hand makes rich" [Proverbs 10:4], and "he that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread" [Proverbs 12:11].

Proverbs 2:18. "Her paths to the dead."] Hebrew, *rephaim*.רְפָאִים See Job 26:5.

Proverbs 3:7. "Be not wise in thine own eyes."] This forbids a man's being disposed to have an high thought of his own piety and holiness, as well as his own reason and judgment, for we know that wisdom is understood most commonly in this book for holiness or true virtue. This is confirmed by the sense in which the Apostle uses the same phrase (Romans 11:25).This sentence is a later addition.

Proverbs 4:23.] See no. 65.*Works, 15*, 68.

Proverbs 5:6. "Her ways are movable, that thou canst not know them."] Or "that you may not know her." She will put on many shapes to deceive you, that

<!-- p. 544 -->

you mayn't find her out, and know what an odious creature she is, and how far from being a true friend to you.

Proverbs 5:14. "I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation."] This is to be joined with the foregoing verse, "And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined mine ear to them that instructed me" Proverbs 5:13]. Men were wont to be taught in congregations and assemblies, then as now.

Proverbs 5:17.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1486–87.

Proverbs 5:18. "And rejoice with the wife of thy youth."] This passage and that in Malachi 2:14, seem to intimate that man should have but one wife at a time, or that only the wife of youth or first wife, is the lawful wife while she lives.

Proverbs 5:23. "Go astray."] SSS.Ibid., col. 1491.

Proverbs 6:18.] There is a sort of men that are, what we call, a designing sort of men. Their character is of that of a selfish and mischievous, sly, underhanded subtilty and intrigue, a deceitful craftiness that is opposite to true wisdom, and contrary to godly simplicity and sincerity. This seems to be the character here intended.

Proverbs 6:27–29.] "The bold presumptuous sinner saith, I may venture upon the sin, and yet escape punishment. I shall have peace, though I go on. He had as good say, I will take fire into my bosom, and not burn my clothes; or I will go upon hot coals, and not burn my feet. 'He that goes in to his neighbor's wife' Proverbs 6:26], however he holds himself, God will not hold him guiltless. The fire of lust kindles the fire of hell." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 477.

Proverbs 6:30–31.] See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1503–4.

Proverbs 7:22. "Correction of the stocks."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1512–13.

<!-- p. 545 -->

Proverbs 8.] What is meant by wisdom in this chapter, see SSS on Proverbs 8:1.Ibid., cols. 1515–16.

Proverbs 8:1–3. "Doth not wisdom cry, and understanding put forth her voice? She standeth in the top of the high place," etc.] Christ instructed and counseled the children of Israel from Mt. Sinai; from thence he cried, spake with a loud and great voice. The blessings and the curses were pronounced from Mt. Gerizim and Mt. Ebal with a loud voice. The temple was built on a mountain. Thence the trumpet was heard to call the people to God. There the testimony was kept. There were the priests and Levites who instructed the people. Jesus taught the people from a mountain, a great multitude being present (Matthew 5, Matthew 6, and Matthew 7). He often taught in the temple on the top of the mountain in the place and times of great concourse. There in the time of the feast of tabernacles, he stood and cried with a loud voice (John 7:37). Christ taught in the synagogues where the Jews always resorted, and ever took opportunities to preach his word when the greatest multitudes were present.

It was on Mt. Zion, or the mountain of the temple, that the apostles chiefly taught the people at Jerusalem after the Holy Ghost was poured out upon them. And as they went to preach the gospel through the world, they chiefly chose to preach in the greatest cities, such as Jerusalem, Samaria, Damascus, Antioch, Ephesus, Athens, Corinth, Alexandria, and Rome. And 'tis agreeable to the Christian institution that the gospel should be preached in public assemblies. The Apostle represents Christ not now as speaking to us from Mt. Sinai, but as speaking to us from heaven, which is, in the most exalted sense, "to stand in the top of high places" when he speaks to us. "She crieth at the gates." The synagogues and churches where the word of God is preached are as it were the gates of the church and the gates of heaven. "She standeth by the way of the places of the paths," which is agreeable to the representation, Isaiah 30:21. "Thou shalt hear a voice behind thee, saying, This is the way. Walk in it." "At the coming in of the doors." God's ministers are to instruct publicly, and from house to house.

Proverbs 8:9.] See Matthew 11:19; Luke 7:35, Luke 12:57; John 10:4–5; John 7:17; Hosea 14:9; Isaiah 35:8; Psalms 107:43; Proverbs 14:6, and Proverbs 15:33, and Proverbs 28:5. [See] the note on Proverbs 28:5.

Proverbs 8:12. "I wisdom."] Here by "wisdom," as throughout the chapter, we must understand Christ, the eternal word and wisdom of God. "Dwell with prudence"

<!-- p. 546 -->

(or "subtilty," as in the margin),I.e. margin of the KJV. "and find out knowledge of witty inventions." Which was most especially and remarkably fulfilled in finding out and contriving the wonderful work of redemption, which was contrived by the wisdom of God, and was determined, agreed upon, and accomplished wholly in and through that person who is the wisdom of God. Ephesians 1:7–8, "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, wherein he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence."

Proverbs 8:17. "I love them that love me."] See John 10:17.

Proverbs 9:13. "A foolish woman."] This represents folly or wickedness itself in opposition to wisdom, that was spoken of in the preceding part of the chapter. They are represented as two rivals for the affections, attachment, and pursuit of mankind. Both are represented as having their houses, both having provided their entertainment, both being very public in their invitations, both inviting the simple and them that want understanding, etc. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1536.

Proverbs 9:18. "Knoweth not that the dead."] Hebrew, *rephaim*.רְפָאִים See Job 26:5.

Proverbs 10:1. "The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father," etc.] The proverbs of Solomon properly begin with this proverb. To engage the attention of the pupil who is addressed as a son,MS: "Son &." the instructor speaks as a father. And then we may suppose the book of Proverbs was prepared for parents to use in instructing their children.

Proverbs 10:2–3. "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing."] They are wholly lost. Though the possessors take much pains to get 'em and to keep 'em, yet "God casts them away." That which he eats, God casts out of his belly. The unrighteous possessor takes care to make his riches a means of his happiness or benefit, but God takes none. Though he takes care to keep it, God won't keep it for him. Yea, he orders things so that they shall be of no benefit to him, shall not support him, keep him alive. His "soul shall famish" nevertheless. But "righteousness will profit." It will do that which riches cannot do. It will truly feed the soul. It is bread and that which satisfies (See Isaiah 55:2.). It will keep the soul from famishing; it will keep it alive, and so will "deliver it from death."

<!-- p. 547 -->

Entries on Proverbs 10-11, showing foolscap that has been almost completely filled in. Courtesy of Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

<!-- p. 548 -->

Proverbs 10:6. "Blessings are on the head of the just, but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked."] Blessings are represented as being "on the head" of the person blessed, probably with some respect to the custom of laying the hand on a person whom another blessed. They shall have a blessing, because they were disposed to give blessing, to wish well to others, to pray for them, and do them good. 1 Peter 3:9, "Blessing, knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing." On the contrary, the wicked are guilty of injuriousness and violence, the mischief and misery of which shall chiefly come upon them, shall bring them to shame and utter confusion, like a malefactor tried, found guilty, and condemned. Manifestation of guilt, just condemnation, shame, and confusion are, according to the style of Scripture, represented by having the mouth covered or stopped.

Proverbs 10:7.] See note on Ecclesiastes 7:1.

Proverbs 10:8. "The wise in heart will receive commandments, but the fool of lips shall fall."] So in the original.יִלָּבֵט שְׂפָתַיִם וֶאֳוִיל Here is an opposition in the words, between the heart and the lips. It implied in the last part of the verse, that he that is a fool in heart is so in lips. Because "of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaketh" [Luke 6:45]. And by our words we shall be justified, and by our words we shall be condemned [Matthew 12:37]. But in characterizing the wise, the heart only is mentioned, because a wise man affects not to show his wisdom, but is rather disposed to hear instruction, and receive command, than to speak and prescribe to others. And in characterizing the fool, the lips are mentioned, because wickedness of heart especially is ready to vent and manifest itself by the tongue, not having the restraint of humility and modesty, and because God is slow to anger, and not ready to punish wickedness till it brings forth its fruit.

Proverbs 10:9. "He that walketh uprightly walketh surely, but he that perverteth his ways shall be known."] Here is an opposition, both between the two characters and events. "He that walketh uprightly" is safe, but not "he that perverteth his ways," let him play the hypocrite, and hide himself never so artfully. If he is not upright, his hiding his wickedness shall not secure him from punishment, for God "will bring to light the hidden things of darkness" [1 Corinthians 4:5].

<!-- p. 549 -->

Proverbs 10:10. "He that winketh with his eye causeth sorrow, but a fool of lips shall fall."] Here are two degrees of external expression of wickedness mentioned,MS: "mention." and what is affirmed is as much as this: He that acts foolishly and sinfully in the least degree, and expresses the wickedness of his heart only with the wink of the eye, brings sorrow upon himself. But he that proceeds further, and expresses the wickedness of heart by wicked words, shall suffer in a greater degree.

Proverbs 10:11. "The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life."] I.e. a fountain of life to himself. "But violence covereth the mouth of the wicked." I.e. the violence or injuriousness of his words shall cover and stop his injurious mouth, i.e. shall bring him to shame and condemnation. See note on Proverbs 10:6.

Proverbs 10:13.] This verseחֲסַר־לֵב לְגֵו וְשֵׁבֶט חָכְמָה תִּמָּצֵא נבוֹן בְּשִׂפְתֵי might have been translated thus. "In the lips of him that hath understanding, wisdom is found; but in the lips is found a rod for the back of him that is void of understanding," i.e. there is found in his lips a rod for his own back. He shall be chastised with the consequence of his own foolish and sinful talk. See Proverbs 14:3.

Proverbs 10:14. "Wise men lay up knowledge, but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction."] The sense probably is this. Wise men conceal or hide (as the wordיִצְפְּנוּ signifies) knowledge. They are not ostentatious of wisdom and holiness, but hide it and lay it up in their hearts as a treasure for future use and benefit. But the mouth of a fool is in haste to utter the folly and wickedness of his heart. The corrupt fountain has an easy and speedy vent by his mouth, by which he speedily brings on guilt and condemnation on himself. See Proverbs 12:23, and Proverbs 14:33, and Proverbs 15:14. See note on that place.

Proverbs 10:16. "The fruit of the wicked to sin."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Proverbs 10:17. "Erreth."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Proverbs 10:20.] The "heart of the wicked" is mentioned, because the heart is the fountain from whence words issue (as Christ says, "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" [Matthew 12:34]), as much as to say, the words of the just are very precious. But the very heart, the fountain from

<!-- p. 550 -->

whence words proceed, is little worth in the wicked. See Proverbs 15:7 and Psalms 37:30–31.

Proverbs 10:21. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for want of wisdom."] "For want of heart," so the wordבַּחֲסַר־לֵב is. There is an antithesis between "lips" and "heart." The heart of a righteous man is a storehouse, from whence he is not only supplied himself (As it is said, "A good man shall be satisfied of himself" [Proverbs 14:14]), but from thence by his lips he feeds many. But a wicked man is so far from that, that he has nothing within him for his own supply, or to keep himself alive. He dies because his heart is empty.

Proverbs 10:23. "It is a sport to a fool to do *mischief*."] The wordזִמָּה rendered "mischief" signifies properly crafty wickedness, whence appears the opposition in the latter part of the verse. "But a man of understanding hath wisdom."

Proverbs 10:25. "As the whirlwind."] I.e. the prosperity of the wicked will last but a very little while. It is like a blast of wind, like a whirlwind, which though it makes a great blustering and ado while it lasts, is presently gone, and all is still and silent; and it is no more seen or heard of. So it is with the wicked. Whatever flourishing appearance they make, and whatever influence in the world they seem to have, and whatever consequence they seem to be of, yet all is soon passed away; and there is an everlasting end to all their prosperity. The similitude here used seems to be something of the same import with that, Ecclesiastes 7:6, "As the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool."

"But the righteous is an everlasting foundation." This [is] a clear Old Testament text for the future eternal life of the godly. The design of the text is to show some great difference between the godly and ungodly, but it shows no such great difference, if there be no future life for the godly. In the former part of the text, 'tis said, "As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more." And so it is with the godly too, if there be no future state, by the testimony of God in himself, in Job 7:7, "My life is wind," and Psalms 78:39, "For he remembered that they were flesh, a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again." The expression is very parallel with that in this place.This paragraph is a later addition.

<!-- p. 551 -->

Proverbs 10:31.] The wordתִּכָּרֵת translated "cut out" signifies indifferently either "cut out," or "cut off," or "cut down." The import of the verse is this. The just man is like a tree that bringeth forth excellent fruit in that his mouth bringeth wisdom, and shall therefore be dealt with as such a tree. But the froward tongue is like a tree that brings forth pernicious fruit, and therefore shall be dealt with as men commonly deal with such a tree, when they cut it down.

Proverbs 11:10.] See Esther 3:15 and Esther 8:15.

Proverbs 11:12. "Holdeth his peace."] I.e. from evil-speaking, reproaches, remarks on others' defects and blemishes, and all manifestations of contempt and ill will in speech.

Proverbs 11:18. "The wicked worketh a deceitful work."] I.e. a work that will deceive him, or that he is greatly deceived in the consequences of. The work that he does, as he views it, seems to promise fair for happiness. His work looks to him as that which yieldsMS: "yield." him great benefit, but his work deceives him, and he'll find himself miserably deceived in it. From the seed that he sows, he promises himself a crop of pleasant fruit; but it will deceive him, for the fruit that it will yield will be gall and wormwood, and will prove the most deadly poison. That this is the sense is evident by the words that follow in the latter part of the verse.

Proverbs 11:23.] Compare this with Proverbs 10:28, and see SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1559–60.

Proverbs 11:29.] I.e. the son that causeth shame, and troubleth the family he belongs to by his wickedness, shall have no inheritance among his brethren, at least none that will do him any good. What [he] inherits shall be wind. It will prove of no service to him, and he shall as it were come to extreme poverty. And the foolish son shall become a servant to his wise brother or brethren. They shall be the heirs, and shall be rich, while [he], being poor, shall be dependent and subject. This sense is much confirmed by Proverbs 17:2.

Proverbs 11:30. "And he that winneth souls is wise."] Or as itחָכָם נְפָשׁוֹת וְלקֵחַ might be rendered, "It is the wise that gaineth souls" (or lives), i.e. that rescues 'em, and so

<!-- p. 552 -->

saves 'em from death. And thus the latter part of the verse is agreeable to the former.

Proverbs 11:31.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1563–64.

Proverbs 12:9.] "It is the folly of some, that they covet to make a great figure abroad, take place, and take state as persons of quality, and yet want necessaries at home, and if their debts were paid would not be worth a morsel of bread. Nay, perhaps pinch their bellies to put it on their backs." There are others "who content themselves in a lower sphere, where they are despised for the plainness of their dress, and meanness of their post, that they may be able to afford themselves not only necessaries, but conveniences in their own houses. They that contrive to live comfortably and plentifully at home are to be preferred to those that affect to appear splendid abroad, though they have not wherewith to maintain it, whose hearts are unhumbled when their condition is low." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 496.

Proverbs 12:10. "The tender mercies of the wicked are cruel."] That which they would have pass for compassion, and their pretended kindnesses, are only a cover for intended cruelties, or a cloak for cruelties they have been guilty of, or are then in the prosecution of, as is often the case with persecutors. How many are there who pretend to lament others' calamities, whose tears are like those of the crocodile.

Proverbs 12:12.] "The root of the righteous yieldeth fruit" that is food to himself and others. He is fed and satisfied from himself without "the net," the artful and wicked devices and practices of evil men. The wicked desires only a net wherewith to fish for himself. The righteous desires to yield fruit for the benefit of others and God's glory. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1568–69.

SSS.This reference, which duplicates that at the end of the previous paragraph, is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1568–69.

Proverbs 12:17.] I.e. "he that speaks truth" shows honesty and uprightness in the manner of his narration. What he says carries evidences of simplicity and uprightness. But in what is said by a false witness, there are marks of deceit very commonly, which may be seen by a discerning, observing person.

<!-- p. 553 -->

This Solomon, who was judge in Israel, being a man of great discerning, had often occasion to take notice of.

Proverbs 12:19. "The lip of truth shall be established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment."] This seems to include these things, viz. that what he says will stand, and will gain more and more credit, when a liar will be found out. And that he that seeks to carry his designs by lying and deceit, though indeed he may seem to have wonderful success for the present, yet this will not hold long. Whereas he that seeks to promote his interest by truth and uprightness, builds on a sure and stable foundation. A liar, a deceitful flatterer, may have great reputation and influence for a little while; but it will vanish away. But the honor and interest of the true upright man will continue, and grow stronger and stronger.

Proverbs 12:20. "Deceit is in the heart," etc.] I.e. their hearts are deceived. They seek to hurt others, but really they cheat themselves; they never will advance their own interest by it. But the counselors of peace, they that seek the good of their neighbors, they take the true course to advance their own prosperity and comfort. This agrees with the Proverbs 12:19 and Proverbs 12:21.

Proverbs 12:23. "Proclaimeth foolishness."] I.e. by ostentation of knowledge.

Proverbs 12:24. "The hand of the diligent shall bear rule, but the slothful shall be under tribute."] The wordרְמִיָּה rendered "slothful" properly signifies deceitful, but yet it seems here to imply both slothfulness and knavery in its import, these commonly going together, for the same word is used, Proverbs 12:27. See Buxtorf.Johannis Buxtorf, *Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum* (6th ed. London, 1646), 703. The meaning seems to be this: That an honest diligence tends to advancement, but that instead of following their business, and seeking a support by an honest industry, [they that] are seeking a subsistence, and pursuing wealth and advance by idle, knavish, and deceitful tricks, shall be brought under and be in subjection to the wise. This sense well agrees with Proverbs 12:19–22. See Matthew 25:21, Matthew 25:23, Matthew 25:26–30; Proverbs 17:2, Proverbs 11:29; Psalms 49:14.

Proverbs 152:25. "Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop, but a good word maketh it glad."] Especially "a good word" from God, the encouraging

<!-- p. 554 -->

words of the Holy Scripture, when God gives an ear to hear, and an heart to understand. The gospel is by way of eminence called the "good word" (Hebrews 6:5). The wordεὐαγγέλιον. "gospel" signifies good news, glad tidings. 'Tis the word of life. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1574.

Proverbs 12:26. "The righteous is more excellent than his neighbor, but the way of the wicked seduceth them."] The wordיָתֵר rendered "excellent" seems more properly to signify "abundant." He abounds more with blessings. But the wicked who seeks abundance is seduced and deceived by the wicked course he takes to obtain it. This sense agrees with Proverbs 12:19–22, Proverbs 12:24.

Proverbs 13:3. "He that keepeth," etc.] As 'tis in "a city besieged; to open the gates betrayeth the safety of it; all watch and ward is about the gate. So the tongue is the gate or door of the soul, by which it goeth out in converse and communication. To keep it open, or loose guarded, letteth in an enemy, which proveth the death of the soul." Manton on *James*, p. 356.*A Practical Commentary on James*.

Proverbs 13:8.] As much as to say, 'Tis true that rich men, when envied for their riches, and brought into danger of their lives by 'em, may ransom their lives by parting with their wealth, but the poor, who have nothing to be envied for, escape and are never called in question. Under many tyrants it has been crime enough to be rich; and that there may be some color for the taking away their lives, they are accused, found fault with, reproached, and censured. But the poor are let alone; they hear none of these things. When the rich Jews were carried captive, the poor of the land were left (2 Kings 25:12). See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1579.

Proverbs 13:10.] SSS.Ibid., col. 1580.

Proverbs 13:12. "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; but when desire cometh, it is a tree of life."] This is true concerning such hopes, expectations, and desires as are spoken of, Proverbs 10:24, Proverbs 10:28, and Proverbs 11:7, Proverbs 11:23, and Proverbs 14:32, and Proverbs 24:14, and Proverbs 21:25, viz. the hope of the wicked, and the desire of the righteous. With respect to the former, wicked men are deceived, and put off from time to time to a further time, are flattered with hopes of happiness

<!-- p. 555 -->

to come at one time and another, which never comes. So his hopes make his heart sick, and his desires kill him, agreeable to Proverbs 21:25. But the desire of the righteous shall be granted, and when it is so, "it is a tree of life," yielding not only most pleasant, refreshing, satisfying fruit, but that life and happiness which is stable, durable, and everlasting. And if we compare one part of this book with another, there is reason to think that they are these hopes and desires that the Spirit of God has respect to in this place.

Proverbs 13:17. "A wicked messenger falleth into mischief, but a faithful ambassador is health."] By "messenger" and "ambassador" here doubtless is meant any officer, servant or person entrusted with any business, or appointed to the management of any affair.

Proverbs 13:19.] The sense of this verse seems to be very much hid in the translation. The meaning seems to be this. The gratification of men's desires or lusts is sweet to 'em, and therefore 'tis an abomination to 'em "to depart from evil." They can't bear to forsake their sin. Job 20:12–13, "Wickedness is sweet in his mouth; he hides it under his tongue. He spares it, and forsakes it not, but keeps it still within his mouth." See SSS.Ibid., cols. 1583–85.

Proverbs 13:23. "Much food is in the tillage of the poor, but there is that is destroyed for want of judgment."] The word "poor" here probably includes righteous and humble in its signification, as it very often does in the Old Testament. "Much food is in the tillage of" him who humbly, and honestly, in a humble trust in God, diligently follows the business of his calling through the blessing of heaven upon them. But on the contrary, very often great men, whose business it is to rule and judge the cause of the poor, are destroyed through the curse of God upon them for their injustice and oppression. This sense is agreeable to many other of Solomon's proverbs, and several in this chapter, particularly Proverbs 13:9, Proverbs 13:11, Proverbs 13:22, Proverbs 13:25. This sense is confirmed by Proverbs 15:6, and Proverbs 15:27. See SSS.Ibid., cols. 1586–87.

Proverbs 14:2. "He that walketh in his uprightness feareth the Lord, but he that is perverse in his ways despiseth him."] As much as to say, He that lives a holy life, that is the man that fears God. "But he that is perverse in his ways," let him pretend and profess what he will, despises him. Like that of Jesus Christ, "He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me" [John 14:21].

<!-- p. 556 -->

Proverbs 14:4.] It appears to me probable that by the ox in this verse the Spirit of God has respect to something beyond that four-footed beast, as in that law, "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn" [Deuteronomy 25:4]. See another sense in SSS.This sentence and the following reference are a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1589–90. See Proverbs 14:23.

Proverbs 14:5.] "A faithful witness will not lie, but a false witness will utter lies."] This is a warning not to trust those that have once been found to be persons that don't make conscience of speaking the truth. If we see not what temptation they have to lie in a particular case, or if they seem never so serious, and are never so peremptory, and use affirmations, yea, and oaths, yet 'tis not wise to depend upon them.

Proverbs 14:6.] This has been remarkably verified in many of the great men of this age who, having great strength of reason but were highly conceited of their abilities, and trusted in 'em, despising others as weak and silly, who have been men of great labor and diligence in their searches after truth in divine matters, and have not found it, but have been woefully bewildered, and confounded, and left of God to run into gross errors. See Proverbs 14:8.This reference is a later addition.

Proverbs 14:8. "Is deceit."] I.e. to himself. The corruption of his heart blinds and deceives him with respect to his own conduct concerning his duty, and the way he takes the nature and issue of it; whereas a holy principle of heart will enlighten his mind with respect to the way of his duty and happiness.

Proverbs 14:9. "A mock at sin."] I.e. they deride others' faults. "But among the righteous there is favor," or benevolence, as the wordרָצוֹן signifies. That is, they will think and speak charitably of others, and be ready to pity, excuse, forgive, and pray for others with respect to the things they do that are amiss. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1592. This reference is a later addition.

Proverbs 14:21–22.] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Proverbs 14:24.] It might more intelligibly have been rendered, "Riches is a crown to the wise," i.e. it is an honor and real benefit to them that are wise, and

<!-- p. 557 -->

use it wisely. "But the foolishness of fools is folly." That is, you can make no better of it. Put fools in what condition you will, let 'em be never so rich, clothe ['em] with robes, set 'em on thrones, still they are no better than fools; and their wealth and high station does but the more expose 'em, and makes the worse fools instead of making them better. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1599.

Proverbs 14:29. "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding."] And his conduct is a great honor to him, gets him the reputation of a very wise man. "But he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly." He thinks hereby to magnify himself, and make those about stand in awe of him, whereas he does but magnify his own folly, and lifts that up to view, and makes it appear great to them that behold him.

Proverbs 14:31. "Reproacheth his maker."] See Proverbs 14:31.JE's reference is circular.

Proverbs 14:33. "Wisdom resteth," etc.] The wordתָּנוּחַ don't signify "remainest," but it signifies having "rest," "quietness," and contentment, i.e. it is not impatient to show itself. It hath rest in being in the heart. It is not uneasy in being confined there, [not] being forward to show itself abroad, and manifest itself by the mouth. The following words, "but that which is in the midst of fools is made known," confirm this sense. They are forward to show their wisdom, and thereby bewray their folly. See Proverbs 15:2.This reference is a later addition.

Proverbs 14:35.] For the true design of this saying, see Matthew 24:45–51.

"Causeth shame." I.e. brings reproach on the king's name and family.This paragraph is a later addition.

Proverbs 15:2.] "Poureth out foolishness."] I.e. in endeavoring upon all occasions to show his wisdom and goodness, to pour it and show it to the utmost, whether the occasion be proper or not, he really "pours out foolishness." See note on Proverbs 14:33.

Proverbs 15:4. "A wholesome tongue" (Hebrew,לֶשׁוֹן מַרְפֵּא "the healing of the tongue") "is a tree of life, but perverseness therein is a breach" (Hebrew,שֶׁבֶר "ruin or

<!-- p. 558 -->

breaking in pieces") "in the spirit."] That speech that is with wisdom and grace is a tree of life. The good that it is a means of, to the persons spoken to, and also the person speaking, is eternal life. But, on the contrary, utter ruin to the soul is the consequence of evil and corrupt communications. See SSS.שֶׁבֶר

Proverbs 15:7. "But the heart of the foolish doth not so."] This implies the contrary concerning the foolish of that which is asserted of the wise, in the former part of the verse, viz. that the lips of the foolish do not "disperse knowledge," together with the reason of it, namely, that they have it not in their hearts. The "heart of the foolish" has no such store or treasure for his lips to disperse. "A good man" (as Christ says) "out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good, and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" [Matthew 12:35, Matthew 12:34]. And an evil tree cannot "bring forth good fruit" [Matthew 7:18].

Proverbs 15:11. "Hell and destruction are before the Lord. How much more then the hearts of the children of men?"] "The wordאֲבַדּוֹן here used for 'destruction' is Abaddon, which is one of the devil's names (Revelation 9:11). That destroyer, though he deceive us, cannot evade or elude the divine cognizance. He sees through all his disguises, though he is sly and subtile. Job 26:6, 'Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering.'" ("Abaddon hath no covering," so the word is, i.e. Satan, the chief of those *rephaim*, spoken of in the preceding verse.) Therefore the argument of the Wise Man is good. "If he sees through the depths and wiles of Satan himself, much more can he search men's hearts, though they are deceitful" and desperately wicked, for men have learnt all their deceitful arts of Satan. (See Jeremiah 17:9–10.) Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 507.

Proverbs 15:13.] This verse is a caution against melancholy, as that which destroys health, debilitates and breaks the mind, and disables it from the use of its natural powers. "A merry heart makes a cheerful countenance." The literal translationיַיטִבפֶּנִים is, "makes the countenance good," which might be rendered "causes a healthy countenance," so that the meaning probably is that a cheerful mind is for a man's health, for "to have a healthy

<!-- p. 559 -->

countenance" is a Hebrew phrase for enjoying health. See Psalms 42:11 and Psalms 43:5.

This sense is abundantly confirmed by Proverbs 17:22. "A merry heart doth good like a medicine," i.e. promotes health. And it may be noted that the wordיַיטִב "do good" there is the same which is here used and translated "makes cheerful." See SSS.This paragraph is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1607–8.

Proverbs 15:14. "The heart of him that hath understanding seeketh knowledge."] And so such an one is more ready to hear than to speak. "But the mouth of fools feedeth on foolishness." I.e. he [is] eager upon foolish and sinful talk, and 'tis what he delights in. 'Tis to him as food that a man loves and is greedy of. In the Hebrew phrase,רָעָה a man is said to "feed upon" or "devour" words when he is forward to speak. So Proverbs 19:28, "An ungodly witness scorneth judgment, and the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity." So Proverbs 20:25, "It is a snare to a man to devour that which is holy, and after vows to make inquiry."

Proverbs 15:21. "Folly is joy to him that is destitute of wisdom, but a man of understanding walketh uprightly."] The literal translationיַיַשּׁר־לָכֶת תְּבוּנָה וְאִישׁ לַחֲסַר־לַב שִׂמְחה אִוֶּלֶת is, "Folly is joy to him that is without a heart, but a man of understanding will direct himself in walking." The meaning seems to be this. The wicked man, who has no principle of true virtue in his heart, commits sin with eagerness, and delight, and relish of heart; and therefore he goes on in ways of sin allowedly without hesitation. But a gracious man has a principle in his heart that directs and governs him, that abhors sin, and relishes and delights in righteousness, by which principle he is led and directed in the right way, as by a spiritual scent, distinguishing good from bad, and inclining him to that which is right. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1610–11.

Proverbs 15:25. "The Lord will destroy the house of the proud, but he will establish the border of the widow."] As by "the poor" in the Old Testament is oftentimes meant those that are poor in spirit, so here and perhaps in some other places, by "the widow" seems to be intended one that is so in

<!-- p. 560 -->

a spiritual sense, or the soul to whom those things are dead that formerly it was wedded [to], as the soul that is weaned from the world and her own righteousness. True Christians are represented as being dead to the world, and the world to them; and so the Apostle compares the person that is weaned from his own righteousness to a woman that has lost her husband. Such widows as these the Apostle calls "widows indeed." 1 Timothy 5:3, "Honor widows that are widows indeed." And 1 Timothy 5:5, "Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day." It seems manifest that by "widow" in this place in Proverbs is meant a widow in this sense by the antithesis, the widow in the latter part of the verse being set in opposition to the proud in the former part.

Proverbs 15:30. "The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart, and a good report" (or "a good hearing," as itטוֹבָה שְׁמוּעָה might have been rendered) "makes the bones fat."] I.e. when we don't wish and hope for what we desire, or think it probable, but see it with our eyes, or hear it with our ears. See Proverbs 13:12.

Proverbs 15:31. "The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise."] I.e.MS: "i.e. that is." this is the way to dwell amongst 'em, and not to depart from 'em, because wholesome reproofs, or reproofs of life, are the proper means of reclaiming persons when they are departing, or are in danger of departing, from among the wise.

Proverbs 15:33. "The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honor is humility."] "The fear of the Lord," a disposition to stand in awe of him, to reverence, and adore, and trust in him, is the way to wisdom; and humility is the way to honor. The fear of the Lord and humility are near akin, and wisdom and honor are near akin. "The fear of the Lord is the *instruction* of wisdom." I.e. a principle of true piety in the heart will wonderfully enlighten the mind in the doctrine of true wisdom, and will guide and direct one in its ways. See John 7:17, and Proverbs 8:9, and the places there quoted.

Proverbs 16:1. "The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the Lord."] Mr. Henry says, that "most read it, 'The preparations of the heart are in man, but the answer of the tongue is

<!-- p. 561 -->

from the Lord.'" I.e. man contrives what and how he will speak, but the happy executing his design, and the success of it, is of God, as it is said, Proverbs 16:9. "Man's heart deviseth his way, but the Lord directs his steps." And in another place, "A man's way is not in himself. 'Tis not of him that walketh to direct his steps" [Jeremiah 10:23].*Exposition, 3* (1725), 510–11.

Proverbs 16:4.] The Wise Man in the expression, "hath made all things," has not respect merely to the works of creation, but also the works of providence. Making and creating is commonly understood in this large sense in Scripture for bringing to pass. Yea, bringing to pass, though not by an immediate effecting, but only by permitting, ordering, and disposing, is called "making" in Scripture. The "making the wicked," here mentioned, is a work of providence. God makes men wicked in the same sense as he said in the ninth of Romans, to make them "vessels of wrath," to harden them, and fit them "to destruction" [Romans 9:22] (of which, see notes, *in loc*.), viz. by so disposing and ordering things in his providence that they, in consequence of his disposals, especially in his permission or withholding restraints, do continue in wickedness, or are hardened in it. They are distinguished from others in being impenitently and obstinately wicked, and are suffered to multiply wickedness, and heap up wrath. And God's end in it is to glorify himself in the day of their evil or ruin. God makes wicked men in no other sense than he creates darkness, which is not by any positive effecting,JE wrote this over "efficiency." but only ordering by withholding light, for darkness is only a negative. Isaiah 45:7, "I form the light, and create darkness. I make peace, and create evil. I the Lord do all these things." These things that are here said to be formed, made, and created are all works of providence, and some of them brought to pass by no positive efficiency, because negative things, works of providence, are said to be created (Numbers 16:30; Isaiah 57:19; Isaiah 41:20; Isaiah 45:8, and Isaiah 48:7, and Isaiah 54:16; Jeremiah 31:22). So that it don't appear that this scripture will justify such an expression as that, that God made some men to damn them. 'Tis most probable that the Wise Man, by "making the wicked," has respect to something that God doth respecting the wicked or reprobates that is distinguishing and peculiar to them. God's distinguishing dealings towards mankind might be expressed thus: That God maketh both the righteous and the wicked in the same sense, i.e. whom he will, he has mercy on and makes righteous, and whom he will, he hardens or leaves to wickedness. But if the

<!-- p. 562 -->

Wise Man had respect only to the bringing the men into being, bearingConjecture for illegible word that Grosart overwrote. guilt and corruption, this is common to all. All in this sense are made wicked, in this sense alike. 'Tis probable that by "making the wicked" here is intended the same as is expressed, Romans 11:7–10, 2 Thessalonians 2:11–12, Psalms 81:12, Isaiah 6:9–10, which is a judicial proceeding and a punishment of sin, though it be a mere sovereign proceeding in God that he distinguishes some by not executing this punishment upon them.

Proverbs 16:6. "By mercy and truth iniquity is purged."] The wordיְכֻפֵּר rendered "purged" is *jecup-par*, which signified "atoned." Therefore by this saying the Wise Man would teach that the legal sacrifices in themselves are of no efficacy to atone for sin, and that nothing can avail to this but spiritual sacrifices, Christ's righteousness consisting in his obedience and faithfulness to God, and mercy to men. And nothing in us can avail as any evidence of our interest in his righteousness, but moral and spiritual dispositions and acts, spiritual offerings to God, whereby we imitate Christ's righteousness, and follow his example.

Proverbs 16:11. "Are the Lord's,… are his work."] I.e. just weights and balances are sacred things which God has appointed, as he did the vessels of the sanctuary, and which is as much of a sin to violate or alter as it would be to alter any of the sacred utensils of the temple from the divine pattern by which they were made. Hence the standard weights seemed to have been kept in the sanctuary, laid up there, as well as the ark and the sacred vessels. Hence we read of the shekel of the sanctuary. "All the weights of the bag," i.e. the just, true weights, are said to be God's "work," i.e. they are God's appointment, as that which God "appointed,"JE deleted "He was, according to an Hebrew idiom, said to have made." as though he had by an immediate command directed how it should be made, as he did how the vessels of the temple should be made. Yea, they are to be looked upon as sacred, as though God had made them with his own hands, as he did the tables of stone that were delivered to Moses in Mt. Sinai.

Proverbs 16:20. "He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good; and whoso trusteth in the Lord, happy is he."] Mr. Henry observes that "Some read the former part of the verse thus, 'He that attendeth to the word shall

<!-- p. 563 -->

find good,'" which is a most literal translation,יִמְצָא־טוֹב עַל־דָּבָר מַשְׂכִּיל and is much confirmed by Proverbs 13:13.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 512. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1623.

Proverbs 16:21. "The wise in heart shall be called prudent, and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning."] The literal translationלֶקֵח יסִיף שְׂפָתֵיִם וּמֶתֶק נָבוֹן יִקָּרֵא לַחֲכַם־לֵב is thus. "To the wise in heart, he that hath understanding shall be called; and the sweetness of the lips shall add to learning." The word "called" is from a wordקָרָא that is used for calling or inviting one to another, and for the calling together a company or congregation. And therefore the meaning seems to be this. They that have understanding shall be gathered about him that is wise of heart, to hear his instructions, and be benefitted by his conversation and his good instructions. His wise speeches, which shall be pleasant and entertaining to them, shall increase their knowledge.

Proverbs 16:22. "Understanding is a wellspring of life to him that hath it, but the instruction of fools is folly."] It might as well have been rendered, "is a wellspring of life in him that hath it," i.e. a fountain of good to others, tending to their life and happiness. What is communicated from them, the instructions they give, are wholesome and of vital influence. But as to what flows from fools, even the best instructions they give are folly, and tends to blind and corrupt the minds of those that are conversant with them, and to lead 'em to mischief and misery.

Proverbs 16:23. "The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips."] This is agreeable to what Christ says,MS: "Say." "A good man, out of the good treasure of his heart, bringeth forth that which is good.… How can ye, being evil, speak good things?… Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" [Matthew 12:35, Matthew 12:34].

Proverbs 16:27. "An ungodly man diggeth up evil."] He "takes a great deal of pains to find out something" wherewith to reproach his neighbor, and blast his reputation. "If none appear above ground, he will dig for it, by diving into what is secret, or looking a great way back, or by evil suspicions and surmises." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 513. The words immediately following in this and the next verse confirm this sense.

<!-- p. 564 -->

Proverbs 16:30. "He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things; moving his lips, he bringeth evil to pass."] These expressions intimate the secret, subtile, sly, deceitful way of his injuring his neighbor. "He shuts his eyes," that is, he conceals his aim and design, as though he did not see or aim at the mischief that will follow, acts as it were as if he were asleep and thought no harm, had no more hand in the evil that befalls his neighbor than if he were all the while asleep. "He moveth his lips." I.e. he whispers. He puts his ill designs in practice in a very secret manner.

Proverbs 17:5. "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker."] I.e. him that in his providence has made him poor, and has made [him] in this respect to differ from others that are ready to mock him, and deride him on that account.

Proverbs 17:8. "Whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth."] I.e. "whithersoever it turneth" from the hands of the giver, "it prospers" to promote his designs, and to gain those to whom it is given to his interests.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. The wordsיַשְׂכִּיל יִפְנֶה אֶל־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר בְעָלָיו בְּעַינֵי הַשּׂחַד אֶבֶן־חֵן might have been translated more literally thus. "A gift is a precious stone in the eyes of its lord" (or its husband, or him that espouses it, i.e. of the judge that is fond of bribes). "It prospers to all that to which it looks," or to which it has respect. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1631–32.

Proverbs 17:12.] This is agreeable to what Christ said to his disciples. "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves. But beware of men" [Matthew 10:16–17].

Proverbs 17:13.] It was declared that the sword should never depart from David's house, because he rewarded Uriah with evil for his good services [2 Samuel 12:10]. Evil did not depart from the house of Eli, and the house of Saul and Jeroboam, and the houses of others that God advanced to the kingdom over Israel, because they rewarded God evil for good. The Jews rewarded Christ, and his apostles, and other disciples evil for good. Therefore evil never departed from them and their posterity. Their house was left to them desolate, and the guilt of Christ's blood was on them and their children.

<!-- p. 565 -->

Proverbs 17:26.]Before this entry, JE deleted "Proverbs 17:26. to strike princes for equity." As, on the one hand, it is not good for judges to do injustice in judgment, and to punish the just, so, on the other hand, when they punish the wicked, and thereby do justice and equity, it is not good to rise up against 'em, and oppose, reproach, or in any respect injure 'em for that.

Proverbs 17:27.] Here see SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1641.

Proverbs 18:1.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1642–44.

Proverbs 18:4. "The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook."] The sense seems to be this. The words of a wise man's mouth are like waters that come from a deep fountain or wellspring, and his words flow from his heart like a flowing brook, from a deep fountain that yields a sufficient, constant supply. The wisdom of his talk is not feigned or forced, but flows naturally, as having the fountain within him. They are not muddy, mixed, and adulterated, but clear, sweet, and refreshing, like waters from a deep fountain. See Proverbs 10:11 and Proverbs 20:5.

Proverbs 18:10. "The name of JEHOVAH is a strong tower."] It is so in several respects. 1. As Christ is the name of God, as he is often called, who is the idea, *Logos*, word, or name of God. 2. As that by which God has made himself known, the word and promises of God, and the whole revelation he has made of him is so. 3. As the name JEHOVAH itself is so, as that exhibits God's infinite perfection, his all-sufficiency, his immutability, and faithfulness. God's calling himself by this name, and sending Moses to the children of Israel in the manner he did with this name, implies in it the great promises of the covenant of grace to them.

Proverbs 18:21. "And they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof."] Itפִּרְיָהּ יֹאכַל יְאֹהֲבֶיהָ might have been as well translated, "Let them that love it" (i.e. life), "eat the fruit thereof," i.e. of the tongue. For the Hebrew tongue always uses the future for the imperative in the third person. This sense is confirmed by Psalms 34:12–13.

<!-- p. 566 -->

Proverbs 18:24. "A man that hath friends must show himself friendly, and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."] The words might be translated more agreeably to the originalמֵאָח דָּבֵק אֹהֵב וְיֵשׁ לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ רֵעִים אִישׁ thus. "There is one of friends" (or one of those that are of that character), "who is so for the sake of showing himself friendly," i.e. a man of disinterested friendship, of pure benevolence, who is a friend not to gain anything, but to benefit the object of his love. "And he is a friend that sticks closer than a brother." Such a disinterested friend may be depended on. Christ is eminently such a friend, and perhaps the Spirit of God may have respect to him. Neither need it seem strange that some of these proverbs should have respect to him; so very evidently does Proverbs 18:10 of this chapter.

Proverbs 19:2. "Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth."] The former partלא־טוֹב נֶפֶשׁ בְּלֹא־דַעת גַּם of the verse might have been translated thus. "Also in the soul's being without knowledge, there is no good." I.e. if the soul be without grace, nothing that that man has, and nothing that happens to him, or that he is the subject of, can be of any benefit to him. "And he that hasteth with his feet sinneth." I.e. he that directly proceeds according to natural appetite and inclination without knowledge, without considering any other consequences, or any higher end than the immediate gratification of his inclinations, runs into nothing but mischief and ruin, and gets no good in the end. The wordחוֹטֵא "sinneth," here as in many other places, is used for coming to punishment and ruin.

Note on Deuteronomy 6:25.This reference is a separate entry.

Proverbs 19:3.] I.e. though men's wicked practices and their evil consequences are the fruits of their own folly and wickedness, yet they lay the blame of it to God and not to themselves. When they feel and fear the terrible consequences of their own sin and folly, then they fret against God, and find fault with his dealings with them, instead of condemning themselves.

Proverbs 19:22. "The desire of a man is his kindness."] That is, this is what in a peculiar manner recommends him to the affection of others, causes him to be beloved and desired, agreeable to many other passages in this book, as Proverbs 19:6 of this chapter, and Proverbs 18:16, and Proverbs 21:14, and Proverbs 17:8. To be a man

<!-- p. 567 -->

beloved, in the Hebrew way of expressing it, is to be a man of desire, as when the angel says to Daniel, "O man, greatly beloved" [Daniel 10:19]. In the original,אִישׁ־חֲמֻדוֹת it is "O man of desire." By a like Hebraism, when the Wise [Man] would signify that a man's amiableness or desirableness in the eyes of others consists in his kindness, he says, "The desire of a man is his kindness."

"And a poor man is better than a liar." A poor man that has but little to give, and can show but little kindness, is better than a rich man that promises much, but only flatters and turns persons off with good words.

Or by "the desire of a man being his kindness" may be meant that his kindness is according to his sincere good will, though he may be poor, and able to help us but little. We ought in such a case to accept such a gift as manifests his hearty desire of our welfare, as God doth. For wherever there is "a willing mind, it is accepted according to what a man hath, and not according to what he hath not" (2 Corinthians 8:12), as Christ accepted what the poor widow threw into the treasury as a greater act of piety and charity than the abundance that was given by the rich, who, many of 'em, were hypocritical and so liars, as the expression is here, in their offerings (Mark 12:43–44).This paragraph is a later addition.

Proverbs 19:28.] Note on Proverbs 15:14.

Proverbs 20:24.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1675–76.

Proverbs 20:26. "He bringeth the wheel over them."] In allusion to the wheel then used in threshing, which dislodged the grains of corn from the stalk where they hung together, fast one by another, as in clusters. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1677.

Proverbs 20:30. "The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil," etc.] The former part of the verse, as well as the latter, relates to the benefit of correction. "The blueness of a wound," i.e. when the skin or flesh is made black and blue by the stripes of the rod of correction, this cleanses away sin.

Proverbs 21:1.] The turning of "rivers of water" here spoken of is not the cutting out a new channel or water course for the water to run in, but God's governing the water of a river in its course by its banks, and turning the

<!-- p. 568 -->

stream hither and thither as he will, as God governs the waters of the sea, and stays its proud waves by the sands, saying, "Hitherto shalt thou come, and no further" [Job 38:11]. As the waters of the sea are great and very forceable, as though they would not be restrained, but yet God breaks their force, and brings them down by the sands. So the stream of many rivers is rapid, and the force of waters mighty, as though they would not be diverted from their course, yet they are under government. They don't go on in a direct course where it as it were seems resolute to go, but is continually restrained, and governed, and is turned from its course hither and thither. God stays and turns the mighty waters by the limits and bounds he has set everywhere, on both sides, throughout the whole course of the river from the head to the mouth. The water han't its own course where the strength of the stream bears, but God cuts out their course for them, and says, Thus far shalt thou go in this course, and then so far shalt thou go in that course. He governs the stream by sands and rocks that he places for limits. This is a very fit and beautiful comparison. As God thus governs the course of the mightiest streams of water, so he governs the hearts of the greatest and mightiest of men.

Proverbs 21:4. "The plowing of the wicked is sin."] The marginal readingI.e. of the KJV. seems preferable, viz. "The light of the wicked is sin." This appears by the Hebrew concordance to be by far the most general signification of the word.See נור, נִיר, נֵר in Buxtorf, *Lexicon Hebraicum el Chaldaicum* (6th ed.), p. 432, where the primary meaning is "*Lucerna, Lumen*," that is, lamp or light. See also Taylor, *Hebrew Concordance, I*, entry 1134 under ניר. By "the light of the wicked" we must understand the show, the proud profession, and appearance they make of great excellency, and their good opinion of themselves by which they shine in their own eyes (This agrees with the signification of the lamps of the foolish virgins [Matthew 25:3].), and their glory, joy, and expectation. So the same word as applied to the wicked is to be understood, in Job 18:6 and Job 21:17, and from time to time in this book, as Proverbs 13:9, and Proverbs 20:20, and Proverbs 24:20. And this agrees well with the former part of the verse. The word properly signifies a candle or lamp. The lamps of the foolish virgins imply all those things that I mention: their self-conceit, their show and profession, their hope and expectation, and their joy and comfort.

Proverbs 21:5. "Hasty."] I.e. with that sort of haste that is spoken of, Proverbs 20:21 and Proverbs 28:20, Proverbs 28:22.

<!-- p. 569 -->

Proverbs 21:6. "Is a vanity tossed to and fro of them that seek death."] The literal translationמְבַקְשֵׁי־מָות נִדָּף הֶבֶל is this. "Is a vanity dispelled, they seeking death." "A vanity dispelled," i.e. their work, their contrivances, and what they get by it vanishes away, like a vapor that is dispelled, or like smoke that is driven away by the wind. Psalms 68:2, "As smoke is driven away." There the same wordנָדַף is used. So again the same word in Psalms 114, "The wicked shall be as the chaff which the wind drives away." So Isaiah 19:7, "Shall wither, and be driven away, and be no more." "They seeking death," i.e. they that thus get riches by a lying tongue.

Proverbs 21:12. "The righteous man wisely considereth the house of the wicked, but God overthroweth the wicked for their wickedness."] A more literal translationלָרָע רְשׁעִים מְסַלֵּף רָשָׁע לְבֵית צַדִּיק מַשְׂכִּיל would be, "The righteous man, wisely considering the house of the wicked, overthroweth the wicked for their wickedness." I.e. he as it were passes sentence upon them, as those that are to [be] overthrown, which is by an Hebraism called "overthrowing them." See Jeremiah 1:10.

Proverbs 21:15. "It is joy to the just to do judgment, but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity."] The wordsאָוֶן לְפעֲלֵי וּמְחִתָּה מִשְׁפָּט עֲשׁוֹת לַצַּדִּיק שִׂמְחָה would be more literally translated, "To do judgment shall be joy to the just" (i.e. it shall issue in their joy and happiness); "but horror shall be to the workers of iniquity," i.e. working iniquity instead of joy shall issue in the sorrow and amazement of the unjust.

Proverbs 21:16. "Congregation of the dead."] Hebrew, *rephaim*. See Job 26:5. See SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1685–86.

Proverbs 21:24. "Proud and haughty scorner is his name, who dealeth in proud wrath."] The wordעוֹשֶׂה rendered "dealeth" is *guosheh*, doeth, maketh, or worketh. The meaning seems to be this. If a man's behavior and practice be haughty, bitter, and wrathful, his true character is determined by it. It demonstrates him to be a "haughty scorner," a proud enemy to God and men, whatsoever good principles he may pretend to act from, whether

<!-- p. 570 -->

superior wisdom, justice, religious zeal, sense of honor, hatred of wickedness, or any other. This is a very important observation, because there is no ill thing which men do so often pretend to proceed from good principles, and christen with good names, as those things that proceed from pride, and spite, or false zeal.

Proverbs 21:27. "How much more when he bringeth it with a wicked mind?"] The wordבְזִמָּה properly signifies a wicked design or device, as Absalom's vow, Jezebel's fast, and the Pharisee's long prayers, when [they] make a show of devotion, that they may the more easily and effectually compass some covetous or malicious design. When holiness is pretended, but some wickedness intended, then especially the performance is abomination (Isaiah 66:5). See more fully, SSS.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2. col. 1690.

Proverbs 21:28.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1690–91.

Proverbs 22:1. "A good name."] I.e. a good character, including a good report. But that real character that is just ground for such a report, the favor that is better than silver or gold, is properly the favor of God.

Proverbs 22:2.] I.e. though there is so great a difference between them, and one has so much more [than] the other, yet both are equally dependent on God for all good. The rich, notwithstanding all his riches and sufficiency, after all is as much dependent on God's help, and his pleasure, and providence, for his well-being as the poor man. They are on a level in this respect. See Proverbs 29:13.

Proverbs 23:2. "And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite."] I.e.
