Ecclesiastes 11:6.] Still it's a continuation of the same discourse. "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand" from giving to the

<!-- p. 605 -->

poor. He had before, in the Ecclesiastes 11:4, compared almsgiving to sowing seed. "Thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that." When you sow your seed, you ben't sure of a crop, but men ordinarily have in this way. So when men give to the poor, they ben't sure that they shall [be] rewarded with temporal prosperity; but 'tis God's ordinary way to reward men with great increase.

"In the morning sow thy seed. In the evening withhold not thy hand." The morning is the time when husbandmen are wont to go forth to sow their seed. The evening is the time when they return home to eat and to drink, and refresh themselves with the fruit of their labors. And therefore that is the proper time to give to the poor, that they mayn't eat their morsel alone. And the evening is the time that the husbandman returns home with the fruits of his field in time of harvest, and so the proper time [to] give God and the poor their part of the fruits.This paragraph is a later entry.

Ecclesiastes 11:8. "Remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many."] I.e. "of darkness," with respect to the light of the sun mentioned in the foregoing verse, days wherein the light of the sun shall to us be extinguished. These shall be many indeed, for they shall be the days of eternity; they never shall be fulfilled.

Ecclesiastes 11:9.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1940.

Ecclesiastes 11:10.] See note on Job 14:22.

Ecclesiastes 12:4. "The sound of the grinding is low."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1945–48.

Ecclesiastes 12:5. "Go about the streets."] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1948–51.

Ecclesiastes 12:6.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 1951–56.

Ecclesiastes 12:7.] Both body and spirit return to their originals. The body returns to the earth from whence that came, and the soul returns to God from whence that came. According to the account we have of man's creation,

<!-- p. 606 -->

the body was made out of the dust, but the soul was breathed forth from God [Genesis 2:7].

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1956–57.

Ecclesiastes 12:9.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1957–58.

Ecclesiastes 12:11. "As goads."] To awaken the consciences of sinners, to prick men at their hearts, "as goads" in the sides of God's people when they are dull and slothful, to quicken them to duty, to excite them to labor. "As nails fastened by masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd." God's people are often in Scripture represented as his building, house, or temple, and particular persons as parts or members of that building. The use of nails is to join the parts of the building, and fix 'em in it, that they may not be removed from their place and use in the building. So the words ofJE deleted "God." the wise masters of assemblies join souls to the true church of God, and fasten in the temple of God, that they may not depart from it (See Revelation 3:12.). They unite their hearts to Christ, the foundation, and to other parts of the building, and engage and fix their hearts in the proper business of their station in God's house. See Isaiah 22:23 and Ezra 9:8.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1958–59.

Ecclesiastes 12:12. "And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness to the flesh."] This properly comes after all that he had said, and goes immediately before his conclusion in the two next verses. Because though many may own that as to the sensitive objects and concerns of the world they are vanity, yet may think himself above these, and that he is employed in what is truly excellent and is the most substantial good, if he be employed in study, and contemplation, and writing, to acquire for himself and communicate to others great speculative knowledge and understanding. But the Wise Man would suggest that this also is vanity, that it is not true wisdom. This alone will not bring any men to their proper perfection and rest; nor is his great end, duty, and happiness but that what he next spake of, viz. practical godliness. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1959–60.

<!-- p. 607 -->

Ecclesiastes 12:13. "This is the wholeKJV reads "whole *duty*." of man."] The Wise Man, by an induction of particulars, had shown that all other things were vanity, or nothing; and now he draws up this conclusion, that this is "the whole," or all.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols 1960–61.

Ecclesiastes 12:14.] This verse proves that to fear God, etc., is the whole of man as to his interest and happiness, because his happiness or misery in the winding up of things will be in proportion as he doth it or neglects it. God will assuredly make it so; and whatever temporal advantages or disadvantages he has, it shall not alter that proportion. It shall be no weight in the scales in the conclusion, and so is to be reckoned nothing now.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1961–62.

### Canticles

The Song of Solomon.] See no. 147.*Works, 15*, 92. See "Miscellanies," no. 303.Ibid., *2*, 389–90. See Isaiah 5:1. See note on Canticles 6:13 and Canticles 8:5. See note on Canticles 1:4, and Canticles 8:8–12, [and] Canticles 1:9. See note on Canticles 1:5, no. 458;Ibid., *2*, 538. "Scripture," no. 460.Ibid., 547–51. JE entered these references at different times and in no clear order on the MS.

The book of Solomon's Song. The figures of speech used in this book, many of them are very agreeable to those used in Isaiah 5:1–7. Besides Christ's being there called "my beloved," compare with that fifth of Isaiah the following parts of this song: Canticles 1:6; Canticles 2:12–13, Canticles 2:15; Canticles 4:12–16; Canticles 5:1; Canticles 6:2–3, Canticles 6:11; Canticles 7:12–13; Canticles 8:11–13. Particularly compare Canticles 1:13–14; Canticles 2:2, Canticles 2:16; Canticles 4:13–14; Canticles 5:1; Canticles 6:2–3; Canticles 7:7–8, with Isaiah 5:7. Also compare these and other places in Solomon's Song with Isaiah 35:1–2, Isaiah 55:13, Isaiah 41:19, Isaiah 60:21, Isaiah 61:3, Numbers 24:6, Psalms 1:3, Jeremiah 17:8, Ezekiel 47:12, Psalms 80:8–15, Isaiah 27:2–3.

See Jeremiah 12:7.This reference and the preceding paragraph are a separate entry.

See "Notes," no. 231.*Works, 15*, 181. See notes on Ephesians 5:18. See no. 336.Ibid., 322.

As it was a common thing in these ancient times to have mystical speeches and parables, so it seems to have been a common thing to have mystical songs. See note on Canticles 2:10–11. See the evidence there is that the Psalms 45 is no common love song or epithalamium. "Miscellanies," no. 1067, §46.MS: "Bk. 6, p. 16, 17, 18, 19." JE presents a variety of arguments against the notion that Psalms 45 is a common love song. For example, he refutes the idea that the person spoken of is either David or Solomon. The account is "inconsistent" with David's marital history, and Solomon was never "a mighty hero in the field of battle and a great conqueror." The individual principally intended is described "as one above mere men." The language of the psalm is not appropriate to any particular person. In fact, "the song is not about external, but about spiritual things," a judgment also evident in its style. See "Scripture," no. 436.*Works, 15*, 520. The ancient Jews about Christ's time "believed that the book of Canticles was chiefly composed

<!-- p. 609 -->

for the Messiah." See Basnage's *History of the Jews*, p. 367.*History of the Jews, from Jesus Christ to The Present Time*. Basnage (1653–1723), who studied in Geneva, served congregations in Rouen, Rotterdam, and The Hague. See note on Canticles 8:5.JE deleted "See 'Scripture,' [no.] 486, Bk. 3." See SSS, preface to this book, and also to the book of Proverbs.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1961–70, and 1429–30.

Canticles 1:1.] Preface to book of Proverbs, SSS, and also to this book.Ibid. See agreement with Psalms 45, "Scripture," no. 507.*Works, 15*, 610–13. No. 507 is the last entry in "Notes on Scripture."

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 1970.

Canticles 1:4.] This verse affordsJE deleted "several." two good arguments that this song is no human love song. 1. Because the first person singular and plural are here used promiscuously. "Draw *me, we* will run after thee. The king hath brought *me* into his chambers. *We* will be glad and rejoice in thee; *we* will remember thy love more than wine." If this was intended for the language of an earthly lover or sweetheart, how comes she to speak of herself thus in the plural number? 'Tis evident 'tis because more than one person is signified, and respect is plainly had to the virgins mentioned in the last clause of the preceding verse, "the virgins love thee." 'Tis the nature of earthly love to dislike a rival, and to be averse to plurality. But she speaks of the virgins' loving her loved,Alexander Grosart added "be" to the front of this word on the MS, making it "beloved." and having enjoyed his love, with manifest approbation and delight. So in the beginning of the Canticles 6, when the daughters of Jerusalem desire to seek the beloved of the spouse that they may enjoy him with her, she don't disapprove of, but forwards it by directing them, according to their desire, where they may find him. See also Canticles 3:10–11. And by using the singular and plural thus promiscuously, 'tis evident that the spouse that is speaking, though one spouse, yet is more persons than one. 2. The last clause, "The upright love thee." (1) It shows that this song is not a profane but an holy love song. Why should a lascivious lover take notice of this with such delight and pleasure, that the upright loved her beloved? The same wordמֵישָׁרִים is used all over the Old Testament to signify the saints. Therefore it might have been translated, "the saints," or "the sincerely godly love thee." (2) When

<!-- p. 610 -->

it is said in the last clause of this verse, "the upright love," 'tis natural to suppose the same to be meant as in the last clause of the preceding verse, "the virgins love thee," and so, that the virgins are the saints, who are spiritual virgins, and that 'tis the saints that were intended by the plural pronoun "we" in the verse. And how well does this agree with what we suppose, viz. that this song is intended as a song of love between Christ and the church, or the assembly of the saints.

"Draw me; we will run after thee." The meaning don't seem to be, "Draw me, and then we will run after thee." But when the spouse says, "we will run after thee," her request seems to be answered, as appears, because in the next words she says, "the king has brought me into his chambers." She had no sooner made this request, but as ever she was aware, her soul "made her like the chariots of Amminadib" [Canticles 6:12].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Canticles 1:5.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1974–75.

Canticles 1:5–6.] See no. 86.*Works, 15*, 75.

"I am black." Denoting her outward meanness, obscurity, and affliction, often denoted by darkness or blackness in Scripture. So Christ was without form or comeliness. This meanness and affliction is in great measure owing to the contempt and hard usage of false churches and false professors, which appears very much in their keeping them under and in a state of servitude to serve their temporal interests, and to maintain their worship. Thus the Protestants in popish countries are obliged to help maintain the Romish church, and the Dissenters in England are forced to pay tithes to the Church of England, and among those of the same profession, true Christians are commonly kept under and obliged to serve false professors.This paragraph is a separate entry. This sentence is a later addition to the paragraph.

"As the tents of Kedar," etc. Externally, in outward form, and by my worldly circumstances, like "the tents of Kedar," black, coarse, and homely, but inwardly and spiritually glorious and beautiful, like the pure, rich, embroidered curtains of Solomon, either in his palace, or temple, or royal pavilion. Like Moses' tabernacle, whose outward covering was badgers' skins, but its inward curtains fine linen, and blue, purple, and scarlet.This paragraph is a separate entry. This sentence is a later addition to the paragraph.

See also no. 458.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 538.

Canticles 1:6.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1975–77.

Canticles 1:8. "Go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock."] SSS.Ibid., col. 1978.

Canticles 1:9. "I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh's chariots."] The horses draw the chariot of the king; so the church as it were draws the chariot of Christ. Christ rides as it were on a chariot of salvation, on the chariot of the word of truth. The word runs and is glorified, and thereby Christ is conveyed; but the church draws this chariot, especially the ministers of the gospel. The church is the pillar and ground of truth. Ministers bring Christ to men, and carry him through the world, and make manifest the savor of his name; and herein they are like the angels who are spoken of as Christ's chariots. The horses that drew the chariots of the king of Egypt were beautiful, strong, and swift, for Egypt was famed above any country for its excellent horses; and Pharaoh had the best in the country to draw his chariots. It was a "company of horses" that drew Pharaoh's chariots united together; so is the church, and so are true ministers of the gospel. Christ proceeds in the course of things in his providence, and especially in his church towards his end that he aims at, and will in the consummation of things arrive to, as a prince proceeds in a chariot towards his royal city, palace, and throne. See notes on Ezekiel's wheels.*Works, 15*, 373–79, 384–86, 388. And he is pleased to make his disciples the instruments of this his progress.

Kings were wont to go forth to war with chariots and horses. So believers, and especially ministers, are like Christ's horses to draw his chariots in war. Zechariah 10:3, "And hath made them as his goodly horse in the battle." Oftentimes the church is represented as his army, as in this song Christ compares her to a "company of two armies" [Canticles 6:13]. So Revelation 19. They are represented as the armies of heaven, following him on white horses Revelation 19:14]. The church in this song is said to be "terrible as an army with banners" [Canticles 6:4]. And in Canticles 4:4, her neck is said to be "like the tower of David builded for an armory, wherein there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men." And Canticles 7:4, the same is represented by a "tower of ivory," and her nose as the "tower of Lebanon." And Canticles 8:10, she is compared to a wall, and her breasts to towers.

<!-- p. 612 -->

*Corol*. Such kind of comparisons as these are a great argument that this song is no human love song. These things agree with the typical representations of the church in the congregation of Israel that went out of Egypt, who went up harnessed, and were encamped in the wilderness, always as an army with banners marshaled in military order.

"Behold, he standeth behind our wall; he looketh forth at the windows, showing himself through the lattice." "Such was the state of the old testament church while it was in expectation of the coming of the Messiah. The ceremonial law is called a 'wall of partition' (Ephesians 2:14), a 'vail' (2 Corinthians 3:13), but Christ stood behind that wall. They had him near them; they had him with them, though they could not see him clearly. He that was the substance was not far off from the shadows (Colossians 2:17). They saw him looking through the windows of the ceremonial institutions, and blossoming through those lattices.… And such is our present state in comparison with what it will be at Christ's second coming. We now see him through a glass darkly. The body is a wall between us and him, through the windows of which we now and then get a sight of him, but not face to face, as we hope to see him shortly. In the sacraments Christ is near us, but it is behind the wall of external signs; through these lattices he manifests himself to us, but we shall shortly see him as he is." (Thus Henry.)*Exposition, 3* (1725), 620. It might be added that such is the present state of the Christian church in comparison of what it will be after the time comes of the church's promised light, prosperity, and glory on earth, that time

<!-- p. 614 -->

eminently signified in the verses here immediately following, represented as a happy spring when the flowers shall appear on the earth, etc. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1989–90.

SSS.All three paragraphs are separate entries. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1989–90.

Canticles 2:14.] Having remained long in obscurity, being driven into secret corners and hiding places by thine enemies, being banished from among men, not appearing in palaces and public places, but dwelling in the wilderness "in the clefts of the rocks" and caves of the mountains, and when in cities and houses hiding thyself in the most secret corners. The church also in low state hides itself from Christ in fearfulness and unbelief, like Adam that hid himself from God among the trees, being of little faith and too much fear by reason of her deformity and nakedness. "Scripture," no. 444.The last sentence and this reference are later additions. *Works, 15*, 526–27.

"My dove!" SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1991–92.

Canticles 2:15. "Take us the foxes, the little foxes that spoil the vines, for our vines have tender grapes."] Which represent either, first, the sins that spoil the graces of the saints in their present infant state, in which their graces are like tender grapes easily damnified. These sins that spoil the graces are represented by foxes, because [of] their sly deceitful manner in which they insinuate themselves, and "little foxes" because the sins that are intended are not what are called gross sins, but other sins which the saints are more incident to. Or, secondly, they represent sly deceivers who don't appear as open and declared enemies to the church, nor their wickedness so great as to be plain and manifest, and tends at first sight to shock the minds of the saints, which sly deceivers do corrupt and spoil young and tender converts in a time of great revival of religion, for such a time is spoken of in the context. Hereby also is signified that Christ would have sin and error nipped in the bud, which though at first they are like young foxes, yet even then they spoil the vines, and if let alone will soon grow great.This sentence is a later addition. Such foxes, to destroy young and tender grapes, were the false prophets and seducers in the Apostle's days, whom the Apostle calls

<!-- p. 615 -->

deceitful workers, who crept into houses and led "captive silly women," etc. [2 Timothy 3:6]. See Galatians 3:1, Titus 1:10–11, 1 Timothy 4:1–2, 2 Corinthians 11:13, Ephesians 4:14, 2 Peter 2:1, 2 Timothy 3:6, Matthew 7:15, Revelation 2:2. See further the parallel between foxes and seducing heretics, in Mr. Hellenbroek's sermon on this verse, from p. 4 to p. 12.This sentence is a later addition. Abraham Hellenbroek, *A Sermon. From Canticles*. False prophets are compared to foxes. Ezekiel 13:4, "O Israel, thy prophets are like the foxes in the deserts."

Canticles 3:1. "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth. I sought him, but I found him not."] This represents the church's seeking Christ (God's people's seeking his gracious returns to his church, and his presence in it), when the church is in a low state, and when it is a dark time as to the interest in the world. Though at such times God's saints have a true love to Christ, and they do sincerely seek him, yet they seek him as it were on their beds in a dull, and a comparatively slothful and sleepy manner. But before Christ remarkably returns to his church, she must be more in earnest. She must arise off from her bed, and "go about the city," etc. Canticles 3:2].

Canticles 3:2. "In the streets, and in the broad ways."] I.e. in the use of public ordinances and means of grace.

Canticles 3:4.] It cost the spouse much to find her beloved, but when she found him she held him so much the faster. So it is with the saints. The longer it is before they find Christ, the more pains, and care, and self-denial it costs them, the more choice they will be of their privilege when they have found Christ, and the more careful not to let him go.

Canticles 3:6. "Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?"] This represents the abundance of merit with which Christ came out of his passion and state of humiliation. In coming out of his state of humiliation, he as it were came out of a dreadful wilderness; and he came forth like great cloud of incense, for then he had finished his purchase. He arose and ascended from this humiliation like a great cloud of incense up to heaven, perfumed with all manner of sweet spices, for when he had finished his passion, he entered into the holiest of all with his own blood, with the incense of his abundant merits, as the high priest of old entered into the holy of holies with a cloud of incense. We read, Ezek.

<!-- p. 616 -->

Canticles 8:11, of "a thick cloud of incense" going up. And another thing that is probably meant by it is Christ's coming forth out of his humiliation in the glory of his divinity. The glory of the divinity is represented by the cloud of glory. While in his humiliation his divinity was veiled; but when he [was] exalted, he reassumed the glory he had with the Father before the world was.

We find this question, "Who is this?" often asked in Scripture on occasion of Christ's coming forth out in his merits, triumph, and glory after his sufferings and conflicts with his enemies. See note on Psalms 24:7–10, no. 308.*Works, 15*, 281–83.

Canticles 3:9–10. "King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon. He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem."] This probably represents the same thing with Jacob's ladder, and the way by which Solomon went up to the house of the Lord, which the queen of Sheba admired so much, even the way of salvation. The chariot was made "of the wood of Lebanon," very durable, for the covenant by Christ is "an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure" [2 Samuel 23:5]. The "pillars thereof of silver," a precious metal, and the whitest and brightest of all metals, representing the righteousness of Christ, which in the affair of our salvation is as it were the pillars that support the building, and which is precious, and perfectly pure, and bright. The "bottom thereof of gold," representing Christ's divinity and the infinite dignity of his person, which [is] the precious foundation of everything that belongs to the salvation of Christ, the foundation on which stands the infinite merit and sufficiency of his righteousness. The stones for the foundations of the temple were costly stones, and the foundation that God lays in Zion is spoken of as a precious stone (Isaiah 28:16). The same was represented by the golden altar of incense. The gold was the foundation on which the incense (representing Christ's righteousness) was offered, and whence it ascended up to God. See note on Canticles 5:11. The covering of the chariot was "of purple," representing the sufferings and propitiation of Christ by which believers are sheltered from the winds and storms of God's wrath. The same was represented by the covering of the tabernacle made of ram skins (the skins of rams offered in sacrifices dyed red). This covering rested on the silver pillars and the foundation of gold. So the sufficiency of Christ's

<!-- p. 617 -->

sufferings depends on his innocency and the perfection of his righteousness performed in his going through his sufferings, and on the infinite dignity of his person. The "midst thereof was paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem." 'Tis said that the bottom thereof was gold. Christ's divinity and infinite dignity is the foundation of that redemption that Christ wrought out, and yet the pavement is said to be love to "the daughters of Jerusalem." In some respects, free and sovereign grace, and eternal electing love to those that were to be believers, is the foundation of redemption. 'Tis the foundation of everything belonging to it, as for them, directed for them, and prepared for them, and applied to them. Everything that was contrived and done for the redemption and salvation of believers, and every benefit they have by it, is wholly and perfectly from the free, eternal, distinguishing love and infinite grace of Christ towards them. We read of God's "chariots of salvation" (Habakkuk 3:8). See SSS on these two verses.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2000–2001. This reference is a later addition.

Canticles 3:10–11.] That "the daughters of Jerusalem and Zion" are so often mentioned in this song as much concerned in what is said of the excellency and love of the bridegroom is an argument that the song is divine, or the bridegroom is Christ, because God's people, the members of the visible church, are so often elsewhere called the daughter or "daughters of Jerusalem and Zion."

Canticles 3:11. "The crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, in the day of the gladness of his heart."] Here, first, the bridegroom was crowned in token of his possession of and dominion over the bride. The church of Christ sets the crown upon Christ's head in the day of his espousals to his bride, i.e. in the conversion of the soul. Christ is crowned as king by God the Father, and not only so, but also by the church, his mother. Crowning a king was a ceremony equivalent to anointing, but Christ is anointed not only by God, but also by his church. See notes on Ezekiel 19:1, Ezekiel 19:5; Daniel 9:25; and Mark 14:3. The soul of a believer, when converted, does set the crown on Christ's head in these two respects. 1. In willingly and joyfully ascribing to him the glory and honor of his dominion over all things, with their whole heart concurring with God the Father in setting the crown upon him, acknowledging that he is worthy of the glory above all others, doing as the four and twenty elders

<!-- p. 618 -->

do who cast down their crowns at his feet (Revelation 4:10), and saying as they do (Revelation 5:12) "with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain," etc. And 2. In choosing of him, and willingly submitting to him as their king by giving up their hearts to Christ, devoting themselves to him, becoming his willing people, setting Christ upon the throne of the heart, and with their own hands and with a joyful heart putting the crown on his head there, giving him the possession of the heart, setting him in the highest place above all other lords or lovers. The church sets the crown upon Christ's head in the day of her espousals with him, in the same manner as when a people in elective kingdoms choose a king. They set the crown on his head, thenceforward honoring and obeying him as their sovereign.

But, secondly, the crown that was put upon the bridegroom in the day of his espousals was rather a crown of joy, of gladness, for crowns were used not only to betoken honor and dignity, but joy. Hence we read from time to time of a crown of joy and rejoicing. And though here by king Solomon's mother and bride both is meant the church, yet it seems as if there should be some distinction in this affair in the espousals of Christ's spiritual bride between the mother that crowns him with joy, and the bride over whom he rejoices. Therefore by his mother here seems especially to be meant the church as holding forth the word of Christ, and administering the ordinances of Christ, whereby souls are converted, and brought forth, and brought to an union and spiritual marriage with Christ. And therefore the ministers of the gospel seem especially to be intended by his mother, for they travail in birth with souls till Christ be formed in them (Galatians 4:19). When the church is spoken of under the character of a mother, the instructing part of the church is thereby especially intended. See Canticles 8:2. See note on 1 Corinthians 15:42, especially towards the latter end of the note. See Hosea 4:4–8, especially note on Hosea 4:5. See also 1 Thessalonians 2:7.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2001–2.

Canticles 4:1. "Thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Mt. Gilead."] The hair is the fruit of the body, and probably here represents fruit in practice, as it does in the law of the leprosy [Leviticus 13]. The hair of the head is the fruit of the head. The head of the spouse may probably representJE deleted "ministers."

<!-- p. 619 -->

the elders of the church, so that by her hair being "as a flock of goats appearing from Mount Gilead" may be meantMS: "meant." ministers and elders being especially as a city set on an hill, that is in open view, and can be seen at a distance, so that their good works appear. They are ensamples to the flock. They adorn the doctrine of Christ in the eye of the world. A fruitful hill appears differently from a barren one, even at a distance, by the flocks that appear feeding upon it.

Hair also in Scripture is made use of to represent thoughts, understanding, meditations, or the fruits of these meditations. So this may represent the living fruits of ministers' studies. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2002–4. This paragraph is a separate entry.

Canticles 4:2. "Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them."] This may probably represent the church's ministers and teachers, who are in this mystical body as the teeth in the natural body. They first take the food of the body, which is the word of God, and by their studies they prepare it for the nourishment of the body, as the teeth do our natural food by chewing it. These are represented by sheep to show that ministers should be harmless and gentle, imitating their Lord and Master in those virtues, agreeable to the rules in the epistles to Timothy and Titus, not like the clergy of the Church of Rome, haughty, voracious, and cruel, more like wolves than sheep. They should be real sheep, and not wolves in sheep's clothing.

They are said to be like a "flock" of sheep. For ministers should act in concert as coworkers and fellow helpers, as the teeth in the body natural, and should often meet together in council, should be congregated as a flock to assist one another in promoting the public good of the church. They are said to be as a flock of "shorn" sheep, for so it is in the original,הַקְּצוּבוֹת to represent that faithful ministers don't fleece their people to clothe themselves, but rather yield their own fleeces to clothe their people. They spend and are spent for the good of their souls. They "every one bear twins," etc., to represent their fruitfulness and success. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2004–5.

"Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, that came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them."] "Ministers are the teeth of the church that, as nurses,

<!-- p. 620 -->

chew the meat for the babes in Christ. (The *Chaldee Paraphrase* applies it to the priests and Levites, who fed upon the sacrifices.)… These are compared to a flock of sheep. Christ calls his disciples and ministers a 'little flock' [Luke 12:32]." Henry.*Exposition, 3* (1725), 625. They are "even shorn." Faithful ministers, instead of fleecing the flocks they have the care of for themselves, yield their fleece to the flock. They are willing to spend and be spent for them. They are as sheep that come up from the washing when about to be shorn. So ministers had need to be pure themselves in order to yield pure spiritual clothing to their people. "Whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren amongst them." Fruitful ministers are not wont to be barren ministers. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2005–6. This paragraph is a separate entry.

Canticles 4:3. "Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet."] "Scripture," no. 486.*Works, 15*, 582–83.

Canticles 4:4. "Thy neck is like the tower of David."] "Scripture," no. 487.Ibid., 583.

Canticles 4:5. "Thy two breasts are like two young roes."] "Scripture," no. 488.Ibid.

Canticles 4:6. "Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and the hill of frankincense."] I.e. I will get me to heaven "till the day break," i.e. till the morning of the day comes of my glorious kingdom and my church's light and joy, either at the commencement of the church's glory on earth, when Christ will descend from heaven to the earth spiritually, or the resurrection day, the morning of the eternal day of the church's consummate glory, when Christ will descend in his human nature. See Canticles 8:14.

Canticles 4:8. "Come with me from Lebanon."] No. 2 28.Ibid., 177–79.

The state that persons, while at a distance from Christ, are in is a wilderness, a state of sin; and this world is a wilderness. Christ here invites his spouse away from sin and the world. Lebanon was the pleasant and delightful part of the wilderness with tall pleasant cedars. Hermon and "the lions' dens," etc., is theJE deleted "terrible, barren, dangerous part of the wi." terrible part of it. Christ earnestly invites us to

<!-- p. 621 -->

come to him, away from the honors and pleasures of the sinful state. And this is the way to be delivered from dangers and dreadful things that belong to this state, and to be delivered from persecutors and all the enemies and afflictions of this world. SSS.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2010–11.

Canticles 4:9. "My sister, my spouse."] No. 336.*Works, 15*, 322.

"One of thine eyes." No. 435.Ibid., 520.

Canticles 4:12.] SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2013–14.

Canticles 5:1. "Drink abundantly, O beloved."] Ephesians 5:18 note.

Canticles 5:2. "I sleep, but my heart waketh."] It may be well explained by those words of Christ to his disciples, Matthew 26:41, "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."

Canticles 5:10. "White and ruddy" (or red).] His whiteness represents his infinite holiness and perfect righteousness. His being red represents the great sufferings and extreme trials under which his righteous and most excellent virtue was manifested. It may also signify his incarnation. The word is אָדוֹם, a word of the same derivation as Adam, man.

Canticles 5:11. "His locks are bushy, and black as a raven."] Christ's perfect age is set forth, Revelation 1:14, by his hair's being "white like wool, as white as snow," or perfectly white. And here his perfect youth is set forth by his hair's being "black as a raven," or perfectly black. Christ hath both perfect age and perfect youth, the perfect bloom and vigor of youth through eternity, or an everlasting youth. He was properly represented with that which signified his age in Revelation 1, where he appears in the quality of a ruler and judge, the great Alpha and Omega Canticles 5:8]. Here when he is spoken of as a bridegroom, he is most properly represented with that which signifies the perfection of youth. See SSS.Ibid., col. 2021.

"His head is as the most fine gold." This probably represents Christ's

<!-- p. 622 -->

divine nature. The head of Christ is God, says the Apostle. Gold seems to have been made use of to signify Christ's divinity or divine dignity before. Canticles 3:10, see note. See SSS on Canticles 3:1.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, col. 2016.

Canticles 5:12.] "Rivers of water," when spoken of mystically, and concerning things holy and divine in Scripture, are perhaps universally put for the Holy Spirit, its influences and fruits. This expression therefore denotes Christ's receiving the Spirit not by measure, and thence divining infinite holiness, and sweet love, and grace as it were appearing in his eyes, which "are as the eyes of a dove," pure and loving.

SSS.This reference is a separate entry. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2021–22.

Canticles 5:13. "His lips are like lilies, dropping sweet smelling myrrh."] Here in the description of Christ's lips, as of several other parts of his body, is signified the mixture of holiness and grace that there is in Christ. His lips' being as lilies represents the purity and holiness of his gospel, not in the least countenancing or encouraging sin; and their "dropping sweet smelling myrrh" represents the grace of Christ to sinners manifested in the gospel.

Canticles 5:14. "His belly is as bright ivory," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 489.*Works, 15*, 584.

"His belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires." The wordמֵעִים translated "belly" signifies bowels, and the same word is so translated, Canticles 5:4. And so it signifies Christ's mercy and love. The glory of Christ's grace and love consists in two things. 1. That his mercy is perfectly pure and holy, represented by his bowels being "as bright ivory." 2. By its being so gentle and so great, seeking such great benefits, so high a happiness for the beloved, on this account his belly is represented as "overlaid with sapphires," a precious stone of the color of the sky, one of the mildest of the colors, and the color of the heavens, representing Christ's mercy being exceeding sweet, mild, and gentle, and that it is so great it seeks nothing less than heavenly glory and blessedness for the beloved. See "Scripture," no. 489.*Works, 15*, 584. This paragraph is a separate entry.

And see SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2023–24.

<!-- p. 623 -->

"His hands are as gold rings set with the beryl." "Great men had their hands adorned with gold rings set with precious stones. But in the church's eye, Christ's hands themselves were as gold rings set with precious stones. All the instances of his power, the works of his hands, all the performances of his providence and grace, are all rich, and pure, and precious as gold." (Henry.)*Exposition, 3* (1725), 632. By Chambers' account, the beryl is like the crystal, but only partakes of a green color. Crystal may properly represent purity and holiness, and green, divine grace and beauty, giving life and joy, as the beams of the sun in the spring, covering the earth with a vivid joyful green. Holiness and grace are wonderfully connected in Christ's works, in the work of redemption, in all parts of it.This paragraph is a separate entry. Chambers, *Cyclopaedia* (2 vols., 2nd ed. London, 1738), entry on "Beryl, or Beryll, βηρυλλος," *I*, [n.p.].

Canticles 5:15. "His countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars."] Signifying the mixture of majesty and grace. Lebanon was a great mountain, which mountains are an appearance in nature that exhibits great majesty. The cedars of Lebanon, also being so very great and high, had a majesty in their appearance. But by their being so fair and flourishing, of so beautiful a green, they exhibited an amiable image of that divine grace which is mild and gentle, and gives life and joy.

"His legs are as pillars of marble, set on sockets of fine gold." Gold seems in this book pretty often to be used to represent Christ's divinity, or the infinite dignity of his person. See notes on Canticles 2:10 and Canticles 5:11. Christ, in the office of our mediation, and in the character of our prophet, priest, king, spiritual husband of the church, etc., stands on the foundation of his divinity, and his infinite dignity and sufficiency consisting therein. 'Tis by his standing on this that he stands so strong. Or these "sockets of fine gold," which are the foundation on which his feet stand, may represent the preciousness and perfect excellency of the ground of the divine proceedings in his providence. It may be observed that in all that is divine, the foundation is represented as peculiarly precious. The foundation of the temple was of precious stones. So the foundations of the New Jerusalem and its streets, the ground on which the inhabitants went, were precious stones and pure gold. In the bridegroom's chariot (Canticles 3:9), "the bottom thereof was of gold" Canticles 3:10]. See also Isaiah 54:11 and Isaiah 28:16. All that belongs to, or can properly be called, the foundation of the divine proceedings in his providence, especially the proceedings of Christ as our Savior in the work of redemption,

<!-- p. 624 -->

whether those perfections or divine dispositions that move him or dispose him to do what he does, or the chief motives and supreme end, is perfectly pure and infinitely excellent.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Canticles 6:2.] The church is Christ's garden. See Canticles 4:12–16. The "beds of spices" are particular churches or congregations of saints included in the church universal.

Canticles 6:4. "As an army with banners."] A well regulated army, or an army of regular forces.

Canticles 6:9. "Her mother."] Note on Psalms 116:16.

Canticles 6:10.] "'Fair as the moon,' the lesser and changeable light, in her sanctification. 'Clear as the sun,' the greater and invariable luminary, in her justification. The inherent holiness of believers being imperfect, and subject to many inequalities; while their imputed obedience is every way complete, and constantly like itself." Hervey's *Meditations*, vol. 2, p. 93.*Meditations and Contemplations* (4th ed.), *2*, 93, n. See note on Joshua 5:1–9.

Canticles 6:13. "O Shulamite," etc.] The wordהַשּׁוּלַמִּית. This is an example of the variation in versification between the Hebrew Bible and the King James Version. is from the same root as Salem and Solomon, and is the same name as Solomon, only in the feminine gender, and signifies "peaceable." Here is observable the wonderful conjunction of the name "peaceable" with a comparison representing her ready for and valiant in war, she being compared to a "company of two armies." See also Canticles 6:10.

See no. 85.*Works, 15*, 75. This comparing the Shulamite to "the company of two armies," or Mahanaim, where the host of angels, having met with Jacob's company, made one company of two armies [Genesis 32], is a clear proof that the lovers that are the subject of this song are no earthly lovers, and that this is a mystical song. See note on Canticles 6:4.This reference and the preceding sentence are a separate entry.

Canticles 7:1. "How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 490.*Works, 15*, 584–85.

<!-- p. 625 -->

Canticles 7:2. "Thy navel is like," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 491.Ibid., 585.

"Thy belly is like a heap of wheat." No. 327.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 310–11.

Canticles 7:4. "Thine eyes are like the fishpools in Heshbon," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 492.*Works, 15*, 585–86.

"The tower of Lebanon." "Scripture," no. 493.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 586–87.

Canticles 7:5. "Thine head," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 494.*Works, 15*, 587.

"The king is held in the galleries." The wordרְהָטִים translated "galleries" signifies "walks." The wordאָסוּר rendered "held" is "bound." By these walks or galleries where Christ is held, or as it were bound, is meant his house, in which God is said to walk (Leviticus 26:12, 2 Corinthians 6:16). Christ is held in these walks as his fixed abode by his delight in his church (Psalms 132:13–14).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Canticles 7:7.] Note that the palm tree is a very tall tree, by the account which *Atlas Geographus* gives of it.Hermon Moll in *Atlas Geographus* discusses the height of palm trees. For example, in his description of Jericho, "call'd the *City* of Palm-Trees," he cites Tacitus' statement that palm trees are "tall and comely" (*III*, 150). His account of Brazil states that the Portuguese there plant palm trees "for Ornament, because of their Height" (V, 252). In the Antilles Islands, he notes, the Royal Palmetto, "one of the most stately Trees in the Universe," grows to a height of 300 feet (*V*, 487).

See further in Wilson's *Christian Dictionary*.Wilson's primary entry on "Palm tree" reads, "It's upright and tall of stature, beareth sweet fruits, and hath the leaves always green and flourishing, being good for shadow" (pp. 461–62). In the supplementary section entitled *A Dictionary of the Song of Solomon*, he compares this "tree, tall and straight, whose Nature is not to be pressed down with weight," to the "Church, which is not made crooked with the weight of afflictions, but rather becometh more upright and strong." Likewise, the "stature of the Spouse [is] likened to a *Palm-tree*, [which] sheweth her spiritual growth in the faith (notwithstanding all her tribulations) tending alwayes upwards to heaven" (*Complete Christian Dictionary* [6th ed.], p. 1134).

Chambers in his dictionary says that the Phoenicians called the palm tree "Phoenix" because, though burnt to the ground, it rose again "fairer than ever." See under the word "Phoenix."*Cyclopaedia* (2nd ed.), entry on "Phoenix, ΦΟΙΝΙΞ," *II*, [n.p.]. It was very straight. See Jeremiah 5:10.

"Thy breasts to clusters of grapes." See "Scripture," no. 495.Each paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 587–88.

<!-- p. 626 -->

Canticles 7:8. "The smell of thy nose like apples."] "Scripture," no. 496.*Works, 13*, 588.

Canticles 7:9.] 'Tis the wine "that goes down (or is swallowed) sweetly," as being most pleasant and refreshing. See this whole verse explained, "Scripture," no. 497.Ibid.

Canticles 8:1.] See no. 8.Ibid., 50.

Canticles 8:2. "Into my mother's house, who would instruct me."] See note on Canticles 3:11, at latter end.

Canticles 8:4.] See no. 395.Ibid., 389–90.

Canticles 8:5. "Who is this that cometh up out of the wilderness, leaning," etc.] See note on Joshua 5:1–9. The several things said in this verse are plainly of a mystical signification, and consequently this song a mystical song.

"I raised thee up." The wordעוֹרַרְתִּיךָ signifies to awake, or cause to rise. We may note from hence that under the same means by which the saints are brought forth or regenerated, they are also renewed and raised up from a low state when fallen into sleepiness and sloth, darkness and sorrow. This "apple tree" probably signifies that "tree of life" (Revelation 22:2), "which bare twelve manner of fruits," the doctrine of the twelve apostles, "the leaves of which tree were for the healing of the nations." See also Ezekiel 47:12. Under this tree the church shall have a spiritual resurrection from its low state.This paragraph is a later addition.

Canticles 8:6. "Upon thine heart."] The love of Christ must be fixed in our hearts unchangeably. "As a seal on thine arm." And must appear in our steadfast and persevering practice and works of righteousness. We must constantly and perseveringly love him with all our hearts, and with all our strength.

Canticles 8:8. "A little sister."] I.e. a younger sister, by a Hebraism.

<!-- p. 627 -->

Canticles 8:8–9. "We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts.… If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver," etc.] By a young woman's having no breasts seems to be a phrase to express her not having come to such maturity as to be marriageable. And the thing intended here is that there [are] elect persons and an elect church not yet brought, not formed and fitted by divine grace, for espousals with Christ. And by what is said in the Canticles 8:9, we are taught that the special gifts of grace in the elect, when they are accommodated to the gifts of nature, everyone in this respect has his own proper gift, the gift that is suitable to his nature, and station, and circumstances in the world, or the station, use, office, and business God intends him for. By "breasts" here seems to [be] signified graces of the Spirit. See SSS.*Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 2045–47.

Canticles 8:8–12.] Who can doubt whether these four verses are of mystical signification, and that therefore this song is designed as a mystical song, and not a mere human love song? What should lead earthly lovers, in singing of each other's beauty and love, to take notice of such things as these? If we suppose the song to be mystical, and that 'tis concerning Christ and his church, a good account can be given of these passages, a very natural interpretation analogous to other scriptures. By the "little sister" we may suppose is meant the same as the younger brother in the parable of the prodigal, and by Solomon's "vineyard" the same with Christ's vineyard so often spoken of in Scripture, and by the "keepers" the same with the keeper of the vineyard and laborers in the harvest in Christ's parable, who partake of the fruit of their labors with Christ. See John 4:36.

Canticles 8:10. "I am a wall, and my breasts like towers; then was I in his eyes as one that found favor."] The wall next to the foundation is the strongest part of the building or city. 'Tis that which immediately rests on the foundation, whereby it is strong. Therefore when the spouse says, She is "a wall," 'tis as much as to say, I rest on Christ, am built on him, and am strong in the Lord. The defense of the wall, and its strength against the enemy, were the towers that were built upon it, as the shield was the defense of the soldier. Therefore the towers on the wall especially represent faith. As the spouse's neck, by which the body is joined to the head, is represented as a tower, Canticles 4:4 (See note *in loc*.), therefore when she says, "My breasts are like towers," it signifies that the church of Christ

<!-- p. 628 -->

lives by faith in Christ, and that it is in the exercises of faith that her graces exert themselves, are manifested, maintained, and bring forth their fruit, by which means it is that the church is accepted of God, is amiable in his sight for Christ's sake in whom she believes, and her graces sweet and delightful in his eyes.

Canticles 8:11.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 2047–48.

Canticles 8:12.] SSS.Ibid., cols. 2048–49.

Canticles 8:14.] Christ says, Canticles 4:6, that he will get him "to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense, till the day break, and the shadows flee away"; that is, that he would leave this world, and ascend into heaven, till the morning of the joyful and glorious resurrection. Here in these words with which this song is finished, "Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like unto a roe or a young hart on the mountains of spices," the spouse prays that Christ would quickly descend from thence, in like manner as [the] book of Revelation is concluded with these words, "Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus" [Revelation 22:20].

<!-- p. 629 -->

### Isaiah

Isaiah 1:5.] This agrees with the history of the times wherein Isaiah prophesied. See 2 Chronicles 28:22 with the rest of the chapter.

Isaiah 1:9. "Except the Lord had left us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should been like unto Gomorrah."] So it was remarkably in the second destruction of the nation by the Romans. There was a remnant of believing Jews, according to the election of grace; and there was another remnant of those in whose loins were the elect Jews that should be called in the latter days, for which elects' sake the days of calamity were shortened. Otherwise, no flesh could have been saved.

Isaiah 2:2. "The mountain of the Lord's house," etc.] I.e. that particular mountain or rock in Jerusalem on which the temple is built that, according to Bedford in his *Scripture Chronology*, was hewn out and formed in the same shape as the altar, and called *Har-el*.*Scripture Chronology*, 568. The temple under the Mosaic dispensation, though it was in a very eminent and conspicuous place, and was visible to a considerable distance in that land, yet it was then in a low and obscure place in comparison of what it is in the times of the gospel, when this very mountain of the house of the Lord shall be set up as it were on the tops of other mountains so as to be higher than the hills, that it may become conspicuous far off, even to the nations of the Gentiles far and near. The other hills that interpose, that hid the prospect under the Mosaic dispensation, shall not hide it under the gospel, for it shall then be above the hills,MS: "hill." and seen over their tops. Thus Christ tells his disciples, who were the beginning of the Christian church, that they were a city set on an hill [Matthew 5:14]. Now all the tribes of Israel flowed into the mountain of the house of the Lord three times a year at their three great feasts, like rivers flowing into a sea; but then all nations shall flow into it. Now the temple and the altar were set on a mountain, but then the mountain of the house itself should be set on the top of a mountain,

<!-- p. 630 -->

as the altar now was on the mountain of the house. See note on Zechariah 1:8, no. 269, the former part of that note.*Works, 15*, 223–24.

This sets forth how far the church under the gospel in its enlargement and glory exceeds the church under the old testament by a figure very much like that used in Jeremiah 3:16–17, where it is foretold that the ark should no more be in use, but Jerusalem itself should be the throne of God instead of the ark, and that all nations should "be gathered to the name of the Lord, to Jerusalem," as now all the tribes of Israel were gathered before the ark, intimating that the church should be so enlarged, that the whole city Jerusalem should be no more to God's whole people than now the ark was to all the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and that the holiness and glory of the church should then so far exceed what now was that the whole city Jerusalem should be as holy as now the ark, the most holy thing in the most holy place of the temple, the most holy house in all Jerusalem. See 2 Corinthians 3:10, Zechariah 14:20–21, Isaiah 23:18, Isaiah 61:6.This sentence is a later addition.

Isaiah 2:3. "Come ye, and let us go up."] "As when the Jews from all parts of the country went up thrice a year to worship at Jerusalem, they called on their friends in the road, and excited them to go along with them." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 8.

"For out of Zion shall go forth the law." See notes on Isaiah 51:4 and Psalms 50:2.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Isaiah 2:5. "O house of Israel, come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord."] Compare this with Revelation 21:23–24 and Revelation 22:5, and see the note on Revelation 21:23–24.

Isaiah 2:20.] Though his idols were silver and gold, and esteemed as most precious things, and were set up in magnificent temples, and had been prized and honored above all things, being adored as gods, yet now they shall be cast away, and left as mere heaps of rubbish, affording lurking places for moles and bats. Such animals as are here mentioned are wont to lurk in heaps of rubbish of old decayed buildings, or stuff and utensils that are cast away.

<!-- p. 631 -->

Isaiah 2:22.] The Isaiah 3 would more properly have begun with this verse.

Isaiah 3:1. "The stay and the staff."] This refers not only to the bread and water next mentioned, but to the other things that follow that they were wont to have dependence upon.

Isaiah 3:1–5.] These things were not only fulfilled in the first destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, but in a remarkable manner in their second destruction by the Romans. They first were bereaved of their water, more prudent men, and of their stay and staff,JE deleted "bread and." of provision, and ammunition, etc.; and then those things followed mentioned, Isaiah 3:4–5. See "Miscellanies," no. 972.*Works, 20*, 254–74.

Isaiah 3:8. "To provoke the eyes of his glory."] See note on Exodus 16:10.

Isaiah 3:10–11.] What is contained inMS: "to." these two verses seems to be an introduction to what follows through the former part of this book, wherein Isaiah proceeds in his preaching to the end of Isaiah 35, agreeably to the direction given him of God in this verse, interchangeably threatening terrible judgments to the wicked that were in Israel, and revealing glorious promises to the righteous among them, as from hence to the end of this chapter, the Prophet says to the wicked, "It shall be ill with him." In the Isaiah 3, he says to the righteous, "It shall be well with him." In the Isaiah 6:12, he again says to the wicked, "It shall be ill with him." And Isaiah 6:13 and Isaiah 7:1–16, he says to the righteous, "It shall be well with him." But Isaiah 3:8 is a threatening to the wicked; Isaiah 3:17–26, to the wicked; Isaiah 8:1–8, to the wicked; Isaiah 8:9–10, [to] the righteous; Isaiah 8:14, part to the righteous, and part to the wicked; Isaiah 8:15, to the wicked; Isaiah 8:16–17, to the righteous; from thence to the end, to the wicked; Isaiah 9:1–7, to the righteous; Isaiah 9:8 to the end, and Isaiah 10:1–6, to the wicked; Isaiah 10:7 to the end, and chs. Isaiah 11 and Isaiah 12 and Isaiah 13 and Isaiah 14, to the righteous; Isaiah 22:1–19, to the wicked; Isaiah 22:20 to the end, to the righteous; Isaiah 24:1–12, to the wicked; Isaiah 24:13 to the end, and Isaiah 25, and Isaiah 26:1–9, to the righteous; Isaiah 26:10–11, to the wicked; Isaiah 26:12 to the end, and Isaiah 27, to the righteous; Isaiah 28:1–4, to the wicked; Isaiah 28:5–6, to the righteous; Isaiah 28:7–8,

<!-- p. 632 -->

to the wicked; Isaiah 28:9–10, to the righteous; Isaiah 28:11–15, to the wicked; Isaiah 28:16, to the righteous; Isaiah 28:17–22, to the wicked; Isaiah 28:23 to the end, to the righteous; Isaiah 29:1–4, to the wicked; Isaiah 29:5–8, to the righteous; Isaiah 29:9–16, to the wicked; Isaiah 29:17 to the end, to the righteous; Isaiah 30:1–17, to the wicked; Isaiah 30:18 to the end, to the righteous; Isaiah 31:1–3, to the wicked; Isaiah 31:4 to the end, and Isaiah 32:1–8, to the righteous; Isaiah 32:9–14, to the wicked; and Isaiah 32:15 to the end, and Isaiah 33:1–6, to the righteous; Isaiah 33:7–14, to the wicked; Isaiah 33:15–17, to the righteous; Isaiah 33:17–18, to the wicked; Isaiah 33:19 to the end, and chs. Isaiah 34 and Isaiah 35, to the righteous.

Isaiah 3:15. "Grind the faces of the poor."] This figure of speech, if we consider what was their way of grinding corn in those days, which was pounding it in a stone mortar with a stone pestle, called the upper and nether millstone […].JE failed to complete this sentence.

Isaiah 3:24. "And burning instead of beauty."] I.e. they shall be burnt and tanned with the sun. (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 14. For they shall be deprived of those veils wherewith they used to shelter themselves from the sunbeams, and shall be led away captive, and made to serve in slavery to their enemies, uncovered and naked.

Isaiah 4:1.] This verse should most properly been made part of the Isaiah 3, and is connected with the latter end of it. The women intended to charm the men, and get husbands by their ornaments there mentioned; but their men were slain with the sword, as 'tis said, Isaiah 3:25. And this that is mentioned in this verse is the consequence. Henry.Ibid.

Isaiah 4:4. "The spirit of burning."] Matthew 3:11.

Isaiah 4:5. "A cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night, for upon all the glory shall be a defense."] 1. Here is reference to the pillar of cloud and fire [that] was a defense to the children of Israel from their enemies when pursuing them (Exodus 14:20), and sheltered them from the burning heat of the sun in those parched deserts of Arabia. See Psalms 121:5–7, and Isaiah 49:10, and Revelation 7:16. 2. Here is reference to the covering of rams' skins and badgers' skins, which in the wilderness was a defense

<!-- p. 633 -->

and shelter for the inward, beautiful, glorious work of the tabernacle, that was as it were the glory of the camp of Israel.

In the Hebrewחֻפָּה עַל־כָּל־כָּבוֹד it is, "Upon all the glory shall be a covering," as in the margin.I.e. margin of the KJV. That covering was a defense to the tabernacle of the congregation from the weather, as the pillar of cloud was to the congregation itself. And as that covering was a defense to that tabernacle of God, so every dwelling place in Zion and all the assemblies of his people, mentioned in the preceding verse, shall be as dear to God as that tabernacle was. He shall look upon every house where Christians dwell as his own dwelling place, and shall dwell there as he dwelt in the temple. See Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 15. The glory of God's people, their most precious treasure, shall be hid safe in God's pavilions and "secret of his tabernacle" (Psalms 27:5). So the life of every Christian is hid with Christ in God, and his treasure is laid up in heaven. See note on Isaiah 10:3. That which was laid up in the sanctuary was most precious of all; God would not order it to be kept there if it was not very precious. God's sanctuary, or pavilions, is from time to time spoken of as a sure defense and safe hiding place (Psalms 27:5 and Psalms 31:20; Isaiah 8:14; Ezekiel 11:16; Psalms 91:1).

Isaiah 5:1.] It renders it the more credible that Solomon's song is a divine song, for the appellation of "my beloved," there often used, is not unsuitable for a divine object, and so that other discourse of that song that is agreeable to such an appellation. For here 'tis evident this appellation is given to God. See Isaiah 5:7. As on the other hand, the appellation of "beloved" is given by God to his saints, in Psalms 60:5 and Psalms 108:6. Jeremiah 12:7, "I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies."

Isaiah 5:18. "Woe to them that draw iniquity," etc.] I.e. that make wickedness their daily labor, as [an] ox does to draw in a team; that laboriously treasure up wickedness and wrath, as the husbandman draws home his sheaves by oxen with cart ropes, and industriously gathers in his harvest; and so draws on and hastens the punishment of sin, as in the next verse. The Prophet had been speaking of wicked men's unjustly enriching them to the oppression of others by getting from them their fields and the produce of them (Isaiah 5:8 and Isaiah 5:17). We sometimes read of persons' sowing iniquity. We here read of their gathering the harvest, and drawing of it in, as husbandmen do sheaves in carts.

<!-- p. 634 -->

Isaiah 5:19.] I.e. that dare God in their practice.This follows a brief Pierpont note on Isaiah 5:19 which strikes the theme of "daring" God, which JE's entry echoes: "Here they stand on yr heads and most contemptuously shake yr heels agst heaven, daring omnipotency itselfe, to do his worst."

Isaiah 5:22. "Woe to them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink."] There is a severe sarcasm in the words, for the Prophet is speaking of the great men and princes in Israel, as appears by the verse following, which should be mighty men, men of glorious fortitude and strength; but they were mighty for nothing but gluttony and drunkenness.

Isaiah 6:2.] Called so from the brightness of their appearance, their appearing as lightning or as a flame of fire, as God is said to make his angels "a flaming fire" (Psalms 104:4), for the radix of the word is שָׂרַפ, that signifies "to burn." Hence fiery serpents are called *seraphim* (Numbers 21:6, Numbers 21:8). See Genesis 3:14.

Isaiah 6:3. "Holy, holy, holy."] See notes on Revelation 4:8.

"The whole earth is full of his glory." In the original,כִּבוֹדוֹ כָל־הָאָרֶץ מְלא "His glory is the fullness of the whole earth," which signifies much more than the words of the translation. God's glory, consisting especially in his holiness, is that in the sight and communications of which man's fullness, i.e. his holiness and happiness, consists. By God's glory here there seems to be respect to that train, or those effulgent beams, that filled the temple, those beams signifying God's glory shining forth and communicated. This effulgence and communication is the fullness of all intelligent creatures who have no fullness of their own.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 6:11–12. "Until the cities be wasted."] That which is spoken in the foregoing verses of Israel, that it is said shall be "till the cities be wasted without inhabitant," etc., being so often applied in the New Testament to the Jews before their last destruction by the Romans, makes it evident that when the Jews' destruction is foretold by the prophets, and they are speaking of their ruin by the Chaldeans, respect is also at the same time had to their destruction by the Romans.

Isaiah 6:13.] As 'tis with the church, it cannot wholly fail because when it seems dead, it shall yet live because its substance is in it, which is "the holy seed."

<!-- p. 635 -->

So it is with a particular saint. He cannot utterly fall away because his seed abideth in him (1 John 3:9). See "Miscellanies," no. 991.This reference is a later insertion. *Works, 20*, 315–20. The people in the captivity were preserved from utter destruction chiefly for the sake of their "holy seed," or that holy posterity that should spring from them like a new set of leaves in the spring after the old leaves had withered and fallen. Though that generation that was carried captive into Babylon were almost wholly a wicked generation, and continued obstinate in their wickedness after the captivity, as appears by the prophecy of Ezekiel, and continued to be followed with God's judgments in their captivity, as appears by many things in Scripture, yet the next generation of their seed or children, many of them, were a holy generation which returned out of captivity, for whose sakes the tree was preserved, as it was in the wilderness. That generation that came out of Egypt were a very corrupt and obstinate generation, and were pursued with God's judgments till they were destroyed. But the generation of their children that entered into Canaan were a holy generation, for whose sake it was that the whole people was not utterly cut off, and did not all fall in the wilderness.

Isaiah 7:3. "And Shear-jashub thy son."] Which signifies "the remnant shall return."יָשׁוּכ שְׁאִר This doubtless has a more special reference to that which is expressly spoken of and foretold, Isaiah 10:21, "The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God," what had its more immediate accomplishment in Hezekiah's time, after the Assyrians had wasted the kingdom of Ephraim, and greatly diminished Judah. See notes on the place.The part of this entry preceding this point is a later addition.

The name signifies "the remnant shall return," whichJE deleted "doubtless points at." probably has some respect to the wonderful return of those 200,000 captives which Pekah and Rezin had carried away, who were brought back not by might, nor by power, but by the spirit of the Lord. Read the story, 2 Chronicles 28:8–15. Though as a pledge of something further, viz. that mentioned, Isaiah 19:21, and also that under the Messiah, mentioned Isaiah 11:11, Isaiah 11:16, [it has respect to] the return of a remnant from Babylon, and the conversion of a remnant in the time of Immanuel, by which they were saved from that state of captivity to sin and Satan in unbelief, in which the rest perished eternally, and were also saved from the last terrible destruction by the Romans.

<!-- p. 636 -->

Isaiah 7:4. "The two tails of these smoking firebrands."] They smoked now as though by and by they would break out into a terrible flame, and set Jerusalem and all Judah on fire, and consume. But though this was what they threatened, king Ahaz is directed not to fear them.

Isaiah 7:8. "Within threescore and five years."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 42–43.Based on the exact number of years after the prophecy, Prideaux equates the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy concerning the destruction of Ephraim with the conquest of the Ten Tribes by Esarhaddon (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 42–43).

Isaiah 7:9. "If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established."] Hence we may note that unless we believe, we shall not have the benefit of absolute promises made to the church, and things that are certainly predicted to come to pass.

Isaiah 7:14.] See "Miscellanies," no. 991, at latter end of that number.This sentence is a later separate entry from the following sentence. *Works, 20*, 320. See note on 1 Kings 14:14–15.

"The Lord himself shall give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Sometimes those things that [are] "mentioned in Scripture" as signs of things predicted ["did not take place"] till after the thing signified has been accomplished, as Exodus 3:12, 1 Samuel 2:34, Isaiah 37:30, Jeremiah 44:29–30, as Ridgley observes from Bp. Kidder, *Body of Divinity*, vol. I, p. 398.Ridgley, *A Body of Divinity, 1*, 398, n. h. Thomas Ridgley (1667–1734) was an English Dissenting theologian. See also SSS on Genesis 3:12.Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 1, cols. 37–38. The child here spoken of is doubtless the same that is spoken of in the Isaiah 9:6, for 'tis evident that there the Prophet still continues to discourse of the same matters, as may be easily seen by observing the connection.This paragraph and each of the three following are separate entries.

"A virgin shall conceive." This denotes and is typical of the purity of Christ's conception. He proceeds from a pure undefiled virgin. There was a typical defilement in the coition of man and woman, as appears by the law of Moses. Christ proceeded from one typically pure, and this was typical of the spiritual purity of the conception, that he was not conceived in sin. The propagation of mankind from the more unclean and vile parts of the bodies of the parents, and from the seed of man that is a typical

<!-- p. 637 -->

filthiness, was typical of the original sin and corruption conveyed by generation.

"The Lord of hosts himself shall give you a sign." The thing here mentioned was a sign that God had mercy in store for them, and it was a sign that neither the nation nor the house of David could be destroyed inasmuch as this blessing was in them. That a child should be born of a virgin was a sign of God's power and ability to preserve them. That his name should be Immanuel, God with us, was a sign that [God] would be with them to preserve them. That this Immanuel was to be born of the house of David was a sign that they need not fear the cutting off the entail of the crown of Israel in the house of David by setting up the son of Tabeal [Isaiah 7:6], or any other way. Henry.*Exposition, 4*, 24–25.

See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 2, 97–108.Kidder mounts a defense of Matthew's application of this prophecy to the Virgin Mary against accusations by Jewish writers that the Evangelist misapplied and misquoted the Prophet. Kidder marshals contextual, linguistical, and hermeneutical arguments to support his position. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726).

Isaiah 7:15. "Butter and honey shall he eat."] That is, he shall feed on the fruits and blessings of Canaan, which are milk (and butter, which is of milk) and honey, which intimates to Ahaz that the land shall yet enjoy prosperity, and shall yield her increase to God's people, and shall yet flow with milk and honey, so that the inhabitants shall have "butter and honey" for their food, agreeable to what is foretold (Isaiah 7:21–22).

Isaiah 7:17.] See no. 242.*Works, 15*, 196–97. This entry was written later than the following separate note which JE crossed out with a large "X." "Isaiah 7:17. 'The Lord shall bring upon thee.' Upon thee, O land of Israel or Ephraim, spoken of in the preceding verse."

Isaiah 7:19.] God avoids comparing the land to a fruitful field because of its spiritual barrenness. He don't therefore say that these insects shall come, and devour the corn, and trees, and fruits of the earth, but "they shall come, and rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes." See Isaiah 9:18.

Isaiah 7:20. "A razor that is hired."] The razor that Ahaz had hired. See 2 Kings 16:7–8. "The hair of the feet." I.e. of the lower parts of the body, so that here by the hair of the head and of the beard and the feet is meant all the hair of the whole body. The whole body was corrupt and leprous;

<!-- p. 638 -->

and in order to its being cleansed, the hair must be all shorn off (Leviticus 14:8–9).

Isaiah 7:25.] "There where briars and thorns were wont to be of use, and to do good service, even in the hedges, for the defense of the inclosed grounds, they shall be plucked up, and all laid in common. There shall be briars and thorns in abundance, there where they should not be, but none where they should be. The 'hills that shall be digged with the mattock' for special use, from which the cattle used to be kept off with 'the fear of briars and thorns,' shall now be thrown open, the hedges broken down, for the boar of the wood to waste it (Psalms 80:12–13). It shall be left at large for oxen to run in, and lesser cattle." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 26.

Isaiah 8:6.] What is meant here by "the waters of Shiloah" may be learnt from John 9:7. "And he said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, which is by interpretation, Sent." 'Tis manifest that the pool of Siloam is there respected as a type of Christ, the fountain of living waters, who by his blood and spirit washes away sin, and restores sight to the blind. And 'tis manifest that the pool of Siloam is the same with the waters of Siloam. 'Tis called the "pool of Siloah" (Nehemiah 3:15). They are said here to "refuse the waters of Shiloah," i.e. they refuse the God of Israel, who was Jesus Christ, who is often spoken of as the husband of the church of Israel. One thing whereby they very lately showed their refusal of him was by their slighting the prophecy and promise of his birth of a virgin as the Immanuel, in the Isaiah 7. They refused these waters because they went "softly." They disliked the God of Judah because they supposed that he did not prosper his worshippers as the gods of other people, and particularly the gods of Syria and Ephraim did, because the kingdom of Judah, where alone his worship had been kept up, and where his temple was, was a small kingdom, and at this time in low circumstances, and did not make such a figure and noise in the world as those other kingdoms. The benefits of the God of Judah were not so visible, were not manifest in such external pomp and glory, as some other kingdoms enjoyed. They refused Christ their God for the same reason that the Jews refused him when he came in the flesh, which was because he did not come with observation and noise, and bring that outward prosperity and glory to their nation as they expected. They refused "the waters of Shiloah," and rejoiced in Rezin and Remaliah's son, i.e. they hankered after the gods of

<!-- p. 639 -->

those kings that they thought helped them to greater power and prosperity, as we may see they did by 2 Kings 16:3–4, and 2 Kings 16:10–11 ff., and 2 Chronicles 28:2–4, and 2 Chronicles 28:25, but especially 2 Chronicles 28:23, which very much clears this explanation. God would convince them of their folly herein by suddenly overthrowing those two kingdoms, and thereby show the insufficiency of their gods to defend them, and would greatly distress Judah, and punish them for hankering after those gods.

Isaiah 8:7–8.] See no. 293.*Works, 15*, 265.

Isaiah 8:8. "And he shall pass through Judah. He shall overflow and go over; he shall reach even to the neck."] That is, he shall overwhelm the whole body, and nothing but the head should be above water. The head of Judah was Jerusalem, as it is said, Isaiah 7:8–9, that "the head of Syria was Damascus, and the head of Ephraim was Samaria." So the head of Judah was Jerusalem. All the rest of Judah should be taken but only this head city. And so it proved when Sennacherib and the king of Assyria came up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them, and laid siege to Jerusalem; but God graciously preserved that from his hands, as 2 Kings 18:13 ff. God did not give this land wholly to be overwhelmed and destroyed because, though the armies of the enemy filled the breadth of the land, yet God kept the head above water because it was Immanuel's land.

Isaiah 8:21. "And look upward."] This is to be joined with the next words in the following verse, "And they shall look to the earth," etc., i.e. they shall look to heaven and earth, but which way soever they turn their eyes, they shall behold nothing but trouble and darkness, dimness and anguish.

Isaiah 9:1. "Nevertheless, the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation."] I.e. nevertheless, there shall a time come when there shall not be such dimness; or such dimness in those regions shall not always continue in "the land of Zebulun," etc. In those regions the captivity and destruction of Israel began, and in the same places the great salvation by Jesus Christ began. See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. 33–34.This reference is a later addition. Kidder notes that the "land of Zebulun" suffered early captivity at the hands of the Assyrians, and that Nazareth in the land of Galilee was a city in the region where Jesus began his public ministry. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1.

<!-- p. 640 -->

"Galilee of the nations." "Most commentators refer this name [to] 1 Kings 9:11–13, supposing that Solomon's giving a tract of land here to Hiram, occasioned it to be filled with foreigners, and to be peopledMS: "People." with a mixture of Phoenicians, Egyptians, and Arabians, according to the account that Strabo gives." Doddridge on Matthew 4:15.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 1*, 198–99, n. c.

Isaiah 9:6. "And his name shall be called Wonderful."] Which shows that this child that was to be born is the same person with the angel that spake to Manoah, that "ascended in the flame of the altar" [Judges 13:20], for he tells Manoah that his name is secret (Judges 13:18). The word is the same in the originalפֶּלֶא that here is translated "wonderful"; and that person was God, for he is there spoken of as being God (Judges 13:22–23). So that here is a prophecy of God's being born, which agrees with the names that follow—"the mighty God, the everlasting Father"—and to the name that he is called by in the Isaiah 7:14, viz. Immanuel.
