And it also confirms that the child here intended is the person that was to be a sacrifice for sin because this person, whose name was secret or Wonderful, ascended up before Manoah "in the flame of the altar." See notes on Judges 13:18 and Judges 13:20.This reference is a later addition. And so it argues it to be the same person that wrestled with Jacob, for when Jacob inquired after his name, he answers, "Wherefore inquirest thou after my name?" [Genesis 32:29], in like manner as he answered Manoah when he inquired after his name [Judges 13:18]. It argues it also to be that Son of God spoken of in Proverbs 30:4. "What is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?"The remainder of this entry is a later addition. See also Revelation 19:12.

"His name shall be called Counselor." Not only because he is man's counselor, but God's. See Genesis 1:26, and the places there cited in my note.

Isaiah 9:6–7.] That this child, this king of Israel here spoken of, is not any mere man is manifest by the way of his managing war, and conquering and destroying his enemies, mentioned in the Isaiah 9:5, which is altogether different from the battles of other kings, which is "with confused noise, and garment rolled in blood," but his "shall be with burning and fuel of fire."

<!-- p. 641 -->

Isaiah 9:8–21.] These things were remarkably fulfilled in the destruction of the land by the Romans.

Isaiah 9:9–10.] No. 243.*Works, 15*, 197.

Isaiah 9:11–12. "Therefore the Lord shall set up the adversaries of Rezin against him."] Ephraim joined with Rezin against Judah, that were God's people, as in Isaiah 7, reference to which is had here. See notes on the preceding verse. Seeing they united themselves with Rezin in his sin, they shall be united with him in his calamity and punishment. "And join his enemies together." As they combined and conspired with the enemies of God's people, so his enemies shall combine together against him. "The Syrians before." Yea, the Syrians themselves that they combined with against God's people, and that they trusted to help them in their wicked design, shall beJE deleted "made a." a scourge to punish that very wicked design.

And by Isaiah 9:20 and Isaiah 9:21. They shall also be made enemies, every man to his neighbor, and be a means of devouring one another, and even themselves. So fierce is God's anger against those that are enemies to his church.

Isaiah 9:18. "Briars and thorns."] See note on Isaiah 7:19.

Isaiah 9:18–21.] These things were remarkably fulfilled at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans.

Isaiah 9:20–21.] See note on Isaiah 9:11–12, second part.I.e. second paragraph.

Isaiah 10:1–4.] These four verses are to be joined with the latter end of the Isaiah 9 as part of what is spoken concerning Israel or Ephraim, which seems evident by the conclusion of the Isaiah 9:21 and the conclusion of the last of these verses, so answering one to another, both concluding, "For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still."

Isaiah 10:3. "And where will you leave your glory?"] I.e. your best, that is most choice and precious with you, that you place your happiness in, and esteem

<!-- p. 642 -->

your highest glory. That which is very choice is called their glory. See Hosea 9:11 notes.This reference and the preceding sentence are later interlineations. To whose trust will you commit this in time of this desolation? Where will you hide it, or lay it up? Persons in time of great danger of desolation are wont to take care of their most valuable possessions, their most precious treasure, to hide that in some very safe place. It is promised to the church and people of God (Isaiah 4:5), that "upon all their glory shall be a defense," or covering to hide it and defend it, as the covering of the tabernacle sheltered the ark of the covenant and other holy things, that were the glory and most precious treasure of the church that is hid in God's pavilion, in the secret of his presence. But where will the wicked leave their glory?

Isaiah 10:16–18.] This was fulfilled in the miraculous destruction of Sennacherib's great army of an hundred, fourscore, and five thousand in one night (Isaiah 37:36).

Isaiah 10:20–22. "The remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob."] The Assyrians and other enemies destroyed and utterly carried captive the ten tribes of Israel. And Sennacherib's army destroyed multitudes of Judah, so that it was but a small remnant that was left of what all Israel was before those invasions, and a smaller still that were by those judgments induced to return to God, as Isaiah 10:21–22. "Shall no more stay upon him that smote them." I.e. they shall not trust in the Syrians, as Pekah, king of Israel, had done, who afterwards smote them, as Isaiah 9:11–12. Nor shall they stay upon the Assyrians, as Ahaz, king of Judah, had done (2 Kings 16:7–8), for which they were punished by being smitten by them in Ahaz's time, for Tiglath-pileser, when he came, "distressed him, and strengthened him not" (2 Chronicles 28:20), and afterwards were more grievously smitten by them in Hezekiah's time when Sennacherib's army took all the fenced cities of Judah excepting Jerusalem.

Isaiah 10:24. "And he shall lift up his staff."] The marginal readingI.e. margin of the KJV. appears to be the right, "But he" (i.e. God) "'shall lift up his staff for thee,' after the manner of Egypt," by Isaiah 10:26, where the expression is repeated.

Isaiah 10:24–34.] What is here spoken was accomplished in the invasion of Sennacherib's army, and their dreadful destruction by an angel, and in his destruction that followed.

<!-- p. 643 -->

Isaiah 10:27. "His burden shall be taken away."] I.e. they shall no longer be under tribute to him, as they had been. See 2 Kings 18:14.

Isaiah 10:34. "By a mighty one."] By a mighty angel. See Isaiah 37:36.

Isaiah 11:1.] "Christ is here called a rod and a branch. Both the words here used signify a weak, small, tender product. Some render the wordsחֹטר and נֵצֶר a 'twig' and a 'sprig.' The enemies of God's people were just before," in the conclusion of the Isaiah 10, "compared to strong and stately boughs," lofty trees of the forest, and cedars of Lebanon. But Christ is compared to a tender sprig. (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 38. By this is denoted his humility and the meanness of his outward appearance, as by the greatness and loftiness of trees and boughs, in the last verses of the Isaiah 10, is meant pride and outward pomp, as also Isaiah 2:11–13. See notes on Isaiah 53:2. See Ezekiel 17:22. See Hervey, *Dialogues*, vol. 3, p. 359.This sentence is a later addition. Hervey, drawing on the contrast in the text, writes, "When those lofty Cedars are leveled with the Ground, *there shall come a Rod*, a Twig shall spring *from the Stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his Roots*. Which, notwithstanding its mean Original, and unpromising Appearance, shall rear its Head to the Skies, and extend its Shade to the Ends of the Earth" (*Dialogues, 3*, 359). "A branch shall grow." See "Miscellanies," no. 991.This reference and the preceding sentence are a separate addition. *Works, 20*, 315–20.

Isaiah 11:10.] "Christ was lifted up from the earth, that as an ensign or beacon he might draw the eyes and hearts of all men to him (John 12:32). He is set up as an ensign in the preaching of the everlasting gospel, in which the ministers as standard bearers display" Jesus Christ and his truth and love. (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 39. The brazen serpent was set up an ensign, or upon an ensign, as it is in the originalעַל־נֵס אֹתוֹ וְשִׂים (Numbers 21:8). Christ should be set up as an ensign to gather together his people, both of Jews and Gentiles, for their march to Canaan, here spoken. See Isaiah 11:11–12. And they should look to Christ, as an army looks to the ensign or standard to see where to go, and how to move, as being that by which the captain leads and guides his army, and keeps 'em together. See note on Exodus 17:15, no. 205.*Works, 15*, 128–29.

"His rest shall be glorious." That is, the rest that this standard or ensign is set up to gather 'em together, and [to] lead his people. The children

<!-- p. 644 -->

of Israel were led to Canaan under ensigns or banners, which rest Joshua brought 'em into. This context speaks of an ensign's being set up to gather Israel, and bring 'em to Canaan a "second time," as Isaiah 11:11–12. This rest shall be glorious. The earthly Canaan, which Joshua brought the children of Israel into, is called "the glorious land" (Daniel 11:16, Daniel 11:41, and Daniel 11:45); but Joshua did not bring the people to their true rest. But 'tis the spiritual Joshua, or Jesus, does that, who brings 'em to the heavenly Canaan (Hebrews 4:8–9). The children of Israel did not fully obtain that rest which Moses promised 'em till Solomon's reign. See 1 Kings 8:56. That rest was glorious, but it was but a type of the glory of Christ's rest. See note on Exodus 13:21. See "Scripture," no. 503.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 601–5.

"An ensign of the people." See no. 205, being note on Exodus 17:15.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 128–29.

Isaiah 11:11–12. "To recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt," etc.] In these two verses there seems to be a distinction made between that remnant of Israel and Judah that Christ should save, and the Gentiles that should be called with them. Note that that remnant of Israel and Judah, that were recovered and converted by the preaching of the apostles, were chiefly those that were dispersed in those countries. That great ingathering that there was by Peter's sermon seemed to have been so (Acts 2:9–11).

Isaiah 12:6.] In the originalצִיּוֹן יוֹשֶׁבֶת it is, "thou inhabitress of Zion," the same that is elsewhere called "the daughter of Zion," i.e. the church.See JE's exposition of the text in his sermon on Isaiah 12:6, preached a first time Nov. 1735, with the doctrine "When God is in the midst of a people, 'tis just cause of exceeding joy and praise in them that so great and holy an one is amongst them" (*Works, 19*, 453–55).

Isaiah 13:19–22.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 808–11.Prideaux cites travelers' reports describing the desolation of the site of the former city of Babylon to confirm Isaiah's prophecy in these verses (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, pp. 808–11).

Isaiah 13:20.] See no. 175.*Works, 15*, 102–3.

Isaiah 14:12–15.] See "Miscellanies," no. 340."Ibid., *2*, 414–15. See also "Miscellanies," no. 1264.Ibid., *2*, 212. No. 1264, entitled "THE DEVIL BEFORE THE FALL THE HIGHEST OF ALL CREATURES," contains JE's discussion of Lucifer or Satan as "the brightest of all the stars" who served as "God's prime minister of state" before his fall.

<!-- p. 645 -->

Isaiah 14:23. "And pools of water."] See Prideaux, Pt. I, pp. 268–69.The inundation of Babylon, here linked by Prideaux to Isaiah's prophecy, was caused by the diversion of the river during the siege of the city (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 268–69).

Isaiah 14:25.] Fulfilled in the destruction of Sennacherib's army by an angel.

Isaiah 14:26.] I.e. this is a specimen of what God would do against all nations that should hereafter be engaged against the church, particularly against the empire of the Babylonians, the destruction of which is foretold in the preceding part of this chapter, and against the spiritual Babylon, the great enemy of the Christian church.

Isaiah 14:29. "The rod of him that smote thee."] I.e. Uzziah. See 2 Chronicles 26:6. When Uzziah was dead, they made reprisals upon Ahaz, and took many of the cities of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:18). But Hezekiah, who began to reign about thirty-two years after Uzziah, destroyed the Philistines (2 Kings 18:8).

Isaiah 15:2. "He is gone up to Bajith and Dihon, the high places."] The places where they worshipped their gods. "To weep," on occasion of this great public calamity, before their gods.

Isaiah 15:5.] The people of Moab, or the daughter of Moab (according to Scripture language), having lost her children slain by the sword, shall howl as "an heifer of about three years old" lows when she has lost her first calf, and also is deprived of both feed and water, for the daughter of Moab shall lose both her children and her substance. See Isaiah 15:6.

Isaiah 15:6.] See note on preceding verse.

Isaiah 15:7. "To the brook of the willows."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 148.Prideaux asserts that this phrase, which he maintains should have been translated "the valley of willows," points to the flat region where Babylon stood with its many rivers and canals, and its abundant willows (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 148).

Isaiah 16:1.] The Prophet gives good counsel to the Moabites to reform what was amiss amongst them, and particularly to be kind to God's people as the likeliest way to prevent the judgments before threatened (Isaiah 16:1–5).

<!-- p. 646 -->

In this Isaiah 16:1, he adviseth them to be just to the house of David, and to pay the tribute they had formerly covenanted to pay to the kings of his line. David made the Moabites tributaries to him. 2 Samuel 8:2, They became his "servants, and brought gifts." Afterward they paid their tribute to the kings of Israel, and paid it in lambs. 2 Kings 3:4, "And Mosha, the king of Moab, was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool." Now the Prophet requires them to pay it to Hezekiah. Let it be raised and levied from all parts of the country, "from Selah," a frontier city of Moab on the one side, "to the wilderness," a boundary of the kingdom on the other side.

Isaiah 16:2.] The comparison is to be understood of such birds as the children of Israel used to keep, as doves particularly, who if they were turned and shut out of their dove houses would not know what to do, nor where to go, no more than Noah's dove when sent out of the ark. As to wild birds, the difficulty was not such with them who had no particular house or certain fixed home, and if they were turned out of one nest could make another. See Hosea 7:10 and Hosea 7:11.

Isaiah 16:3–5.] God here adviseth the Moabites to be kind to the seed of Israel as the likeliest way to lengthen out their tranquillity. The Prophet foresaw some storm coming upon the people of God, perhaps the good people of the Ten Tribes, or of the two tribes and an half on the other side Jordan, whose country joined to that of Moab, and who by the merciful providence of God escaped the fury of the Assyrian army, had their lives given 'em for a prey, and were reserved for better times, but were put to the utmost extremity to shift for their own safety. The danger and trouble they were in was like the scorching heat at noon. He bespeaks a shelter for them in the land of Moab, and that they would not discover those that absconded among them, nor deliver them up to the pursuers that made search for them. "Bewray not him that wandereth," nor deliver him up as the Edomites did (Obadiah 13-19), but "hide the outcasts." This was that good work by which Rahab's faith was justified and proved to be sincere (Hebrews 11:31). Thus when Daniel foretold theMS: "destruction of Bes Belohazzar ‹Judgments of God on Nebuchadnezzar›." judgments of God on Nebuchadnezzar, he advised him to break off his sins by righteousness, and his transgressions by showing mercy to the poor, if it might be a lengthening of his tranquillity (Daniel 4:27). In the fourth and fifth

<!-- p. 647 -->

verses, God assures Moab of the mercy he had in store for his people, that they should not long need their kindness, and that they should ere long be in a capacity to return their kindness. Though the throne of the Ten Tribes be sunk and overturned, yet the throne of David should be established in mercy. It was their interest to make Hezekiah their friend by doing him justice, paying him his due tribute, and treating his people with kindness in the time of their affliction, because God would soon consume their oppressors, as he did by destroying Sennacherib's army, and then his throne should be established. They should not insult even the calamities of those that God was about so wonderfully to fight for and deliver. When they saw the calamity of God's people, they would be in danger of thinking that now they were going to be utterly ruined, and so to insult 'em, and help forward the affliction; but they were mistaken.

Isaiah 16:8. "They are come even unto Jazer; they wandered through the wilderness. Her branches are stretched out; they are gone over the sea."] Hereby is represented the exceeding fruitfulness of the land of Moab in vineyards. See Genesis 13:10. The vine of Moab was so spreading and flourishing that it reached "even to Jazer," a city in the tribe of Gad. The luxuriant branches of their vines wandered "through the wilderness" of Moab, and beyond the Dead Sea that was upon the borders of their country.

Isaiah 16:13. "Since that time."] I.e. since the time spoken of, Isaiah 16:6, when Moab first began to show his pride, and haughtiness, and wrath against God's people, and to threaten and insult them.

Isaiah 16:14. "As the years of an hireling."] I.e. it is only the more strongly to denote that the time is limited and determined, agreeable to Job 7:1 and Job 14:6, and not that three years were any more the years of an hireling, than two years or one year, as is evident by Isaiah 21:16.

Isaiah 17:6–7.] Thus after the captivities of the Ten Tribes, there were yet some of them left in the land in Josiah's time that joined with Judah in the true worship of God (2 Chronicles 34:9 and 2 Chronicles 35:18). And some of them returned when the Jews returned from captivity, as evident by 1 Chronicles 9:3, and Luke 2:36; James 1:1; Acts 26:7.

Isaiah 17:12–14.] Fulfilled in the destruction of Sennacherib's army by the angel.

<!-- p. 648 -->

Isaiah 17:13. "A rolling thing before the whirlwind."] See Psalms 83:13.

Isaiah 17:14. "Behold at eventide trouble."] I.e. trouble to God's people. Rabshakeh and his army shall be very troublesome in the evening, but "before the morning he is not."

Isaiah 18:1. "Shadowing with wings."] I.e. covering with wings, or protecting the chickens when under the covert of the hen's wings, in their way of expressing it, were under the shadow of her wings. Egypt and Ethiopia were lands shadowing the Jews with their wings. They had their dependence upon 'em for safeguard and protection. Isaiah 20:5–6, "And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory. And the inhabitants of this isle," etc. They trusted in the shadow of these countries (Isaiah 30), and the "trust in the shadow of Egypt" shall be your confusion. So Isaiah 30:2.

Isaiah 18:2. "*Saying*, Go, ye swift messengers."] The word "Saying," which is not in the original,קַים מַלְאָכִים לְבוּ seems to be ill supplied. The words, "Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled," seem rather to be the words of the Most High, signifying that the messengers shall be disappointed and ashamed of the nation that they had entered into alliance with, being a nation that were in such miserable circumstances that their alliance could be of no benefit to 'em. See Isaiah 30:4–5, which place abundantly confirms this interpretation.This paragraph was written as a separate entry later than the following paragraph.

"Whose land the rivers have spoiled." I.e. the rivers of Chaldea, Euphrates and Tigris, Pison and Gihon,Pison and Gihon are two of the four rivers that issued from the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:10–14). Ancient traditions held that the four encircled the entire earth. that were in those days called "the rivers." See note on Isaiah 28:17.

Isaiah 19:1. "The Lord… shall come into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence."] Joseph and Mary, when they fled into Egypt from Herod, came to "Hermopolis, a city of Thebais. There it was that Jesus being carried into a temple, all the statues of the idols fell down, as may be collected from Eusebius, *Demonstration Evangel*.,*Demonstration of the Gospel* sets out to prove Christianity by reference to the Old Testament. Athanasius,

<!-- p. 649 -->

*Lib. de Incarnatione Verbi*,Athanasius (c. 296–373), Bishop of Alexandria, author of *The Incarnation of the Word of God*. and other ancient writers." Reading, *Evangelical History*, p. 51.William Reading, *The HISTORY of Our Lord and Saviour JESUS CHRIST* (4th ed. London, 1737), pp. 50–51. Part I contains the history of Jesus, "from the Conception to the Imprisonment of John the Baptist."

Isaiah 19:1–2 ff.] Fulfilled in the intestine divisions of Egypt, and wars between the twelve confederated sovereigns of the land falling out among themselves, and at last all conquered by Psammitichus. See Prideaux, *Connection*, vol. 1, p. 46.*Old and New Testament Connected* (10th ed.), Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 46–47. See Henry.This reference is a later addition. *Exposition, 4* (1725), 54.

Isaiah 19:17. "And the land of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt."] I.e. the destruction that they shall see brought upon Judah their ally, and the power of the common enemy which shall be seen in the conquest of Judah. See Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 55.

Isaiah 21:1.] "Babylon is here called the desert, or plain of the sea, because it was a flat country, and full of lakes like little seas, and was abundantly watered by the many streams of the river Euphrates." (See Henry.)Ibid., 58. Herein it was a type of the spiritual Babylon, that "great whore that sitteth upon many waters" [Revelation 17:1]. It is said to Babylon, Jeremiah 51:13, "O thou that dwellest upon the waters." "Some think it is here called a desert because though now it was a populous city, yet in time it should become a desert." Henry.Ibid.

Isaiah 21:2. "The treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously."] This is agreeable to the manner of Babylon's being taken the first time, when Gobrias and Gadates, two of the king of Babylon's principal nobility and governors of provinces of the country, being injured by their master, revolted and went over to Cyrus, and betrayed their provinces into his hands, and enabled him to penetrate into the heart of the country, and were guides to Cyrus's forces when they entered the city in the night. Those that entered

<!-- p. 650 -->

it at one end had Gadates, and those at the other had Gobrias for their guides.Gobrias, a Persian, and Gadates, an Assyrian, slayed the king of Babylon when Babylon fell to the Persians under Cyrus. See Prideaux, Pt. I, pp. 160 and 171.*Old and New Testament Connected* (10th ed.), Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 160, 171.

"The treacherous dealer dealeth treacherously." This is alsoJE deleted "especially." agreeable to the manner of Babylon's being taken the second time, when the city was taken by the treachery of Zopyrus. See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 266–67.Zopyrus, loyal to Darius, feigned desertion and deceived Babylon, thereby contributing to its conquest by Darius and the Persians (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 266–67). See the preceding paragraph.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"All the sighing thereof have I made to cease." I.e. the sighing of the captived people with which Babylon was full.This paragraph, also a separate entry, has been relocated from the place where JE erroneously entered it.

Isaiah 21:3.] What is said in this verse is very agreeable to the sudden and surprising manner in which Babylon was taken. See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 170 ff.The conquest of Babylon and the slaying of its king and courtiers occurred during the time of a great annual festival in a night of drunkenness and reveling in the city (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 170 ff.).

Isaiah 21:4.] This also is exceeding agreeable to [the] manner of Babylon's being taken, for Babylon was surprised, and the hearts of the inhabitants surprised with terror and amazement in the night, and the night of their pleasure. See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 170 ff.See the preceding note (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 170 ff.).

Isaiah 21:3–4.] These two verses were literally fulfilled in Belshazzar.

Isaiah 21:5] This verse seems to have reference to Babylon's being taken in the time of a feast.

Isaiah 21:9. "And all the graven images," etc.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 347.Prideaux interprets the destruction of the temples and images of Bel and Merodach in Babylon by Xerxes as fulfillment of this prophecy (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 347).

<!-- p. 651 -->

Isaiah 21:11–12. "Watchman, what of the night?" etc.] One is represented in vision as calling to the Prophet "out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night?" etc., the usual call to a watchman in the night to inquire what he has observed. The watchman replies, "The morning cometh, and also the night. If ye will inquire, inquire ye; return, come." The answer is, There is a morning coming, a short time of light and prosperity in Idumea, and then follows a dark night quickly upon it. Therefore if ye inquire of the Lord, don't be hypocritical, but in good earnest in it, showing a disposition to comply with the direction that shall be given (See Ezekiel 7:16, Lamentations 5:21, Jeremiah 31:18.), and improve this morning, this short day of grace and space to repent in, to return to God from whom you Idumeans have departed, and come immediately before the night comes.

It was now a time of night, a dark time in Idumea as well as the neighbor nations. A dark cloud hung over them, for the king of Assyria's armies were now ravaging the neighboring countries (See the foregoing ch., Isaiah 20:1, and 2 Kings 18.); andJE deleted "Edom." Idumea seemed to be in imminent danger. But 'tis here foretold that this cloud should blow over. These armies should not destroy Idumea. This night of darkness should pass away by the miraculous destruction of Sennacherib's army, and a morning of light and peace follow to continue a little while. But it should soon be followed with a dark night, when Nebuchadnezzar should actually destroy Idumea, agreeable to Jeremiah 27:3–11, and Jeremiah 9:26, and Jeremiah 49:7–22. They are exhorted to take this opportunity to return to God, to improve this day of God's patience.

The Edomites were justly accounted backsliders, having forsaken the God of Isaac their father, as the Ammonites are spoken of as backsliders (Jeremiah 49:4), having forsaken the God of their father Lot. Therefore they are here fitly called upon by the Prophet to return.This and the preceding paragraph are later additions.

Isaiah 21:12. "The morning cometh, and also the night."] The day of the Lord, that is a lightsome day to some, is darkness and not light to others. The acceptable year of the Lord is also the day of vengeance of our God. When God's hand is known towards his servants, his indignation is known toward his enemies.This sentence is a later addition.

<!-- p. 652 -->

Isaiah 21:13. "In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge," etc.] You "that used to keep the high roads with your caravans, shall be obliged to quit them, and lodge 'in the forest in Arabia.'" Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 59.

Isaiah 21:14.] Probably "theJE deleted "inhabitants." land of Tema" lay next to that of Dedan,Tema and Dedan were localities in Arabia. so that the Dedanim, when they fled from the drawn sword and bent bow Isaiah 21:15], came thither. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 59.

Isaiah 21:16.] See notes on Isaiah 16:14.

Isaiah 25:7.] The "covering" that is here spoken of is the covering of ignorance and blindness that hinders them from discerning spiritual things. In the Isaiah 29:10, the ignorance of the prophets, and rulers, and seers is represented by that, that God had "covered" them.

Isaiah 25:11.] He that "spreadeth forth his hands" intimates that he will employ and exert his power vigorously for his people and against their enemies, that he will work with a strong hand and a stretched-forth arm. Yea, in that great day he shall as it were stretch forth both his hands. He shall be doing and bringing great things to pass on every side, and continually. Thus he will surmount all opposition from the evil of the world. Sin and calamity, which are often in Scripture represented by water, he shall vigorously and mightily appear above them, and go through them.

Isaiah 26:7.] Or, "God's way to the just is uprightness." See Hervey's *Dialogues*, vol. 2, p. 221 margin.Hervey writes, "Not—*The Way of the Just is Uprightness*—This is a Sense, scarcely consistent with Humility; and by no means proper, to introduce a devotional Address to the great JEHOVAH. Rather—*GOD's Way to the Just is Uprightness*; or, still more emphatically, *Uprightnesses*. Is in all Respects irreprovable, excellent, admirable; suited to his sacred Attributes of Wisdom, Goodness, and Truth" (*Dialogues, 2*, 221–22, note).

Isaiah 27:9.] The altar of wicked men is their own dignity and worthiness. On this altar they offer up their sacrifices to God; and this is the altar which in their eyes sanctifies the gift, as the dignity of Christ's person was the altar on which he offered his sacrifice. Isaiah 27:12. "Shall beat off."] I.e. "shall beat off" the enemies of my people, and make the whole land between the river of Egypt and Euphrates clear, that Israel may possess the whole, as the heathens were beat off and driven out of the land of Canaan when they came out of Egypt. This was the borders of the land which God promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), and 'tis prophesied that this should be Israel's possession in gospel times (Zechariah 9:10, Psalms 72:8).

Or else the wordsםִצְרָים עַד־נַחַל הַנָּהָר מִשִּׁבֹּלֶת יְהוֹה should have been translated, "The Lord shall strike off," or "smite away," or "powerfully and suddenly remove,JE deleted "both the or destroy." both the channel of the river and the stream of Egypt," for so the words might properly have been rendered; and so this prophecy is much like that, Isaiah 11:15.

Isaiah 28:1. "Woe to the crown of pride, to the drunkards of Ephraim."] The drunkards here spoken of were the chief and leading men in the land, men in office, and of authority and influence, as appears by the Isaiah 28:6–7, therefore called "the crown" and "the crown of pride," for their pride mentioned and described in the Isaiah 28:14, Isaiah 28:15, and Isaiah 28:22. Drunkenness is most unsuitable in rulers, judges, and officers because it caused them to err in judgment and their public work (Isaiah 28:7). Ecclesiastes 10:16–17, "Woe to thee, O land," etc.

The land of Ephraim was a country full of fat and fertile valleys abounding with fruitful vineyards. The "head" of those "fat valleys" was the royal family, or the king and his court. "Which are on the head"עַל־רֹאשׁ אֲשֶׁר might as well have been rendered, "which is on the head," i.e. the crown, or glorious beauty.

<!-- p. 655 -->

Isaiah 28:5. "In that day shall the Lord of hosts be for a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty," etc.] Instead of that "crown of pride," and that "fading flower upon the head of the fat valleys," mentioned in the Isaiah 28:1.

When Ephraim was destroyed, the residue of the people was Judah and those that joined with them. This was fulfilled in the days of Hezekiah, but more fully in the days of the Messiah.

Isaiah 28:7. "But they also have erred," etc.] This is Judah as well as Ephraim. They apostatized after the reformation in Hezekiah's time, and the bigger part of them erred in Christ's and the apostles' times.

Isaiah 28:9–11.] In the Isaiah 28:9, those that are the subjects of divine teaching are represented as little children lately weaned from the mother's breast. So all must become as little children in order [to] the being true disciples, and must also be weaned from worldly enjoyments, which are as it were the mother's breasts to natural men. What is said in the Isaiah 28:10–11 seems to allude to the method of instructing children, viz. by little and little, by continued and often repeated precepts and instructions, and particularly the manner of teaching them to read, which was to teach them a line at a time, and so one line after another. And God's speaking to them "with stammering lips" seems to allude to our way of talking with children wherein we are wont to conform to them, and stammer, or talk brokenly, as they do. But that God would speak to 'em in a strange language is the thing chiefly intended. See Isaiah 33:19.This reference and the preceding sentence are a later addition. But God seems here to have a special eye to the times of the gospel when God dealt with the church as a mother does when weaning of it from the breast. See notes on Genesis 21:8–9. And he gradually instructed his people in the spiritual and sublime doctrines of the gospel as they were able to bear and receive them. There was "precept upon precept, line upon line, here a little, and there a little," much after the same manner as when a father instructs a child. And then God spoke to them with another tongue, as the apostles did at the pouring out of the Spirit of God at Pentecost and afterwards. And these very words are applied to that by the Apostle (1 Corinthians 14:21).

The church then was in her weaning state, weaning from the carnal ordinances, the breasts of the Jewish church, the mother of God's people, which was typified by Isaac's weaning [Genesis 21:8]. (See notes.) Speaking to the church "with stammering lips and another tongue" was

<!-- p. 656 -->

then accomplished in two respects. 1. By the apostles' and others' speaking and preaching the gospel with strange tongues. And 2. By the calling of the Gentiles, a people of strange tongues, whereby they became the teachers of the Jews, for the church is the pillar and ground of truth to exhibit it to the world.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 28:11.] Here in this chapter the Prophet speaks interchangeably of blessings upon God's people, and judgments upon the drunkards of Ephraim. In the Isaiah 28:5–6 are concerning the one, and the Isaiah 28:7–8 of the other; Isaiah 28:9–10 of the one, and the Isaiah 28:11–13 of the other; the Isaiah 28:16 and part of the Isaiah 28:17 of the one, and the following words of the other.

Isaiah 28:15. "When the overflowing scourge shall pass through."] Reference is here had to what was said in the Isaiah 28:2.JE wrote this as an addition to the following entry on the same verse by Pierpont: "intrench yms within ye line of yr own carnal confidences."

"We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement." This has respect to their covenant with Egypt, which they looked upon to be so powerful, and a people that had so much the power of life and death, that they thought that making a covenant with them was a kind of making a covenant with death. This covenant of theirs with Egypt is often spoken of by the Prophet, as Isaiah 31 throughout, and Isaiah 30 at the beginning. "For we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves." By lies and falsehood is meant the same false, deceitful refuge; not that they called it falsehood, but that God knew it to be so. He knew that Egypt, whom they trusted in, would be treacherous to them, and would be false to their covenant with them, and this is the bed on which they would rest, and the covering with which they would cover themselves, as Isaiah 28:20.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Isaiah 28:16. "He that believeth shall not make haste."] Compare this with Deuteronomy 20:3. "Let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble." In the original,יָחִישׁ לא "Do not make haste."

Isaiah 28:17. "Judgment also will he lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet."] I.e. in building upon that foundation.

<!-- p. 657 -->

Entries on the book of Isaiah, showing the extra double pages of foolscap. Courtesy of Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

<!-- p. 658 -->

"The hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place." By the hail is meant the northern army of Assyria, as northern armies are represented by hail in Revelation. This "hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies," that is, Egypt. (See note on Isaiah 28:15, above.) "The waters shall overflow the hiding place," i.e. the waters of the river Euphrates. The coming of the armies of Chaldea is compared to the overflowing of that river (Isaiah 8:6–8). So 'tis said, Isaiah 18:2 and Isaiah 18:7, "whose land the rivers have spoiled," i.e. the rivers of Chaldea, viz. Tigris, Euphrates, etc.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 28:18. "When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then shall ye be trodden down by it."] Still referring to what was said in the Isaiah 28:2–3.

Isaiah 28:23.] This parable is ushered in with a solemn preface demanding attention, as Christ used often to annex these words to his parables, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."See, for example, Mark 4:9.

Isaiah 28:23–29.] What is designed here seems to be that God deals with his people as a prudent husbandman with his field and with his grain, for God's people are his "husbandry" (1 Corinthians 3:9). Christ says his "Father is the husbandman" (John 15:1), and under this comparison God here shows what is the reason of the afflictions and judgments that he brings upon them. God had, in the preceding part of the chapter, been setting forth the judgment that should be brought on the land. He here teaches the gracious design he had in it to his people, as 'tis common throughout this prophecy to intermix threatenings of judgments with promises of succeeding mercy. Here, first, God deals with his people as a prudent husbandman deals with his field. First he plows his field, and breaks the hard clods, and makes smooth the roughnesses of it, makes plain the face of it, and so fits and prepares it, and then sows his seed. So God, by the afflictions he brings on his people, he doth as it were plow and mellow the hard ground, and breaks the hard clods, and evens their roughnesses to fit them to receive the seed, and to bring forth good fruit. And as the plowman plows the ground no more and no longer than is needful to fit it for the seed ("Doth the plowman plow all day to sow?"), so God will afflict his people no more, and hold 'em under affliction no

<!-- p. 659 -->

longer than to fit them for spiritual good. And as the husbandman suits his seed to his ground, he casts in "the wheat in the principal place," as it is rendered in the margin,I.e. margin of the KJV. and the barley and the rye into ground that is suitable for them. So God deals with his people. He deals with everyone according to their needs, deals forth those blessings that are most fit for them. That which is fit for one is not fit for another. Everyone has his distinct sort of gifts, and brings forth their distinct sort of fruit, each one according to his capacity, temper, and circumstances. If the husbandman has this discretion in managing his field, much more shall he have in dealing with his people who gives the husbandman that discretion, and is the fountain of all wisdom and prudence.

Secondly, God deals with his people in the afflictions he brings upon them as the husbandman deals with his grain when he threshes it. The end of his threshing it is not to break or bruise the grain, but to cleanse it, to separate it from the husk, and fit it for the owner's use. So God's end in the afflictions he brings on his people is not to injure his people, but to purify them, and to separate them from their sins, and wean them from the world, and fit them for God's use. And as the husbandman uses discretion in threshing his grain—one sort of grain he threshes in one manner, and another in another, as shall best suit the several sorts of grain, and tend most to separating of it from the husk without bruising it—and the husbandman shows his discretion also in the degree of his threshing, he won't be ever threshing it. He'll thresh no longer than till he has separated the grain, and not so as to bruise it. So God deals wisely with his people in the degree and kind of afflictions he brings on them. He will bring various afflictions on various sorts of persons, such [as] are suitable for them; and he will afflict them no more than is for their good. Thus is God wonderful in counsel, and excellent in working, and does everything in the wisest and best manner. God's people are elsewhereJE deleted "frequently compared to." called his grain, and his harvest, and the like. See the Isaiah 27:7–10.

Isaiah 29:1–2.] The Jews were wont (as Bedford, in his *Scripture Chronology*, says, p. 568) to call the altar "Ariel,אֲרִיאֵל or the lion of God." Here God "calls Jerusalem itself by the same name, the one being remarkable for devouring sacrifices by fire, and the other as remarkable for devouring men

<!-- p. 660 -->

by slaughter. And now he threatens, that he would distress Ariel the city, and it should be as Ariel the altar, with abundance of slain about it." See *Scripture Chronology*, p. 670. Those that are slain in war are elsewhere compared to those that are slain and offered on the altar in sacrifice, as Isaiah 34:6, Ezekiel 39:17 ff. And the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem is particularly called God's sacrifice (Zephaniah 1:7–8).

"Ariel," the lion of God, and "Harel,"הַרְאֵל the mountain of God, seem both to be names of the altar, as in Ezekiel 43:15–16. See the original.This sentence is a later addition. So they also seem both to be names of the city of Jerusalem, the holy city, which is sometimes called "God's holy mountain," and here is called "Ariel." And probably they might both be names of the mountain of the temple, which Bedford thinks was hewn out in just the same shape with the altar. The altar itself was so great that it was like a little mountain. All three of these—the mountains on which the city was built, and the mountain on which the temple stood, and the altar—were types of Christ, who is often in Scripture compared to an high rock or mountain, and is the Lion of God.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 29:5 ff.] In this context is first a prophecy of God's judgments on Jerusalem, and then follows a prophecy of the destruction of her enemies by whom this judgment was brought upon her, and this latter begins with this verse.

Isaiah 29:6.] See Psalms 81:7, Revelation 16:18 ff., and Revelation 11:19.

Isaiah 29:9. "Stay yourselves, and wonder."] I.e. "stay yourselves" on Egypt, and on your rulers and prophets, mentioned, Isaiah 29:10, Isaiah 29:14. And you shall wonder what they stagger at; they shall strangely fail you.

Isaiah 29:16.] Their altering God's commands and the religious constitution of Israel,JE later deleted "and his worship," and replaced it with "and the religious constitution of Israel." and finding fault with his institutions, as though he had not appointed and ordered things in the best and wisest way, and imagining that they could mend it, is as if the potter's clay should rise up and find fault with the wisdom of the potter, as though he had not made it right or in the best manner. See Isaiah 29:13. So Antichrist changed times and laws.JE added this sentence at the same time he altered the beginning of the entry.

<!-- p. 661 -->

Isaiah 29:17.] This signifies the rejecting the Jews, and calling of the Gentiles.

Isaiah 29:18.] 'Tis the same book spoken of in the Isaiah 29:11–12.

Isaiah 30:1. "That cover with a covering, but not of my spirit."] I.e. that they are not directed to by my spirit, as in the next verse.

Isaiah 30:2.] Israel's trusting in Egypt, their old taskmasters, is a type of persons' trusting in their own righteousness for salvation, or which is the same thing, trusting in the law, that as we are by nature holds in bondage, and is a taskmaster like the Egyptians. It sets us a task that we can never do. Israel, in trusting in Egypt, trusted to an enemy that would at last appear against them, and not for them. So those that trust in the law to justify, trust in that which will condemn them. John 5:45, "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one that accuseth you, even Moses, in whom ye trust."

Isaiah 30:8–10.] Such passages as these are a notable evidence that these books of the prophets were not forged by the Jews, and were not received with such respect, and made so much of by them, but because they were of divine authority.

Isaiah 30:12. "And trust in oppression and perverseness."] Or as it is in the margin,I.e. margin of the KJV. "in fraud and perverseness." The same is meant as in Isaiah 28:15. By making "lies" their refuge, and hiding themselves "under falsehood," i.e. in Egypt. (See notes on that verse.) This appears by what follows in this chapter.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. God, on account of the wickedness of the Egyptians of old in oppressing his people, and the exceeding stubbornness and perverseness of Pharaoh and the Egyptians under God's commands and chastisements, forbid his people ever having any intercourse, or making any alliance with that people,JE deleted "any more." to all generations as a proper testimony of their abhorrence of this their "oppression and perverseness" (Deuteronomy 17:16, Exodus 13:17, Numbers 14:3–4). Therefore when instead of giving such a testimony of their abhorrence of their "oppression and perverseness," they made alliance with this people, they did as it were make friendship with "oppression and perverseness." And when they trusted in them, they trusted "in oppression and perverseness."

<!-- p. 662 -->

Isaiah 30:25. "In the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall."] This day seems to be the same time spoken of in Revelation 16:18–20. "And there was a great earthquake," etc. "And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. And great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath. And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found." And there probably in this place may be some reference to what had been said before, Isaiah 2:12 ff. "For the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon… all the high mountains, and upon all the hills that are lifted up, and upon every high tower, and upon every fenced wall." And Isaiah 25:12, speaking of Moab as implying the whole company of the enemies of the church, "And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust." And Isaiah 26:5, "For he bringeth down them that dwell on high; the lofty city, he layeth it low. He layeth it low, even to the ground; he bringeth it even to the dust."

Isaiah 30:27-31:9.] See no. 218.*Works, 15*, 151–53.

Isaiah 30:29.] See note on John 8:12. It was probably the custom when the people were about to go up to Zion, to the feasts of the Lord there, that they rose early while it was yet night, and that then they arose with songs and instruments of music. See note on Jeremiah 30:6.

Isaiah 31:1–2.] As they are strong, so he is wise, and able to baffle their strength; or he is wise as well as they. The Egyptians boasted of their wisdom and policy, as Isaiah 19:11–12. And they were famed for their policy in the world, and on this account the people of Judah trusted in them.

Isaiah 31:3. "Horses flesh, and not spirit."] Here I would observe that they of old time under the old testament accounted spirits a distinct kind of beings or substances from bodies, and so that when the spirit of man is spoken of, a distinct substance from his body is meant; and also that spirits are a much more perfect kind of beings than bodies are; and also that they were a sort of beings capable of subsisting in themselves without dependence upon flesh or body. The body is called the sheath of the spirit (Daniel 7:15), as it is in the original.נִדְנֶה בְּגוּ רוּחִי

<!-- p. 663 -->

Isaiah 31:5. "As birds flying."] The comparison of a lion in the foregoing verse represents the power with which God would defend his people, and anger towards their enemies. The comparison in this verse represents the mercy with which he will defend them, and tenderness and love toward them. God's care of his people is often represented by that of birds towards their young. Here 'tis represented as though God would come with like speed and great concern to defend his people, as birds do when their young are attacked.

"'Passing over he will preserve it.' The wordעָבַר for 'passing over' is used in this sense only here, and Exodus 12:12, Exodus 12:23, Exodus 12:27, concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites, when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this refers here. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that destroyed and drew his sword only against the besiegers." (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 90. The like should be afterwards from time to time with respect to the Christian church.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 31:9. "Fire is in Zion."] See no. 378.*Works, 15*, 362–63.

Isaiah 32:1. "And princes shall rule in judgment."] Psalms 45:16, 1 Samuel 2:8, Revelation 5:10, Matthew 19:28.

Isaiah 32:2.] No. 261.Ibid., 207–8.

Isaiah 32:2. "As rivers of water in a dry place."] See no. 213.Ibid., 144–45.

Isaiah 32:3.] Which intimates that at other times men see, and yet their eyes are dim or blind, and hear, and yet are deaf. And there seems to be respect here to what was said in the Isaiah 6:9, "Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not," which Christ refers to, Matthew 13:13–14. "They seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand. And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Esaias which saith, By hearing ye shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing ye shall see, and shall not perceive." And this

<!-- p. 664 -->

Prophet refers to this again in the Isaiah 43:8. "Bring forth the blind people that have eyes, and the deaf that have ears."

Isaiah 32:5. "The vile person shall no more be called liberal," etc.] 'Tis a note of a very evil and corrupt time when very bad men, becauseMS: "many that ‹the Generality›." the generality are a great deal worse, are accounted good.

Isaiah 32:14. "Dens forever."] This is a plain instance of the word "forever" being used in Scripture for a limited time, or till the end of that age or course of things in providence, or that grand period the end of which in many respects resembles the end of the world. This prophecy seems to have an eye to several things. 1. The destruction of many of the cities of Judah by Sennacherib, some of which were probably never rebuilt again. 2. The destruction of all the cities of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar, many of which never were rebuilt again. Last, the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, which is not built again till the end of that grand period of many ages, the end of the church's troubles, and the Spirit be poured from on high, etc., as in the next verse.

Or rather, it signifies that the wicked hypocritical city should forever be destroyed, that Jerusalem that is built afterwards is not represented as being the same. 'Tis no revival of that false church that was before, which is sunk forever, but is a New Jerusalem. As in repentance, the old man is destroyed forever and its former comforts; the comforts that are afterwards are of another kind and from another source. "The forts and towers" which it is said "shall be dens forever" represent the false confidences, and high, and towering, and self-confident imaginations of hypocrites.

Isaiah 32:15.] Note on Isaiah 35:1.

Isaiah 32:17. "And the work of righteousness shall be peace."] See note on James 3:18.

Isaiah 32:19.] "The city shall be low in a low place."] Not exalted with high towers which shall be forever demolished, as Isaiah 32:14, but shall be low and humble "in a low place," in a secure valley sheltered from the violence of the tempest by mountains round about. See Isaiah 32:2 and Isaiah 32:18. Low in the valley,

<!-- p. 665 -->

secured from the force of the wind, but beside plentiful waters for her supply. See next v.JE deleted "See Psalms 72:6."

Isaiah 33:17–19.] The Prophet seems to speak here interchangeably of hypocrites, mentioned in the Isaiah 33:14, and the sincere, spoken of in the Isaiah 33:15 The former part of this Isaiah 33:17 is to be understood of the one; the latter part, "they shall behold the land that is very far off," is to be understood of the other, that is, the wicked shall be carried captive into a far country (Deuteronomy 28:49, Deuteronomy 28:64; Isaiah 13:5). And so the Prophet continues speaking of them, in the Isaiah 33:18 and again the Isaiah 33:19, as of the righteous. See no. 214.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 145–46.

Isaiah 33:21.] "Jerusalem had no considerable river running by it," as the royal cities in Egypt, and Assyria, and Chaldea, "and most great cities had, nothing but the brook Kidron, upon which account their enemies despised them." Nor did the children of Israel deal much in ships, as Egypt, and Assyria, and Chaldea did, and carried on their wars in considerable measure by them.JE deleted, "Their cry was in the ships." See Isaiah 43:14. But in God there shall be more than an equivalent. The glorious *Jehovah* will be to Jerusalem "a place of broad rivers and streams." Thus we read of a river running through the New Jerusalem [Revelation 22:1]. But if there be broad rivers and streams about Jerusalem, may not these yield an easy access to the fleet of the invader? No, these are "rivers and streams in which shall go no galley with oars," or gallant ship. If God himself be the river, it must needs be inaccessible to the enemy. God's people need not fear, "though the earth be removed," for there is a river that "makes glad the city of God" (Psalms 46:2, Psalms 46:4). See Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 97.

Isaiah 33:23. "They could not spread the sail. Then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey."] There is probably here some reference to the same time that is foretold in Isaiah 60:9.

Isaiah 34:4. "Rolled together as a scroll."] See note on Revelation 6:14.

<!-- p. 666 -->

Isaiah 34:5. "For my sword shall be bathed in heaven."] I.e. in the blood of those that are in heaven, the kings and princes of the earth that are in the foregoing verse, as often elsewhere, compared to the stars or host of heaven. And herein the Holy Ghost seems to allude to God's coming forth with the sword of his vengeance against that multitude of angels, principalities, and powers in heavenly places that sinned in heaven, casting them down from thence. So also in Revelation 6:12–15, and Revelation 12:7–9. God's sword's being "bathed" seems to hold forth the same with God's sword's being "made drunk with blood" (Jeremiah 46:10).

Here probably is some reference that the Spirit of God has to the terrible destruction of the angels. God's sword was once bathed in the blood of angels in heaven, the consideration of which may well be a terror to other enemies of God, and particularly to the followers, subjects, and children of these fallen angels, the people of God's curse, the inhabitants of Idumea, which is Satan's kingdom on earth. As God's sword has been bathed in heaven in the blood of angels, it shall come down from thence with like fury to be bathed in like manner in the blood of those that have subjected themselves to Satan as their king, and listed under him as their captain. As the sword of God's vengeance was first wielded in heaven against the angels, so the other terrible judgments that God executes against them when he destroys their kingdom on earth is represented as being in a war that is carried on in heaven against the devil and his angels, particularly in the destruction of his Romish kingdom (Revelation 12), of which Idumea is a type. Satan, by exalting himself to the throne of the kingdoms of this world, and usurping the authority of God of this world, is in Scripture represented as ascending to and reigning in heaven. The devils are principalities, and powers, and spiritual wickedness in heavenly places.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Isaiah 34:6. "The Lord hath a sacrifice."] See note on Zephaniah 1:7–8.

Isaiah 34:9–10.] See no. 276, concerning the destruction of Sodom.*Works, 15*, 232–33.

Isaiah 34:11. "Stones of emptiness."] I.e. bound stones.וְאַבְנֵי־בֹהוּ It shall be measured and marked out to confusion and emptiness. See Lamentations 2:8.

<!-- p. 667 -->

Isaiah 34:16.] The "book of the Lord" here meant is this book, or the book of this prophecy, wherein the things mentioned in the two foregoing verses are mentioned, as appears by comparing these words with the foregoing and following. When it is said here, "Seek you out of the book of the Lord," etc., the meaning is, Hereafter when the event shall prove whether this prophecy be true or no, then read this book, and examine this prophecy, and compare it with the event, and see if anything fails. See if any one of these doleful creatures fails of possessing Idumea and Bozrah, and everyone with their mate, i.e. see if the prophecy ben't most exactly fulfilled.

*Corol*. Hence, the books of the prophets should be regarded by the church of God as part of the canon of sacred Scripture, as well as the books of Moses; they are the books of the Lord, or *Biblia*.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 35:1. "The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them."] I.e. for the beasts of the desert, the satyr and the owl, etc., spoken of in the last verses of the Isaiah 34. That which used to be a wilderness and a solitary place where they used to haunt, and was therefore a doleful place, it shall be new, be glad, and rejoice at their absence. They shall no more dwell there (See Isaiah 35:7 and Isaiah 35:9.), and so it shall cease to be a wilderness and solitary place any longer. It shall be turned in[to] a pleasant fruitful field, and shall "blossom as the rose," as it follows. And the place that used to be as a flourishing prosperous field shall be turned into a wilderness and solitary place, henceforward to be the haunt of those doleful creatures, as in Isaiah 29:17 and Isaiah 32:15.

Isaiah 35:6–7.] See note on Exodus 17:6.

Isaiah 35:10. "And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads."] Here is an allusion to the manner of the children of Israel when they went up to the house of the Lord at the feasts of the Passover, Pentecost, and tabernacles, who were wont to go singing and playing with instruments of music, as appears by Isaiah 30:29, and also Psalms 42:4, and probably with other tokens of joy, as a garland or crown of joy on their heads. For we often read of a "crown of rejoicing"E.g. 1 Thessalonians 2:19. in Scripture, which doubtless we should not, were

<!-- p. 668 -->

it not the manner amongst the Jews to manifest their joy by a crown or something of that nature on their heads.

Isaiah 36-39.] The history that we have in this and the following chapters is thus inserted into this book of Isaiah's prophecies, and after the prophecies in the foregoing chapters, because the great works of God towards his people and their enemies recorded in this history is a fulfillment of some of these prophecies, and is a specimen and earnest of other things, even the principal things contained in those foregoing prophecies, which respect God's judgments on his people by their enemies, and the great destruction that God will bring on the proud and powerful enemies of his church, and the great deliverance and prosperity which he will bring to pass for them, as Christ's transfiguration soon followed Christ's prediction of his coming in his kingdom as an earnest of it.

Isaiah 37:7. "Behold, I will send a blast upon him."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 35.Prideaux equates the "blast" with the hot winds that can kill travelers in the Arabian desert (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 35).

Isaiah 37:30–31.] The sign mentioned in the Isaiah 37:30 is a type of what is promised in the Isaiah 37:31: the corn's springing again after it had been cut off with the sickle, and bringing forth another crop from the roots that seemed to be dead, and so once and again represents the church's reviving again as it were out of its own ashes, and flourishing like a plant after it had been seemingly destroyed and past recovery. When the enemies of the church have done their utmost, and seem to have gained their point, and to have overthrown the church so that the being of it is scarcely visible, yet there is a second life in it that will cause it to flourish again, and to "take root downward, and bear fruit upward." This was fulfilled now at this time, for the king of Assyria had already taken and carried captive the Ten Tribes, and Sennacherib had also taken all the fenced "cities of Judah" (as in the Isaiah 36:1), and had ravaged all the country round about; and Jerusalem only remained. And Rabshakeh had in his own imagination already swallowed that up, as he had also in the fearful apprehensions of the Jews themselves. But yet God wrought wonderful deliverance. But this had a more remarkable accomplishment in the Jews' return from

<!-- p. 669 -->

their captivity, and has often been wonderfully accomplished. These revivals of the church, they are all shadows and resemblances of the last resurrection, which is in Scripture represented by the springing of a plant out of the earth, from a seemingly dead root or seed, as Isaiah 66:14. "Your bones shall flourish like an herb." And Isaiah 26:19, "Thy dead men shall live; together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in the dust; for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead." So John 12:24 and 1 Corinthians 15:36–38.

The remnant that was escaped of the house of Judah appeared like the hopeless remnant of the corn after the top and fruit was cut off with the sickle; but yet it again took root downward, and bore fruit upward once and again, once now after the land had been wasted by the kings of Assyria, first the Ten Tribes, and then the kingdom of Judah, and again after the destruction of the land by the king of Babylon, to represent which the corn revived after it was cut down twice going. See Psalms 72:6.This and the following paragraph are later additions.

"The fruits of the earth were devoured by the Assyrians." "The Assyrians had reaped what they had sown, and the next year was the sabbatical year." Henry on 2 Kings 19:29.*Exposition, 2* (1725), 462.

Isaiah 37:38.] God pours contempt not only on this great king, but on his god. He had cast great contempt on the God of Israel, and made as though he were unable to defend Jerusalem from his power, as Isaiah 36:18–20, and in the Isaiah 37:10–13 of this chapter. This God of Israel, that he so despised as though much inferior to his god, now shows how unable his god is to defend him by ordering it so that he should be slain in the very temple of his god in whom he trusts, in his sanctuary, and in the secret of his presence, and that while he was there worshipping of him, and imploring his help under his present low and distressed circumstances, and slain too by his own sons.

Isaiah 38:5–8.] Here the resurrection of Hezekiah, the king and captain of the church (as he is called, 2 Kings 20:5), is given as an earnest of the church's resurrection and salvation, as Isaiah 38:6. And at the same time there is a resurrection of the sun, or coming back and rising again from the west whither it had gone down, which is also a type of the resurrection of Christ, the Sun of righteousness. The sun was brought back ten degrees, which probably brought it to the meridian. The Sun of righteousness has

<!-- p. 670 -->

long been going down from east to west, and probably when the time of the church's deliverance comes from her enemies, so often typified by the Assyrians, the light will arise in the west, and rise higher and higher till fixed in a meridian light, and so shall no more go down, agreeable to the Prophet. See note on Numbers 24:17.

Isaiah 38:12. "As a shepherd's tent."] "The shepherd's tent is soon removed, for the flocks must not feed long in one place." Boston's *Fourfold State of Man*.This paragraph is a later addition. *Human Nature in its Fourfold State* (4th ed.), 280–81.

"I have cut off like a weaver my life." I.e. as a weaver when he has finished his piece of cloth cuts off the thread, and cuts out the piece out of the loom, cuts it off from the thrum, so I, though I have been very busy in the world, and been filling up my life with many great acts, yet now in my thoughts and expectations I cut off the thread like a weaver. I put an end to the thread and series of all my designs and projects, having in my apprehension done all the work that God had for me to do.

Isaiah 38:13. "I reckoned till morning, that, as a lion, so will he break all my bones."] This passage seems to look as though the last agonies of death, and struggles with the king of terrors, were very terrible.

Isaiah 38:18.This entry has been marked by JE, Jr., with a large asterisk and the following: "(Quote the whole)." He also added "Isaiah 38:19" to the biblical citation. "For the grave cannot praise thee; death cannot celebrate thee. They that go down to the pit cannot hope for thy truth."] The death that is here spoken of is that which is death indeed, or is properly so called. The state of death is here spoken of as 'tis originally, and as being still a state of death, and not as 'tis changed by a redemption from a state of death to a state of life, or so as to be made a more glorious sort of life. Hezekiah speaks of that death wherein men do really die, or are truly dead, and not that improperly so called, wherein men are a thousand times more alive than they were before, and are immortal and beyond a possibility of dying. Death, as 'tis originally, and when 'tis properly death, is a state wherein men can't "praise God," nor "celebrate" him, nor "hope for his truth." 'Tis a state of evil without any good. 'Tis, as Job says, "a land of darkness, as darkness itself, and the shadow of death without any order, and where the light is as darkness" [Job 10:22].The quotation marks on this and the two preceding sentences were added by JE, Jr. 'Tis a state wherein there is no good done, no good enjoyed, no good hoped for.

<!-- p. 671 -->

'Tis a state of absolute emptiness of any good act or principle, happiness or hope. They that are in hell are in such a state of death. Such was death originally; such was death as it was threatened to our first parents. And very commonly, when death is spoken of in the Old Testament, 'tis in this notion of it, for the change of a state of death into a state of more glorious life was not fully revealed under the old testament. Life and immortality is brought to light by the gospel [2 Timothy 1:10]. 'Tis under this notion that death seems to be spoken of in Ecclesiastes 9:4–6, where it is said that "a living dog is better than a dead lion," and that "the dead have no more a reward," and that "they have no more a portion forever in anything done under the sun." Hezekiah did not mean that they that are redeemed from the power of the grave, they that get the victory over death and shall never die (as Christ promises to believers), "shall not praise God, nor hope for his truth."The quotation marks on this and the preceding sentence were added by JE, Jr.

Isaiah 38:18–19, together with Isaiah 38:11 and Isaiah 38:22.]JE, Jr., crossed out the biblical reference on the MS in an attempt to combine this paragraph with the preceding entry. We see in this instance that the better men are, the more terrible would it make death if there were no future state; for the better they are, the more they love God. Good men have found the fountain of good. Those men who have an high degree of love to God do greatly delight in God. They have experience of a much better happiness in life than others, and therefore it must be more bitter to them to have their beings eternally extinct by death. Thus this seemed to be above all other things the sting of Hezekiah's affliction in his expectation of death, that he should no more have any opportunity of communion with God, and worshipping and praising him, as appears by these two verses, together with the Isaiah 38:11 and Isaiah 38:22, there not being at that time a clear and full revelation of a future state. Hence we may strongly argue a future state; for 'tis not to be supposed that God would make man such a creature as to be capable of looking forward beyond death, and capable of knowing and loving him, and delighting in him as the fountain of all good, and should make it his duty so to do, which will necessarily increase in him a dread of annihilation, and an eager desire of immortality; and yet so order it that that desire should be disappointed, so that his loving his Creator should in some sense make him the more miserable.

<!-- p. 672 -->

Isaiah 40-66.] "At this chapter begins the latter part of the prophecy of this book, which is not only divided from the former by the historical chapters, that come between, but seems to be distinguished from it on the scope and style of it. In the former part, the name of the Prophet was frequently prefixed to the particular sermons, besides the general title, as Isaiah 2:1, and Isaiah 7:3, and Isaiah 13:1. But this is all one continued discourse, and the Prophet not so much as once named. That consisted of many burdens, many woes; this of many blessings. There the distress the people of God were in by the Assyrian, and their deliverance out of that, were chiefly prophesied" (and the future distresses of the church of God, and their great deliverance and prosperity in the days of the gospel are spoken of chiefly under these types). "But these things are here spoken of as things past (Isaiah 52:4); and the captivity in Babylon, and their deliverance out of that, which were much greater events, of more extensive and abiding concern, are here largely foretold" (and the future distresses, and glorious deliverances, and prosperity of the church in gospel times prophesied of under these types.) "As if this part of this book were designed for a prophetical summary of the New Testament, it begins with [that] which begins the gospels, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness' (Isaiah 40:3), and concludes with that which concludes the book of the Revelation, 'the new heavens and the new earth' (Isaiah 66:22)."Henry, *Exposition, 4*, 109.

It seemsMS: "'Tis probable ‹It Seems›." that Isaiah had the revelation of these glorious times of the gospel at the latter part of Hezekiah's reign, after those things had happened that we have the history of in the Isaiah 63-65, when Isaiah was in his old age. 'Tis remarkable that Moses, Isaiah, David, and the apostle John all seemed to have lived to a very great age, and all had their brightest and most glorious revelations of the future good that God would accomplish for his church in their old age, and little before the death. After [they] have long traveled toward heaven, when they come near to it, they began as it were to be in the dawning of the light of it. Isaiah prophesied about eighty or ninety years. See Roberts' *Key of the Bible*.Roberts discusses Isaiah's prophetic career as spanning the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, which he calculates as a period of sixty-four years (p. 414).

Isaiah 40:2. "Double for all her sins."] No. 317.*Works, 15*, 293–94.

<!-- p. 673 -->

Isaiah 40:3–4.] See note on Luke 3:4–5.

Isaiah 40:6.] John the Baptist was sent to prepare the way for Christ to follow by preaching the law, and thereby convincing men of their own utter insufficiency and helplessness, and thus showed that all flesh, all the strength and worthiness of men, is as grass that withers and fades away Isaiah 40:7].

Isaiah 40:15. "As the small dust of the balance."] I.e. considering the deity as in one scale, and all nations in the other, and the nations weigh nothing, there [is] no account to be made of their weight, as men in weighing make no account of the small dust that sticks to the balance.

"He taketh up the isles as a very little thing." See "Scripture," no. 485.This paragraph is a later addition. *Works, 15*, 582.

Isaiah 40:17.] I know of no place in the Bible where the infiniteness of the Divine Being is more plainly asserted.

Isaiah 40:21.] In this verse God seems to have respect to that tradition there was amongst the heathen concerning the true God and his works that had been delivered down from Adam, and Noah, and the first fathers of the nations, which traditions were found amongst the heathen long after Isaiah's time.

Isaiah 40:28. "The Creator of the ends of the earth."] I.e. of the whole earth from end to end, and particularly of those ends of the earth whence their troubles arose, and whither they were carried captive and dispersed, and of those nations that came from thence, or dwelt there, and oppressed them.

"Fainteth not, neither is weary." This is here observed because God's people's being faint and weary is here taken notice of in the two next verses. Though the church be weary, and faint, and discouraged, yet her God, her Redeemer, is not discouraged. Though their strength fails, yet his don't fail.

Isaiah 41:2.] The "righteous man" here spoken of is Abraham. See Genesis 14:14–15. See concerning this and the following verses, in note on Genesis 14:15–16 ff., no. 302.*Works, 15*, 274–76.

<!-- p. 674 -->

Isaiah 41:8. "Jacob whom I have chosen."] This epithet especially belongs to Jacob rather than to Isaac or Abraham, because God chose him before Esau his brother, though they were children of the same parents, and twins in the womb together, and though Jacob was the youngest, and chose them before they were born, or either of them had done good or evil.

Isaiah 41:15–16.] Here is threshing and winnowing, but no corn. All proves chaff; the wind carries all away. This difference is there between the effect of the threshing and winnowing of the righteous, and that of the wicked. The former is only to purify them, to separate them from the husk and chaff; the other is to destroy them. They prove nothing, and come to nothing in the threshing and winnowing, as God said to Belshazzar, "Thou art weighed in the balances, and found wanting" [Daniel 5:27]. God's church is often threshed, but it proves something else besides chaff. It is the corn of God's floor (Isaiah 21:10 and Isaiah 28:27–28). It is purified, but not destroyed by threshing. God's church stands through all generations, though the great monarchies of the earth that seem, like great mountains, to appear as great and to stand as fast, come to nothing, at length prove as the chaff that the wind drives away, as it was with Nebuchadnezzar's great image. See Revelation 2:27.

Isaiah 41:18–20.] See no. 437.Ibid., 521.

Isaiah 41:19.] The trees here mentioned are "all evergreens," as the Bishop of Petersborough observes in *Defense of Christianity*, p. 21, which represents the lasting durable nature of the blessings and comforts of the church after the days of her mourning are ended, and the everlasting duration of her happiness.Edward Chandler (1668?–1750), identified as the Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield on the title page, lists the cedar, myrtle, fir, pine, and box trees as "most desireable," in *A Defence of Christianity* (2nd ed. London, 1725).

So were most of those trees evergreens with which they were wont to keep the feast of tabernacles, mentioned in Nehemiah 8:15 and Leviticus 23:40. Indeed, "willows of the brook" are mentioned, for they represent the perpetuity and unfailing nature of the saints' life and joy another way. See Jeremiah 17:8 and Psalms 1:3; Numbers 34:6.This paragraph is a later addition.

<!-- p. 675 -->

Isaiah 41:22. "Former things."] I.e. "former things" that they have, great acts of power and wisdom that show them to be gods, or "former things" that they foretold before they came to pass. See note on Isaiah 43:9. The challenge that God makes in this and the next verse agrees well with the character that he claims as his prerogative in Isaiah 41:4. "I the Lord, the first, and with the last." See no. 438.*Works, 15*, 521–22.

Isaiah 41:25.] See no. 331.Ibid., 314–16.

Isaiah 41:26. "That we may say, He is righteous."] I.e. that his cause is good, and he is just in his pretensions in claiming the honors of a good. See Isaiah 41:21.

Isaiah 41:27. "The *first* shall say to Zion."] The same that says he is "the first, and with the last" (Isaiah 41:4).

Isaiah 42:1. "Behold my servant," etc.] This is to be connected with the Isaiah 41:27–29. "For I beheld, and there was no man," etc.; "even amongst them, and there was no counselor." When God beheld the world thus destitute of any to guide, or enlighten, or help them out of their extreme misery, then God sent his servant and his elect, etc.

Isaiah 42:2. "He shall not cry, nor lift up," etc.] "It shall not be proclaimed, 'Lo, here is Christ, or Lo, there' [Matthew 24:23], as when great princes ride in progress, or make a public entry. He shall have no trumpet sounded before him, nor any noisy retinue to follow him." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 118.

Isaiah 42:3.] See no. 79.*Works, 15*, 73. "Smoking flax." Perhaps what there is reference to is "the wick of a lamp" or candle "when first beginning to kindle," that is liable to be put out by a little wind or the least violence of motion. Doddridge on Matthew 12:20.*Family Expositor, 1*, 317.

Isaiah 42:4. "Isles shall wait for his law."] See in my book of notes on Revelation. By mistake there written, next page after number 40.*Works, 5*, 142–43.

<!-- p. 676 -->

Isaiah 42:8.] See no. 479.Ibid., *2*, 576–77.

Isaiah 42:9. "Former things."] No. 438.Ibid., 521–22.

Isaiah 42:10–12.] The songs of the Lord of old were very much confined to the temple at Jerusalem. When the Jews were in a strange land, they hung their harps on the willows, and could not sing the Lord's song (Psalms 137:2–4). Now the songs of holy joy and praise shall be sung all the world over. The Gentile nations shall share equally with the Jews in new testament blessings, and therefore shall join in the new testament praises and acts of worship. The conversion of the Gentiles is often foretold under this notion of their singing praises with God's people, as appears by Romans 15:9–11. See Isaiah 24:16.

Isaiah 42:18–20.] In these verses is a comparison between the Jews and Gentiles as they should be in gospel times. The one were deaf, and yet heard; were blind (accounted so by the Jews, and accounted so by themselves), and yet saw; were brought to the saving knowledge of the gospel. With the other that was Israel, God's servant, to whom were committed the oracles of God, and sent of God to communicate this precious treasure to others, it was the reverse. They see, and yet were blind; they heard, and yet were deaf, as Christ charged them. Seeing they saw, and saw not; hearing they heard, and understood not.
