They saw many things, and yet did not observe. They *opened the ears* of others. They were in their own apprehension pure and *perfect*. As the Apostle says, Romans 2:17–20, "Behold, thou art called a Jew, and restest in the law, and makest thy boast of God, and knowest his will, and approvest the things that are more excellent, being instructed out of the law, and art confident that thou thyself art a guide of the blind, a light of them which are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes, which hast the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law." Thus it was [with] the Jews, especially with their teachers, the priests, and scribes, and Pharisees. Thus they saw many things, and observed not; and opened the ears, and yet heard not themselves, as it follows in [the] Romans 2:21. "Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?"

Isaiah 43:3. "Ethiopia and Seba for thee."] See an account how this was done (2 Chronicles 14:9 ff.).

<!-- p. 677 -->

Isaiah 43:9. "And show us former things. Let them bring forth their witnesses."] I.e. former effects of their power, or let 'em tell us of former things, things that are already come to pass, according as they before declared, and let them bring their witnesses that they declared it before, and that it came to pass as they predicted. God hath often done this; he declared former things from the beginning before they come to pass (Isaiah 48:3, Isaiah 48:5; also Isaiah 44:7–8, and Isaiah 45:21, and Isaiah 46:9–10, and Isaiah 42:9). "Or let them hear, and say, It is truth." It seems to me itאֱמֶת וְיֹאמְרוּ וְיִשְׁמְעוּ should have been rendered, "*And* let them hear, and say, It is truth," i.e. the witnesses, and not, "*Or* let them."

No. 438.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 521–22.

Isaiah 43:21–28.] In this prophecy of the great gospel salvation, the freeness of God's grace in it as not being at all for our righteousness is largely insisted on here in the Isaiah 43:21, and also in the Isaiah 43:4, and Isaiah 43:7, and Isaiah 43:25, and beginning of Isaiah 44. The sovereign good pleasure of God and his electing love is represented as the grand original of all these blessings, and in the Isaiah 44:22 and following verses is particularly shown how it is not and cannot be for any sacrifice offered by those that are the subjects of these blessings, or any righteousness, or anything given, offered, or done by them, or anything whatsoever of their own (Isaiah 43:26). And it is particularly shown that they have nothing of their own but sins, either in themselves and in their ancestors. When the children of Israel were redeemed out of Egypt and had Canaan given them, which was a great type of the gospel redemption, great care was taken to instruct the people that it was not for their righteousness. So here, when the redemption of the children of Israel out of Babylon is spoken of (Isaiah 43:14), another great type of gospel redemption, and their redemption is prophesied of under that type, great care is also taken to inform the church that 'tis not for their righteousness. Thus this doctrine of justification by free grace, without the works of the law or our own righteousness, is the doctrine both of the old and new testament. And this confirms it, that when the Apostle so much insists on justification without the works of the law, he means without any moral goodness of ours whatsoever. Justification is the thing here especially spoken [of], as appears by [the] Isaiah 43:25–26. See Isaiah 48:9–11, with the context.

<!-- p. 678 -->

Isaiah 44:3.] That one thing meant here by God's pouring "floods on the dry ground," is his pouring out his Spirit on heathen lands or nations,MS: "nation." we may learn by what David says when he wasJE deleted "absent." in a land distant from the sanctuary of God, and destitute of all the ordinances of his worship,JE deleted "in an heathen country." Psalms 63:1–2, with the title, where he calls the wilderness of Judah "a dry and thirsty land, where no water is," because it was destitute of those things that he says he thirsts for, viz. God's ordinances, and worship, and the means of grace.

Isaiah 44:7. "Who, as I, shall call, and shall declare it, and set it in order for me, since I appointed the ancient people?"] God is here speaking to his church in the days of the gospel made up not only of Jews but Gentiles, or speaking to the Gentile nations, or heathen gods, as Isaiah 41:21–22 ff., and Isaiah 43:9, and Isaiah 45:20–21, and Isaiah 46:8–10. By the "ancient people" here is meant the nation of Israel, the people that God anciently separated, constituted, and appointed as his covenant people.JE deleted "in the wilderness." God called, declared, and set in order the great things here spoken of soon after he appointed that ancient people. The things here spoken of that God then declared are the things spoken of in the preceding verses, viz. God's pouring water on the thirsty, etc., and his calling the Gentiles, or bringing them in great multitudes to subscribe to the Lord, and call themselves "by the name of Jacob" Isaiah 44:5], etc. The predictions here referred to are probably that great promise in the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, "In thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed" [Genesis 28:14]; and that by Balaam, Numbers 24:6–7, "As the valleys are they spread forth, as the gardens by the river's side, as the trees of lign aloes which the Lord hath planted, as the cedar trees beside the waters. He shall pour water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters"; and Deuteronomy 32:36–39, and Deuteronomy 32:43, which compare with this chapter, Isaiah 44:1–8, and with Isaiah 40:1–2, Isaiah 40:12 ff., and Isaiah 41:4, Isaiah 41:22, and Isaiah 42:7–9, and Isaiah 43:9–12 with the context, and Isaiah 45:21–22, and Isaiah 46:9–10. And see also Deuteronomy 33:26–29, and compare what is there said with these passages in Isaiah and their contexts.

Isaiah 44:22. "Sing, O ye heavens, for the Lord hath done it. Shout, ye lower parts of the earth."] Hereby is signified the same as in Revelation, where

<!-- p. 679 -->

those that are "in heaven" and those that are "under the earth" are represented as praising God [Revelation 5:13], i.e. the angels of heaven, and departed saints whose bodies are buried in the lower parts of the earth. They behold and rejoice at the redemption of Israel, and the prosperity of the church, yea, at the recovery of one lost sheep. See Isaiah 49:13.

"Sing, O ye heavens." Romans 8:19 ff.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Isaiah 44:27. "That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers."] This is probably said when speaking of the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and of Cyrus and his taking Babylon, because the way in which he took Babylon was by drying up the river Euphrates.

Isaiah 45:1–2.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, 134–35, 147, 171.Prideaux describes the construction of the walls and gates in the city of Babylon, and he explains why the gates were left open at the time of the conquest by Cyrus (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 134–35, 147, 171). The brazen gates next to the river were left open for him, and God also the same night remarkably opened the gates of the palace.

"And I will loose the loins of kings." I.e. I will deprive them of strength and preparation to resist or withstand thee. Here God foretells that he "will loose the loins of the kings" that he shall fight against, but that he will gird his loins (Isaiah 45:5). God remarkably loosed the loins of Belshazzar and the princes of Babylon before Cyrus, when he caused them to quit all manner of care of their own defense, to cease to stand with loins girt to resist the enemy, to quit their arms and leave open the gates next to the river, and to drown them in luxury and drunkenness.

Isaiah 45:5–7.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 304.Prideaux suggests that these verses in Isaiah may have provided Zoroaster with ideas on which he constructed his theology regarding the origins of good and evil as well as the perpetual struggle between the two (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 304).

"I have girded thee." See note on Isaiah 45:1–2. God is here said to "create darkness," though it be a mere negative thing, and is made only by withholding light. This will justify us in understanding only of an effectual permission when God in Scripture is represented as causing the sins of men. See the doctrine of Zoroaster probably derived from this chapter, "Miscellanies," no. 1359.*Works, 23*, 713. No. 1359, entitled "EXTRACTS FROM DR. CUDWORTH CONCERNING THE OPINIONS AND TRADITIONS OF HEATHEN PHILOSOPHERS AGREEABLE TO TRUTH CONCERNING MATTERS OF RELIGION," contains extensive citations from Ralph Cudworth, *The True Intellectual System of the Universe* (London, 1678). The entry closes with a parenthetic comment, "(N.B. These things seems to have been derived from what God says to Cyrus the Persian by the prophet Isaiah, in Isaiah 45:1, Isaiah 45:5–9, Isaiah 45:21–25.)"

<!-- p. 680 -->

Isaiah 45:9–10. "Woe to him that striveth with his Maker," etc.] These verses are to teach the Jews in captivity submission to God in their captivity and great calamities, to fit 'em for that deliverance spoken of in the following verses. God is here spoken of as Israel's Maker. See Isaiah 45:11.

Isaiah 45:17–18.] See "Miscellanies," gg.*Works, 13*, 185.

Isaiah 45:19. "I said not unto the seed of Jacob."] The seed of him that wrestled with God, and as a prince had power with God, and prevailed.

Isaiah 45:20. "Ye that are escaped of the nations."] See Zechariah 14:16 note.

Isaiah 45:21. "Tell ye, and bring them near; yea, let them take counsel together. Who hath declared this from ancient time? Who hath told it from that time? Have not I the Lord? And there is no God besides me, a just God and a Savior."] "With what daring expressions to all creatures doth God challenge the honor of founding this covenant of love and peace wholly to himself? No creature did so much as put in his opinion in this counsel, or contribute anything to it, but he would go away with the whole glory himself. 'Tis not meant of the deliverance from Babylon, as some interpret it, which is evinced by the following verses, to the end of the chapter, as also Isaiah 45:17, where it is called 'an everlasting salvation,' which will admit of no shame or confusion, 'world without end,' a salvation that lasts as long as eternity endures. Justice and mercy are comprehended as the great things he glories in. 'A just God and a Savior.' He finds a way to have a valuable satisfaction of his justice, wherein should be bound up an eternal security to the sinner, a great priest for our guilt, and a beautiful pattern for our imitation. Justice should triumph in the punishment, mercy in the redemption, the creature in the fruits redounding from both." Charnock's second vol., pp. 265–66.Charnock, "A Discourse of God's Being the Author of Reconciliation," *Works* (1684) *II*, 265–66.

Isaiah 45:22–23.] See note on Matthew 28:18–19.

Isaiah 45:23.] By this it appears that when God makes a positive declaration of a future thing that he will accomplish, though there be nothing in it of

<!-- p. 681 -->

the nature of a promise by which any other can challenge a right, yet God is obliged by that declaration so that he can't declare it "in righteousness," if he should fail of accomplishing what he declares. This is implied here in that expression, "the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness." And God, in saying "the word is gone out of my mouth," does as much as say, I can't recall my words, but stand obliged by 'em.

"In righteousness." This shows that by righteousness in Scripture is sometimes meant truth or veracity. So it very often is.

Isaiah 45:24.] See Psalms 71:16.

Isaiah 46:1–7.] BelIdentified by some as an alternate name of Baal. and Nebo, the gods of Babylon, were first carried by men, borne on their shoulders (Isaiah 46:7); and then afterwards, when Babylon was destroyed, they were carried by the beasts. When the Medes and Persians destroyed Babylon, they took the cattle of Babylon, and made them carry the gods of Babylon away into captivity; and they were a great burden to the poor cattle, for the images were made of gold and silver (Isaiah 46:6), and they were very great and heavy. And these gods of Babylon were not able to deliver either the men, or so much as the beasts of the city. They [that] were called the protectors of bothHere "[but yet they]" has been interlined in a different hand, identified as that of Grosart. must go into captivity. Yea, they themselves must go into captivity. They not only could not preserve the cattle from being led away captive, but they could not deliver 'em from that grievous circumstance of their captivity, of carrying them, who were so heavy a burden, to 'em. It was quite otherwise with the God of Israel. He did not need to be supported and borne by his people, much less by their beasts. But on the contrary, his people were supported by him. He carried them "from the womb, and even to hoar hairs" (Isaiah 46:3–4).

Isaiah 46:9. "The former things of old."] No. 438.*Works, 15*, 521–22.

Isaiah 47:9.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 265.Prideaux recounts the desperate and barbarous measures used by the Babylonians against their own population during the siege by Darius. In order to make their provisions last longer, they slaughtered all women and children except the favored wife and a maidservant of each man. This Prideaux saw as the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 265).

<!-- p. 682 -->

Isaiah 47:11.] What is said in this verse is very agreeable to the surprising manner of Babylon's being taken.

Isaiah 47:13. "And save thee from these things that shall come upon thee."] I.e. by foretelling what is like to come, and forewarning thee of what is approaching. It shows how vain the pretenses of these astrologers, etc., was that they could not foretell the city's danger, for their desolation came suddenly, and they knew not of it beforehand, as 'tis said in the foregoing verses. Herein did God manifest the truth of what he says of himself (Isaiah 44:25).

There was a remarkable fulfillment of these things the night that Babylon was destroyed, that night those astrologers, etc., were called to interpret the handwriting on the wall that pronounced the fatal sentence so speedily to be executed on Babylon, and on the astrologers themselves, but could not do it [Daniel 5:7–8]. That night their great ignorance appeared, and that night they with other Babylonians were destroyed and became "as stubble" Isaiah 47:14].

Isaiah 49:2. "In the shadow of his hand hath he hid me."] It is an Hebraism that seems to signify no more than this, viz. he hath held me, or grasped me, within his hand, as one grasps a sword or shaft in his hand. What is covered round in the grasp of the hand is said to be hid "in the shadow of the hand." See Psalms 17:8.

Isaiah 49:22. "Upon their shoulders."] See note on Deuteronomy 33:12.

Isaiah 49:23. "And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers."] I.e. to nurse thy children, thy sons and daughters, spoken of in the foregoing verse, that the Gentiles shall bring "in their arms" and "upon their shoulders." 'Tis not meant that the kings shall stand in the relation of nursing fathers, and queens thy nursing mothers to thee, for that hardly well agrees to what follows. "They shall bow down to thee with their face to the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet," which don't so well suit with the relation of fathers and mothers as of servants. 'Tis meant they shall be thy nourishers and nurses, not to thee, but for thee to thy children. Tutors and nurses are a sort of servants in great houses, and that a sort of servants or ministers are meant here is confirmed from Isaiah 60:10 and Isaiah 60:16.

<!-- p. 683 -->

Isaiah 49:24–25.] In the twenty-fourth, the question is put whether theJE deleted "lawful captive shall be delivered." captivity "of the just" (as it is in the original)יִמָּלֵט צַדִּיק וְאִם־שְׁבִי should be delivered. In the next verse, the answer is made that the prey of the "violent" (as it is [in] the Hebrew),יִמָּלֵט עָרִיץ וּמַלְקוֹח i.e. the very unjust, should be delivered. God did not look on the taking his people captive so innocent a thing as others did.

Isaiah 50:11. "Ye shall lie down in sorrow."] I can't think of any other lying down that can reasonably be supposed to be here intended than lying down in the grave (and so in hell), the same lying down that is spoken of, Deuteronomy 31:16. "Thou shalt lie down with thy fathers." (So it is in the original.)עִם־אֲבֹתָיךָ שֹׁכֵב הִנּךָ Job 20:11, "Which shall lie down with him in the dust." Job 21:26, "They shall lie down alike in the dust." Job 27:19–20, "The rich man lieth down, but he shall not be gathered. He openeth his eyes, and he is not. Terrors take hold as waters," etc. Jeremiah 3:24–25, "Shame hath devoured the labor of our fathers. We lie down in our shame."

Isaiah 51:4. "Hearken unto me, my people; and give ear unto me, O my nation; for a law shall proceed from me, and I will make my judgment to rest for a light of the people."] Here seems to be a prophecy of a new revelation to be made of God's mind and will, and a new dispensation or establishment of religion, for any constitution or establishment by divine revelation is called a "law" in the Old Testament. So that gracious covenant and those free promises established to Abraham is called a law.JE deleted "1 Chronicles 16:15 ff." Psalms 105:8 ff., "He hath remembered his covenant forever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations. Which covenant he made with Abraham, and his oath unto Isaac, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant, saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance." So the whole of the revelation of God's will is called a law throughout the Psalms 119. Counsel and advice is sometimes called a law. Proverbs 1:8, "Forget not the law of thy mother," and Proverbs 6:20. And Proverbs 13:14, "The law of the wise is a fountain of life." As the first law went out of Mt. Sinai, so the second went out of Mt. Zion. Isaiah 2:3 and Micah 4:2, speaking of gospel times, "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem."

<!-- p. 684 -->

It might as well have been translated, "*A law* shall go forth out of Zion," as here 'tis said, "*A law* shall proceed from me," for the word in both places is תוֹרָה, without any diversity. And when it is said, "A law shall proceed, or go forth, out of Zion," 'tis meant that a law shall be given at Mt. Zion in the same manner as 'tis said, Deuteronomy 33:2, "The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up from Mt. Seir unto them; he shined forth from Mt. Paran, and he came with ten thousands of his saints. From his right hand went a fiery law for them." As there 'tis said, "The Lord *shined forth* from Mount Paran," and that "from his right hand went a fire of law for them" (for so it is in the original),לָמוֹ אֵשׁדָּת מִימִינוֹ i.e. to "enlighten" them. (See notes on the place.) So here 'tis said, "A law shall proceed from me, and I will make my judgment to rest *for a light of the* people."This paragraph is a later insertion.

And we find that Mt. Sinai and Mt. Zion are opposed one to another by the Apostle in this respect, that as the law went forth out of the one, so the glorious gospel went forth from the other (Hebrews 12:18–22 and Hebrews 12:25–27). This new law went forth out of Mt. Zion or Jerusalem in two respects. First, as it went forth from the spiritual Mt. Zion, from heaven, and the church of God (Hebrews 12:25). And also as it first went forth from Jerusalem when the Spirit was poured out on the apostles on the day of Pentecost, which was the same day that the law was given at Sinai, and a day kept in commemoration of that event.

See note on 1 Chronicles 23:26.

Isaiah 51:8.] This verse is a proof of the indefectibility of the church.

Isaiah 51:9. "Arm of the Lord."] It may be understood of the Son of God, as Eli's offspring are called his "arm." See 1 Samuel 2:31, SSS, on that verse.*Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, cols. 39–40.

"Art thou not it that hath cut Rahab, and wounded the dragon?" See note on Psalms 74:13–14.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"Rahab." No. 255.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 205.

Isaiah 51:16. "And covered thee in the shadow of mine hand."] I.e. have held thee, or grasped thee, in mine hand as an instrument wherewith to do these great things. See notes on Isaiah 49:2.

<!-- p. 685 -->

Isaiah 52:2. "Shake thyself from the dust."] Here is reference to what had been said in the Isaiah 51:23.

Isaiah 52:7.] See no. 108.*Works, 15*, 81. This was remarkably verified in what we have account of in Luke 19:37–38. "And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, saying, Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord. Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest."

Isaiah 52:8. "Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing."] See note on Jeremiah 30:6.

"See eye to eye." See Jeremiah 32:4 and Jeremiah 34:3. 'Tis as much as to say, "shall see face to face," as appears by these places in Jeremiah. This is fulfilled: 1. By the apostles (the most eminent watchmen of the Christian church seeing) and conversing with Christ. They saw the Redeemer of Israel immediately and personally, not as the prophets of old did. It was an essential requisite of an apostle that he should be one that had seen Christ the Lord (Acts 1:21, 1 Corinthians 9:1, 1 Corinthians 15:8). 2. In the clear knowledge of divine things, and great degrees of spiritual understanding, which they shall have in the time of the latter-day glory. 3. In the beatifical vision the church shall have of Christ at his last appearing, spoken of by the apostle Paul (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the Apostle (1 John 3:2).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Thy watchmen "shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion." When he "shall bring Zion again," as he brought the people once out of Egypt, and then was seen among them by Moses, their watchman, "eye to eye," or face to face, for the words translated, "Thou art seen face to face" (Numbers 14:14), in the originalנִרְאָה בְּעַיִן אֲשֶׁר־עַיִן are the same as here, "eye to eye." The accusative case understood is Jehovah. 'Tis as much as to say, When Jehovah shall bring again Zion, thy watchmen shall see Jehovah face to face. They then, in general, shall have that which is spoken of as so great and peculiar a privilege of Moses, and granted to no other prophet under that old administration (Numbers 12:6–8 and Deuteronomy 34:10).This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 52:10. "Made bare his holy arm."] "This may allude to the habit generally worn by the Easterns, and especially by persons of rank, which was a

<!-- p. 686 -->

long robe without sleeves, so that when the arm was stretched out to perform any action which required strength, it would appear uncovered." Doddridge, notes on John 12:38.*Family Expositor, 2*, 311–12, n. b.

Isaiah 52:15. "The kings shall shut their mouths at him."] I.e. they shall be silent, attending to his wonderful doctrine and instructions, as it follows, "for that which had not been told them," etc. They shall shut their mouths as learners in acknowledgment of his superior wisdom, and as a testimony of their desirousness to hear and learn, as Job says, Job 29:21–22, "Unto me they gave ear, and waited, and kept silence at my counsel. After my words they spake not again."

They shall be silent in token also of their admiration.

Isaiah 53:1. "Our report."] 'Tis the same report spoken of in the Isaiah 52:15 which, it is said, many nations and kings should hear and consider. This report in that verse is spoken of as what the Gentiles should hear of, though in this verse 'tis spoken of as what the Jews would not believe, but reject.

Isaiah 53:1–2.] See no. 78.JE wrote this note before the preceding entry. *Works, 15*, 73.

Isaiah 53:2. "A tender plant."] Which denotes, in the first place, a small plant, not a great tree that makes a great show. Christ did not appear as one of the great men of the world, one of the tall cedars, but as one of the meaner sort of men, one of the lesser and lower sort of plants. He was but a small tender twig.

Secondly, his being a tender plant denotes his liableness to suffer, his exposedness to the malice of his enemies, etc. He was a branch that might easily be bruised or broken, not a stiff strong tree. He had no such strength of guards and armies, as earthly princes, to defend him. He voluntarily appeared in such circumstances wherein he should be exposed to the calamities of life and the malice of foes.

This verse has respect to Christ's appearing in mean and low circumstances without outward pomp and splendor. Great outward glory is in Scripture often compared to a tree growing high, and large, and flourishing in its pride (Psalms 37:35, Daniel 4:10 ff., Isaiah 10:33–34, Ezekiel 31:3–4 ff., Isaiah 2:13 with context, and Job 29:19–20). And therefore Christ's being

<!-- p. 687 -->

destitute of earthly glory is by his being "a root out of a dry ground," not like a tree planted in a fat soil or by streams of water, that flourishes, and grows large, and makes a great show. Christ is in Scripture often compared to a root, plant, or branch. The Jews expected such a branch as this, but on the contrary he is "as a root out of a dry ground" that grows low, and spreads but little, and makes no gay appearance. It was a low bush and not a mighty tree that was seen burning on Mt. Sinai [Exodus 3:2], and was not consumed, which was a type of Jesus Christ.This paragraph and the following paragraph are a later insertion.

The same thing is signified by his being without form, or comeliness, or beauty. Earthly pomp and glory of wealth, power, and magnificence is called "comeliness" in Scripture, as Ezekiel 27:10; and so it is called "beauty" (2 Samuel 1:19, and Isaiah 13:19, Isaiah 28:1, Ezekiel 27:3–4, Ezekiel 27:11, and Ezekiel 28:12, Ezekiel 28:17).

See notes on Isaiah 11:1. See Ezekiel 17:22.

There is "no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty." Comeliness and beauty are sometimes put for outward pomp, state, and magnificence (Ezekiel 27:1–2, Ezekiel 27:10–11; Job 40:10; Ezekiel 32:18–19). And particularly it is often put for the pomp and state ofJE deleted "earthly." princes and men in authority (Proverbs 31:29–32; Isaiah 33:17; Ezekiel 28:12, Ezekiel 28:17; Isaiah 28:1, Isaiah 28:4–5).This paragraph is a later addition.

Particularly we find the pomp and magnificence of great earthly princes is compared to the stateliness and beauty of a great, tall, spreading, flourishing tree in a fruitful soil with a multitude of waters at the root (Ezekiel 31:2–10). (Compare Daniel 4:12, Isaiah 10:33, and Psalms 37:35) And this stately flourishing appearance of such a tree [is] called its beauty or comeliness (Isaiah 53:3, Isaiah 53:7–9). And therefore here, when the Messiah is spoken of as being not like such a stately flourishing tree with many waters at the root, but as a low tree, a bush, a weak "tender plant," and "root out of a dry ground," or having no waters at the root, it is natural that we should understand that the Messiah should come without this pomp and glory of earthly princes, yea, in a state and with an appearance that should be the reverse of it.This paragraph is an even later addition.

Isaiah 53:8. "He was taken from prison and from judgment."] I.e. when he was brought "to the slaughter," as in the foregoing verse. This shows the way in which he was put to death. He was first imprisoned, taken and bound

<!-- p. 688 -->

as a malefactor, and then judged, arraigned before the judgment seat of men, and by them condemned.

"And who shall declare his generation?" See John 7:27.

"For he was cut off out of the land of the living." Christ was so in two respects. He was cut off by temporal death, and so from among the living in this world. And then he was cut off from the congregation of the Lord, cast out as accursed from among God's people, or from the church of God, which are called "the living ones," and their land, orJE deleted "their privileges." their state, "the land of the living." See notes on Genesis 3:20, "Scripture," no. 322, no. 399;*Works, 15*, 304–6, 396–99. and note on Ezekiel 26:20, and on Daniel 9:26.This and the two preceding paragraphs are separate entries.

Isaiah 53:10. "It pleased the Lord to *bruise* him."] This is not the same wordשׁוּף that is used in Genesis, "It shall *bruise* thy head," etc. [Genesis 3:15]. "This wordדָּכָא signifies to pound as in a mortar," as Mr. Charnock observes, vol. 2 of his *Works*, p. 308.Charnock, "A Discourse of God's Being the Author of Reconciliation," *Works, II*, 308.

"He shall prolong his days." The Prophet had been speaking of his death, and now speaks of his making "his soul an offering for sin," and yet here says, "he shall prolong his days." This is a plain prophecy of the resurrection of Christ. Prolonging his days is joined with seeing his seed because 'tis not to be supposed that a man can live to "see his seed" multiplied unless he lives long.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Isaiah 53:11. "He shall see of the travail of his soul."] The pains that Christ endured for sinners were as it were the travail pains by which he brought forth his children, even those many that he shall justify by his knowledge, because "he shall bear their iniquities," spoken of in the following words. The pains of death that vol. 3, p. 66 ὠδῖναί, i.e. travail pains. If ministers are said to travail in birth with souls, much more did Christ.

"By his knowledge." The word *dhanath*דַּעָת is very often used for righteousness, holiness, and piety. See Job 21:22, and Job 33:3, and Job 36:12; Psalms 119:66; Proverbs 1:4, Proverbs 1:7, Proverbs 1:22, Proverbs 1:29, and Proverbs 2:5–6, Proverbs 2:10, and Proverbs 5:2, and Proverbs 8:9–10, and Proverbs 9:10, and Proverbs 10:14, and Proverbs 11:9, and Proverbs 12:1, and Proverbs 13:15–16, and Proverbs 14:7, Proverbs 14:18, and

<!-- p. 689 -->

Proverbs 15:7, Proverbs 15:14, and Proverbs 18:15, and Proverbs 19:25, Proverbs 19:27, and Proverbs 20:15, and Proverbs 21:11, and Proverbs 22:12, and Proverbs 23:12, and Proverbs 24:5, and Proverbs 30:3; Ecclesiastes 2:21, and Ecclesiastes 7:12; Isaiah 5:13, and Isaiah 11:2, and Isaiah 28:9, and Isaiah 33:6; Jeremiah 3:15, and Jeremiah 22:16; Hosea 4:1, Hosea 4:6, and Hosea 6:6; besides many places where the verbיָדַע this noun comes from is used in an agreeable sense, concerning which I have not examined the concordance, and other words of like signification.Buxtorf, for example, links יָדַע, "to know," with the following Latin verbs—*scisco, nosco, agnosco, cognosco, animadverto*, and *percipio*—all of which involve some process of acquiring knowledge; and he cites numerous biblical examples of its use (*Lexicon Hebraicum et Chaldaicum* [6th ed.], pp. 283–85. See also Taylor, *Hebrew Concordance, I*, entry 734 under ידע). But Isaiah 42:19–21 is particularly worthy of observation.This paragraph is a later addition.

Isaiah 53:12. "Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great."] No. 15.*Works, 15*, 52.

Isaiah 55:1–3.] Here is a free invitation to come and take of the waters of life after the description of the glory of the New Jerusalem, as it is in the latter end of the book of Revelation. The description that is given of the New Jerusalem in the Isaiah 66:11–12, is like that which we have in Revelation.

Isaiah 55:8.] Their thoughts and ways here spoken of are the same spoken of in the foregoing verse, that they are exhorted to forsake. And possibly 'tis meant that therein God's ways are so different from their ways that they are exhorted to forsake, that he was so ready to pardon and show mercy to them. The wicked are not merciful, or of a forgiving spirit, but of the contrary spirit.

Isaiah 55:10.] This verse is to be joined with the fifth; the particle "For" connects it with that. The other verses come in as a parenthesis. That which is spoken of Isaiah 55:5, viz. the conversion of the nations, or the earth's bringing forth everywhere multitudes of converts through God's word and spirit, is here in this Isaiah 55:10, as 'tis in many other places, compared to the earth's bringing forth a glorious harvest through the influence of the rain.

Isaiah 55:12–13.] In these verses is an allusion to the going forth of the Jews out of Babylon, and returning to their own land, the mountains and hills

<!-- p. 690 -->

of which had long lain waste and desolate, but now should on their return as it were rejoice andJE deleted "clap their hands." "break forth into singing," and should put off their mournful dress, the briars and thorns they were clothed with while they lay desolate and uncultivated, and should now be covered with fir trees and myrtle trees.

Isaiah 56.] See sermon on 1 Corinthians 16:1–2, p. 18.JE's sermon on 1 Corinthians 16:1–2, preached fall 1730–spring 1731, with the doctrine "That 'tis the mind and will of God that the first day of the week should be the day that should be especially set apart for religious exercises and duties amongst Christians" (MS, p. 4). For the text of this sermon, see *Works, 17*, 220–50. Page 18 of the MS contains a typological comparison of the sabbath of rest the Israelites enjoyed after coming out of the Red Sea with the Christian sabbath to be kept on the day of Christ's resurrection from the grave. See pp. 237–38.

Isaiah 56:3–4 ff.] Here is plainly a prophecy of the abrogating of some of the laws of Moses in gospel times, as particularly those in Deuteronomy 23:1–3. See note on 1 Chronicles 23:26 and Jeremiah 3:16–17.

Isaiah 56:5.] The calamity of eunuchs in Israel consisted in two things chiefly. 1. They had no place allowed 'em in God's house. 2. They had no posterity to keep up their name. 'Tis with reference to these that the promises in this verse are made.

Isaiah 56:9–11. "All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, yea, all the beasts in the forest."] As much as to say, Ye may come, ye have opportunity to come safely, for there are no watchmenJE deleted "to keep you off." nor dogs to defend the flock, as it follows in the next verse. The "watchmen are blind"; they can't see when wild beasts are coming to devour the flock. They are ignorant and unskilled in their business. Yea, [wild beasts] may easily devour the flock for all them. "They are all dumb dogs; they cannot bark" to scare away wild beasts from the flock, or to give notice of their approach. And then they'll be asleep; they take no care of the flock.

Isaiah 57:3.] See Warburton, vol. 3, pp. 396–97.Warburton observes that the Israelites were "prone to Idolatry in prosperous Times," but returned to God in times of adversity. Sometimes their idolatry even included abuse of the memorials of their own deliverance as, for example, the monument of twelve stones at Gilgal (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed. London, 1742], vol. 2, Pt. 2 [i.e. vol. 3]).

<!-- p. 691 -->

Isaiah 57:5.] It seems that the devil led the idolaters of these times to perform these barbarous and unnaturally cruel acts of worship in dark, and solitary, and dismal places, as in dark valleys or caves, and "clifts of the rocks," delighting to bring his worshippers to such places, which were images of hell. Thus children were offered in the valley of the son of Hinnom [2 Chronicles 33:6].

Isaiah 57:8.] They kept remembrances, memorials, or images of their idols in their houses "behind the doors and the posts."

Isaiah 57:10. "Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way."] I.e. in the length of thy way that thou goest before thou overtakest or findest what thou seekest, as appears by the words following, "Thou hast found the life of thine hand." I.e. thou hast not found thine hand dead, and so found thyself utterly without strength to help thyself with the works of thine own hand; or thou hast imagined that thou hast found thy living, or what thou mightest live upon by the works of thine hand, by those works spoken of, Isaiah 57:12.

Isaiah 57:15. "That inhabiteth eternity."] Eternity that God inhabits is here spoken of as something infinitely before and infinitely above the whole creation, even above the highest heavens, "the high and holy place" spoken of in the following words. It is the eternal state of his own infinite glory and blessedness in which the persons of the Trinity dwell together, infinitely above heaven, and in which they ever did dwell.

Isaiah 58:13.] Honoring, "not doing our own ways, nor finding our own pleasure, nor speaking our own words," is not restrained to the sabbath. But in the first place, in this a particular positive duty is mentioned as what will be required under the gospel, when the ceremonial law shall cease, and then a compliance with moral duties or obedience in general, as in Isaiah 56:2, and Isaiah 56:4, and Isaiah 56:6.

Isaiah 59:4. "Bring forth iniquity."] See [note on] Deuteronomy 6:25.

Isaiah 60:1. "The glory of the Lord is risen upon thee."] Probably here is an eye had to that glorious effulgence or appearance of glorious brightness, for that was what they commonly understood by "the glory of the Lord." This glory or body of light was the symbol of the presence of Christ, the Sun of righteousness. 'Tis here represented as though this glory should

<!-- p. 692 -->

rise upon Zion, that had long sat in darkness, like the sun. For that city shall have no need of the light of the sun, nor of the moon to shine, for the glory of God shall be her light, and be her sun, as Isaiah 60:19–20, and Isaiah 24:23, and Revelation 21:23. When daylight is come, and the sun risen, then 'tis time to rise and no longer to sleep. See Ephesians 5:14.

Isaiah 60:7. "The house of my glory."] So called because it was the house where God was wont to manifest himself by that visible brightness that was commonly called "the glory of the Lord," that is called the Shekinah. The glory of the Lord was supposed to dwell there over the ark above the mercy seat when it was not visible. And therefore when the ark was carried captive, they said in Israel, "The glory is departed from Israel" [1 Samuel 4:21].

Isaiah 61:2. "To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord."] Some reference seems to [be] had to the year of jubilee wherein universal liberty was proclaimed in Israel. This was a kind of "acceptable year" to God, a year in which God was therefore pleased to order liberty to be universally granted.

Isaiah 61:4.] This verse that speaks of the wastes that shall be built being so "old," and the desolations that shall be repaired being "of many generations," and also the parallel place, Isaiah 58:12, doMS: "do plain that." plainly [show] that the glorious salvation and restoration of God's people, so much spoken of in this book, is something different from the restoration from the Babylonish captivity, which at longest was but of seventy [years], which was no more than the duration of one generation. And there are some passages in some of the other Prophets that show the same thing concerning parallel prophecies in them of a future glorious restoration of God's people, as Ezekiel 16:55 and Ezekiel 38:8, where the mountains of Israel are spoken of as having "been always waste" (i.e. for very many ages), till the time that they should be "gathered out of many people," which is doubtless the same gathering that is spoken [of] in the Ezekiel 37, particularly Ezekiel 37:12, which [was] their restoration after they were dead, but had been dead so long that their bones were become very dry, as Ezekiel 37:2–3. See Psalms 74:3.

Isaiah 61:8. "I hate robbery for burnt offering."] This seems to be given as a reason why God will take away the riches of the Gentiles from 'em, and

<!-- p. 693 -->

give it to his people. And as in all these prophecies of the glory of the church, from the Isaiah 40-66, there is an allusion to the church's deliverance out of Babylon as the type of the church's deliverance out of the spiritual Babylon or antichristian church. So the riches of the Romish church seems to be here especially intended, which the ecclesiastical persons used unjustly to drain the people of under a pretense of offering it to God, or devoting it to a religious use. But [God] hates this "robbery for burnt offering"; and therefore their wealth shall be taken from them, and given to his true church.

Isaiah 62:3.] It is here promised that God's people shall be "a crown of glory," etc., "in the hand," and not upon the head of the Lord, because.…JE deleted this unfinished entry with a large "X."

Isaiah 62:11. "Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him."] God first works his work, and then gives the reward. We are created of him "in Christ Jesus unto good works" [Ephesians 2:10]. He first gives the work, and then gives the reward of the work. A work of humiliation and reformation shall go before him, and a reward of peace, and comfort, and peace with him. Or possibly, 'tis the reward he receives of his own work in conflicting with his enemies, and treading the wine press, mentioned in the Isaiah 63.

Isaiah 63:1. "Who is this that cometh," etc.] This is connected with the Isaiah 62:11 where it is proclaimed, "Behold, thy salvation cometh; his reward is with him," etc.

Isaiah 63:11. "Where is he that brought them up?"] Here God looks to the Mediator, that "angel of his presence," spoken of in the preceding verses, the person that had espoused the church of Israel. Thus he beholds the face of his anointed, and turns away his face from beholding their transgressions.

Isaiah 64.] The prayer in this chapter begins with the Isaiah 63:15.

Isaiah 64:2. "The fire causeth the waters to boil."] This has some respect to the terrible ferment that things will be put into, when God shall appear wonderfully for his church, through the corruption that is in the heart of

<!-- p. 694 -->

men, which is sometimes represented in Scripture by water, and will be as opposite to that spirit that then will be poured out as water is to fire.

Isaiah 64:6. "And we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away."] Alluding to the leaves in the fall of the year which fade, and then the wind blows them off.

Isaiah 65:5. "Which say, Stand by thyself," etc.] Prideaux says concerning the Pharisees, the greatest sect among the Jews in Christ's time, as follows. "These men, by reason of their more nice and rigorous observance of the law according to their traditions, which they had superadded to it, looked on themselves more holy than other men, and therefore separated themselves from those, whom they thought sinners and profane, so as not to eat or drink with them. And hence from the Hebrew word *pharas*,פָּרַד which signifieth 'to separate,' they had the name of Pharisees, which is as much as to say 'Separatists.' And although their chief separation was from the common people whom they called *am haaretz*,הָאָרֶץ עַם i.e. 'the people of the earth,' and reckoned them no other than the dung thereof, yet by reason of their hypocritical pretenses to greater righteousness than others in the observance of the law, they drew the common people after them." *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 481–82.*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 481–82.

Isaiah 65:17–18. "New heavens," etc.] Christ speaks of himself as the restorer of the world after it has been destroyed, in Psalms 75:3.

Isaiah 65:20. "An infant of days, nor an old man that hath not filled his days."] Both these expressions signify the same thing. "An infant of days," i.e. one that has lived many days, and yet is an infant. By "days" in Scripture is sometimes meant a long time or old age. So Job 32:7, "I said, Days should speak." "An old man that hath not filled his days," i.e. an old man that is yet young, has obtained no good, nor done none, that never yet has attained happiness, nor answered his end, any more than if he had died an infant.This paragraph was written after the following three paragraphs.

"For the child shall die an hundred years old." I.e. though it dies in childhood, it shall die with the attainments of one an hundred years old, not only in perfection, but happiness. It was looked upon a great happiness

<!-- p. 695 -->

to have long life. The child that dies in childhood yet shall be fully happy.

"But the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed." I.e. though he lives till he is an hundred years old, though he seems to prosper and be let alone, yet the curse shall certainly overtake. It shall be evident and apparent that he is, notwithstanding his having long life, all his seeming prosperity, a cursed miserable creature. See Ecclesiastes 8:12, which well explains this passage, and Ecclesiastes 6:3–6.

The godly person, though he dies a child, hath full happiness, and possesses the promise of long life, viz. eternal life; but the wicked person, though an hundred years old, is miserable and is subject to the threatened curse, which is death, though he seems to live out his days, and die full of days.

As to the godly, though they die when they are children, and so seem to be cut off in the beginning of their days, which the world looks on as the greatest curse that can befall 'em, and the greatest fulfillment of the curse of God's law, which is death, yet they shall die blessed in full happiness and possession of long life. But as to the wicked, though they seem to prosper, though they live to an exceeding great age, which the world looks on as the greatest blessing and the greatest fulfillment of God's promised blessing, which is life, yet they shall be indeed accursed.

See Warburton, vol. 3, p. 665.This reference is a later addition. Warburton writes about changes Isaiah describes as attendant on the new dispensation—a new religion and a new law. Earlier patterns will no longer prevail. "For we must remember, that *long Life* for Obedience, and *sudden and immature Death* for Transgressions, bore an eminent Part in their Rewards and Punishments: Now these are expressly said to be abrogated in the Dispensation promised, it being declared that the Virtuous, tho' dying untimely, should be as if they had lived an hundred Years; and Sinners, tho' living to an hundred Years, as if they had died untimely" (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed., London, 1742], vol. 2 in 2 Pts. [i.e. vol. 3]). Part II in vol. 2 begins with p. 366.

Isaiah 66:1. "The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool."] The mercy seat in the temple is no longer God's throne, but heaven. And the ark and temple are no longer God's footstool, as they used to be called (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalms 99:5, and Psalms 132:7–8; Lamentations 2:1; Isaiah 60:13). The glorious times shall come wherein the whole habitable world shall be blessed with as honorable tokens of God's presence, not only as [the] land of Canaan, but as the temple, yea, as the holy of holies and the ark that had God's glory upon it. See Jeremiah 3:16–17; Isaiah 60:2, and Isaiah 2:5. See note on Revelation 21:23–24. Also compare Haggai 2:7 (with notes) and Isaiah 6:1, Isaiah 6:3.

<!-- p. 696 -->

Isaiah 66:3. "He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog's neck; he that offereth an oblation, as if he offered swine's blood; he that burneth incense, as if he blessed an idol."] The time especially pointed at in this place, as in the beginning of the Isaiah 65, seems to be the time of setting up Christ's kingdom in the days of the gospel when the Jews were rejected and the Gentiles called. Here as there is represented the wickedness of the Jews in Christ's and the apostles' days, which though it did not consist in external idolatry and such visible forsaking of their law, as in some former times, yet was no less heinous. They abounded in sacrifices, and were very strict as to the ceremonies of the law of Moses, but their wickedness was as great in God's sight as if they had acted in contradiction to the law of Moses in the most visible and gross manner by worshipping idols, offering swine's blood, etc. Yea, their very religion and external conformity to the law was no less abominable by their hypocrisy and self-righteousness.

Isaiah 66:14. "Your bones shall flourish like an herb."] See note on Isaiah 37:30–31.
