### Jeremiah

Jeremiah 1:5.] See no. 13.*Works, 15*, 52.

Jeremiah 1:11–12.] "An 'almond tree' was one of the forwardest trees in the spring. It flourished!, saith Pliny, in the month of January, and by March hath ripe fruits. Hence it is called in the Hebrew *shakedh*,שָׁקֵד 'the hasty tree.'" So Aaron's rod was the rod of an almond tree. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 211.

Jeremiah 1:13.] The face of the "seething pot" was that side or part of the pot that was outwards, exposed to view, being next to the hearth or to the mouth of the furnace over which the pot boiled. That way that the face of a seething pot in this sense was, that way was the fire and fuel brought.

Jeremiah 2:2. "The kindness of thy youth."] See Judges 2:17 and Judges 2:22.

"The kindness of thy youth." Nos. 282, and 296, 478, 499, 500.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 238–40, 267–68, 576, 592–94.

Jeremiah 2:3.] "'All that devoured him did offend'; so it should be read. Those were reckoned offenders, that devoured the first fruits, or anything that was holy to the Lord." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 213.

Jeremiah 2:12. "Be astonished, O heavens," etc.] If we saw sin against God as it is, it would appear an horribly dreadful evil. We should be amazed and struck with astonishment and a kind of terror or horror at the sight of such an evil much more than now we are, at any particular atrocious acts as the most inhuman unnatural acts of cruelty and the like; and we should not then at all wonder that so dreadful a punishment is threatened for sin. As we are not sensible of the dreadfulness of our sins, so were not the children of Israel of the dreadfulness of theirs, of which God thus speaks, as appears by Jeremiah 2:19, Jeremiah 2:23. And yet that was no argument

<!-- p. 698 -->

that their sin did not expose 'em to a dreadful punishment, as appears by Jeremiah 2:35. See Jeremiah 16:10. See a fulfillment of these two verses, Matthew 27:45.This sentence is a later addition.

Jeremiah 2:14. "Is Israel a servant," etc.] That he is thus turned out of the house, for the servant abideth not in the house forever, and given up to bondage and slavery.The last seven words are a later addition.

Jeremiah 2:18. "To drink the waters of SihorA location linked to Egypt.… and to drink the waters of the river."] Instead of "the fountain of living waters," mentioned, Jeremiah 2:13.

Jeremiah 2:23–24. "Thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways; a wild ass," etc.] "'A swift dromedary traversing her ways,' a female of that species of creatures, hunting about for the male. 'A wild ass used to the wilderness,' not tamed by labor, and therefore very wanton, 'snuffing up the wind at her pleasure,' when she comes near the he ass; and on such an 'occasion, who can turn her away?' Who can hinder her from that which she lusteth after? 'They that seek her' then 'will not weary themselves' for her, for they know it is to no purpose, but will have a little patience till she is big with young, till that month comes which is the last month which she fulfills (Job 39:2), when she is heavy and unwieldy" (when the fruit of her lust and wantonness is mature), "and then 'they shall find her,' and she cannot outrun them. The time will come when the most fierce will be tamed, and the most wanton will be manageable; when distress and anguish comes upon them, that is the month in which you may find them." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 217.

So the time was coming when the fruit of Israel's wantonness, and untowardness, and unbridled lusts should be mature; and then they should be tamed with sorrow and distress. "In the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us" (Jeremiah 2:27). See Hosea 5:15.

Jeremiah 2:25. "Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst."] Implying that by going to Egypt and to other strangers for help, she would get nothing but thirst and nakedness. Thy lovers, with whom thouMS: "they." playest the harlot, will not clothe thee, nor feed thee.

<!-- p. 699 -->

Jeremiah 2:32.] See no. 14.*Works, 15*, 52.

Jeremiah 3:10. "Hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly."] I.e. in the time of the reformation by king Josiah. "In the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, when they were disposed to idolatry, the people were so too; and all the country was corrupted with it. And when they had a good king that reformed them, they did not heartily concur with him in the reformation. God tried whether they would be good in a good reign, but the evil disposition was still the same." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 220–21.

Jeremiah 3:16–17.] They had been wont to call the ark "the throne of the Lord," but now Jerusalem shall be so called. That which is spoken of these verses could not be done without a change of the law, so that here is an implicit prophecy that the law shall be changed in gospel times. See note on 1 Chronicles 23:26, and Isaiah 56:3–4, and Zechariah 14:21. That also implies a change of the law, in Isaiah 61:6 and Jeremiah 16:14. Concerning these two verses, see note on Isaiah 2:2. See also no. 285, the last paragraph in that note.*Works, 15*, 246.

Jeremiah 3:19.] In this verse faith and perseverance are represented as the great conditions of the possession of the inheritance of God's children.

Jeremiah 3:25. "We lie down in our shame."] I.e. we die or perish in our shame. See note on Isaiah 50:11.

Jeremiah 4:9. "The prophets shall wonder."] Seeing the event so exceeding contrary to their confident expectations and those smooth things they had so often prophesied.

Jeremiah 4:10. "Then said I, Ah, Lord God," etc.] There is an ellipsis in the words. It is as much as if he had said, "Ah, Lord God, according to these prophets, thou hast deceived this people very greatly indeed, saying, Ye shall have peace, whereas the sword reacheth unto the soul. For they have been very peremptory and abundant in declaring that there should be peace, and that there was no danger of these calamities; but how exceeding contrary is the event."

Or it is as if he had said, "Then said I" (as expressing and foretelling

<!-- p. 700 -->

the language of these prophets in this disappointment and amazement of theirs), "Ah, Lord God," etc.JE crossed out the balance of this paragraph with a large "X." If we understand the words thus, the ellipsis is no more strained than that in Jeremiah 6:24. "We have heard the fame thereof," i.e. the people of Zion shall say, "We have heard the fame thereof." And there the Prophet expresses the people's future language, as here the future language of the false prophets.This paragraph is a later addition.

Jeremiah's words contain an irony against the prophets, and he speaks what he supposes must naturally be their language in their wonderment and amazement when this dreadful event should come so contrary to their predictions. As to such an ellipsis, there is no difficulty in allowing it, they being frequent in this prophecy, as in Jeremiah 4:13, "Woe unto us! For we are spoiled!" i.e. the people of that time shall say, "Woe unto us," etc. Jeremiah 4:19, "My bowels, my bowels," etc., i.e. the people ofMS: "or." Jerusalem shall cry out, "My bowels," etc. Jeremiah 4:22, "For my people is foolish," etc., i.e. God says, My people shall cry out thus, for they are foolish. Jeremiah 6:4, "Arise, let us go up at noon," i.e. Jerusalem's enemies shall say, "Arise." Jeremiah 6:9, "Turn back thine hand as the grape-gatherer," etc., i.e. God says to the enemy, "Turn back," etc. Jeremiah 6:24, "We have heard the fame thereof," i.e. the people shall say, "We have heard," etc. See also Jeremiah 8:15; Jeremiah 9:18; Jeremiah 10:19, Jeremiah 10:21, Jeremiah 10:23; Jeremiah 12:5.

Jeremiah 5:13. "And the prophets shall become wind," etc.] This verse is [a] continuation of what the people say whereby they belie the Lord. They say, "It is not he; neither shall evil come upon us; neither shall we see sword nor famine" Jeremiah 5:12]. "The prophets" that threaten sword and famine "shall" prove to be "but 'wind,' for 'the word' of God 'is not in them.' 'Thus it shall be done unto them,' i.e. what the prophets threaten us with 'shall be done unto them.'" They threaten us with sword and famine, and sword and famine shall come upon themselves and not on us. It may be a threatening of theirs against the prophets, as much as to say, We will do to them according to what they have prophesied against us. "Do they frighten us with famine? Let them be fed 'with bread of affliction.' So Micaiah was (1 Kings 22:27). Do they tell us of sword? Let them perish by the sword (Jeremiah 2:30)." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 230.

<!-- p. 701 -->

Jeremiah 5:14. "Because ye speak this word."] I.e. that threatening word against God's prophets, in the end of the foregoing verse, "Thus shall it be done unto them." The manifestation of malice and a persecuting spirit against the dispensers of God's word filled up the measure of their sin, and did in a peculiar manner render the word of God in the mouths of those ministers of God of baneful influence to them.

Jeremiah 5:22.] No. 294.*Works, 15*, 265–66.

Jeremiah 6:2–3.] It is probably intended a comely and delicate woman that is a shepherdess dwelling in a tent. The shepherds with their flocks, such as were in Arabia, the posterity of Kedar, Midian, and others who were shepherds, and were often wont to encroach upon and invade their neighbors' territories with their flocks, and eat up their pasture, and carry away their cattle, such as these shall come up against this delicate, feeble, helpless shepherdess, and shall eat up her pasture with their cattle, and carry away her flocks, and spoil her tent, and do violence to her person. Such a kind of robbers the Chaldeans themselves, that were now coming against the Jews, formerly had been. See Job 1:17. TheJE deleted "true." church of God is represented as a shepherdess feeding her flock (Canticles 1:7–8). So is the people of Judah in this prophecy (Jeremiah 13:19–22), for 'tis the people or church of Judah is there spoken to, as is evident because the pronouns are feminine. These shepherds here spoken of that should eat up the pastures of "the daughter of Zion" with their flocks are the same with the pastors, spoken of, Jeremiah 12:10, who should destroy God's vineyard, and tread his portion under foot, and make his "pleasant portion a desolate wilderness." See note on that place.

Jeremiah 6:4–5.] The enemies of Jerusalem speak as men in care to make dispatch, as those that would leave nothing undone till tomorrow. "Arise, let us go up at noon," though it be in the heat of the day. "Woe to us! The day goeth away," etc., and we are not doing our work. We sit still, and slip our opportunity. "Arise, let us go by night," though in the dark nothing shall hinder them.

Jeremiah 6:11. "I will pour it out upon the children abroad, and upon the assembly of the young men together."] See notes on Lamentations 3:27 and Ezekiel 14:22.

<!-- p. 702 -->

Jeremiah 7:11. "A den of robbers."] Robbers in the wilderness of Arabia were wont to shelter themselves in dens of the mountains. So many wicked men, false professors, shelter themselves in their wickedness in the house of God. They shelter and defend themselves from the reproach of men with a cloak of religion, and by attending the outward duties of worship. They defend themselves from their own consciences, trusting in their own righteousness, though they live in a violation of the rules of morality. See note on Matthew 21:13.

Jeremiah 7:15.] Shiloh was in the tribe of Ephraim, as in Psalms 78:67–68. God first took away his ark from that tribe, and delivered it into captivity, and afterwards delivered the people also into captivity. So likewise the ark that was nowMS: "new." in the tribe of Judah should go from them into captivity, and the people should also be delivered into captivity.

Jeremiah 7:21. "Put your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat flesh."] "The law of the burnt offering was, that it was none of it to be eaten, but the whole burnt and consumed upon the altar. So that if the Jews had done what the Prophet bids them (Jeremiah 7:21), they had acted contrary to the law of the burnt offering. And his directing them so to do, is only hinting to them, that it was of no moment to be exact in their sacrifices, without amending their lives." Shuckford's *Connection*, vol. 3, p. 136.*Sacred and Prophane History* (2nd ed.), p. 136, n. r.

'Tis as much as to say, "'Put your burnt offerings,' that were to be wholly burnt, unto your peace offerings, which the offerer had a considerable share of," and feasted upon; and make a feast for yourselves of both. "Keep your sacrifices to yourselves. Let them all be served up at your own tables, for they are no way acceptable at God's altars." Henry.This paragraph is a later addition. *Exposition, 4* (1725), 240.

Jeremiah 7:22–23.] I.e. "in the day when" God first "brought 'em" to treat with him at Mt. Sinai, and first entered into covenant with them there, he then said nothing about ceremonial observances; but what he insisted on was that they should obey his voice, i.e. that audible dreadful voice which they heard from Mt. Sinai which spake the Ten Commandments or moral law, and not any ceremonial precepts. See Exodus 19 and Exodus 20, especially Exodus 19:5–6. This is said to be in the day when God brought 'em out of Egypt, because when they came out of

<!-- p. 703 -->

Egypt it was to meet with God at this mountain. And this was the first solemn covenanting with the nation after they were brought out of Egypt.

Jeremiah 7:29. "Cut off thine hair, O Jerusalem, and cast it away."] "In token both of sorrow and slavery, Jerusalem must now cut off her hair, and cast it away. The wordנֵזֶר is peculiar to the hair of the Nazarites, which was the badge and token of their dedication to God, and is called their crown. Jerusalem had been a city that was a Nazarite to God, but now must cut off her hair, must be profaned, degraded, and separated from God, as she had been separated to him. And it is time for those that have lost their holiness to lay aside their joy." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 240–41.

Jeremiah 7:31. "Which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart."] The meaning is not, I did not command to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to Moloch, and it never came into my heart to offer such sacrifices to [a] false god. But the meaning is, I never commanded them to offer any such sacrifices even to myself, nor did it ever once come into my heart to require parents to "put such a faceHenry reads "force." on their natural affection in honoring me." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 241.

Jeremiah 7:33.] See no. 105.*Works, 15*, 102.

Jeremiah 8:4. "Shall they fall, and not arise? Shall he turn away, and not return?"] *Q.d*. "'Shall men fall, and not arise?' If men happen to fall to the ground, to fall into the dirt, will they not get up again as fast as they can? Shall a man turn aside out of the right way? Yea, 'tis possible the most careful traveler may miss his way. But then as soon as he is aware of it, will he not return? Yes certainly, he will with all speed, and thank him that showed him his mistake." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 242.

Jeremiah 8:6. "Everyone turneth to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle."] They went on with full career in their sins, thoughtless and regardless of those dreadful dangers that they run themselves into.

<!-- p. 704 -->

Jeremiah 8:7. "Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times… but my people know not the judgment of the Lord."] See note on Ecclesiastes 8:5–6.

Jeremiah 8:11. "For they have healed," etc.] The Prophet in this verse evidences what he had said in the foregoing, viz. how the prophets and priests were given to covetousness, and dealt falsely. They dealt falsely or unfaithfully in that they were false to their trust; they were not thorough in the work of their office, which was to heal the hurt of the daughter of God's people. This they were unfaithful in in that they did it slightly, and so as would be to no purpose. And they dealt falsely in that they deceived the patient; they pretended he was cured, and that it would be well with him, when it was no such thing. They were given to covetousness. They acted as a covetous physician that aims at nothing but his pay, if he can but make his patient believe that he is cured, so as to get his fees, aims at no more.

Jeremiah 9:12. "Who is the wise man that may understand this, and who is he to whom the mouth of the Lord hath spoken, that he may declare it?" etc.] God in these words has respect to their prophets that pretended to be wise men and men to whom the mouth of the Lord had spoken.

Jeremiah 9:24.] "'Tis not the knowledge that they are directed to glory [in], but the thing known, viz. that God is the Lord that exerciseth loving-kindness, etc., which renders him that trusts in him more safe and sure of success than our own wisdom and strength, etc., mentioned in the preceding verse. And whereas it is said, "Let him glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am," etc., it don't mean that he should glory in his knowledge, but in it that God is "the Lord that exerciseth loving-kindness and judgment," etc., as a thing known and certain.

Jeremiah 10:16. "The portion of Jacob."] God is so called here, and again, Jeremiah 51:19. This is the portion that Jacob had, as he had the birthright, and inherited the blessing. The great portion and inheritance of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, which their seed inherited, was that God was their God, as God told Jacob, Genesis 28:13, "I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac." And as God said to Abraham in Genesis 17:7–8, "And I will establish my covenant between me, and thee, and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to thee and thy seed after thee. And I will give unto thee, and to thy seed after thee, the land wherein thou art a stranger, all the land of Canaan

<!-- p. 705 -->

for an everlasting possession; and I will be their God." And as God said to Moses, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6).

"The rod of his inheritance." See no. 176.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 103.

Jeremiah 10:17. "Gather up thy wares."] I.e. pack up thy effects. It was probably a common form of expression among that people when they would signify to any that they must make haste, and prepare to be gone, and finally to depart.

Jeremiah 11:12–13.] What is said in these verses imports that their gods should not and could not help them, though they had so many of them, and though they built so many altars to them.

Jeremiah 11:15. "And the holy flesh is passed from thee."] The particle "and," or the prefix ו, here couples these words with the first words in the verse, "What hath my beloved to do in my house." So that the meaning is this: My beloved has no more "to do in my house," nor with the "holy flesh" of my sacrifices or peace offerings that were wont to be eaten there.

Jeremiah 11:18–19.] What the Prophet would signify in these verses is that it was God [that] informed him of the conspiracy of the men of Anathoth against his life. "He knew nothing of it himself, so artfully had they concealed it. He came to Anathoth, meaning no harm to them, and therefore fearing no harm from them, like a lamb or an ox that thinks he is driven as usual to the field, when he is brought to the slaughter. None gave him any notice of his danger. But the Lord himself was pleased to give him knowledge of it that he might save himself,JE deleted "and so he escaped." as the king of Israel did on the notice that Elisha gave him (2 Kings 6:10). Thus he came to know it. God showed him their doings. Such were their devices, that the discovering of them was the defeating of them." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 255.

Jeremiah 11:20.] See no. 38.*Works, 15*, 58.

Jeremiah 11:23. "And there shall be no remnant of them."] Their punishment is agreeable to their sin. They intended to destroy Jeremiah, both root and branch (Jeremiah 11:19); and therefore there shall be no remnant of them.

<!-- p. 706 -->

Jeremiah 12:3.] See no. 177.Ibid., 103.

Jeremiah 12:5.] If the injuries done thee by the men of Anathoth make such an impression upon thee, what wilt thou do when the princes and chief priests at Jerusalem set upon thee with all theirMS: "thy." power? This was the case afterwards (Jeremiah 20:2 and Jeremiah 32:2).

Jeremiah 12:8. "As a lion in the forest, it crieth out against me."] "It crieth out against God in the threatenings and slaughter it breathed out against his prophets, that speak to them in his name. And what is said and done against them, God takes as said and done against himself." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 258.

Jeremiah 12:9. "Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird."] The originalצָבוּעַ הַעַיִט is "a bird that is tinged or colored," i.e. with blood. Some read it, "a bird with talons." So the margin.I.e. margin of the KJV. What is intended seems to be a bird of prey. In the foregoing verse God's heritage was compared to a beast of prey, in this verse to a bird of prey. Thus their wickedness is represented. The words that follow in this verse represent her punishment. "The birds round about her are against her," i.e. I will cause the birds round about to assemble themselves to devour and make a prey of this bird of prey. "All the beasts of the field come to devour," i.e. I will cause all the beasts of the field that are round about to devour and make a prey of this beast of prey, this lion of the forest.

Jeremiah 12:10. "Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard," etc.] I.e. "The Chaldean generals that made themselves masters of the country, and eat it up with their armies, as easily as the Arabian shepherds with their flocks eat up the fruits of a piece of ground." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 258. See note on Jeremiah 6:2–3.

Jeremiah 12:12. "The spoilers are come up upon all high places."] I.e. upon all the fortresses and strong places.

Jeremiah 13:1–2 ff.] Concerning the symbolical actions of the prophets, see Warburton, *Divine Legation*, vol. 2, pp. 83 ff.Warburton describes the mixed discourse of words and actions common in the early ages of the world and especially among Eastern peoples. He cites numerous instances of such actions by prophets in the Bible, including Jeremiah. Such actions were not deserving of the charge of absurdity or fanaticism. On the contrary, he writes, "*Information by Action* was, at this Time, and Place, a *very familiar Mode of Conversation*" (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed. London, 1742], vol. 2, pp. 83–87).

<!-- p. 707 -->

Jeremiah 13:11.]*Works, 15*, 53. See no. 19.

Jeremiah 13:12.] See no. 178.Ibid., 103.

Jeremiah 13:21. "What wilt thou say when he shall punish thee, for thou hast taught them to be captains, and as chief over thee?"] I.e. by thy showing such a servile spirit towards the heathen nation, so meanly to follow them, seek to them, and act as esteeming them above thee, their gods better than thine, their religion, laws, and constitution more excellent than thine, and by being so forward in the times of thy distress to seek to them for help, and basely to trust in their shadow, and so to become a sort of servants and tributaries to them. Thou hast by these things led them to despise thee, and so hast encouraged and tempted them to invade thee, and take much upon them, and domineer over thee,MS: "them." and insult thee.

Therefore what wilt thou say when thou are punished for this thy folly, when thou hast thus brought it on thyself? Thou wilt be found inexcusable, and your mouth will be stopped.

Jeremiah 13:22. "Are thy skirts discovered, and thy heels made bare."] Thus they used to deal with prisoners taken in war. They drove 'em into captivity, "naked and barefoot" (Isaiah 20:4).

Jeremiah 14:6. "And the wild asses did stand in the high places."] The air in this time of great drought was so hot that they could not breathe. Therefore they get to the highest places they can where the air is coolest, and there pant, and snuff up the wind, and make a noise like hissing dragons.

Jeremiah 15:1.] Moses and Samuel were two noted intercessors whose intercession had prevailed for Israel. Concerning Samuel, see 1 Samuel 7:9.

Jeremiah 15:11. "Well with thy remnant."] "I.e. 'with the remainder of thy life,' for so the wordשֵׁרוּת signifies. The residue of thy days shall be more comfortable

<!-- p. 708 -->

to thee than those hitherto have been. 'Thy end shall be good'; so the Chaldee reads it." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 268.

Jeremiah 15:12.] This is a continuation of what God says in the foregoing verse to Jeremiah for his comfort, signifying his defense from the Chaldeans. Though they were strong as iron, and should come against the land with swords and other iron weapons, yet they should not be able to hurt him, for God had hisMS: "him." iron too (Jeremiah 15:20, and Jeremiah 1:18), and stronger iron than their weapons, as the northern iron and steel is stronger than other iron. See also Ezekiel 3:8–9.

Jeremiah 15:19. "If thou return, then will I bring thee again."] If thou recover thy temper, and art reconciled to thy work, and shake off these distrustful discontented thoughts and passions, and not give way to them, for the people must return to thee. But thou must not return to them. Thou must not be unbelieving and froward like them. "If thou dost thus return, I will bring thee again, and thou shalt stand before me." If thou wilt believe and look to me for help, I will help thine unbelief, and restore strength and courage, and renew the influences of my spirit upon thee.

Jeremiah 16:10. "Wherefore hath the Lord pronounced all this great evil against us?"] See note on Jeremiah 2:12.

Jeremiah 16:13.] The state of the Jewish church in Babylon very much represented the state of the Christian church under the tyranny and oppression of the Church of Rome, the great antitype of Babylon, for the church was there almost extinct. The Jews that were carried captive, almost all of them, had corrupted themselves, and apostatized from God before they were carried away, though they kept up something of the form of religion. And when they were carried to Babylon, they did not reform, but there served other gods, and had lostOr: "left." the outward ordinances and the very form of the worship of the God of Israel. See Deuteronomy 4:28 and Deuteronomy 28:64. So also the church of Israel was in Egypt, another type of the spiritual Babylon. See note on Exodus 3:13.

Jeremiah 16:15.] See no. 37.*Works, 15*, 58.

<!-- p. 709 -->

Jeremiah 17:1.] The "sin of Judah" remains upon their hearts after all means used to rub it out, like letters that are engraven in a firm rock or flint; it remains from generation to generation, as it follows in the next verse, "Whilst their children remember," etc. "It is graven upon the horns of your altars." I.e. the name of the same idols that seem to be engraven on their hearts are graven on the horns of their altars as being the gods that those altars are consecrated to. It probably was a custom to engrave the names of the gods they worshipped on the altars on which they were wont to sacrifice to them. And when it is said their sin is graven on the horns of their altars, hereby may be meant their idol's name, for a people's idol was frequently wont to be called their "sin," as Hosea 10:8. Deuteronomy 9:21, "I took your sin, the calf that ye had made." Amos 8:14, "They sware by the sin of Samaria." And this agrees with the latter part of the Jeremiah 16, particularly the Jeremiah 16:20.

It may be further observed that atonement for sin was wont to be made with the blood of the sacrifices put "upon the horns of the altar" (Leviticus 4:7 and other places). But their putting the blood of the sacrifices offered to their idols on their altars, instead of taking away their guilt and memory of it, and blot[ting] out the handwriting that was against them, that it did but fix it, and engrave it in indelible characters. And so, indeed, did the sacrifices offered to the true God, if they did not repent of and forsake their sins. As he that attends the Lord's Supper, that sacred memorial of Christ's sacrifice, does but seal his own condemnation instead of receiving the atoning virtue of that sacrifice, if he does it without repentance and reformation.This paragraph is a later addition.

Jeremiah 17:3. "O my mountain in the field."] I.e. my possession, or lot, or inheritance. The possessions of the children of Israel were either in the city or in the field, and the land of Canaan was a very mountainous country. And the mountains being the most distinguished places, the possessions or inheritances of such and such families in the field used to be called by the mountains they included. And probably the phrase of "such an one's mountain," or "such an one's hill," used to signify the inheritance of such a person or family that lay upon and about such an hill. So elsewhere the children of Israel are called God's vineyard planted on a "fruitful hill" (Isaiah 5:1). Thus the mountain in the land of Gilead was named after the family that possessed it, viz. the family of Gilead. And so a mountain in the tribe of Ephraim was called after the name of the tribe that

<!-- p. 710 -->

possessed it. That which was called Mt. Ephraim was not any particular mountain; but the whole original possession of the tribe of Ephraim, being a mountainous country, was called Mt. Ephraim, as is evident by Joshua 17:15. Yea, the whole possession of the tribe of Ephraim seems to be called Mount Ephraim (Judges 7:24). The mountain of Samaria was called after the name of Shemer, the man that possessed it (1 Kings 16:24). So such and such mountains that were in the possessions of such a people were put for their whole possession. Deuteronomy 2:5, "Because I have given Mount Seir unto Esau for a possession." Mount Seir, as it was understood among the children of Israel, included great part of Arabia where the Edomites dwelt, which being a mountainous country, was all called Mt. Seir. Thus Mt. Sinai, being within the limits of that country, was mentioned as a part of Seir. Deuteronomy 33:2, "The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them." Judges 5:4, "Lord, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled," etc. The "field of Edom," or Edom's inheritance in the field, and Mt. Seir are the same thing. So God's inheritance in the field, and his mountain in the field, are the same, viz. the land of Canaan. And Caleb, when he sought for his possession, he says, "Give me this mountain" (Joshua 14:12). And the whole possession of the children of Israel is called a "mountain." Deuteronomy 3:25, "I pray thee, let me go over, and see the good land that is beyond Jordan, that goodly mountain, and Lebanon." And the same is called the mountain which God's right hand had purchased. Psalms 78:54, "And he brought them to the border of his sanctuary, even to this mountain, which his right hand had purchased." The southern part of this land, which was once the possession of the Amorites, was once called "the mountain of the Amorites"JE deleted "because they were a principal nation that possessed it." (Deuteronomy 1:7, Deuteronomy 1:20). See note on Deuteronomy 1:20. But that by God's "mountain in the field" is meant his possession or inheritance is more evident still from Exodus 15:17. "Thou shalt bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of thine *inheritance*." The land of Canaan is there represented as God's field or mountain of inheritance, and the children of Israel the trees, or vines, or plants that are planted in it. Mountains that were tilled, and sowed, or planted were probably called "mountains in the field" to distinguish them from mountains that were improved by them as fortresses and places that they built, for they had many such mountains which are often spoken of in the Scripture. But God's people, or the land of his people, is fitly compared to the other sort of mountains that are manured, are God's husbandry, whereon

<!-- p. 711 -->

trees, vines, or plants are planted. And God is more fitly compared to mountains that are fortresses and places of habitation, as he often is in Scripture.This entry has several rearrangements made in accord with JE's directions.

Jeremiah 17:12. "A glorious high throne," etc.] This and the two next verses seem to be brought in as the language of those that trust in the Lord, spoken of, Jeremiah 17:7–8. The "glorious high throne," from the beginning spoken of, is heaven (Psalms 11:4, Isaiah 66:1–2, Hebrews 8:1 and Hebrews 9:24). The words are brought in something after the same manner with the Jeremiah 16:19. The true church glories that although that earthly sanctuary, which belonged to Israel according to the flesh, was like to be destroyed, yet they, the spiritual Israel, had an everlasting sanctuary which was God's throne on high out of the reach of all enemies.

The phrase, "from the beginning," in the Old Testament either signifies the same as "from everlasting," or "from the beginning of ages." See Psalms 119:160, Proverbs 8:23, Isaiah 48:16. That this true sanctuary is "from the beginning" is mentioned as an argument that it cannot be overthrown, in like manner as God's word's being true "from the beginning" is mentioned as an evidence that it will never fail, in Psalms 119:160. "Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth forever."This paragraph is a later addition.

Jeremiah 17:13.] There seems to be some reference here to what was said in the Jeremiah 17:7–8. There he "whose hope the Lord is" is said to be "as a tree planted by the waters, that spreadeth out her roots by the rivers," which waters are there spoken of as living or unfailing waters, that don't fail "in the year of drought," etc. And here "the Lord, the hope of Israel," is said to be "the fountain of living waters." See Revelation 22:1.

Jeremiah 17:16. "I have not hastened from being a pastor to follow thee."] Or "after thee," as it is in the original.אַחֲרֶיךָ I.e. I have not made that haste in taking this office upon me as to go before thee, and not after thee. I did not show a forwardness in this matter so as to take this office on myself before I was called of thee, or so as to run before I was sent. I was not so fond of the business and errand that I am sent upon, viz. the denouncing such awful judgments on my people, for I have not desired the woeful day, as it follows.

<!-- p. 712 -->

Jeremiah 17:16, Jeremiah 17:18.] What we find in these verses is a confirmation that when the prophet Jeremiah and other inspired penmen of the Old Testament imprecated judgments on their enemies, these parts of their writings are not of private interpretation, or that they did therein express their private inclinations and desires, but spoke prophetically the mind of, cursed them in the name of the Lord, or foretold that these judgments should come. For here Jeremiah, in the Jeremiah 17:16, solemnly appeals to God that he had not "desired the woeful day." But yet in the Jeremiah 17:18, he prays that the evil day might be brought on his enemies.

Jeremiah 17:24–26.] It is that which will hold true, that whatsoever people do strictly observe God's sabbath, they are a religious people. Otherwise such promises would not here be made to this single duty.

Jeremiah 17:25. "Riding in chariots and on horses."] See Bp. Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, p. 373, taken with the rest of "Dissertation IV."In Dissertation IV entitled "Christ's Entry into Jerusalem," Sherlock links the punishment of Judah and Israel for having chariots and horses in their armies with their trusting in armies rather than in the Lord for their strength and security. Likewise, the coming Messiah was to be meek and lowly, not a king surrounded by pomp and chariots (5th ed.).

Jeremiah 18:9–10.] If, when I am about to make that nation or kingdom a vessel to honor, it be marred in my hand, "then I will repent of" what I proposed, and will make them a vessel to dishonor, as Jeremiah 18:4.

Jeremiah 18:14. "Will a man leave the snow of Lebanon?"] See Proverbs 25:13.

Jeremiah 20:7. "O Lord, thou hast deceived," etc.] "The wordsוָאֶפָּת פִתִּיתַנִי may very well be read thus, 'Thou hast persuaded me, and I was persuaded.' 'Tis the same wordפָּתָח that is used, Genesis 9:27, margin.I.e. margin of the KJV. 'God shall persuade Japheth.' And Proverbs 25:15, 'By much forbearance is a prince persuaded.' And Hosea 2:14, 'I will allure her.'" Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 285. This refers to what passed between God and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:4–10 and Jeremiah 1:17–19).

Jeremiah 20:10. "Report, say they, and we will report it."] This is not what they say to Jeremiah, but one to another. They earnestly desired and sought after some false witness, some evil and slanderous report, that they might spread and propagate, or that they might inform the rulers against him.

<!-- p. 713 -->

Jeremiah 20:14 ff. "Cursed be the day wherein I was born," etc.] How great an evidence is to be gathered from this and other like passages of the Old Testament of a future state of reward to the saints. Jeremiah was a man of affliction in this life. 'Tis evident that as long as he lived he met with opposition, hatred, and continual affliction, so that he was heartily weary of life, and wished he had never been born. This affliction was followed with no remarkable alteration from affliction to prosperity, as it was in Job. But while he lived, he lived to see nothing but those things that were most grievous to his heart, which made his being in this world far worse than no being. Now if there be no future state, how is this consistent with the frequent declarations of God in the Old [Testament] that those that fear him are blessed and happy, and his promises that it shall be well with them, that he will be their defense and exceeding great reward, etc., which the Old Testament is full of, and with what God said and promised to Jeremiah in particular (Jeremiah 1:8, Jeremiah 1:18–19; and Jeremiah 15:11), and also with the promises God makes by Jeremiah to the righteous, which he applies to him in this very context (Jeremiah 20:11–13)?

Jeremiah 21:9. "His life shall be given unto him for a prey."] I.e. he shall save his life, but with much difficulty and hazard, as a prey is taken from the mighty. And he shall have joy in so narrowly escaping with his life in a time of such general destruction, that shall be like theirs that divide the spoil. They thought to have made a prey of the camp of the Chaldeans, being flattered by their false prophets, as their ancestors did of the camp of the Assyrians (Isaiah 33:23). But they will be sadly disappointed, if by yielding at discretion they can but save their lives; that's all the prey they must promise themselves.

Jeremiah 22:10. "Weep ye not for the dead."] I.e. "for Josiah. Jeremiah had himself been a true mourner for him, and had stirred up the people to mourn for him (2 Chronicles 35:25). Yet now he will have them go out of mourning for him, though it was but three months after his death, and to turn their tears into another channel, and weep for" Shallum, i.e. Jehoahaz, that was carried captive into Egypt, whose "case was much more deplorable." Henry.Ibid., 289.

Jeremiah 22:16. "Was not this to know me, saith the Lord?"] See James 1:27.

<!-- p. 714 -->

Jeremiah 22:19.] Jerusalem herein was a type of the spiritual Jerusalem, and a type of heaven into which the wicked that are dead, and unclean, and loathsome shall have no part, but shall be shut out, as those were out of the New Jerusalem that are characterized, Revelation 22:15, "For without are dogs," etc. And we are told, Revelation 21:27, that "there shall in no wise enter in there anything that defileth, nor whatsoever worketh abomination." The carcasses of these unclean beasts were dead; so are the souls of natural men who are also unclean. They were not suffered to have a place within the gates of Jerusalem; no more have wicked men in the mystical church. Those carcasses without Jerusalem were very loathsome, stinking, and nauseous; so are the souls of the wicked. These unclean beasts, while alive, were allowed a place in Jerusalem, but when dead were cast forth, and suffered no more to be brought in. So wicked men, while alive, may have a place in God's visible church; but when dead, they are cast forth, and shall be shut out of heaven. Their carcasses lay rotting, and stinky, and eaten of worms. So shall the souls of the wicked be tormented without the New Jerusalem after they are dead. See Isaiah 66:24 with Jeremiah 22:20, compared with Mark 9:44, Mark 9:46, Mark 9:48.

Jeremiah 22:20.] Jephthah's daughter went up and down the mountains to bewail her virginity [Judges 11:38]. Here the daughter of Zion is called upon to go up the mountains to bewail the loss of her lovers. What is here translated "the passages," in the originalעֲבָרִים is *abarim*. Abarim was an high mountain in the border of Moab. Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim were each of them high mountains in the borders of the land of Israel, next to those nations with whose idols God's people had committed whoredom: Lebanon next to Tyre, and Sidon, and Syria; Gilead next to the Ammonites; Abarim next to the Moabites. The daughter of Zion is called upon to go up on those mountains from whence she might behold the countries where her lovers had dwelt, and see 'em now desolate, and there lament and bewail her bereavement of 'em.

Jeremiah 22:24.] Concerning the name Coniah. "As I live, saith the Lord, though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim," etc. I.e. Jeconiah or Jehoiakin. The name Jeconiah is compounded with the name Jehovah or Jah, for the greater honor. God here leaves out his own name out of his name, and calls him simply Coniah, in contempt denying him the honor of any relation to him. The prophets, speaking by inspiration, do sometimes change the

<!-- p. 715 -->

names of persons and places for the greater honor. Thus Pashur is called Magor Missabib (Jeremiah 20:3). Bethel is called Beth-aven by the prophet Ezekiel.Here JE is mistaken. The only references to Beth-aven in the prophetic books occur in Hosea (Hosea 4:15, Hosea 5:8, and Hosea 10:5). JE deleted with three large "X's": "And so it is probably that Jehoahaz has his name changed by the Prophet, Jeremiah 22:11 of this chapter."

Jeremiah 22:30.] "In Jeconiah, or Jehoiakin, the line of David was extinct as a royal line. Some think he had children born in Babylon because mention is made of his seed being 'cast out' there (Jeremiah 22:28), and that they died before him. We read in the genealogy, 1 Chronicles 3:17, of seven sons of Jeconiah Assir, i.e. Jeconiah the captive, of which Salathiel is the first. Some think they were only his adopted sons, and that when it is said, Matthew 1:12, 'Jeconiah begat Salathiel,' no more is meant, but that he bequeathed to him what claims and pretensions he had to the government, the rather because Salathiel is called 'the son of Neri' (Luke 3:27), of the house of Nathan (Luke 3:31). Whether he had children begotten, or only adopted, thus far he was childless, that none of his seed ruled as kings in Judah. He was the AugustulusRomulus Augustulus was the last Roman emperor of the West (475–476). of that empire, in whom it determined." (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 292.

It appears the more likely that Salathiel, of whom came Christ, was not the natural offspring of Jeconiah, and so that Christ was not descended of him, and that the Spirit of God intended to imply that when he says here, he shall be "childless," and "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah," because the Holy Ghost in the Jeremiah 23, a few verses forward, in the continuation of the same discourse of reproof to the princes of Judah (Jeremiah 23:5), does expressly foretell that God would raise up "unto David a righteous Branch" that should "reign and prosper," etc. Now it is not at all probable that God should here with great solemnity declare that Jeconiah should be "childless," one that himself should "not prosper," and that should have "no man of his seed that should prosper, sitting on the throne of David, and ruling in Judah," and yet a few sentences after in the continuation of the same discourse, he should foretell that a king should arise and sit on the throne of David, that should prosper, reigning or ruling over his people, and saving Judah, meaning one of Jeconiah's posterity.

Jeremiah 23:18.] 'Tis as much as to say, Not one of you "hath stood in the counsel of the Lord," etc. You say with great assurance, We stand "in the counsel

<!-- p. 716 -->

of the Lord," or "*in the secret* of the Lord," as the wordבְּסוֹד signifies. We have perceived and heard his word. We have marked it, and heard it, and 'tis certainly so, whereas you speak nothing but lies. There is not one of you have heard or perceived anything from me, or have the least reason to make so solemn and positive a declaration, signifying that you are sent by me.

Jeremiah 25:30. "And utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall mightily roar upon his habitation."] I.e. *from* heaven, "his holy habitation" above; *upon* Jerusalem, "his habitation" below; not "from Jerusalem," or Mt. Zion, as Joel 3:16. For now Jerusalem is one of the places against which he roars.

Jeremiah 26:9.] That which they persecute the prophet Jeremiah for is the same thing that they charged as a great crime upon Stephen, and for which they put him to death. See Acts 6:13–14.

Jeremiah 26:20–24.] What is here said concerning the prophet Urijah we are not to take as a continuation of the words of the princes, but as the words of "the historian himself that penned the book, Jeremiah himself or Baruch, who, to make Jeremiah's deliverance the more wonderful, takes notice of this passage that happened about the same time, for both were in the reign of Jehoiakim, and this in the beginning of his reign (Jeremiah 26:1)." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 305.

Jeremiah 27:1–3.] There is an ellipsis in these words, and there are some words to be understood at the beginning of the Jeremiah 27:3 that are not expressed. We are to understand it thus. "The word had come to Jeremiah from the Lord in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, saying, Make thee bonds and yokes, and put them upon thy neck," in token of Judah's subjection to the king of Babylon which was then soon to begin. And afterwards, viz. in the beginning of Zedekiah's reign,JE deleted "God commanded Jeremiah, saying, Send these bonds and yokes which I commanded thee long since to put upon thy neck to the king of Edom and the king of Moab, etc." the word was renewed with this addition, viz. that he should not only put these bonds and yokes on his own neck, but "send them to the king of Edom," etc.

That things that are diverse and that come to pass at different times should in this manner be connected in the narration, as though they

<!-- p. 717 -->

happened at the same time and were only different parts of the same event, need not seem incredible. This is not more strange than an instance we have in the Jeremiah 29:24 ff. There Jeremiah's words to the captives in Babylon, in a second letter to them, being about the same subject, are connected with the words of the preceding letter, as though it were a continuation of the same discourse when, indeed, it was the words of another letter written afterwards, occasioned by what Shemaiah had written to the Jews in Jerusalem in reply to that first letter of Jeremiah.

Jeremiah 28:17. "In the seventh month."] That sabbatical month wherein were so many solemn feasts, that joyful month that began with the feast of trumpets, and on the tenth day [of] the month had the day of atonement, which was followed with that most joyful feast of tabernacles, which held for eight days together (See Numbers 29.). It was a joyful month, especially in the temple where these joyful feasts were celebrated, and to the priests. This false prophet Hananiah seems to have been of the priests, for he was of Gibeon, a priests' city (Jeremiah 28:1). So the wicked priests and officers that were in Israel died in the beginning of that glorious happy reign of Israel. So when the light of that glorious day of the church of God, so often spoken of in prophecy, begins to take hold on the ends of the earth, the wicked shall be shaken out of it. And particularly will God at that time terribly execute his wrath on false prophets, and the priests and ministers of the false church, and false ministers of the visible church. When Christ makes his joyful entry into Jerusalem, he will scourge buyers and sellers out of his temple.

Jeremiah 29:24. "Thus shalt thou also speak to Shemaiah."] See note on Jeremiah 27:1–3.

Jeremiah 30:7.] See note on Matthew 24:21–24 ff, no. 292, especially §8.*Works, 15*, 256.

Jeremiah 30:11. "In measure."] It would have been more agreeable to the use of the word *lammishpat*לַמִּשְׁפֶּט to have translated it, "in mercy." See also Jeremiah 46:28.

Jeremiah 30:21. "And their nobles shall be of themselves."] No. 236.*Works, 15*, 187–88.

<!-- p. 718 -->

Jeremiah 31:2. "The people which were left of the sword."] I.e. of God's destroying judgments whereby so many of that wicked congregation were consumed in the wilderness. God brought them into a wilderness, and kept them a long time there, and there in a terrible manner slew multitudes of them. But yet he did not make a full end; but there was a remnant that were redeemed, that found favor, were brought into Canaan. So although God shall deliver his people into captivity, and they shall be carried away captive, and sore judgments shall be executed, yet there shall be a remnant that shall find favor, and return.

Jeremiah 31:5. "Plant vines,… and eat them as common things."] I.e. they shall "plant vines," and live and continue in the possession of their vineyards till the fruit is brought forth, and till they, according to the law, may eat the fruit freely, as being now common. According to the law of Moses, after they had planted any tree or vine, and it had begun to bear fruit, they were forbidden to eat the fruit till the fifth year (Leviticus 19:23–25). And on the fifth year, after the vine began to bear, when they might freely eat the fruit, the fruit was said to be common. Therefore in Deuteronomy 20:6, where it is said in our translation, "What man is he that hath planted a vineyard, and hath not yet eaten of it?" In the originalחִלְּלוֹ וְלא it is, "hath not yet made it common." So when it is threatened in our translation, Deuteronomy 28:30, "Thou shalt plant a vineyard, and shalt not gather the grapes thereof," in the originalתְחַלְּלֶנּוּ וְלא תִּטַּע כֶּרֶם it is, "Thou shalt plant a vineyard, and shall not use it as common meat." The promise in this place in Jeremiah is the reverse of that threatening.

Jeremiah 31:6. "For there shall be a day that the watchmen," etc.] Mt. Ephraim is specified probably the rather, because it was in the kingdom of Ephraim, or the Ten Tribes, who after they separated from Judah forsook the worship of God at Jerusalem, the place which God had chose. Jeroboam forbid their going up to Jerusalem to worship [1 Kings 12:28]. Mt. Ephraim was upon the border between the kingdom of Israel and Judah, where it seems the kings of Israel were wont to keep watchmen for the defense of the kingdom of Israel from Judah, and to hinder communication, and probably to prevent any from going up to Jerusalem to worship. Here it is prophesied that those "shall cry, Arise ye, and let us go up to Zion unto the Lord our God."The remainder of this entry is a later addition. Or else, what is referred to is this, viz. it is very likely

<!-- p. 719 -->

that it was the manner in the tribes of Israel when they were about to go up from all parts of the land to the house of the Lord at the time of their three great feasts, they were wont to rise very early before day in order to set out on their journey, thereby giving a properMS: "properly." testimony of their forwardness and engagedness in the affair of going up to Zion, where God dwelt, to worship him there, as the children [of Israel], when they left Egypt to go to Canaan, the promised land, set out on their journey very early while it was yet night. And 'tis likely that it was the manner for the watchmen to wake the people by calling upon them aloud to arise and go to Zion, and that they waked them with singing and instruments of music, and that the people also, when they arose, answered with music and joyful songs. See Isaiah 30:29 and Isaiah 52:8.

Jeremiah 31:9. "I will cause them to walk by the rivers of water."] Though they pass through a dry and thirsty desert, God "will cause them to walk by rivers of water," as he did when they came through the desert of Arabia towards the promised land from Egypt. There a great desert between Judea and Chaldea, the dry deserts of Arabia, did almost compass round the land of Israel.

Jeremiah 31:15.] "In Ramah nothing was heard but lamentation and bitter weeping at the time of the general captivity, more than in other places, because there NebuzaradanNebuzaradan, a court offical of Nebuchadrezzar. had the general rendezvous of his captives, as appears, Jeremiah 40:1, where we find him sending Jeremiah back from Ramah. Rachel is said there to weep 'for her children.' The sepulcher of Rachel was between Bethlehem and Ramah. Benjamin, one of the two tribes, and Ephraim, head of the Ten Tribes, were both descendants from Rachel. She had but two sons, the elder of which was one for whom his father grieved, and refused to be comforted [Genesis 37:35], because he thought he was not. The other she herself called Benoniבֶּן־וֹנִי [Genesis 35:18], 'the son of my sorrow.'" That voice of lamentation was heard in Ramah, of mothers for children, that might, "to speak poetically," be represented by Rachel's weeping for her children. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 319.

Jeremiah 31:22. "A woman shall compass a man."] The plain meaning of this, as it here comes in, and by observing the manner in which the word "compassed"

<!-- p. 720 -->

is elsewhere used, seems to be this: that God, who governs and orders all things in his providence, has brought to pass a strange thing with respect to this backsliding daughter here spoken. That instead of being sought to by her lovers for her lovers, or merely setting herself forth to attract their love and laying herself in their way, she goes and woos them for their love, pursues them, and besets them that she may obtain them (Ezekiel 16:33–34).

The Latin word for "woo" is *ambio*, which signifies "to compass." But concerning the opinion that interprets this of the blessed Virgin's conception of Christ, see what is said in Poole's *Synopsis*, which is worthy of notice.This sentence is a later addition. See *Synopsis Criticorum, III* (London, 1673), cols. 897–99.

Jeremiah 31:29. "The fathers have eaten a sour grape."] See note on Ezekiel 9:5–6.

Jeremiah 31:29–33.] See Warburton, vol. 3, p. 455.Warburton contextualizes God's purpose in giving Israel and Judah "a NEW *Dispensation*, in which a future State of Reward and Punishment was to be *brought to light*," one in which God "will abrogate the Law of punishing Children for their Parents Crimes" (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed. London, 1742], vol. 2, Pt. 2 [i.e. vol. 3]).

Jeremiah 31:32. "Not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers in the day that I took 'em by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt."] That covenant was as it were founded in that redemption out of Egypt. And therefore when [God] made that covenant with the people, he prefaced it thus: "I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage" [Exodus 20:2]. Therefore 'tis natural from [what] the Prophet here says of God's making a new covenant, not according to that made in the day of that redemption and founded on that redemption, but a very different and far better covenant: I say, it is natural to suppose that this new covenant would not be a covenant founded on that redemption, but on some other, and far better, and more glorious redemption. See Isaiah 43:18 and Jeremiah 23:7–8.

"Which my covenant they brake." This refers especially to their making and worshipping the golden calf. "Though I was as an husband unto them." See Poole's *Synopsis, in loc*.,*Synopsis Criticorum, III* (London, 1673), cols. 900–901. but especially in these words as cited by the Apostle (Hebrews 8:9). See also Owen on Hebrews 8:9, p. 264a–b.This entry has several later additions. John Owen joins the debate concerning the Jeremiah text by interpreting the parallel passage in Hebrews 8:9 to mean that God dealt with the Israelites "as a Husband with a Wife that breaketh Covenant," no longer regarding them with "love, tenderness and affection," but rather allowing them to wander in the wilderness until "they were consumed" (Hebrews 6–10).

Jeremiah 31:33.] See no. 179.*Works, 15*, 104. See sermon on Ezekiel 11:19, exposition on the text.No extant copy of this sermon has been located. See notes on Galatians 5:18, *Ans*. to second *Inq*.

Jeremiah 32:39–40.] See "Miscellanies," no. 729, *Corol*. 1.*Works, 18*, 356–57.

Jeremiah 33:6. "And will reveal unto them the abundance of truth and peace."] Here is probably respect to that marvelous revelation of the boundless riches of divine grace that should be made by Christ, and the redemption he should work out. And 'tis likely there is a reference to some preceding prophecies of it, as particularly that in Psalms 72:3. "The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness." Psalms 72:7, "In his days shall the righteous flourish, and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth." So Psalms 85:8–13 and Psalms 89:1–2, Psalms 89:14–16, Psalms 89:24. See Psalms 37:11.

Jeremiah 33:16. "This is the name wherewith he shall be called."] See Ezekiel 48:35 and Exodus 17:15.

Jeremiah 33:18. "Neither shall the priests the Levites want a man," etc.] See note on Deuteronomy 33:8.

Jeremiah 33:20–21.] This intimates not only the perpetuity of the kingdom and church of Christ in this world "to the world's end, but that its condition in this world should be intermixed, and counterchanged, prosperity and adversity succeeding each other as light and darkness, day and night. But this is plainly taught us, that as sure as we may be, that though the sun will set tonight, it will rise again tomorrow morning, whether we live to see it or no; so sure we may be, that though the kingdom of the Redeemer in the world may for a time be clouded and eclipsed by corruptions and persecutions, yet it will shine forth again, and recover its luster in the time appointed." This was proper to be revealed now to Jeremiah at a time when the sun was just a-setting on the Jewish church, and a very dark and dismal night coming on. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 330.

<!-- p. 722 -->

Jeremiah 34:22.] It was before Jerusalem's first destruction by the Babylonians, as it was before her second destruction by the Romans, in this respect, that God [gave] the people warning of its approaching destruction by its being compassed with armies. And then those armies were again removed for a little space to give opportunity to the people still to do those duties that were necessary for their escape, as particularly here was opportunity for any of the people that believed the word of God by Jeremiah to do as he directed 'em: Go forth, and make peace with the king of Babylon, and subject themselves to his government, whereby their lives might be saved (See Jeremiah 21:8 ff.), as before the last destruction, those that believed Christ's word had opportunity to flee to the mountains, and so to escape that terrible destruction. We have particular account of the occasion of the Babylonians' departure from Jerusalem, in the Jeremiah 37.

Jeremiah 35:6–8.] Jonadab herein acted as a prophet. He had an extraordinary direction, without doubt, to give his children such a command. Otherwise, it is unaccountable that he should do it; neither would his posterity have been obliged by it. And then the thing that he commands them is evidently typical of what is spiritual. It typifies a living as pilgrims and strangers on the earth spiritually. Their not drinking any wine represents a living in the mortification of carnal appetites, a life of abstinence from sensual pleasures. Their building no houses, nor sowing seed, nor planting vineyards, but dwelling in tents, signifies that God's people have here no settled dwelling place, that this world is not their country, not their home, that they have butMS: "been." little to do with these things, that they are to treat those things with neglect, and that they don't treat them as settling upon them, but use [them] as transient pilgrims and strangers, looking for another country.

Jeremiah 37:12. "To separate himself thence."] I.e. from Jerusalem, or as it is in the margin,I.e. margin of the KJV. "'to slip away from thence.' 'In the midst of the people.' I.e. amongst the people who, in that interval of the siege, went out into the country to look after their affairs there. He endeavored to steal away in the crowd." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 339.

Jeremiah 38:11–13] God, in improving sinful men to bring souls up out of the horrible pit, and out of the miry clay, out of the pit wherein there is no water, does as it were make use of "old cast clouts and old rotten rags."

Jeremiah 38:19–20.] Hence we may observe that there is not that danger in obeying God's commands and following his counsel as we are ready to think there is. Those things that we are afraid will be the consequence, the lion in the way, commonly would prove a shadow if we would resolutely go on.

Jeremiah 39:3. "And sat in the middle gate."] A gate "in the middle wall that divided between one part of the city and the other. Here they cautiously made a halt, and durst not go forward into so large a city, amongst men that perhaps would sell their lives as dear as they could, till they had given directions for the searching of all places, that they might not be surprised by any ambush. They 'sat in the middle gate,' from thence to take a view of the city, and give orders." And now was fulfilled what Jeremiah prophesied long since, Jeremiah 1:15, that "the families of the kingdom of the north should set every one his throne at the entering of the gates of Jerusalem." "Rabsaris and Rabmag are supposed not to be names of distinct persons, but the titles of those whose names go before. Sarsechim was *Rabsaris*,רַב־סָרִיס i.e. captain of the guard; and Nergal-sharezer, to distinguish him from the other of the same name that is put first, is called *Rabmag*,רַב־מָג i.e. camp muster, either mustermaster or quartermaster." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 343.

Jeremiah 39:4. "By the way of the king's garden, by the gate betwixt the two walls."] See note on Ezekiel 12:3–6.

"The word which came to Jeremiah," etc.] This is the title of this part of the book, but refers properly to "the word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord," that begins Jeremiah 42:7, the story that here intervenes betwixt this title and that which is properly "the word which came to Jeremiah" after he was sent back from Ramah, coming in only as an introduction to that word of the Lord.

"When he had taken him being bound in chains, among all that were carried away." "It should seem that Jeremiah was very honorably fetched

out of 'the court of the prison' by the king of Babylon's princes (Jeremiah 39:15). Henry.Ibid., 345.

London, 1742]).

Jeremiah 46:17.] Concerning the pride and great boasts of this king of Egypt, see Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 132.*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 132.

Jeremiah 46:18. "Surely as Tabor is among the mountains, and as Carmel by the sea."] I.e. as these great mountains are firmly fixed in their places, and none can remove them, so is the decree and word of God concerning the destruction of Egypt. The steadfastness and immutability of God's word is elsewhere compared to the stability of mountains. Psalms 36:6, "Thy righteousness is like the great mountains."

Jeremiah 46:28. "In measure."] See note on Jeremiah 30:11.

Jeremiah 49:2–3.] Rabbah, the chief city, is represented as the mother; the other cities are the daughters. Jeremiah 49:7–22.] See of the accomplishment of this and other prophecies against Edom, Prideaux's *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 281–82.Prideaux maintains that references to the land of Edom in the Old Testament, with one exception, refer to that country between the Lake of Sodom and the Red Sea. Jeremiah 49:10–11. "His seed is spoiled, his brethren, and his neighbors, and he is not. Leave thy fatherless children; I will preserve them alive. And their brethren and neighbors being destroyed, "He is not" that shall say, or "There is none" that shall say, "Leave thy fatherless children" under my care, and "I will preserve 'em alive. And let thy widows trust in me."JE deleted "Henry." See *Exposition, 4* (1725), 364. And therefore men, women, and children shall be all slain.

Jeremiah 50:2. "Bel is confounded; MerodochThe god of Babylon. is broken in pieces."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, p. 347.Prideaux describes the destruction and pillaging of the temples of Babylon by Xerxes, king of Persia (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 347).

Jeremiah 50:8. "And be as the he-goats before the flock."] I.e. be forward in this good design of returning to Zion, and be ready to assist and lead others on to it, and do what you can everyone to promote others' going, and to show 'em the way. Thus it ought to be in the affair of turning from sin to God, of which the going out of Babylon to Zion was a type. See Psalms 51:13; John 1:41–42, John 1:45–46; Luke 22:32. And in this manner ought persons to behave themselves in the affair of returning out of the mystical Babylon, and in all times of public reformation.

Jeremiah 50:24. "I have laid a snare for thee," etc.] This is most agreeable to the way in which Babylon was taken. The city was so strong that it never [could] have been taken by open force. But they were surprised by the stratagem of their enemies, when they were most secure, in the very time of their mirth and voluptuousness, in the dead of the night, when they were drowned in drunkenness and sleep.

Jeremiah 52:25. They were both discharged, as we read before.John Lightfoot reconciles conflicting details in the accounts of the siege of Jerusalem given in Jer. and II Kgs. "Now *Jeremy* agrees exactly in all the account but this, that he saith, he took away seven men that were near the King; which he did indeed, but slew but five of them, for the other two *Jeremy* and *Ebedmelech* were delivered: Now of their Story the Penman hath given you account before, and therefore when he saith here, that all these were taken at *Jerusalem*, and slain at *Riblah*, he himself had been the interpreter there how to understand it suitable to the relation in the Book of *Kings*" (*A Chronicle of the Times, and the Order of the Texts of the Old Testament. Wherein the Books, Chapters, Psalms, Stories, Prophecies, &c. are reduced into their proper order, and taken up in the proper places, in which the natural Method and genuine Series of the Chronology requireth them to be taken in*, in *The Works of the Reverend and Learned John Lightfoot D.D. Late Master of Katherine Hall in Cambridge; Such as were, and such as Never before were Printed* [2 vols. London, 1684], *I*, 129).
