### Lamentations

Lamentations 1:7. "The adversaries saw her, and did mock at her sabbaths."] Jerusalem was the city of their solemnities, the city of sabbaths, where they were wont to meet to keep their festival and holy days. Those, while they enjoyed them, were very much the glory of that city. It was much upon the account of them that it was called the "holy city." Her enemies now robbed her of all this glory. They no more went up to Jerusalem to solemnize their holy days. "The ways of Zion mourn because none cometh to her solemn feasts," as Lamentations 1:4. Her enemies insulted her on this account, as men, when they have overcome their enemies, and brought them into miserable circumstances, are wont to insult them, and mock at their former prosperity that they used to glory in. Those sabbaths were some of the pleasant things, that are spoken of in the verse, that she remembered in the days of her affliction that she enjoyed in days of old. See Lamentations 2:6.

Lamentations 1:10. "She hath seen the heathen entered into her sanctuary," etc.] They entered into the holy place "into which no Israelite was permitted to enter, though never so reverently and devoutly, but the priests only. The stranger that comes nigh even to worship there shall be put to death. Thither the heathen now crowded in rudely, not to worship but to plunder." Yea, they thus crowded into the holy of holies, where the high priest alone was allowed to enter, and that but once a year with the utmost devotion, though "God had commanded that the heathen should not so much as 'enter into the congregation' (Deuteronomy 23:3)." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 381.

Lamentations 2:12. "Their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom."] I.e. they poured out their lives, and breathed their last in their mothers' bosom.

Lamentations 2:13.] "We commonly endeavor to comfort our friends by telling them that their case is not singular, nor without precedent. But Jerusalem's case will not admit of this argument." Henry.Ibid., 387.

<!-- p. 729 -->

Lamentations 3:27. "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth."] The great calamities that [were] brought on Jerusalem and Judah were for the destruction of the elder people, but for the good of many of the rising generation who were hereby humbled and fitted for the great mercy God afterwards bestowed upon them. See Jeremiah 6:10–11, and note on Ezekiel 14:22.

Lamentations 3:38. "Out of the mouth of the Most High proceedeth not evil and good?"] 'Tis an interrogation: Doth not both evil and good proceed out of the mouth of the Lord?, implying an affirmation. The words in the originalוְהַטְּוֹב הָרָעוֹח תֵצֵא לא may be rendered, "proceed not this evil and this good," i.e. the evil and good mentioned in the preceding part of the chapter. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 390.

Lamentations 4:1. "The stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street."] By the "stones of the sanctuary" are probably meant the "sons of Zion," spoken of in the next verse. See Lamentations 2:19, 1 Peter 2:5.

Lamentations 4:6. "No hand stayed on her."] The wordחוּל signifies "remained." She was destroyed in a moment, and no hand of man, no hand of an enemy, abode or remained long upon her, as upon Jerusalem.

Lamentations 4:14. "They have wandered as blind men."] Being blind leaders of the blind, "God said of corrupt judges, Psalms 82:5, 'They know not, neither will they learn; they walk on in darkness.'" Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 394.

Lamentations 4:15. "They cried unto them, Depart ye," etc.]JE deleted "The pronoun 'they' is a relative without any antecedent." Here is a verb of the third person plural without a nominative case expressed, as is frequent in the Prophets. It is as much as to say, They shall be bid to depart. God in his providence will not suffer these polluted wretches to have anything more to do with the sacred things of his house, but shall drive them away with great abhorrence, as it were with a loud cry. TheJE deleted "relative." pronoun "they" understood may intend God that dwelt in his temple, and the holy angels that were conversant there, and his holy prophets that spake in his name. It may intend the same that are spoken of, Ezekiel 9:1, "them that have

<!-- p. 730 -->

charge over the city," or else them that have a special charge over the temple.

Or the pluralJE deleted "number." verb may be used here when the nominative case that is understood is God, *Elohim*, to which we have an instance parallel in Genesis 20:13. "God caused me to wander," *Elohim hithgnu*,אֱלהִים אֹתִי הִתְעוּ where *hithgnu*, "caused to wander," is in the plural number. Here see Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration of the Messiah*, Pt. II, pp. 28–29.This sentence and the following three are a later addition. Kidder asserts, "It is common among the sacred writers, that an active verb, that hath no *person* going before it, is to be understood as a *passive* or *impersonal*; and the careful observing of this manner of speech will remove many difficulties, that might otherwise disturb us." This principle he applies to passages that seem to make God the author of human sin. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 28–29. See an instance of that manner of speaking Bp. Kidder speaks of, in Proverbs 13:10. "Only by pride cometh contention." In the originalמֵצָּה יִתֵּן רַק־בְּזָדוֹן it is, "Only in pride will he give contention." The plural number is used here much after the same manner as it is, Daniel 4:25, "*They* shall drive thee from men." Daniel 2:30, Proverbs 24:8.

"They said among the heathen." Still the pronoun is used in the same manner. And they that said thus among the heathen are the same that cried, Depart, etc. See also Daniel 7:5, and Daniel 11:2 and Daniel 11:7; Job 34:20, margin. The next verse [Lamentations 4:16] explains it.This entry has numerous reworkings and realignments.

Lamentations 4:16. "The anger of the Lord hath divided them; he will no more regard them."] That is, God has forever separated 'em from the temple and holy things, as those that are unclean, etc.

Lamentations 5:12. "Princes are hanged up by their hand."] I.e. by the hand of those mentioned in the foregoing verse, the Chaldeans, the same enemies that ravished the women in Zion.

<!-- p. 731 -->

### Ezekiel

Ezekiel 1.] Concerning Ezekiel's wheels, see no. 389.*Works, 15*, 373–79.

Ezekiel 1:1. "In the thirtieth year."] I.e. in the thirtieth year of his life. Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*.*Scripture Chronology*, 681. Thus God first began to reveal himself to him in the same year wherein, if he had been in the land of Israel, he would have begun to enter on the execution of his office as a priest (Numbers 4:2–3, Numbers 4:22–23, Numbers 4:29–30). Ezekiel, by reason of his captivated state, could not receive the honor at that time that the priests were wont to receive at that age of entering on the execution of their office. But this was made up to him by his being at that time called to be a prophet. And he began his ministry at the same time that Christ began his ministry, who was the great prophet and high priest of his church.

Ezekiel 1:2. "In the fifth day of the month."] 'Tis probable it was on the sabbath day, because we read, Ezekiel 3:16, that "at the end of seven days," which we may well suppose to be the next sabbath, "the word of the Lord came" to him again. Thus John "was in the Spirit on the Lord's day" [Revelation 1:10], when he saw the visions of the Almighty.

Ezekiel 1:4.] The same appearance that the prophet Ezekiel here expresses, "as the color of amber," seems to be what the apostle John saw and expresses by "pure gold, like unto clear glass" (Revelation 21:18, Revelation 21:21), i.e. transparent gold, yet appearing of an excellent purity and brightness. It was such an inexpressible appearance that Ezekiel saw that he represents by the color of amber as coming the nearest of it in appearance of any natural body, being yellow and something of the color of gold, and yet transparent. So instead of the brazen sea in Solomon's temple, John saw "a sea of glass mingled with fire" (Revelation 15:2). Or else it represented the color of flesh, but transparent, or both flesh and gold, as a color between both. See note on Ezekiel 1:27.

"And a fire enfolding itself." No. 393.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 387–88.

<!-- p. 732 -->

Ezekiel 1:12.] "They made no blunders or mistakes which would give them occasion to turn back to rectify them; their work needed no correction. They minded no diversions" nor obstacles in their way. "As they turned not back, so they turned not aside." The motions of providence are steady and regular; and whatever the Lord pleaseth, that he doth, and is never put upon new counsels. Whatever difficulties lay in the way of these wheels, they were sure to get over them; and their motion was never interrupted. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 403.

Ezekiel 1:19–21. "And when the living creatures were lift up from the earth, the wheels were lift up."] When God's wisdom, power, justice, and goodness so lead and direct, the wheels of providence are elevated above the ordinary course of things, yea, above the course of nature, as in the working of miracles and the extraordinary changes that are brought to pass in the world by the supernatural work of God's Spirit on the hearts of men.

Ezekiel 1:27.] That color, which is here said to be "as the color of amber," was probably a flesh color but only transparent, that the fire that was within might shine through it. Fire represents the divine nature, as the divinity was commonly represented by fire or the Shekinah. The flesh color represents the human nature, so that here is the divinity dwelling in flesh, or God incarnate, because the person that Ezekiel had here a vision of was Jesus Christ. See Ezekiel 1:4, and also Ezekiel 8:2. Or the color is "as the color of amber," as a color somewhat resembling both that of flesh and gold, to represent both Christ's incarnation and his preciousness, for this stone which God lays in Zion is elect, precious. He is infinitely precious to God the Father, and is precious to believers. (See note on Ezekiel 1:4.) Christ is the wisdom of God, the same wisdom as that spoken of in the Proverbs 8:10–11, of which it is there said, that it is to be received "rather than gold," and that it is "better than rubies, and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it." And Proverbs 8:19, "My fruit is better than gold, and my revenue than gold, yea, than fine gold; and my revenue than choice silver." In the description that is given of Christ in Canticles, it is said, Canticles 5:11, that "his head is as the most fine gold."

Ezekiel 3:16. "And it came to pass at the end of seven days."] "I.e. on the seventh day after the vision" we had an account of in the two foregoing chapters.

<!-- p. 733 -->

"And 'tis very probable that both this and that were on the sabbath day," as John "was in the Spirit on the Lord's day," when he saw the visions of the Almighty (Revelation 1:10). "The people on the sabbath had not the convenience of temple or synagogue; only it should seem they had a place by the 'riverside, where prayer was wont to be made,' as Acts 16:13. There they met on the sabbath day, where their enemies upbraided them with 'the songs of Zion' (Psalms 137:1–3). There Ezekiel met them, and 'the word of the Lord' then and there came to him." Henry.Ibid., 410.

Ezekiel 4:1. "Take thee a tile."] "'Twas Jerusalem's honor, that while she kept her integrity, God had graven her upon the palms of his hands (Isaiah 49:16). And the names of the tribes were graven in precious stones on the breastplate of the high priest [Exodus 39:14]. But now the faithful city is become a harlot, a worthless brittle tile or brick is thought good enough to portray it upon." Henry.Ibid., 412.

Ezekiel 4:3.] The iron wall betweenJE deleted "God and the city." the Prophet and the city represents the immovable, insuperable wall of separation between God or Christ and the city, for God's prophets represent him, and speak and act in his name, as appears by Jeremiah 13:1–11, and Hosea 1:2, and other places.

Ezekiel 4:5–6. "Three hundred and ninety days," etc.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 124–25.Taking "days" for "years" in prophetic style, Prideaux dates this last captivity 390 years from the apostasy of Jeroboam, thereby fulfilling the word of the prophets, especially Ezekiel (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 124–25).

The Prophet, in lying on his side bearing the iniquity of the people, also represents God or Christ, as in Ezekiel 4:3. And it signifies God's bearing, and being burdened and wearied for so long a time, their sins.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ezekiel 4:7. "And thine arm shall be uncovered."] Signifying that God would make bare his arm, and make his hand and his displeasure very manifest in the distress and destruction of that city.

Ezekiel 4:8.] The "bands" that were laid upon the Prophet represented the sins of the people, which are elsewhere represented as a grievous burden and hard bondage to God (Amos 2:13, Isaiah 43:24, Ezekiel 6:8).

<!-- p. 734 -->

Ezekiel 4:9–13.] Still the Prophet, in thus eating and drinking his bread and water "by measure," represents Christ, either in himself, or in his visible church or body. The people offered polluted bread to Christ, and robbed him in tithes and offerings, and were very sparing and scant in the fruit they brought forth to God during these three hundred and ninety years. And Christ's people, as the consequence of this, afterwards eat bread by measure, and water by measure, and eat polluted bread. They were driven to eat many unclean things in the siege, to eat anything they could lay hands on, without any regard to the distinction the law made between clean and unclean, and among other things, to eat the flesh of their own children. And afterwards they eat unclean things in their captivity among the Gentiles.

Ezekiel 5:1–4.] Here again, as in the preceding chapter, the Prophet represents God, and his hair represents the people. Christ's church adhere to him, and as it were grow out of him as a man's hair, for his people are members of his body. A man's hair is a sort of natural clothing. Christ's church are represented as his clothing; so Aaron's garments were typical of Christ's church (Psalms 133:2). Christ's seamless coat [John 19:23] represents the union of his church. Jeremiah's girdle represents God's church (Jeremiah 13:1–11). The hair is a natural ornament; so Christ's church is spoken of as Christ's attire and ornaments (Jeremiah 2:32). The hair is the ornament of the head, and a kind of natural crown. The hair is often understood to [be] a kind of natural crown and ornament in what the Scripture says of it (Jeremiah 7:29, Ezekiel 16:7, John 11:2 and John 12:3, Luke 7:38, Luke 7:44, Ezra 9:3, Nehemiah 13:25, Isaiah 3:24, 2 Kings 2:23, Jeremiah 16:6, Ezekiel 27:31, Jeremiah 48:37, Isaiah 15:2–3, Micah 1:16, Isaiah 22:12, Jeremiah 47:5, Ezekiel 7:18, Amos 8:10, 2 Samuel 10:4–5, 1 Chronicles 19:4–5).This sentence is a later interpolation. So is the church of Christ to Christ. Psalms 60:7, "Ephraim is the strength of my head," i.e. its beauty, ornament, and crown. See Isaiah 52:1. "A virtuous woman is said to be a crown to her husband" [Proverbs 12:4]; so is the church to Christ, who is her husband. The saints are a crown of rejoicing to faithful ministers of Christ who have been the instruments of their salvation; much more are they so to Christ himself, who is the author of their salvation.

"Then take thee balances, and weigh and divide the hair." "This intimates the very exact directing of God's judgments, according to equity (by him men and their actions are weighed), and the proportion which divine justice observes in punishing some by one judgment, and others by another." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 415.

<!-- p. 735 -->

Ezekiel 5:3–4. "Thou shalt also take of them a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. Then take of them again, and cast them into the fire, and burn them in the fire."] The small number that were preserved and bound in his skirts represented that little handful of people which were left under the government of Gedaliah, who also, most of them, came to a miserable end, some slain by Ishmael, and most of the rest afterwards destroyed in the destruction of Egypt. See Jeremiah 40, and four following chapters.

"For thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel." The wordsיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵלכָּל־בֵּית תֵצֵא־אֵשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ literally translated are thus, "Out of it shall proceed fire upon all the house of Israel," i.e. out of that fire into which this hair is cast, viz. the fire of God's wrath, the fire spoken of in the explication of these signs, or reddition of these similitudes (Ezekiel 5:13).

Ezekiel 5:7. "Therefore thus saith the Lord, Because ye multiplied more than the nations that are round about you."] "I.e. multiplied idols and altars, gods and temples; multiplied those things, the unity of which was their praise, 'more than the nations which were round about.' Israel's God is one, and his name one, his altar one. But they, not content with this one God, multiplied their gods to that degree, that according to the number of their cities, so were their gods, and their altars as heaps in the furrows of the field, so that they exceeded all their neighbors, in having gods many and lords many. They corrupted revealed religion more than the Gentiles had corrupted natural religion." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 416.

Ezekiel 6:13.] "There they had offered sweet odors to their idols, but there shall their dead carcasses send forth a stinking smell." Henry.Ibid., 419.

Ezekiel 6:14. "Towards Diblath."] 'Tis called Diblathaim (Numbers 33:46), "that great and terrible wilderness," which is described, Deuteronomy 8:15.

Ezekiel 7:12. "Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn."] Here it may be asked, What occasion would the seller have had to mourn more than the buyer, if there had been no captivity approaching? When men make bargains, both buyer and seller aims at their own advantage. *Answ*. The Prophet here has respect to buyers and sellers of inheritances. Inheritances were not wont to be sold in Israel unless a man was become poor,

<!-- p. 736 -->

and was obliged to sell his inheritance. And it was looked upon a great calamity to a man when he was thus obliged to sell his inheritance. And therefore God, in mercy and tenderness to them, required that "the land should not be sold forever," but that a redemption should be granted. See Leviticus 25:23–25. But at this time neither had the seller any occasion to mourn, nor the buyer to rejoice, for it made no alteration in the circumstances of one or the other, because the whole land was about to be broken up and left desolate, and they were all to be carried away out of it into captivity.

Ezekiel 8:2. "As the color of amber."] Note on Ezekiel 1:27.

Ezekiel 8:6–12.] See Warburton, vol. 2nd, pp. 296 ff.Warburton links the "great abominations" committed by Israel (Ezekiel 8:6) and the "idols of the house of Israel" portrayed on the wall (Ezekiel 8:10) as evidence that the Jews "*were extremely fond of* Egyptian *Manners, and did frequently fall into* Egyptian *Superstitions*," and that many of the laws given by Moses "*were instituted partly in Compliance to their Prejudices, and partly in Opposition to* Egyptian *Superstitions*" (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed. London, 1742], 2, pp. 296–300).

Ezekiel 8:16. "About five and twenty men."] Which is the number of the false idolatrous church, as twelve is of the true, being the root of 666, the number of the beast (Revelation 13:18). See also Ezekiel 11:1–2.

Ezekiel 9:2. "Came from the way of the higher gate, which lieth towards the north."] Either because the Chaldeans came from the north, Jeremiah 1:14, "Out of the north shall an evil break forth"; or because "the image of jealousy" was set up at "the door of the inner gate that looks towards the north" (Ezekiel 8:3, Ezekiel 8:5), and at "the door of the gate of the Lord's house, which was towards the north," the women sat that wept for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). These destroying angels came in at that gate of the temple to show what it was that opened the door for them, and brought 'em in to destroy the city.

"And they went in, and stood beside the brazen altar." These destroying angels receive their orders from God, standing at the brazen altar, as we read, Revelation 14:18, that an "angel came out from the altar, that had power over fire, and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sickle, and gather the cluster of the vine of the earth." These angels stood beside the altar, because the fire on the altar represented the wrath of God; and this fire, being not appeased with sacrifice, it burnt towards the inhabitants of the city whose sin had enkindled

<!-- p. 737 -->

the fire. Therefore instead of the priests' standing at the altar to appease God's wrath with sacrifice and intercede for the people, destroying angels stand there, to be animated and set to work by that flame, and to execute the purposes of God's wrath on the people, and act as ministers of him who would be a consuming fire to them.This paragraph is a later addition.

Ezekiel 9:5–6.] 'Tis a great evidence that infants are guilty of sin,The preceding six words are a later addition. that when these destroying angels were sent on that errand to execute God's fury upon the people (Ezekiel 9:8), and that reason was given for it, that their iniquity required such terrible vengeance, and that it was a just recompense of their sin (Ezekiel 9:10), I say, that when these angels came on such an errand, and also had express direction to spare some, to avoid 'em with great care, and not come nigh 'em, yet they are directed to smite and slay utterly without any pity all the rest, young and old, and even little children. Those that they are with such great care to except and not come near are excepted expressly, because they had approved themselves not partakers in the sins of the city. And therefore who can imagine that at the same time orders should be given to smite and slay utterly, without their eye sparing or having pity, those that were a great deal more evidently free from having any share in the sin of the city, because they are not capable of sinning, which is the case of little children if they have no original sin; which orders would not surely have been given with such circumstances merely for the sins of their parents, if they had no sin that was properly their own, as we may be the rather assured, because God himself did so fully and largely declare to this Prophet, that children should not die for the iniquity of the fathers, nor for any iniquity that they were not properly guilty of, in the Ezekiel 18 of this book.

Ezekiel 9:7. "And he said unto them, Defile the house."] "It should seem these destroyers made some difficulty of putting men to death in the temple, but God bids them not boggle at it." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 428.

Ezekiel 10:5. "Voice of the Almighty," etc.] This is a great evidence that the living creatures don't represent either angels or men, but something infinitely above all creatures.

<!-- p. 738 -->

Ezekiel 10:7. "And one cherub stretched forth his hand from between the cherubims [unto the fire], and took thereof, and put it into the hands of him that was clothed with linen, who took it, and went out."] This man "clothed with linen" seems to represent Christ. He has coals of divine vengeance put into his hands by God's justice, and not by any created angel. Christ, in acting as judge of the wicked to execute vengeance on his enemies, to break them with a rod of iron, etc., don't act in any dependence on any created angel. He receives nothing from them, but they receive all from him. He receives none of the weapons of his vengeance from them, but from the justice of God. This cherub that puts fire into the hand of Christ seems to be the same with the angel that "had power over fire" (Revelation 14:18), who cried unto "him that had the sharp sickle," to thrust in his sickle, "and gather the cluster of the vine of the earth." The angel that "had power over fire," or over God's wrath, is the attribute of God's justice. This hand that took fire from between the wheels was a hand that belonged to the face of the eagle, one of the faces of the cherub, for as each of these living creatures had four faces, so each had four wings and a hand under each wing, a hand belonging to each face (Ezekiel 1:6, Ezekiel 1:8). The hand that now took these burning coals probably belonged to the face of the eagle. See "Miscellanies," ww,*Works, 15*, 191–95. and "Revelation," no. 70, Ibid., 5, 162–65. and note on Revelation 14:15.

Ezekiel 10:19.] The Shekinah, or "glory of the God of Israel," made four removes: first, "to the threshold of the house," or temple (Ezekiel 9:3); secondly, to the east gate of the court of the temple, which is mentioned here; thirdly, from hence to the top of Mt. Olivet (Ezekiel 11:23); lastly, from thence into heaven (Ezekiel 11:24).

Ezekiel 11:1.] The "five and twenty men" here spoken of "were not the same with the five and twenty whom the Prophet saw 'at the door of the temple,' worshipping towards the east (Ezekiel 8:16). Those seem to have been priests or Levites, for they were 'between the porch and the altar.' But these were princes, sitting in the gate of the Lord's house to try causes (Jeremiah 26:10); and these here are charged, not with corruptions in worship, but with maladministration of the government. They devised mischief under pretense of concerting measures for the public safety, as Ezekiel 11:2." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 431.

<!-- p. 739 -->

Ezekiel 11:3. "This city is the caldron, and we be the flesh."] They gloried in being the proper inhabitants of Jerusalem, the holy city, and trusted in that privilege. It seems to have been a proverbial expression among the Jews when they would signify that any properly belonged to a city, house, or country, and were the proper inhabitants. See note on Ezekiel 11:15. These princes, by using this proverbial, did not only signify their trust in the privilege of being the proper inhabitants of Jerusalem, but their resolution that they would not go out of the city to the Chaldeans, as Jeremiah advised, by which they brought ruin on the city. See note on Ezekiel 11:6 and Ezekiel 11:8.

Ezekiel 11:6. "Ye have multiplied your slain," etc.] The princes and rulers, spoken of in the Ezekiel 11:1–3, had multiplied the slain in the city, not only those whom they by the sword of justice had unjustly put to death under color of law, but those whom they by their willfulness and pride unwisely exposed to the sword of war. All that had fallen and should yet fall in Jerusalem by the sword of the Chaldeans, they that advised 'em to stand it out (contrary to the advice of the prophet Jeremiah), should be accounted the murderers of.

Ezekiel 11:8. "Ye have feared the sword, and I will bring the sword upon you."] I.e. ye feared if you hearkened to Jeremiah's advice in going out to the Chaldeans, that they would kill you. But you shall not avoid being slain by them by refusing so to do.

Ezekiel 11:15.] God owned them that were already carried captive to Babylon as good figs, and declared it was for their good that he had sent 'em to Babylon. But the inhabitants of Jerusalem, those that remained there, abandoned 'em, supposing they were abandoned by God and sent far off as not worthy of any part in the land, but that they which were left behind alone were worthy. This they gloried in, and so did in effect vaunt it over their brethren, and bid them begone, and keep at a distance, for God has given the land wholly to us, and you are not worthy to have a part with us. "This city is the caldron, and we the flesh." See note on Ezekiel 11:3.

Ezekiel 11:21. "But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things."] I.e. have their hearts and dispositions conformed to the disposition of their false gods, to the dispositions of devils, and their temper and practice conformed to the characters and accounts given of their idols, and the ideas they had of them, their wantonness, intemperance, injustice, cruelty, etc.

<!-- p. 740 -->

Ezekiel 11:23.] Thus when God was departing from the city Jerusalem before its destruction, he goes up out [of] the city, and ascends to heaven from the same mountain that Christ ascended from.This remainder of this entry is a later addition. It was now the same person that ascended, that afterwards ascended hence in his human nature. When God left his people in wrath at the time of their destruction, he is represented as going and returning to his place, i.e. to heaven (Hosea 5:15). God, in the Ezekiel 43:2–4, is represented as returning again to the city and temple in the same chariot of the cherubims in which he departed as what should be in the future glorious restoration of his church. When Christ left that people before their first destruction by the Babylonians, he ascended into heaven from the same mountain from whence he afterwards ascended when he left them before their second destruction by the Romans.This sentence is a later addition.

Ezekiel 12:3–6. "Therefore, thou son of man, prepare thee stuff for removing," etc.] This is to represent Zedekiah's flight out of the city in the utmost confusion. He should remove from one place to another in the daytime, and shall carry forth his stuff as one preparing for a flight on the approaching evening, that he might be ready with his stuff near the place in the wall where he would make his escape. And because all the doors and gates were so guarded by the enemy that he durst not pass through them (see Jeremiah 52:7 and 2 Kings 25:4), he should dig through the wall, and carry his goods away clandestinely; and he should carry them on his own shoulders for want of a servant to attend him. He should do this in the twilight, that he might not be discovered; and he should cover his face, as being afraid to be known.

King Zedekiah, it seems, after the princes of the king of Babylon came into the city, and sat in the middle gate, fled first in the daytime to the king's garden, that was a place that was walled in by itself, and was near the outward wall of the city, and there lay concealed all the evening. But as soon as ever the evening came on, even in the twilight, they went out of this garden by the gate of the garden that opened next to the wall of the city into the space between the two walls, the wall of the garden and the wall of the town, and dug through the wall of the town, and fled out. See Jeremiah 39:4.

Ezekiel 13:4–5.] These false prophets, instead of doing the part of good shepherds to the flock, to watch carefully over them and defend the fold, to

<!-- p. 741 -->

make up the fence, and go and stand in the breach, to keep out the wolf, they were like the foxes that slyly stole over the fence, and caught the lambs, and ran away with them, and made a prey of them.

Ezekiel 13:10. "And one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered mortar."] See note on Jeremiah 8:11. They pretended to build up a wall for their defense from enemies or from the weather, and made them believe that it was a strong fortress or secure shelter, and that they were secure, and might rest quietly in it. Whereas, indeed, it is a poor, feeble business of no significancy. The rain will wash it away, the wind will rent it, because 'tis cemented "with untempered mortar." And the inhabitant shall find himself naked and exposed to all the force of the storm, and the hailstones shall come upon his head.

Ezekiel 13:18. "The women that sew pillows to all armholes."] As mothers probably were wont to do when they led their children with leading strings, they sewed little pillows to their clothes under the armpits, that the leading strings might not hurt them. This was necessary among them, for their children had no bodice or stays to fasten their leading strings to. The teachers of the people are their leaders (Isaiah 9:15–16, Luke 6:39). And God, in leading his people by the prophets, is spoken of as leading them as parents are wont to lead their children (Jeremiah 31:32 and Hosea 11:2–3). And the prophets among the people are spoken of as fathers among children (2 Kings 2:12, 2 Kings 13:14; Genesis 45:8). And the prophetesses were represented as their mothers (Judges 5:7). And therefore it was the mere nature to compare their leading the people to the way of mothers' leading their children.On "leading strings," see *Works, 15*, 28, 278. These false prophetesses were like the false prophets, spoken of in the preceding verses, who saw visions of peace, and "daubed with untempered mortar." They were all for contriving to lead the people in such a manner as to make them and keep them easy.

"And make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature." What in our translation is called "kerchief" was probably a kind of a crown that the women used to make for an ornament to the head. These prophetesses did not only make the people [easy] by telling them no calamity should come, but they crowned 'em as having done well, done their duty, and promised 'em a reward, even a crown of life. See Ezekiel 13:22.

"To hunt souls." Implying that instead of being the mothers of God's people, they were their destroyers. Instead of treating them as their dear children, truly seeking their ease and honor, as they pretended, they

<!-- p. 742 -->

treated them as wild beasts, as the huntsman does his game. They hunt for the precious life.

Ezekiel 14:14. "Though these three men, Noah," etc., "they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness."] This shows that it is no new notion lately first thought of in the world, that one may be favored of God for the sake of another's righteousness. It was old as Ezekiel's time. And 'tis not spoken of here as a false or unreasonable notion, as though there were no such thing as one's being accepted for the sake of another's righteousness, but only that the wickedness of the land was so great that the righteousness of these eminently holy men would not be sufficient to avail for them, or at most that the righteousness of men is of so little worthiness that it is not sufficient to recommend any more than themselves. But the righteousness of Christ is sufficient. 'Tis so excellent and worthy in God's account that 'tis sufficient to procure favor for the vilest of sinners. Herein is Christ a more excellent and sufficient mediator than Noah, Daniel, or Job, or the most holy and eminent of mere men.

Noah was in the old world, but saved only himself and his family. Daniel was in Babylon when it was destroyed, and only saved himself. Job saved only himself by his righteousness when all his children were destroyed. Each lived in a very degenerate time: Noah in the old world, Job when all nations were falling away to idolatry, Daniel in a most degenerate time in Israel.

Ezekiel 14:22. "Both sons and daughters."] In that corrupt time in Israel, it was the rising generation that God especially intended mercy for, as it was in the wilderness. See Lamentations 3:27 and Jeremiah 6:10–11.

"Shall come forth unto you." I.e. shall be brought forth out of the land of Israel that is devoted to destruction, unto you that are already here in captivity.

Ezekiel 15:2.] Man is very fitly represented by the vine. Its weakness, its dependence on other things which support it, well represents man's dependence on God, and his subordinate dependence on other things, his helplessness and misery if left alone. What a multitude of things does man depend upon for his subsistence and well-being, as the vine takes on many twigs to hold itself up. And it well represents man by its being useless any other way than by its fruit. The fruit of the vine does the more fitly represent the blood and benefits of Christ, the Son of man.

<!-- p. 743 -->

Ezekiel 16:6. "I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood."] Doubtless 'tis something very remarkable and wonderful that God would here signify by this emphatical repetition. And the emphasis lies partly in those words, "when thou wast in thy blood," the circumstances that she was in when God showed mercy on her, and partly in those words, "I said unto thee, Live," showing the wonderfulness and excellency of the favor God showed her in these circumstances. The thing that God would have so much remarked, and to have such special notice taken of, is the absolute freeness and sovereignty of his grace in bestowing life upon her. He said to her, Live, when she was polluted in her blood, while she was in her sin, and so not for her righteousness, or in any wise moved by her moral purity. God is not moved by this, either in converting or justifying the sinner, for he both renews and justifies the ungodly. See Titus 3:3–7, 1 Corinthians 6:11, Ephesians 2:1–13, Romans 4:5. This also signifies God's showing mercy to the sinner when he is helpless, for what is more helpless than an infant cast out in its blood.

"I said to thee, Live." This signifies that life in her was wholly the effect of God's power, and wholly the fruit of his mere good pleasure, which is further signified by the Ezekiel 16:8, "Thy time was the time of love."

Ezekiel 16:8. "I spread my skirt over thee."] Sinners' nakedness is covered with Christ's clothing.

Ezekiel 16:43. "Because thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth."] The days wherein God did those things for her, mentioned in the former part of the chapter.

Ezekiel 16:49. "Neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy."] Hence we learn that the poor, the wicked, are the objects of our charity. For 'tis not probable that those "poor and needy" in Sodom, here spoken of, were only godly persons where there was scarce any that were righteous, not ten in the whole city, and it may be none but Lot, who was not poor, but rich.

Ezekiel 16:51–52.] See Romans 1:32 and Romans 2:1 notes.

Ezekiel 16:57–58.] The sense of these verses seems to be this. Before thou didst come to be so grossly and openly flagitious, and before the appointed time was come for openly judging thee according to thine abominations,

<!-- p. 744 -->

even then thou didst suffer much for thy lewdness and thine abominations. Thou didst fall under the "reproach of the daughters of Syria, and all that are round about her," and the contempt of "the daughters of the Philistines." And if so, how great will be thy disgrace and punishment now thy wickedness is fully discovered, and the proper time of thy judgment. What is here said of the daughters of Syria and the Philistines seems to refer to the descent made upon Judah by the Syrians in the days of Ahaz, and soon after another by the Philistines (2 Chronicles 28:5, 2 Chronicles 28:18).

Ezekiel 16:60. "Nevertheless," etc.] That is, although thou hast not remembered the covenant betwixt us, but hast despised the oath in breaking the covenant, and though I will deal with thee as thou hast done, and will have no regard to my covenant with thee, as thou has disregarded, yet hereafter I will remember my covenant with thee.

Ezekiel 16:61. "I will give them to thee for daughters."] Here the Gentiles that are represented by Sodom are spoken of as those that should hereafter become children of God's Israel, or of that church of God which proceeds from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And in this chapter those that were the posterity of these patriarchs according to the flesh are not reckoned in the sight of God as their posterity, but rather the posterity of the heathen nations that formerly had possessed the land, as in Ezekiel 16:44–45, and also Ezekiel 16:3. How agreeable is this to the New Testament doctrine (Romans 2:28–29; John 8:39; Romans 9:6–7, Romans 4:11 ff., Romans 11:17 ff.; Galatians 3:15 ff., Galatians 6:16; Revelation 2:9; Galatians 4:25–31).

Ezekiel 17:22. "Of the highest branch of the high cedar."] One of the royal race of David, and "the highest branch," as he was of the highest line, and legal heir to the crown. "A tender one." See Isaiah 53:2 notes, and notes on Isaiah 11:1.

"'The highest branch,' the furthest of all from the root, for soon after he appeared, the house of David was all cut off and extinguished. But the nearest of all to heaven, for his kingdom was not of this world. He was taken 'from the top of the young twigs,' for he is the man, the branch, 'a tender plant, and a root out of a dry ground' [Isaiah 53:2], but a branch of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he may be glorified." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 455.

<!-- p. 745 -->

Ezekiel 17:23. "Fowl of every wing."] I.e. men of all nations, and not only of the children of Israel.

Ezekiel 17:24. "Brought down the high tree, and exalted the low tree," etc.] This is fulfilled several ways. The Jewish church was the "high tree" and "green tree." They had been highly exalted and favored of God, for there was no nation so great, that "had God so nigh to 'em," as they (Deuteronomy 4:7). They were also high in opinion of themselves, being an exceeding self-righteous people. But [God] exalted the Gentiles that were the "low tree," she that was desolate. The same thing is signified in the song of Hannah [1 Samuel 1:1–10]. It is fulfilled again by the victory the Christian church got over the heathen empire, and so in the victory she will obtain over Antichrist. Christ also seems to be meant by the "low tree" and the dry tree. See Ezekiel 21:26.

Ezekiel 18:4. "Behold, all souls are mine."] Not only the soul of the father, but the soul of the son are from me. The soul of the son is not from the father, but 'tis immediately created by me. Nor has the soul of the child to be looked upon as a communication of the father's soul, or an adjunct to it, or any otherwise so related to it as that the guilt of one should be the guilt of the other. The soul of the father and son do stand separately related to me, and subject to my law by and for themselves. And therefore "the soul that sins, it shall die"; and the child shall not be punished for its immediate father's sin.

Ezekiel 18:20. "The soul that sinneth it shall die."] See note on Ezekiel 9:5–6.

Ezekiel 19:1–5.] The kingdom or people are spoken of as the mother of the prince that makes him king. Thus "we read of Solomon's 'crown wherewith his mother crowned him' (Canticles 3:11)." Henry.Ibid., 461.

Ezekiel 20:1.] "By what the Prophet saith to them, Ezekiel 20:32, it should seem their inquiry was whether, now they were captives in Babylon at a distance from their own country, where they had not only no temple, but no synagogue, for the worship of God, it was not lawful for them, that they might ingratiate themselves with their lords and masters, to join with them in their worship, and do as the families of these countries do, that 'serve

<!-- p. 746 -->

wood and stone'? This matter [was palliated]This insertion is from Henry's text. as well as it would bear, like Naaman indenting with Elisha for leave to bow in the house of Rimmon, in complement to the king. But we have reason to suspect that their inquiry drove at this. Note, those hearts are wretchedly hardened that ask God leave to go on in sin, and that when they are suffering for it, they came and sat demurely with a show of devotion before the Prophet (Ezekiel 33:31)." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 462–63.

Ezekiel 20:5. "And made known myself to them in the land of Egypt."] See note on Exodus 3:13.

Ezekiel 20:27. "Yet in this your fathers have blasphemed me."] I.e. in the very same thing your fathers of later generations, your more immediate ancestors, have done like your ancestors of old, mentioned in the foregoing verses, notwithstanding those judgments for their sins there mentioned.

Ezekiel 20:32. "And that which cometh into your mind."] See note on Ezekiel 20:1.

Ezekiel 20:34–37.] As God, when he brought the children of Israel "with a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm, and with fury poured out," and brought [them] in the wilderness of Arabia, so God would bring 'em from the countries wherein they were scattered with a mighty hand, etc., and would bring 'em "into the wilderness of the people," before he brought ['em] "into the bond of the covenant," before he brought 'em into the Canaan of the kingdom of heaven, or of the gospel state, which Jesus the true Joshua was to bring them into. From the time of the captivity till the coming of Christ, the Jewish church was as it were in a wilderness. God made 'em "to pass under the rod" to humble 'em, and to prove 'em, as he did the children of Israel in the wilderness. They were in "the wilderness of the people." They were continually molested, invaded, and overrun by the nations of the world in that remarkable season of changes, overturnings, uproar, and confusion among the nations of the earth. This interval was a time wherein God shook the heavens and the earth. The kingdoms of the world were never [so] shaken; never were such wars and such great revolutions, in so short a space. And the children of Israel were not unconcerned in this confusion. They were affected

<!-- p. 747 -->

by all the great revolutions that happened in that space of time. They were brought "into the wilderness of the people."

Ezekiel 20:37. "And I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant."] As the shepherd causes his sheep "to pass under the rod," when he tithes them, as they go past out of the fold, that he may mark which is for God. See Leviticus 27:32 and Jeremiah 33:13.

Ezekiel 20:38–39. "I will purge out from you the rebels," etc.] In the timeMS: "time these that." that these rebels shall no longer be accounted of Israel, they shall not any longer be accounted of God's Israel merely because they descended from Abraham and Jacob. Only those shall be accounted Christians, and shall enjoy the privileges of Christians, and shall be suffered to dwell in the land of Christians, but such as are of a good conversation, agreeable to that in Isaiah 60:21, "Thy people shall be all righteous." "As for you, O house of Israel," etc.

"As for you" that now dwell in the land of Israel, and are reckoned amongst my people, and yet are rebels that serve other gods, don't pretend to be of my people no more. Don't make profession of my name. Go out among the heathen. Don't reckon yourselves of Israel. Don't pretend to have anything to do with me. Don't pollute my holy name with your gifts and with your idols; agreeable to Revelation 3:15, "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot. I would thou wert cold or hot." This is very naturally introduced by the preceding verse, as when Christ comes,Here JE crossed out "only." only those that areHere JE crossed out "righteous." rebels shall not be accounted of Israel, shall not dwell among [them]. So I had rather now that such would not pretend to be of my people. God had said in the preceding part of the chapter that he would not be inquired of by them. He would not so far own 'em to be his people for this reason, because they polluted themselves with their gifts and with their idols.

Rebels do but sojourn "in the land of Israel," as Ezekiel 20:38. They are strangers there; they don't belong there.

Ezekiel 20:46.] Probably meaning the land of Judea by "the south field" or "forest of the south," the same as is explained in the beginning of the next chapter. Chaldea was much to the north of Judea, and therefore the invasion

<!-- p. 748 -->

of the Chaldeans is spoken of as evil out of the north. This whole parable is explained in the beginning of the next chapter.

Ezekiel 20:47. "Every green tree, and every dry tree."] I.e. both the righteous and the wicked. See Ezekiel 21:3, with Luke 23:31. The Prophet, Ezekiel 17:24, speaks of drying up "the green tree," and causing "the dry tree to flourish," meaning by the "green tree" the Jews who were visibly righteous and very self-righteous, and by the "dry tree" the Gentiles who were wicked.

Ezekiel 21:10. "It contemneth the rod of my son, as every tree."] I.e. it makes no distinction between the rod of my son and other trees. It shows no respect or reverence to it, so but that it cuts it down as it would an ordinary [tree]. This may have respect to two things. By the "rod" of God's son is [meant] either the king of Judah, or the royal line of David, God's son, as he typified Christ. See Ezekiel 21:12–14. Or it means Christ, who is indeed God's Son, and is often called a rod, and a branch, or sprout. And then this place is parallel to that, Zechariah 13:7, "Awake, O sword, against the man that is my fellow."

Or it may mean the nation of Israel, who are called God's "son" (Hosea 11:1). By the Ezekiel 21:12, it seems that both the prince and the nation are meant by the rod.

Ezekiel 21:22. "Open the mouth in the slaughter."] I.e. "open the mouth" to shout when they are going to the slaughter or battle, or in words immediately following (1 Samuel 17:20).

Ezekiel 21:27. "If the wordעַוָּה. Here the versification differs between the KJV and the Hebrew Bible. In the latter, this word is in Ezekiel 21:32. be translated "overturn," then 'tis probable that this is a prophecy referring to the many changes that there were of the supreme power amongst the Jews from the captivity till Christ came. The supreme power was often shifted, one while in the hands of the Persian emperors, another while in the hands of the Syrians, etc. The crown and diadem was often overturned. If the word be translated "perverted," as it is in the margin,I.e. margin of the KJV. by that must be understood being given to them that had no right to it, causing of it to be usurped first by Persian, then by Syrian kings, and then by the Romans. He "whose right it is" is Christ.

<!-- p. 749 -->

God is the proper and rightful king of Israel, as God taught the people when they first asked [for] a king. Christ was their king; they were his possession, as he had bought them, and it was he especially that brought 'em out of Egypt, and was wont to appear to 'em.See JE's "Sermon Ten" on Isaiah 51:8, in his series preached in 1739 with the doctrine, "The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world" (*Works, 9*, 246–47).

Probably the word "overturn" or "pervert" is mentioned three times because of the three monarchies the church of the Jews were subject to, as "woe" is rehearsed three times in Revelation 8:13, meaning three distinct calamities or woes, and as "holy" is expressed three times by the angels [Isaiah 6:3], answerable to the number of the persons in the Trinity.

"And it shall be no more." That is, the crown that shall be taken off, and diadem that shall be removed (Ezekiel 21:26). The supreme power over Israel shall be no more in the royal line of David, but shall be removed away, and shall be overturned from one to another till Christ shall come; and then it shall be again in the hands of the royal offspring. See this more fully explained in "Miscellanies," "Fulfillment of Prophecies of the Messiah," §14.This sentence is a later addition. In "Miscellanies," no. 1068, entitled "Fulfillment of the Prophecies of the Messiah," section 14, as designated by JE's original numbering, includes a discussion of the changes in civil authority before Christ came. Ezekiel's prophecy, JE wrote, "was exactly fulfilled: the supreme civil power among the Jews being removed from the house of David soon after the captivity, and seated in the high priests of the family of Jozadeck, and removed from them to the Asmonean family of the posterity of Mattathias, and then removed from them to Herod, with whom it remained till Christ came." JE underscored that "the crown is changed from one family to another three times" before the Messiah appears (pp. 19–20).

Ezekiel 21:29. "Whiles they see vanity unto thee, whiles they divine a lie unto thee, to bring thee upon the necks of them that are slain, whose day is come, whose iniquity shall have an end."] The Ammonites were not destroyed till after the destruction of Jerusalem by reason of their being let alone. Sometime after they had see'd the destruction of the Jews, the people that they hated, they grew very insolent, and triumphed over Jerusalem, and trod on the necks of the Jews that were slain, because their day was come, etc. And they thus trampled on the dead bodies of the Jews, the rather because their false prophets and diviners assured them that the sword never should come to them at all, but that they should remain in perpetual safety. They supposed that now the sword of the Chaldeans had slain the hated Jews, it should return into its sheath. But God tells 'em it is still drawn and furbished "for the slaughter," and

<!-- p. 750 -->

should not return into the sheath till God had judged them with it, as in the Ezekiel 21:28 and Ezekiel 21:30.

Ezekiel 21:31.] Or "I will blow" up "the fire of my wrath" against thee, for they were as the fuel, as in the next verse. See Ezekiel 22:21.

Ezekiel 22:28. "Daubed them with untempered mortar."] See Ezekiel 13:10–11.

Ezekiel 22:30.] 'Tis an allusion to a valiant man that, when a breach is made in a wall by the enemy, goes and stands in the gap, and keeps out the enemy, and defends the besieged city or camp. So an eminently godly man defends a people by fervent prayer when beset with God's judgments and wrath, and God begins to break in upon them. For he that is powerful in prayer is compared to a valiant man in fight. Thus 'tis said of Jacob, that "as a prince he had power with God, and had prevailed" [Genesis 32:28]; he had as it were overcome God. So in the New Testament, that "the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force" [Matthew 11:12], alluding to an enemy's taking a city. See in the Ezekiel 13 of this same prophecy, Ezekiel 13:4–5, Ezekiel's speaking there of the prophets as he doth here. "O Israel, thy prophets are like foxes in the deserts. Ye have not gone up into the gaps, neither made up the hedge for the house of Israel to stand in the battle in the day of the Lord." It becomes the spiritual leaders of a people thus to be spiritually valiant, and by their valor, by their faith and fervency in prayer (Jeremiah 27:18), to defend their people, as it becomes the captains and leaders in an army to be valiant, and to be able to stand in the front of the battle, and to defend those that follow them.

It seems also to allude to a person's interposing, in such a case, that is beloved and esteemed by the enemy besieging, out of pity to the besieged, when he sees that their wall is broken, and they are just ready to be destroyed, interposes and stands himself in the breach between the sword of the enemy and the people, either offering his own breast to the enemy's sword in their room, to satisfy their rage, or to stop and assuage them by virtue of his merit and esteem of them. Moses in these senses stood in the breach, Psalms 106:23. "Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them," herein being a notable type of Christ. Thus Aaron ran into the camp, "and stood between the dead and the living," i.e. between God's wrath and the people, with

<!-- p. 751 -->

incense in his hand, a type of prayer and of merit; "and the plague was stayed" (Numbers 16:47–48).

Ezekiel 23:17–19. "And her mind was alienated from them.… Yet she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot in the land of Egypt."] "They had enough of the Chaldeans, grew sick of them, as Jehoiakim and Zedekiah did. 'Her mind being alienated from [them],' she courted the Egyptians, would come into an alliance with them, and to strengthen their alliance would join with them in their idolatries, and then depend upon them to be their protectors from all other nations. For so wise, so rich, so strong, was the Egyptian nation, and come to such perfection in idolatry, that there is no nation now they can take such satisfaction in as in Egypt." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 478.

Ezekiel 23:34. "Thou shalt break the shards thereof, and pluck off thine own breasts."] "For indignation at the extreme bitterness of the cup, being 'full of the fury of the Lord' (Isaiah 51:20), as men in great anguish tear their hair, and throw everything from them. Finding there is no remedy, but it must be drank, thou shalt have no manner of patience in the drinking of it." Henry.Ibid., 479.

Ezekiel 24:6–7. "Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it!… For her blood is in the midst of her; she set it upon the top of a rock; she poured it not upon the ground, to cover it with dust."] The law required that they should not eat flesh with the blood, but that the blood should be poured on the ground, and covered "with dust" (Leviticus 17:13). Flesh dressed and eaten with the blood was polluted, abominable flesh. The people of Jerusalem are here compared to such flesh in the caldron. "Her blood is in the midst of her." She is like a pot whose scum is in the midst of it. When bloody flesh is boiled in a pot, the blood rises in a scum. The sin of the people is compared in these words to two things. 1. To the blood and scum, which is the pollution and abomination of bloody flesh. 2. To the wickedness of those that shed blood of men, and did not cover it with earth, as they were required to do the blood of beasts, but were so open and daring in it as to "set it on the top of a rock."

<!-- p. 752 -->

Ezekiel 25:4–5. "To the men of the East.… Rabbah a stable for camels, and the Ammonites a couching place for flocks."] After Nebuchadnezzar had made the cities and country desolate, the people inhabiting Arabia, who are often called "the men of the East," and whose wealth, we learn by many scriptures, lay in their cattle, and abounded in camels and flocks, should come and take possession of their country and cities, and should make even their royal city "a stable for their camels," etc. Henry.Ibid., 485.

Ezekiel 26:4. "I will also scrape her dust from her," etc.] See the accomplishment, Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 692–93.Prideaux describes Alexander the Great's siege and battle at Tyre (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, pp. 692–93).

Ezekiel 26:5. "Spreading of nets in the midst of the sea."] See no. 256.*Works, 15*, 205.

Ezekiel 26:12. "And shall lay thy stones, and thy timber, and thy dust in the midst of the water."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 692–93.Prideaux interprets this passage as a prophecy of Alexander the Great's conquest of new Tyre, effected by his building a causeway to the island city from the rubbish of old Tyre (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, pp. 692–93).

Ezekiel 26:14. "A place to spread nets upon."] No. 256.*Works, 15*, 205.

Ezekiel 26:20. "Set thee in the low parts of the earth, in places desolate of old."] The cities of Sodom and Gomorrah were sunk and set "in the low parts of the earth." And so were many of the cities of the old world, being buried deep in the earth by the new strata of earth, that the flood brought over them and left upon them.

"And I shall set glory in the land of the living." "The land of the living" here is set in opposition to the pit and "the low parts of the earth," whither the people of old time are gone, viz. the inhabitants of the old world and of Sodom and Gomorrah, i.e. hell. And therefore by "the land of the living" here is meant the land of the saints, the land of those that shall be saved from death and hell, and have spiritual and everlasting life, the land of God's church. There is no reason to understand this as a promise of great prosperity to the whole habitable earth after Tyrus's ruin, but that God should accomplish glorious things for his church, whose calamity they had rejoiced at (Ezekiel 26:2), would advance its glory in the

<!-- p. 753 -->

land of Canaan as he did in and after the days of Cyrus (This sense is greatly confirmed by Ezekiel 28:25–26.),This parenthetical remark is a later addition. and did greatly advance its glory, both on earth and in heaven, the proper land of the church in the days of the Messiah. The Holy Spirit seems to mean the same thing (at least chiefly) in the book of Psalms by this expression, "the land of the living" (Psalms 27:13, and Psalms 116:9, and Psalms 142:5). By "the book of the living" (Psalms 69:28), the Psalmist apparently means "the book of the righteous," the same that in the New Testament is called "the book of life" [Philippians 4:3]. So by "the land of the living" is meant the same as "the land of the righteous," or "land of uprightness," as it is called, Psalms 143:10. See notes on Genesis 3:20, "Scripture," nos. 322 and 399.*Works, 15*, 304–6, 396–99. The land of Israel was "the land of the living," because it was a land where God gave the blessing of spiritual and eternal life. Psalms 133:3, "As the dew that descended on the mountains of Zion, where the Lord commanded the blessing, even life for evermore." Here we don't only read of one Mt. Zion, but of "the mountains of Zion," meaning the mountains of Israel, of the church, the mountains of which are used to signify the whole land of Israel very often in Scripture. The saints are called by the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 4:11, οἱ ζῶντες, "they that live," or "the livers."

Ezekiel 27:8.] "The common sailors they had from other countries. The inhabitants of Arvad and Sidon were their mariners. These came from cities near them. But the pilots and masters of the ships, that had the command in their fleets, were of their own city, such as they could put confidence in." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 490.

Ezekiel 27:26. "Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters; the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas."] "Tyre is as a great ship richly laden, that is split or sunk by the indiscretion of her steersmen. 'Thy rowers' have themselves 'brought thee into great' and dangerous waters. The governors of the city, and those that had the management by their public affairs, by some mismanagement or other, involved them in the war with the Chaldeans, which was the ruin of their state." Henry.Ibid., 491.

Ezekiel 28:8. "Thou shalt die the deaths of them that are slain in the midst of the seas."] "That have no honor done 'em at their death, but their dead

<!-- p. 754 -->

bodies are immediately thrown overboard without any ceremony, to be a feast for fish. Tyre is like to be 'destroyed in the midst of the sea' (Ezekiel 27:32). And the king of Tyre shall fare no better than the people." Henry.Ibid., 493. It may also be observed that "great waters" are often made use of in Scripture as a symbol or signification of great misery and the wrath of God. And the sea or the deep is in Scripture often an emblem of hell, and the fish of the sea of devils.For parallel comments on these biblical symbols, see *Works, 11*, 58, 72, 84, 131, and 132.

Ezekiel 28:14. "Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth, and I have set thee so."] I.e. either "I have set thee" as one of the cherubims in the house of God, that stretch forth their wings, and cover the mercy seat, for those cherubims were without doubt anointed, as the ark and the mercy seat were, and all the vessels of the tabernacle and temple, i.e. all the furniture thereof. The king of Tyrus had assumed to himself great honor. And God had exalted him to great honor in his providence, and that even upon his holy mountain to be next to God himself, like one of the angels that were next to his throne, like the cherubims that dwelt in the holy of holies, and were next the mercy seat or throne of God in the temple.

Or "the anointed cherub that covereth" may be taken as an appellation proper to Christ, who is the angel of the Lord, and whose name is Christ, or the anointed, and who eminently may be called the "cherub that covereth," that is, that covereth with the wings of his protection, who shelters his people under the shadow of his wings from wrath and from all evil, who gathers them as an hen gathers her chickens under her wings, whose peculiar character it is to be the Savior, or he that covereth. And when it is said, "Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth, and I have set thee so," the meaning seems to be, Thou hast usurped the honor and power of the anointed cherub; thou hast put thyself in his place. And I, in my providence, "have set thee so"; I have suffered thee thus to usurp, and have in my providence set thee in Christ's place, and have ordered it so that by thy usurpation thou shouldst have that dominion and honor that belongs alone to this anointed cherub. In what is said here of the king of Tyrus, an eye seems to be had to Antichrist, who is upon God's holy mountain, who hath set himself in Christ's seat, and sitteth in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God, calling himself Christ's vicar on earth. See "Miscellanies," no. 980.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 20*, 296–99.
