Ezekiel 29:9. "Because thou hast said, The river is mine own, and I have made it."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 132.Prideaux relates the story of Apries' violent death at the hand of Amasis, citing it as a fitting end for one whose conceit of himself and his boasts, including the statement in this verse, had been a challenge to the power of God (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 2, p. 132).

Ezekiel 29:13–21.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 112. They were a "base kingdom" Ezekiel 29:14] in that henceforward they were never governed by princes of their own. A kingdom is said to be base, when under the dominion of a foreign prince (Ezekiel 17:14).*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 112.

Ezekiel 29:18.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 131.Nebuchadnezzar and his army, after defeating Tyre, ravaged Egypt and gathered rich spoils from that country, which fulfilled prophecies by Ezekiel, according to Prideaux (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 131).

Ezekiel 29:21.] No. 469.*Works, 15*, 561–62.

Ezekiel 30:5. "The men (or children) of the land that is in league."] The land of the Jews is so called because they, contrary to God's revealed will, entered into a league with *Egypt*, which they trusted to for their safety from the Chaldeans. Now those that fled into Egypt fall with it, agreeable to Jeremiah's prophecies.

Ezekiel 30:6. "They also that uphold Egypt shall fall."] "See the justice of God. Egypt pretended to uphold Jerusalem when that was tottering, but proved a deceitful reed; and now they that pretend to uphold Egypt shall prove no better." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 498.

"From the tower of Syene." See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, p. 131.Prideaux describes Nebuchadnezzar's conquest of Egypt as extending from Migdol to Syene, the latter near the border of Ethiopia (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, p. 131).

Ezekiel 30:10. "By the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon."] They that undertook to defend Israel from Nebuchadrezzar, seeing they were treacherous, and would not fulfill their engagements, shall fall themselves by the same foe that Israel through their treachery fell by.

<!-- p. 756 -->

Ezekiel 30:21–22.] "One arm of that kingdom might well be reckoned broken, when the king of Babylon routed the forces of Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish (Jeremiah 46), and made himself master of all that pertained to Egypt, 'from the river of Egypt to Euphrates' (2 Kings 24:7)." (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 499. The other arm was broken, when his army that he sent against the Cyrenians was cut off, and thereupon a great part of his own people revolted from him, and [he] was "forced to flee into the upper Egypt towards Ethiopia." Prideaux, Pt. I, pp. 127–28.*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 127–28.

Ezekiel 31:17. "Slain with the sword."] See note on Job 19:29.

Ezekiel 32:26. "There is Meshech and Tubal."] "There lies the Scythian power, which about this time was busy in the world. Meshech and Tubal,Meshech and Tubal were countries in Asia Minor. those barbarous northern nations, had lately made a descent upon the Medes, and caused their terror among them, lived among them upon free quarter for some years, making everything their own they could lay their hands on. But at length Cyaxares, king of the Medes, drew them by a wile into his power, cut off abundance of them, and obliged them to quit his country." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 505.

Ezekiel 32:27. "Their iniquities shall be upon their bones."] A plain hint at a future punishment.

Ezekiel 34:23.] Here is an allusion to David's occupation before he was called to Saul's court, which was that of a shepherd, as Psalms 78:70–72.

Ezekiel 36:2. "The ancient high places."] I.e. fortresses. See note on Deuteronomy 32:4 and Deuteronomy 32:13.

Ezekiel 37:7–9.] His "prophesying upon the bones" was a representation of preaching God's word to these that are spiritually dead; and "prophesying to the wind," saying, "Come from the four winds, O breath," represented the prayer that ought to accompany preaching in order to the success of the word in men's conversion. Men may be prepared for conversion by doctrinal knowledge, common illumination, and conviction "without the Spirit" of God, for all natural men are in the New Testament

<!-- p. 757 -->

represented as wholly without the Spirit, i.e. however they may be the subjects of common influences of the Spirit, yet the Spirit of [God] is not at all communicated to 'em in his own proper nature. Nor is he united to them as any principle in them, or any stated inhabitant in their souls. This is a confirmation that saving grace differs from common grace not only in degree, but in nature and kind. See "Miscellanies," no. 1103.*Works, 20*, 486–87.

Ezekiel 38-39.] Concerning GOG AND MAGOG, see no. 433.Ibid., 15, 514–17.

Ezekiel 38:17. "Of whom I have spoken in old time," etc.] This is a good proof that those glorious prophecies of Isaiah and other former prophets, which insist so much on the great deliverances which God would accomplish for Israel, and the terrible destruction of their enemies, han't respect only to the destruction of Babylon, and the redemption of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, but have respect to things to be brought to pass long after that, for Ezekiel prophesies in the time of the captivity. And yet he speaks of this that he here foretells (which is spoken of as much foretold by former prophets), as that which is to be accomplished long after that time, and after the people had been resettled in their own land after a long captivity. See Ezekiel 38:8, Ezekiel 38:12, Ezekiel 38:16.

See note on Isaiah 61:4.

Ezekiel 38:22. "And great hailstones."] Revelation 16:21.

Ezekiel 39:6. "A fire on Magog."] Revelation 20:9.

Ezekiel 39:8–10.] See Psalms 46:9 note.

Ezekiel 39:17. "A great sacrifice."] See note on Zephaniah 1:7–8.

Ezekiel 40:16. "And upon each post were palm trees."] Palm trees were the emblems of saints. Every post has one of these engraven on them. "And it had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, upon the posts thereof" Ezekiel 40:26]. Hereby seems to be symbolically represented the same thing that is contained in that promise of Christ, Revelation 3:12. "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God." See Ezekiel 40:22, Ezekiel 40:26, Ezekiel 40:31, Ezekiel 40:34, Ezekiel 40:37.

<!-- p. 758 -->

Ezekiel 40:31. "And the going up to it had eight steps."] See also Ezekiel 40:34 and Ezekiel 40:37. The ascent into the outer court at each gate was by seven steps. (See Ezekiel 40:17, Ezekiel 40:22, and Ezekiel 40:26.) But the ascent into the inner court at each gate was by eight steps, to signify that the nearer God's people approach, the more swift are the advances by which they make progress in holiness, get above the world, and approach to the heavenly state.

Ezekiel 42:15–20.] The holy ground about the temple "extended each way 500 reeds, each reed above three yards and a half, so that it reached every way about an English measured mile, which (the ground lying square) was above eight miles round. Thus large were the suburbs, as I may call them, of this mystical temple, signifying the great extent of the church in gospel times." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 535.

Ezekiel 43:12. "Shall be most holy."] In the originalקֱדָשִׁים קַדֶשׁ it is, "holy of holies." Formerly only that part of the temple where was the ark and mercy seat was called" holy of holies"; but now not only the whole temple, but the whole mountain of the house shall be so called.

Ezekiel 43:15. "The altar shall be four cubits."] See notes on Isaiah 29:1–2.

Ezekiel 45:25.] Passing over the feast of Pentecost without any mention of it, after God had declared the ordinances for the Passover, he comes directly to the feast of tabernacles, because the state of the church here represented is not that which was in the apostles' days, or the benefits and glory that it had by the outpouring of the Spirit in the first fruits of it that was then, but the joyful and glorious state of the church after the fall of Antichrist, when there should be a more full ingathering of God's elect, which was represented by the feast of tabernacles, when although the death and sacrifice of Christ signified in the Passover will then be remembered and greatly celebrated, yet the glory of that first outpouring of the Spirit in the apostles' days, bringing in the first fruits of the Christian church, shall be as it were forgotten as worthy no more to come into mind. The glory of that last outpouring of the Spirit shall so much exceed it, the former shall have no glory in this respect by reason of the glory that excelleth. See note on Zechariah 14:16–19, "Scripture," no. 396.*Works, 15*, 390–92.

<!-- p. 759 -->

Ezekiel 46:15.] Here is mention of a morning sacrifice, but no evening sacrifice, because in the glorious time here spoken of there be a continual and increasing day, but no evening, intimated by that in Isaiah, "Thy sun shall no more go down," etc. [Isaiah 60:20].

And that in Zechariah, "It shall be one day, not day and night; but at evening time it shall be light" [Zechariah 14:7]; and typified by the sun's standing still in Joshua's time [Joshua 10:13].

Ezekiel 47:1. "Waters issued out from under the threshold of the house."] So probably that which is signified by these waters will first arise from some mean, obscure part of the church of God. The threshold of the door is the meanest and lowest part of the house. So it was a "stone cut out of the mountains without hands, that smote the image" (Daniel 2:34 and Daniel 2:45). See note on Daniel 2:45.

Ezekiel 47:11.] The "miry places" and "marishes" are neither land nor water, aptly representing wicked professors that are neither cold nor hot. Marshy places are made barren by the water, and not fruitful. Such places are cloyed and glutted with water, and are hindered from being fruitful when other places are fertilized by the water. Marishy places yield neither the produce of the land in the useful growth of that, nor yet do they yield fish, the proper produce of the water.

"Shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt." Referring to what had been said before, Ezekiel 47:8, where we are told that the waters of the sanctuary, "being brought forth into the sea, the waters shall be healed," i.e. shall be cured of their saltness, and shall be made sweet and fit for use to quench thirst, etc.; but the miry places and marshes thereof (by which perhaps is meant the marishes of the sea, the salt marshes), shall be forever given up to their saltness, and never shall be made sweet.

<!-- p. 760 -->

### Daniel

Daniel 2:30. "But for their sakes," etc.] It seems as though the words in the originalיְהוֹדְעוּן לְמַלְכָּא פִשְׁרָא דִּי עַל־דִּבְרַת might properly have been rendered thus, "To the end that they might make known the interpretation to the king," i.e. that God might make known. The plural number here seems to be used in the same manner that it is, Daniel 4:25. And Lamentations 4:15, "They cried unto them, Depart ye," etc.

Daniel 2:32–33.] 'Tis not unlikely that the Greek philosophers and poets might first take their notion of their four ages—the golden, silver, brazen, and iron ages—first from this dream of Nebuchadnezzar's and Daniel's interpretation of it, for it was about this time that philosophers first appeared among the Greeks. And 'tis known that they took many of their notions from the Chaldeans and the wise men or magicians of this country, of whom Daniel was reckoned the most famous, and was called their master [Daniel 5:11]. About this time, in particular, Pythagoras traveled into Babylon, and continued there for twelve years, and was an auditor of the magicians, of whom Daniel was the master, who interpreted this dream of the king of Babylon, which made a great noise through that city and country.

Daniel 2:34–35.] When God sends forth his word, when he sends forth the rod of his strength out of Zion in the latter days, God's word shall run and be glorified. And everything that stands in its way shall be broken in pieces before it, whether it be gold, or silver, or brass, or iron, or clay. However strong that is that is set up in opposition, it shall be broken in pieces. Brass and iron shall be as clay, no more able to withstand it than weak clay. And however magnificent, bright, and glorious, and precious in the esteem of men, it shall be broken in pieces. There shall be no difference between bright and precious gold and silver, and vile clay; all

<!-- p. 761 -->

shall be broken in pieces together. All alike shall become as the chaff of the summer threshing floor that the wind drives away, light and worthless, nothing accounted, scattered by a blast of wind, and trodden underfoot. Thus it shall be proclaimed at that time, "All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof as the flower of the field. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, because the spirit of the Lord bloweth upon it. Surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, but the word of our God shall stand forever" (Isaiah 40:6–8). And thus shall be fulfilled that in the Isaiah 2:12–17, and Isaiah 41:15–16, and Isaiah 64:1–2, [and] Isaiah 5:15.The remainder of this paragraph is a later entry. Then the interest of infidelity and heresy, however strengthened by the arguments of theJE deleted "learned." men of great abilities, and though mightily established, having full and strong possession, all seeming to be strong and irrefragable like iron and brass, and the curious, beautiful schemes of philosophers, which had been adorned with the greatest eloquence, and a fine style, and highly valued by the world as silver and gold, shall come to nothing, shall become as the chaf that the wind drives away.

Daniel 2:45. "A stone cut out of the mountains without hands."] Dr. Barrow (second volume of his *Works*, p. 104) interprets this thus: "A slender instrument coming forth out of some remote and secret place, without any considerable influence of human endeavor."Fourth edition. See note on Ezekiel 47:1.

Daniel 3:1 ff.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. I, pp. 142–43.Prideaux discusses the dimensions, mass, and value of Nebuchanezzar's golden image (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. I, vol. 1, pp. 142–43).

There is no doubt but that thisMS: "Thing." image made by the king of Babylon, so costly, vast, and wonderful, tending to fill the gazing crowd with admiration, was in divine providence and in the Scripture history a designed type of that image that the king of the spiritual Babylon commanded to be made, and commanded all to worship, and causes all that will not worship it to be killed, which we read of, Revelation 13:15, and that this burning, fiery furnace of Nebuchadnezzar is a type of the cruel popish persecutions.

<!-- p. 762 -->

Daniel 3:25.] See no. 100.*Works, 15*, 79.

"Like the Son of God."] See "Fulfillment of Prophecies of the Messiah," pp. 20 ff.JE contextualizes Nebuchadnezzar's comment concerning the fourth form in the fiery furnace by stating that "the doctrine of the ancient prophets" asserted "that the Messiah was the Son of God," the name applied to the divine person appearing from time to time "in a glorious visible form." Among those privileged to receive visitations were Jacob, Moses, Joshua, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and others. Even the heathen had traditions from the Israelites concerning the Son of God or a divine person appearing as a man, which JE links with Nebuchadnezzar's observation ("Fulfillment of the Prophecies of the Messiah," §16, pp. 20–21). See also "Controversial Book," p. 218.This paragraph is a later entry. JE writes, "One of the names by which that divine person, that was with the Jews in the wilderness and that dwelt with them in the land of Canaan, was known among them, was 'the son of God.'… This person, it was evident, was not the first person in the deity, or he that acted first in the affairs of God's kingdom." This person had appeared from time "in the form of a man" to the ancient patriarchs and the Jews, and was "famed among the heathen nations." "And therefore, when Nebuchadnezzar saw a person with Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the burning fiery furnace in such a visible form, he at once supposed it to be this person that he had heard of, that used thus to appear; and therefore he says the form of the fourth is like to [the] Son of God [Daniel 3:25]" ("'Controversies' Notebook: Justification," *Works, 21*, 381).

Daniel 4:8. "In whom is the spirit of the holy gods."] This manner of expression among the Chaldeans, which we have several times in this [chapter], probably arose from some traditional notice that the heathen had of the Trinity. See "Miscellanies," nos. 955 and 970.*Works, 20*, 227–29 and 253–54. They had some traditional notice of the Son of God, as Daniel 3:25 of the preceding chapter.

Daniel 4:15. "With a band of iron and brass."] I.e. "that it may not be raked to pieces, or trodden to dirt, and to show that it was reserved for better days, let it be hooped round 'with a band of iron and brass' to keep it firm." (So Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 569. This sense is favored by Daniel's interpretation, Daniel 4:26. "And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; *thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee*." Compare 1 Samuel 25:29.

Daniel 4:25. "They shall drive thee."] Here see Job 18:18, the Hebrew;יְנִדֻּהוּ וְּמִתֵּבֵל אֶל־חֹשֶׁךְ מֵאוֹר יֶהְדְּפֻהוּ and Job 34:20, the Hebrew;בְיָד לאֹ אַבִּיר וְיָסִירוּ וְיעֲבֹרוּ עָם יְגֹעֲשׁוּ לָיְלָה וַחֲצוֹת יָמֻתוּ רֶגַע and Luke 12:20, the Greek.εἶπεν δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός ἄφρων, ταύτη τῇ νυκτὶ τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπαιτοῦσιν ἀπο σοῦ ἃ δὲ ἡτοίπασας, τίνι ἔσται

<!-- p. 763 -->

"They shall drive thee from men." See note on Daniel 2:30 and Lamentations 4:15.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Daniel 4:27.] By "the poor" here are probably especially intended God's people that were then held captive under Nebuchadnezzar. God's people go by this appellation, "the poor," in Scripture. This was God's quarrel with the king of Babylon, that he "opened not the house of his prisoners" (Isaiah 14:17).

Daniel 4:30–33.] There is probably no sin that is so frequently punished with distraction as pride. We see in innumerable instances spiritual pride punished with a sort of distraction, men lostOr: "cast." to a strange unaccountable wildness and extravagance in religious matters, as though in these things they had not the use of the faculties of rational creatures. Men thinking themselves wise and lifted up with a pride of their knowledge do often become fools in such a very surprising manner and degree.

This fall of Nebuchadnezzar, this remarkable change made in him by the judgment of God, does in many things resemble the fall of the Satan or Lucifer, the grand rebel angel, to which the fall of the king of Babylon is compared in Isaiah 14. Nebuchadnezzar was not only vastly debased, cast down from the highest outward glory to the mean state of a beast, but probably like a very fierce, furious beast, that it was dangerous coming nigh him. It seems to have been with him as it was with the demoniac that was possessed with the legion of devils, of whom we read that he "wore no clothes, neither abode in any house" [Luke 8:27]. And though "he had been often bound with fetters and chains, yet the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters had been broken in pieces" [Mark 5:4]. And he was driven into the wilderness, and no man could tame him, nor durst any man pass by that way. 'Tis said in the Daniel 5:21, that "his dwelling was with wild asses," a most wild, untamable kind of creature. Thus Nebuchadnezzar was driven from men. And this is the best account that can be given how it should come to pass that he should be suffered to live in the open field, and that he was not confined. Thus Nebuchadnezzar, from the height of his pride and glory in that glorious [palace] that was near the place where the Garden of Eden was, was cast down into the most vile circumstances to be like a beast, and not only so, but like a devil.

<!-- p. 764 -->

Daniel 5:24. "Then was the part of the hand sent from him."] I.e. from God. When thou wast come to this height of wickedness, God sent this part of a hand; "and this writing was written."

Daniel 5:25 ff.] "The signification of these words is, 'he hath numbered, he hath weighed, and they divide.' *Mene*,מְנֵא *mene*; that's repeated, for the thing is certain. It signifies, both in Hebrew and Chaldee, 'he hath numbered and finished.' *Tekel*;תְּקֵל that signifies in Chaldee, 'thou art weighed,' and in Hebrew, 'thou art too light.' *Upharsin*,וּפַרסִין which should have been rendered *Pharsin* or *Peres; Pharsin* in Hebrewפַּרְסִי signifies the Persians; *Paresin* in Chaldee signifies 'dividing.' Daniel puts both together." Thus Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 575.

The two last words, *Tekel* and *Pharsin*, being interpreted by Daniel in two senses according as the words will allow, taking the sense of the words as they signify both in Hebrew and Chaldee, is an indisputable evidence of two things. 1. That the words of God, especially the words of prophecy, may well be supposed sometimes to have several senses. See note on Hosea 11:1. Yea, further, 2. That when the same words allow of two senses or translations entirely different and not dependent or related one to another as type and antitype, yet we may well suppose that the Holy Ghost has respect to both oftentimes. And when both senses are what the language properly allows, both are instructive and agreeable to the analogy of faith, we may well interpret 'em of both.

This handwriting on the wall is applicable to all wicked men when the time is come for 'em to die, for then God "has numbered and finished" their day. "And after death comes judgment when they are weighed in the balances, and found wanting." And after that God "divides," i.e. gives them to their enemies as a prey. They are then given over into the hands of devils as their prey. See Henry.Ibid., 576. And then also their worldly possessions, that they placed their happiness in, are taken from them, and divided to others.

Daniel 5:31. "And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old."] "Some observe, that he being now sixty-two years old in the last year of the captivity, he was born in the eighth year of it;

<!-- p. 765 -->

and that was the year when Jeremiah was carried captive, and all the nobles, etc. See 2 Kings 24:13, 2 Kings 24:15. Just at that time when the most fatal stroke was given, was a prince born, that in process of time should avenge Jerusalem upon Babylon, and heal the wound that was now given. Thus deep are the counsels of God concerning his people; thus kind are his designs towards them." Henry.Ibid. We may note further that those who were carried away in that captivity were especially the objects of God's gracious designs and promises of a merciful return. Those were the good figs spoken of, Jeremiah 24.

Daniel 6:22. "My God hath sent his angel."] The lions' den into which Daniel was cast was a type of the same thing with Nebuchadnezzar's burning fiery furnace, and that which seems principally typified by both is hell. The lions in this den are types of devils. And the angel of the Lord that came into the den amongst the lions to deliver Daniel from them was probably the same person that came into the burning fiery furnace to deliver Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the flames, viz. the angel of the covenant, "the Son of God" [Daniel 3:25]. Christ, our Good Shepherd, was as it were thrown to the lions, and encountered them, and shut their mouths that they cannot devour us.

Daniel 7:4.] It "had eagle's wings," whereby it was wont to fly upon the prey, referring to the swift progress Nebuchadnezzar made in his conquests. "I beheld till the wings thereof were plucked, and it was lift up from the earth, and made stand on the feet as a man, and a man's heart was given to it." The plucking of his wings seems to refer to the putting a stop to the progress of Nebuchadnezzar's arms, and stripping him of his glory that he vaunted himself in by his distraction. And his being "lift up" and set in an erect posture, and having "a man's heart" given to him, refers to what came to pass when Nebuchadnezzar was restored from his distraction. While he was distracted, he had a beast's heart, and went in the prone posture of a beast. But when he came to him [self], he lift up his eyes to heaven. He was restored to the erect posture of a man, and had a man's heart given him. Till then he always had rather the heart of an unreasonable, wild, furious beast than a man. But now he was brought to some reasonable consideration and rational apprehensions of things.

Daniel 7:5. "Three ribs in the mouth of it between the teeth of."] These ribs seem to be the bones of his prey. The ribs, rather than other bones, were

<!-- p. 766 -->

represented perhaps because the ribs are those bones which are next the vitals; and the sight of them did naturally excite the idea of his tearing and devouring the vitals of his prey. Not one rib, but three at once are seen in his mouth, the better to represent his extraordinary voraciousness.

Daniel 7:8. "Little horn."] The popes may well be so represented, not only as the order and succession came at first from a small beginning, a pastor of a particular congregation, but as the particular popes were not the sons of nobles, of no royal or noble blood (for the popedom descends not by inheritance), but are originally most of them private men. And many of them of very mean birth are servants that reign, one of those things which the earth can't bear.

Daniel 7:13. "Came with clouds of heaven."] See note on Hebrews 12:1.

"I saw in the night visions." No. 279.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 235–37.

Daniel 7:25. "And think to change times and laws."] This expression shows that what is here prophesied of under the representation of the little horn is some great apostasy of God's visible people that had been in the enjoyment of his word and ordinances. See Isaiah 24:5 and Ezekiel 5:6.

"Change times." See note on Isaiah 29:16, and see Isaiah 24:5.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Daniel 8:10. "It cast down some of the stars to the ground."] The customMS: "custom of." the heathen had of consecrating eminent men into stars after their death probably arose from traditions from the ancients of the glorification of the saints after their death in heaven, where they shine forth as the stars with God and the blessed angels.

Daniel 8:14. "Unto two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings."] So it is in the original, "νυχθήμεραι, so many natural days, reckoned as in the beginning of Genesis by the evenings and mornings, because it was the evening and morning sacrifice that they most lamented the loss of. Two thousand three hundred days makes six years, and three months, and about eighteen days; and just so long they reckon from the defection of the people procured by MenelausMenalaus, an unscrupulous high priest during the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes in the 2nd century B.C.E. the high priest in the one hundred

<!-- p. 767 -->

and forty-second year of the kingdom of the Seleucidae, the sixth month of that year, and the sixth day of the month (so Josephus dates it), to the cleansing of the sanctuary, and the reestablishment of religion among them, which was in the one hundred forty-eighth year, the ninth month, and the twenty-fifth day of the month. 1 Maccabees 1:54" Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 587.

Daniel 9:7.] See no. 81.*Works, 15*, 74.

Daniel 9:23–24.] Daniel, in the foregoing prayer wherein he prayed for the restoration of Israel, sought and hoped for all those great and glorious blessings which in the prophecies of Jeremiah and other prophets were usually annexed to their return from their captivity, which were to accompany or follow the coming of the Messiah. Therefore the angel, in answer to his prayer, is [sent to] him with such a message as he is concerning the Messiah.

Daniel 9:25. "Messiah the prince."] Called so the rather in this place because in the foregoing verse he had been spoken of as to be anointed. He seems therefore here to be called the Messiah, or anointed, with reference to that.This paragraph was added after the following materials.

"Messiah the prince." The same that is called one of the "chief" of the princes, or "the first of the chief princes," as 'tis in the margin (Daniel 10:13), and that the angel, speaking to Daniel in Daniel 10:21, calls "your prince," i.e. Israel's prince, or the prince of God's people, and Daniel 12:1, "the great prince that standeth for the children of thy people."

"The Messiah." Christ is the Messiah, or Christ, or the anointed, in several respects, and called so on several accounts. 1. As he is in his divine nature only, without any consideration of his human nature, or his office of mediator, consider him only as the eternal *Logos*. And he is Christ, or the anointed, as he is the object of the infinite love and delight of the Father, and as the Father doth eternally pour forth the Spirit of love (which is typified in Scripture by oil) infinitely upon him. 2. In his human nature he is Christ, or the anointed, as the Spirit is given not by measure to him, as he was conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, and the Spirit abode upon him, and dwelt in him from the first moment of his existence in that degree and measure as to be a bond of union with the eternal *Logos* so as to be the same person. 3. He is the Messiah, or

<!-- p. 768 -->

the anointed, in his office of mediator, for God the Father poured forth the Holy Spirit abundantly on him to consecrate him to and qualify him for this work at his conception and birth, and more publicly and visibly at his baptism when the Spirit descended upon him like a dove, and abode upon him, and God proclaimed with a voice, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased" [Mark 1:10–11]. 4. He is Christ, or the anointed, not only as he is anointed of God, but as he is anointed by the church, or by every believing soul, by the exercise of the grace of the Holy Spirit towards him, and as it were pouring out his soul in divine love upon him, as Mary poured the precious ointment on Christ's head. See note on Mark 14:3. This was typified by Jacob's anointing the stone on which he rested in Bethel. See notes on that story in the twenty-eighth of Genesis, the second part. Thus David, the greatest of all the personal types of Christ, was not only anointed by God by the hand of the prophet Samuel, but also by his people Israel (2 Samuel 2:4, 2 Samuel 2:7).

Daniel 9:26. "Messiah be cut off."] The word in the originalכָּרַת here rendered "cut off" especially signifies two things in the Old Testament. First, being slain or destroyed. See as in Hosea 8:4, Obadiah 1:9, Zephaniah 3:6–7, Genesis 41:36, Leviticus 20:5, Isaiah 11:13, 1 Kings 11:15–16, Zechariah 13:8, Micah 5:9, Ezekiel 30:15, 1 Kings 18:4, Ezekiel 17:17, Isaiah 48:9, Jeremiah 51:62, Nahum 3:15, and in innumerable other places. Secondly, a being separated from among God's people, and cast out of his church as accursed. (See note on Genesis 17:14.) And in both senses 'tis commonly used when speaking of a punishment inflicted as the fruit of God's curse. In Psalms 37:22, 'tis threatened that "they that are accursed of him should be cut off." In both senses the Messiah was cut off. Thus he is said to be "cut off out of the land of the living" (Isaiah 53:8). Though the word there be not the same in the original,גָּזַר yet it seems to be of the same signification. See note on that place.

"Shall the Messiah be cut off, but not for himself." Such kind of negatives as this, to signify something positive, are frequent in the prophecies of this book. So Daniel 2:34, and also Daniel 2:45: "a stone cut out of the mountains, which was not in hand," as it is in the original.בִידַיִן דִּילָא אֶבֶן הּתְגְּזֶרֶת So Daniel 2:44, "The kingdom shall not be left to other people." Daniel 8:22, "Four kingdoms shall stand up out of the nation, but not in his power." Daniel 8:24, "His power shall be mighty, but not by his own power." Daniel 11:4, "His kingdom shall

<!-- p. 769 -->

be divided towards the four winds of heaven, and not to his posterity, nor according to his dominion which he ruled." Daniel 11:20, "He shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle."This paragraph and the following paragraph are separate entries.

"Desolations are determined." In this expression, and again in that in the latter part of the Daniel 9:27, "the consummation, and that determined," there seems to be reference to former prophecies, and particularly Isaiah 10:22–23. "For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return. The consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness. For the Lord of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land." The word "consumption" is the same in the originalכָּלָה with that here translated "consummation," and it seems to be the very same destruction of the Jews that is there foretold as here. The same is called "the overflowing scourge (Isaiah 28:15, Isaiah 28:18–19), which is spoken of there, Isaiah 28:22, in the same terms. Isaiah 28:22, "A consumption, even determined upon the whole earth," or the whole land. Indeed, the consumption begins at Jerusalem, and passes through the whole earth. It comes first on Jerusalem, and then passes from her to her destroyers. So the matter is represented in the next chapter, Isaiah 29; and so the matter is represented here in Daniel. So the matter is frequently represented elsewhere in Scripture with respect to destructions and consumptions of God's visible people.

Daniel 10:5.] This seems to be the same person that John saw in the Revelation 1, viz. Jesus Christ, and not to be the same person, in the Revelation 1:10 and Revelation 1:18 that speak of Michael, who is Christ, as one that helped him. That person did not appear in the same form with this. It was one that was a messenger from this glorious person to speak to Daniel and strengthen him in his name. The same that is here spoken of is spoken of again, Daniel 12:6–7.

Daniel 10:21. "Noted in the *scripture* of truth."] The wordכְּתָב signifies "writing," and is so used, Esther 8:9, and elsewhere in the Old Testament. What is meant is probably the book of God's decrees, the same with the book sealed with seven seals that the Lamb opened (Revelation 5).

"But Michael your prince." The prince of Israel or God's people that is here called Michael is, in the Daniel 9:25, called by the name of Messiah.

<!-- p. 770 -->

Daniel 11:5–6.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 105–107.Prideaux identifies the "king of the south" as the king of Egypt and the "king of the north" as the king of Syria, whose alliance was cemented by the marriage of the daughter of the former to the latter (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 105–7).

Daniel 11:6.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 105–107, 111–12.Prideaux details the royal intrigues that in his judgment fulfilled the prophecies of Daniel regarding the fates of the kings of Egypt and Syria (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 105–7, 111–12).

Daniel 11:7–9.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 112–14.The military conquests of Ptolemy Euergetes over the kingdom of Syria, and the plunder that he brought back to Egypt, including precious metals and religious images, form the narrative Prideaux provides (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 112–14).

Daniel 11:10–19.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 197–201.Prideaux links the fulfillment of the prophecies of Daniel in these verses with the career and actions of Antiochus the Great, king of Syria (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 197–201).

Daniel 11:20.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 213–14.The "raiser of taxes" Prideaux identifies as Seleucus (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 213–14).

II, vol. 3, pp. 216–19).

Daniel 11:22–45.] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, pp. 288–90.Antiochus Epiphanes' designs upon Egypt and its treasures, as well as his persecution and oppression of the Jewish nation, are the subject of Prideaux's comments (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 288–90).

Daniel 11:24. "He shall scatter among them the prey, and spoil, and riches."] See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, p. 268.Antiochus, according to Prideaux, had exhausted his treasury by his extravagance in gift-giving, thereby fulfilling Daniel's prophecy (*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, p. 268).

Daniel 12:1.] See notes on Matthew 24:21–24 ff., no. 292, especially §§9 and 10.*Works, 15*, 251–64, especially 256–59.
