Daniel 12:11.] Dr. Goodwin in his *Exposition of Revelation* observes that from the time that TitusTitus Flavius Vespasianus (39–81) took part in the Roman suppression of the Jewish revolt in 66–70, and subsequently served as emperor of Rome. took away the "daily sacrifice," *anno* 69 or 70, to the time of Wycliffe'sJohn Wycliffe (c. 1330–84), early English theologian and reformer. preaching, *anno* 1359 or 60, is 1290 years.Thomas Goodwin, *An Exposition upon the Revelation*, in *The Works of Thomas Goodwin, D.D., Sometime President of Magdalene Colledg in Oxford* (5 vols. London, 1681–1704), *II*, 184–87.

Daniel 12:13.] This implies that Daniel shall share in the enjoyment of the glory and joy of these happy times, and shall have a lot and portion with others in it. See "Miscellanies," no. 811.*Works, 18*, 520–22.

<!-- p. 772 -->

### Hosea

Hosea 1:2. "The beginning of the word of the Lord by Hosea."] Hosea's prophecy was "the beginning of the word of the Lord." There was a set and succession of prophets that God raised up in the times of Uzziah and Jeroboam, and succeeding times, who left their prophecies in writing. And Hosea was the first of these. Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 645.

Hosea 1:3. "GomerThe name of Hosea's wife, Gomer, גּמֶר, relates to the Hebrew verb, גָּמַר, "to bring to an end, or complete." the daughter of Diblaim."] "Which name may be interpreted, a complete and final desolation, the effect of a general corruption." Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 646.

Hosea 1:4. "Call his name Jezreel."] This child seems to be so named not only to signify that God was about to [do] some great thing with respect to Jezreel, with respect to both the city of Jezreel and the kingdom of Israel, of which Jezreel was one of the royal seats, as in this and the following verse, but also to signify what God would do, viz. the things that are foretold here in this chapter, where in the first place God's anger towards Israel is foretold, Hosea 1:4–10, and then God's mercy towards them is foretold in the Hosea 1:10–11. So this name seems to intimate both God's anger and his mercy towards that people, his anger in that God would not have the child called Israel, but Jezreel, which seems to signify the same that is in this chapter foretold, viz. that they were not God's people, and he would not have mercy on them, but [they] should be removed and dispersed, for Jezreel signifies "dispersion." But yet it carries in it an intimation of mercy afterwards, because though they should be dispersed, yet they should be "the dispersed of God," as the wordיִזְרְעֶאל, "God sows." signifies. The name seems to denote their approaching captivity, because it signifies the scattered or dispersed of God, and also seems to denote their future return, for though it signifies dispersed of God, yet it also signifies the seed of God, or those that are dispersed and sown as

<!-- p. 773 -->

seed. See Hosea 2:22–23. Now seed, though at present it seems to be thrown away and to die, yet it is in order to a future new life, and a being gathered again with great increase; and so the Prophet foretells that it shall hereafter be with Israel. And therefore the time of their return, or the time when the harvest that springs from this seed is gathered, is called in the Hosea 1:11 "the day of Jezreel," or the day of the seed of God.

"Jezreel." See no. 247.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 199–200.

Hosea 1:5. "I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel."] There "probably their armory was kept, or it may be there some noted battle was fought, wherein the kingdom of Israel was very much weakened." (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 609. And probably there was [the] last struggle with the Assyrians, the decisive battle in which the king of Israel and the royal family were taken, for that was one of the royal seats.

Hosea 1:7.] This was remarkably fulfilled in the days of Hezekiah in the miraculous destruction of Sennacherib's army. Bedford, *Scripture Chronology*, p. 646.

Hosea 1:9.] The names of these children signified awful judgments that God would bring upon Israel. And they were all the children of whoredoms, the children of a woman that was an harlot, to signify that those calamities were the natural fruit and product of the wickedness of the church of Israel that is called an "harlot," and especially of her idolatry which is called "whoredom."

Hosea 1:11. "Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head."] "This had a literal accomplishment when the Galileans, who inhabited the part of the country that belonged to the Ten Tribes, and probably for the most part were descended from them, so heartily joined with those that were properly called Jews, in following Christ, and embracing his gospel. And his first disciples were partly Jews and partly Galileans. The first that were blessed with the light of the gospel were of the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:15). And though there was no good will at all between the Jews and Galileans, yet upon their believing in Christ, they were happily consolidated; and there were no remains of the former disaffection

<!-- p. 774 -->

they had one to another. Nay, when the Samaritans believed, though between them and the Jews there was a much greater enmity, yet in Christ there was a perfect unanimity (Acts 8:14).

"They all agreed to appoint over them one head, even Jesus Christ. Note, that to believe in Christ is to appoint him to ourselves for our head, i.e. to consent to God's appointment, and willingly commit ourselves to his guidance and government"; and by this union in one head it is that Christians are united together. "'And they shall come up out of the land.' It is an allusion to the manner of Israel and Judah before they were divided into two kingdoms. They all used to go up from all parts of the land to Jerusalem to worship. Psalms 122:4, 'Thither the tribes go up.'" The Ten Tribes then used to go up out of their land to worship with the tribe of Judah. Henry.Ibid., 611. When the children of Israel and Judah used to [go] up to worship, it seems as though they used to go up in troops or great companies (See Psalms 42:4.), under captains or leaders that were to lead them to the mountain of the house of God.

Probably every distinct tribe went up under one head, so that their going up from all parts of the land to the mountain of the house of God resembled the manner of their coming up out of Egypt to Canaan, which was under the guidance of the heads of the tribes and the standards of the four principal tribes, and all under one head, Moses, and afterwards Joshua or Jesus. In allusion to that, the gathering together of the people under Christ is compared, in Isaiah 11:10. See notes *in loc*. And there were certain men that were the heads of the tribes in Israel, not only while they were in the wilderness, but when they were settled in the land of Canaan, as appears by 2 Chronicles 5:2, and 1 Chronicles 27:16 ff., Joshua 14:1, and Joshua 19:51, and Joshua 21:1. See Dickinson's *Reasonableness of Christianity*, pp. 88–89.In *The Reasonableness of Christianity*, Jonathan Dickinson (1688–1747), a Presbyterian minister and theologian in New Jersey, asserts that each of the Ten Tribes held the scepter, or "power of government," at one time or another, not only the tribe of Judah. And by that forementioned expression in [the] Psalms 122:4, "Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the Lord, unto the testimony of Israel," it looks as if a whole tribe went up together. Here the great union of Judah and Israel is foretold, as if they should not only become one people, but that the very distinction of tribes should cease. They should be united, and go up together to the mountain of the house of God in one company under one head, as one tribe used to do.

Christians all have one head to conduct 'em, and bring 'em to God

<!-- p. 775 -->

and to heaven, theJE deleted "temple of his glory, even Jesus Christ." mountain of God's holiness, and the temple of his glory.

"The day of Jezreel." See note on Hosea 1:4.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hosea 2:1.] This verse seems properly to belong to the latter part of the preceding chapter where the Prophet was foretelling how that the children of Israel, after they had been rejected from being the people of God, should in the latter days return again, and be his people, as in the Hosea 2:10. Those that God here speaks to are "the children of Judah and the children of Israel," spoken of in the Hosea 2:11; and the command respects the time there prophesied of when they should be united under one head. In the Hosea 1:8–9, it was declared that God now calls Israel *Lo Ammi*עַמִּי לֹא and *Lo Ruhamah*;רֻחָמָה לֹא but here 'tis foretold that when God shall have mercy on 'em, and restore 'em in the latter days, they shall be called *Ammi* and *Ruhamah*, i.e. "my people" and "beloved" again, as they had aforetime. The same is foretold again in the Hosea 2:23 of this chapter, and we may take this as a further predicting and explaining that happy union that there should be among God's people, spoken of in the Hosea 1:11. Though they had been greatly divided, Judah and Israel shall own one another for God's people, and beloved, and for brethren and sisters one to another; and so shall Jews and Gentiles.

Hosea 2:2. "Plead with your mother, plead."] Speaking to the children of the church of Israel, whom the children of Judah are directed to own for brethren and sisters in the foregoing verse, for though they are not the same persons that now are her children that then will [be], yet they are spoken of as if they [are the] same persons, after the manner of prophecy, as if it was the same mother and the same children that now are rejected that then shall be recovered.

"Plead with your mother, for she is not my wife." As much as to say, I call her "your mother," because "she is not my wife," as God, when he was angry with Israel, speaking to Moses, calls them "thy people, which thou hast brought out of Egypt" (Exodus 32:7).This paragraph is a later addition.

<!-- p. 776 -->

Hosea 2:3–5.] See no. 248.*Works, 15*, 200.

Hosea 2:14. "Therefore I will allure her."] I.e. I will court or woo her again, as a young man does a virgin that he desires to make his wife. God had been speaking of her going after other lovers, and how he had repudiated her on that account. Nevertheless, God promises that in the latter days he will court her again, and again make her his wife, as Hosea 2:19–20. All the following part of the verse, viz. "and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her," is to be taken together as exegetical of this, or to show after what manner God will deal with her when he is about to woo or allure her. He will speak pleasantly and comfortably to her, as a young man does to a maid that he courts. But I will first "bring her into the wilderness," and there bring her to herself, and make her sensible that she needs me, and that I am worthy to be received for an husband. See Hosea 2:7. His bringing her into the wilderness, as he now threatened (Hosea 2:3 and Hosea 2:12), was to humble her, and fit her to be spoken comfortably to. The manner how she should be brought into the wilderness is described from Hosea 2:6.

Hosea 2:15. "And I will give her vineyards from thence."] I.e. the vineyard which God destroyed (Hosea 2:12), or others instead of them "from thence," i.e. from the wilderness. God would turn the wilderness into a fruitful field for her, that she might know that God gave her her vineyards, and not her idols (Hosea 2:7–8), as she supposed (Hosea 2:12). She should "suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock,… the pure blood of the grape (Deuteronomy 32:13–14).

The "valley of Achor" was the place where the children of Israel were troubled by Achan. "The valley of Achorעָכוֹר, or "trouble." signifies the 'valley of trouble,'" and that was the place where they stoned Achan, and put away the troubler. The meaning of it seems to be that their being troubled for sin and convinced of it, as the children of Israel send out the troubler, and putting away sin, and killing this troubler, is the way in which God's people shall come to light and comfort, and in which a door of hope is opened to them. "The valley of Achor was a very fruitful valley." God will give his people precious fruits and comfort that shall be the earnest of their future inheritance in the heavenly Canaan. Upon their trouble for sin, and forsaking, or upon their repentance, as it follows, "she shall sing there," etc. See Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 615.

<!-- p. 777 -->

"And she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt." This plainly refers [to] that triumphant song that Moses and the children of Israel sung when they came up out of the Red Sea, which was indeed the day when they came up out of the land of Egypt (See "Miscellanies," no. 160, §12.).*Works, 13*, 315–16. The occasion of their singing should in several respects [be] like that. It should be an occasion of their deliverance from a state like that that they were then delivered from. God, in the foregoing part of the chapter, threatens that they should be brought [to] such a state as they were in in Egypt. See notes on Hosea 2:3. But now the Prophet is foretelling their deliverance from such a state. And besides, the Prophet is speaking of their joy after convictions for sin and repentance of it, which is intended by his giving them hope and joy in the valley of Achor. See notes on the former part of the verse. In this their humiliation they shall pass through affliction and a kind of death, wherein they shall die unto sin, as the children of Israel had great affliction and distress in Egypt under their cruel taskmasters, types of man's sins, and were brought to extremity at the Red Sea, and almost to despair, when their old taskmasters were ready to swallow 'em up, and Pharaoh, the type of the devil, ready to seize 'em, and passed through the waters of a great deep, by which great sorrow, and darkness, and death are often represented in Scripture. In repentance God's people have their sins slain, as the children of Israel had their enemies killed in the Red Sea. Repentance is as it were the sea or gulf through which God's people pass in their departure out of the spiritual Egypt, or state of slavery to sin and Satan.Each of the three paragraphs is a separate entry.

Hosea 2:22–23. "And they shall hear Jezreel. And I will sow her unto me in the earth."] God, in promising to "sow her," alludes to the name Jezreel, which signifies the "seed of God," or the "sown of God."

Hosea 3:5. "And shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days."] By this text it appears that by the "fear of the Lord" in the Old Testament is meant something else besides a mere fear of the effects of the divine anger.

Hosea 4:2. "And blood toucheth blood."] "I.e. abundance of murders are committed in all parts of the country, and as it were in a constant series and succession. *Caedes aliae aliis sunt contiguae*.The figurative sense of this Latin is, "Everyone is touched by murder." A stream of blood runs down

<!-- p. 778 -->

among them, even royal blood. 'Twas about this time that there was so much blood shed, in grasping at the crown. Shallum slew Zechariah, Menahem slew Shallum, Pekah slew Pekahiah, and Hoshea slew Pekah. And the like bloody work, it is likely, there was among other contenders. So then, the land was polluted with blood: 'twas filled with blood from one end to the other." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 620.

Hosea 4:5. "And I will destroy thy mother."] Here the prophets and priests mentioned in the two foregoing verses, the teaching and leading part of the church of Israel, are called the "mother," and the common people that are taught and educated by them are called the "children," as in the next verse. See note on Canticles 3:11, the last part; and Canticles 8:1–2; and 1 Thessalonians 2:7.

Hosea 4:7. "Therefore will I change their glory into shame."] I.e. the glory of the priests, who are as the mother among the people (Hosea 4:5). God advanced the priests to great dignity, and conferred great glory upon them. He threatens here to change their glory into shame.

Hosea 4:8. "They eat up the sin of my people."] I.e. the priests eat their idolatrous offerings and sacrifices. As the true sacrifices that were offered to God are called their "holy things," so their sacrifices to idols are called their "sin." These the priests lived upon; and therefore "they set their heart on their iniquity," i.e. on their idolatry, that was so gainful to them.

Hosea 4:12. "Their staff declareth unto them."] "'Tis probable that this refers to some wicked method of divination by a staff, as Nebuchadnezzar divined by his arrows (Ezekiel 21:21)." Henry.Ibid., 622.

Hosea 4:15.] Gilgal seems to have been one of the places where they were wont to worship and sacrifice (Hosea 9:15 and Hosea 12:11, and Amos 4:4 and Amos 5:5). Their pretense for it probably was God's dignifying the place by ordering that there the children of Israel should first enter Canaan, having so miraculously passed over Jordan, and that there were those twelve stones that God appointed as a monument of their great men, and that there the congregation was circumcised, and had their reproach rolled away, and there kept their first Passover in Canaan, and that there God appeared

<!-- p. 779 -->

to Joshua and told him the place whereon he stood was holy (Joshua 5), and there the people formerly offered sacrifices and burnt offerings by Samuel's direction (1 Samuel 10:8 and 1 Samuel 11:15).

"Neither go ye up to Beth-aven." Bethel is so called by the Prophet. Their pretense for worshipping and sacrificing there was that God there appeared to their father Jacob in so merciful and wonderful a manner, and told him that that was the house and the gate of heaven, and that Jacob had promised that when he returned from Mesopotamia that should be God's house, and that he there offered offerings to God on the stone that was his pillows. And so the name hitherto had been Bethel, the "house of God." But for the wickedness and idolatry that it was now the appointed place of, it is called no longer Bethel, but Beth-aven,אָמון בֵּית the "house of iniquity."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hosea 4:16. "Now the Lord will feed them as a lamb in a large place."] This is spoken of Judah, mentioned in the preceding verse.

Hosea 4:18. "Their drink is sour."] I.e. it is dead, lost all its sweetness and spirit, and is fit for nothing but to be thrown away. Deuteronomy 32:33—there they are represented by bitter grapes and poisonous wine, here to dead drink, that this is therefore incurable and irrecoverable.

"Her rulers with shame do love, *Give ye*." "I.e. they love bribes." Henry.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Exposition, 4* (1725), 622.

Hosea 4:19. "The wind hath bound her up in her wings."] Ready to carry her away swiftly to a great distance, and to scatter her to the four quarters of the world.

Hosea 5:1–2. "Ye have been a snare on Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor. And the revolters are profound to make slaughter."] I.e. they were crafty and cruel one towards another, and laid snares to catch and destroy their neighbors, as hunters used to lay snares on these mountains in pursuit of their game.

Hosea 5:6. "They shall go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the Lord."] I.e. they shall go with their flocks and herds to offer in sacrifice to God, to appease his wrath, and make him propitious.

<!-- p. 780 -->

Hosea 5:8.] "Gibeah and Ramah were two cities near together in the confines of the two kingdoms of Judah and Israel, Gibeah a frontier town of the kingdom of Judah, Ramah of Israel, so that the warning is hereby sent to both kingdoms. 'Cry aloud at Beth-aven,' i.e. Bethel," this lying in the eastern part of the land, and being the chief place of their idolatry, God probably so ordered it that it was one of the first "seized by the enemy. And therefore the trumpet is not sounded there, but you hear the outcries of them that shout for mastery mixed with theirs that are overcome." Bethel was their sanctuary, the seat of their god; yet here they cry aloud in distress. "'After thee, O Benjamin.' Ephraim is already vanquished, their sanctuary seized, and the enemy will soon be upon thy back, O Benjamin," in the kingdom of Judah. Bethel was a city near the borders of the tribe of Benjamin. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 624.

Hosea 5:9. "Among the tribes of Israel have I made known what shall surely be."] Three of the tribes are mentioned in this and the preceding verse, viz. Judah, of which Gibeah was a city, and Benjamin, the two tribes of the kingdom of Judah, and Ephraim, the chief of the Ten Tribes, a city of which was Ramah. It might be looked upon as sure as if it were already come, and were proclaimed by sound of trumpet, and the cries of the conqueror and conquered, as mentioned in the foregoing verse.

Hosea 5:11. "Ephraim is oppressed and broken in judgment, because he willingly walked after the commandment."] I.e. the common people of Ephraim are cruelly oppressed and broken in judgment by their rulers, which is a punishment of God upon them for submitting to their unlawful and wicked commands, viz. the command of Jeroboam and the succeeding kings of Israel, who obliged all their subjects by a law to worship the calves at Dan and Bethel, and never to go up to Jerusalem to worship. They were willingly subject to their authority in this, and now they suffer cruel oppression by that authority against their wills.

Hosea 5:13.] See 2 Kings 15:19 and 2 Kings 17:4, 1 Chronicles 28:16 and 1 Chronicles 28:21.

Hosea 6:2. "After two days."] Colossians 2:12–13 and Colossians 3:1.

Hosea 6:6.] "Mercy and the knowledge of God" in this verse seem both to signify all piety or godliness so far as it respects the moral duties of religion.

<!-- p. 781 -->

Both express the whole of religion, the latter with regard to the foundation of it, the former, viz. mercy, with regard to the essence of it, or that in which it more essentially consists. For mercy in this prophecy seems to [be] put for all religion of the heart, and to signify the same as charity in the New Testament. In the Hosea 6:4, where it is said, "Your goodness is as the morning cloud," in the originalוְחַסְדְּכֶם it is "your mercy."JE deleted with a large "X" the following: "And so Hosea 10:12, 'Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy.' Both terms seem to signify all moral goodness, as in the next verse. 'Ye have plowed wickedness, and reaped iniquity.'" So in Isaiah 57:1, "The righteous perisheth, and merciful men are taken away; the righteous are taken away from the evil to come." By "merciful men" is meant the same as good men.

Hosea 6:8–9. "Gilead is a city of them that work iniquity, and is polluted with blood. And as troops of robbers wait for a man, so the company of priests murther in the way by consent."] In the former of these verses is shown how the Levites were guilty of murder, in the latter the priests. Ramoth Gilead, the city here spoken of, was a city of the Levites, and was one of the cities of refuge, which was appointed for the protection of men's lives; but instead of that, it proved the contrary. It is probable that the Levites there were polluted with blood two ways: 1. By protecting them, "for a bribe, that had been guilty of willful murther," when they fled there; and 2. In delivering "those to the avenger of blood" that had only accidentally slain others, "when they were poor and had nothing to give them." See Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 628.

"They commit lewdness." "The word signifies such wickedness as is committed with deliberation." Henry.Ibid.

Hosea 6:11. "Also, O Judah, he hath set an harvest for thee."] I.e. "he hath set an harvest for thee" to reap, as thou hast plowed iniquity and sown wickedness. So he hath appointed a time wherein thou must reap what thou hast sown. See Hosea 10:13. "When I returned the captivity of my people." I.e. when these captives of Judah, which were taken by the men of Israel, were restored in obedience to the command of God sent them by Oded the Prophet (2 Chronicles 28:8–15), God delivered thee then because the appointed time of harvest was not come, your iniquity was not full, the harvest was not ripe. But I did not intend it for a final deliverance,

<!-- p. 782 -->

but only turned aside mine anger for a while, and appointed another time of harvest.

'Tis probable that among those that were then carried captive there was a number that were truly God's people, though Judah in general was become exceeding corrupt, and that it was for their sakes that God did so extraordinarily interpose for the return of those that were then carried captive. There seems to be a distinction made here between Judah and God's people. Though God had returned the captivity of his people in an extraordinary manner, yet he had set an harvest for Judah, that was become a corrupt and wicked people, and were not owned as God's people. It was for the elect's sake, for the blessing that was in that captivity, that God did not destroy them then. But though God had mercy on his people, yet let not the wicked think to escape. God at the same time appointed another time for their destruction.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hosea 7:1. "The thief cometh in, and the troop of robbers spoileth without."] The thief breaketh into the house, and stealeth within doors; and the troop of robbers spoileth without. "They commit falsehood." I.e. in their pretenses and shows of amendment and healing, they are guilty of vile dissimulation.

Hosea 7:4. "They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker," etc.] Here is a sudden transition from one comparison to another, or two comparisons in one, as is common in Scripture. The sinners of Ephraim are in this verse compared to two things, viz. to an oven heated, and to the dough leavened, and kneaded, and so fitted to be cast into the hot oven. They are compared to "an oven heated," because their hearts are so heated with lust. They are compared to dough leavened. Leaven is used as a type of wickedness in the Scripture. Their ripening in wickedness is compared to kneading and leavening because, as hereby the dough is fitted to be cast into the oven, so by men's ripening in wickedness men are fitted for destruction. As the baker casts in the leaven into the dough, and kneads it, and then waits till the mass be thoroughly fermented, and then casts it into the oven, so the devil casts the leaven of wickedness into men's hearts, and continually labors more and more thoroughly to establish and confirm the heart in sin, and to form the nature to it, as the baker thoroughly mixes leaven with the dough by kneading. And oftentimes Satan gets wicked men to that pass. Their hearts are so dreadfully

<!-- p. 783 -->

hardened in sin, they seem to be so given up to the power of it, that Satan is in a great measure secure of 'em. He waits till the measure of their sin be filled up, and till they are thoroughly ripe for destruction, and sets his heart at rest about them as not much fearing but that sin will have its perfect work in them, and so bring forth death, as the baker, after he has leavened and kneaded the dough, sleeps till the oven heats, and till the leaven hath thoroughly fermented and fitted, to be cast into the oven. See Hosea 7:6.

Hosea 7:6.] See notes on Hosea 7:4.

Hosea 7:8. "Ephraim hath mixed himself among the people."] I.e. with heathen and idolaters. "Ephraim is a cake not turned." Half roasted and half raw, of but a partial righteousness. As they have mixed themselves among the people, so their religion is mixed with wickedness.

Hosea 7:9. "Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth it not."] "Some devoured them by open wars, as 2 Kings 13:7, when 'the king of AssyriaBoth Henry and the KJV read "Syria." made them like the dust by threshing'; others, by pretending treaties of peace and amity, in which they extorted abundance of wealth from them, and made them pay dear for that which did them no good, but which afterwards they paid dearer for (2 Kings 16:9)." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 630.

Hosea 7:11. "Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart."] There are two properties of the dove in which Ephraim is compared to her. 1. That she is silly and without understanding, for though the dove be noted for innocency, yet not for wisdom. In this not the dove, but the serpent excels. Her silliness especially appears in her being easily, above all birds, decoyed into a net or snare; so Ephraim was decoyed into the net of their enemies, Egypt and Assyria. See in the latter part of this and the following verse. 2. Another property is their cowardice; they are without courage. They are easily scared and frighted, and fly at anyone's approach, even from those that would give them meat. So Ephraim fled from God, that would feed them (Hosea 7:13), though they hasted to the bait of them that would destroy them.

Hosea 7:12. "I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard."] I.e. as the law of Moses declares, which has from time to time been read to them

<!-- p. 784 -->

in their solemn assemblies, and particularly as the congregation of Israel in the wilderness heard, to whom God first revealed the law with its annexed promises and threatenings.

Hosea 7:14. "And they have not cried to me with their heart."] No. 250b.*Works, 15*, 201–2.

Hosea 7:15. "Bound and strengthened their arms."] See 2 Kings 13:16–17 and 2 Kings 14:25–26.

Hosea 8:9.] '"They are gone to Assyria,' to engage the king of Assyria to help them; and herein they are as 'a wild ass alone by himself,' foolish, and headstrong, and unruly. They will have their way, and nothing shall hold them in. They take a course by themselves; and the effect will be, that like a wild ass by himself, they will be the easier and surer prey to the lion." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 634.

Hosea 8:11.] They sinfully made these altars, and sinfully offer sacrifices on them, and therefore shall only be a means of enhancing their sin and guilt instead of expiating of it, as they designed.

Hosea 8:13. "They shall return into Egypt."] I.e. they shall again return into the like slavery and bondage under heathen masters that they were in in Egypt (Deuteronomy 28:68). And probably many of them actually fled into Egypt for refuge when the king of Assyria [came] to destroy it, for Israel at that time was in alliance with Egypt, in whom they put great confidence for defense from the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:4–5). There may probablyMS: "probable." be reference to their flying into Egypt to avoid destruction from the king of Assyria, in the Hosea 9:6. "For, lo, they are gone because of destruction. Egypt shall gather them up; Memphis shall bury them."

Hosea 9:7. "Israel shall know it."] Though they would not believe it when forewarned of by the prophets, and though they hearkened to their false prophet (mentioned in the next clause) that they should have peace, yet their experience should convince 'em.

<!-- p. 785 -->

Hosea 9:8. "The prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways."] I.e. by all his prophecies, all that he says and does, pretending to speak or act in the name of the Lord, he brings the people into a snare. The people are brought into great calamity and ruin by hearkening unto them, as a bird is by going after the bait that is in a snare. "And hatred in the house of his God." I.e. he brings God's hatred on himselfI.e. the false prophet. and on the people that hearkens to him in the places of their solemn worship. The people, by following the counsel and guidance of their false prophets in their public worship, provoked God to destroy them. Gilgal was one of these places of public worship. See Hosea 4:15, Hosea 12:11; Amos 4:4, Amos 5:5. And therefore 'tis said, Hosea 9:15, that there God "hated them," and that he would "drive them out of his *house*," and "love them no more."

Hosea 9:10. "I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness."] I.e. I took delight and pleasure in them, as a poor traveler would do if he found grapes in a parched and desolate wilderness where he had most need of 'em and least expected them. "As the first ripe in the fig tree at her first time." Fig trees bore two crops in a year. (See notes on Mark 11:13, no. 2 26.)*Works, 15*, 175–76. Their forefathers are here compared to the first ripe figs of the first crop. These first ripe figs were much accounted of, both because they were the first that came, and because they were more than ordinarily delicious (Isaiah 28:4).

Hosea 9:15. "All their wickedness."] I am ready to think that this is what is intended by the phrase, "All wickedness of theirs is in Gilgal," and that itבַּגִּלְגָּל כֶּל־רָעָתָם ought to have been so translated, i.e. "there is all manner of wickedness of theirs in Gilgal," the word *Cōl* only signifying the greatness of the wickedness they committed there. "The learned Grotius conjectures that there is a mystical sense here. Golgotha in Syriac is the same with Gilgal in Hebrew;גִּלְגָּל, a place where sacrifices were offered. and therefore he thinks this may have reference to their putting of Christ to death at Golgotha, which was the great sin of the Jewish nation, and of which it might truly be said, All their wickedness was summed up in that." (Henry.)*Exposition, 4* (1725), 628. And of that it might truly be said that there God hated them so as to cast them out of his house, and love them no more, for the Jewish nation, we know, were cast off for that sin. If we

<!-- p. 786 -->

understand this as implying this mystical sense, 'tis no more than what is agreeable to the application of that text in the New Testament, Jeremiah 31:15, "In Rama was a voice heard, lamentation and bitter weeping," etc. [Matthew 2:18].

Hosea 10:1.] See Warburton, vol. 3, p. 398.Warburton asserts that "the Prophet *Hosea* assures us, that the *Day of Prosperity* was the constant Season" of Israel's idolatry. This passage therefore is "most clear Proof that their Defection from the God of *Israel* was not a Doubt of his Power, but a wanton Abuse of his Blessings." Warburton warned, "This the Deists would do well to consider" (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed., London, 1742], vol. 2, Pt. 2 [i.e. vol. 3]).

Hosea 10:2. "Their heart is divided."] They halted between God and Baal, for they hypocritically pretended to worship the true God, as appears by many passages in this prophecy. And their hearts were also divided between many false gods, for instead of serving but one God, to whom their hearts should be only and wholly devoted, and whom they should sacrifice to at but one altar, they had many gods and many altars that their hearts were divided to, as in the preceding verse they had some altars to the true God, and others to Baal, some to one idol, and others to another.

Hosea 10:3. "Because we feared not the Lord, what then shall a king do unto us?"] What can we expect from a king when we have forfeited the favor of God?

Hosea 10:4. "Judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field."] "In the field that is plowed for good corn." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 639.

Hosea 10:5.] The "glory thereof" is theJE inserted and then deleted "golden." images. The people and the priests shall mourn, as they did in Israel at the carrying away of the ark by the Philistines, saying, "The glory is departed" [1 Samuel 4:21]. They carried away those golden images into Assyria for a present to the king of Assyria.

Hosea 10:7.] Though he is a king, yet it shall appear that with all his greatness and royal magnificence, he is but a bubble.

Hosea 10:8. "The sin of Israel."] That is, their idol, the golden calf of Beth-aven, or Bethel (here called Aven), spoken of, Hosea 10:5–6.

<!-- p. 787 -->

Hosea 10:9–10.] See no. 252.*Works, 15*, 202–3.

Hosea 10:11. "And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, that loveth to tread out the corn."] That is, for the sake of the gain of it, that she might have the opportunity to fill her own belly with the corn, which is agreeable to what is said of Ephraim in the Hosea 10:1 of this chapter, and Hosea 9:1. "But I passed over upon her fair neck." Her neck was fair and delicate because she, having been used only to the easy and pleasant work of treading out the corn, her neck had not been worn and gauled with the yoke. But I will pass over her fair neck, as the husbandman does when he puts a yoke upon his cattle. I will put a yoke upon her neck that she may do harder work than tread out the corn. I will cause her to draw the plow in the field.

"I will make Ephraim to ride," etc. See no. 253.Ibid., 203–4.

Hosea 10:12. "Break up your fallow ground."] That has hitherto been neglected, and unoccupied, and overgrown with weeds and thorns, and utterly unfit to receive good seed, and bring forth good fruit. "It is time to seek the Lord, till he come and rain righteousness upon you." The husbandman must plow and sow, looking up to God for rain to nourish the seed, and make it bear fruit. We can do nothing without God, as the husbandman, when he labors, depends on the rain and blessing of heaven for a crop; but God is wont to give his blessing in the way of our diligence when we seek it of him. If our plowing and sowing be righteousness, the rain will be righteousness.

Hosea 10:13. "Iniquity."] Note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Hosea 11:1.] This verse is in the New Testament applied to Christ being called out of Egypt when a child. Christ is sometimes in the Prophets called "Israel." But by this we may see that the Holy Ghost has an eye to many things, and has so contrived his words that the same expression shall be adapted to many things at the same time. See note on Daniel 5:25 ff.

Israel, when [God] called him "out of Egypt," was not only a child, because he was young at that time as a nation, but that generation that God loved and brought into Canaan were literally children when God called

<!-- p. 788 -->

'em out of Egypt. God, speaking of them, Numbers 14:31, calls 'em "little ones." See note on Jeremiah 2:2–3.This paragraph and the preceding reference are a later addition.

Hosea 11:2. "They called them."] See note on Lamentations 4:15.

Hosea 11:4. "I drew them with the cords of a man."] In contradistinction to those with which brute beasts were wont to be managed and led. I drew them with cords that were fit to draw a reasonable creature, fit to affect his reason, toJE deleted "work upon." attract his will, and to incline him willingly to follow, as Psalms 110. "Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power" Hosea 11:3].

Hosea 11:5.] "He shall not return into the land of Egypt," but to a country vastly further distant from their own, and whence they can have far less hopes of ever returning. Because they refused to return to me, therefore I will send 'em so far from their own land that they shall never return to that.

Hosea 11:7. "They called them to the Most High."] See note on Lamentations 4:15.

Hosea 11:10. "When he shall roar, the children shall tremble from the west."] I.e. when God roars by the voice of his word, which [is] sometimes compared to thunder, and sometimes to the roaring of a lion, for the powerfulness of it. "The children," i.e. the children of Israel, who is called God's "son" in the Hosea 11:1, "shall tremble." 'Tis the character of the godly that they tremble at God's word. When the word of [God] is blessed to bring persons to repentance, and to reclaim them from their evil ways to God, the first effect it commonly works in them is fear.

"From the west," whither they have been dispersed to the ends of the earth. The success of the gospel amongst both Jews and Gentiles was chiefly westward.

Hosea 11:11. "Tremble as a bird out of Egypt."] As a dove (that before was spoken of as a very fearful bird, Hosea 7:11), when it is afraid, flies with all haste to the windows of the dove house of its owner, so shall the children, when they tremble at God's word, fly to the goodness of the Lord. In Hosea 7:11, God speaks of their being fearful with a sinful cowardice that made 'em fly from their owner, that would feed them, after the bait of the fowlers, that would destroy them. This place speaks of a contrary sort

<!-- p. 789 -->

of fear that would drive them to their owner. When they tremble, they shall fly out of Egypt and Assyria to the land of Israel, as before they fled out of this land to Egypt and Assyria. "And I will place them in houses," where they may be safe and secure from what they are afraid of. I will secure them in dove houses; and they shall not be left wandering about without place of rest or security, as a bird cast out of her nest, or dove turned out of the dove house (Isaiah 16:2).

Hosea 12:1. "Ephraim feedeth on wind."] I.e. on vain hopes of help from man. "He followeth after the east wind," in following after creature confidences, Assyria and Egypt. "He daily increaseth lies and desolation." No. 258.*Works, 15*, 206.

Hosea 12:4. "He found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us."] So God found Jacob. "Justly are they upbraided with this, for in that very place they had now set up one of the golden calves, and had turned Bethel into Beth-aven," and therefore it follows, as in the next verse. Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 645.

Hosea 12:5. "Even the Lord God of hosts; the Lord is his memorial."] His memorial that appeared to Jacob at Bethel was Jehovah, and not Baalim. See Genesis 28:13. When God there appeared to him, he said, I am Jehovah; and there Jacob promised that Jehovah should be his God (Genesis 28:21). And when Jacob returned from Padan-aram, and came to Bethel again, he commanded his household to "put away their strange gods" (Genesis 35:2).

God's names, titles,MS: "title." and attributes are the memorial of him. There is no need of a calf or any other image to represent him. God's name "Jehovah"יְהוָֹה signifies much the same with "I am that I am," which seems to signify that God is not like anything else besides himself, that they should represent him by an image.

Hosea 12:7–8. "He is a merchant."] The word in the originalכְּנַעַן is, he is "Canaan," the signification of which word is "merchant." Probably these two things are signified by [this], viz. that he is a merchant, and also that he is like Canaan, in whose room he succeeded. And to put 'em both together, it

<!-- p. 790 -->

signifies that he was a wicked merchant, or wicked in their dealings with one another, or with their neighbors.

Hosea 12:8. Here they plead their success and prosperity in their way as an argument that it is right, as though God blessed them in it, and thereby testified his approbation of it. They also seem to plead their good reputation. They carried on their craft so secretly that they passed for honest men. They were well thought of, as the Pharisees who devoured widows' houses, and yet colored all over with a pretense of great strictness. They were so secret and subtile in their fraudulent dealings that they carried all with a pretense of great fairness, and were very careful that none of their iniquity should be discovered by their neighbors. "They shall find none iniquity in me that were sin." Nothing very bad, nothing but what is excusable, nothing to bring God's judgments upon me, as my prosperity is a witness. By sin is often understood that which is a ground of God's curse and divine judgments. Deuteronomy 15:9, "And he cry unto the Lord against thee, and it be sin unto thee." So Deuteronomy 24:15. 1 Kings 12:29–30, "And he set up one in Bethel, and the other in Dan. And this thing became a sin." And 1 Kings 13:34. Psalms 109:7, "Let his prayer become sin."

Hosea 12:11. "Heaps in the furrows of the field."] I.e. heaps of dung as thick and numerous as they. Their gods are called dungy gods, and their altars are compared to dung heaps.

Hosea 12:12–13.] No. 260.*Works, 15*, 207.

Hosea 13:7.] God here compares himself in his judgments on the people to these beasts of prey as being suitable to the metaphor. Under the people are represented, in the two foregoing verses, a flock or herd, first in a wilderness, and then in a fat pasture.

Hosea 13:10.] See Warburton, vol. 3, p. 412.Warburton discusses the Israelites' demand for "a king and princes" which was motivated by their hope that each of them might become distinguished officers of state under such leaders and benefit thereby. The contrast with the rule of the judges was striking. "They could get nothing, when their Affairs led them to their Judges poor Residence, in the *School of the Prophets*, but the GIFT *of the Holy Spirit: which a Courtier… would not prize*." The Prophet therefore cautioned "that they should take care, when they demanded a King." (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed., London, 1742], vol. 2, Pt. 2 [i.e. vol. 3]).

<!-- p. 791 -->

Hosea 13:11. "I gave thee a king in mine anger."] Viz. Saul. "And took him away in my wrath," viz. when the king of Israel was taken by the Assyrians, and the kingdom destroyed.

Hosea 14:2. "Take with you words."] I.e. instead of sacrifices to expiate your iniquity.

Hosea 14:7. "As the wine of Lebanon."] "Lebanon is famous for excellent wine. See Pococke,Edward Pococke (1604–91), a distinguished Orientalist and biblical commentator, who wrote *A Commentary on the Prophecy of Hosea* (Oxford, 1685). vol. 2, p. 103, and Maundrell,MS: "Maundrel." Henry Maundrell (1665–1701), a traveler in the Orient, author of *Aleppo to Jerusalem at Easter, A.D. 1697* (Oxford, 1703). p. 35.… And Le BrunPierre Le Brun (1661–1729), an author who wrote extensively about liturgy and the Mass. tells us, that the wine of Cannobin there, is the richest and finest in the world." *Treatise of the Future Restoration of the Jews and Israelites*, p. 45, margin.Samuel Collett, *A Treatise of the Future Restoration of the Jews*, p. 45, n. 59. The citation from Collett is from a section entitled "Of the happy State of the Israelites in their own Land, for some Years after their Restoration; With a Description of the Land, and the Goodness of it."

Hosea 14:9.] See Proverbs 8:9, and other texts there referred to in my notes.

<!-- p. 792 -->

### Joel

Joel 1-2. The two first chapters of Joel.] See Warburton, vol. 3, pp. 639 ff.Warburton discusses the double prophecies of desolation found in these chapters of Joel, locusts in a primary sense and the Assyrian army in a secondary sense. He details the artistry of the Prophet, who in the Joel 1 describes the locusts as a people, but their ravages as those of insects. In the Joel 2 he describes the enemies as locusts and their actions as men of war. In this fashion the Prophet joins the "*two* Senses so closely as to obviate all Pretense for a Division to the Injury of the Holy Spirit," thus confirming a double sense (*Divine Legation of Moses* [2nd ed. London, 1742], vol. 2, Pt. 2, [i.e. vol. 3], pp. 639–43).

Joel 2:2. "As the morning spread upon the mountains."] I.e. as the clouds which appear spread upon the mountains in the morning.

Joel 3:2. "I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat."] All that we are to understand by this is that there shall be a great destruction of the enemies of the church very parallel with that which was in Jehoshaphat's time in the valley of Berachah, which is here called "the valley of Jehoshaphat," of which destruction we read in 2 Chronicles 20, and a destruction of which that was a remarkable type and image, as the enemies of the church are said, in Revelation 16:16, to gather themselves "together to a place called Armageddon," i.e. the mountain of Megiddo, signifying that this battle was represented by that of Deborah and Barak, by Sisera and his host, which was at Megiddo (Judges 5:19). God will with his great power plead with all the enemies of his church when they assemble themselves, and come up against the church to besiege and destroy it, as the Moabites, Amorites, and Edomites came then against Judah and Jerusalem, as in the Joel 3:9 and following verses. God will judge them, as he then judged the enemies of Judah in the valley of Jehoshaphat. See 2 Chronicles 20:12. And it shall in many respects be very parallel with that destruction.

Joel 3:6. "Ye have sold unto the Grecians."] See Ezekiel 27:13.

<!-- p. 793 -->

### Amos

Amos 1:6–13.] See no. 221.*Works, 15*, 156–58.

Amos 3:4.] I.e. will God roar in his wrath against man, if he be not by sin made a prey for his wrath? Here seems to be reference to the words that God had spoken against the people, spoken of, Amos 3:1.

Amos 4:1.] 'Tis the great women and ladies of Samaria are here threatened. Their husbands or fathers, who were rulers or leading men in Samaria, are called "their masters."

Amos 5:24.] A "mighty stream" that bears all before it, bears down all obstacles. Rulers should so govern that nothing should be able to stop the stream of justice. It should be like a river that will have its course, whatever dams are endeavored to be made. It will either tear down obstacles, or get above them.

Amos 5:25. "Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years?"] It is probable that all sacrifices offered by the congregation in general were intermitted during that thirty-eight years that the children of Israel wandered in the wilderness after their murmuring at the report of the spies, for so much as circumcision was not observed. Therefore it soon came to that, that the greater part of the congregation was uncircumcised, and so were unqualified to attend the feasts, sacrifices, and worship of the sanctuary. And therefore we read no more of any Passover kept after they left Mt. Sinai. That the main rites and institutions of the ceremonial law were thus neglected so long a time so soon after their institution showed two things. 1. The wickedness of the people, as it was owing to that, that they were driven back into the wilderness, and that they were let alone in their wickedness. Thus Moses, as the prophet of God under his direction, was restrained from putting them upon the observance of the ceremonial law, but was ordered to leave 'em

<!-- p. 794 -->

to their own negligent, disobedient hearts in this affair. (See note on Joshua 5:4–6.)

2. It showed how little God regarded the performances of the ceremonial law that he should so suffer them to be neglected for so long a time so soon after their institution. It was to the Prophet's purpose to observe both these things, as it was also to St. Stephen's purpose when he cites these words of the Prophet (Acts 7:42–43).

Amos 5:26.] See Millar's *History of the Propagation of Christianity*, vol. 1, p. 170.Millar explains the reference to bearing the tabernacle of Moloch and images of Chiun by describing similar practices at the feast honoring the goddess Isis in Egypt in his discussion of parallels with the dedication of the golden calf by Aaron and the Israelites. Robert Millar, *History of the Propagation of Christianity* (3rd ed., 2 vols. London, 1731).

Amos 5:27. "Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus."] Many of the people had been carried captive by the Syrians into Damascus and the country depending upon it. But a worse captivity was coming when they should be carried into captivity to a much greater distance. Yea, they should be carried into a worse and more distant captivity than the inhabitants of Damascus themselves. The captivity of Israel under Shalmaneser was far beyond that of Damascus under Tiglath-Pileser, and much more grievous and destructive. They were carried into Kir (Amos 1:5). But the utmost parts of Media, whither the Ten Tribes were carried, was probably far more distant. Kir probably was somewhere in the country of Babylonia, and therefore Stephen cites this place thus: "I will carry you away beyond Babylon" (Acts 7:43).

Amos 6:1. "That are at ease in Zion."] The originalבְּצִיּוֹן הַשַּׁאֲנַנִּים more literally is, "that are at rest," or "in tranquillity in Zion." The meaning is, "that trust in Mount Zion." To "rest in" and to "trust in" are the same thing. The following words, "*And trust in* the mountain of Samaria," confirms this to be the sense. "Which are named chief of the nations." In the originalהַגּוֹיִם רַאשִׁית נְקֻבֵי it is, "the *beginning*," or "*head*," or "*first fruits* of the nations." That is, these two mountains or cities were the capital cities, and esteemed the holy cities (consecrated to God as his first fruits), of these two nations of Judah and Israel. "To whom the house of Israel came." I.e. all the posterity of Jacob were wont to come up to these two mountains for judgment and for defense.

<!-- p. 795 -->

Amos 6:2. "Be they better than these kingdoms, or their border greater than your border?"] These words,גַת־פְלִשְׁתִּים וּרְדוּ רַבָּה חֲמַת מִשָּׁם וּכְֽוּ רְאוּ כַלְנֵה עִבְכוּמִגְּבֻלְכֶם גְּבוּלָם אִם־רַב הָאַלָּה מִן־הַמַּמְלָכוֹת הֲטוֹבִים as the verse is translated and pointed in our version, imply (according to the ordinary use of such interrogations in the Hebrew tongue) that they were not better than these kingdoms. But the verse ought to have been rendered thus: "Pass ye unto Calneh," etc., "and see whether they were better than these kingdoms, or whether their border was greater than your border."

"Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; from thence go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Be they better than these kingdoms, or their border greater than your border?" It seems that the interrogation was intended to be answered in the affirmative, as much as if it had been said, Were they not better, etc. Calneh was an ancient city built by Nimrod (Genesis 10:10), which it seems now lay in ruins. Hamath was destroyed [by] Sennacherib, who boasts of his destroying the gods of Hamath [2 Kings 18:34]. Gath, likewise, was made desolate by Hazael (2 Kings 12:17).This paragraph is a separate entry.

Amos 6:6. "That drink wine in bowls… and are not grieved for the afflictions of Joseph."] Here is probably an allusion to the story of the chief butler whose business was with Pharaoh's wines, who, when he was restored to his butlership, and was in prosperity, remembered not Joseph, but forgot him.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. Or rather, to their merciless, unnatural ancestors, the sons of Jacob, who took Joseph, and "stript him out of his coat of many colors, and took him, and cast him into a pit," etc., and then "sat down to eat bread," being not at all concerned at the calamity of Joseph, nor grieved for him when they "saw the anguish of his soul" (Genesis 37:23–25 and Genesis 42:21). See note on Psalms 80:1.

Those that are here spoken of as eating "the lambs out of the flock" Amos 6:4], and drinking "wine in bowls," etc., and not being "grieved for the afflictions of Joseph," are the rulers of the people, as is evident because they are charged with causing "the seat or throne of violence to come near" Amos 6:3]. And by "Joseph" is meant God's church, his people that are distinguishingly beloved, as Joseph was, and who were chiefly of the lower kind of people, their younger brethren. Joseph in his sufferings was a type of the church. 'Tis probable that that was literally true of Joseph's brethren, that when they persecuted and afflicted him, they eat

<!-- p. 796 -->

the lambs or kids out of the flock, for they were shepherds, and they were then feeding sheep; and the flesh of the sheep and lambs was their common food. And we read that when they had sold Joseph, they killed a kid of the goats, and dipped the coat in the blood. And doubtless they eat that kid.

Amos 6:7. "Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive."] The great men and rich men were first carried captive out of Judah and Jerusalem, as 'tis such as are here spoken of. See Isaiah 3:2–3, 2 Kings 24:14.

Amos 6:10. "A man's uncle shall take him up."] One thing denoted by this is that the young men shall die first. Young men used to do such services as carrying forth the dead. See Acts 5:6, Acts 5:10. But now old men are forced to do it.

"Hold thy tongue, for we may not make mention of the name of the Lord." When being asked whether any more are left alive, and he shall answer, "No," or "There is an end," as it is in the original.אָפֶס וְאָמַר On that occasion he that makes that answer shall begin to break forth with great affection and grief, and as is usual on such occasion, to make mention of God's name in bitter exclamation, as calling for God's mercy and pity, or remarking the awful hand of God. He shall bid him hold his tongue because they were so held under the power of watchful enemies, who were enemies to God, that they might "not make mention of the name of the Lord." See Amos 8:3.This paragraph is a separate entry. This reference is a later addition.

Amos 6:12. "Shall horses run upon a rock? Will one plow there with oxen?"] By "a rock" here is meant such a steep rocky mountain full of precipices as were common in that country, and are often meant by the word "rock"סֶלַע in the Old Testament. There is no running a race here with horses. If any should attempt, they would take a direct course to break their own necks, and destroy themselves. Nor can [one] "plow there with oxen." This is to set forth how much in vain the labors of God's prophets and messengers were with that people, and how ill they treated them.

The work of ministers is sometimes in Scripture compared to the running of a race. But the messengers of God in their labors among that perverse people were like men that attempted to run a race on horses on a

<!-- p. 797 -->

rocky mountain, eminently exposing themselves to wounds and death. Again the work of ministers is often compared to the labors of the husbandmen, and to the labors of the ox. These would attempt to plow in vain in the midst of such rocky hills and precipices.

Amos 6:14. "From the entering in of Hemath to the river of the wilderness."] The wordנַחַל translated "river" signifies valley or brack, as well as river. What is meant seems to be some valley or brack in the southern parts, in the utmost border of the land, next to the wilderness of Arabia, some stream running either into the Great Sea or the Salt Sea.

Amos 8:1–2.] Summer fruit is fruit that is quick ripe. This is made use of to represent the hastening of judgments for sin, and things ripening apace for the ruin of the wicked inhabitants of the land, or as it was, fruit in a basket, summer fruit already ripe and gathered, ready to be eaten. It might signify that the people were already ripe for destruction, just ready to be destroyed, as summer fruits are gathered not to be laid up, but to be eaten presently.

Amos 9:9.] By sifting the house of Israel is not only meant scattering them, but trying them with great afflictions and temptations amongst all nations, by which trials not the least grain should fall on the ground. They should not destroy the righteous, but "all the sinners of my people shall die," as in the next verse. They should not endure the trial, but should be as the chaff which the wind drives away.

Amos 9:12.] "Edom was the standing name of that nation which was descended of Esau, as the Israelites were of Jacob. But an apostle in Acts 15:17 applies what is said of Edom (if we adhere only to the private interpretation of the prophecies, and regard not the signification of proper names) unto mankind in general. For the interpretation of Edom is 'man'; and the wordאֳדֹם is used, as a collective, for mankind, as they are all of one blood and frame." *The Creation the Ground-Work of Revelation*, p. 52.Andrew Wilson, *Creation the Ground-Work of Revelation*. Wilson (1718–92), a physician and philosopher, practiced medicine in Edinburgh and London.

<!-- p. 798 -->

### Obadiah

Obadiah 1:15. "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee."] The land of Edom was desolated by the Nabatheans in the time of the Jews' captivity in Babylon. See Prideaux, Pt. II, pp. 281–82.*Old and New Testament Connected*, 10th ed., Pt. II, vol. 3, pp. 281–82.

Obadiah 1:16. "As ye have drunk upon my holy mountain."] I.e. as ye my people have drunk of the cup of affliction and tremblings, "so shall all the heathen drink," etc.

Obadiah 1:16–17.] The Jews returned to their land after it was desolated, but the Edomites never. See Prideaux, *Connection*, Pt. II, p. 281 margin.Ibid., n. b.

<!-- p. 799 -->

### Jonah

Jonah 1.] See no. 97.*Works, 15*, 78–79.

Jonah 2:4.] Jonah took ship to go to TarshishTarshish was a far-off, unidentified port. to flee from the presence of the Lord. But God took a most effectual course with him to make him confess that there was no place where he could be hid from God's sight, or be out of his hands. The storm that was raised in the sea, and tossed the ship in which he was, convinced him that he was not out of the presence of God. Afterwards he was cast into the sea, was swallowed by a whale, and went down to the bottom of the sea under the roots of the mountain. The waters compassed him about to a vast height, and the earth with her bars was about him; and he was as it were in the belly of hell. Then he was ready to think that surely he was cast out of God's sight. But God [made] it to appear that he was there also, by so wonderfully and miraculously preserving him there, hearing the silent petitions and cries of his heart there where he could speak no words, and by bringing him up from thence.

Jonah 3:5. "So the people of Nineveh believed God," etc.] The special reason why the men of Nineveh so much regarded Jonah as one sent from God, and a true prophet, seems to have been because they were convinced by the great miracle of Jonah's being preserved so long in the whale's belly, and at last cast up alive on the dry land. For this was the sign of the prophet Jonah, and that which was a sign to the Ninevites, that was so regarded by them, that caused them to repent at his preaching, as is plainly intimated in Luke 11:29–30, Luke 11:32; Matthew 12:39–41. Christ came to Jerusalem and the Jews to warn them of approaching destruction, as Jonas came to Nineveh. And the destruction was at about the same distance, about forty years after Christ's resurrection; and the like sign, only greater, was given to them that had been given to the Ninevites. "For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly," so Christ was

<!-- p. 800 -->

"three days and three nights in the heart of the earth." But the Ninevites repented, but this generation repented not.

Jonah 4:6–11.] This gourd represents man or the life of man. It was a feeble, tender, dependent, frail vine. It came up suddenly, and was very short-lived. It came up in a night, and perished in a night. It was green and flourishing, and made a fine show one day, and was withered and dried up the next. The worm that smote the gourd represents death. The gourd was killed by a worm, a little thing; so a very small matter proves the death of man. The frailty of man was well represented by such an emblem at this time when God had threatened the destruction of so great a multitude of mankind.

The gourd was very pleasing and refreshing to Jonah while it lasted, as life is sweet. It was very desirable to him upon that account, that it defended him from scorching heat. So is life desirable as it holds man back from the dreadful state of death. Jonah had pity on the gourd, that is, on himself for the loss of it, and thought himself wronged that he was deprived. But how much more should he have had pity on the many thousands of Ninevites when God had threatened them with the loss of life, the thing represented by the gourd, a so much more desirable enjoyment than the gourd. And if he found fault with God that he did not spare to him the shade of the gourd, why might he not well have pity on the Ninevites, and spare their lives? Jonah insisted upon it, that he did well to be angry for God's taking away the gourd, and yet was angry with God for not taking away the lives of the Ninevites. So unreasonable was he, and so much more did he regard the honor of being a true prophet than the lives of such a multitude.

<!-- p. 801 -->

### Micah

Micah 2:4. "Hath changed the portion of my people."] I.e. changed it as to its owner, taken it from its former possessors, and given it to others. The following expressions confirm this meaning.

Micah 2:6. "They shall not prophesy to them, that they shall not take shame."] They will not let the prophets prophesy, because they will "not take shame." They esteem the words of the prophets a reproach to 'em, and therefore hate them for their words.

Micah 2:7. "O thou that art named of the house of Jacob, is the spirit of the Lord straitened?"] I.e. do you think to be able to restrain the spirit of God, to tie it up to your limits, and prescribe to it what it shall say, or to restrain it as to what it shall bring to pass? "Are these his doings?" You are named of the house of Jacob, call yourselves his children. But do you do the works of Jacob? "Do not my words do good to him that walketh uprightly?" Instead of their being uneasy and grieved by it, they are refreshed; instead of esteemedMS: "esteemed it." as their reproach and wound, they esteem [it] as a precious ointment that heals, and revives, and invigorates them.

Micah 2:13.] See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. 107e–108a.Kidder notes "the Jews themselves grant" that this passage is "to be understood" of the Messiah, an opinion expressed by "their ancient writers." *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 107–8.

Micah 3:11. "The priests thereof teach for hire."] This is not against an established maintenance, for such had the priests by the law of God, but against their refusing to teach the people, when they upon occasions come to them to inquire of the law of God, unless they would pay 'em for it.

Micah 4:6. "Will I assemble her that halteth."] Zephaniah 3:19 and Luke 14:21.

<!-- p. 802 -->

Micah 4:13. "Arise and thresh," etc.] Zion is here spoken of as compared to a heifer, for with such they used to thresh, or by their treading out the corn (Hosea 10:11). "And I will consecrate their gain," etc.] By beating in pieces many people, they shall get their substance and gain from them, as the thresher gets the grain from the sheaves that are threshed.

Micah 5:2. "Whose goings forth."] "Dr. Pococke observes that the 'going forth' is used for a 'word which proceedeth out of the mouth' (Deuteronomy 8:3), and is therefore very fitly used to signify the eternal generation of him who is called the Word of God, that was 'in the beginning with God' [John 1:2]." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 724. See this text particularly considered, "Scripture," no. 501a.*Works, 13*, 594–98.

Micah 5:7. "As a dew from the Lord, as the showers upon the grass, that tarrieth not for man, nor waiteth for the sons of men."] The wordsיְקַוֶּה and יְיַחֵל in the original translated "tarrieth" and "waiteth" signify such a waiting as carries in it expectation, hope, and dependence. And 'tis the "grass" that is spoken [of] that don't expect, or hope, or wait for supplies from man, hoping for showers or dews from them who can't give rain, but look for showers only from God. And therefore 'tis expressed that there should be a dew on the grass "from the Lord." See Job 29:23 and Jeremiah 14:22. See also 2 Kings 6:33.

Micah 5:10–11.] See Bp. Sherlock's *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, p. 382.Sherlock cites the prophets Micah and Hosea to confirm "that the Character given of the Messias, that he should ride on an Ass, was in opposition to the Pride of their warlike Kings, who by their great Strength in Chariots and Horses had ruined themselves and their People." The point was that "God would be to them instead of Armies and fortified Towns" (Dissertation IV, "Christ's Entry into Jerusalem," *Use and Intent of Prophecy*, 5th ed.).

Micah 7:11. "In that day shall the decree be far removed."] The decree spoken of is that decree or awful sentence pronounced in the foregoing chapter, Micah 7:13–16.

Micah 7:16. "Their ears shall be deaf."] 'Tis a figurative expression representing as though their senses should be perfectly overcome and stupefied by the greatness of the things they should see and hear, as the sight is dazzled, and men are struck blind by a sudden and great light and glory, and their ears deafened with a sudden, great, and astonishing sound.

<!-- p. 803 -->

### Nahum

Nahum 1:6. "The rocks are thrown down by him."] They were wont to build their fortresses on high steep rocks, or rocky mountains. These are the strongest places, but these shall be no defense "before his indignation." But these rocky mountains shall be "thrown down by him."

Nahum 1:11. "A wicked counselor."] This has reference to Sennacherib or Rabshakeh "who counseled the Jews to despair of the divine protection, and surrender themselves to the king of Assyria, and endeavored to put 'em out of conceit of Hezekiah's reformation." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 736.

Nahum 1:12. "Though they be quiet."] I.e. secure. Henry.Ibid.

Nahum 2:2.] What God does to his own people in turning away their excellency, marring all their glory, is mentioned as an evidence that God undoubtedly [will] destroy the glory of Nineveh. Nebuchadnezzar, who was to destroy Nineveh, was one whom God had determined to improve as such a great and universal instrument of his wrath to all nations in those parts, that he should destroy the whole land of Jacob, as the excellency of the Ten Tribes had been destroyed before. God had determined to empty the whole land. And if the day was a day of such great wrath as to reach and swallow up that people, and Nebuchadnezzar was appointed to be the instrument of it, it would be unreasonable for Nineveh to expect to be distinguished and defended. If the sword be as it were thus bathed in heaven, it would come down on Nineveh.

Nahum 2:7. "And Huzzab shall be led away captive, she shall be brought up, and her maids shall lead her as with the voice of doves, taboring upon their breasts."] Huzzab is either the queen of Nineveh, or Nineveh itself under the emblem of a great princess. See the Nahum 3:4. "'Her maids' of honor 'shall lead her,' because [she] is weak and faint, 'with

<!-- p. 804 -->

the voice of doves,' i.e. with the voice of mourning and lamentation, taboring upon their own breasts for grief and vexation, as if they were drumming upon them, for so the wordמְתֹפְפוֹת signifies." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 737–38.

Nahum 2:8. "Nineveh of old is like a pool of water."] Not like running of water like the passing streams from rain or snow. See Job 24:18–19. But the waters of a standing lake, which are settled, and remain unmoved of old, and from generation to generation, and stand till they putrefy. The representation is something like that. Jeremiah 48:11, "Moab hath been at ease from his youth; and he hath settled on his lees, and hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel; neither hath he gone into captivity."

"Stand, stand, shall they cry; but none shall look back." When the people are fleeing, some shall endeavor to keep 'em back, [but it] will be in vain. The soldiers shall flee, and in vain will their commanders cry after them to stay, and not to flee. They shall be so under the power of fear that nothing shall restrain their flight.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Nahum 3:11. "Thou shalt be hid; thou also shalt seek strength because of the enemy."] I.e. thou shalt run, and skulk, and hide thyself, seeking some refuge and defense from the enemy.

Nahum 3:16–17.] These that are here called "merchants" probably were their mercenary soldiers, which should be a great multitude; but these hired soldiers should be such as there would be no dependence upon, let their multitude be never so great. Instead of helping them in time of danger, they should fly away like the cankerworm that turns into a flying insect. They should fly away with all they can get. They shall as it were suck the wealth and life of the land, and spoil it like a parcel of cankerworms or locusts, and then should be gone. "Thy crowned and thy captains," i.e. the princes and foreign chiefs that you shall hire, should be like so many great grasshoppers, that while the season is cool abide by you, but when the heat of the war comes on, shall be gone, as grasshoppers leave the hedge in the heat of the day.

<!-- p. 805 -->

### Habakkuk

Habakkuk 1:3. "Show me iniquity."] See note on Deuteronomy 6:25.

Habakkuk 1:12.] This verse literally translated, as Mr. Glas observes, is thus. "Art not thou from everlasting, Jehovah, my God, my Holy One? We shall not die, Jehovah. To judgment thou hast placed him; to rebuking thou hast founded him." So Mr. Glas applies these words to the Messiah. See *Notes on Scripture-Texts, No. 5*, p. 5.*Works* (2nd ed.), *III*, 218.

Habakkuk 2:3–4 ff.] These two verses, together with the following verses to the end of the fourteenth, contain that which is very parallel with Revelation 13:10. These two verses speak of the patience and faith of the saints in expectation of what God had promised to them concerning the destruction of the literal Babylon that held them captive, and the church's consequent deliverance and glory. And in the following verses is set forth how they that led others into captivity should go into captivity, and how they that killed others with the sword should be slain themselves, particularly Habakkuk 2:7–8, Habakkuk 2:10. And in the Habakkuk 2:14 is set forth how that the earth after this should "be filled with the knowledge of the Lord." So the Spirit, speaking in the Revelation 13, speaking of the destruction of the spiritual Babylon, says, "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity. He that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and faith of the saints" Revelation 13:10]. And the Revelation 14, at the Revelation 14:6–8 and following verses, speaks of the whole earth's being filled with the knowledge and worship of the true God by the preaching of the gospel "to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people," as attending the downfall and dismal punishment of Babylon, and thus adds these words, Revelation 14:12, "Here is the patience and faith of the saints."

Habakkuk 2:4. "His soul which is lifted up."] See note on Deuteronomy 8:17.

<!-- p. 806 -->

Habakkuk 3:2. "Revive thy work in the midst of the years," etc.] See "Scripture," no. 483.*Works, 15*, 580–81.

Habakkuk 3:3–6.] See note on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210.Ibid., 135–40.

Habakkuk 3:4. "He had horns coming out of his hand."] Or rather, bright beams. See Buxtorf's *Lexicon*.Buxtorf defines קָרַן with the Latin verbs *splendere* and *radiare*, both of which mean "to shine" or "to beam" (*Lexicon Hebaicum et Chaldaicum* [6th ed.], p. 660). 'Tis probable that the special occasion for observing this was when God stretched forth his hand to deliver to Moses the two tables of stone, after he had engraven the law on them, when "from his right hand proceeded a fire of law for them," as 'tis said, Deuteronomy 33:2 (See notes on the place.). When God delivered the law with his right hand, there came from that right hand a glorious and awful brightness that struck Moses with awe and fear like lightning (as we have often an account of God's appearing with such a kind of brightness), and this betokened the omnipotent power there was in the right hand to enforce the law given, and thus therein "was the hiding of his power." Thus an exceeding brightness denoted great power in Revelation 18:1. "And after these things I saw another angel come down from heaven, and the earth was lightened with his glory." The time when God thus gave the law the last time seems to have been when he passed by and proclaimed his name (Exodus 34). Then when Moses saw God's back parts, he saw his right hand with these bright beams, either writing the law on the tables, or delivering them to Moses. The wordקַרְנַים translated "horns" is in the dual number, which confirms the reference to the two tables of stone.This sentence and the following paragraph are later additions.

"And there was the hiding of his power." Hervey translates it, "his powerful hiding." See *Dialogues*, vol. 3, p. 108 margin.Hervey adds, "a most secure Refuge, a Sanctuary absolutely inviolable." He also states, "Uncontroulable and omnipotent Power was lodged in the great JEHOVAH'S Hand; and this was the sure Defence, this was the impregnable Garrison, for all his People" (*Dialogues, 3*, 108, note).

Habakkuk 3:9. "According to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word."] God had sworn to give this land to the tribes of Israel. It was his oath to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob, and repeated many a time to the tribes of Israel.

<!-- p. 807 -->

Habakkuk 3:11. "At the light of thine arrows."] See no. 208.*Works, 15*, 131–34.

Habakkuk 3:13. "The head out of the house of the wicked."] I.e. out of the family of the wicked.This paragraph is a separate entry written later than the following paragraph.

"By discovering the foundation unto the neck." That by the wound which thou with thy sword gavest to the head, it was cut through or split down quite to the foundation of the head where it is set onto the neck.

<!-- p. 808 -->

### Zephaniah

Zephaniah 1:4 "And the name of the Chemarims with the priests."] "We read of these in the history of Josiah's reformation. 2 Kings 23:5, 'He put down the idolatrous priests.' The word is the *chemarim*.הַכְּמָרִים The word signifies 'black men.'… They seem to have been immediate attendants on the service of Baal. They shall be cut off 'with the priests,' the seculars with the regulars." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 753.

Zephaniah 1:7–8. "A sacrifice."] Wicked men in their destruction are a sacrifice to the justice of God. Christ is the great high priest to offer sacrifices to God. For [them] that obey him, he offers himself a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice; as to others, he will offer them up a sacrifice to God's vindictive wrath. For Christ is the person to whom the Father hath committed the destruction of his enemies as well as the salvation of his elect people. See Isaiah 63:1–2 ff., Psalms 2:9, and Revelation 19, and innumerable other places. The wicked are also a sacrifice, as their destruction is for the deliverance and salvation of God's people; and so they are as it were a ransom for them (Isaiah 43:3, Proverbs 21:18).

Zephaniah 1:11. "Howl, ye inhabitants of Maktesh, for all the merchant people are cut down; all they that bear silver are cut off."] "Maktesh was a low part of Jerusalem, deep like a mortar, for so the wordמַכָתַּשׁ signifies. The goldsmiths lived there (Nehemiah 3:32), and the merchants." Henry.*Exposition, 4* (1725), 754.

Zephaniah 2:11. "Will famish all the gods of the heathens."]KJV: "gods of the earth." They shall no more be fed with offerings and sacrifices, nor their desires gratified by the homage that is now paid them.

<!-- p. 809 -->

Zephaniah 3:11.] That rejoicing or glorying in their pride, and being haughty because of God's holy mountain, was eminently the sin of the people in the day that Christ appeared in the world.
