See Taylor's note on Romans 13:11, p. 448 of his book.Taylor writes about the "beautiful and lively Metaphor in this and Romans 13:12, involving night and day," the former pointing to the "present, imperfect State of Trial," the latter to the prospect of "Salvation and Glory" (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*).

Romans 14:1–3.] Here see Taylor's *Paraphrase and Notes*.Taylor paraphrases the intent of the Apostle in these verses as a call "to exercise Love and Gentleness, with Regard to any religious Differences" among Gentile converts and Jewish Christians whose obligations and pollutions differ. He calls for "mutual Forbearance, Unity and Peace" (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, pp. 297–98).

Romans 14:2. "For one believeth he may eat all things; another, who is weak, eateth herbs."] There was no meat that was killed and sold among the heathen but what was some way or other offered to an idol. So that the

<!-- p. 1033 -->

first Christians, in such populous cities as Rome, where they must buy all their provision at the heathen markets, could scarce come at any meat but what was offered to idols, or some way polluted, not being drained of the blood, etc.

Romans 14:10.] Judge and "set at nought" has reference to the same spoken of in the Romans 14:3, where we read of judging and despising. One party judged the other as licentious and wicked; the other party despised and set at nought him that differed from him as silly, superstitious, foolishly scrupulous, etc.

Romans 14:15. "Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died."] That is as much as to say, Will you not put yourself so much out of the way as to restrain your appetite, though you thereby expose your brother to be destroyed, for whom Christ put himself so much out of the way as to die to save him from being destroyed?

Romans 14:20. "Destroy not the work of God."] Christians are God's "workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works" [Ephesians 2:10]. We are God's husbandry. We are God's building. We should not destroy this building, but edify it or build it up, as in the preceding verse.

Romans 14:21. "Stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak."] They were made weak thus. The Jewish converts had been bred up in an extraordinary reverence for the ceremonial law. And when they saw that other Christians did not observe those laws, but allowed themselves to eat things that had been by those laws forbidden, and that they had been bred up in an abhorrence of as unclean, and argued that it was agreeable to the Christian institution for 'em so to do, and that it was a liberty allowed them by the gospel, they were in danger of being put out of concert of the gospel by that means, and to be weakened in their esteem and faith of it, that it indulged those liberties that they had such an inrooted and habitual abhorrence of, that they were stumbled and made weak in Christianity, or they were offended by being led in the same practice while they doubted of the lawfulness of it, for "he that doubteth is damned," as Romans 14:23.

Romans 14:22. "Hast thou faith?"] That is, to believe this doctrine of the gospel that these things are lawful, such a faith as the Apostle professes in the Romans 14:14.

<!-- p. 1034 -->

Romans 15:1.] Taylor says itὀφείλομεν δὲ ἢμεῖς οἰ δυνατοὶ τά ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάξειν. should have been translated, "But we that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak," this verse standing "in immediate connection with the Romans 14:23." See Taylor's notes.*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, p. 451.

Romans 15:5. "Like-minded according to Christ Jesus."] That is, of a mind like unto Christ's mind, in the respect mentioned in the Romans 15:3.

Romans 15:6–12.] The Apostle, in the preceding part of the chapter, had been exhorting the Jewish and Gentile Christians to receive one another, notwithstanding differences of opinion about lesser matters. He exhorts those Jewish Christians that were scrupulous about unclean meats to receive the Gentile Christians that were not so, and also exhorts those Gentile Christians not to despise the Jewish Christians for their scrupulousness. And here in the Romans 15:6, he makes use of this as an argument, "That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," intimating that a respect to the glory and praise of God, that has been so gracious to both of them in giving Christ to them, and who is the Father of Jesus Christ that is the common Lord and Savior of both of them, should induce them thus to receive one another. And therefore [he] adds, Romans 15:7, "Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God." I.e. receive ye one another "to the glory of God," as Christ has received both of you, both Jews and Gentiles, "to the glory of God," or that the glory of God might be shown forth upon and declared by both. And then he goes on, in the Romans 15:8–9, to show how Christ glorified God in receiving each of them, and how he by receiving them gave each occasion to glorify him. In the Romans 15:8 he shows how he glorified God by receiving the Jews, and gave them occasion to glorify him. He glorified the truth and faithfulness of God in fulfilling the promises made to their fathers, and so the Christian Jews have great reason to glorify him. "Now I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers." And in the Romans 15:9 he shows the great cause he had given the Gentile Christians to glorify him by the great and wonderful mercy he had showed them in bringing of them out of so miserable a state of heathenish darkness, wherein they were aliens and strangers, etc., to be the people of God. So that both had

<!-- p. 1035 -->

great cause to glorify God, the same Father, for being received by Christ, the same Lord, unto the same privilege of a blessed union and communion with him, and therefore ought with one head and mouth to glorify God, as the Apostle had said before, Romans 15:6.

The texts he here cites from the Old Testament are very pertinent to these two things he had insisted, viz. how Jews and Gentiles should cordially join one with another, as with one heart and mouth, in glorifying God, and also how God had glorified himself in what he had done for each in sending Christ, etc. Romans 15:9, "I will confess thee among the Gentiles, and sing unto thy name." That shows how the Jews should unite with the Gentiles in glorifying God. The words next cited, Romans 15:10, show how the Gentiles should join with the Jews in glorifying God. "Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people." And the next words, Romans 15:11, show how both should unite in praising God: "all the Gentiles," and "all the people," i.e. the Jews. And the former part of the next verse, viz. Romans 15:12, "There shall be a root of Jesse," confirms what the Apostle had said, Romans 15:8, that God had glorified his truth to the Jews in sending Christ of their nation. "There shall be a root of Jesse." And the latter part of the verse confirms Romans 15:9, viz. God's mercy to the Gentiles, etc.This paragraph is a later addition, causing JE to add Romans 15:10–12 to the heading of the original entry.

Romans 15:12–13.] These two verses confirm that by "hope" is meant faith in Christ, for when it is said, "in him shall the Gentiles trust," in the originalἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσιν. it is, "in him shall the Gentiles hope"; and then it follows, "the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing," referring to the joy of the Gentiles in trusting in Christ, spoken of, Romans 15:10–11. (See note on Hebrews 6:19, no. 284.)*Works, 15*, 240–42. So where the word in our translation is "trust," it is "hope" in the original, in the following places: 1 Timothy 4:10, 1 Timothy 6:17, John 5:45, Ephesians 1:12, 1 Timothy 5:5, 1 Peter 3:5.

This confirms that the Old Testament "trust" is the same with the New Testament "faith," for 'tis evident trusting in God and hoping in God are often used in the Old Testament, as faith and hope are in the New.This paragraph is a later addition.

Romans 15:13. "And peace."] In this the Apostle refers to the unanimity between Jews and Gentiles he had been so much insisting on.

<!-- p. 1036 -->

Romans 15:15. "In some sort."] ἀπὸ μέρους, "with respect to a part" of you. See Taylor's note, p. 453 of his book.Taylor adds that here ἀπὸ μέρους "signifies the *Gentile* Part of the Church at *Rome*" because of the way that Paul construes his commission "as the Apostle of the Gentiles" (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*).

Romans 15:17. "I have therefore whereof I may glory through Jesus Christ in things pertaining to God."] The Apostle by this phrase, "things pertaining to God," means sacred things pertaining to the temple or the priesthood, or those affairs of God's people wherein their intercourse with God is maintained, and God is most immediate[ly] ministered to. Thus this phrase is used by this Apostle in Hebrews 2:17, and Hebrews 5:1. This phrase the Apostle uses here, because that thing he has respect to as his great honor, and which he speaks of in the preceding verse, is what he did as God's priest in "offering up the Gentiles," etc. Dr. Doddridge has this note on this place. "Raphelius very justly observes, that this phrase has a peculiar propriety when applied to sacerdotal affairs, and especially victims presented to God, of which the Apostle is here speaking. Other texts are illustrated by this remark, particularly Hebrews 2:17. See Raphelius, *Not. ex Xen., in loca*."*Family Expositor, 4*, 184, n. e. The work in reference is Georg Raphel, *Annotationes philologicae in Novum Testamentum ex Xenophonte collectae* (1720).

Romans 16:1. "A servant of the church."] See Taylor's note on the verse.Taylor suggests that this phrase might have been translated "a Diaconess of the Church" because it seems likely that the custom in Corinth did not allow the male deacons to distribute resources to women in need as that would have been regarded as an indecency and a scandal to Christians. Therefore it is probable that women were chosen as deaconesses to attend the needs of other women (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, pp. 455–56).

Romans 16:20. "Bruise Satan under your feet shortly."] Agreeably to what God promised of the seed of the woman [Genesis 3:15]. The Apostle probably has respect to the Christian church prevailing to the overthrow of heathenism in the empire in Constantine's time. It was suitable to intimate this to those Christians who were Romans, and dwelt in the capital city of that heathen empire.

Romans 16:22. "I Tertius."] Which Dr. Doddridge supposes to be the same with Silas, being a name signifying the same with the Latin word *Tertius*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 198, n. c.

<!-- p. 1037 -->

### I Corinthians

1 Corinthians 1:24.] See no. 155.*Works, 15*, 94.

1 Corinthians 1:27. "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise," etc.]This verse and the two following are the final lines in JE's conclusion to his treatise on free will. See *Works, 1*, 439. God by this method shows Satan that his understanding and wisdom is of infinitely further reach than his. All Satan's strife and contrivance is to get the powers, and honors, and riches, and wisdom of the world onMS: "of." his side, and to improve them in his interest. God shows that his wisdom stands in no need of such helps, but he knows how to order the meanest and most despicable means so, and so to contrive things with them as to baffle all the policy of Satan, and confound all the strength that he has on his side. As king would show his superior policy if he should so contrive things, as without the trouble of raising armies and fleets, and providing arms and ammunition, or taxing his country, and the like, should successfully carry on a war against a powerful enemy with mighty forces, and should baffle and confound them from time to time, though they lay out themselves to the utmost, by some very inconsiderable, despicable means, and with very little ado.

1 Corinthians 1:28.] Possibly by "things that are not," the Apostle has a special respect to the Gentiles who are not a people, and by "things that are," the Jews, as Mr. Locke thinks.Locke, *Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 9, n. m.

1 Corinthians 1:30.] All our good is contained in these four things mentioned, viz. "wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption." The good of the fallen creature can't be better distributed and summed up than in these four things. All our good consists in the good of greatness, which is wisdom; and in our good of excellency, which is our sanctification or deliverance from sin, and infusion of holiness; and in our relative good, which

<!-- p. 1038 -->

is righteousness, or justification, or being no longer the objects of God's anger, and becoming the objects of his favor and love; and in our good of enjoyment, or a deliverance from misery, and being brought to happiness, joy, and glory or redemption.

Here in this verse is shown our dependence on each person in the Trinity for all our good. We are dependent on Christ, as he is made to us wisdom, etc. We are dependent on the Father, in that 'tis of that he is made these things to us. 'Tis the Father that has given him, and sent him into the world. And 'tis the Father that accepts of him, that what he has done may procure these benefits for us. We are dependent on the Holy Spirit, as 'tis of him that we are in Christ. 'Tis he that brings us to close with Christ, and gives us faith in him, whereby we come to receive of him these benefits.

These four benefits answer to the four evils that we are subject to in our fallen state, viz. "ignorance, guilt, sin, and death." Bates, *Harmony*, p. 84.William Bates, *Harmony of the Divine Attributes* (4th ed., London, 1697), 84. Bates (1625–99) was a prominent English preacher.

1 Corinthians 2:6.] "In the Jewish discipline there were two sorts of persons, ἀσκηταί, 'beginners,' that did exercise themselves in virtuous actions and endeavors. Then there were others whom Philo calls τέλειος, 'perfect.' They were those who had attained to somewhat, and made some progress in the matters learned." Manton, on *James*, p. 354.Manton, *Practical Commentary Upon James*.

1 Corinthians 2:11–12.] In these two verses is contained an invincible argument for the insufficiency of human reason without a divine revelation in things of that nature which the gospel reveals, viz. the mind and purpose of God concerning his acceptance of and favor towards the sinful children, the way, terms, purpose, and fruits of that favor, viz. that these things are entirely dependent on God's free pleasure, or merely these are things freely given us of God. And therefore 'tis impossible any should know them naturally but God, him or the Spirit of God, as no man knows what the mind of man is, but the spirit of man that is in him.

1 Corinthians 2:14–15.] See notes on Galatians 5:17, especially the last paragraph before the corollaries.

<!-- p. 1039 -->

1 Corinthians 2:15–16.] See no. 156.*Works, 15*, 94–95.

1 Corinthians 3:15.] The allusion is to a man that is asleep in his house that he has built when it takes fire, and has his house and all his sustenance in it consumed, loses all, and but narrowly escapes with his own life by running through the fire. Such a man suffers loss; he loses the works of his hands, the house that he has built, hoping that it would be a safe and comfortable habitation for [him], and also the fruits of his labors that he hath gathered into his house, and has been laying up in store for himself for his future maintenance and comfort. He loses all the reward of his labors. He loses his garments, which are also burnt up, and escapes naked, and with great difficulty saves his own life, escapes through great fear and terrible amazement, and is vehemently scorched with the fire, though he escapes being consumed. When the Apostle here speaks of a man's building in the text and context, he alludes to a man's building an house for himself to dwell in. A straw building is very likely to [be] burnt. Such Christians as spend their time in building such a superstructure are asleep and know not what they do. They are not wakeful but slumbering Christians that do thus, and such only as are asleep are like thus to be surprised with and to suffer by fire burning their house over their heads.

1 Corinthians 3:19. "For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness."] These are the words of Eliphaz in Job 5:13, by which it is manifest that though Job's three friends misapplied their doctrines in inferring from 'em Job's hypocrisy, yet their sayings are justly cited as canonical scripture. In their general doctrines, as Mr. Henry observes, they "spake the pious sense of the patriarchal age."*Exposition, 3* (1725), 28. Job 5:11, which is also the words of Eliphaz, seems to be referred to by the Virgin Mary in her song (Luke 1:52).

1 Corinthians 3:21. "All things are yours."] See Luke 12:44.

1 Corinthians 4:3–4. "Yea, I judge not mine own self."] I.e. I don't undertake to determine concerning myself, mine own uprightness and faithfulness, as expecting that you or others should be governed by what I judge and declare of myself. "For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified." I.e. my own conscience don't condemn me, but yet I am not hereby justified to you. "He that judgeth me is the Lord." I claim, and

<!-- p. 1040 -->

being approved of, and treated by, and submitted to by no further than the Lord; my proper judge does attest my fidelity.

1 Corinthians 4:6. "Above what is written."] I.e. above, what I have just now written, in the direction I have given in this epistle, how ye should esteem of ministers that plant and water, etc.

No. 157.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 95.

1 Corinthians 4:9.] "The Apostle seems here to allude to the custom of bringing those last upon the theater, who were to be destroyed by wild beasts." Mr. Locke.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 26, n. a.

1 Corinthians 4:12. "And labor, working with our own hands."] This manner of expression plainly intimates that it was not ordinarily looked upon as belonging to a minister of the gospel that he should follow any bodily labor.

1 Corinthians 4:13. "The filth of the world, and the offscouring of all things."] Dr. Doddridge says there were among the heathen certain "wretches taken from among the dregs of the people, offered as expiatory sacrifices to the infernal deities, and loaded with curses, affronts, and injuries, in the way to the altars, at which they were to bleed," that were called by these names, καθάρματα and περίψηματα, for which he cites Dr. Henry More,Henry More (1614–87), the Cambridge Platonist, author of *The Theological Works of the Most Pious and Learned Henry More* (London, 1707). Dr. Whitby, and Suidas,This is a reference, most likely, to the text of Suidas, the lexicographer, published as *Souidas. Suidœ lexicon, Grace & Latine* (Cambridge, 1705). and Dr. Ridley,Glocester Ridley (1702–74), author of *The Christian Passover. Four Sermons in which the Doctrine of the Lord's Supper is laid down* (London, 1736). and says that "BosLambert Bos (1670–1717), author of *Antiquitatum Graecarum praecipue atticarum* (1649). illustrates this sense of the word κάθαρμα by a very large and judicious collection of Greek quotations."*Family Expositor, 4*, 255.

1 Corinthians 5:1. "Not so much as named among the Gentiles."] I.e. "not known. That the marrying of a son-in-law and mother-in-law was not prohibited by the laws of the Roman Empire may be seen in Tully;Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 B.C.E.), Roman orator and man of letters. but yet it was looked

<!-- p. 1041 -->

on as so scandalous and infamous, that it never had any countenance from practice. His words in his oration *pro Cluentio*, §4, are so agreeable to the present case, that it may not be amiss to set them down. *Nubit generosocrus, nullis auspicibus, nullis auctoribus. O scelus incredibile et praeter hanc unam in omni vita inauditum*."I.e.," The mother-in-law marries the son-in-law with no favorable signs, no witnesses. O the unbelievable wickedness, unheard of in all the world before this one!" Locke's commentary.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 32, n. h.

1 Corinthians 5:4. "And my spirit."] See notes on 1 Corinthians 14:32.

1 Corinthians 5:7. "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump."] Leaven was a type of sin, partly upon this account, that it was a remainder of the old lump, and so is a fit type of the old man, or our original corruption.JE deleted "Bread derives its leaven." A lump of dough derives its leaven from a former lump, as we derive original corruption from our parents.

1 Corinthians 5:11. "No not to eat."] The Apostle doubtless means not only eating at the Lord's Table, but at any table, by the manner of expression, "No not to eat," or "No not so much as to eat." The Apostle would not express himself so of eating at the Lord's Table, which is the highest act of communion; but he evidently speaks of some lower act. And that 'tis a common eating will further appear, if we consider that it was the manner of the Jews at that time to abstain from eating with those that they looked upon as unclean. Therefore they would not eat with the Gentiles, as Galatians 2:12. And so they would not eat with publicans and sinners. Hence they found so much fault with Christ for eating with them (Matthew 9:11 and Mark 2:16). But Christ commands that excommunicated persons should be unto us "as an heathen man and a publican" [Matthew 18:17]. It was not only the custom of that age and nation to refuse to eat bread with those that they looked upon [as] polluted, but we find it was so among the Egyptians (Genesis 43:32).

1 Corinthians 6:6. "Goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers."] "Josephus observes, that the Romans (who were now masters of Corinth) permitted the Jews in foreign countries to decide private affairs, where nothing capital was in question, among themselves. And from hence Dr. Lardner argues the justice of this rebuke of St. Paul." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 267, n. d.

<!-- p. 1042 -->

1 Corinthians 6:14. "Will also raise us up."] This is mentioned as confirming what the Apostle had said in the foregoing verse, of the body's being "for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." He will raise up the body as his own, as what he purchased, and what is united to him, and is to be so in the most perfect and glorious manner to all eternity.

1 Corinthians 6:18. "Every sin that a man doth is without the body."] I.e. other sins immediately respect some object *ad extra*. Some are committed more immediately against God, and others against our neighbor. "But he that committeth fornication sins against his own body." He pollutes and defiles that. The Apostle comprehends our whole duty under three virtues, Titus 2:12, viz. sobriety, righteousness, and godliness. The second respects our neighbor; the last respects God, and the first ourselves. Fornication is a violation of the first (1 Timothy 2:15), and so is a sin immediately against ourselves, our own bodies.

1 Corinthians 7:2.] A plain text against polygamy, especially as expressed in the original. ἴδιον ἄνδρα signifies "own, peculiar to herself," as Mr. Wall in his *History of Infant Baptism*, p. 99, observes.William Wall, *History of Infant Baptism* (2 vols., 3rd ed. London, 1720), I, 99. Wall (1647–1728) was a minister and biblical scholar.

1 Corinthians 7:14.] "ἡγίασται, sanctified, ἅγιά, holy, ἀκάθαρτά, unclean, are used here by the Apostle in the Jewish sense. The Jews called all that were Jews, holy; and all others they called unclean. Thus *proles genita extra sanctitatem*Literally, "a child born without moral purity," or unclean. was a child begot by parents while they were yet heathens; *genita intra sanctitatem*Literally, "[a child] born in the condition of purity," or holiness. was a child begot by parents after they were proselytes. This way of speaking St. Paul transfers from the Jewish into the Christian church, calling all that are of the Christian church saints, or holy, by which reason all that are out of it were unclean." Locke, *in loc*.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 42, n. d.

1 Corinthians 7:15. "A brother or sister is not under bondage."] See note on Matthew 5:32.

1 Corinthians 7:25. "I have no commandment of the Lord."] I.e. no commandment for them. Christ had given him no positive commandment for them about it, one way or t'other, whether virgins should marry or should not. But it don't follow from hence that the Apostle had not the direction of

<!-- p. 1043 -->

the Spirit of God in the judgment he gave of what was best; neither doth the Apostle determine so. But he says in the last verse 1 Corinthians 7:40], that he thinks he has, and 'tis now determined that he had, by this book's being put into the canon of the Scripture. When the Apostle says he has "no commandment of the Lord," he don't mean that he has no direction or commandment of the Spirit of God what to say by way of advice, but if he had, it was no positive command to them, either to act, or not to act, as he says, in the 1 Corinthians 7:6, "I speak by permission, not by commandment."The remainder of this entry is a later addition. "Yet I give my judgment as one that hath obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful." The wordπιστός. translated "faithful" might (more agreeably to the Apostle's design) have been rendered "worthy to be credited" or "regarded," i.e. worthy to be regarded in his advice, intimating that God by his mercy gave him wisdom, and directed his judgment in the advice he gave, though his advice was only general advice, and not any commandment to any particular person. The Spirit of God itself may have the determination of circumstances with persons themselves, though he directs in giving general advice that is infallibly good as general advice, and yet the advice [may] not be of the nature of a particular positive institution or command, because the determination of their particular case is left by Christ to their own judgment.

1 Corinthians 7:36.] See no. 153.*Works, 15*, 94.

1 Corinthians 7:37. "Virgin."] "παρθένον seems used here for the virgin state, and not the person of a virgin. 1. Because the resolution of mind here spoken of must be in the person to be married, and not in the father that has power over the person concerned, for how will the firmness of the mind of the father hinder fornication in the child who has not that firmness? 2. The necessity of marriage can only be judged of by the persons themselves. A father cannot feel the child's flames which make the need of marriage. The persons themselves only know whether they burn, or have the gift of continence. 3. Because, if 'keep his virgin' had here signified 'keep his children from marriage,' the expression had been more natural to have used the word τέκνα, which signifies both sexes, than παρθένος, which belongs only to the female." Mr. Locke.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 46, n. p.

<!-- p. 1044 -->

1 Corinthians 7:38. "So then," etc.] It may be objected, how can this be when it is our duty to do as well as possibly we can, and if we do not, we sin, and don't do well? *Ans*. It is said that the same man that does well in marrying would do better in not marrying, for he not having the gift of continency would do ill not to marry. Both he that marries, and he that marries not, may do the best that they can do; and yet one do better than the other. For he that marries not has a further gift to improve than the other, viz. the gift of continence. A man that has a gift may do better in improving his gift than another that has it not, and does not improve it, though he does well. He that has ten talents does better in gaining ten more with them than he that has two talents does in gaining two more, though he does well. He that has money does better in giving to the poor than he has not does in not giving, though he does well.

1 Corinthians 7:40. "I think also I have the Spirit of God."] The word δοκῶ here used don't always signify merely having opinion, as Luke 17:9, "I trow not," in the original, οὐ δοκῶ. See also Acts 15:28, "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost," ἔδοξεν τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι. "δοκῶ ἔχειν often signifies the same with ἔχω. Compare Luke 8:18, Matthew 13:12, 1 Corinthians 10:1–2, 1 Corinthians 14:37. And the ambiguity of the expression, 'appear to have,' seems exactly to correspond to the ambiguity of this original phrase." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, n. l.

1 Corinthians 8-10.] See sermon on 1 Corinthians 10:16.JE's sermon on 1 Corinthians 10:16, n. d (no. 156, summer-fall 1729), with the doctrine: "The thing designed in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper is the communion of Christians in the body and blood of Christ." See below, note on 1 Corinthians 10:16.

1 Corinthians 8:3. "But if any man love God, the same is known of him."] That is, God is "known of him," or by him. He that loves God has the only true knowledge of God, "by a construction like that of the original of Acts 10:36, where οὗτος plainly refers to the immediate antecedent." So Doddridge.*Family Expositor, 4*, 294.

"But if any man love God, the same is known of him. "Which last words in the original are ἔγνωσται ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, "is made to know of him," or "is taught of him." The Apostle, though writing in Greek, yet often uses the Greek verbs according to the Hebrew conjugations. So 1 Corinthians 13:12, ἐπιγνώσομαι, which according to the Greek propriety signifies "I shall be known," is used for "I shall be made to know." And so Galatians 4:9.This paragraph is a separate entry. JE crossed it out with a large "X" on the left side of the entry. The preceding Doddridge entry on the same verse is the later entry.

<!-- p. 1045 -->

1 Corinthians 8:4. "An idol is nothing in the world."] "Dr. Whitby shows this was a common aphorism among the Jewish doctors, to which the word אֱלִילִים, the name given them, did probably allude." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 294, n. c.

1 Corinthians 8:5.] "The heathens had supreme sovereign gods, whom they supposed eternal, remaining always in the heavens. These were called θεοί, 'gods.' They had besides another order of inferior gods, gods upon earth, who by the will and direction of the heavenly gods governed terrestrial things, and were the mediators between the supreme heavenly gods and men, without whom there could be no communication between them. These were called in Scripture 'Baalim,' i.e. lords, and by the Greeks Δαίμονες. To this the Apostle alludes here." Locke, *in loc*.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 49, n. u.

1 Corinthians 9:5.] "Sister" is to be understood in the same sense here, as in 1 Corinthians 7:15, Romans 16:1, James 2:15.

1 Corinthians 9:9.] The business and labors of a minister of the gospel is on many accounts fitly compared to that of the ox that labors in a man's husbandry, and particularly to this labor of the ox here spoken of, viz. treading out the corn, his chief work being to explain and apply the word of God to his hearers, and as it were bringing out that spiritual food from the veil or husk it is wrapped up in on the plant whereon it grew, that it might be fitted for our use.

1 Corinthians 9:14. "Even so hath the Lord ordained," etc.] When he said, "The laborer is worthy of his hire" [Luke 10:7].

1 Corinthians 9:16.] See no. 152.*Works, 15*, 94.

1 Corinthians 9:26. "I therefore so run, as not uncertainly."] By this it is evidence that assurance is not to be obtained so much by examining and thinking as by action.

1 Corinthians 9:27. "Lest, when I have preached to others," etc.] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus: "Lest, after having served as an herald, I should be disapproved." And in his notes says, "I thought it of importance to retain the primitive sense of these gymnastic expressions. It is well known to those

<!-- p. 1046 -->

who are at all acquainted with the original, that the word κηρύξας, expresses the discharging the office of an herald, whose business it was to proclaim the conditions of the games, and display the prizes, to awaken the emulation and resolution of those who were to contend in them. But the Apostle intimates, that there was this peculiar circumstance attending the Christian contest, that the person that proclaimed its laws and rewards to others was also to engage himself, and that there would be a peculiar infamy and misery in miscarrying in such a circumstance. Αδόκιμος, which we render 'castaway,' signifies one who is disapproved by the judges of the games as not having fairly deserved the prize."*Family Expositor, 4*, 310–11, n. n.

1 Corinthians 10:2. "And were all baptized unto Moses."] See note on Psalms 68:8–9, no. 210, *Corol*. 2; *Works, 15*, 139–40. and note on 1 Peter 3:20; and SSS, on Psalms 77:16.This reference is a later addition. *Synopsis Criticorum, II* (London, 1671), Pt. 2, cols. 1067–68.

1 Corinthians 10:8. "Neither let us commit fornication."] "This was common at many idolatrous feasts among the heathen; and it was the more proper for the Apostle to caution these Christians against it, as it was proverbially called the Corinthian practice, κορινθιαζειν, being, as many have observed, equivalent to *scortari*.I.e. to whore. Strabo tells us that in one temple of Venus at Corinth, there were no less than a thousand priestesses, who made prostitution a part of their devotion to the goddess." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 315, n. e.

1 Corinthians 10:11. "Ends of the world."] See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 3, pp. 162–65.Kidder discusses the variety of expressions used in the New Testament to speak of the days of the Messiah, or the "time of Christ's appearance and kingdom," pointing also to the use of these terms by Jewish writers. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), 162–65.

1 Corinthians 10:13. "No temptation… but such as is common to man."] I.e. no trial or affliction, but such as is adapted to the weak, frail nature of man. In the original it is ἀνθρώπινος, such as is human, or adapted to the human nature. See 2 Samuel 7:14.

<!-- p. 1047 -->

1 Corinthians 10:16.] See sermon on the verse, for explaining the meaning of the text, and context, and the scope of these three chapters, viz. the eighth, ninth, and tenth.See above, entry on 1 Corinthians 8-10. JE's explanation of the text and context of this sermon on 1 Corinthians 10:16 focuses on the Apostle's effort to dissuade the Corinthian Christians "from eating things offered to idols." In response to those who maintained that the ceremonial law was abrogated and therefore they might eat things offered to idols at heathen festivals, Paul argued in the 1 Corinthians 8 that weaker brethren would be offended by such actions and the Christian name dishonored. In the 1 Corinthians 9, he points to his own example of self-denial "for the sake of others," including "refraining from marriage" and "taking no wages for his labor in the ministry." In the beginning of 1 Corinthians 10, he links this situation to the judgments against Israelites who are things offered to idols, which was viewed as "visible communion or fellowship in the worship of devils."

1 Corinthians 10:17. "Are all partakers of that one bread."] "Eisner has an admirable note on this text, to prove that eating together in a religious manner hath been, in almost all nations, a token of mutual friendship. See Mr. Low-man's *Hebrew Ritual*,Moses Lowman published *A Rational of the Ritual of the Hebrew Worship; in which the Wise Designs and Usefulness of that Ritual are Explain'd, and Vindicated from Objections* (London, 1748). On Lowman, see *Works, 5*, 55–59. p. 54, and Maimonides, quoted by him there. See more especially, Cudworth's *Discourse Concerning the True Notion of the Lord's Supper*,Ralph Cudworth (1617–88), the Cambridge Platonist, published the *Discourse* in 1642. ch. 1 and ch. 6. And it is certain also that by sacrifices and the feasts on them, they held communion with the real or supposed deity to which they were presented, as the author of *A Discourse on Sacrifices* has shown at large." Doddridge's note, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 319, n. b.

1 Corinthians 10:20. "I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils."] "Eisner has proved at large from incontestable authorities, that the demons were considered as present at these sacrifices, and as taking their part with the worshippers in the common feast, by which means, as Maimonides expresses it in a very remarkable passage, friendship, brotherhood, and familiarity was contracted between them, because all eat at one table, and sat down at one board." Doddridge's note, *in loc*.Ibid., 320, n. c.

1 Corinthians 11:4–5.] I.e. "the man, 'having his head covered,' dishonoreth Christ his head, by appearing in a garb not becoming the authority and dominion which God through Christ has given him over all the things of this world" (Christ, whom God hath appointed head over the universe,

<!-- p. 1048 -->

hath committed to him some of his authority, and made him his image and representative. See 1 Corinthians 11:7.), "the covering [of] the head being a mark of subjection. But on the contrary, a woman praying or prophesying in the church with her head uncovered dishonoreth the man, who is her head, by appearing in a garb that disowns her subjection to him." Mr. Locke.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 67. See preceding verse.

1 Corinthians 11:5.] How a woman's praying or prophesying at all is consistent with a woman's not speaking in the church, see Taylor's note on Romans 16:1.The Greek custom of keeping women in a state of separation apart from men, Taylor explains, means that sometimes they exercised devotions apart from their husbands. The prohibition against women praying and prophesying in the church or public assemblies did not prohibit women from such activities in "separate Meetings, which consisted of none but women." Taylor also reviews the contested judgments of commentators regarding this practice (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, pp. 456–59). "For that is even all one as if she were shaven." For a woman to have her head shaven was looked upon "so shameful a thing that it often was inflicted as a proper punishment on women of the most abandoned character." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 329.

1 Corinthians 11:10. "Because of the angels."] I.e. because of the presence of men that are Christ's representatives, bearing some of his authority and dominion in this lower world, who are the image and glory, and made a little lower than the angels, these thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers in that respect, that they are crowned with glory and honor, and set over the works of God's hands. See 1 Corinthians 11:3–5, 1 Corinthians 11:7; and notes on 1 Corinthians 11:4–5. "For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels." The Apostle probably here means church officers, using such terms as he knew the Corinthian Christians would be likely to understand, the Apostle having probably before taught them that ministers were a kind of angels, angels of the churches. Here is a gradation to be observed in the Apostle's discourse in this place. He speaks of three kinds that are honorable: the woman that is the image and glory of the man; and the man, who is the image and glory of God; and the angels, who are above men, are the image and glory of God, have the image of his knowledge, glory, and authority in a higher sense than men. So it was with ministers of the gospel, before whom women appeared in church assemblies. These had greater knowledge, and light, and greater authority, and represented Christ in a higher manner than the rest of the

<!-- p. 1049 -->

congregation, and therefore might be accounted a rank higher than the other males of the congregation. For this cause especially ought the women to have power on their heads in the congregation, that they were thereJE deleted "not only." in the presence of the men,JE deleted "but of the pastors of the church who were as it." some of which were not only men, but as it were angels.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 Corinthians 11:14. "Doth not even nature itself."] See no. 49.*Works, 15*, 64. "Judge in yourselves," the Apostle says in the foregoing verse. "Is it comely that a woman pray to God uncovered?" Is it not shocking to your nature? And so this is what is meant in the 1 Corinthians 11:14. Is it not shocking to you to see a man with long hair, to see a man appear after so feminine a manner? Is not there that within you, in your nature, that is against it? As now it would be shocking to a man to appear publicly in women's clothing, it would be shocking to the nature of a modest woman to go abroad with her breasts naked. There is that within her in her nature that would teach her, or make her to be ashamed. But yet in some parts of the world the custom is and has been such that it would not be at all shocking to the most modest; their nature would not teach 'em to be ashamed. If any man now should be so impudent as to appear publicly in a woman's garment, it might very well be said, as the Apostle here does, "Judge ye in yourselves. Is this comely?" Is it not even shocking to nature to see a man come thus to the worship of [God]? Don't your nature teach you to be ashamed when you appear so? And yet possibly these same habits in after ages, or in some other nations, may be decent and comely for a man to appear in.

"The Grecian women, excepting the heathen priestesses, when they came into public assemblies, used to appear in their veils, as we find in Homer and many other ancient writers." Doddridge, *in loc*.This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 4*, 331, n. c.

1 Corinthians 11:17. "I praise you not."] These words here, and also in 1 Corinthians 11:22, have reference to what the Apostle had said before, 1 Corinthians 11:2.

1 Corinthians 11:21. "Another is drunken."] Herein they did at this holy festival of Christ as they used to do at the festivals of their idols.

<!-- p. 1050 -->

1 Corinthians 11:22. "And shame them that have not."] I.e. by sending them away empty, for as the Apostle says, "One is hungry, and another is drunken" 1 Corinthians 11:21]. The rich come and eat, or at least drank all which they themselves of their own cost provided, and sent the poor away hungry. For it seems that in the primitive church the Lord's Supper was made use of, partly as a feast of charity, to feed the poor, and satisfy the hungry; and by reason of their having of it so, very often it considerably answered this end. There those that had no houses of their own to eat and drink, or nothing in their houses to eat and drink, might come freely to the house of, and be satisfied at the Lord's Supper; and thereby was better represented Christ's preparing the gospel feast for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind. Hereby was signified well also how that gospel blessings were free for the poorest and meanest, and those that had no money or price, as well as the richest. Or if that was not the sense wherein they were shamed, yet the poor were shamed in that they were denied the spiritual advantage of partaking of the Lord's Supper, for it seems they would not let them partake that could not help bear the charge of the provision. The sacrament being so frequent, the charge was considerable, and also by reason of their eating and drinking so largely, as 1 Corinthians 11:21–22, 1 Corinthians 11:34.

1 Corinthians 11:22–23. "Shall I praise you? I praise you not. For I have received of the Lord that which I also delivered unto you."] The Apostle in these words has reference to what he had said before to the Corinthians, 1 Corinthians 11:2. "Now *I praise* you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, *as I delivered them unto you*."

1 Corinthians 11:27. "Wherefore whosoever," etc.] Inasmuch as by the bread and wine is represented Christ's body and blood, bruised and spilt in death, as the Apostle observed in the foregoing verse, therefore those that so contemned, and negligently and profanely treated these signs, they by fair construction slighted the thing signified, viz. the body of Christ, and the crucifying of it, and implicitly manifested a Consent to his death. If any had stood by when Christ was crucified, and made a light matter of it, and showed their slight by their behavior, and had treated the body of Christ when slain with indignity, it might justly be imputed to 'em as a partaking in his murder. There are two ways of eating the body and drinking the blood of Christ. One is as a prey, to satisfy hatred and blood-thirstiness. Job 31:31, "O that we had of his flesh!" Thus the murderers of Christ eat of his flesh, and drank his blood; and thus unworthy partakers

<!-- p. 1051 -->

of the Lord's Supper do. Secondly, another way of eating and drinking is from love and gracious appetite, so as true disciples and worthy partakers do feed on Christ.

1 Corinthians 11:28. "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup."] "καὶ οὕτως. These words, as to the letter, are rightly translated, 'and so.' But that translation, I imagine, leaves generally a wrong sense of the place in the mind of an English reader. For in ordinary speaking these words, 'Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat,' are understood to import no more than these, 'let a man examine, and then let him eat,' as if they signified no more but that examination should precede, and eating follow, which I take to be quite different from the meaning of the Apostle here, whose sense the whole design of the context shows to be this. 'I here set before you the institution of Christ. By that, let a man examine his carriage, καὶ οὕτως, and according to that, let him eat. Let him conform the manner of his eating to that.'" Thus far Mr. Locke.*Paraphrase and Notes on First Corinthians*, 72, n. c. Οὕτως, *ita*, properly signifies "after that manner," which the word "so," as it stands in the English translation, is not ordinarily understood to signify, but only the succession of time. This direction of the Apostle implies no more than this, that they should with great care and strictness see to it that they conformed their eating the Lord's Supper to the institution which the Apostle had now particularly laid before them, and had done so before, but they for want of care had greatly departed from it, which they were exceeding prone to do by reason of their being new in Christianity, and having before been used to the heathen rites in their sacrifices and solemn festivals, and being now led aside by bad examples and false Judaizing teachers, who perhaps led 'em to imitate the Jewish festivals, particularly that of the Passover, wherein they eat or drank plentifully, and wherein they eat in separate companies, each private family apart by themselves, which it seems they conformed to (1 Corinthians 11:21). For want of thus examining themselves in their eating by the institution, it seems they did not discern the Lord's body, as it follows. They did not take notice of the use and end of the bread and wine they made use of.

1 Corinthians 11:29.] If you eat and drink unworthily, not examining and judging yourselves, you will by eating and drinking but expose yourselves to God's judgment and condemnation. The end of coming to the Lord's Supper,

<!-- p. 1052 -->

and eating his flesh and drinking his blood, is that we may thereby have justification and life. And so all that eat and drink worthily shall, but they that eat and drink unworthily the body and blood of Christ will avail 'em nothing to their justification and salvation, but on the contrary will be to their condemnation.

1 Corinthians 11:31–32.] What the Apostle here says of judging ourselves is with reference to what he said before of examining ourselves (1 Corinthians 11:28); and what he says of being judged seems to be with reference to what he said before of eating and drinking judgment to ourselves 1 Corinthians 11:29]. If we would examine and judge ourselves, we should not be judged; or if we were judged, it would not be to condemnation, but only as being chastened as children, that we might escape condemnation. If we would judge ourselves, i.e. if we would critically try our behavior by the institutions and rules of Christ, taking care strictly to conform ourselves thereto. See note on 1 Corinthians 11:28.

1 Corinthians 12:2. "Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led."] I.e. by invisible agents, by evil spirits, ye were acted by them, and carried away by them. The wordsἤγεσθε and ἀπαγόμενοι. translated "carried away" and "led away," in the original are of the same root. This sense suits with the following verse. Evil spirits don't influence men to acknowledge Christ as Lord, and to adore him; they carry 'em a contrary way.

1 Corinthians 12:3. "Wherefore I give you to understand," etc.] It seems to be a rule for the distinguishing a good spirit, or the Spirit of God in his miraculous gifts, from an evil spirit, the same that is given, 1 John 4:2. "No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." I.e. he can't say so by the influence of any other spirit, but the Holy Spirit.

"No man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed." "This probably refers to the Jews who, while they uttered blasphemies against Christ themselves (1 Timothy 1:13), and extorted them, if possible, from those they apprehended to be his disciples (Acts 26:11), pretended to the gifts of the Spirit, by which they undertook to cast out devils." Doddridge, *in loc*.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 4*, 343, n. b.

<!-- p. 1053 -->

1 Corinthians 12:5. "And there are differences of administrations."] That is, offices. The word in the original is διακονιῶν, ministrings or services. These different offices are reckoned up (1 Corinthians 12:28 ff).

1 Corinthians 12:10. "To another the discerning of spirits."] The Apostle don't speak of discerning the true spirit of God in others from an evil spirit, but of discerning the particular gifts of the Spirit of God that others were endued with, which gifts are called spirits. See note on 1 Corinthians 14:32. God gave to some of them a miraculous gift of discerning what particular gifts others were endowed with, in order to the church's making improvement of them, that it might be known who were qualified and fit to be set apart to such and such offices in the church. Thus Timothy was set apart to the office of a bishop. The spirit that he had was discerned to be such as fitted him eminently for that office (1 Timothy 1:18 and 1 Timothy 4:14).

By the gift of "discerning of spirits" they could not only discern what spirit anyone was endued with, but when others spoke, they could discern whether they spoke by the Spirit, or by inspiration, or no. See 1 Corinthians 14:29.

1 Corinthians 12:13. "By one Spirit we are all baptized into one body… and have been all made to drink into one Spirit."] 'Tis expressed "in terms taken from the sacraments of the Christian church; the sacraments of initiation and confirmation," viz. baptism and the Lord's Supper. In the one, we are baptized with water; in the other, we drink wine. Both are symbols of the Holy Ghost. See Bennet, *Christian Oratory*, vol. 2, pp. 128–29.*Second Part of the Christian Oratory*. These excerpts are from a sermon by Bennet on 1 Corinthians 12:13 entitled "Of the Unity of the Church" (pp. 114–42).

1 Corinthians 12:23.] "As to those parts, which decency and custom teaches us to conceal, we contrive not only to cover, but also as far as we conveniently can, to adorn by covering." These words which are translated, "upon these we bestow more abundant comeliness," τούτοις τιμὴν περισσοτέραν περιτίθεμεν, properly signify "we surround with more abundant honor." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 350, n. c and d.

"And those members of the body." Matthew 20:27 and Matthew 23:11.These references are a separate entry.

1 Corinthians 12:26. "If one member be honored, all the members rejoice with it."] The whole man rejoices in the clothing with which we honor our more

<!-- p. 1054 -->

uncomely parts. The whole is looked upon as interested in the ornaments put upon any one part. See note on 1 Corinthians 12:23 above.

1 Corinthians 12:28. "Governments."] It being so that Christians in those days were so generally endued with extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, it made the case of the church then very different from what it is now. For then,JE deleted "all." those that had those extraordinary gifts became pastors in the exercise of those gifts, and so far as they were thereby qualified. Thus any male member of the church that had the gift of prophecy might do the part of a pastor, so far as the exercise of that gift extended, or in prophesying. So anyone that had the word of wisdom, or knowledge, or a spirit of revelation, or doctrine, or exhortation, or gift of tongues, might do the part of pastors in the exercise of those gifts. All that had those extraordinary gifts thereby became a kind of extraordinary officers in the exercise of those gifts, and so far as that extended, and accordingly used to officiate in the church. This is evident by this, and the Romans 14, and also the Romans 12. So far as any person had a miraculous gift by the immediate and extraordinary influence of the spirit of Christ on their minds, so far were they (as Christ, who is the head and fountain of all church office power, and therefore when they were in the exercise of that gift) to be submitted to by the church, as if Jesus Christ himself spake and acted, for it was not they indeed that spake and acted, but Christ in them. Christ, by giving of them such a miraculous gift, marked out a person for such work in the church.

But it can't be argued from hence that there are so many distinct standing offices in the church as there were extraordinary gifts.

A spirit of government, or an extraordinary and miraculous qualification for the exercise of that part of the pastor's office which consists in judging, reproving, rebuking, admonishing, etc., he that had this gift was authorized to do this part of a pastor's work; and the church submitted to him herein that they discerned had this gift, for they had a discerning of spirits (among other gifts of the Spirit) among them. But this no more argues that government was a distinct standing office than that exhorting was, for some that had a gift of exhorting were in the exercise of that gift to do the part of a pastor, and no otherwise (Romans 12:8). One had an extraordinary gift of the Spirit in doctrine, another in counseling and exhorting, another in reproving, admonishing, and judging of offenders. But these are only so many different parts of a pastor's office,

<!-- p. 1055 -->

and may indeed all be referred to preaching and declaring the word of God. All this is confirmed from Romans 12:6–8. The spirits of Christians,JE deleted "in those days." which they had in an extraordinary manner dwelling in them, sometimes directed in judging offenders. Thus the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 5:4, directs the Corinthians to excommunicate the incestuous person in the name of his spirit.

1 Corinthians 12:31. "But covet earnestly the best gifts."] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus. "Ye contend earnestly about the best gifts," and says, "I doubt not but this is the just rendering of ζηλοῦτε τὰ χαρίσματα τὰ κρείττονα. For it seems contradictory to suppose, that after the Apostle had been showing them that these gifts were not at their own option, and that they ought not to emulate the gifts of each other, nor aspire to superiority, he should in effect unsay all again, and give them contrary advice."*Family Expositor, 4*, 352, n. h. JE marked this entry with a vertical line near the left margin.

1 Corinthians 13:8.] See sermon on this verse, throughout the doctrinal part and First Inference.JE's sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 (no. 897), preached May 1748, with the doctrine, "The extraordinary influences of the Spirit of God imparting immediate revelations to men were designed only for a temporary continuance while the church was in its minority, and never were intended to be steadily upheld in the Christian church. "JE identifies prophesying, knowledge, and tongues as extraordinary gifts of the Spirit that are the product of immediate revelation, by contrast with the graces of the Spirit—faith, hope, and charity. The former gifts are no longer needed because the means of grace are available. "It is not to be expected that any of those gifts that imply divine revelation should be bestowed in these days because the canon of the Scripture has long since been complete." See *Works of Jonathan Edwards*, 25, *Sermons and Discourses*, 1743–1758, ed. Wilson H. Kimnach (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 2006), 275–311. See also no. 305, notes on this and three following verses.*Works, 15*, 277–79.

1 Corinthians 13:12. "For now we see through a glass darkly."] The word in the original signifies a looking glass, and what we translate "darkly" would have been literally translated, "in an enigma or dark saying." Such are those sayings by which God reveals himself to us in this world, and tells us what manner of being he is. That he might speak to us in our manner, he represents him [self] by such words as we use about other things, which indeed are applicable to God only figuratively, or dark shadows and distant resemblances, as 'tis in the words of an enigma or riddle. See "Miscellanies," no. 710.Ibid., 18, 335–39.

"The exact rendering of δι᾽ ἐσόπτρου is 'by means of a mirror.' And

<!-- p. 1056 -->

the Seventy use this word for the women's looking glasses, or mirrors of metal (Exodus 38:8)." Doddridge, *in loc*.This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 4*, 359, n. i.

1 Corinthians 13:13. "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; and the greatest of these is charity."] "Charity is the very grace and ornament of heaven, the employment and the pleasure of blessed spirits. Nor can faith and hope ever be parted from true religion. For there is no being so great as not to depend on faith in God, and trust in his power and wisdom, or to be above hoping anything from his goodness and benevolence. And therefore the Apostle says expressly of faith and hope, that they shall remain, with charity, the greatest of the three. Other gifts are bestowed for the service of the church, such as tongues, miracles, and the like; and they may well cease, when the occasion which required them ceases. But faith, hope, and charity are not occasional gifts, but are essential to religion, and must continue as long as religion itself." Dr. Sherlock's *Several Discourses Preached at Temple Church*, p. 268.Thomas Sherlock, *Several Discourses Preached at the Temple Church* (4 vols. London, 1756–61), I, 268. This selection is drawn from Discourse XIV, Pt. I, which concerns the topic of faith. Vol. I does not have a volume number on it.

"Hope." Note on Hebrews 6:19, no. 284; no. 304.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 240–42, 276–77. No. 304 is a later addition.

1 Corinthians 14:13. "Wherefore let him that speaketh in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret."] He that had the gift of tongues understood what he himself spake, as is evident by several passages in the chapter. But a person might have the understanding of an unknown tongue, and yet not be well able to interpret, i.e. he might not be able to render what he spake into another tongue readily so as fully to express the same sense, and maintain the purity of the idiom of the tongue into which what he says is rendered. See *Miscell. Sacra*, vol. 1, pp. 55–56.Herman Witsius, *Miscellaneorum Sacrorum, I*. Bk. I, entitled "*Prophetis et Prophetia*," the section from which JE draws these comments, discusses various modes of revelation, including ecstasy, visions, soothsaying, divination, and communication through angels.

1 Corinthians 14:14. "My understanding is unfruitful."] I.e. though I understand myself (See 1 Corinthians 14:4.), yet my meaning is unprofitable to others.

1 Corinthians 14:15. "With the understanding also."] I.e. in an intelligible manner so as to communicate my understanding. See verse preceding and following, and 1 Corinthians 14:19.

<!-- p. 1057 -->

1 Corinthians 14:20. "Brethren, be not children in understanding."] He that speaks in an unknown tongue, and don't interpret, don't speak with the understanding, talks like a child that repeats words after others, and don't understand what he says. This is to enforce the advice that the Apostle had given before, that he that speaks in an unknown tongue should pray that he might interpret, and that they might speak with the spirit and with the understanding also, that they might speak words that the Holy Ghost dictates, as children do after their parents, and know not what they say.

The Apostle adds this, "Howbeit in malice be ye children," because it seems they must be as little children, as Christ taught; but the Apostle would let 'em know that this should not be in understanding, but in malice.

1 Corinthians 14:24. "He is convinced of all; he is judged of all."] I.e. of, or by, all of you by your prophesying.

1 Corinthians 14:24–25.] There are many instances of this inward conviction of the conscience that happen by the preaching of the word of God faithfully and skillfully when it is done without inspiration. But when the preacher is inspired, and speaks by a spirit of prophecy, which directly reveals the most secret things and often the secrets of men's hearts, the preacher may be under infinitely greater advantage thoroughly and effectually to convince the hearer, as Christ often convinced his hearers by telling them the secret things they were conscious of in their hearts, as the woman of SamariaJE deleted "and others." [John 4] in particular.

1 Corinthians 14:32. "And the spirits of the prophets."] 'Tis diverse spirits considered as in them, i.e. as it becomes a principle in them. It is diverse principles in diverse persons. One has a spirit of prophecy; another has a spirit of knowledge, another a spirit of faith, another spirit of working miracles, etc. Thus these different principles are called spirits in the 1 Corinthians 14:12, but considered in himself, he is but one Spirit, as the Apostle teaches, 1 Corinthians 12:8–11. The Apostle, in the 1 Corinthians 12:14, calls the Spirit of God in him his spirit. So again the Apostle directs them to cast out the incestuous person in the name of his spirit, because the Spirit of God miraculously dwelling in him directed to it (1 Corinthians 5:4).

1 Corinthians 15:4. "Rose again the third day according to the scriptures."] Particularly according to that scripture, Psalms 16:10, "which intimates that he should

<!-- p. 1058 -->

not see corruption in the grave," because commonly "bodies begin to corrupt on the fourth day, agreeable to John 11:39." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 4*, 379.

1 Corinthians 15:11. "Therefore whether it were I or they," etc.] There was no such thing as any difference among the Apostles in the doctrines that they preached, or as one's finding fault with what another taught; but all acknowledged each other's doctrine. It appears by this and several other places, as 2 Peter 3:15–16; Jude 3 and Jude 17; Galatians 1:17–19, Galatians 1:22–24; Galatians 2:7–9; Galatians 2:9 of this context; Romans 16:7; 1 Corinthians 4:9, and 1 Corinthians 9:5, and 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 2:20; 2 Peter 3:2; Revelation 18:20; Revelation 21:14. And it appears by the history of Paul's life in the Acts, that he owned the doctrine of the other apostles, and that his was agreeable to theirs, so that there was no difference between him and them, or amongst Christians that had been converted and taught by them about doctrines that were taught and received. Paul at his first conversion was sent to Ananias, a disciple of the other apostles, of him to be baptized and have his eyes opened. And Paul relates of himself, Galatians 1:23, that then he preached "the faith that once he destroyed," and that was the doctrine of the other apostles. And after he was converted, he assayed to join himself to the disciples at Jerusalem, and that he was with the apostles, coming in and going out at Jerusalem. The disciples at Antioch, where the church was first established by the other apostles, send Paul and Barnabas, who carried their charity to the church at Jerusalem, which was founded and taught by other apostles. Those who had not their Christianity of Paul were chosen by him to be his companions in his labors, to assist him in preaching the gospel, as Barnabas, and Mark, and Silas, etc.

Paul and Silas were separated and sent forth from Antioch by disciples of other apostles, and [Paul] is sent by them again to Jerusalem about circumcision. He goes to the other apostles for their determination, acknowledging their authority to teach and determine as the apostles of Christ, and then carries their determination. Thus he is acknowledged by the churches of Antioch and Jerusalem that were founded by other apostles, and by the other apostles themselves, for they send him with their determination, with a commendation (Acts 15:26). And other like instances might be mentioned. The apostle Paul acknowledges the church of Jerusalem to be the mother of other churches, and that they were indebted to them as having received their faith from them (Romans 15:25–27). Again Luke, who was the companion of Paul, his writing so

<!-- p. 1059 -->

much in honor of the other apostles in his gospel and history of the Acts of the Apostles, is an argument that Paul gave 'em all that honor that he did. The Apostle, in the 1 Corinthians 15:9 of the context, owns the church that was built only on the foundation of the other apostles to be the church of God. Jesus Christ, when he first appeared to Paul, called the church that Paul persecuted himself, saying, "Why persecutest thou me?", and "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest" [Acts 9:4–5]. Also see Acts 22:19–20.

Now if the apostles had not the doctrine they taught by revelation, it was a strange thing there should be no difference among them, for they taught a multitude of strange and wonderful things that were never before in any such manner so plainly, particularly, and expressly taught by anyone whatsoever. If all was of their own invention, it was strange they did not differ in their schemes.

1 Corinthians 15:17. "And if Christ is not risen, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins."] Because his not being risen: 1. Would be an argument of his insufficiency as a Savior. If he were unable to deliver himself from death, it would have been an argument that he was not able to deliver us. If he was a physician that could not heal himself, there would be cause to apprehend that he was not sufficient [for those] whose diseases were so much worse. And then this was the appointed way of his restoring us, viz. by his restoring himself. We were to be saved no otherwise than in him and with him as members of him, and so to be justified in his justification, which was his resurrection, to be delivered in his deliverance, to have victory in his victory, to triumph with him, to be raised up together with him, and made to sit together in heavenly places in him. And then if God the Father had not thus opened his prison doors, it would have been an evidence that he was not satisfied. And besides, if he had not risen, he would not have been alive to intercede for us, and fulfill the work of salvation he had laid a foundation for in his suffering in his kingly office. So were things constituted in the affair of our redemption, that these things were to be done by Christ as God-man and the head of the human nature. And, 2. If Christ were not risen, it would be an evidence that he was an impostor, for the grand evidence of his mission and appointment as our Savior was his resurrection, which Christ foretold as such, and the determination of that grand point was put on that issue.

1 Corinthians 15:19. "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable."] "It is quite foreign to the purpose, to argue from this text,

<!-- p. 1060 -->

as some have done, that 'if there were no future state, virtue would make men more miserable than they would otherwise be.' It is evident St. Paul speaks, not here of the case of good men in general, if their hopes of future happiness should after all be disappointed, but of the case of the apostles and other preachers of Christianity, if amidst all their hardships and persecutions, they were not supported by their hope. Destitute of this amidst the extremest sufferings, they must have been perpetually subjected to the upbraidings of their own minds, for sacrificing every view of happiness in this world or another, to advance what they knew to be a pernicious falsehood. Perhaps there never were men on earth so criminal and so wretched as they must on this supposition have been." Doddridge, *in loc*.Ibid., 385, n. c.

1 Corinthians 15:20. "But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the first fruits of them that slept."] "Where he refers to the law concerning the first fruits. When the harvest was ripe, they were to bring a sheaf of the first fruits for a wave offering, with a burnt offering at the same time (Leviticus 23:9–11). Nor might they eat bread, parched corn, or green ears, till they had made their offering of first fruits. But having done this as the law required, the whole mass and substance of the harvest was hallowed, this offering of the first fruits being instead of all the rest, to which he alludes, Romans 11:16. 'If the first fruits be holy, the lump is holy.' Now with reference hereto, the Apostle calls the resurrection of Christ the 'first fruits'; it having as it were hallowed the dead bodies of the saints, and consecrated them to a new life. He rose not only as first in order, but his resurrection was a representation and figure of ours; showed not only that it might be, but that it should be; he rose as our head; when the natural body was raised, the mystical was raised also. 'By his resurrection he dissolved the tyranny of death,' saith one of the Fathers, 'and raised the whole world or church.' Which is no more than what the Apostle intimates in these words, 'He hath raised us up together with Christ' (Ephesians 2:6). He rose for us, went into heaven for us, as our 'forerunner' (Hebrews 6:20)." Bennet's *Christian Oratory*, p. 165.Benjamin Bennet, *The Christian Oratory: Or, The Devotion of the Closet Display'd* (2nd ed. London, 1728), pp. 165–66. See Isaiah 26:19.

1 Corinthians 15:21–23. "Since by man came death," etc.… "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."] I.e. all that are in Christ. The

<!-- p. 1061 -->

words impart no more, for the Apostle speaks of no more being made alive in Christ than are in him. The Apostle in these words has respect only to the resurrection of the saints, as is evident by the words that follow in the next verse. "But every man in his own order: Christ the first fruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming." Indeed, this resurrection only can well be called a "being made alive," for this only is in Scripture called a "resurrection to life." John 5:29, "And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life, and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation." Daniel 12:2, "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt." This "resurrection to life" is alone meant by the word "resurrection" elsewhere, as Luke 20:35. "But they which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection of the dead." And Philippians 3:11, "If by any means I might attain to the resurrection of the dead." And 'tis this "resurrection to life" the Apostle evidently has a special respect to, in the foregoing verses, and indeed throughout this whole chapter, as appears by 1 Corinthians 15:14, 1 Corinthians 15:17–20, 1 Corinthians 15:23, 1 Corinthians 15:29–32, 1 Corinthians 15:35, and all the following part of the chapter, especially the 1 Corinthians 15:45, taken with the foregoing and following, and compared with these words we are now treating of. Therefore those that would argue from hence that Christ, as the Second Adam or as men's surety, procures the resurrection of the wicked as well as of the just, argue without foundation.

1 Corinthians 15:24.] See "Miscellanies," nos. 86 and 609.*Works, 13*, 250–51; *2*, 143–45. See Mastricht, p. 1096b;This sentence is a later addition. Mastricht writes, "*Sextus* hujus dispensationis passus, qui erit in traditione regni, de qua textus loquitur Revelation 11:15. dicens *regna mundi* futura, *Domini & Christi ejus, & Dominus Deus omnipotens*, ut *Rex regnaturus* vs. 17. quod etiam distinctius repraesentat Apostolus 1 Corinthians 15:24–29" (*Theoretica-Practica Theologia* [Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715], p. 1096, col. 2). and note on v. 28. See "Miscellanies," no. 736;*Works, 18*, 360–63. Pfaffius, p. 439.This sentence is a later addition. Christoph Matthew Pfaff's comments on this text are cited in *Works, 18*, 363, n. 4. His observations on Christ's continuing heavenly reign include this closing note: "*Regnum denique gloriam, quod Christo competit, sequentibus effatis biblicis indigitatur*" (*Institutiones theologiae dogmaticae et moralis*).

1 Corinthians 15:25–26. "For he must reign till he hath," etc.] These two verses confirm me in it, that those great enemies of Christ—Antichrist, and Mahometanism, and heathenism—shall be overcome and subdued under

<!-- p. 1062 -->

Christ's feet, and the whole world be brought into a visible subjection to Christ before the resurrection and last day. That is intimated here and in the Psalms 110:1, that is here referred to, that that shall be the design that shall be carried on all the while that Christ sits at God's right hand, all the while that he reigns, that is, in his mediatorial kingdom, viz. the subduing all Christ's "enemies under his feet." And as soon as this is done, he shall resign up the kingdom to the Father, as having done his work. We shall therefore doubtless see this work gloriously carried on before that time comes and the last stroke is given.

1 Corinthians 15:28.] See no. 158.*Works, 15*, 95–96.

1 Corinthians 15:29.] See no. 20.Ibid., 53–54. The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. "Baptized for the dead." 'Tis no objection against supposing that by "the dead" here the Apostle has respect to Christ, who those that he wrote against supposed to be a dead man, that the word is in the plural number, as is evident, Matthew 2:20, "they are dead"; by Matthew 9:8, "and glorified God, which had given such power unto men"; and also John 4:38, "other men labored, and ye are entered into their labors," where by "other men" Christ means himself, as seems plain by the context. John 3:12, "Earthly things," when only one thing is intended. ὑπέρ is used in such a sense as here, in John 11:4, Romans 1:5, Philippians 1:29, Acts 5:41, 2 Thessalonians 1:5.

The Apostle uses the third person plural, "What shall *they* do that are baptized for the dead?" and "Why are *they* then baptized for the dead?" because he has a special respect to those heretics themselves that infested the church of Corinth, and taught that there was no resurrection of the dead. They themselves had baptized for Christ. And if Christ be yet dead, what will they do? And if this be what they believe, that Christ is still dead, why would they go to be baptized for the dead? How inconsistently did they act with themselves in it! For if this be the case, their baptism did 'em no good. Their faith is vain, and they are yet unwashed from their sins. Matthew 21:7, the plural number is twice used for the singular. See the original,ἤγαγον τὴν ὄνον καὶ τὸν πῶλον, καὶ ἐπέθηκαν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῶν καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια, καὶ ἐπεκάθισεν ἐπάνω αὐτῶν. and compare it with the other Evangelists.The last two sentences are a later addition.

There are instances also in the Old Testament of the plural number being put for the singular: dried up mighty rivers, whereas it was but one

<!-- p. 1063 -->

river, viz. Jordan. So Habakkuk 3:8. "Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? Was thine anger against the rivers?" And another instance in the New not mentioned before, Matthew 26:8. "But when the disciples saw it, they had indignation, saying, To what purpose is this waste?", when but one disciple is meant, viz. Judas. (See this text more fully spoken to, in answer to a question proposed to be answered before the Association,I.e. the Hampshire County Association. The Hampshire County Association Minutes (MS, Forbes Library, Northampton, Mass.), contain no identifiable reference to such a question or discussion, nor is the MS to which JE refers extant. in one of my drawers.)I.e. the drawers of JE's scrutore, or writing desk. For a photograph of the desk, see the frontispiece in *Works, 13*. Mark 1:21, "Immediately on the sabbath day"; in the Greek it is τοῖς σάββασιν, in the plural number. So the plural is in like manner put for the singular in Matthew 12:2, and Matthew 28:1; and Acts 13:14. See also Matthew 27:44, Genesis 19:29, Judges 12:7, Psalms 137:1, 1 Samuel 28:13, Genesis 21:7, Exodus 32:31, 1 Samuel 10:12, Genesis 27:29. See 1 Samuel 17:43, "That thou comest to me with staves." 1 Samuel 28:13. 2 Chronicles 24:25, "And for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest," when only one son is meant, viz. Zechariah, whom we read of, 2 Chronicles 24:20–21. (See SSS on 2 Chronicles 24:25, where are quoted several instances from heathen writers.)Poole, *Synopsis Criticorum, I* (London, 1669), Pt. 2, col. 852. Genesis 21:7, "Who would have said that Sarah should have children suck?" Genesis 46:1, "All the souls of his sons and his daughters," when he had but one daughter, viz. Dinah. See also Genesis 46:7. Genesis 36:25, "The children of Anah were Dishon." Genesis 46:23, "And the sons of Dan, Hushim."This and the preceding paragraph are a later addition.

1 Corinthians 15:33. "Evil communications corrupt good manners."] What the Apostle had said in the verses immediately preceding showed how this doctrine of no resurrection tended to "corrupt good manners." Such a principle removes the main enforcement of Christian self-denial, and opens a door for all manner of licentiousness. For if it be so, men will be mere Epicures, and say, Let us enjoy our pleasures, for tomorrow we die.

1 Corinthians 15:34.] Seeing that it is so that these heretical doctrines tended to corrupt the practice, such as were tainted with them needed this advice to awake to righteousness, and forsake their corrupt practices. They denied the resurrection of the body, but they stood in need of the resurrection of the soul to rise or awake to righteousness. "For some men have not the knowledge of God." They were not aware that they needed advice to

<!-- p. 1064 -->
