### Ephesians

Ephesians 1:1. "By the will of God."] No. 268.*Works, 15*, 222–23.

Ephesians 1:5. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ."] Christians have their blessedness in heavenly places, for they are not of the world. That is not their country, not their home. Their inheritance, their house, their treasure, their food, their ornaments, their friends, society, and entertainments are "in heavenly places." Their enjoyments are not in an earthly paradise, for they are not of the first Adam, who was of the earth, earthy. They are taken out of that stock. They are the children of the second Adam, who was a quickening spirit and the Lord from heaven. And therefore, because they belong to Christ or are in Christ, their blessings are spiritual and "in heavenly places," and not earthly, in Eden, or any other earthly country.

Not in the earthly Canaan, the ancient land of promise. When God promised blessings of old to his people, frequently these words were added to the promise: "In the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee." But now the gospel promises are not blessings in an earthly Canaan, but in heavenly places. See Dr. Owen's *Works*, vol. 1, p. 40.This paragraph is a separate entry. John Owen, in his treatise entitled ΧΡΙΣΤΟΛΟΓΙΑ: *or, A Declaration of the Glorious Mystery of the Person of Christ with the Infinite Wisdom, Love and Power of God in the Contrivance and Constitution thereof*, asserts that "all divine truth relating to the saving knowledge of God is treasured up in him [i.e. Christ]." That wisdom "concerning the vocation, sanctification and salvation of the church" is called "treasures" because it is "precious and unvaluable… preferred above all earthly treasures" and because it is "unsearchable" (*Works of John Owen*).

Ephesians 1:4. "Chosen us in him."] See "Miscellanies," no. 769, at the end of that number, and no. 1245.*Works, 18*, 414–18; 25, 177–81. Both of these entries focus on the concept of election.

"That we should be holy and without blame before him in love."] Love is the fulfilling of the law, the principle of a Christian's obedience, the sum of Christian holiness. Christians avoid sin; and so being without

<!-- p. 1093 -->

blame is from love, the spirit of adoption, and not from a slavish fear, God "having predestinated us unto the adoption of children," as it follows in the next verse.

Ephesians 1:9–10.] See "Miscellanies," no. 702, §12.*Works, 18*, 296–98. See "Miscellanies," no. 781.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 18*, 450–52. JE deleted "and 833."

Ephesians 1:12–13. "Who first trusted in Christ.] I.e. the Jewish Christians. "In whom ye also trusted." I.e. the Gentile Christians. See Romans 1:16 and Acts 3:26.

Ephesians 1:14. "Until the redemption of the purchased possession."] 'Tis evidently an allusion to the law in Israel, in the twenty-fifth of Leviticus, that when a man was waxen poor, and was forced to sell his possession, there should be a redemption of it granted. One of his kinsmen might redeem it for him, and he might return to it again.

Ephesians 1:15. "Wherefore I also."] In the foregoing verses the Apostle had observed to the Ephesians that they were predestinated to the praise of God's glory, and sealed with the spirit of promise to the praise of his glory, or that they might praise his glory, or the fruit of which was their praising his glory. "Wherefore I also," says the Apostle, praise upon your account. This seems to be the connection.

Ephesians 1:17. "The Father of glory."] God may be so called, as he is the Father of Christ. And so this be the same with what goes immediately before, only diversely expressed, for Christ is the brightness of his Father's glory [Hebrews 1:3]. See Revelation 21:23.

Ephesians 1:18. "Of his inheritance in the saints."] Respect seems to be had here to what was said in the Ephesians 1:14, and this "inheritance" here spoken of seems to be the same with the "possession" there spoken of.

'Tis "his inheritance in the saints."This sentence and the following four are a later addition. 'Tis his inheritance in being the saints' inheritance, for the saints and he are one. 'Tis the inheritance they possess by partaking with him. 'Tis "his inheritance in the saints," as 'tis that inheritance which he in those his members possesses; they enjoy it in him, and he in them. They are raised up with him, and set with

<!-- p. 1094 -->

him "in heavenly places" Ephesians 1:20], as it follows in the next words and Ephesians 2:5–6. 'Tis called the inheritance of Christ in his saints, as the sufferings of the saints are called the sufferings of Christ in the saints (Colossians 1:24).This sentence and the following two are a later addition. As here the Apostle speaks of the glory of Christ's inheritance in his saints, so in 2 Thessalonians 1:10 he says that at the day of judgment Christ "will come to be glorified in his saints." See note *in loc*. The saints' future reward is called Christ's glory (2 Thessalonians 2:14).This sentence is a later addition.

"The glory of his inheritance in the saints." On further consideration, it appears to me the true sense is, "his inheritance in heaven." In the Greek it is, ἐν τοῖς ἀγίοις, which might have been literally translated, "in the holy places," which, if we suppose the Apostle means heaven by it, would have been very agreeable to the way ofMS: "of the." speaking the Apostle uses in the next verse but one, when he means "in heaven." He expresses it thus, ἐν ἐπουρανίοις So in Ephesians 2:3. So in Ephesians 2:6 and Ephesians 3:10. In Hebrews 1:3, he expresses it thus, ἐν ὑψηλο/ς, "in the high." The same is expressed in Luke 2:14, ἐν ὑψίστοις, "in the highest." If it may thus be called the "heavenly," the "high," and the "highest," it may as properly be called the "holy." The land of Canaan was called the "holy land," and the city of Jerusalem is called the "holy city," Mt. Zion the "holy mountain," as also the mount on which Christ was transfigured (2 Peter 1:18), and the temple the "holy place," often in the Old Testament and New. But heaven and the New Jerusalem is most eminently the holy land, the holy city, and the holy mountain, God's holy temple, and the holy place. See Revelation 21:2, Revelation 21:10; and Revelation 22:19. ἐν τοῖς ἀγίοις is a phrase used by the Seventy for "in the holy place," as Psalms 68:35; Exodus 29:30. So τὰ ἅγια and τῶν ἀγίων, etc., are used, Exodus 28:35; 1 Kings 8:8, 1 Kings 8:10; 1 Chronicles 6:49, and 1 Chronicles 23:32; 2 Chronicles 5:11, and 2 Chronicles 29:5. So τὰ ἅγια is abundantly used by them for the sanctuary. Leviticus 19:30, and Leviticus 20:3, and Leviticus 21:12; Numbers 10:21; 2 Chronicles 29:21; Jeremiah 51:51; Ezekiel 5:11, and Ezekiel 8:6, and Ezekiel 9:6, and Ezekiel 23:38–39, and Ezekiel 24:21, and Ezekiel 25:3, and Ezekiel 37:26, Ezekiel 37:28, and Ezekiel 43:21, and Ezekiel 44:1, Ezekiel 44:5, Ezekiel 44:7, Ezekiel 44:9, Ezekiel 44:11, Ezekiel 44:15–16, and Ezekiel 45:4, Ezekiel 45:18, and Ezekiel 47:12, and Ezekiel 48:10; Leviticus 10:4; Numbers 3:28, Numbers 3:32, and Numbers 4:12, Numbers 4:15, and Numbers 8:19, and Numbers 18:5; 1 Chronicles 24:5. So the Apostle, Hebrews 9:2, Hebrews 13:11, and Hebrews 8:2. And the Apostle in the same chapterI.e. Hebrews 9. uses it for the most holy place, Hebrews 9:8 and Hebrews 9:25, and Hebrews 10:19. And in the same chapter,I.e. Hebrews 9. Hebrews 9:12, [and] Hebrews 10:19, the Apostle calls heaven by the name of τὰ ἅγια. So again, Hebrews 9:8 and

<!-- p. 1095 -->

Hebrews 9:11. ἐν ἀγίοις is put for God's "holy hill" in Psalms 15:1, by which we must understand heaven; and the phrase is used for "in heaven," in Isaiah 57:15, by the Seventy, "I dwell in the high and holy place."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ephesians 1:19–22.] See "Scripture," no. 502.*Works, 15*, 599–601.

Ephesians 1:19–23.] It seems manifest by these verses that the saints shall partake with Christ, not only in his resurrection and ascension into heaven, but also in his exaltation there, "far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion," and in having "all things put under his feet" [Ephesians 1:21–22]. And the reason of it is couchedConjecture for illegible word. JE deleted "given." in the Ephesians 1:23, viz. that the church is his body.

Ephesians 1:21–22. "Far above all principality, and power," etc., "and every name that is named, not only in this world, but that which is to come."] By "the world to come" here and in Hebrews 2:5, the Apostle seems chiefly to intend that world that is spoken of in the Old Testament as a new world that should succeed this, new heavens and a new earth. Indeed, the heavenly world that now is may be called "the [world to] come," because it is in the glorified state of redeemed souls there, and in that happiness that saints and angels are there brought into by Jesus Christ, God-man, the beginning of the new heavens and new earth. The saints and angels in heaven now enjoy an anticipation of the glory of that world to come. And so the New Jerusalem, or Jerusalem which is above, now is in heaven, though the principal time for its setting up be future.

*Corol*. By this it is evident that Christ's dominion over the world as God-man will not be at an end when this world shall come to an end, and he shall have delivered up the kingdom to the Father; and also by Hebrews 2:5.

Ephesians 1:23. "The fullness of him that filleth all in all."] Nos. 235 and 481.*Works, 15*, 185–87, 578. The second reference is a later addition.

"Which is his body, the fullness of him that filleth all in all." These latter words, "that filleth all in all," are here naturally brought in, because it is by Christ's descending first to earth and to death, and then ascending into heaven, "far above all principalities and powers" (spoken of or implied in the context), agreeable to Ephesians 4:10. And what is very wonderful indeed is here observed, viz. that of him that thus filleth all things,

<!-- p. 1096 -->

or is the fullness, the glory, and happiness of all things, the church is the fullness or the glory and joy, as the woman is said to be the glory of the man.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ephesians 2:1.] This verse is exegetical of the Ephesians 1:19–20, or to show the exceeding greatness of the power that wrought in Christ, when he was raised from the dead, wrought in them.The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. This verse is to be connected with the Ephesians 2:5. What comes between is a parenthesis. "This," says Dr. Doddridge, "is one instance among others, of Paul's beginning a sentence, and then throwing in a very long parenthesis, and taking up again the words with which he began. Compare Ephesians 3:1, Ephesians 3:14; Ephesians 4:2; 1 Timothy 1:3, 1 Timothy 1:18."*Family Expositor, 5*, 134, n. a.

Ephesians 2:6. "And made us to sit together in heavenly places."] I.e. either 1. In places of heavenly honor and dignity, places above any place of earthly honor and trust. Believers sit in the place of priests unto God, and in the place of kings. They are in places of heavenly dominion and divine dignity. But it is in Christ, by virtue of their union with him, they are partakers of his honors and dominion. The devils are called in the Ephesians 6:12, "spiritual wickedness in heavenly places," ἐν ἐπουρἀίοις, the same word as here, because the devil had usurped God's throne, and reigned as God, and had divine honors paid him. Or 2. Christ hath "made us sit together in heavenly places," as he hath virtually made us sit together in mansions of glory above with Christ. When persons are converted, they have a right and title given them to heavenly glory. They have then God's faithful promise that they shall then sit with Christ in heavenly places. So that we, in our conversion, have communion with Christ in both his resurrection and ascension. When a person is converted, he has communion with him in his resurrection; he is "quickened together with Christ," as Ephesians 2:5. And he has also therein communion with Christ in his ascension; they do then as it were ascend to heaven with Christ.

"And has made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus." The meaning is not, "hath made us sit together with one another," but "together with Christ," as 'tis said in the foregoing verse, "He hath quickened us *together with Christ*." So the Apostle goes on in this verse, "He hath

<!-- p. 1097 -->

raised us up together with him, and hath made us sit *together with him* in heavenly places." This is more plain by looking at those two verses as in the original: συνεζωοποίησεν τῷ Χριστῷ… καὶ συνήγειρεν καὶ συνεκάθισεν ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις ἐν Χριστῷ ῎Ιησοῦ. 'Tis here evident that the ούν with which each verse is componedConjecture for illegible word at edge of column. has respect to the same thing, and that each one denotes the communion the saints have with Christ in being quickened, and also raised up, and set in heavenly places. The import of the original would perhaps have been more naturally suggested to us if the translation had been thus: He hath jointly quickened [us] with Christ, and jointly raised us up, and jointly set us in heavenly places in Christ. And whereas in the last clause there is added, "in Christ Jesus," 'tis to denote that the saints ascend into heaven, and reign in glory there "with him" and "in him," which more fully expresses the manner in which the saints have communion with Christ in his ascension to heaven, and that dignity and glory that he possesses there, as sitting with him in his throne.This paragraph is a later separate entry.

Ephesians 2:7 "The ages to come."] Nos. 300 and 504.*Works, 15*, 272–73, 605–8. The second reference is a later addition.

Ephesians 2:12. "That at that time ye were without Christ," etc.] The first of these things here mentioned are the foundation of all the rest that follow. A being "without Christ" is the foundation of "being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel," etc. And the last thing here mentioned is the sum of all the rest. A being "without God in the world" is the sum of all evil. A being "without Christ," and "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise," and without hope, are all summed up in being "without God in the world."

"Without God in the world." ἄθεοι ἐν κόσμῳ, "atheists in the world." "Both the Christians and the heathens, as Dr. WhitbyDaniel Whitby, author of *A Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament* (2 vols. London, 1703). well observes here, called each other 'atheists,' though both worshipped some deity real or imaginary, because each supposed the other to reject that which was the true object of adoration." Doddridge, *in loc*.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 5*, 144, n. d.

Ephesians 2:13. "Ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ."] "There seems to be an evident allusion here to the privilege of

<!-- p. 1098 -->

those Israelites, who were not under any ceremonial pollution, or who were cleansed from their guilt by the blood of atonement, and so had free liberty of entering the temple, and conversing with God, upon which account they are called 'a people near unto him' (Psalms 148:14). Compare Exodus 19:4, Exodus 19:6; Leviticus 10:3; and Psalms 65:4." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, 145, n. e.

Ephesians 2:14. "Middle wall."] Alluding to the wall in the temple that separated the court of the Gentiles from the court of the Jews, on the pillars of which was "this inscription, 'Let no alien enter into the holy place.'" Wells' *Sacred Geography*, vol. 4, p. 55.*Historical Geography of the New Testament* (2nd ed.). "Vol. 4" appears on the spine of the binding.

Ephesians 2:15.] Christ abolished in his flesh the law of commandments by destroying or abolishing his flesh in his crucifixion (Colossians 1:22), and that three ways. 1. Those ordinances were as it were the flesh of Christ mystical. They are called carnal ordinances. The carnality of the church consisted in them. They were ordinances fitted for Christ mystical in the flesh, or for the church in its carnal state. So Christ himself, while in the flesh, was subject to those ordinances; but when he died, and his flesh was abolished, he ceased to be subject to those carnal ordinances, for he ceased to be in a carnal state, but rose to a spiritual state. And it was fit that the church should have communion with her head in this, that Christ mystical should be as Christ personal, that that also should cease any longer to be in a carnal state, but should rise with Christ to a spiritual state, where there is no such use of carnal ordinances. It was not fit that Christ's mystical body should remain in a carnal state after Christ's flesh was abolished, and he was risen from the dead to a spiritual state. It was fit that whole Christ should be in a spiritual state after that, both head and members, both his real and mystical body.

2. The church did as it were die in Christ. He that was the head of the church, and represented the church before God, died; and therefore the law since that has no more dominion over the church, for the law has dominion over the church no longer than while he liveth. Christ, while he lived, was under the law; but when he died, he was free from the law. When he rose again, he was no longer subject to the ceremonial law, for he rose to a spiritual life, and to live in another world. The ceremonial law is made only for the inhabitants of this world. So neither was the

<!-- p. 1099 -->

church that died and rose in him. Thus Christ abolished the law of commandments in his flesh through death. See Romans 7, at the beginning. See also Colossians 2:20.

3. Christ by his death abolished guilt, and held forth to theJE deleted "church." world aJE deleted "full and perfect." proper and complete atonement and full satisfaction for sin, which made that old legal dispensation no longer proper or meet to be kept up in the church; but a dispensation of greater liberty was suitable to succeed this. The legal way in which God treated his church had its ground very much in the concealment of the proper atonement for sin, or its being but very obscurely revealed. Therefore they were kept under a yoke of bondage. The church, while a minor, differed nothing from a servant, but was under tutors and governors; and they received a spirit of bondage unto fear [Romans 8:15]. Their sacrifices and legal purifications were to renew and keep up a sense of guilt; and therefore all fell, of course, when once Christ crucified, the great sacrifice and perfect atonement of guilt, was revealed. The end of the ceremonial law was to cause that all might stand self-condemned, and be shut up to the grace that should afterwards be revealed. Thus Christ blotted out "the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, that was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross" (Colossians 2:14).

Ephesians 2:19. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God."] "I know not how far there is room to distinguish nicely between the signification of these two words, ξένοι and πάροικοι, 'strangers and foreigners.' If there be, the latter signifies something more than the former; and I doubt not, but it alludes to the case of sojourning strangers among the Jews, who were not incorporated by complete proselytism into the body of the Jewish people, and made, as such proselytes were, συμπολῖται, 'fellow citizens' with equal privileges. And perhaps when οἰκεῖοι τοῦ θεοῦ, 'domestics of God,' is added, it may have some relation to that peculiar nearness to God in which the Jewish priests were, and refer to that great intimacy of unrestrained converse with God, to which we Christians are admitted. In which respect our privileges seem to resemble, not only those of the people praying in the common court of Israel, but of the priests worshipping in the house itself. Nay, it is elsewhere added, by a figure which seems beautifully to rise even on this, that we have confidence

<!-- p. 1100 -->

'to enter into the holiest of all by the blood of Jesus' (Hebrews 10:19)." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, n. k.

Ephesians 2:20. "The apostles and prophets."] That by "prophets" here is not only meant the prophets of the New Testament, but the prophets of the Old Testament, several things confirm. 1. The preceding discourse of the Apostle, concerning the union of the church of the Jews built on the foundation of the prophets of the Old Testament, and the church of the Gentiles built on the foundation of the apostles of Christ, naturally led him to speak of the whole church constituted both of Jews and Gentiles, as one city "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets," united in one foundation. 2. We find prophets in like manner spoken of unitedly, as by their word, the joint rule of Christians. 2 Peter 3:2, "That ye be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandments of us the apostles of the Lord and Savior." 3. The teachers of the Old Testament and New are here united, as the elders of the Old Testament and New are represented as united, constituting the twenty-four elders, viz. the twelve patriarchs of the Old Testament, and twelve apostles of the New, and in the names of the twelve patriarchs written on the gates, and of the twelve apostles on the foundation of the same city. But yet 'tis probable the prophets of the New Testament are also intended, especially Mark and Luke, which is confirmed by Ephesians 3:5 and Ephesians 4:11.

Ephesians 3:9. "Which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God."] I.e. "which from the beginning of the world" God hath designed, and had in view, and aimed at, in all his providences ever since the beginning of the world, though this his aim was not made known till now. "Who created all things by Jesus Christ." This is here mentioned from respect to the reason why God "created all things by Jesus," viz. because the creation of all things was with an aim and subordination to that great work of Christ as mediator, viz. the work of redemption. It was not only God's design in all the works of providence from the beginning of the world, as in the foregoing words, but also in the creation of the world itself. And therefore God "created all things by Jesus Christ." Christ was to be the great means of God's glory, and that by which chiefly he was to be so was the work of redemption, which he was to work out, and to which all other works, and even the creation of the world itself, were subordinate, which

<!-- p. 1101 -->

the following verse confirms. It was meet therefore that, seeing the principal work was to be wrought by Christ, that other works subordinate thereto should be so likewise. And therefore both the beginning of the world and the end of the world are by Christ, for both are subordinate to the great purposes of the work of redemption. He is therefore both the creator and the judge of the world. He is, as he says in the Revelation, the Alpha and the Omega [Revelation 1:8]. See "Miscellanies," no. 833.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 20*, 43–44.

It seems pretty plainly implied, Proverbs 8:27–31, that the world was created with subordination to the designs of Christ's love to the children of men.This sentence is a later addition.

Ephesians 3:10. "The manifold wisdom of God."] Not only in the work of redemption itself, but in his providences and works from the beginning of the [world till] now, God's design in these manifold works of his was made known. Now it appeared what he aimed at in the great and various works which he hath wrought from age to age, which till now "had been hid in God," as in the foregoing verse. But now the wisdom of God appears to the angels in the event of all, in the accomplishment of the great thing aimed at.

See no. 169.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 99.

Ephesians 3:19. "Fullness of God."] Job 11:8–9.

"Be filled with all the fullness of God." That by "fullness" is meant good, moral, and natural, appears by observing the phraseology of the New Testament in other places, and is confirmed by Genesis 1:2, compared with the context. "The earth was without form and void." In the original, it is *Tohu, Bohu*,תֹהוּ and בֹהוּ both which words signify vanity and emptiness. This is to show what the creature was in itself before it received its goodness or fullness from the Spirit of God. Immediately after, we are told how that "the Spirit of God moved," or hovered, or brooded "on the face of the waters," by which things by degrees were brought out of this state of emptiness, and became good. We read of one thing after another that emerged that was good; and at the conclusion of the whole, we are told that all was very good. So that first all was empty and void, to show what the creature was in itself; but after the Spirit of God had brooded on it, and infused of a divine fullness or good into it, then all was very good,

<!-- p. 1102 -->

so that goodness that is afterwards spoken of is set in opposition to that emptiness, spoken of Ephesians 3:2. So that the goodness that the creature receives from God and its fullness are the same thing. (See note on Genesis 1:2.) We find that all evil, both natural and moral, is often in Scripture called "vanity."This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ephesians 4:1. "Walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called."] I.e. let your walk be such as that vocation is worthy, or such as is in some measure answerable to the worthiness of your honorable vocation. 'Tis meant such a walk as their calling deserved, not such an one as deserved such an high and honorable calling. This seems plainly to [be] the import of such an expression here, and also Colossians 1:10, [and] 1 Thessalonians 2:12. And the same is intended as in Philippians 1:27. "Only let your conversation be as becometh the gospel of Christ."

Ephesians 4:9–11. See "Miscellanies," no. 702, §3 and §12.*Works, 18*, 289–90, 296–98.

"Descended into the lower parts of the earth."] Nothing more is designed by this than the parts below the surface, to distinguish it from Christ dwelling on the surface of the earth as the living do. Elsewhere the dead are called those that are under the earth, because such commonly are buried in the interior parts of the earth within the surface.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ephesians 4:13.] See no. 50.*Works, 15*, 65.

Ephesians 4:25.] All union in society is founded in truth. Take away truth and all, and you destroy all human converse; and there could be no living, nor trading, nor dwelling together. For if there be no truth, we are unfit to be trusted; and so it overthroweth all commerce in the world. Especially therefore is truth becoming those who not only are united with others in civil society, but in Christian society, in which they are all one body, and "members one of another."

Ephesians 4:30. "Whereby ye are sealed."] "This term of 'sealing' seems to be a metaphor taken from merchants' putting some seal or mark upon their commodities, by which they may be known to be theirs." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, 183, n. q.

<!-- p. 1103 -->

Ephesians 5:5. "An idolater."] Note on Colossians 3:5.

Ephesians 5:6. "Children of disobedience."] Note on 1 Peter 1:14.

Ephesians 5:18. "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be ye filled with the Spirit."] As much as to say, In this there is no excess. It is no matter how full ye are of the Spirit. A being full of wine, or being "drunk with wine," were expressions of the same import in those days. Thus when the apostles were filled with the Spirit at Pentecost, some "mocking said, These men are full of new wine" [Acts 2:13]. There is excess in being full of wine, but no excess in being filled with the Spirit. There is no excess in spiritual enjoyments. We may be drunken with the Spirit, and there is no excess in that, as 'tis said, Canticles 5:1, "Drink, and be drunken, O beloved."

The Apostle here seems to have reference to that in Canticles 5:1. He was afraid that they would misunderstand that as a liberty to Christ's beloved ones to be drunk with wine, but he explains the meaning of it to 'em. *Corol*. Hence we may learn the authority of that book of Canticles.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Ephesians 5:20.] "Giving thanks in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ" imports two things. 1. That we should praise God for our mercies, as being sensible that 'tis by Christ and him only that we receive our mercies. And that the mercy of God towards those that are so unworthy is glorious and worthy of praise, because 'tis bestowed in this way through such a mediator. That which is the principal and most essential thing in praise for mercy is a sense of the gloriousness of the exercises of God's mercy to us. And they that are sensible that the exercises of divine mercy towards them are glorious only as they are in and through Christ, or as they are members of Christ, they praise God in Christ, or in the name of Christ, or as members of Christ. They only that ascribe to God the glory of his mercy as in Christ, do ascribe to God the true glory of his mercy; and therefore they only do acceptably praise God. If we give thanks to God for mercy under the notion of absolute mercy, we shall but dishonor God instead of glorifying him, for that notion of absolute mercy is dishonorable to God. See "Miscellanies," no. 648.*Works, 18*, 188.

2. To give thanks in the name of Christ is to offer our thanks through his hands, as being sensible that these our offerings ben't worthy to be accepted but on his account. See Colossians 3:17.

<!-- p. 1104 -->

Ephesians 5:26.] "I apprehend here is an allusion to the methods taken in Eastern countries, to purify the virgins that were to be presented to the royal embrace (Compare Esther 2:3, Esther 2:9, Esther 2:12; and Ezekiel 16:7–14.)." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, n. b.

Ephesians 5:30–32.] See "Shadows of Divine Things," nos. 5, 9, 12, 56.*Works, 11*, 52–54, 67.

"This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the church." "A mystery is that which hath one thing signifying, and another thing signified, as in Revelation 1:20. 'The mystery of the seven stars and of the seven golden candlesticks.' The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, etc. So when the Apostle here had said of Adam's marriage, and adds, 'I speak concerning Christ and his church.' Which is all one with that John saith in the Revelation, as if the Apostle should have said, The mystery of Adam's marriage is the marriage of Christ and his church; that is, this is that which is intended by it, and which God had in his eye. A parable is called a mystery in Scripture, as in Luke 8:10. Why? Because it holds forth a similitude, and a thing signified thereby. So in Daniel 2:28. Nebuchadnezzar's dream is called a mystery. 'There is a God in heaven,' saith Daniel there, 'which revealeth mysteries.' So it is in the original,רָזִין גָּלֵה בִּשְׁמַיָּא אֳלָהּ אִיתַי because he dreamed one thing, and another thing was intended by it." Dr. Goodwin's *Works*, vol. 1, Pt. 3, pp. 54–55.This paragraph is a separate entry. See no. 232.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 181–82.

Ephesians 5:31. "A man leave his father and mother."] Psalms 45:10.

Ephesians 5:32–33. "This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the church. Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife as himself."] This is a great mystery having respect to Christ. This, I say, belonged!, εἰς Χριστὸν,JE deleted "(So it is in the original)." is to be applied to Christ. "NEVERTHELESS let every one of you in particular," etc., as much as to say, It is not only to be applied to Christ and the church of Christians in general, but is also to be applied to each one of you that is an husband in particular with regard to his own wife.

<!-- p. 1105 -->

Ephesians 6:12. "Spiritual wickedness in high places."] "τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις. 'Spirits who became the authors and abettors of wickedness even while they abode in heavenly places.'… There is somewhat peculiar in the form of the expression in the original. Mr. Locke paraphrases it thus, 'The spiritual managers of the opposition to the kingdom of God.'" Doddridge, *in loc*.This reference is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 5*, 216 and n. c.

"Wickedness in high places." See Isaiah 24:21.

Ephesians 6:15. "Your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace."] I.e. with such a preparation going your journey through the wilderness, or going the Christian warfare, and running the Christian race, as the gospel of peace when effectual is a means of, and such as is agreeable to the genius of the gospel of peace, consisting especially in a peaceable spirit, or a spirit of Christian meekness and calmness of mind, which fits persons eminent for the Christian warfare, and to go through this world so full of enemies and injuries. See note on Canticles 7:1, "Scripture," no. 490.*Works, 15*, 584–85. A meek and quiet spirit is in the sight of God of great price, more beautiful than an outward adorning of gold and costly array. And therefore there Christ says to his spouse, "How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince's daughter!"

Ephesians 6:16. "Above all."] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "Upon all," and says, "This best answers the particle ἐπί here used, and best expresses the allusion to the situation of the shield, as covering the other pieces of armor, which has here a beautiful propriety, as truth, righteousness, and peace are sheltered as it were by faith, from the assaults which otherwise might overbear them."*Family Expositor, 5*, 218, n. f.

### Philippians

Philippians 1:7.] Dr. Doddridge thus translates this verse. "As it is just in me to be thus affected towards you, because you have me in your hearts, both in my bonds, and in my defense and confirmation of the gospel, as you are all partakers with me in the grace,"Ibid., 233–34. which seems agreeable to the original.καθώς ἐστιν δίκαιον ἐμοὶ τοῦτο φρονεῖν ὐπὲρ πάντων ὑμῶν, διὰ τὸ ἔχειν με ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμᾶς, ἔν τε τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀπολογίᾳ καὶ βεβαιώσει τοῦ εὐαγγελίου συγκοινωνούς μου τῆς χάιτος πάντας ὑμᾶς ὄντας.

Philippians 1:23.] Dr. Doddridge translates this verse thus. "For I am borne two different ways, having a desire to be unbound and be with Christ, which is better beyond all expression."*Family Expositor, 5*, 242–43.

"Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ," etc. Who can doubt but that when the departed saints are with Christ, it is in those mansions that Christ has prepared for them in his Father's house, that he speaks of in John 14:2–3? "In my Father's house are many mansions. If it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you to myself; that where I am, there ye may be also." The Apostle here speaks of his going to be where Christ is. And who can doubt but that it must be in the place that Christ speaks of in that place in John, among the mansions in his Father's house, in the place that Christ had prepared for him? For Christ says not a word of his coming to take his disciples to himself to be where he is, but only in those mansions in the place that he should prepare for them. And who can doubt but that those mansions in his Father's house, among which Christ was then going to prepare a place for them, was in heaven, in the place where Christ was then going to his Father?This paragraph is a separate entry.

<!-- p. 1107 -->

Philippians 2:6. "Thought it not robbery," etc.] See Mr. Joseph Edwards' sermon on *Christ, God-Man*, pp. 48 ff.Joseph Edwards' *Christ God-Man. A Sermon Preached before the University of Oxford, At St. Mary's, On Sunday, July 30, MDCCXLIX. With a Preface, Occasioned by a Book lately published entitled Memoirs of the Life and Writings of Mr. Whiston, in relation to the Divinity of our Saviour, and the Controversy concerning it* (London, 1749), was designed to acquaint young readers with the Arian controversy and to refute William Whiston's views on it. JE received this sermon from John Erskine in Scotland along with other pamphlets in late June 1752. See *Works, 16*, 489, n. 1. The closing section is a response to those who would strip Christ "of his Godhead." This passage in Philippians, Joseph Edwards asserts, was employed by Arians "in their abominable War against Heaven, and the Son of God, and God." Yet, he contends, it does not support Arianism, but rather is "as clear, and certain a Demonstration as any other, of our Saviour's being God" and of his having willingly emptied himself of "native Privileges." This he also construes as "a wonderful Example of Condescension and Humility" (pp. 48–56). See also Hervey's *Dialogues*, vol. 3, pp. 66–67.Hervey interprets ἁρπαγμὸν to denote "the *Act* of plundering or taking the Spoil." Therefore "the Text most naturally implies, that *CHRIST* counted it no Act of Robbery; no Invasion of Another's Prerogative; but looked upon it as his unquestionable Right, to be *equal with GOD*, and to receive Divine Honours." Hervey continues, "If this signifies a *real* and *proper* Equality, the proof seems, to me at least, irrefragable" (*Dialogues, 3*, 66–67, note).

"Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God." Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it thus: "*Who, being long* before his appearance in human flesh, *in the form of God*, and having been from eternal ages possessed of divine perfections and glories, when manifesting himself to the patriarchs and prophets of old, *thought it not robbery* and usurpation *to be* and appear *as God*, assuming the highest divine names, titles, and attributes, by which the Supreme Being has made himself known, and receiving from his servants divine honors and adorations." And in his notes he says, "Bishop BurnetGilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury or Sarum, who wrote *An Exposition of the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England* (London, 1699). well observes, that the Socinian interpretation is extremely cold and insipid, as if it were a mighty argument of humility, that though Christ wrought miracles, which they strangely think signified by the phrase of 'being in the form of God,' yet he did not set up himself for supreme deity.… 'To be and appear as God.' So ἴσα θεῷ is most exactly rendered, agreeable to the force of ἴσα in many places in the Septuagint, which Dr. Whitby had collected. The proper Greek phrase for 'equal to God' is ἴσον τῷ θεῷ, which is used in John 5:18. Mr. PierceThomas Pierce (1622–91), one-time Dean of Salisbury and a vigorous controversialist. thus paraphrases the clause before us, 'He was not eager in retaining that likeness to God,' of which he was before possessed. And he observes, that had it referred to what was considered as future, the expression would have been ἔσεθαι, not εἶναι, and

<!-- p. 1108 -->

further pleads that the Apostle's design here is not to caution the Philippians against coveting what they had no claim to, but to engage them, after the example of Christ, to give up their own right for the advantage of others."This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 5*, 249–50, and nn. b and c.

Philippians 2:7.] He emptied himself. See notes on Ephesians 1:22–23, no. 235.*Works, 15*, 185–87.

Philippians 2:8. "Obedient unto death."] Isaiah 50:5–6.

Philippians 2:11.] See no. 146.Ibid., 92.

Philippians 2:15–16. "Among whom ye shine as lights in the world, holding forth the word of life."] Dr. Doddridge thus paraphrases this. "Amongst whom, be concerned that ye may shine as elevated lights in the dark world about you, that you may direct those that sail on this dangerous sea, and secure them from suffering shipwreck on those fatal rocks, which everywhere lie in their way." And in his notes says, "Monsieur SaurinJacques Saurin (1677–1730), pastor of the French Church at the Hague. has observed that the word φωστήρ has this energy, and alludes to the buildings which we call lighthouses, the most illustrious of which was raised in the island of Pharos, when Ptolemy Philadelphus built that celebrated tower, on which a bright flame was always kept burning in the night, that mariners might perfectly see their way, and be in no danger of suffering shipwreck upon the rocks, which they were to pass in their entrance into the haven of Alexandria."*Family Expositor, 5*, 253–54 and n. i. This sense is confirmed by the immediately following words, "holding forth the word of life," the word being here represented as that light by which they are to shine, exhibiting it not only in speech, but by a practice agreeable, which word is a light that will so direct, as to preserve from death, and lead in the way of life, and so is "the word of life."

Philippians 2:17. "Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy," etc.] Dr. Doddridge translates it thus: "For if I should even be poured forth as a drink offering, on the sacrifice and ministration of your faith," etc., and observes upon it, that "the heathens sometimes used blood, mingled with wine, in their libations poured on the sacrifices offered

<!-- p. 1109 -->

in honor of their idol deities. Compare Psalms 16:4. The Apostle considers the faith of the Philippians as an acceptable sacrifice presented to God; and if he incurred martyrdom for his zeal to promote it, he might speak of his blood as a libation poured out upon occasion of it, with greater beauty and propriety than most commentators have observed."Ibid., 256–57 and n. a.

Philippians 2:30. "Not regarding his life, that he might supply your lack (or deficiency) of service towards me."] Dr. Doddridge says, "The Apostle considers them as disposed to have rendered him what service they could in person; but not having an opportunity to do it themselves, the good Epaphroditus was in this respect their proxy and representative, and was willing, if it were possible, to perform to the Apostle in his own person all the kind offices which their whole society could have rendered, had they been present as he was." And [he] observes that "the journey and change of air might contribute to his disorder, as well as the assiduity of his attendance on Paul, and dispatching his affairs in all weathers, and perhaps at all hours."Ibid., 260–61 and nn. f. and g.

Philippians 3:2. "Beware of dogs."] "The Jews used to call the Gentiles 'dogs,' and perhaps St. Paul may use this language, when speaking of their proud bigots, by way of retaliation." Doddridge, *in loc*.Ibid., 263, n. c.

Philippians 3:3.] "Which worship God in the spirit."] And not by such external rites as circumcision. "Have no confidence in the flesh." I.e. in such carnal ordinances and external privileges.

Philippians 3:6.] "Touching the righteousness which is in the law, blameless."] The context leads us to suppose that he means only in external conformity to the law, for he is speaking of those things that he had whereof he might glory IN THE FLESH, i.e. in that which is external.

Philippians 3:9. "The righteousness which is of God through faith."] Why the righteousness by which we are justified is so called, see "Miscellanies," nos. 1177,*Works, 23*, 93–94. and 1271.Ibid., 216.

<!-- p. 1110 -->

Philippians 3:10.] It seems to me that by "the power of Christ's resurrection," the Apostle here means the power that wrought that effect of the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. He sought that he might experience the same power in himself, raising him to newness of life, agreeable to Ephesians 1:18–20. "That ye may know… what is the exceeding greatness of his power, according to the working of his mighty power, which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead." The Apostle expresses the same in the next verse in other words. What this same Apostle says, Romans 6:3–11, clearly explains what the Apostle means by being "made conformable to his death," that he might also be to his resurrection.This sentence is a later addition.

Philippians 3:14. "High calling."] Dr. Doddridge supposes here to be an allusion to the proclamation made before the opening of the course at the Olympic games, to contend for such and such a prize.*Family Expositor, 5*, 269, n. n.

Philippians 3:15.] See no. 18.*Works, 15*, 53.

Philippians 3:16. "By the same rule," κανόνι.] The word κανών, as Dr. Manton observes, was agonistical. In their races in the Grecian games, "between the two terms, the starting place and the goal, there was a way marked out called κανών, the rule, which was a white line marked out, the path wherein they were to run. If they transgressed, or went over it, or beside, they did not νομὶμως ἀθλῆαι, 'strive lawfully,' and so were not crowned [2 Timothy 2:5]." Manton's *Sermons*, vol. 5, p. 323.Thomas Manton, *A Fifth Volume of Sermons Preached by the Late Reverend and Learned Thomas Manton, D.D*. (London, 1701).

Philippians 3:20. "For our conversation is in heaven."] Or "we are free of the heavenly city." Philippi was "a Roman colony, and free of the city of Rome," whose emperor Nero "would have himself called Σωτὴρ τῆς οἰκουμένης." See *Present State of Republic of Letters*, vol. 1, p. 449.From a review of Edmund Chishull, *Antiquitates Asiaticae Christianuam Aeram antecedents*, in *Republick of Letters, I* (June 1728), 437–52.

Philippians 4:5. "The Lord is at hand."] "Miscellanies," no. 842.*Works, 20*, 57–64.

<!-- p. 1111 -->

Philippians 4:8. "Think on these things."] The Apostle, in the immediately preceding verses, had told them what they should not exercise their thoughts about, viz. outward things, things pertaining to their worldly interest. Philippians 4:6, "Be careful for nothing." Now he tells them what they should think about, what should be the objects of the greatest exercise of their thought-fulness and care.

Philippians 4:12. "I am instructed."] Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it, "I am as it were initiated into this great mystery," and says in his notes, "This is well known to [be] the peculiar sense of μεμύημαι.… And the Apostle, by the choice of this word, seems to intimate to every Greek reader how much he esteemed these good dispositions of mind here spoken of, beyond all their boasted initiations, whatever mysteries they might be supposed to contain."*Family Expositor, 5*, 283 and n. b

### Colossians

Colossians 1:1. "By the will of God."] No. 268.

Colossians 1:10. "Walk worthy of the Lord."] See note on Ephesians 4:1.

Colossians 1:15. "The firstborn of every creature."] Dr. Waterland,Daniel Waterland (1683–1740), an Anglican theologian who wrote in defense of the divinity of Christ. as cited by Hurrion in his *Knowledge of Christ Crucified*, observes that this "comes not up to the force, nor meaning of the original. It should have been, 'firstborn before the whole creation,' as is manifest from the context, which gives the reason, why he is said to be πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως. It is, because 'he is before all things, and by him were all things created'" Colossians 1:16–17].*Knowledge of Christ, and Him Crucified*, p. 127, n. i.

"The image of the invisible God." "Miscellanies," no. 777.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 18*, 427–34.

Colossians 1:16. "Thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers."] "Miscellanies," no. 838.*Works, 20*, 53–54.

Colossians 1:20.] "Dr. Whitby would render it, 'By him to make all things friendly in him, making peace between them by the blood of his cross.' And I apprehend that to be the true sense, and the only sense in which things in heaven can be said to be reconciled.… When a breach commenced between man and the blessed God, the angels, as faithful subjects, must join with him against the rebellious creature." Doddridge, in loc.*Family Expositor, 5*, 304, n. f.

Colossians 1:24. "That which is behind in the sufferings of Christ."] Not that anything was behind or lacking, needful to perfect his satisfaction and purchase, but something was "behind of the sufferings of Christ" that were appointed before the consummate glory of the church. For it was appointed that Christ should suffer first in his person, the head, and then

<!-- p. 1113 -->

after that, in his members, and that in this way the glory of the church should be brought to pass, and in a sense by the means of both, so that after the suffering of the head, the suffering of the members was behind.

Colossians 2:3. "In whom are hid all the treasures."] "Miscellanies," no. 982.*Works, 20*, 301–302.

Colossians 2:9. "For in him dwelleth all the fullness of the Godhead bodily."] Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it thus. "For in him dwelleth all the fullness of the Godhead bodily and substantially, so that the human nature is the temple of the deity," and says in his note upon it, "I assuredly believe that, as it contains an evident allusion to the Shekinah in which God dwelt, so it ultimately refers to the adorable mystery of the union of the divine and human natures, in the person of the glorious Emmanuel, which makes him such an object of our hope and confidence, as the most exalted creature, with the most glorious endowments could never, of himself, be."*Family Expositor, 5*, 313 and n. d.

Colossians 2:11.] See no. 69.*Works, 15*, 69.

Colossians 2:12. "Risen with him."] Hosea 6:2.

Colossians 2:14.] Ephesians 2:15 note.

"Handwriting of ordinances." The Apostle alludes to the handwriting upon the wall against Belshazzar, in which he was condemned, and the curse of God was denounced against him.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Colossians 2:15. "And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it."] 'Tis not meant that "he made a show of them openly," and triumphed over them upon the cross. If the Apostle had meant so, the Apostle would probably have said, "triumphing over them upon it," not "in it." Christ is here said to triumph in his cross in no other sense than the Apostle elsewhere says he gloried in it (Galatians 6:14). The time of Christ's hanging on the cross was not the time of Christ's triumphing; it was the battle. The triumph was afterwards. Indeed, Christ did in a sense overcome Satan upon the cross; he did that by which he was overthrown. But it was not then known by Satan.

The time of the triumphing was when Satan, by the event, see himself

<!-- p. 1114 -->

overthrown. It was when the victory was openly shown, whenJE deleted "See sermon on the words, exposition of the text." JE's sermon on Colossians 2:13–15, n. d. (no. 255, Aug. 1731–Dec. 1732), with the doctrine: "When a sinner is converted, then Jesus Christ triumphs over his enemy the devil" (MS, p. 4). JE's exposition of the text explains Christ's triumphing over "Satan and the powers of darkness" on the cross through the "conversion of sinners." The cross was the "means" by which the victory was obtained; the effects were seen later. The time of Christ's triumph was after his resurrection and ascension when multitudes were converted. The "spoils" Christ took from Satan were sinners. The public show of that victory was the "remarkable success" the church enjoyed in the three centuries following Christ's death. Christ "made a show of them openly," as is expressed here. The time of Christ's hanging on the cross was the time of Satan's triumphing. There never was such a triumphing in hell as there was then; that was Satan's hour (Luke 22:53).

Christ triumphed in the cross, that is, in the virtue, fruits, and consequences of it, when the success of his crucifixion openly and remarkably appeared after his ascension. The Apostle is here in this place speaking of the triumph Christ had over the devil in the conversion and justification of sinners, mentioned in the two preceding verses.

Christ had the greater triumph in his victory over Satan, and Satan the greater disgrace for that victory's being obtained by the cross, and that upon two accounts. 1. Because the means by which he obtained the victory was in itself so weak and despicable, and appeared so unlikely (1 Corinthians 1:17 ff.). Thus David had the greater triumph over Goliath in that he prevailed against him with only a staff, a sling and a stone [1 Samuel 17:49], and Sampson with his jawbone of an ass [Judges 15:15]. 2. Because the cross was the very thing whereby Satan thought he overthrew Christ. Thus David had the greater triumph over Goliath in that he slew him with his own sword.

Colossians 2:16. "With respect to an holy day."] This don't include the sabbath. The word is ἑορτή, a "feast."

Colossians 2:18–19.] "To divert men from Christ, the one and only Mediator, the devil very early introduced the mediation of angels, his servants, therein pretending a greater exercise of humility than others attained to. The apostle Paul has taken notice of this, when he speaks of 'a voluntary humility, and worshipping of angels, and not holding the head.' It was alleged, that to go immediately to Christ would be too great a boldness, and discover too little sense of our own unworthiness; but to implore the intercession of angels would discover our humility. But the Apostle charged this invention with pride and ignorance, when he called it an

<!-- p. 1115 -->

'intruding into things which they have not seen' and a being 'vainly puffed up with a fleshly mind.' He condemned it as will-worship, and not holding of Christ 'the head'; for if Christ be God-man, Mediator, there is no need to employ any other. And whilst men expect more easily to obtain pardon, grace, and glory by the mediation of others than of Christ, they practically disown his care, condescension, and kindness, as head of the church. He is nearer to us, both in nature and affection, than the angels, and is appointed of God as the one and only Mediator. And therefore 'tis not humility, but pride, 'tis not religion, but rebellion and superstition, to set up or make use of any other mediator. The Apostle, instead of deterring us, has encouraged us, to 'come boldly to the throne of grace, seeing we have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who is passed into the heavens for us' [Hebrews 4:14, Hebrews 4:16]. 'I can (saith one of the ancients) more safely and more comfortably speak to my Jesus than to any one of the holy spirits of God; Christ is more engaged to me (that is, as God-man, Mediator, and Redeemer) than to any of the celestial spirits.'" Hurrion, *Of Christ and Him Crucified*, pp. 181–83.*Knowledge of Christ, and Him Crucified*.

"Voluntary humility and worshipping of angels." "It evidently appears from several passages in Philo, to have been the opinion of that learned Jew, that angels were messengers who presented our prayers to God, as well as brought down his favors to us. He represents this view of the matter as most humble and reverential, and there is no doubt but it prevailed among other Jews (Compare Tobit 11:14; Tobit 12:12, Tobit 12:15.)." Doddridge, *in loc*.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 5*, 317, n. 1.

Colossians 2:20. "Why, as though living in the world."] This world is not the country of the church. Christ, after he rose from the dead, was no longer a proper inhabitant of this world, and therefore was no longer subject to the ceremonial law. So is the church, which is mystical Christ, dead and risen with Christ. Christ is the representative of the church, and therefore the church have communion with him in this alteration of his state. See notes on Ephesians 2:15.

See notes on Ephesians 2:15, especially second paragraph.This reference is a separate entry.

Colossians 2:22.] This verse Dr. Doddridge translates, "All which things tend to corruption by the abuse of them, according to the commandments and doctrines of men."*Family Expositor, 5*, 321.

<!-- p. 1116 -->

Colossians 2:23.] This verse Dr. Doddridge translates thus: "Which things have indeed a pretense of wisdom, in will worship, and humility, and severity to the body, to the dishonorable satisfying of the flesh." And he says in his notes, "that οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι, he takes to be a meiosis,I.e. a belittling; a making something smaller than it is. to express what is dishonorable."*Family Expositor, 5*, 321–22 and n. c. This sense is the more natural because it is plainly implied in the foregoing words, in the Apostle's manner of speaking, that they sought honor by their show and pretense of wisdom and humility. They thought they acted very worthily and honorably in these things, and recommended themselves to the just esteem and commendation of God and men.

Colossians 3:1. "Risen with Christ."] Hosea 6:2.

Colossians 3:3–4. "Ye are now dead, and your life is hid."] Dead men are hid; they are out sight. "Your life is hid." The world don't see that you live. They don't see that you are happy, but look upon you miserable, because you deny yourselves, and don't gratify the flesh, nor give yourselves that enjoyment of earthly things which they do. They don't see what 'tis that you live upon. They don't know how, nor in what, nor by what means you enjoy comfort and happiness. The world looks upon you dead, as you are indeed dead to the world. But your conversation is in heaven. You live above the world. Your life, and comfort, and happiness is in God, whom the world sees not; it is in heaven with Christ. But though now ye are hid like dead men that are out of sight, yet when Christ, who is your life, shall appear, ye shall be hid no longer, but then shall appear with him, and shall appear with him in glory. Then your life shall appear; then shall it appear that you are alive and happy.

Colossians 3:5. "Covetousness, which is idolatry."] As idols were wont to be made of silver and gold, so silver and gold are the idols that these spiritual idolaters worship.

Colossians 3:9. "Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have [put] off the old man with his deeds."] Stops seem here to be wrong made, which makes it more difficult to understand the sense. The stop that is made at the end of the preceding verse ought rather to have been at the end of these words, "Lie not one to another." For this is one of those disuniting sins

<!-- p. 1117 -->

mentioned, of which the words in this and the two next verses are mentioned as a common reason why we should avoid them, viz. because in the new man these disuniting distinctions, by which the carnal world is divided, are abolished, and Christ is all in all.

Colossians 3:16. "Let the word of God dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns," etc.] Dr. Doddridge translates it, "with psalms," etc., and he paraphrases it, "And let these seasons, whether of public worship or private conference, be diversified with the use of David's psalms, or other evangelical hymns and spiritual songs."Ibid., 328.

Colossians 3:17. "And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus."] *Ques*. Why must we do whatsoever we do in the name of Christ? *Ans*. Because nothing can be acceptable to God as from us, but in and through Christ, as Hebrews 13:21, "Working in you that that is well-pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ," and 1 Peter 2:5. Therefore when we come to God to do anything Godward, we must always bring Christ with us, that what we do may be accepted, i.e. we must have a sense of our unworthiness of acceptance in ourselves, and must hope for acceptance on his account. *Ques*. But why can't what we do be accepted but by Christ? *Ans*. 1. We are infinitely ill-deserving creatures, and all our good is nothing when put in the scales with our unworthiness. And then, 2. We are condemned creatures, and 'tis against the law that anything should be accepted from us as we are in ourselves. 3. The third reason why nothing that we do can be accepted but by Christ is because there is nothing that we do but what is in a sense corrupt. Even the holy actions and gracious exercises of the godly are so. They ben't merely attended with the exercises of corruption that precede and follow them, and are mixed with them; but they are themselves corrupt. Take 'em as they are in their dimensions and manner of exerting them, even the exercises of grace in a godly man are manifestations and expressions of corruption. The act most simply and absolutely considered is good; but consider it in its measure and the manner of exertion, and they are an expression of corruption. All the godly man's acts of love are defectively corrupt or sinfully defective. There is that defect in them that may well be called the corruption of them. That defect is properly sin, an expression of corruption, and what tends to provoke the just anger of God, not because the exercise of love is not proportionable or equal to God's

<!-- p. 1118 -->

loveliness or to his kindness, but because 'tis soJE deleted "far from being equal." very disproportionate to the occasion that is given for the exercise of love, considering God's loveliness, and the manifestation that is made of it, or the manifestation and exercise of his kindness, and man's capacity and the advantages to be sensible of it and the like, together. A negative expression of corruption may be as truly sin, and as truly odious, and as just cause of provocation as a positive. Thus if a man, a worthy and excellent person, should from mere generosity and goodness exceedingly lay out himself, and should with great expense and suffering save another's life, or redeem him from some extreme calamity, and when he had done all, that other person should never thank him for it, or express the least gratitude any way, this would be a negative expression of his ingratitude and baseness, but is equivalent to an act of ingratitude or a base unworthy spirit, and is as truly an expression of it, and brings as much blame as if he, by some positive act, had much injured another person. And so it would have been only in a lesser degree, if gratitude was but very small, bearing no proportion to the benefit and obligation, or if for so great and extraordinary a kindness he had expressed no more gratitude than would have been becoming towards a person that had only given him sixpence, or had done him some such small kindness. If he had come to his benefactor to express his gratitude, and had done after this manner, he might truly be said to have acted basely, unworthily, and odiously. He would have shown a most ungrateful spirit, and his doing after such a manner would be justly abhorred by all. And yet the gratitude, that little that there was of it, and so far as it went, was good.

And so it is with respect to our exercises of love and gratitude to God. They are defectively corrupt and sinful, and might justly be odious and provoking to him, taken as they are upon the like account, and would be so, were it not that the sin and corruption of them is hid by Christ. God as it were don't see the odiousness and iniquity of them, and so accepts them for Christ's sake, which but of him would be worthy of his detestation. See sermon on 1 Peter 2:5, the three reasons of the doctrine.This reference is a later addition. JE's sermon on 1 Peter 2:5, n. d. (no. 261, Aug. 1731—Dec. 1732), with the doctrine, "The good works of the godly can't be accepted any other way, than in and through Christ" (MS, p. 5). JE asserts three reasons that good works cannot make persons acceptable: "all their goodness is nothing when put in the scales with their unworthiness"; when considered separately, all are condemned wholly by the law and are objects of divine wrath; and even the "best works of the godly are so polluted" that they are not "fit to be accepted" except through Christ.

*Corol*. Hence the saints may be said to be rewarded for their good works for Christ's sake, and not for the excellency of their works in themselves

<!-- p. 1119 -->

considered, for as we have shown, as they are in themselves, they are odious, and might be just cause of provocation. They ben't rewardable therefore as they are in themselves. They are accepted through Christ; and 'tis therefore for Christ's sake that they are rewarded, for God's rewarding them is a testimony of his acceptance. They are rewarded for Christ's sake in this sense, viz. that 'tis for his sake that God looks upon [them] as fit to be accepted and rewarded. See "Miscellanies," nos. 627 and 41.*Works, 18*, 155–56; 13, 223–24.

"Giving thanks to God and the Father." See Ephesians 5:20.This reference is a separate entry.

Colossians 4:16. "And that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea."] The Apostle don't mean any epistle of his to the Laodiceans, but as is evident by the words of the original,καὶ τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας ἴνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε. some epistle written from Laodicea. It evidently appears that the "words from Laodicea" belong to the epistle as deciphering that, and don't refer to the reading. Nor can it be supposed that the Apostle means any epistle that he had written from Laodicea to some other church. 'Tis not probable that he would decipher the epistle that he meant by the place that he wrote from, but by those that he wrote to. The Apostle was not wont in his epistles so much as to mention the places that he wrote them from.

The Apostle therefore probably means some epistle that the Laodiceans had written to him, for as the Apostle was wont to write to churches, so they were wont to write to him about their spiritual and ecclesiastical concerns (1 Corinthians 7:1).

It seems the Apostle designed this epistle to the Colossians should serve as an answer to the epistle of the Laodiceans, and therefore orders it to be read amongst them. Colosse and Laodicea were near one to another, and probably were in like circumstances, and had the like occasion for the Apostle's determination, instruction, and advice concerning those subjects that the Apostle especially treats of in this epistle, particularly about the ceremonies of the law of Moses, and the tenets and concerns of philosophers which some endeavored to obtrude upon the Christians in Colosse, and Laodicea, and the region thereabouts. The Laodiceans had written to the Apostle about those things. The Apostle had an eye to what they had written in this his epistle, and therefore would have the Colossians to read it for their better understanding of this his answer.

### I Thessalonians

1 Thessalonians 1:3. "Work of faith, and labor of love, and patience of hope."] "All these" (says Dr. Doddridge) "are plain Hebraisms, for 'active faith, laborious love, and patient hope,' and might very properly have been so translated." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor*, 5, 352, n. a.

The proper evidence of the genuineness of faith is its activity, orJE deleted "operativeness." its being operative. The proper evidence of the genuineness of love is its being laborious and self-denying. The proper evidence of a genuine hope is patience or perseverance in waiting for the hoped for reward, through all intervening labors and sufferings.

1 Thessalonians 2:12. "Worthy of God."] See note on Ephesians 4:1.

1 Thessalonians 3:11. "Now God himself," etc.] By this verse it appears that Christ is the proper object of invocation, not only in some particular thing in which he, in the exercise of his office, is more peculiarly concerned, but for any mercy that we need, even as God the Father.

1 Thessalonians 3:13. "At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints."] This and those other parallel texts—the 1 Thessalonians 4:14, "Them also that sleep in Jesus will God bring with him"; and Jude 14, "Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints"—do plainly show that the saints are in heaven with Christ before their resurrection.

1 Thessalonians 4:13–18.] See "Miscellanies," no. 639.*Works, 18*, 170–73.

1 Thessalonians 4:14. "Even so also them that sleep in Jesus will God bring with him."] This passage, together with the 1 Thessalonians 3:13, "at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints," and also

<!-- p. 1121 -->

Jude 14, "the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints," and Zechariah 14:5, "and the Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with thee," seem to make evident that the souls of the saints do neither sleep while the body is dead, nor yet is in any place called Hades, different from the highest heavens, because when Christ descends at the day of judgment, he'll bring the saints with him from thence, as is evident by these places.

1 Thessalonians 4:16–18.] Concerning the Apostle's speaking as though Christ's coming would be while they were alive, see "Miscellanies," no. 842.Ibid., 20, 57–64.

1 Thessalonians 5:17. "Pray without ceasing."] This implies praying morning and evening. See "Miscellanies," no. 1115.Ibid., 347–48.

### II Thessalonians

2 Thessalonians 1:5–7.] See Numbers 12:3–4, Ecclesiastes 7:8, Psalms 76:9 and Psalms 45:4, Romans 12:19–20, Psalms 48:4 ff., Isaiah 11:4 and Isaiah 29:19–20.

2 Thessalonians 1:10. "When he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and admired in all them that believe."] When he ascended after his resurrection, he was glorified in his person. Now at the day of judgment, he shall be glorified in his saints, in the members of his mystical body. Then he shall be admired in his saints in whom he is now despised, and reproached, and persecuted, as in the foregoing verses. See note on Ephesians 1:18. The 2 Thessalonians 1:12 of this chapter confirms this interpretation. There the Apostle prays that "Christ may be glorified" in them now 2 Thessalonians 1:12], i.e. glorified in what is seen in them, in the beauty and glory of that holiness in which they appear to the world.

2 Thessalonians 1:11. "That our God would count you worthy of this calling."] Dr. Manton on this place observes, that besides a worthiness of meetness and suitableness which the saints have, "There is *dignitas dignationis*, or worthiness of acceptance. So it is taken, Acts 5:41. They went away 'rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Christ,' that this honor was put upon them. So we in common speech say, Such a one counted me worthy of his company, or his presence, or conference with him, or to sit down at his table; by these phrases of speech, not ascribing any worth to ourselves, but condescension in vouchsafing the honor to us. So here, the Apostle prayeth that they may be accounted 'worthy of this calling'; that is, that God would vouchsafe 'em to partake of his grace and glory. This worthiness is nothing else but God's gracious acceptation of a sinner through Jesus Christ, calling them to this grace through the knowledge of the gospel, and giving them eternal life because they are worthy; which noteth liberality in the giver, but no worth in the receiver. So it is taken, Luke 21:36, 'That ye may be counted worthy to stand before the Son of man.' And Revelation 3:4, 'They shall walk with me in white, for they are worthy.' Because in Christ they are accepted as worthy, having given them a right by his grace. All is to be ascribed to

<!-- p. 1123 -->

God's dignation; for Christ's sake God doth take our carriage in good part, though many failings." Manton's *Sermons*, vol. 5, p. 469.Manton's sermon on 1 Thessalonians 1:11, in his *Fifth Volume of Sermons*, pp. 467–82.

There is this distinction to be observed, viz. the worthiness which commends to love, and the worthiness or value which love puts on the beloved. When God hath set his love on any, his love sets a high value upon them, i.e. a great worthiness. There is difference between the value that is the foundation of love, and the value of which love is the foundation. See note on Revelation 3:4.

2 Thessalonians 2:1. "By the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."] ὑπὲρ τῆς παρουσίας. This Dr. Doddridge translates, "With respect to the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ," and supposes "ὑπὲρ to be used for περί here," as he observes it is, 1 Corinthians 8:23, JE follows Doddridge on this erroneous citation; there is no 1 Corinthians 8:23. and says that "VitringaCampegius Vitringa (1659–1722), a Dutch theologian and biblical commentator, author of *Observationum sacrarum libri primus* [—*sextus*] *in quibus de rebus varii argumenti, & utilissimae investigationis, theologicè ac criticè, disseritur* (2 vols. 1683–1708). has said so much to vindicate this rendering, that he could not but prefer it."*Family Expositor, 5*, 407 and n. a.

2 Thessalonians 2:1–3]. There appears a necessity…JE deleted this unfinished entry and the marginal reference to it.

See "Miscellanies," no. 842.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 20*, 57–64.

2 Thessalonians 2:4. "So that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, showing himself that he is God."] Dr. Doddridge observes "that the Pope on high days has been wont to set himself on a high throne, in the temple of God, to be there adored, and that he permits his parasites expressly to boast that he is God, and to give him divine titles, in some of their licensed authorized works."*Family Expositor, 5*, 413.

2 Thessalonians 2:7. "The mystery of iniquity doth already work."] See Poole's *Synopsis, in loc*., vol. 5, pp. 990 [col. 2], d–e and 991 [col. 1], a–b.*Synopsis Criticorum, IV* (London, 1676), Pt. 2. Vol. 5 is vol. IV, Pt. 2.

"Mystery of iniquity." No. 329.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 313.

2 Thessalonians 2:14. "To the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ."] I.e. the glory that he possesses, as Christ prayed that his disciples might behold

<!-- p. 1124 -->

the glory which had [been] given him [John 17:24], and that his joy may be "fulfilled in themselves" [John 17:13]. So they are said to drink of the river of his pleasures, and to see light in his light [Psalms 36:8–9]. And Christ says that the glory that the Father had given him, he had given them [John 17:22]; and they enter into the joy of their Lord [Matthew 25:21], are called "into his marvelous light" [1 Peter 2:9], have his kingdom given them, are kings and judges in the kingdom of heaven, and sit with him in his thrones.

2 Thessalonians 3:5. "Patient waiting for Christ."] The words in the [text] are ὑπομονὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ, "the patience of Christ," which doubtless signifies such patience as becomes a follower of Christ, and is an imitation and participation of the patience he exercised.

2 Thessalonians 3:17. "Which is my token in every epistle."] The Apostle commonly made use of an amanuensis in writing his epistles. But to prevent counterfeits, he added the salutation at the end with his own hand. To this purpose, [see] Doddridge.*Family Expositor, 5*, 421–22.
