### I Timothy

1 Timothy 1:1. "By the commandment of God our Savior."] No. 268.*Works, 15*, 222–23.

1 Timothy 1:5. "Now the end of the commandment is charity."] The Apostle here tells what is "the end of the commandment," because the commandment or law was what they jangled about.

1 Timothy 1:9. "The law is not made for a righteous man."] This may be given as a reason why the precepts of the moral law were not expressed by God to our first parents, as well as that positive precept of not eating the forbidden fruit. There is not that need of God's expressly and particularly forbidding these and those immoralities to one that is perfectly righteous in his nature, either for the making known his obligation, or for the enforcing it. As to one that is of a corrupt nature, God in his infinite wisdom never would have seen cause expressly to reveal the moral law, had it not been for transgressions or man's disposition to sin.

See notes on Galatians 5:18, *Ans*. to the 2nd *Inq*.This reference is a separate entry. See "Scripture," no. 196 (*Works, 15*, 113–15).

"In lege Dei post peccatum duo sunt consideranda. I. Norma et directio ad ὑποταγήν. II. Vis frenandi, et compescendi terrore et metu, ac denique juste condemnandi. Quando ergo Apostolus docet, legem justo positam non esse, non intelligit id de primo ac praecipuo legis opere, quod ipsi essentiale est, sed de altero illo accidentario, quod per et post peccatum superaccessit, et a quo justi per Christum liberati sunt." Witsius, *Oeconom, Lib*. I, *cap*. III, sec. 9.This excerpt from Herman Witsius (1636–1708) reads, "In the law of God, since the entrance of sin, two things are to be considered. 1. The *rule* and direction to *obedience*. 2. *The power of bridling and restraining* by terror and fear; and lastly, of *justly condemning*. When therefore the apostle teaches, that the law was not made for a righteous man, he does not understand it of the primary and principal work of the law, which is essential to it, but of that other accidental work, which was added to it on account of and since the entrance of sin, and from which the righteous are freed by Christ" (*The Œconomy of the Covenants, between God and Man. Comprehending A Complete Body of Divinity* [3 vols. New York, 1798], *I*, 78–79), first published in Latin as *De œconomia fœderum Dei cum hominibus* in 1677. This is taken from a citation of Rawlin

<!-- p. 1126 -->

on *Justification*, p. 27.Rawlin, *Christ the Righteousness of his People*. The word in the original that is translated "made" is κεῖται, "*put* for a righteous man," or "*laid* upon a righteous man."This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 Timothy 1:13.] The Apostle don't tell us what his blasphemies were, but no doubt can be made but that he, with other blasphemies, blasphemed and reproached that Spirit that the Christians were indued with, for such were the circumstances of the church of that day. The gift of the Holy Ghost was a thing so notorious and great, and what drew the eyes of the world so much on the Christians, that it could not be otherwise than that those that reviled and persecuted the Christians must revile that Spirit, which was the great seal and testimony by which the truth of their profession was confirmed in the sight of the world, and especially must it be so at that day when Paul was a persecutor, when the Spirit of God had so lately in so remarkable a manner poured out on the Christians at so public a time. He doubtless reviled that Spirit, as the Jews used to do in Christ before he was crucified, calling it Beelzebub, and as others did on the day of Pentecost when it was first poured out, saying that the apostles were drunk [Acts 2:13]. And therefore the Apostle here says, he "obtained mercy" because he did it "ignorantly" and "in unbelief." If he had done it against light and knowledge, it would have been the unpardonable sin.

1 Timothy 1:14.] See John 16:27.

"But the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus." This seems to be by the figure which is called hendiadys,A grammatical term referring to the expression of an idea by two nouns connected by "and," instead of by a noun and an adjunct. and by faith and love are not meant two proper distinct things. But 'tis as much as to say, a loving faith, or that faith whose life and spirit is love, or that faith which works by love, as when it is said, "He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire" [Luke 3:16], i.e. with a fiery Spirit, or a Spirit that shall be like fire.This paragraph is a separate entry.

1 Timothy 1:19. "Concerning faith have made shipwreck."] It seems that it should rather have been rendered, "concerning *the faith*," i.e. concerning the doctrine of the gospel, for the original is περὶ τὴν πίστιν, and this best agrees with the metaphor of making shipwreck. For herein the gospel, or doctrine of faith, is represented as a treasure committed to their care, as a treasure is committed into a ship, and so to the care of the master,

<!-- p. 1127 -->

to be carried safe to such a port. But they, through their unskillfulness and carelessness, "have made shipwreck" of it, and lost it. Or if by "faith" is meant an inherent qualification, doubtless they made shipwreck of it, as Simon Magus did, of whom we are told that he believed when others believed [Acts 8:13], but never had a true faith, for 'tis plain by what the apostle Peter says, he then remained "in the gall of bitterness, and bond of iniquity." And it must be such a faith as the stony-ground hearers had, who, at the same time that they believed, had no root in themselves [Matthew 13:5–6], and so were not true saints, and such a faith as those had of whom we are told that they believed on Christ, but Christ did not commit himself to them, for he knew what was in men. He knew that what was in them was not right, was not to be depended.

1 Timothy 2:4. "Who will have all men to be saved, and come to the knowledge of the truth."] By "the knowledge of the truth" here is doubtless meant the knowledge of gospel truth, whereby it is evident that it is not meant that God will have all men to be saved in any sense inconsistent with the doctrine of absolute election and particular redemption. For it can't be argued from the text that God would "have all men to be saved," any more than he would have all "come to the knowledge of the" gospel. But those that are against the doctrine of election do allow that there is such a thing as an election of nations and peoples to a church state, and to the enjoyment of the means of grace, or (which is the same thing) that be here purposed, that some should have the gospel, or "come to the knowledge of the truth," and that others should not.

1 Timothy 2:15.] Dr. Doddridge thus paraphrases the former part of this verse. "Yet let them not be despised or upbraided on this account, considering on the other side, that she was also happily instrumental in producing the great promised Seed, who was derived from a woman, without any human father; and so they may be saved, as I may say, by childbirth."*Family Expositor, 5*, 452.

1 Timothy 3:15. "Pillar and ground of truth."] See Turretin, vol. 1, p. 103.The sixth question in Turretin's second topic, *De Scriptura Sacra*, asks "From what source does the divine authority of the Scriptures become known to us? Does it depend upon the testimony of the church either as to itself or as to us?" Turretin states, "The church is called 'the pillar and ground of the truth'… not because she supports and gives authority to the truth (since the truth is rather the foundation upon which the church is built, Ephesians 2:20), but because it stands before the church as a pillar and makes itself conspicuous to all." Against the views of Roman Catholics, Turretin says that the church is not a foundation, or a substructure of the truth (*Institutio Theologiae Elencticae*). See Dennison, ed., *Institutes of Elenctic Theology, I*, 85, 93–94. The church is the pillar that supports and holds forth the truth to the view

<!-- p. 1128 -->

of the world, as a candlestick is as it were a pillar to support and hold forth the light that is set in it. And therefore churches in Revelation 1 are called "golden candlesticks" Revelation 1:12], as here the church is called "the pillar of truth." The church is set to hold forth light to the world, and therefore Christ says, Matthew 5:15–16, "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light to all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Which is the very argument the Apostle seems to make use of with Timothy in this verse, to behave himself well in the church of God in which he was set to be a light.This paragraph and what follows are later than the Turretin reference.

See Philippians 2:15–16.

1 Timothy 3:16. "Justified in the Spirit."] See Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. 49–51.Kidder justifies Christ's reference to his miraculous works in his conversation with the disciples of John the Baptist, for Kidder asserts that "miracles are a good proof of the truth of a doctrine." The critical distinction, however, is between true miracles (i.e. those by the power of the Spirit) and false ones. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 49–51.

1 Timothy 4:1–3. "Doctrines of devils, or demons… forbidding to marry."] "This injunction of celibate, or monastic life, was one great part of the doctrine of demons, being one of the superstitions Pythagoras brought out of Egypt, when he returned into Greece. He forbad marriage to those of his sect, and erected a cloister of virgins or nuns, the charge of which he gave to his daughter. Plato held the same sentiment, and Heraclitus, and Democritus, and Zeno the prince of the Stoics, who never touched a woman." Thus Bochart. See Gale's *Court of the Gentiles*, Pt. 2, Bk. 2, ch. 6, p. 150.Theophilus Gale, *Court of the Gentiles*, Pt. II (Oxford, 1670).

"Commanding to abstain from meats." "Pythagoras commanded his disciples to abstain from all things that had life. He held that all things dedicated to God were holy, and so not to be used in common uses. Thence that fishes were not to be eaten." Ibid., p. 151.Ibid.

1 Timothy 4:5.] I.e. "being warranted to use it by the 'word of God,' if we don't forget to acknowledge God in it by prayer and praise." See Evans' *Christian Temper*, vol. 2, p. 103.John Evans' Sermon V on Luke 21:34, entitled "Temperance," has the doctrine, "That Christians are strongly obliged to maintain a strict guard against intemperance" (p. 93). In it he argues against "licentiousness" in food because the ceremonial law against certain meats has been abolished. See *Practical Discourse concerning the Christian Temper* (2nd ed.), *II*, 87–109.

<!-- p. 1129 -->

1 Timothy 4:8. "Bodily exercise (γυμνασία) profiteth little."] Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it thus. "That bodily exercise, about which many are so solicitous, and in the pursuit of which they go through so many fatigues, in preparing for and attending the public games, is profitable to but very little, the best rewards of it being but of a very transient and fading nature."*Family Expositor, 5*, 469. The Apostle has reference againMS: "against." to these games in the advice he gives Timothy (as here), in 1 Timothy 6:12.

1 Timothy 4:10. "The Savior of all men."] See Turretin, Pt. 2, p. 501.The fourteenth question in Turretin's fourteenth topic, *De Officio Christi Mediatorio*, asks "Did Christ die for each and every man universally or only for the elect?" Turretin's answer is the latter. He writes, "It is gratuitous to say that Christ is the Savior of those for whom salvation is indeed acquired, but to whom it will never be applied. Even the very word 'to save' denotes the actual communication of salvation." Turretin sees this passage in Timothy as consistent with that view by interpreting the word "Savior" in the first clause as the "preserver" of all, both man and beast, but in the latter clause as reference "strictly and properly with regard to believers," one being bodily salvation and the other spiritual salvation (*Institutio Theologiae Elencticae* [Trajecti ad Rhenum, 1696], *II*, 501). See Dennison, ed., *Institutes of Elenctic Theology, II*, 455, 461.

"This," says Dr. Doddridge, "seems a title parallel to that in Job 7:20, 'preserver of men.' But he is especially the Savior of believers, as he extends to them the noblest and most important deliverances."This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 5*, 470, n. e.

1 Timothy 5:3. "Widows indeed."] "Here is, as CalvinJohn Calvin (1509–64), French theologian and reformer who led the Protestant reformation in Geneva. justly observes, an allusion to the Greek word χήρα, which signifies a person in distressed and indigent circumstances." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, 475, n. b.

1 Timothy 5:8. "But if any provide not for his own, and especially for those of his own house."]JE marked this unfinished entry with a large "X."

1 Timothy 5:9.] Concerning such widows as are here spoken of, see Taylor's note on Romans 16:1.*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, pp. 455–59. See also JE's entry on Romans 16:1.

<!-- p. 1130 -->

1 Timothy 5:11. "For when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry."] It appears probable from 1 Timothy 5:15, that the Apostle here has in eye some particular instances of a strange behavior of some young widows that had been taken into the number, a regard to which instances very much governs his language. As much as to say, If you take in young widows, no wonder if they, through a wanton disposition, behave themselves as those which you have tried of this sort. No wonder if they gad about from house to house, grow idle, trifling busybodies, and are wanton in their behavior, and marry in a dishonorable manner such as they have first been wanton with.

'Tis probable that in the instances [to] which the Apostle had respect, or one of them at least, a young widow that had been taken into the number, through her wantonness had yielded to the enticements of an heathen man, and finally had married him, which occasions such a manner of expression as "waxing wanton AGAINST CHRIST," and "cast off their *first faith*" 1 Timothy 5:12]. When the Apostle says, "For when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ," etc., the expression imports no more than this. There will be danger of such things happening in younger widows.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Timothy 5:17. "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honor."] I.e. don't look upon it too much that they should live above the rest, that they should live more honorably than their neighbors, and be exalted in outward circumstances above [them]. Ye should look upon them as worthy of it, for their works' sake. See note on Proverbs 27:18.

What the Apostle probably had in view when he used this expression of "DOUBLE Honor" to the ELDER was the law that gave a DOUBLE portion to the ELDER brother.This paragraph is a later addition.

1 Timothy 5:24.] "Beforehand," i.e. before the day appointed for judgment, the proper time for manifesting what men are, and what state they are in. Their corruptions do as it were hasten to judgment. God in his providence, in the trials he brings upon them, shows what they are in the sight of the world; and God would have 'em judged in his house by being cut off, excommunicated, whereby God's judgment as it were takes place before its proper time. For this is God's judgment; what they bind on earth is bound in heaven.

<!-- p. 1131 -->

1 Timothy 5:25.] If the words in the originalὡσαύτως καὶ τὰ ἔργα τὰ καλὰ πρόδηλα, καὶ τὰ ἄλλως ἔχοντα κρυβῆναι οὐ δύνανται. be carefully considered, they will lead to this sense: As the evil works of some men are manifest beforehand, and others that are hid now are manifest afterwards at the day of judgment, so it is with good works. The good works of some are manifest beforehand. And those good works that are truly good, that are otherwise, that are not manifest now, yet will be manifest afterwards at the day of judgment; they cannot finally be hid.

1 Timothy 6:19. "That they may lay hold on eternal life."] A most beautiful expression for the purpose that the Apostle intended it, naturally intimating that they that were rich had much to beat them back, and to oppose and hinder their coming at so glorious a prize. The Apostle therefore would have them use these means he here directs to as an earnest to obtain it, notwithstanding the peculiar difficulties that were in the way of rich men's obtaining it, if by any means they might violently press through the opposition, and reach forward, and lay hold of it.

The Apostle probably had in his eye what Christ said concerning the difficulty of rich men's obtaining eternal life, and might possibly have some reference to what he himself had said just before (1 Timothy 6:9–10). The original wordἐπιλάβωνται. seems to have very much the same force as our English word "lay hold," naturally intimating opposition to the obtaining a thing, or danger of mistingI.e. missing. of it. So in Matthew 14:30–31, where we read that when Peter was sinking in the tempestuous sea, "Jesus stretched forth his hand, and *caught* him." The wordἐπελάβετο. in the original is the same. See also how he uses the same word,ἐπιλαβοῦ. 1 Timothy 6:12, where the Apostle speaks of fighting the way through to reach this prize, and seems to allude to those that strove for the prize in the Olympic games.

2 Timothy 1:1.] According to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus."] By this the Apos…JE deleted this unfinished entry.

"The will of God." No. 268.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 222–23.

2 Timothy 1:12. "That which I have committed unto him."] In the original, παρακαταθήκην. The gospel, in 2 Timothy 1:14, is also called παραθήκη. "Philo and Josephus have many passages in which both the soul and the law are in different views called παραθήκη, 'the depositum of God.'" Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, 513, n. f.

2 Timothy 1:13.] It seems to me probable that by "the form of sound words" here spoken [of], the Apostle means the solemn charge that he gave Timothy at his ordination concerning what doctrines he should preach, or that part of the charge wherein were committed to him the doctrine that he should preach. The 2 Timothy 2:2 confirms me in this, where the Apostle charges Timothy to commit the same things to other "faithful men" that he should ordain for teachers that he had heard of him "among many witnesses," where he seems evidently to refer to some public, solemn transaction wherein the doctrines of the gospel were committed to him "among many witnesses." And what is intended don't seem to be only hearing the doctrines of the gospel preached and taught as ordinary Christians do, but some committing of these doctrines to teachers in a way peculiar to them, because he adds, "the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." These faithful men had the true doctrines of the gospel committed to them already, as all Christians had; but the Apostle speaks of another committing.

2 Timothy 1:14.] "That good thing" here spoken of is that "treasure" spoken of, 2 Corinthians 4:7, of which "the form of sound words," mentioned in the preceding verse, is the vehicle.

<!-- p. 1133 -->

2 Timothy 1:15. "This thou knowest, that all those that are in Asia be turned away from me."] Dr. Doddridge paraphrases it thus. "Thou knowest this, that all those of Asia, who are at Rome, and were known to me by a profession of Christianity, are turned from me, and have proved treacherous friends, after all their forward pretenses."Ibid., 516.

2 Timothy 2:8.] That is, according [to] that gospel that I committed to thee when I laid on mine hands on thee. See 2 Timothy 2:13–14.

2 Timothy 2:13.] Dr. Doddridge renders it thus, "If we are unfaithful, he abideth faithful," and says in his notes, "So I think εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν should be rendered, as it stands opposed to πιστός." And he paraphrases the verse thus. "If we are unfaithful and false to our engagements, he abideth faithful, and will steadily adhere to those rules of judgment and distribution, which he hath so solemnly laid down in his word (Compare Matthew 10:33.). For we may be sure he cannot deny himself by frustrating his own public declaration."Ibid., 522 and n. d.

2 Timothy 2:18.] See no. 137.*Works, 15*, 89.

2 Timothy 2:19.] "Many critics have justly observed, that the word σφραγίς often signifies an inscription, or the mark made by a seal, as well as the seal itself. See Revelation 9:4. And the expression is here used with peculiar propriety, in allusion to the custom of engraving, upon some stones laid in the foundation of buildings, the name of the persons by whom, and the purposes for which, the structure is raised." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 5*, 526, n. a.

2 Timothy 3:16–17.] See Mastricht, pp. 17–18.Under the heading "De Sacra Scriptura," Mastricht writes, "Artificium illud *vivendi Deo*, cum non sit potentia *naturalis*, ad quam *non docti*; sed facti simus; verum facultas *acquisita*: regulam omnino exigit, qua dirigatur, & quidem *a Deo* praescriptam, prout jam ante monuimus: quam, praeter *vitam* Christi, & *conscientiam* propriam; supra in *verbo* Dei, seu *Scriptura* posuimus. Quae, ut *norma* est vivendi; sic communis etiam *complexus*, praeceptorum ac regularum, eo tendentium; quo nomine Theologiae *principium* indigitatur. Hujus contemplationem, superstruemus verbis, quae ex 2. ad Timoth. Cap. III. Vers. 16. 17. praemisimus." He also discusses the inspiration of Scripture and its varied uses, including doctrine, reproof, correction, and teaching, as well as its goals of piety, morality, and spiritual formation (*Theoretico-Practica Theologia* [Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715], pp. 17–18).

<!-- p. 1134 -->

2 Timothy 4:3. "After their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears."] Here are two expressions, viz. "heaping to themselves teachers after their lusts," and "having itching ears." 'Tis the same thing expressed in different words. The former expression denotes as much as that "their lusts are manifest in their hearing," or in the teachers and doctrines that they hear. The latter expression denotes that "their lusts work in their ears," which is the same thing with being manifest and exercised in their hearing. Here the lust of the heart is compared to an itch, that consists in an eager, restless appetite, but is no regular appetite, but a distemper of the body. So men's lusts are distempered, restless appetites of the soul.

2 Timothy 4:8. "At that day."] The day of judgment is called "THAT DAY," here, and 2 Timothy 1:12, and Luke 10:12.

2 Timothy 4:17. "Preaching might be fully known."] "Might be carried on with confidence"; so the original, πληροφορηθῇ, here signifies.

<!-- p. 1135 -->

### Titus

Titus 1:1. "According to the faith of God's elect."] "'For the faith.' This is the proper signification of κατὰ πίστιν, in this connection, which expresses the end to which his labors tended. Compare 1 Timothy 6:3. See *Raph. ex Xen., in loc*." So Doddridge.*Family Expositor, 5*, 559, n. a.

Titus 1:15. "Unto the pure all things are pure.] They have a taughtConjecture for unclear word. eye and a pure heart. They use and enjoy all unto the Lord, and give God thanks. They eat, and drink, and do all they do to the glory of God. But to others is nothing pure, for their mind and conscience is defiled. They eat and drink with conscience of an idol, as the same Apostle expresses himself elsewhere, i.e. every enjoyment is used with an idolatrous respect. With a view and regard, they are conscious to an evil design in what they do. And therefore their act as done by their minds is an evil act; 'tis against their light. Every act therefore is with a defiled conscience.

Titus 3:11. "Being condemned of himself."] Lardner, in vol. 6 of his *Credibility*, pp. 819–20, mentions the following interpretation as the interpretation of St. Cyprian and others. "A heretic is said to be condemned of himself, because (while a fornicator, an adulterer, a murderer, and other vicious persons, are cast out of the church by the priests), heretics pass sentence upon themselves, and of their own accord depart from the church: which departure is a condemnation passed upon them by their own consciences."Nathaniel Lardner, *Credibility of the Gospel History*, Pt. II, vol. 4 (1740, which is vol. 6), pp. 819–20. For more on Lardner, see *Works, 5*, 66–67.

<!-- p. 1136 -->

### Philemon

Philemon 6.] "The communication," etc.] Dr. Doddridge translates it, "the communion of thy faith."*Family Expositor, 5*, 591.

Philemon 11.] "In time past… unprofitable," etc.] Dr. Doddridge observes that the name "Onesimus" signifies "profit."Ibid., 594, n. c.

<!-- p. 1137 -->

### Hebrews

Hebrews 1:3. "Who being the brightness of his glory."] It was Christ, the second person of the Trinity, that was wont to appear of old in that effulgence of glory that was commonly called "the glory of the Lord."

"The express image of his person." χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. "That is, saith Leigh,Edward Leigh (1602–71), author of *Critica Sacra, or Philologicall and Theologicall Observations upon all the Greek Words of the New Testament in order alphabeticall*, &c (London, 1639). answering to the divine perfections, as the impression on the wax does the engraving of the seal. It is observable that Philo calls the *Logos*, χαρακτὴρ καὶ εἰκών θεοῦ." So Doddridge, *in locum*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 10, n. f. It seems to be well translated "express image," meaning an image that exactly answers the original, as the impression does the seal. But it may be observed that whatsoever is the express or exact image of a thing is, in the Apostle's sense, equivalent or of equal value with that thing, it having a full answerableness. This seems to be signified in Hebrews 10:1. "The law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices… make the comers thereunto perfect," intimating that if they had been the very image exactly answerable, they would have been equivalent, and might have answered the same purpose.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 1:6. "Again, when he bringeth," etc.] The Apostle has probably here some reference to the Psalms 97, where we have a prophecy of the Messiah's coming into the world, on which occasion it is said, Psalms 97:7, "Worship him, all ye gods." But fact or event (in which that prophecy was fulfilled), was whatJE deleted "actually." was at Christ's birth, that we have some intimation in the Luke 2, where we are told that on that occasion, there appeared "a multitude of the heavenly hosts, saying, Glory to God in the highest," etc. [Luke 2:13–14]. At that time, when the Son of God appeared a poor little infant in a stable and manger, then God said, Let all the angels of God worship him. And then the angels had a great trial of their obedience, greater than ever they had before.

<!-- p. 1138 -->

Hebrews 1:9. "Thou hast loved righteousness," etc.] "This refers to that unparalleled instance of the love of moral rectitude, which Christ hath given in becoming a sacrifice for sins, by his atonement doing more than ever hath been done by any rational agent towards displaying his love of righteousness, and hatred of iniquity." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 13, n. o. See Romans 8:3.

Hebrews 2:1. "Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed."] I.e. if Christ be so much greater than the angels, we ought to give "earnest heed," for the not giving heed to the word spoken by them was severely punished, as he observes in the next verse.

"Lest at any time we should let them slip." I.e. by not keeping them in practice, in the same sense as Christ speaks of keeping his commandment. We should keep it as a jewel committed to our care that we are apt to lose, is apt to slip from us. He that don't persevere in obedience, lets the command slip. The thing which the Apostle here warns against is apostasy, the same that he is abundant in warning against in other parts of this epistle (Hebrews 3:6, Hebrews 3:12–14; Hebrews 4:1, Hebrews 4:11; Hebrews 6 throughout; Hebrews 10:23, Hebrews 10:25–39; Hebrews 12:1–4, Hebrews 12:15–17, Hebrews 12:25–29; Hebrews 13:1, Hebrews 13:7–9, Hebrews 13:13–14, Hebrews 13:20–21.This paragraph is a later addition.

Hebrews 2:5. "For unto the angels."] The mentioning in the foregoing verse God's bearing those that heard Christ witness by "signs and wonders, and divers miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost," leads the Apostle to observe this honor, that Christ was above the angels, that God had put in subjection to him the world to come.

"Whereof we speak." In these words the Apostle probably has reference to what he had spoken before, Hebrews 1:2, of Christ's being "appointed heir of all things," and Hebrews 13:13, of God's saying to him, "Sit on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool."This paragraph is a later addition.

"World to come." See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 3, pp. 162–65.Kidder discusses this and other terms used by Jewish writers and by the New Testament for the days of the Messiah, or the time of Christ's appearance. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 162–65. See "Miscellanies," no. 1260b.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 23*, 196–98.

"Put in subjection the world to come." The renewed state of things brought to pass by Christ, called "the new heavens and new earth," is here called "the world to come," although already come in its beginnings.

<!-- p. 1139 -->

Even as the blessings of Christ's kingdom and of this new creation are called "good things to come," ἀγαθά μέλλοντα (Hebrews 9:11 and Hebrews 10:1), though they were already come in their beginnings. Note that the time when Christ came, and offered up himself, and ascended into heaven is called "the end of the world" (Hebrews 9:26), συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων, "the end of ages," the finishing as it were of the old world. So the kingdom of heaven, the new state of things that followed, is called "the world to come," the new world, the future or succeeding ages, μέλλοντος αἰῶνος (Hebrews 6:5), and here, οἰκουμένην μέλλουσαν.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 2:6.] See notes on Psalms 8:6 ff.

Hebrews 2:7. "Thou madest him a little lower than the angels."] Mr. Charnock understands it as 'tis in the margin.I.e. margin of the KJV. See vol. 2 of his *Works*, p. 1093.Charnock, "A Discourse of the Necessity of Christ's Exaltation," *Works, II*, 1093. βραχύ τι, "a little while," a short space. Thus the place in the Psalms 8 here referred to, as they are according to the mind of the Holy Ghost to be understood in different senses of both Adams Hebrews 2:4], so this word, which is capable of two interpretations, viz. a "little degree" and a "little while," is to be applied in one sense to one, and in another to the other.

Hebrews 2:8. "But now we see not yet all things put under him."] In these words the Apostle has respect to what he had said before, Hebrews 2:5, signifying that it was "the world to come," or a certain future state of things, wherein all things were to be subjected to Christ.

"In subjection under him." See Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. 118e–119a.This reference is a separate entry. Kidder features prophecies in the Old Testament that speak of all nations serving the Messiah, and he declares those prophecies have been fulfilled "in a great measure" in Christ's kingdom that is spread over the world. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 118–19.

Hebrews 2:11. "For both he that sanctifieth… are all of one."] This the Apostle says here because he had called believers "sons," in the foregoing verse. "They are all of one," two ways: they are all of one heavenly Father God, and all of one earthly father Adam.

Hebrews 2:16.] The particle "for" connects the verse with the fourteenth, with these words, "Forasmuch as the children are partakers of flesh and

<!-- p. 1140 -->

blood, he also took part of the same." The Apostle mentions the angels here because he had been speaking in the foregoing part of the chapter of Christ's being made "lower than the angels" Hebrews 2:9],The remainder of this paragraph is a later addition. and of the privilege of the saints above the angels, in the latter part of the foregoing chapter, in that they, being united to Christ, that was so much above the angels. The angels were all their "ministering spirits" [Hebrews 1:14]. What the Apostle says in this verse shows the unspeakable and infinite privilege of the saints above the angels. So that 'tis the elect angels that the Apostle has the most direct respect to in this verse.

Hebrews 3:1.] "Both are properly mentioned, 'Apostle and High Priest,' as the author was to show, that as an apostle, Christ was superior to Moses, and as an high priest, to Aaron. He is called an apostle as sent from God, with full commission for the important affair he came to transact, apostle signifying messenger." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 24, n. b.

"Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus." Not only the Apostle's brethren, but Christ's brethren, as in the Hebrews 2:11 and Hebrews 2:17. "Partakers of the heavenly calling," not only partakers with the Apostle, and partakers one with another, but partakers with Christ in his heavenly calling as an high priest, for no man taketh this honor to himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron. Christians are spoken of, in the Hebrews 2:17, as the brethren of him who is "a merciful and faithful high priest." And they are not only so, but they are also partakers of his heavenly calling as high priest, for they also are priests unto God through him, and as united with him. 1 Peter 2:4–5, "To whom coming, as unto a living stone,… ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood." And so 1 Peter 2:9. "Ye are a royal priesthood, an holy nation." So Revelation 1:6 and Revelation 5:10; and Exodus 19:5–6; Isaiah 61:6. They are priests with Christ, as they are partakers of his heavenly calling and his holy unction. 1 John 2:20, "But ye have an unction from the Holy One." Believers are fellows with Christ in his anointing, as in the Hebrews 1:9. "God hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows." They are partakers with him in his unction, as the precious ointment that was poured on Aaron's head ran "down to the skirts of his garments" (Psalms 133:2).This paragraph is a separate entry.

<!-- p. 1141 -->

Hebrews 3:4.] By this he argues that Moses was not the builder of the house, because he was a man, and this house not such a house as men build, but such an one as he only is the builder of that builds all things, who is God.

Hebrews 3:5. "For a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after."] All that was said and done by Moses, and indeed throughout the Mosaical dispensation, which we have account of in the Old Testament, was chiefly for a testimony of those things that should "be spoken after," to introduce the gospel which Christ was to reveal.

Hebrews 3:6-4:11.] See no. 309.*Works, 13*, 283–84.

Hebrews 3:12. "In departing," etc.] Having respect to that which he quotes from the Psalmist, in the Hebrews 3:10, "They do always err in their hearts," etc.

Hebrews 3:13.] "While it is called today."] In this expression there is probably reference to that time then near at hand when the nation in general, the unbelieving part of 'em, were to [be] given up to awful destruction, when God would swear in his wrath against them, as he did against their forefathers in the wilderness.

Hebrews 3:14. "Partakers of Christ."] It might have been rendered, "Christ's partners," for so the word *metochoi*μέτοχοι. is used in Hebrews 1:9 and Luke 5:7. So that 'tis the same as if it had been said, "partakers with Christ," which is what the Apostle means particularly, "partakers with him" in his rest. Compare Hebrews 3:11 and Hebrews 4:5, Hebrews 4:9–10.

Hebrews 4:1–11.] See no. 309.Ibid. See also note on John 5:17.

Hebrews 4:2.] Dr. Watts, in his *Orthodoxy and Charity*, says that the words should be translated, "To them was the gospel preached as well as unto us." See p. 4.Isaac Watts, *Orthodoxy and Charity united: In several Reconciling Essays on the Law and Gospel, Faith and Works* (London, 1745). This reference to Watts derives from "Essay I. The Substance or Matter of the Gospel" (pp. 1–34). Here see Taylor's *Key*, p. 118, margin.Taylor writes, "The Apostle runs a Parallel between the State of the antient *Jews* in the Wilderness, and that of *Christians* under the Gospel, while in this World." Both had a promise given to them; both had glad tidings preached to them; for both, the grace given to them was "to produce Faith and Obedience" (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, p. 118, n.).

<!-- p. 1142 -->

"For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them," etc.] Dr. Doddridge renders it, "'For we are made partakers of good tidings, as they also were,' i.e. of the promised rest." And in his note on the preceding verse, he observes, "The example is most suitable, being taken from their own ancestors, the evil being the same, namely, unbelief, the time resembling it just after the establishment of a new constitution, and the consequence the same, the exclusion from rest. The superior dignity of Christ above Moses, and the superior excellence of heaven above Canaan, greatly confirm the force of the argument."This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 6*, 32 and n. d.

Hebrews 4:3–5.] In order to understand the Apostle's reasoning in this place, it must be taken notice of that by the expression of "entering into my rest," the Apostle understands entering in with God into rest, and being partakers with him of his rest, his comfort and refreshment (Exodus 31:17).

Hebrews 4:3. The Apostle argues that we, if we believe, may enter into rest, inasmuch as God's swearing that the unbelievers should not enter implied that if they had believed, they might have entered. "Although the works were finished from the foundation of the world," i.e. that don't hinder that God's rest was so long ago, inasmuch there is another rest of God from the work of redemption, as the Apostle observes in the Hebrews 4:10.

Hebrews 4:5. "And in this place again, If they shall enter into *my rest*."] In the expression, "my rest," in the Psalms 95, the Apostle plainly understands something besides the rest which God had provided, or the rest that he had promised. He understands the rest that God himself enjoys. For God's rest, spoken of in the preceding verse (with which these words are connected), was God's rest in this sense. And so in the improvement the Apostle makes of these words in Psalms 95 in the following verses, he exhorts Christians to seek to enter into Christ's rest in that sense, viz. to seek to be partakers of the rest that Christ enjoys, that he entered into when he had finished and ceased from his works, as God did from his.

Hebrews 4:6.] See Taylor's *Key*, p. 117e.Taylor notes, "και, 'and,' in *Greek*, as well as [ו] in *Hebrew*, sometimes signifies [though]." Therefore Hebrews 4:6 should be translated, "*Seeing then* it is so, *it remains*, or follows, *that some must enter into it; though they, to whom it was first preached, entered not in because of Unbelief*" (*Paraphrase with Notes on the Epistle to the Romans*, p. 117, n.).

Hebrews 4:7. "Today, after so long a time, as it is said, today."] The Apostle adds these words, "after so long a time," but argues that that is implied, "as it

<!-- p. 1143 -->

is said, today," or because "it is so expressed, today," which he intimates is as much as if it had been said, "Even today, after so long a time."

Hebrews 4:7–9.] See note on Psalms 95:7–8.

Hebrews 4:11. "Into that rest."] That is, into Christ's rest. Be partaker with him in the rest that he rested.

Hebrews 4:12.] It is not meant that the word pierces to the dividing the soul from the spirit, the joints from the marrow, as some have supposed, which is very unintelligible, but dividing asunder these things themselves. The word in its powerful efficacy in mortification and conversion, emptying the soul of itself, and parting it from sin, and weaning it from the world, and bringing to a thorough self-denial or self-renunciation, does as it were cut the soul asunder. 'Tis an exceeding difficult thing for a man thus to renounce sin, and the world, and himself. It is like laying down his life; the soul in this work is as it were cut asunder. The joints, the parts of the body that are naturally closely joined, are parted. Yea, the very bone itself is as it were divided through the midst of the marrow.

"For the word of God is quick and powerful," etc. It seems probable by the context that here is an allusion to the word which God spake at Mt. Sinai, with thunders, and lightnings, and a voice too piercing, awful, and tremendous that the people could not endure it, the same word that is spoken of, Hebrews 12:19–20. And the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of WORDS, which voice they that heard entreated that the WORD should not be spoken to them anymore, for they could not endure that which was commanded. That penetrating awful word presignified the amazing wrath that the disobedient would be exposed to; so more plainly and awfully does the word spoken by Christ. See Hebrews 12:25:29.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 4:14. "A great high priest."] See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. me and 112a–b.Kidder declares that Jesus is "a priest of the highest order" following his ascension, a priest after the order of Melchizedek. The high priest of old was but a type of Christ as high priest. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 111–12.

Hebrews 5:7. When he had offered up prayers and supplications."] See note on Luke 22:44, no. 255, and no. 311.*Works, 15*, 172–75, 285. These two "Scripture" references are later additions.

<!-- p. 1144 -->

"Offered up… with strong crying and tears," etc. Job, when he did the part of a mediator or priest with God for his friends, offered prayers and sacrifices together.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 5:8. "Obedience by the things which he suffered."] Isaiah 50:5–6.

Hebrews 5:9. "Eternal salvation unto all them that obey him."] See no. 142.*Works, 15*, 91.

Hebrews 6:1–3.] See no. 74.Ibid., 70–71.

Hebrews 6:3. "And this will we do, if God permit."] And this the Apostle actually proceeds to do in the beginning of Hebrews 7, where he resumes his subject of Christ's priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, which he broke off from in the Hebrews 6:11 because of weakness in knowledge. And all that is Hebrews 6:11–20 of the chapter comes in by way of digression.

Hebrews 6:4–6.] What is meant by their being "enlightened," etc., see no. 74; Ibid. and how they were guilty of the sin against the Holy Ghost, see no. 227.Ibid., 176–77.

That when the Apostle speaks of them who "have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost," he has a special respect to them that had received the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Ghost, is evident from this. The Apostle here has respect to the same persons that he spake of in the Hebrews 6:2, but there he is speaking of them that had been the subjects of the laying on of hands, which was a rite used in conferring the Holy Ghost in his extraordinary gifts.This paragraph is a separate entry.

See no. 299.*Works, 15*, 272. See note on Hebrews 6:8 infra. That the persons here spoken of were such as never were regenerated, see "Scripture," no. 501b.This sentence and the two preceding short references are later additions. *Works, 15*, 598–99.

"For it [is] impossible for those who were once enlightened," etc. It may be observed that those of the Jews or Hebrews who were unbelievers were wont to ascribe the miraculous operations of Christ and his followers, which were the extraordinary influence of the Holy Ghost, to the

<!-- p. 1145 -->

devil. They had no other way to account for them on their principles. And therefore we may well suppose that those of the Christian Hebrews, who themselves had partook of those extraordinary gifts and operations of the Spirit, that apostatized, and renounced Christianity, and again joined with the unbelieving persecuting Jews (for such are especially spoken of here), I say, we may well suppose that they ascribed those miraculous gifts and powers, which they themselves had while professing Christians, to the devil, as other unbelieving Jews did who were generally most malignant, spiteful enemies to Christ and all Christians. And therefore they were guilty of the very same thing with those scribes and Pharisees who ascribed Christ's miracles to Beelzebub, who were guilty of unpardonable blasphemy against the Holy Ghost.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 6:6. "They crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame."] Those that crucified Christ would have committed the unpardonable sin had they crucified him, and openly reproached him and the Spirit he taught and acted by, against light, as these the Apostle speaks of do. ['Tis] probable the Apostle in these words may have some respect to those words of Christ when they were crucifying him, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" [Luke 23:34], intimating that if they had known, there would be no forgiveness for them.

Hebrews 6:8.] The malice of those apostates and persecutors who committed the unpardonable sin is with special fitness compared to briers and thorns. See Canticles 2:2, Ezekiel 28:24, Micah 7:4, Ezekiel 2:6, Isaiah 10:17, 2 Samuel 23:6–7.

Hebrews 6:10. "For God is not unrighteous to forget," etc.] This is spoken in the same sense as that inMS: "in the." 1 John 1:9, "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins." God's righteousness obliges him to reward the saints' good works; then it obliges him to forgive sinners upon repentance. See note on Nehemiah 9:8, and note on Isaiah 45:23.

Hebrews 6:11.] Here the words, "to the end," are to be joined not with the immediately preceding words, "the full assurance of hope," but those going before, "show the same diligence." The Apostle, in the preceding verse, had observed the labor and diligence which had appeared in them. He here exhorts that this be continued "to the end," in order to

<!-- p. 1146 -->

the full assurance of hope. The Apostle is still pursuing the advice he began the chapter with, to avoid apostasy, and to go on to perfection.

Hebrews 6:12. "Inherit the promises."] An evidence that those saints that are dead are in a state of reward, and not in a state of inactivity and insensibility, for the wordκληρονομέω. translated "inherit" signifies to possess by inheritance. And 'tis also hereby evident that they ben't only reserved in a state of rest and repose in order to their promised reward, but have that happiness and glory already in possession in a great degree, as also appears by Revelation 14:13. See "Miscellanies," no. 1280.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 23*, 226.

Hebrews 6:15. "Obtained the promise."] This is an evidence that the saints in heaven are acquainted with the affairs of the church here on earth, and also that a considerable part of their happiness consists in seeing the dispensations and works of God's grace towards the church on earth, and the discoveries of his glory therein. For how could Abraham be said to have "obtained the promise" of multiplying his seed, after he had by faith expected it, and patiently waited for it, unless he had seen it, and so enjoyed it, or rejoiced in it? Though Abraham obtained Isaac, a pledge of the promise while he lived, yet it seems that something further is here intended by Hebrews 6:12.

Hebrews 6:19. "Hope we have as an anchor of the soul."] No. 284;*Works, 15*, 240–42. note on Romans 15:12–15.This reference is a later addition.

Hebrews 7:2.] By this it is evident that the Holy Ghost sometimes intends to teach us divine mysteries by the signification of names.

Hebrews 7:3. "Without father, without mother."] "It has been observed by many… that several ancient writers of character among the heathens speak of persons' being born of no father, or without a father, when they mean only to express by it that their father was unknown.… Eisner hath some remarkable quotations to show that it was usual among the Greeks to say of a person, that he was ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ, 'without father, without mother,' when his parents were unknown.… But the reason in Eisner's

<!-- p. 1147 -->

opinion is that there was no trace of his parentage in the sacerdotal genealogies, he being without priestly descent, ἀγενεαλόγητος, as it immediately follows." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 55–56, n. b.

Hebrews 7:16. "Who is made, not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life."] "Who therefore, we may assure ourselves, is made and constituted, not according or in regard to the law of the carnal commandment, which contained so many things of an external and comparatively of a carnal nature, and which considered men as dwelling in mortal flesh, and so to succeed each other, but according to the undecaying power of an indissoluble and endless life." Doddridge, Paraphrase.Ibid., 59.

Hebrews 8:1. "Set on the right hand of the throne."] See no. 310.*Works, 15*, 284–85.

Hebrews 8:5. "According to the pattern showed thee in the mount."] The Apostle means that that mount represented heaven. He was charged to make 'em according to the pattern showed in the mount, signifying that they were to be images and shadows of heavenly things, "patterns of things in the heavens," as Hebrews 9:23.

Hebrews 8:9. "Continued not in my covenant."] This refers especially to their making the golden calf.

Hebrews 9:1. "Then verily the first *covenant*."] "Our translators strangely supply the word 'covenant' instead of 'tabernacle,' whereas most copies read σκηνή, 'tabernacle,' and that undoubtedly suits the connection best." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 71, n. a.

Hebrews 9:4. "Which had the golden censer."] See Owen, on the place, pp. 313e and 314.Owen argues that the term θυμιαήριον may be translated "altar" as well as "censer," referring to overlaid with gold (Hebrews 6–10).

"The golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded." Both these represented Christ with regard to that spiritual nourishment, life, and refreshment we have by him. By the manna, the children of Israel

<!-- p. 1148 -->

had food. By the rod that smote the rock once and again, they were supplied with drink. Here was a memorial both of their bread from heaven and water out of the rock.

"Wherein was the golden pot that had manna." See note on Revelation 2:17, no. 262.This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 15*, 208–209.

Hebrews 9:11. "Good things *to come*."] In this expression is reference to that in Hebrews 9:9, "which was a figure for the time *then present*." "That is to say, not of this building", τοῦτ᾽ ἔστιν οὐ ταύτης [τῆς] κτίσεως "not of this creation." The Apostle did [not] express his full meaning in the foregoing clause, "a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands." And therefore he explains himself here to intend something further that these words taken strictly imply. He signifies that he intends not merely a "tabernacle, not made with hands," but not brought into being according to the common course of things in this old creation, but made by God (as the human nature of Christ was the tabernacle here meant) in an extraordinary, supernatural manner. Thus the Apostle seems to use the phrase, "not made with hands," in 2 Corinthians 5:1. This tabernacle was not formed according to the course of things in this old creation, but it is of the new creation, which the Apostle often calls "the world to come," the things of which he in this verse calls "good things to come." See reasons confirming this interpretation in Poole's *Synopsis*,*Synopsis Criticorum, IV* (London, 1676), Pt. 2, cols. 1316–17. and Owen, *in loc*., pp. 363e and 364a–b.Owen points to the conception of Christ as an act of divine power without parallel whereby the Virgin Mary conceived apart from natural generation (Hebrews 6–10).

Hebrews 9:13. "Sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh."] That is, cleansed from legal, typical impurities, which were external impurities, or impurities that come by external things, such as touching the dead body of a man, etc. Or if "the blood of bulls" were offered for sin, the purification was only with respect to what was external. They might be admitted to external privileges after, that they might not before.

These ceremonial purifications had no proper and direct influence to any purification, but only with regard to what was external and temporal. Dr. Doddridge on Hebrews 9:9 of this chapter says, "The Mosaic sacrifices were never intended to expiate offenses to such a degree, as to deliver the sinner from the final judgment of God in another world, but merely to make his peace with the government under which he then was, and to furnish

<!-- p. 1149 -->

him with a pardon, pleadable against any prosecution, which might be commenced against him in their courts of justice, or any exclusion from the privilege of drawing near to God, as one externally at peace with him, in the solemnities of his temple worship."This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 6*, 74, n. f.

Hebrews 9:14.] The Apostle is probably led, when speaking of sins in this place, to make use of the appellation "dead works" from allusion to pollutions by dead bodies, for the cleansing from which the ashes of the heifer, spoken of in the preceding verse, were appropriated. See Numbers 19.

Hebrews 9:15. "For the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament."] Dr. Doddridge renders ἐπί not "under," but "against," and translates the verse thus: "And he is in this respect the mediator of a new covenant, that death being undergone, for the redemption of transgressions, against the former covenant," etc.*Family Expositor, 6*, 78.

Hebrews 9:15–18.] See what I have written under the title of "Shadows of Divine Things."*Works, 11*, 60–61.

Hebrews 9:19–22.] It may be inquired what it typifies when not only persons, but utensils were purged with the blood of sacrifices? How are anything but persons purged by the blood of Christ when other things are not capable of guilt? *Ans*. "It denotes that all things are sanctified and pure, to those whose souls partake of the atonement of Christ, and whose sins are remitted through his bloody death; but to a guilty and defiled soul and conscience, everything is defiled." See Watts, third volume of *Sermons*, p. 134.Isaac Watts, *Sermons on Various Subjects, Divine and Moral: With a Sacred Hymn suited to each Subject. In Three Volumes, Design'd for the Use of Christian Families, as well as for the Hours of Devout Retirement* (3 vols. London, 1721–29), *2*, 134.

How to reconcile the account here given with the account given by Moses, see Owen, *in loc*., pp. 425c–429.This sentence is a later addition. Hebrews 6–10.

Hebrews 9:23. "Purified with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these."] "It may perhaps seem strange, that celestial things should be spoken of as needing to be purified and cleansed. But

<!-- p. 1150 -->

it is to be considered, that as the sacred dwelling and vessels were esteemed to be polluted by the Israelites, who in various degrees had access to them, so heaven would have been as it were polluted by the entrance of such sinners as we into it, had not the blood of Christ intervened." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 81, n. f.

Hebrews 9:24.] Concerning the holy of holies, a type of heaven, see Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, pp. 113–15.Kidder cites ancient Jewish and rabbinic sources to support the notion that learned Jews regarded the holy of holies as "a type of the highest heavens." *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 1, 113–15.

Hebrews 9:26. "The end of the world."] See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 3, pp. 162–65.Kidder links this phrase with others used by ancient Hebrews and writers of the New Testament to refer to the days of the Messiah. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 162–65.

"At the end of the world." "'At the conclusion of the ages.' So συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων is most exactly rendered, meaning the last of the dispensations God ever intended to give mankind."This paragraph is a separate entry. Doddridge, *Family Expositor, 6*, 82, n. g.

Hebrews 9:27–28.] See Dr. Owen, *in loc*., pp. 467–68, in places marked thus | in the margin.JE's copy of Owen has not been located. Owen distinguishes the "particular judgment" of individuals following death from the "general judgment" at the second appearance of Christ. At the latter, believers are freed from condemnation of the law by Christ's offering, his suffering and death (Hebrews 6–10).

Hebrews 9:28. "Appear the second time."] No. 312.*Works, 15*, 285–86.

"Shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation." "I doubt not, but there is indeed, as LimborchPhilippus van Limborch (1633–1712), a Dutch Arminian theologian and author of *Commentarius in Acta Apostolorum et in Epistolas ad Romanos et ad Hebrœos* (1711). supposes, an allusion here to the high priest coming out to bless the people, who were waiting for him in the temple, when the great day of atonement was over, and as he then appeared in his golden garments, whereas before he had officiated in the plain dress of a common priest, and as the trumpet of the jubilee on that year sounded to proclaim the commencement of that happy period. There is not perhaps an image that can enter into the mind of men, more

<!-- p. 1151 -->

suitable to convey the grand idea which the Apostle intended to convey by it, than this would be to a Jew, who well knew the grand solemnity to which it referred." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 82, n. i. See Leviticus 9:22–23, Numbers 6:23–26, Deuteronomy 21:5.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Hebrews 10:1. "A shadow of good things to come."] No. 288.*Works, 15*, 247–48.

Hebrews 10:1–3.] Concerning the argument for the insufficiency of the ancient sacrifices from their being often offered. The Wise Man argues the vanity of all earthly enjoyments, and that temporal food is not man's true good, from that, that the occasions for eating still return. If a man eats, yet the need of eating returns. Satisfaction is not obtained; his need and his appetite remains. The demands of nature are not answered, so but that still it continues demanding, so that after a man has repeated his eating from day to day many years, yet he needs, and his nature craves, as much as when he first came into the world. Ecclesiastes 6:7, "All the labor of man is for his mouth, yet the appetite, or" (as in the original)תִמָּלֵא לא וְגֵם־הַנֶּפֶשׁ "*the soul*, is not filled." See also Ecclesiastes 1:5–9, with the context. The argument is of the same sort with that which the Apostle here makes use of to show the vanity of the ancient sacrifices, and their insufficiency to answer the end of a true atonement, that they did not satisfy because the demands of justice still remained, and its appetite returned, as in the other case the demands of nature. They were never able to make the comers thereto perfect. The occasions of offering them returned continually. And therefore if Solomon's argument be good, the Apostle's is certainly good also.

Hebrews 10:5. "A body hast thou prepared me."] See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 2, 89–92, Kidder argues that the Apostle's phrase is equivalent in sense to the Psalmist's, "mine ears hast thou opened." In support of that contention, he discusses the meaning of "boring the ear" of a servant who refused his liberty. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 2, 89–92. See also JE's sermon, *The Sacrifice of Christ Acceptable*, on Psalms 40:6–8, in *Works, 14*, 442–43. and Owen, *in loc*., p. 28b–e.Owen discusses the use of the ear as a metaphor for obedience and compliance with the commands of God, the ear being the means of receiving those instructions. The Apostle's citation of Psalms 40:6 frames this observation. By synecdoche, in Scripture the ears are put for the whole body. God the Father prepared a body for Christ whereby he was free to do the will of God (Hebrews 6–10).

<!-- p. 1152 -->

"The ingenious and learned Mr. *Saurin* supposes the Seventy there…"JE deleted this unfinished entry from *Family Expositor, 6*, 87, n. e, with two "x's." Jacques Saurin (1677–1730), pastor of the French church at The Hague, was the author of theological treatises, including *Discours historiques, critiques, theologiques et maraux* (1720), and numerous volumes of sermons, translated from French to English.

Hebrews 10:10.] The meaning of this, and how these words, with those in the two preceding verses, prove that we are saved by the positive righteousness of Christ, as well as by his atonement, see "Miscellanies," no. 1106.*Works, 20*, 488.

Hebrews 10:12. "Sat down on the right hand of God."] No. 310.Ibid., *2*, 284–85.

Hebrews 10:20. "Through the veil."] No. 340.Ibid., 324–25.

Hebrews 10:22. "Our bodies washed with pure water."] See Owen, *in loc*., p. 65c–e.Owen rejects the view held by some, that this passage refers to the ordinance of baptism required before admission to the church. Rather the expression of washing the body is figurative and points to "*the assistance of the Sanctifying Spirit*" in keeping and preserving believers "from all outward and actual Sins," for the body is the instrument of such deeds (Hebrews 6–10). "Referring to the custom of washing their bodies in clean water, before they went to worship at the temple, especially on their solemn days." Doddridge, *in loc*.The Doddridge citation is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 6*, 92, n. d.

Hebrews 10:25. "Not forsaking the assembling ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another daily, and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."] The exhorting here spoken [of] is not private exhorting in conversation, but public exhorting in their assemblies, as seems manifest by the connection of this latter part of the verse with the former part. And yet no argument can be drawn from it in favor of laymen's public exhorting in the manner of many in these days, which will appear by the following considerations. 1. If the Apostle only means thatJE deleted "certain of." those officers among them, whose special business it was to act as teachers and exhorters, should daily exhort their brethren, it is not disagreeable to Scripture phrase for the Apostle to express himself as he does, "exhort one another." We have a parallel instance, Hosea 4:4, "Let

<!-- p. 1153 -->

no man strive, nor reprove another, for thy people are as they that strive with the priest," where though the Prophet speaks of one's "reproving another," he means that it would be in vain for the priests to exhort the people whose business it was to teach and exhort them. 2. The Apostle might the rather use this manner of speech, "exhort one another," to signify the public exhortations to be given by [those] who were especially called to that business, because in that day there were not only their ordinary officers or pastors who were exhorters, but many of their congregations endowed with extraordinary gifts of teaching and exhorting, who were a kind of extraordinary officers in the church of Christ, that were wont publicly to teach and exhort in the exercise of those gifts. But yet this will by no means justify their public exhorting, who are neither ordinary nor extraordinary officers in the church.

Hebrews 10:25, Hebrews 10:27. "But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries."] There is a connection between this verse and the Hebrews 10:25 ("Not forsaking the assembling yourselves together, and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."). The "judgment and fiery indignation" the Apostle speaks of was to be on that day that he then spoke of as approaching. They should not forsake the assemblies of Christians, because the day was approaching wherein judgment and indignation should devour those that were not found among Christians in their assemblies. The opposite or adverse party that persecuted them should be destroyed by it. This was remarkably fulfilled on the adverse Hebrews on that day that was then in all senses in a near approach, even the day of the destruction of Jerusalem.

Hebrews 10:25–29.] How such as are here spoken of committed the sin against the Holy Ghost, see notes on Hebrews 6:4–6, no. 227.*Works, 15*, 176–77.

"For if we sin willfully," etc. Hebrews 10:26]. See Owen, *in loc*., pp. 76–77, 80–85, at places marked in the margin.This paragraph is a separate entry. Owen discusses at length the Apostle's account of the willful sinning of those who once received the truth, stating that the voluntary abandonment of the gospel and its dudes is the highest sin. The indignation of God with apostates will manifest itself in a fiery final judgment. Such adversaries maliciously oppose the doctrine and truth of the gospel. Their sin will be punished by death without mercy, which judgment by God is righteous (Hebrews 6–10).

<!-- p. 1154 -->

Hebrews 10:26. "Sin willfully," etc.] By sinning after coming to" the knowledge of the truth," the Apostle means apostatizing from Christianity after we are come to the knowledge of it, as is evident by the context, particularly by the Hebrews 10:23 and Hebrews 10:25, and by the latter part of the chapter. So sometimes the word "sinning" is used, as particularly in 1 John 3:9. "Whosoever is born of God sinneth not, for his seed remaineth in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God," i.e. he cannot fall away or apostatize, as many that those that the apostle John wrote [to] were acquainted with, had done. But they remained Christians, because the Seed of God, of which they were begotten and became Christians, remained in them.

"Sin willfully." The Apostle means the same as with proud malice, or "with an high hand," in Numbers 15:30–31. The phrase in the originalרָמָה בְּיָד is "with an high hand," or rather "hand lifted up," as of one going to strike another. The same wordיָד וַיָּרֶם is used, 1 Kings 11:26, "He lift up his hand against the king." But he has here reference to that place in the law of Moses, which he speaks of, 1 Kings 11:28. See no. 230.*Works, 15*, 179–81. See Mastricht, p. 362, col. 1, §13.In Bk. 4, ch. 3, under the title "De Peccato Actuali," Mastricht writes, "XIII. *Quinto exprincipio*, est vel ex *ignorantia*, Acts 3:17. 1 Corinthians 2:8. 1 Timothy 1:13. Quando peccator *ignoratse* peccare: vel ex *infirmitale* Galatians 4:1. Hebrews 5:2. quando peccator tentationi alicui *succumbit*; vel ex *malitia* seu elata manu Numbers 15:27. Numbers 15:28. Numbers 15:30." (*Theoretico-Practica Theologia* [Ed. nova, Trajecti ad Rhenum & Amstelodami, 1715]). See "Miscellanies," no. 475, towards the end.This paragraph is a separate entry. This sentence is a later addition. *Works, 13*, 521–22.

Hebrews 10:29. "And hath counted the blood of the covenant wherewith he was sanctified."] There are these things that satisfy me, either that by him that was sanctified by "the blood of the covenant" is meant Christ himself, and that the Apostle alludes to the law of Moses where it was commanded that Aaron and his son should be hallowed with the blood of the sacrifice (Exodus 29:21), or if he intends the person himself that despises it, that he intends only a sacramental sanctifying, alluding to Moses'sprinkling the blood of the covenant on all the people, thereby sealing the covenant (Exodus 24), viz. that these expressions here seem evidently to be taken of those laws, the expression of "blood of the covenant," and that of "an unholy thing," and that he treats throughout this whole book of those laws, and here speaks of Moses' law, as in the foregoing verse. It showed the profaneness of him that despised Moses'law or covenant,

<!-- p. 1155 -->

that he despised it though consecrated with blood, and after it had been sealed by sprinkling blood on the people. He showed a contempt of that blood by which it had been sealed, as though it had not been an holy thing. So the covenant of grace is sealed by the blood of Christ in baptism, and the person sacramentally sanctified. He therefore that despises Christ, he profanes that blood, as though he accounted it "an unholy thing." See "Miscellanies," no. 689, especially §6.This reference and the following paragraph are later additions. *Works, 18*, 255–56.

"Hath done despite to the Spirit of grace." The word for "hath done despite," in the original is ἐνυβρίσας, which signifies "hath reproached in a petulant, proud, and insolent manner." See "Miscellanies," no. 703.*Works, 18*, 309–14.

Hebrews 10:33. "While ye were made a gazingstock" (a public spectacle) "by reproaches and afflictions."] "Like men exposed on a theater as infamous." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 98.

Hebrews 10:37. "For yet a little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry."] It can't be justly inferred from these words that the Apostle expected Christ's last coming to judgment in that generation. All that can reasonably be understood by them than this was that the time of their sufferings was short, and it would be but a little while before they should be wholly delivered from all their enemies and their oppressions, and should receive the recompense of the reward they hoped for. This appears both by the context and drift of what the Apostle here says, and also by the place referred to in the Old Testament. For if this and the next verse be compared with Habakkuk 2:3–4, it will be exceeding manifest that the Apostle refers to what is there said, where God says by the Prophet, "The vision is for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it, because it will surely come, it will not tarry. Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him, but the just shall live by his faith." The thing that it is there said will come and not tarry is God's people's deliverance from the oppression of their enemies, especially from the Babylonish captivity, as appears by the context.

Hebrews 10:38. "Now the just shall live by faith; but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him."] This whole verse is a quotation of or reference

<!-- p. 1156 -->

to Habakkuk 2:4, "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him, but the just shall live by his faith." "We render the phrase in Habakkuk, 'lifted up.' And it is observable, that the alteration of a single letterעפלה to עפל changes the reading into this sense, in which the Seventy have taken it." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 100, n. k.

Hebrews 11:1.] See no. 107.*Works, 15*, 81. The word ὑπόστασις here used signifies "confidence" in 2 Corinthians 9:4, and 2 Corinthians 11:17, and Hebrews 3:14. Concerning the meaning of the word "substance," or ὑπόστασις, in this, see Owen, *in loc*., pp. 3–5, at places marked in the margin.This sentence and the preceding sentence are later additions. The term ὑπόστασις, according to Owen, rendered "substance," refers more properly to a "*real subsistence* (of nature)… in contradiction unto appearing Phantasms." The result is confidence without fear in the believer who is the subject of justifying faith, which is the saving faith of the elect. The "things hoped for" are "all things of present Grace and future Glory" promised by God. They have real subsistence for the person of faith (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 11:3.] See Owen, *in loc*., p. 12 and p. 14, at places marked in the margin.Owen asserts the instrumental role faith plays in assuring believers that the world was created "out of nothing, which is contrary to the most received Principle of Natural Reason," i.e. that "nothing comes of nothing." The believer gains this understanding by assent to divine revelation in the word of God. Owen denies any "*preexisting material Cause*" involved with creation, identifying the power of God as the only "*efficient Cause*," responsible first for producing the chaotic mass of substance out of nothing, and men framing all things in beauty and order (Hebrews 11–13).

Hebrews 11:4.] See note on Genesis 4:3–4, "Scripture," no. 453.*Works, 15*, 533–34.

"And by it he being dead yet speaketh."JE applied this text to David Brainerd in the Appendix to the "memoirs of his life" derived from his "private writings." He hoped that Brainerd might "still be as it were the instrument of much promoting the interest of religion in this world." See *Works, 7*, 540. See Owen, *in loc*., pp. 20–21, at the place marked in the margin.Owen ascribes multiple consequences to the declaration concerning the faith of Abel, who "yet speaketh" after his death. Many interpreters point to Abel's fame and reputation in later generations as the meaning. Owen, however, maintains that the Apostle intends that the blood of Abel speaks from the ground. "*There is a Voice in all innocent blood shed by violence*." Thus murders are avenged "sooner or later by God himself." This statement is also a pledge that God, "in due time," will punish "murderous Persecutors" of the church, which is "instructive unto Faith and Patience in suffering" for believers (Hebrews 11–13). Agreeable to the Doctor's exposition is Revelation 6:9–11 and Revelation 8:3–4.

<!-- p. 1157 -->

Hebrews 11:5–6. "Before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God, for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."] The Apostle refers to that testimony which the Scripture gives of Enoch, that he "walked with God" [Genesis 5:22], which expression implies friendship, and friendly intercourse, and mutual complacence. For how can two walk together, except they be agreed? And therefore the Apostle might well say, that "he had this testimony, that he pleased God." And he most properly observes that there is no pleasing God in this sense, no maintaining friendship and mutually complacential intercourse, without believing that God is, and without believing "that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him," in the sense explained in my distinct note on Hebrews 11:6. When the Apostle says, "he that cometh to God," he may be well understood to mean, "he that comes to him to walk with him." He unites himself to him in friendly complacential union and intercourse. Dr. Doddridge here says in his note, "Raphelius hath shown, that the original word προσερχόμενον is applied in the Greek classics, to coming to God by prayer; and it is used in Hebrews 10:1, Hebrews 10:22, and Hebrews 12:22–23, for approaching to God in any act of divine worship. He therefore justly observes, that it may here be taken in a larger sense, and refer to that steady course of piety and virtue which is implied in pleasing God, or walking with him."*Family Expositor, 6*, 105, n. h.

Hebrews 11:6. "He that cometh to God."] I.e. he that has real access, admittance, and acceptance, comes so as to be truly united to God, and walk with him. "Must believe that he is." I.e. "must believe that he is" *as God*, which implies his having supreme glory, all-sufficiency, and dominion, a believing those things concerning God which are implied in that name of God, I AM. "Diligently seek him." Seeking God in Scripture commonly implies trusting in God, or the exercise of true faith. The word is ἐκζητεῖν, which is a strong expression. And what the Apostle means seems to be "seeking him with the whole heart," as the phrase is, Psalms 119:2, seeking him in reality, in earnest, and with a true fervor of soul. See Poole's *Synopsis, in loc*., p. 1358, right column, d, place marked in margin.*Synopsis Criticorum, IV* (London, 1676), Pt. 2, col. 1358. "Must believe that he is a rewarder." I.e. that it is not in vain to seek him and trust in [him], that one may do it with safety and just confidence of success, and a firm persuasion that he is sufficient, faithful,

<!-- p. 1158 -->

and ready to bestow the benefit we trust in him for. The wordμισθαποδοσία is used to signify success and benefit (Hebrews 10:35). There is forgiveness with God that he may be feared [Psalms 130:4]. He hath not said to the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain. Blessed are all they that trust in him.

Hebrews 11:7. "Noe… became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.] "He was pronounced by God a righteous person, though his character was not absolutely free from imperfections.… Bp. CumberlandRichard Cumberland (1631–1718), Bishop of Peterborough, author of *Origines Gentium Antiquissimœ; or Attempts for Discovering the Times of the First Planting of Nations* (London, 1724). observes, that Noah is the first to whom the name of 'righteous man' [Genesis 7:1] is applied in Scripture." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 106 and n. k.

Hebrews 11:10. "Looked for a city which hath foundations."] This is here said because tabernacles, mentioned in the foregoing verse, hath no foundations, and because 'tis a movable thing, and is designed for no settled abode, but is such as travelers are wont to lodge in, who are traveling through a strange country amongst a people they are disunited from, and that are inhospitable to them, and therefore don't lodge in their houses. But the "city that has foundations" is that wherein they shall dwell in a fixed manner as the proper citizens.

"For he looked for a city…"]JE deleted this unfinished entry.

Hebrews 11:14. "Declare plainly that they seek a country."] "The original word, πατρίδα, is very emphatical; it signifies as it were a native country, or country in which their father dwelt, and is opposed to that in which they were strangers and pilgrims." Doddridge, *in loc*.*Family Expositor, 6*, 109, n. n.

Hebrews 11:16. "God is not ashamed to be called their God."] Note on Matthew 22:31–32, no. 379.*Works, 15*, 363–65.

Hebrews 11:21. "Leaning on the top of his staff."] See Numbers 21:18. The passage in Genesis here referred to seems to be Genesis 48:2, or probably those two passages, Genesis 47:31, and Genesis 48:2. See note on Genesis 47:31. See also note on Numbers 21:18.

<!-- p. 1159 -->

"Leaning on the top of his staff." "This agrees with the Greek and Syriac translation of Genesis 47:31. And WolsiusJohann Christoph Wolf (1683–1739), evangelical theologian and orientalist in Wittenberg, author of *Curae philologicae et criticae in IV. SS. Evangelica et Actus apostolicos* (1725). adds, that the Seventy always render the Hebrew word מִטָּה, 'a staff.'
