Revelation 10:1.] Most fitly doth Christ here appear with a rainbow about his head, which was given of old as a token and seal of the covenant God made with Noah and all flesh, that the flood should no more pass over the earth. For now Christ appears to promise and swear to his church, Revelation 10:6–7, that there should be that end to the time of her troubles, which is in Scripture compared to the waters of Noah on this very account, because God thus sware that there should be an utter end to them, and that they should return no more. Isaiah 54:9, "For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth, so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee."

Revelation 10:1–2.] The angel's being "clothed with a cloud," and setting "his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the earth," signifies his having power to accomplish what he sware (Revelation 10:6–7). It represents his having all power over heaven, and the earth, and sea, that is, the whole universe, and so having power to bring that great event about which he sware at the time appointed. His being "clothed with a cloud" represents his having all power in heaven as his habitation, and as it were the house that he puts on; and his setting his feet on the earth and sea represents his having all

<!-- p. 1218 -->

power over this lower world, it being his footstool. He had power over heaven, earth, and sea, as he was the heir of his Father who made [them], as he observes in his oath (Revelation 10:6). God's power over heaven and earth, and his creating them, is here made use of to encourage the church that was ready to faint through the length of the time of her troubles, as it is, Isaiah 40:26–28 ff.

Revelation 10:2. "And he set his right foot upon the sea, and his left foot on the earth."] "Revelation."Ibid., 104.

Revelation 10:3–4.] What these "seven thunders" uttered was concerning the precise time when there should be an end to the long-continued time of the church's troubles, concerning which the angel swears in the next verse, for that oath has reference to something that had been uttered before as fixing the period. He swore that the time should be no longer. No longer than what? Why, no longer than that precise time that had before been uttered by the loud voice of the angel and the seven thunders that accompanied it, which seven thunders seems to be the voice of the seventh trumpet, spoken of, Revelation 10:7, as it were explained in seven parts. The angel came down from heaven on this errand to limit the time of the church's troubles, and therefore he came with a rainbow about his head. See note on Revelation 10:1. And therefore what St. John is required to seal up is the same that Daniel was required to shut up and seal (Daniel 12:4, Daniel 12:9). It is that appointed time spoken of, Hebrews 2:3.

*Corol*. Hence 'tis in vain to expect that the precise time of Antichrist's fall should be known till it be accomplished.

"And cried with a loud voice, as when a lion roareth. And when he had cried, seven thunders uttered their voices.… Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered," etc. A clear full declaration of the marvelous expressions and manifestations of the all-sufficiency and glory of God in his mysterious and wonderful works, especially in his dispensations towards the moral world, is represented by a great thunder. See note on Job 26:14, with the note on the preceding verse.This paragraph is a later separate entry.

"And cried with a loud voice, when a lion roareth." Christ is now come to declare that the time of the church's troubles shall be no longer, and to reveal the time of the church's deliverances from her enemies that she had been oppressed by for so long a time. Now therefore he utters his voice, as "when a lion roareth," agreeable to ancient prophecies concerning

<!-- p. 1219 -->

God's appearance for his church when that time should come. Isaiah 42:13–15, "The Lord shall go forth like a mighty man; he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war. He shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long holden my peace; I have been still, and refrained myself. Now will I cry like a travailing woman; I will destroy and devour at once. I will make waste mountains and hill, and dry up the pools. And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not," etc. Isaiah 31:4, "For thus hath the Lord spoken unto me, Like as a lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them. So shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof." Hosea 11:9–11, "I will not return to destroy Ephraim.… They shall walk after the Lord. He shall roar like a lion; when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble from the west." Joel 3:16–17, "The Lord also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake. But the Lord will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel. So shall ye know that I am the Lord your God dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain. Then shall Jerusalem be holy, and there shall no strangers pass through her any more."This paragraph is a later addition.

Revelation 10:6. "That there should be time no longer."] It is not meant that there shall be the end of time, according to the modern use of that phrase, viz. that the world shall be at an end, for the Scripture is a stranger to such an use of the word "time," in contradistinction to eternity, orThe last five words are a later interlineation. to signify the duration of the present state of things after the resurrection. But the time here meant is the time before the church's deliverance, the continuance of those many troubles and overturnings that are to precede the time of the church's rest and glory here on earth, and the fulfilling of those glorious things so often spoken of in the word of God. And this is what is meant by the "mystery of God," its being "finished, as he hath declared to his servants the prophets" Revelation 10:7]. The accomplishment of these things are the great objects of the church's hope and expectations, and what they continue long wishing and waiting for. And here the angel, for their comfort, swears that it shall no longer be delayed. The words might be rendered, *diuturnitaten non fore amplius*.I.e. "The length of time is about to be no longer." What the angel swears

<!-- p. 1220 -->

here is the same thing that the angel swears, Daniel 12:7–8. And if we compare the oath there sworn to this, and the circumstances there mentioned, it will appear evidently to be the same, and that here an eye is had to that. And I believe in what is said here in the Revelation 10:7, "as he hath declared to his servants the prophets," respect is had to the prophet Daniel, and what is said there in the Daniel 12 of his prophecy. Respect is here had to the same thing that the church earnestly inquires about in the Daniel 6:9–11. "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held. And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth? And white robes were given to every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellow servants," etc. This season is that which the angel here swears shall be no longer. The word is the same, χρόνος. The angel here in his oath has respect to the same thing, and speaks for the comfort of these souls under the altar. That oath of the angel in Daniel was in answer to the like question, as in the preceding verse. "And one said unto the man clothed in linen, which was upon the waters of the river, How long shall it be to the end of these wonders? And I heard the man clothed in linen, which was upon the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand unto heaven, and sware by him that liveth forever and ever, that it shall be for a time, times, and an half; and when he shall have accomplished to scatter the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished."

The angel's swearing then that the time should be no longer seems to intimate that the time will be long expected as well as earnestly desired before it comes, as seems also to be intimated by the forementioned interrogation in Daniel 6, and Daniel 6:11–12, and as this event proves to be. For how long has the fall of Antichrist already been expected? This is that "appointed time" spoken of, Habakkuk 2:3. See notes on that place.

See remarks on Mr. Lowman's interpretation of this oath, "Revelation," "Remarks on Lowman," second last paragraph.This sentence is a later addition. *Works, 5*, 252.

"That liveth forever and ever." When the angel swears "that the time should be no longer," he properly swears by him who endures, and lives, and reigns forever through all time, to and beyond the end of time, to order all that comes to pass in time, and to fix the seasons. He whose duration is eternal and unlimited alone fixes the limits of time. The eternity

<!-- p. 1221 -->

of God, as well as his creating and governing all things, are properly here made use to comfort the church concerning the period of her troubles, here as they are in Isaiah 40:26–28. See the note on Revelation 10:1–2.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"That there should be time no longer." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 104.

Revelation 10:7. "The mystery of God should be finished."] "Revelation," no. 76.*Works, 5*, 172–73.

Revelation 11:1. "Rise, and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and them that worship therein."] This signifies that God [will] preserve and uphold his church, and will not suffer any of his elect people to perish in this time of general overthrow. Particular limits and bounds shall be set which God will maintain. So much shall be measured out for God that he will keep in the time of this great apostasy. The enemies of God and his people, though they so greatly prevail as though they would tread all things under their feet, yet they shall not be able to bring their devastations within these limits, into that part that God hath measured out for himself. At those measured bounds God will say to the overflowing destruction, Hitherto shalt thou come, and no further. Christ will have his church in the exact and determinate number. He'll have the exact portion that God hath given him in the worst of times. It signifies much the same thing as sealing the servants of God "in their foreheads," in Revelation 7:3 and Revelation 9:4.

Revelation 11:3.] Concerning the beginning of the 1260 days, see extracts from Bower's *History of the Popes*, pp. 9–10.The extracts are in JE's notebook, identified as "Notebook C" relating to the *History of the Work of Redemption* project, which contains his reading notes derived from Archibald Bower, *History of the Popes*. Bower (1686–1766) was at times in and out of the Catholic Church and the Society of Jesus. For more on him, see *Works, 5*, 68–69. On "Notebook C," see *Works, 9*, 545, 547. On pp. 9–10, JE writes, "Bower's *History* seems much to confirm that with the pontificate of Boniface the III, which began Feb. 19, 607, began the reign of Antichrist. That this was the true epoch of the 1260 days." According to Bower, Boniface was responsible for advancing the power and authority of the Pope which had been declining for some time. For example, he obtained by decree the title of "Universal Bishop" and was declared "Head of the whole Catholic Church," thus introducing the notion of "papal supremacy," a process JE records from Bower as "antichristian, heretical, blasphemous, diabolical."

"Two witnesses." A small number in this time of general apostasy and persecution, and yet a sufficient number; for in the mouth of two witnesses were things to be established. Therefore were the apostles sent

<!-- p. 1222 -->

forth two and two, to testify that the kingdom of heaven was at hand [Mark 6:7].This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 11:5. "Fire proceedeth out of their mouth."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 104–5.

Revelation 11:6. "These have power to shut heaven."] See "Revelation," no. 86.Ibid., 198–99.

Revelation 11:7.] The slaying of the witnesses is a thing that don't yet remain to be accomplished. See "Revelation," no. 90.Ibid., 201–8.

See an exposition of this prophecy of the witnesses in Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. 3, p. 40.Kidder identifies the two witnesses as the Albigenses in Spain and the Waldenses in Savoy. He links the slaying of the witnesses to their slaughter by forces allied with the See of Rome, and their final destruction to the efforts of the Duke of Savoy in 1686. *Demonstration of the Messias* (2nd ed. corr., 1726), Pt. 3, 40.

"Mr. Fleming observes that from the death of Andrew Pallicka, the last Bohemian martyr, to the appearance of CarolstadiusCarlstadt (c. 1480–1541), whose real name was Andreas Rudolff-Bodenstein von Karlstadt, was a German reformer whose religious views were more radical than Martin Luther's. He eventually left Saxony for Switzerland. and ZuingliusUlrich Zwingli (1484–1531), a Swiss reformer who carried out a program of religious and political reform in Zurich. at the beginning of the Reformation, was just three years and a half. Bp. Lloyd imagined it was fulfilled in the slaughter of the Albigenses and Waldenses, in the year 1686; and they arose in 1690" (which is agreeable to the forecited exposition in Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*). "Perhaps three days and a half may be mentioned in reference to the state of a dead body, which will seldom keep longer without corruption." Doddridge.This paragraph is a separate entry. *Family Expositor, 6*, 517, n. i.

Concerning the time of slaying the witnesses. Dr. Goodwin, in his *Exposition on the Revelation*, observes that Mr. BrightmanThomas Brightman (1562–1607), biblical commentator and author of *Apocalypsis Apocalypseos, idest Apocalypsis D. Joannis analysi et scholiis illustrata* (1609, translated London, 1644). supposes the slaying of the witnesses to be the victory of Charles V over the Protestants, 1547, and that condemning of the Scriptures about that time by the Council of Trent, just three years and a half after which they revived and enjoyed peace, which since they have had. I think he intimates that the

<!-- p. 1223 -->

reformation of Britain was about that time.Thomas Goodwin, *An Exposition Upon the Revelation*, in *The Works of Thomas Goodwin, D.D. Sometime President of Magdalen Colledg in Oxford* (4 vols. London, 1681–97), *II*, 144. Here JE deleted "See in history concerning this, if this be so. If so." This perhaps is the falling of "the tenth part of the city" [Revelation 11:13].

The history of these things given in the "Supplement" to the second volume of the *History of Popery*, secs. 16–18, in many things agrees well with the prophecy.The "Supplement" carries on "the *History of POPERY* to the End of the Council of Trent" in 22 sections. In secs. 16–18, Henry Care provides a detailed account of ecclesiastical and imperial history beginning in the year 1547 with the defeat of the Elector of Saxony. He also discusses the continuing sessions of the Council of Trent and the forced submission of Protestant princes to it. The conflict between the emperor and the Pope is at the center of this narrative, but war between Protestant and Catholic parties as well as political intrigue fill these pages. Sec. 18 closes with the resignation of Charles V as emperor in 1555 and his apparent "conversion" to Protestant ideals, as described by Care (*History of Popery, II*, 616–39). The sudden and happy revolution in favor of the Protestants was in the year 1552, but we may suppose several years were taken up in the events signified by the witnesses ascending into heaven in the sight of their enemies Revelation 11:12]. And Queen Elizabeth came to the crown in the year 1558.

It is observed in the above-mentioned treatise of Dr. Goodwin, that in England in Queen Mary's days, though her reign lasted five years, yet the killing and martyring of the Protestants in her days lasted but three years and a half the time before being taken up in preparation, getting statutes made, etc.This and the two preceding paragraphs are a separate entry. Goodwin, *Exposition Upon the Revelation*, in *Works, II*, 148. JE's pattern of "citation" is illustrated here. Goodwin writes, "In like manner, in *England*, after that, in Queen *Mary's* days, whose Reign, although it lasted five whole Years, yet the first part of her Reign was spent in *making War* against the Witnesses, or (as I may so speak) in the Preparations of War against the Witnesses, in getting Statutes made for their Burning, &c. and the *killing* and martyring of them was but for three years and an half."

"Where also our Lord was crucified."] "When one sees" (says Dr. Doddridge) "their places of worship everywhere adorned with images of a crucified Savior, one would think that these persecutors intended to crucify Jesus in effigy."*Family Expositor, 6*, 516, n. h. Although they would have it taken as a testimony of their great regard and honor to Christ, probably divine providence intends it as a standing representation of what is the truth, viz. that that church, above all societies in the world, have been the crucifiers of Christ, and have been constantly from age to age crucifying him afresh. should be understood as a sign of their honoring the memory of the prophets and their abhorring the deed of their murderers; but divine providence intended it as a representation of their building their sepulchers by adding to 'em abundantly others of the same kind that suffered the like cruelty.

"Here is the mind that hath wisdom." The "seven heads" Revelation 17:1] are seven mountains. It is not meant that this mark of the woman, that she sits on seven mountains, is so mysterious that 'tis a point of extraordinary wisdom to find her out by it, for that was very easy, and everybody knew what that was that was set upon seven mountains. But the meaning is, This is the key to wisdom in this matter, or to a right understanding who this woman is. Concerning the number of the beast, see Wilson's *Christian Dictionary* under the word "Number."In the supplementary section entitled *A Dictionary of that Mystical Book, called The Revelation of St. John*, Wilson writes under the heading "Number is six hundred sixty six" the following: "A name consisting of so many and such Numerall letters, as being counted summed and up, do make the number of 666, which is the number of the Beast; both the first Beast, (to wit, the *Romane* Emperor, and Empire) and the second Beast; (to wit, the *Romane* Pope and Papacy) for under the Beast is comprehended no one particular man, but an order and succession of men, even a Kingdome." Then follows a long historical account of this viewpoint, beginning with Irenaeus. Revelation 14:13.] The great importance and certain truth of what is here declared to John is here denoted two ways, viz. 1. By a special command to John to write it, that it might stand upon record for the comfort and joy of the saints in all ages. 2. In that the truth of it is established by two witnesses, that are both divine persons. First, 'tis declared by a voice from heaven, which was the testimony of the Son of God, the same person spoken of in the next verse. At the same time it was inwardly revealed to John by the Holy Spirit, confirming what the voice of the Son had declared, "Yea, saith the Spirit," etc.

There is a sort of paradox in the words they speak, as though they shall leave their works behind, and yet as if their works followed them. They shall leave the labor and toil of their work behind, but the reward and sweet fruit of their labors shall follow them.

<!-- p. 1231 -->

"Blessed are the dead that die in the Lord from henceforth." There seems to be a special respect here to that rest and glory that the church shall be advanced to after those events spoken of in the immediately preceding verses, viz. the fall of the mystical Babylon, and God's terrible wrath executed on the enemies of the church at that time, the same thing which is spoken of in the Revelation 20 as the rising of those that were beheaded for the testimony of Jesus, etc. Revelation 20:4], and their living and reigning with Christ. When the church thus rises to its great promised rest and glory, then they that died "in the Lord," especially the martyrs that went through great sufferings and labors for Christ, shall rest from their labors and suffering, i.e. the church that before was suffering and afflicted shall rest, and be comforted and rewarded, as when Christ rose from the dead, he rested from his labors, and began to receive the reward of his works. Even the very individual persons that before had labored and suffered shall then in a peculiar manner have their comfort and reward, as the saints in heaven see and partake of the glory and prosperity of the church on earth, and as their happiness and glory will be exceedingly advanced at the time of the destruction of Satan's kingdom, and the setting up of Christ's kingdom in this world.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 15:3. "And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb."] The song that they sing is on the like occasion with that on which the children of Israel, the church in the wilderness, sung the

<!-- p. 1232 -->

song of Moses, their head and leader, the song they sung with him when he brought them up out of the Red Sea. This song is sung on occasion of which that was a type, viz. their victory over Antichrist, the spiritual Pharaoh or king over that church that is spiritually called Egypt.

But yet it may more properly [be] called "the song of the Lamb," for as Moses in that affair was the head and leader of the church of Israel, so is the Lamb in this. Moses, in that victory over and deliverance from Pharaoh, was but a type of this victory of the church over the spiritual Pharaoh. As Moses and the congregation of Israel then sung and rejoiced together, so doth the Lamb and the church on this.

And therefore the words that 'tis here said they sung are very much like some of the words, both of the song of Moses and also another song in the Psalms wherein the Psalmist personates Christ, which probably respect is had to here when it is said, they sung "the song of the Lamb." The words are very much like the Exodus 15:11. And in the Exodus 15:4 here seems to be respect to what is said in that song (Exodus 15:14–16). The other song that there seems to [be] a reference to is the Psalms 111 in which the Psalmist seems to personate Christ, and therefore so 'tis a song of the Lamb. 'Tis a song that Christ sings with his church, as Moses sang his in the congregation of Israel. And therefore 'tis said in the Psalms 111:1, "Praise ye the Lord. I will praise the Lord with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation." That song was on occasion of some great deliverance God wrought for his church from their enemies, as appears by the Psalms 111:6 and Psalms 111:9. And perhaps there is some reference in it to what is spoken of Christ in the last verses of the Psalms 110, viz. that "the Lord at his right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath," and that he should "judge among the heathen, and fill the places with the dead bodies, and wound the heads over many countries" [Psalms 110:5–6]. The words that are here sung in the Revelation 15:3, "Great and marvelous are thy works, Lord God Almighty," are much like those in the Psalms 111:2–4. "The works of the Lord are great.… His work is honorable and glorious. He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered." And these words, "Just and true are thy ways," are very much like Psalms 111:7. "The works of his hands are verity and judgment.… They stand fast forever, and are done in truth and uprightness." God is here spoken of as king of saints; and so he is there, though the expression is not used. He is spoken of as their "covenant," and they are called "his people" (Psalms 111:5, Psalms 111:9). These words, "Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name" [Revelation 15:4], are like what we

<!-- p. 1233 -->

find, Psalms 111:1, Psalms 111:2, Psalms 111:9–10. "Praise ye the Lord. The works of the Lord are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure in them. Reverend is his name. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." These words, "For thou only art holy," are like these, Psalms 111:9, "Holy and reverend is his name." These words, "All nations shall come and worship before thee, for his judgments are made manifest," are like those, Psalms 111:6, "He hath showed his people the power of his works, that he may give them the heritage of the heathen." Psalms 111:4, "He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered." Note that that psalm is an alphabetical psalm, which some think denotes a peculiar excellency.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 17:5.] "The word MYSTERIUM" used anciently to be "engraven on the Pope's mitre." See *History of Popery*, vol. 1, p. 179.Henry Care explains "that the three Crowns encompassing" the Pope's mitre were "mythologized" as signifying "the Rule he bears in *Heaven, Earth*, and *Purgatory*." But Revelation 17:5 links this mystery to "Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots, and Abominations of the Earth," undermining any sense of such papal power or rule.

Why called Babylon, see "Revelation," no. 79.This reference is a later addition. *Works, 5*, 191.

"MOTHER of HARLOTS, and Abominations of the Earth." Old Babylon was the mother of idolatry, where false religion and false worship first began, and whence it was diffused through the earth. The Church of Rome in this respect was like her, as in her is coined all manner of superstition and false worship, and from thence is spread abroad in the world.This paragraph is a later addition.

"And upon her forehead was a name written, "MYSTERY." "Revelation."This paragraph is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 118–19.

Revelation 17:9–10. "The seven heads are seven mountains.… And there are seven kings."] By this it is most manifest that the Spirit of God may have an eye to several very different things in the same prophetical description, for this [is] a plain instance against which there is no disputing. Seeing God himself tells us that it is so of one vision or prophetic description, why mayn't we suppose that it may be so with respect to others also?

Revelation 17:11. "And the beast that was, and is not."] "Revelation."Ibid., 119.

<!-- p. 1236 -->

Revelation 17:12.] Concerning the "ten kings," see "Revelation," "Extracts from Lowman," at the end.Ibid., 250.

"And the ten horns which thou sawest, are ten kings." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 119–20.

Revelation 17:17. "To fulfill his will."] "To fulfill his will" against spiritual Babylon, and building up the spiritual Jerusalem, as is said of Cyrus against the literal Babylon, and with respect to the literal Jerusalem. Isaiah 44:28, "That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure; even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built," etc.

Revelation 17:18. "The woman which thou sawest is that great city."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 120.

Revelation 18:2.] Why called Babylon, no. 79, "Revelation."Ibid., 191.

Revelation 18:3. "And the merchants of the earth," etc.] That by merchants here in this prophecy of the destruction of spiritual Babylon (See Revelation 18:2.) is meant the clergy or teachers that were in her seems manifest by what is parallel to it in the prophecy of the destruction of old Babylon in Isaiah 47:15, where 'tis evident that by her "merchants" is meant their teachers, by the two foregoing verses.

"And the merchants of the earth are waxed rich." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 120.

Revelation 18:6. "Reward her even as she rewarded you."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 120.

Revelation 18:8. "Therefore shall her plagues come in one day."] "Revelation."Ibid.

"Utterly burnt with fire." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 121–22.

Revelation 18:9. "The kings of the earth."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 122.

Revelation 18:17. "And every shipmaster."] "Revelation."Ibid.

<!-- p. 1237 -->

Revelation 18:20. "Rejoice over her, thou heaven, and ye holy apostles and prophets, for God hath avenged you on her."] The saints will rejoice in seeing vengeance executed on their enemies, upon several accounts. 1. Because they will herein see glorious justice executed, which they will have a more lively sense of in the punishment of that wickedness by which they have so extremely suffered. In that, they will have a more lively sense of the wickedness, for their suffering so much by it. 2. They will rejoice, because herein they will see God's love and tenderness towards them in his severity towards their enemies. Herein will be verified what God [said] of his saints, that he that touched them, "touched the apple of his eye" [Zechariah 2:8], and what Christ said, Matthew 18:6, "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea." 3. They will from self-love rejoice to see just punishment executed upon those that have so greatly injured them. A desire of just revenge for injuries in a creature, simply and absolutely considered, is not evil, any more than for a creature to hate another creature is absolutely an evil. The saints in heaven may and will hate the damned; they may therefore delight in seeing just revenge executed for their injuries to them. Desire of revenge is a principle of the human nature. Self-love necessarily implies such a principle. 'Tis a fruit of the corruption of nature no otherwise than other appetites of the human nature, viz. in its inordinate exercise. The reason why we ought not to desire revenge on our fellow creatures here is because we ought not to hate them, but love them, not because there ought not to be such a principle in our nature as a desire of just revenge for injuries, but because in the circumstances we are under, and mankind is under here, love ought to prevail above it. But when these reasons of love cease, and our enemies become proper objects of our hatred, then we may delight to see just revenge executed upon them.

A Christian spirit destroys a desire of revenge towards our personal enemies here in this world two ways, viz. 1. Humility and an abasing thought of our own nothingness and vileness lessens the offense. If we think ourselves little and vile, we shall not look on the offense of an injury and affront so heinous, shall not resent it so much on our own account. 2. A Christian spirit disposes to look upon other grounds we have to love them as superior to this ground of hatred. But those grounds of love hereafter will cease; and though they are in themselves little, yet God will for Christ's sake magnify them by greatly resenting and dreadfully revenging injuries that have been done them. And the saints from self-love,

<!-- p. 1238 -->

together with a sense of the worthiness of Jesus Christ their head, will humbly approve of God's thus magnifying them, and shall in Jesus Christ, and as falling in with God, humbly magnify themselves, and rejoice in God's vengeance upon their carnal enemies.

Why may not the saints' love to themselves work the same way that God's love to them doth? God's love to them causes him to desire to see their injuries revenged. And why may not their love to themselves as well cause them to rejoice in a just revenge of their own injuries? Or it may be argued thus. If God's love to the saints disposes him to desire the revenge of their injuries, why may not their fellow saints, who fall in with God in loving those saints, also fall in with God in delighting in the revenge of their injuries from love to them? And if their love to others may cause them to rejoice in the revenge of their injuries, why may not their love to themselves as well cause them to rejoice in the just revenge of their own injuries? See "Miscellanies," nos. 600 and 640.Ibid., *2*, 141–42, 173–75.

See Job 22:19.This reference is a later addition.

Revelation 18:21. "And a mighty angel took up a stone."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 122.

Revelation 18:23. "For by thy sorceries were all nations deceived."] "Revelation."Ibid.

Revelation 19:3. "Her smoke rose up forever and ever."] "Revelation."Ibid., 122–23.

Revelation 19:4. "The four beasts fell down."] "Revelation."Ibid., 123.

Revelation 19:5. "And a voice came out of the throne, saying, Praise our God."] This may be looked upon as the voice of Christ, who "is in the midst of the throne" (Revelation 5:6), who overcame, and is set down with the "Father in his throne" [Revelation 3:21]. "The throne of God and the Lamb" are the same (Revelation 22:1). This is not the voice of God the Father, because the voice says, "Praise OUR God." But supposing it to be the voice of Christ, this well agrees to what Christ says, "Go tell my brethren, Behold, I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" [John 20:17]. Thus Christ leads the heavenly church in their praises. In the following verse

<!-- p. 1239 -->

we have an account of the church's compliance, and following of Christ in praising God. See Numbers 23:21.This reference and the following sentence are a later addition. Christ speaks of praising God "in the great congregation," in Psalms 22:25, and Psalms 35:18, and Psalms 40:9–10.

Revelation 19:6. "Lord God omnipotent reigneth."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 123.

Revelation 19:12. "A name written, that no man knew but he himself."] See Isaiah 9:6, and Judges 13:18, and Psalms 30:4.

Revelation 19:13.] One thing that confirms me that the design here is not only to represent Christ's garment as dipped in the blood of his enemies, but also dipped in his own blood, was Joseph's garments being dipped in the blood of the kid that was slain in his room, in which affair Joseph was without doubt a type of Christ. See note on Genesis 37:31. By this it appears that Christ's garments being represented as dipped in his own blood is agreeable to the mind of the Holy Spirit.

Revelation 19:14. "Followed him on white horses."] As coming to judge the nations, as judges formerly, when going to the place of judgment, were wont to ride on "white asses." See Revelation 20:4 and Judges 5:10.

Revelation 19:17.] This "angel standing in the sun" seems most probably to be Jesus Christ, the great antitype of the sun. Christ, who appeared and fought for Israel in Joshua's time, which was then represented by the sun's standing still to fight for them, now appears "standing in the sun" on the behalf of the spiritual Israel. He who is Lord over all things, over beasts, and birds, and every living thing (Psalms 8:6–8), he now commands all the fowls of heaven to gather themselves together to eat the flesh of kings, etc., as David, when he fought with Goliath, said that he would "give the carcasses of the hosts of the Philistines unto the fowls of the air," etc. [1 Samuel 17:46]. So Christ, the true David, now calls on the fowls of the air to come to devour the carcasses of the enemies of his church.

Revelation 19:19. "And the kings of the earth."] "Revelation."Ibid. The verse numbers on this and the following verse in the KJV text in the "Blank Bible" are incorrect.

Revelation 19:21. "And the remnant were slain."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 123.

<!-- p. 1240 -->

Revelation 20:2.] Concerning the time when this "thousand years" is to begin, see "Notes on Revelation," nos. 16, 21, 25, 27, 35b, 50, 53, 60, 69, 29.Ibid., 129–32, 135–36, 138, 146–47, 158, 162.

Revelation 20:4. "Lived and reigned *with Christ*."] See "Miscellanies," no. 827.Ibid., *2*, 537–38.

"And I saw the souls of them that were beheaded… and they lived," etc. I.e. they lived in those that succeeded them in the same profession and the same spirit. This is according to the style of prophecy. So the children that returned from captivity in Babylon are represented as those children of Rachel that were carried captive (Jeremiah 31:15–17), though but few of the same persons returned. So in the Revelation 11:11, the two witnesses that were slain for their testimony, and whose dead bodies were not suffered to be put in graves, are said to arise, and stand upon their feet in the sight of their enemies, whereas it is not intended that the same martyrs that were slain should arise.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 20:5. "But the rest of the dead lived not again until the thousand years were finished."] There is an account in the foregoing prophecies of two sorts of persons that were slain with the sword. First, the martyrs that were beheaded or slain for the witness of Jesus, and for the word, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image. We have an account of the slaying of these in the times of the power and prevalency of the beast in his war with the saints, when it was given to them to war with them, and overcome them, and kill them (Revelation 13:7, Revelation 13:10, Revelation 13:15; Revelation 17:6). These are summarily represented in the Revelation 18:24. "And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth." The others were the opposers of true religion, and the enemies of God's church and people, that were slain by Christ and his armies when his wrath came, and the time for him and his armies to prevail in that great battle which he fought with them, when he came forth with all his glorious hosts against them. These we have an account of in the latter part of the Revelation 19, and particularly in the Revelation 19:21. "And the remnant were slain with the sword of him that sat upon the horse, which sword proceeded out of his mouth. And all the fowls were filled with their flesh" [Revelation 19:21]. These prophecies therefore speak of those two sorts of slain, one in the Revelation 19:21, and the other in the conclusion of the Revelation 18. The former are

<!-- p. 1241 -->

spoken of here as those that should live again, and reign "with Christ a thousand years." The other, that are called "the rest of the dead" Revelation 20:5], or slain, it is said shall not live "again till the thousand years" are finished. And in the Revelation 20:7–8 following, we have an account how that "when the thousand years are expired," these also live again. Then again appears a great multitude of opposers and enemies of God's church in the same spirit with these that had been slain by the sword of him that sat on the horse.

"This is the first resurrection." As the beloved disciple in this chapter, speaking of the first and second death, seems to have respect to the repetition of the expression in the first threatening of death, "Dying thou shalt die," as Revelation 20:14, so in speaking of the first and second resurrection, he also seems to have some respect to the repetition of the expression in the first great and plain promise of the resurrection, in Isaiah 26:19, whence the Jews very much received their hope of a resurrection. "Thy dead men shall live; together with my dead body shall they arise." The Prophet here is evidently speakingMS: "Speaks." of a spiritual resurrection, as appears by the foregoing, and yet in the latter expression 'tis evident that a resurrection of the body is included. These two expressions, as they follow one another in the original, seem more naturally to signify two benefits, and not merely to be exegetical one of another, than in our translation.This paragraph is a separate entry.

"Revelation," nos. 48 and 66.These references are a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 144–45, 160.

Revelation 20:6.] 'Tis much the more likely that in what is here said of "the second death," reference is had to the first threatening to Adam, "Dying thou shalt die" [Genesis 2:17], as though two deaths were threatened, because this book doth much refer to that story in the first chapters of Genesis, speaking of paradise and "the tree of life" (Revelation 2:7; Revelation 22:2), and of the river running through paradise (Revelation 22:1), and the enmity between the serpent and woman and her seed (Revelation 12), and here in Revelation 20 "that old serpent" that tempted our first parents (Revelation 20:2).

As the threatening of death for sin is expressed thus, "Dying thou shalt die," repeating the word that signifies death, so the promises of life to the obedient often in like manner contain a repetition of the word that signifies life, "Living he shall live." So Ezekiel 18:9, Ezekiel 18:17, Ezekiel 18:19, Ezekiel 18:21, Ezekiel 18:28; and Ezekiel 33:13, Ezekiel 33:15, Ezekiel 33:16, which probably there is reference to here in speaking of

<!-- p. 1242 -->

two resurrections. Both the book of Genesis and that of Ezekiel are referred to in this context, the latter in what is said concerning Gog and Magog; and the prophecy of Ezekiel is often referred to in this book.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 20:9. "And fire came down from God out of heaven."] Ezekiel 39:6.

Revelation 20:12. "And the books were opened."] I.e. the Bible. The word is *Biblia*.βιβλία. The books of Scripture, these books were those that were called "the books" in the ancient church. These were the books of the church. These are the books of God. It is supposed that by the expression of "the books" will be understood certain particular books so called, and that the name of the books determines what books, or else it would not be said in the next words, "and another book was opened." Another than what? Why another book than "the books." It supposes that such particular books were denoted by that name of "the books," and these doubtless were the books of Scripture. These the world is to be judged by, or according to the law that is found written in them. Even those that have not had the light of Scripture shall be judged by the same rule of judgment that is found here laid down.JE deleted "and by the same law."

Revelation 20:14. "This is the second death."] In calling this "the second death," there seems to be respect had to the repetition there is made of the threatening to our first parents, "dying thou shalt die" [Genesis 2:17], as signifying two deaths, as the repetition of the word "woe" in this book (Revelation 8:13) implies so many distinct woes. See "Scripture," no. 77.*Works, 15*, 72. See the second sermon on Genesis 3:11, pp. 8–10 of that sermon.JE's second sermon on Genesis 3:11 (no. 504), preached Feb. 1739, with the doctrine: "The act of our first father Adam in eating.… Twofold heinousness. 1. That which only concerned Adam personally. 2. That which equally belongs." (MS, p. 23). JE's discussion of the threat of death which accompanied God's command to Adam not to eat of the fruit of the tree includes a discussion of the second death in the lake of fire. He suggests that the Hebrew idiom, which is translated in the margin as "dying thou shalt die," reflects the assumption of the author concerning two deaths—one temporal, one eternal. He concludes, "when temporal death is past, it may be said one death is past; and behold, there comes on the other death, which is the second death."

Revelation 21:1. "New heavens and new earth."] What the Apostle says, Hebrews 12:26–28, is a great confirmation of that sense of this which I have given.

<!-- p. 1243 -->

"A new heaven, and a new earth." "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 140–42, 158, 159, 198. See also "Miscellanies," "Table."These references are a separate entry. *Works, 13*, 141–42.

"There was no more sea." "Revelation."This reference is a separate entry. *Works, 5*, 124, 165–66.

Revelation 21:2. "Coming down from God out of heaven."] "To 'come down from heaven,' or 'from God,' in Scripture language, means the divine original of a thing," says Mr. Lowman.*Paraphrase and Notes on Revelation*, 259, n. b. Thus the saints are elsewhere said to be from above, as the wicked are said to be from beneath. The church of Christ is wholly from God, of heavenly original. The saints are all born of God, his workmanship, elected, redeemed, regenerated, sanctified, and made happy from thence. Of God are they, in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. All that belongs to the spiritual being and glory of the New Jerusalem is from God. "Of him, through him, and in him are all things" [Romans 12:36].

Dr. Doddridge says, "He apprehended. John saw in the vision an appearance of a city, which seemed (like the sheet which Peter saw [Acts 10:11]) to be let down from heaven, and appeared pendent, as it were in the air."This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 6*, 591, n. b.

Revelation 21:4. "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."] See note on Revelation 7:17.

Revelation 21:11.] See "Scripture," no. 265, the "first evidence."*Works, 15*, 214–17.

A "jasper stone" is green, the color that is of all others the most easy to the eyes. Whence we may infer that the visible brightness and glory that will be seen in heaven, especially in the human nature of Christ, the person who is the brightness of God's glory (See note on Revelation 21:23.), I say, though this light will be exceeding great, and doubtless immensely exceeding the coruscation of the sun, yet it will not be at all painful to the eyes of the saints, as the light of the sun is to us, but shall be perfectly easy. It shall be immensely strong and glorious, and yet infinitely sweet and pleasant. And so the spiritual glory of God that shall be manifested shall not be all overbearing to nature, though they shall have such a transcendent

<!-- p. 1244 -->

discovery of it, as a little of a sight of God's glory is here. See Revelation 4:3.

"Her light was like unto a stone." The wordὁ φωστήρ. signifies "luminary."The last two paragraphs of this entry are later additions.

Revelation 21:14. "And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb."] The apostle Paul is not here excluded. How he is included, see note on Acts 13:2.

Revelation 21:16. "Twelve thousand furlongs."] Fifteen hundred miles in compass each side, three hundred seventy-five miles long.

Revelation 21:18. "Pure gold like unto clear glass."] See note on Ezekiel 1:4.

Revelation 21:21. "And the street of the city was pure gold."] "Scripture," no. 306.*Works, 15*, 279.

Revelation 21:23. "The Lamb was the light thereof."] The wordὁ λύχνος. signifies the "candle."

"The glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof." These ben't mentioned as two things, but as one; one is exegetical of the other. The glory of God is the light thereof, in the Lamb's being the light thereof, for Christ is the brightness of God's glory. 'Tis by this effulgence of glory that God shines and manifests himself on earth, both under the old testament and new. It was this person of the Trinity that was wont to appear and manifest himself in that visible brightness and effulgence to the children of Israel, that was wont to be called the "glory of the Lord." And under the new testament we behold the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. And in heaven and in the resurrection world God still appears and manifests himself by the same brightness of his glory. "No man hath seen God at any time," nor ever will see him, but only as "the only begotten Son of God, which is in the bosom of the Father, declares him" [John 1:18]. Colossians 1:15, "Who is the image of the invisible God," which intimates to us that God the Father is invisible, and can never be seen immediately, but only by Christ his image. See Ephesians 1:17. The glory of God is compared to the sun, and is spoken of as rising as a sun (Isaiah 60:1). The visible bright disk of the sun is a natural image of the second person of the Trinity, as the substance of the sun is of the Father, and the

<!-- p. 1245 -->

heat and light of the Holy Ghost. See note on Exodus 16:10. 'Tis not here represented as though the New Jerusalem was enlightened by two lights or two suns. The expression don't seem to hold forth more than one light. "The Lamb is the light thereof." If there were two lights, why doth he speak of the light? Why is it not said that the Lamb is one of the lights thereof?This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 21:23–24. "The city had no need of the sun," etc.,… for the glory of God did lighten it.… And the nations of them that are saved shall walk in the light of it."] Lowman has this note here. "This part of the prophetical description seems to be taken from the Shekinah, or glory of God, in the several divine appearances. This is represented as a bright and glorious light. The holy of holies, the seat of God's presence in the temple, had no other light than that of the Shekinah, or the glory, that shone over the mercy seat between the cherubim. How strong is this figurative representation, to show that this happy state of the church shall be without comparison, more glorious than any former state of the church had been? The Shekinah, or glory of God's presence, shall not be shut up or concealed in one part of the temple, but shall be spread through the whole extent of this spacious city, and every inhabitant shall enjoy the full felicity represented by it."*Paraphrase and Notes on Revelation*, 266, n. 1. Whereas, it is here said, "The nations of them that are saved shall walk in the light of it." Let this be compared with Isaiah 2:5, taken with the preceding verses that speak of the nations that shall be saved that shall resort to Jerusalem. See also Psalms 89:15, and compare these two verses, taken with the Revelation 22:1, with Psalms 36:8–9.

Revelation 21:24. "And the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honor."] "Miscellanies," no. 838.*Works, 20*, 53–54.

Revelation 22:1. "A pure river of water of life, clear as crystal."] This river is the river of God's pleasures [Psalms 36:8], as it is elsewhere called, and is the Holy Spirit, and therefore proceeds both from the Father and the Son, from the throne of God and the Lamb. The fountain of all good flows out in this stream. Christ himself has told us what the living water is, or which is the same thing, the water of life, viz. that is, the Spirit of God (John 7:38

<!-- p. 1246 -->

John 7:38, and the prophet Isaiah, Isaiah 44:3). 'Tis called "a pure river, clear as crystal," to denote the holiness of it, for God's Spirit is the Holy Spirit. 'Tis the holiness of God in abstract; and therefore when a river is made use of as an emblem of it, 'tis meet that it should be a river of extraordinary pure and clear water, clear as crystal. 'Tis water of life in several respects. 'Tis the water that gives life, and wherein the eternal life of the saints consists. And not only so, but 'tis living water; 'tis water that is alive. 'Tis not passive water, as common water is, but 'tis the Spirit of God, a living divine person, yea, the person who is the life of God in abstract. Infinitely perfect life is as it were the matter of this river. See note on John 7:38–39.

See Psalms 36:8–9.This reference is a later addition.

"Proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." God himself is "the fountain of living waters" (Jeremiah 2:13 and Jeremiah 17:13). He is the fountain of the waters of that river that those that trust in the Lord are "planted by," spoken of there in the Jeremiah 17:8.This paragraph is a separate entry.

Revelation 22:2. "In the midst of the street of it."] "Revelation."*Works, 5*, 124.

Revelation 22:3. "No more curse."] See Mr. Robe's *Sermons*, vol. 2, pp. 224–26.James Robe (1688–1753), a Scottish Presbyterian minister and revivalist, interprets these words as an indication that in heaven, or the New Jerusalem, there shall never be pronounced "the censure of the ANATHEMA, or excommunication in the highest degree" against any person or thing. The words intend "an everlasting exemption and freedom from all destruction" in the heavenly state by contrast with reference to curses effected in three previous states: "1st, To the state of the first inhabitants of heaven.—2dly, To the state of the earthly paradise.—And, 3dly, To the state of the church militant upon earth." In the first, God cast "the angels that sinned" out of heaven. In the second, God drove man (Adam and Eve) from the "terrestrial Paradise." In the third, God "pronounced and executed" the great anathema "upon the wicked" (*Second Volume of Sermons*). JE and Robe exchanged correspondence in the early 1740s. See *Works, 16*, 107–10.

Revelation 22:3–4.] Of old but one of all God's people was allowed so to serve him, and minister to him as to come to his throne, viz. the high priest; and he but once a year. But in heaven all shall dwell near God's throne, and shall see his face continually, whereas the high priest saw no more than God's back parts once a year, and that probably inferior to what Moses did. The high priest only had God's name written in his forehead, but in heaven all shall be admitted to an higher privilege than he, for they shall be kings

<!-- p. 1247 -->

and priests to God, and shall have all his name written "in their foreheads."

Revelation 22:3–4. "And his servants shall serve him. And they shall see his face, and his name shall be on their foreheads."] "There was a custom prevailing among many of the heathen, to inscribe on their foreheads the names, or symbolical marks, of the deity they worshipped. But the near connection between this clause, and that which relates to their serving God in the offices of devotion (for that λατρεύω signifies), makes me think it more natural to refer this to the inscription of 'Holiness to Jehovah,' written on the mitre of the high priest. And so it naturally leads us to reflect upon that intimate approach to the blessed God, with which all these happy souls shall be honored." Doddridge.*Family Expositor, 6*, 602, n. b.

Revelation 22:5. "For the Lord God giveth them light."] Psalms 36:9, and Psalms 89:15; and Isaiah 2:5.

Revelation 22:11. "He that is unjust," etc.] See sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13;JE's sermon on 1 Corinthians 13:8–13 (no. 978), preached May 1748, with the doctrine, "The extraordinary influences of the Spirit of God imparting immediate revelations to men were designed only for a temporary continuance while the church was in its minority, and never were intended to be statedly upheld in the Christian church." In the body of the sermon JE discusses "the last visions" of the book of Revelation as they relate to the day of judgment. He interprets Revelation 22:11 as Christ's indication that "henceforward no more revelations are to [be] expected from me, no more means of grace, no more means to reclaim men from sin." Whoever does not take advantage or improve the means now available will "continue in his unrighteousness and filthiness" forever, for Christ will come quickly to the judgment (p. 291). See *Extraordinary Gifts of the Spirit Are Inferior to Graces of the Spirit*, in *Works, 25*, 275–311. and "Scripture," no. 470.*Works, 15*, 511–12.

Revelation 22:14.] See Dr. Watts, *Orthodoxy and Charity*, pp. 65 ff.Watts, in "Essay II. The Form of the Gospel," points out multiple senses of the word "justification." There are, he asserts, biblical passages that speak of justification by works (James 2), by words (Matthew 12:37), and by fulfilling commands, as in this text (*Orthodoxy and Charity* [1745], 65–73).

"That they may have a right to the tree of life." Dr. Doddridge translates it, "may have the privilege to eat of the tree of life."This paragraph is a later addition. *Family Expositor, 6*, 607.

"Every Christian, who is admitted into heaven, may be said [to have a twofold right to it], viz. there is a right of inheritance which is by faith, whereby we are justified, and become the children of God, and join theirs

<!-- p. 1248 -->

with Christ.… And there is also a right of congruity or fitness, which arises from actual holiness of heart and life, whereby we are prepared for the actual possession of this inheritance. So an infant may have a right of inheritance to his father's estate, by his birth or adoption; but he has not a right of congruity or fitness, till he grow up to the age of discretion." Watts, *Works*, vol. 2, p. 577.This paragraph is a later addition. Watts, *Works* (1753), *II*, 577.

Revelation 22:16. "The bright and morning star."] The more fitly so called, because the time when he rose from the dead, when he rose from the night of his death, from the night of his humiliation, was very early in the morning, as the morning star arises from under the earth early in the morning.

Revelation 22:17. "The Spirit and the bride say, Come."] Here seems to be reference to what had been said, Revelation 19:9, "Blessed are they that are called to the marriage supper of the Lamb." "The bride says, Come." She has authority to invite guests to her own wedding. Her invitation is, indeed, the invitation of Christ, for 'tis the expression of that desire and wish that arises from the spirit of Christ in the bride. So "the Spirit and bride say, Come."

See note on Isaiah 55:1–3.This reference is a later addition.

Revelation 22:19. "God shall take away his part out of the book of life."] See "Miscellanies," no. 689, especially §4 and §9.*Works, 18*, 253–54, 257.

### Appendix C. Financial Accounts of Edwards' Children

The "Children's Accounts," located on the closing pages of the MS numbered as pp. 902–4, raise as many questions as they answer. One must speculate how Edwards is "borrowing" from his children in some cases at a point when they were still toddlers or infants. Perhaps he was taking funds from an amount that he and Sarah set aside for an inheritance or for an "allowance," though the modern notion of an allowance seems inappropriate especially because of the age of the children at the point when some of the records were entered. If a separate ledger of such accounts exists, it has not been located or identified. Perhaps the funds were ultimately intended as a dowry for the daughters or as an asset to be used for the education of the sons. These accounts reflect the care Edwards took to be accurate and to repay in full the debts to his children. They also cast light on the complexity of the currency situation in eighteenth-century New England.On currencies in colonial America, see John J. McCusker, *Money and Exchange in Europe and America, 1600–1775: A Handbook* (2nd ed. Chapel Hill, Univ. of North Carolina Press, 1992).

<!-- p. 1266 -->

The teaspoons we got for our three eldest children came to 1£—1*s*—9*d*. for each of the three couples, making and all. The silver came to 12*s*—9*d*., and the making to 9*s*. Sarah is debtor 12–9, the price of the silver, which is to be subtracted out of what we have used of her money, the price of the making, 9*s*, being given for the use of the money and of the spoons. The other two children paid 3*s*—11*d*. of their own silver that was not set down so that they are made debtors but 8*s*—10*d*., which is to be subtracted from the account of money borrowed of them, the 9 shillings for the making being also given them for the use of the money and spoons.
